Russian Suspect Identified in Execution of Ukrainian POWs at Vovchansk Plant
Ukrainian prosecutors have revealed the call signs of 4 Russian servicemen suspected of involvement in the execution of 3 Ukrainian prisoners of war at the Vovchansk Aggregate Plant during the summer of 2024, as reported by ASTRA.
The announcements follow the confirmation of a life sentence for Russian soldier Sergey Tuzhilov, known by the call sign "Altay," whose appeal was recently rejected by the Appeals Court in Kharkiv.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to investigative findings, elements of the 1st Motorized Rifle Battalion of the 82nd Motorized Rifle Regiment, belonging to the 69th Motorized Rifle Division of the 6th Army of the Russian Leningrad Military District, occupied the plant during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Between June and July 2024, 3 captured Ukrainian servicemen were executed at the site. A battalion commander using the call sign "Enot" allegedly issued orders to kill the captives following torture.
The executions were carried out by servicemen with the call signs "Kot" and "Altay," who fired shots into the backs of the captives' heads while escorting them.
Two additional soldiers, identified by the call signs "Koba" and "Voodoo," provided security and guarded the prisoners during transport. According to ASTRA, the commander and the two guards face charges carrying penalties of 10 to 15 years in prison or life imprisonment.
Independent journalists identified the individual using the call sign "Koba" as Ruslan Kabanov, born in 1985 in the Murmansk region. Prior to his deployment, Kabanov lived in Luga, Leningrad region, and worked for a local forestry enterprise.
Contacted regarding his involvement, his spouse stated that she had not communicated with him since July 2024. She noted that he joined the military directly from prison, where he was serving a sentence for criminal offenses, and confirmed that local authorities officially declared him dead less than a month ago.
Ukrainian investigators documented the crime in cooperation with Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence. Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor Oleksandr Filchakov highlighted that the case offered a rare legal opportunity, as one suspect was held in Ukrainian custody, enabling direct trial proceedings rather than an in absentia trial.

Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield connection 'stable' again

Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield connection 'stable' again
Ukraine has regained a "stable" connection to the Starlink and Starshield satellite communications systems, Kyiv's defence minister said on Saturday. Recent disruptions to the connection led to tensions with Washington over the SpaceX-made network crucial to the Ukrainian army's operations.
The Starlink satellite communications system and its military version Starshield are operating again at speeds over 400km per hour, Kyiv's defence minister said on Saturday, after over a week of service restrictions that slowed connections and disrupted military operations.
"The ministry of defence's monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield. We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable," Evhenii Khmara told reporters.
The Ukrainian military does not disclose the systems' maximum operating speeds, and the defence ministry did not say whether service had been fully restored.
Read moreUkraine’s Pavlohrad refuses to yield to Putin despite unrelenting bombardment
"Monitoring systems had previously recorded disruptions to the Starlink/Starshield service. The speed metrics have now returned to normal," the ministry said.
The restrictions, first reported on October 14, undermined Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and disrupted frontline communications, Ukrainian officials said.
Sources said connection speeds had been reduced to about 160 kph or less.
Ukraine's problems with SpaceX-owned Starlink came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow while pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries
Read moreWhy have US-Ukraine relations soured ahead of the midterms?
Neither SpaceX boss Elon Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. Trump said on Friday that if problems with access to Starlink communications systems in Ukraine persisted, he would "get it straightened out".
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Russian air defense systems downed a SCALP air-launched cruise missile, four Neptune long-range cruise missiles, and 1,297 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Air defense systems have shot down a French-made SCALP air-launched cruise missile, four Neptune long-range cruise missiles, and 1,297 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
The Ukrainian armed forces have lost approximately 1,190 troops over the past 24 hours as a result of actions by Russian armed forces in the special military operation zone, the Russian Defense Ministry reported. According to the ministry, the enemy lost over 200 personnel in the area of responsibility of the Battlegroup North, over 215 due to the actions of the Battlegroup West; up to 180 in the sector of the Battlegroup South, over 350 in the Battlegroup Center’s sector, over 205 in the area of responsibility of the Battlegroup East and up to 40 in the sector of the Battlegroup Dnepr.
Russian forces have struck energy and transport infrastructure facilities used to support the Ukrainian military. "Operational-tactical aviation, attack drones, missile forces, and artillery of the Russian armed forces struck energy and transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian military, as well as storage and launch sites for long-range unmanned aerial vehicles. Additionally, temporary deployment points for Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries were hit across 147 areas," the ministry said in a statement.

Russian attacks kill 4, injure 78 across Ukraine over past day, as drone strikes Kyiv residential building in the morning

Russian attacks kill 4, injure 78 across Ukraine over past day, as drone strikes Kyiv residential building in the morning
Russian attacks over the last day killed four people and injured 78 across Ukraine over the past day, as Moscow strikes at Kyiv in the morning of Oct. 24, local authorities report.
In the early hours of Oct. 24, a Russian drone struck a residential building in Kyiv’s Obolon District, injuring two people, and cauing a fire, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported.
On Oct. 23, Russian forces attacked the city of Chernihiv in Chernihiv Oblast during the day, killing one man and injuring at least 25 people, local authorities said.
An air raid alert was declared in Chernihiv at around 1:40 p.m. local time due to a missile threat. Minutes later, Ukraine's Air Force reported drones and a Banderol low-cost cruise missile heading toward the city.
Chernihiv City Council said two private businesses were targeted in the Russian attack but provided no further details.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian shelling of a residential area in the front-line city of Kramatorsk killed one person and injured six more, including three children, the Donetsk Oblast Prosecutor's Office reported on Oct. 23.
In Sloviansk, another front-line town in Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks throughout the previous day killed one 62-year-old woman and injured four people, Sloviansk Mayor Vadym Lyakh wrote on Oct. 24.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, a Russian attack on the city of Dnipro killed one and injured eight people, while three more people were injured in the Pidhorodnenska community, according to regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha.
In Zhytomyr Oblast, a Russian drone attack in the city of Zhytomyr injured nine people on Oct. 23, including two children, Ukraine’s police force reported.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian forces injured seven people, including a 12-year-old girl and a 13-year-old boy, Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Synehubov said. Homes, businesses, and gas stations were also damaged or destroyed in the strikes, he added.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian forces struck residential areas across the region, injuring six people on Oct. 23, the Kherson Oblast Military Administration reported.
In Ukraine's southern Odesa Oblast, three people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, as Russia struck a recreational building, an administrative building, and a warehouse, said regional governor Oleh Kiper.
In Sumy Oblast, Russia carried out 40 attacks on 25 settlements, injuring five people in several communities over the past day, the regional military administration said. In total, the air alert sounded for more than 18 hours, the administration added.
Overnight, Russian forces launched 126 drones, 61 of which were jet-powered, Ukraine’s Air Force reported. Ukraine managed to suppress 101 drones, including 50 jet-powered drones, the Air Force said.
Russia ramped up production of jet-powered drones this year, which are much harder to shoot down than their propeller powered predecessors, while Ukraine has managed to improve the interception rate over the last month.

British woman dies trying to save sons on Bahamas snorkelling trip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:43:09 UTC
18:43:09 KST

A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling.
The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday.
The force said they believed she was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island of North Bimini when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
The police said that in an attempt to rescue her boys, “the woman was also swept away”. The children were later rescued from the water.
The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support.
Bimini is a small island group between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland.
The islands are best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and are also home to a world-leading shark research centre.
In a statementposted on social media, the Royal Bahamas police force said: “According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini ferry dock.
“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.
“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.
“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.
“She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. Foul play is not suspected at this time.”
An autopsy would be carried out to help determine the exact cause of death, the statement said.
A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.
“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”

France mounts huge security operation as protesters prepare to march
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24

18:42:10 KST

France mounts huge security operation as protesters prepare to march
PARIS, Oct 24 - French security forces fanned out across Paris on Saturday ahead of protests that authorities fear could turn violent, with Interior Minister Laurent Nunez urging police to be "hyper-reactive" against troublemakers and looters.
Soldiers from an anti-terrorism military unit patrolled the Champs-Elysees avenue while police vans circled the Arc de Triomphe, looking to protect some of the capital's most famous sites from any repeat of the unrest that shook France last week.
Nunez has mobilised 70,000 police nationwide for Saturday's demonstrations, 10,000 more than on October 17, when a wave of vandalism and looting raised questions about the government's ability to maintain order.
Anger over living costs and strained public services has drawn students, workers and unions onto the streets in recent weeks, but authorities say radical militants and bands of young looters have exploited the protests to sow chaos.
Speaking to police in Paris, Nunez warned officers that they would face attempts to target shops, public institutions and security forces.
"We have to be ultra, ultra responsive. We have significant calls for disruption from political groups and quite simply from criminals," he said. "It is going to be a long day."
SHOPS, MUSEUMS, OPERA SHUT
Many shopkeepers in Paris boarded up storefronts, while luxury retailers beefed up security.
Business groups have urged stores to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend.
Lidiya Shevchenko, a sales assistant at a Graziella Braccialini store in Paris, said she doubted many customers would venture out to browse luxury boutiques during the day.
"I suppose the mood is just as important when it comes to shopping," she said.
Several of Paris' best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musée d'Orsay and the Opera House, will close for the day to avoid being caught up in any turmoil. More than 20 metro stations were also shut.
The location of Saturday's main Paris demonstration remained unclear after police sought to move organisers away from the city centre towards the southeastern fringes of the capital.
"The declared route poses serious risks of disturbances to public order, notably because of the high concentration of businesses similar to those targeted during the weekend of October 17-18," the Paris police prefecture said.
The last-minute decision angered some on the left.
"Once again, those in power are creating disruption for the marches and impossible deadlines for organisations to reorganise themselves. These methods are multiplying across the entire country," hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon wrote on X.
DEMONSTRATION IN ORLEANS AGAINST FAR RIGHT
Authorities have sharply restricted demonstrations across much of France. Marseille reversed an earlier ban and authorised a union march, while protests remain restricted in central Lyon. Union rallies will also go ahead in Strasbourg, but bans remain in force in several other cities including Nancy, Metz, Besancon, Belfort, Rouen, Le Havre, Toulon and Limoges.
The first authorised march began mid-morning in Orleans, about 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, to protest against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally, which is holding a congress in the city this weekend.
"We have come to tell the far right, face to face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party.
Tensions were heightened by a shooting west of Paris on Friday in which a gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl. REUTERS

Zoom Versus The Hague: Anatomy of a Russian Sleight of Hand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:41:00 UTC
18:41:00 KST

Before 2022, Izium was an ordinary town in Kharkiv region. It had more than 46,000 people, the Siverskyi Donets River, Kremenets Hill, factories, schools, hospitals and markets.
Oleshky, on the left bank of the Dnipro River opposite Kherson, was home to around 24,000. Enerhodar depended on its nuclear power plant, the largest in Europe. That life ended when Russia came.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russian troops seized Izium in the spring of 2022 and held it until Sept. 10, 2022. After liberation, about 10,000 people remained in the town, roughly a fifth of its pre-war population. Local officials estimated that around 80 percent of the town had been destroyed. In a forest on the outskirts, investigators found a mass burial site: 447 bodies, most of them civilians, many bearing signs of torture.
Oleshky has been under occupation since the first days of the full-scale invasion. After the destruction of the Kakhovka dam in June 2023, around 90 percent of the town was flooded. The occupation authorities did not evacuate residents.
Today, about 1,700 people remain in the town center. According to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, no food supplies have reached Oleshky since May 26, 2026. At the end of August, Russian checkpoints blocked all civilian movement and declared the town a “grey zone.”
The approach roads are mined, and humanitarian organizations have no access. For months, Ukrainian forces have been delivering food to residents by drone, in repeated runs; One night alone brought in four tonnes.
Moldova Expels Russian Diplomat After Drone Crash
On Oct. 15, the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor’s Office screened the documentary “Evidence” at Filmhuis Den Haag. Journalist Veronika Marchenko made it together with the prosecutors, with support from the GIDNA project of the Future for Ukraine foundation and from Project Expedite Justice.
GIDNA, led by clinical psychologist Anna Hruba, provides free and anonymous support to women who have survived conflict-related sexual violence. The team’s ongoing work is supported by the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR).
The director had access to official investigation files and closed interrogations. The film covers torture, sexual violence, unlawful detention and executions. It tells the story of a girl who lost her parents and grandmother when a Russian airstrike hit a residential building, and follows the investigation into the killing of a local forensic expert with a disability. It also shows the work of prosecutors and investigators after liberation: exhumations, forensic examinations, identification of specific perpetrators.
After the screening, the coordinator of the Ukraine accountability cluster at the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs moderated a discussion. The audience included Ukraine’s Ambassador to the Netherlands Andriy Kostin, diplomats from other countries, international journalists, and representatives of the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor’s Office and the International Criminal Court.
The hall was full. The film was later shown to the Ukrainian community in Amsterdam.
Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, noted that Russia is trying to prevent information about its crimes from spreading internationally, but despite provocations and attempts to disrupt them, the screenings went ahead.
A week later, Moscow responded with a group video call.
The so-called international “telebridge,” titled “Zaporizhzhia Region: Escalation of the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ Terrorist War,” was initiated by the Russian delegation to the Vienna negotiations on military security together with Rodion Miroshnik, ambassador-at-large of the Russian foreign ministry.
It was moderated by the head of the delegation, Yulia Zhdanova. Rossotrudnichestvo and its network of “Russian Houses” handled the organization.
HUR made the purpose of the operation public before it began. The aim was to divert attention from Russia’s war crimes, above all the catastrophe in Oleshky, to discredit the Ukrainian military and to weaken partners’ support for Kyiv.
Moscow had no answer to the evidence shown in The Hague. So it staged its own show. It responded to Izium by talking about Zaporizhzhia, and said nothing at all about Oleshky.
The main speaker was Miroshnik. He is a former press secretary to Ukraine’s ousted president, Viktor Yanukovych, and a former Party of Regions member of the Luhansk regional council. Since 2014, he has served in the occupation structures in the Luhansk region, and he is under sanctions.
Alongside him spoke the occupation “governor” of Zaporizhzhia region Yevhen Balytskyi, the “head” of Enerhodar Maksym Pukhov, reserve Major General Mykola Plotnikov, and Yuri Chernichuk, appointed by Russia as director of the occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant.
Viewers were also shown “witnesses” and “victims” prepared in advance for the broadcast.
The announcements promised diplomats from 80 countries and representatives of the UN, the OSCE, BRICS and the CIS. The actual line-up: staff of Russian embassies, Rossotrudnichestvo branches in Zambia, Kuwait, Uzbekistan, Nigeria, Bulgaria, Venezuela, Mongolia and Malaysia, and propagandists from Russia Today.
Simultaneous interpretation into three languages was meant to create the impression of an international format. No discussion was planned.
The occupation “governor” and the “head” of Enerhodar explained how Ukrainian forces were supposedly violating the rights of civilians in occupied territory that they themselves control.
The script was predictable. Miroshnik produced casualty figures for the occupied part of Zaporizhzhia region: 508 civilians killed since February 2022. He tied a supposed three- to fourfold rise in strikes to the EU’s €90 billion loan. Chernichuk spoke of a “blockade” of the nuclear plant.
All of it came from the occupation authorities themselves. The territory is closed to independent investigators, journalists and international missions. After Izium was liberated, prosecutors, forensic experts and international journalists worked on the ground, and every body from the mass grave underwent forensic examination.
The link to the European loan has a clear addressee. Moscow is speaking to the Western taxpayer: Your money is killing civilians. The goal is to split support for Ukraine at a time when funding for 2026 and 2027 has already been approved and is being disbursed.
Oleshky has gone months without proper food, water or medical care. Moscow has not explained why. It held a Zoom call about “Ukrainian crimes” in a neighboring region instead. It gave no answer to what was shown in The Hague either, only its own staff and witnesses prepared in advance.
Russian channels and Rossotrudnichestvo websites will now circulate recordings of the call. They will be presented as a “broad international discussion.” No one will check how many people actually joined or who they were. For the domestic audience and for Moscow-friendly countries of the Global South, what matters is the picture: diplomats, interpretation, “witnesses,” numbers.
In The Hague, the audience saw material from criminal proceedings, forensic findings and testimony from people who survived occupation and found the courage to speak. The film was shown in the city that hosts the International Criminal Court, to lawyers, diplomats and journalists free to ask any question. Every episode can be tested in court.
The Russian telebridge was built from statements by the people who run the occupation and from “testimony” prepared for broadcast. It was shown in a closed video call to Russia’s own staff. Nothing in it can be verified, and no one intended it to be.
In liberated Izium, investigators found a mass grave. Oleshky is still occupied, and food is not allowed in. Moscow answered with a video call among its own people. Russia could open these territories to independent investigators and let food into Oleshky today. It chose another Zoom.

Kiev retreats on Nazi collaborator tribute – Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:39:23 UTC
18:39:23 KST

Kiev retreats on Nazi collaborator tribute – Warsaw
Kiev has moved to block a planned tribute to Nazi collaborator Roman Shukhevich, who was involved in the killing of an estimated 100,000 Poles during World War II ethnic purges, officials in Warsaw have claimed.
The reported retreat comes amid a series of disputes between the two countries in recent months over Kiev’s veneration of Nazi-linked figures that have eroded Polish support for Ukraine in its conflict with Russia.
The controversy erupted on Tuesday when the Lviv Regional Council in western Ukraine voted to declare 2027 the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and to celebrate the 120th anniversary of its commander Roman Shukhevich while deciding to organize “cultural, memorial, scientific, and mass media events,” as well as exhibitions and national patriotic rallies on the occasion.
The move triggered a fierce response in Poland, which regards the UPA as perpetrators of genocide against Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia and Shukhevich as a key “architect” of the massacres. Before becoming a UPA leader, Shukhevich served in Nazi Germany’s Nachtigall Battalion and the German-controlled 201st Schutzmannschaft Battalion, which operated in occupied Belarus.
On Wednesday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk condemned the resolution as “unwise” and “suicidal tactics,” saying it “harms Ukraine,” while Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called the move “unacceptable,” warning that it would deepen divisions between the neighboring countries. Meanwhile, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski called for the resolution’s key sponsor, Lviv regional lawmaker Svyatoslav Sheremeta, to be put on a list of individuals deemed undesirable in Poland.
Following the backlash, Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said on Wednesday that officials of Vladimir Zelensky’s office had assured Warsaw that the controversial resolutions would not come into force. On Friday, Tusk echoed the claim, saying that Zelensky had personally signaled he would not endorse the resolution, adding that the Ukrainian leader was “unhappy” with the situation.
This also came after the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry called the Shukhevich tribute in Lviv “counterproductive to our current efforts aimed at further developing Ukrainian-Polish relations.” The ministry stressed that the local authorities had sought no advice from government bodies to assess the consequences of their actions.
An unnamed source in Zelensky’s office cited by Ukrainskaya Pravda went so far as to describe the decision as a “catastrophe.” “Ukraine looks erratic. We have just resolved the previous crisis – and now this,” the source said, accusing regional officials of pursuing “cheap one-day hype” despite knowing all too well what the resolution would lead to.
While senior Ukrainian officials apparently distanced themselves from the controversy, the Lviv council’s original announcement remains accessible as of Saturday. Sheremet also previously defended the resolution, saying “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honor their memory.”
The dispute is the latest in a series of heated clashes between Kiev and Warsaw over Ukraine’s continued veneration of nationalist figures that collaborated with Nazi Germany during World War II.
In May, Zelensky awarded an elite Ukrainian special operations unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA,” prompting another diplomatic uproar, with Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripping the Ukrainian leader of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state decoration.

Czech coalition advances media overhaul in rushed overnight vote
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:38:26 CEST
18:38:26 KST

PRAGUE, Oct 24 (Reuters) - In a rare overnight vote, the Czech ruling coalition pushed public media funding changes through a first parliamentary hurdle despite criticism that they could weaken broadcaster independence.
The populist government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, backed by the far-right SPD party, has frequently criticised public and private media coverage of its policies and accused some outlets of bias.
Opposition parties have compared the proposed changes with reforms in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who oversaw a major expansion of pro-government media.
The government says it is scrapping the 205 crown ($9.45) monthly household broadcasting fee to ease costs for consumers. Funding would instead come from the state budget.
The proposal was brought to the floor outside the planned order of proceedings on Friday. Speaker Tomio Okamura of the SPD limited debate and scheduled the vote for 4:36 a.m. (0336 GMT) on Saturday.
The coalition’s majority then voted to send the bill to committees for further discussion.
SUNDAY PROTEST PLANNED
Hundreds of protesters gathered outside parliament, with some remaining overnight. Local media reported that several people unsuccessfully tried to enter the building.
Critics say the changes would weaken the broadcasters and make them more vulnerable to political pressure. Czech Television is the country’s most-watched broadcaster across major age groups, while public media are among the most trusted news sources in the country, according to a 2025 Reuters Institute survey.
The proposal would cut funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio by about 15%, possibly as early as next year, and keep nominal funding unchanged for several years.
“There is no war for independent media,” Babis said on Facebook late on Friday. “There is no fight for democracy and no nationalisation of media is being prepared.”
The proposal and its fast-track treatment drew criticism from the broadcasters, international journalism groups and institutions including universities and the Catholic Church.
“The bill goes against the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), which requires adequate, stable and predictable funding for public service media,” the European Federation of Journalists said in a statement.
Journalists and other employees at the broadcasters announced a strike for November 3, while a civic group called a public protest for Sunday.
($1 = 21.6880 Czech crowns)
(Reporting by Jan Lopatka. Editing by Mark Potter)

“The Ministry of Defence’s monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield. We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable,” Evhenii Khmara told reporters.

Ukraine’s problems with SpaceX-owned Starlink came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow while pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Neither SpaceX boss Elon Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House.
Trump said on Friday that if problems with access to Starlink communications systems in Ukraine persisted, he would “get it straightened out”.

How much must the world cut emissions to return to 1.5°C?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:37:45 UTC
18:37:45 KST

How much must the world cut emissions to return to 1.5°C?
The Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return, published on October 21, outlines a scenario in which global temperatures peak at 1.7°C to 1.8°C above preindustrial levels around midcentury before returning to 1.5°C or below by 2100. The scenario has about a 50% chance of success.
The required cuts are measured against 2025 emissions levels. Emissions would also need to fall 69% by 2040, the report says.
Current national climate pledges fall far short. Even if countries fully implement their existing commitments, emissions would decline by only 5% to 8% by 2030 and 11% to 15% by 2035.
UN Secretary General António Guterres said the world could still limit the scale and duration of warming above 1.5°C.
Under current policies, global warming could reach 2.8°C this century and continue rising afterward, the report warns.
If countries meet their existing climate pledges and maintain similar efforts, warming could reach 2.6°C. Even if they fulfill their pledges and achieve additional net zero targets, temperatures would still rise by about 2.1°C.
Every 5 years of continued CO2 emissions at current levels could add about 0.1°C to peak warming, the report estimates.
Returning to 1.5°C would also require removing and permanently storing around 320 billion tons of CO2 from the atmosphere over the course of this century. That is equivalent to roughly 8 years of global CO2 emissions at 2024 levels. The report cautions that technological and economic challenges make achieving this uncertain.
Renewable energy
Despite the gap between current efforts and the required cuts, UNEP points to progress since the adoption of the Paris Agreement.
Renewable energy has expanded rapidly, coal and oil supplies have grown more slowly than previously projected, and climate policies have reduced emissions in several countries and sectors.
An assessment of more than 220 policy evaluations found that electricity sector policies reduced emissions by an average of 9%. Economic measures, including carbon taxes and emissions trading systems, cut emissions by 5% to 13% across the sectors studied.
However, these gains remain concentrated in particular countries, sectors and periods. Governments need to expand and sustain successful measures to achieve the necessary global reductions, the report says.
New targets for 2035 and 2040
To align with the lowest possible 1.5°C overshoot scenario, global renewable electricity capacity would need to reach at least three times its 2025 level by 2035 and 4.5 times that level by 2040.
Over the same period, the energy intensity of global economic output would need to fall by at least 30% by 2035 and 40% by 2040, relative to 2025.
The report also calls for major cuts in fossil fuel use. By 2035, the shares of coal, oil and gas in total global energy supply would need to fall by at least 55%, 15% and 5%, respectively, compared with 2025. By 2040, the required reductions would reach 75%, 30% and 35%.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that more than half of the estimated heat-related deaths in 854 European cities between 2000 and 2025 were attributable to human-induced climate change.

5th Asian Para Games: Kazakhstan finishes 9th with 50 Medals
Kazakhstan finished ninth overall at the 5th Asian Para Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Japan, capturing 50 medals — 12 gold, 16 silver, and 22 bronze, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Kazakh Sports Committee.
150 athletes from Kazakhstan competed across 12 sports: Para athletics, Para swimming, Para judo, Para taekwondo, Para powerlifting, Para table tennis, Para shooting, Para archery, Para cycling, sitting volleyball, boccia, and wheelchair tennis.
The national team achieved its strongest results in Para judo, securing 13 medals—five gold, one silver, and seven bronze. Moreover, it topped the sport's team standings.
Para judo gold medalists included Ibragim Nurmakhanuly (J2, -70 kg), Bexultan Kulmurza (J2, -81 kg), Zhurkamyrza Shukurbekov (J2, over 95 kg), Aktolkyn Seilbekova (J1, over 70 kg), and Zarina Raifova (J2, over 70 kg).
Zhanbota Amanzhol earned silver in the men's J2 -95 kg division.
Galymzhan Smagululy, Yermek Nurkabayev, Baglanbek Onalbek, Yerlan Otepov, Alfiya Tlekkabyl, Dayana Fedossova, and Ayala Mereke each claimed bronze medals.
In Para swimming, Kazakhstan collected 10 medals (one gold, five silver, four bronze).
Dias Kenzhebek claimed gold in the men's 100-meter backstroke S10 event, while adding silver medals in the 100-meter freestyle and 200-meter individual medley, alongside a bronze in the 100-meter butterfly.
Ali Turganbekov earned a silver medal in the men's 100-meter breaststroke SB4. He captured another silver medal as part of Team Kazakhstan in the mixed 4×50-meter medley relay, competing alongside Natalya Zvyagintseva, Zulfiya Gabidullina, Aisultan Kulkeyev, and Siyazbek Daliyev.
Team Kazakhstan claimed an additional silver medal in the mixed 4×50-meter freestyle relay, featuring a team of Natalya Zvyagintseva, Aisultan Kulkeyev, Siyazbek Daliyev, and Zulfiya Gabidullina.
In addition, Roman Potapov, Viktor Volkov, and Alina Sinelnikova secured bronze medals in their respective disciplines, adding to the national team's medal count.
In Para cycling, the national team captured nine medals: four gold, four silver, and one bronze.
Nail Yermukhambet became a two-time Asian Para Games champion in the men's B class, winning gold in both the road race and individual road time trial.
Anastassiya Kalaus also secured two gold medals in the equivalent women's events. Furthermore, she earned a silver medal in the 4,000-meter individual track pursuit.
Kirill Ilyukevich claimed two silver medals in the road race and individual road time trial, as well as a bronze medal in the 4,000-meter individual track pursuit. Zhuldyz Kainarova won a silver medal in the women's road race.
In Para powerlifting, Team Kazakhstan pocketed six medals: one gold, two silver, and three bronze.
David Degtyarev became the Asian Para Games champion in the men's -54 kg division, lifting 192 kg to set a new Asian Para Games record. Tursynay Kabyl won a silver medal in the women's -41 kg category, while Alina Solodukhina earned silver in the -45 kg class.
Stanislav Shakiyev and Aizhan Berimkulova took bronze medals in their individual events. Additionally, the Kazakh men's team, comprising Yerbolat Karibay, David Degtyarev, and Stanislav Shakiyev, won a bronze medal in the team competition.
In Para athletics, Kazakhstan captured four medals — two silver and two bronze.
Islam Salimov earned silver in the men's long jump T13, while Dastan Mukashbekov secured silver in the men's shot put F36. Bronze medals in the shot put were claimed by Ivan Zaleznyak (F36) and Makhambet Serikkaliyev (F53).
Additionally, Aisulu Suleimenova set a new Asian record in the women's 100 meters T62, clocking a time of 16.18 seconds.
In Para table tennis, Kazakh athletes took four bronze medals, marking the national team's first-ever podium finishes in the sport in Asian Para Games history.
In Para archery, Team Kazakhstan won two medals — one silver and one bronze.
In the men's doubles W1 class, Nurshat Toleukassym and Temirlan Seitkamal took silver, marking Kazakhstan's first-ever Para archery medal at the Asian Para Games.
Nurshat Toleukassym also earned a bronze medal in the men's individual W1 event.
In Para shooting, Yerkin Gabbasov became the Asian Para Games champion in the men's R1 10m air rifle standing SH1 event.
In sitting volleyball, the Kazakh men's national team clinched the silver medal. Kazakhstan defeated Iraq 3–2 in the semifinals before falling 3–0 to Iran in the gold medal match to complete the tournament as runners-up.
Thus, Kazakhstan concluded its campaign at the 5th Asian Para Games with 50 medals, including 12 gold, 16 silver, and 22 bronze, and finished ninth overall in the final standings.
The 5th Asian Para Games took place from October 18 to 24, 2026, in Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya, Japan.

Kim Jong-un has travelled to China over a newly opened bridge marking the North Korean leader’s first known trip abroad in more than a year, South Korean officials have said.
A government source told the Yonhap news agency on Saturday that Kim had arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong, in Liaoning province, after taking a train from Pyongyang to Sinuiju and crossing the New Yalu River Bridge.
Yonhap also reported that the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, had travelled to the city. Kim’s trip was not announced in advance and had not been confirmed by Pyongyang or Beijing by Saturday evening.
China will mark the anniversary on Sunday of its entry into the 1950-53 Korean war on the North’s side.
Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum devoted to China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.
Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.
The 3km bridge opened in mid-October, 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.
The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June, his first trip there in seven years.
Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.
Xi will host the Apec summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.
Reuters reported on Friday, however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.

Swimmer Tsanko Tsankov prepares for his final Oceans Seven challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:29:19 UTC
18:29:19 KST

Author
Diana Tsankova
News
Swimmer Tsanko Tsankov prepares for his final Oceans Seven challenge
In August, the swimmer crossed the English Channel between Britain and France
Saturday 24 October 2026 11:40
Saturday, 24 October 2026, 11:40
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Goals that test the limits of human endurance, and the satisfaction of overcoming the fears and doubts that stand between you and a cherished dream – these are at the heart of the story of an athlete who has completed six of the seven toughest swimming marathons on the planet. Driven by a desire to conquer ever higher and seemingly unattainable peaks, he is already preparing for his final challenge in the Oceans Seven.
In 2020, Tsanko Tsankov dreamt of becoming the first Bulgarian to swim across the Strait of Gibraltar, with its strong currents, fierce winds, high waves and sharp temperature changes. Two years later, he fulfilled that ambition by swimming from Europe to Africa, going on to add five more major feats to his impressive record.
“Behind me now are the Strait of Gibraltar, the Cook Strait in New Zealand, the Catalina Channel in the United States, the Molokai Channel in the Hawaiian Islands – the longest marathon in the world, the North Channel – the Everest of swimming, and a month ago I also swam across the English Channel”, Tsanko Tsankov told Radio Bulgaria.
PHOTO Burgas municipality
For his latest 35-kilometre marathon, the swimmer had a twelve-hour window to attempt the crossing. Over the course of a week, he had to be ready at any time of day or night to enter the water, as the exact day and time were determined by a local team.
“This marathon swim has the longest history – 151 years – and is considered the birthplace of open-water swimming”, Tsanko Tsankov says. “I swam for hours through vast fields of venomous jellyfish that stung me the entire time. The channel has extremely strong currents, especially during the final few kilometres, when they usually flow against you and require immense effort to overcome.”
He was injured during one of the toughest stages – the final kilometres, when he was exhausted and at risk of hypothermia after long hours in the water in a horizontal position. As he tried to leave the water and climb onto the large rocks at Cap Gris-Nez, he lost his balance, fell and suffered cuts to his left arm and lower legs.
PHOTO BTA
Tsanko Tsankov knew the freedom of gliding through the waves before he could even walk.
“I was born and raised in Burgas, and since childhood I have had a strong bond with the sea”, he recalls. “Back then, I used to spend hours on end in the water during the summer, and that is where my love for open-water swimming was born. It gives me an extra sense of freedom, and I feel the sea is my second home.”
In addition to conquering almost all of the toughest swimming marathons on the planet, he holds world records in winter swimming, set in extreme conditions with water temperatures just below zero degrees Celsius. These include records over 1,000 metres, the longest distance, and in the 450-metre freestyle.
Before each challenge, the champion thoroughly researches the location where he will spend hours swimming. “I try to leave as few unknowns as possible”, he states. Success, however, depends above all on mental resilience – the ability to endure pain and discomfort for hours on end. That is why, in marathon swimming and elite sport in general, 70 per cent of an athlete’s performance comes down to mental attitude.
PHOTO Instagram /tsanko.tsankov1
“I try to do a large part of my preparation in conditions similar to those I will face. For example, for the English Channel crossing, I did 90 per cent of my training in the Black Sea in my hometown. Twenty-five of those sessions took place after 10 p.m. in pitch darkness, to prepare for swimming alone at night far out at sea, which many people fear. Another fear when swimming over deep water is the presence of marine life – including stingrays, sharks, whales, killer whales, venomous jellyfish and other dangerous creatures. So you have to visualise the experience in advance to know what awaits you.”
While he chooses open water over the safer environment of the swimming pool and faces the unknown every time, on dry land Tsanko Tsankov prefers peace and quiet: “I love the peaceful moments when I have the opportunity to reflect, plan my schedule and spend time with my family.”
PHOTO Facebook /Tsanko Tsankov
He also devotes time to around 400 young swimmers at the sports club he chairs. He motivates those who have chosen to follow in his footsteps through personal example as well as words – encouraging them to dream, turn their dreams into goals and never give up when things get difficult. And when the swimmer himself is on the verge of exhaustion, with miles of open water still ahead, he pictures the places where he feels best, his loved ones and the sun shining over his hometown.
One day, once he has fulfilled his goals, Tsanko Tsankov will retire from marathon swimming and ice swimming. Before that, however, next summer he plans to conquer his seventh “peak” by swimming across the Tsugaru Strait in Japan. And in early 2027, he will compete in the European Ice Swimming Championships and the World Cup.
Tsanko Tsankov has now swum more than 57,000 kilometres in training and competition – more than the circumference of the Earth at the equator. “I don’t know how far my strength will take me – the results will show”, he says, adding with a smile: “One thing is certain – I have swum much more than I have walked in my life.”

British ships defy Chinese warnings in South China Sea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:27:12 BST
18:27:12 KST

Two Royal Navy patrol ships have finished a ten day exercise in the South China Sea alongside Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore, working with fifth generation fighters, a Singaporean submarine and New Zealand boarding teams, according to the Royal Navy.
HMS Spey and HMS Tamar led the British contribution to Bersama Lima 2026, the annual exercise of the Five Power Defence Arrangements, whose name means Together Five in Malay. The participating navies brought corvettes, frigates, patrol ships and a submarine, and the exercise built from familiarisation scenarios to a two day war game.
Before sailing, the crews spent a week learning each other’s vessels, systems, procedures and the language they would use at sea so that they could work together once the pace picked up. The maritime phase covered boarding and searching suspect vessels, naval gunfire directed onto targets ashore by soldiers embarked in the ships, a submarine hunt and an air defence exercise supported by aircraft.
Commander Tom Lindsey, the commanding officer of HMS Tamar, said: “Bersama Lima was an excellent opportunity to put my ship’s company through their paces and refresh their war-fighting skills with our Five Power allies.
“There was a great breadth to this iteration of Bersama Lima: fifth-generation fighter jets, international boarding teams and Singapore’s newest submarine which, combined with the level of competence and professionalism showed, levelled up the experience gained.
“These war-fighting serials demonstrated that we can put a task group together in short order and successfully operate together to achieve a spectrum of scenarios.”
Tamar hosted a Royal New Zealand Navy Deployable Boarding Team which was put through repeated serials investigating suspected illegal fishing and narcotics smuggling, work the team and the ship will be doing for real on their next mission.
Able Seaman Mansfield, one of Tamar’s seaman specialists, said: “Driving a Kiwi boarding team up to a suspect vessel with a second sea boat, armed to the teeth, was a surreal experience which really brought the exercise to life.
“We also got the opportunity to replenish underway at sea where we exchanged some goods from home with HMAS Stalwart, who sent Tim Tams [Australia’s favourite biscuit] in return!”
A sailor from HMS Spey said: “It was a privilege to attend Bersama Lima 26 alongside our FPDA partners, an exercise which demonstrates over five decades of commitment to training and working together.
“Throughout the harbour phase, HMS Spey’s sailors took the opportunity to learn from each of the Five Power nations and share their skills to enhance interoperability and build stronger friendships in the region.”
Each British operation in the region since has drawn the same response as Beijing previously accused Britain of flexing its naval muscles over the 2021 carrier deployment. After HMS Spey passed through the Taiwan Strait in June 2025, Senior Captain Liu Runke, spokesman for the navy of the People’s Liberation Army Eastern Theatre Command, said British remarks about the transit had distorted legal principles, and that troops remained on high alert and would resolutely counter all threats and provocations.
When Spey exercised navigation rights and freedoms around the Spratly Islands in May this year, China’s ambassador to the United Kingdom said the 2016 arbitration award was illegal, null and void and that the British position would not shake China’s resolve, as this publication reported at the time. In July the Chinese Embassy in London told Britain to stop stirring up trouble after it backed a statement on the same award, and the embassy’s position was set out again as the two ships entered the sea at the start of this month.
Spey and Tamar are Batch 2 River class offshore patrol vessels, each crewed by around sixty sailors. They have been forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific since 2021 under Operation Highwall. The Five Power Defence Arrangements date from 1971 and remain the only standing multilateral defence arrangement in the region involving Britain.
Spey is now heading to south-east Asia for several weeks of patrols and diplomatic engagement, while Tamar is making for Australia and New Zealand by way of Pacific island chains, where she will carry out maritime security patrols and counter illegal fishing.

Owners of mobile phones that are not set to update their time automatically, or users who prefer not to rely on automatic updates, can adjust their devices manually. They can also restore automatic date and time synchronization at any point.
Android
Android menus vary across models, but time settings are generally found in the device's main Settings menu or under the clock settings.

iPhone
In Settings, select "General," then "Date & Time." Turn off "Set Automatically," select the appropriate time zone and adjust the clock manually.

Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield operating at 400 kph after week of throttling
KYIV, Oct 24 - The Starlink satellite communications system and its military version Starshield are operating again at speeds over 400 km per hour, Kyiv's defence minister said on Saturday, after over a week of service restrictions that slowed connections and disrupted military operations.
"The Ministry of Defence's monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield. We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable," Evhenii Khmara told reporters.
The Ukrainian military does not disclose the systems' maximum operating speeds, and the defence ministry did not say whether service had been fully restored.
"Monitoring systems had previously recorded disruptions to the Starlink/Starshield service. The speed metrics have now returned to normal," the ministry said.
The restrictions, first reported on October 14, undermined Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and disrupted frontline communications, Ukrainian officials said. Sources said connection speeds had been reduced to about 160 kph or less.
Ukraine's problems with SpaceX-owned Starlink came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow while pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Neither SpaceX boss Elon Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House.
Trump said on Friday that if problems with access to Starlink communications systems in Ukraine persisted, he would "get it straightened out". REUTERS

Ray-Ban Meta Audio Review: The Best Smart Glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

I am very lost in Los Angeles. I’m also sweating because I'm running as fast as I can, slapping my hands against the wet glasses frame on my face to boost the volume of the pulsing techno beats blasting into my ears—and anyone else’s if they happen to be nearby. It’s only the second time I’ve gone on a run in the city, and I decide to let myself get completely off course.
“Hey Meta,” I pant. “I need to get back; tell me where to go.”
The music dims, and the AI agent barks turn-by-turn directions in my ears. After getting turned around a couple of times, I eventually make it back. The navigation wasn’t perfect, but it got me where I needed to be.
This feature has long been available in Meta’s smart glasses. But now I’m wearing the new Ray-Ban Meta Audio, camera-free glasses the company announced in September. The only big change between these and Meta’s other glasses is the lack of a camera, but losing that one feature makes a world of difference.
It makes sense that Meta started with cameras on its glasses. After all, its primary breadwinner is Facebook, a visual platform driven by all the photographs and memes your uncle can use AI to generate. The platform is designed to capture content and beam it to the world—sometimes whether people like it or not.
It took waves of privacy controversies for Meta to finally ditch the cameras. People have found the camera-enabled glasses creepy, calling Meta’s products “pervert glasses” because they have been used by weirdo pickup artists to record people without consent. Some users also shared techniques for removing the indicator light on the glasses designed to let people around the wearer know they’re recording. (Meta released a software fix for this that disables the cameras entirely if the indicator light has been tampered with.)
It didn’t help that the company tried to put facial recognition technology on the glasses, which it denied at first, then later admitted to, and removed. In September, the company was sued for its facial recognition systems. (Meta insists that all the very public pushback did nothing to encourage it to release audio-only glasses.)

What to watch on TV this week: Israeli election satire and a Hersh Goldberg-Polin tribute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:14:54 UTC
18:14:54 KST

It isn’t only the political parties that are fighting for your vote; the election-night comedy shows are also engaging in a battle. Checkout (Kupa Rashit) on KAN 11 and Keshet’s Eretz Nehederet (Wonderful Country) on Channel 12 are both broadcasting after the news on the evening of October 27.
The polls will still be open, and at that point nobody will know the results, so KAN and Keshet are betting Israelis would rather take some time to laugh a little.
The Checkout episode was planned about a year ago, and it will focus more on the staff and customers of the forlorn Shefa Issachar supermarket than on any politician or party.
Some of the Checkout writers recently gave an interview to The Jerusalem Post, and Daniel Salganik said of the election episode: “It was a challenge.... We had to make an episode that would somehow feel topical a year into the future. But if, from the outset, your ideology isn’t Left or Right and your only ideology is ‘Is it funny?’ then it’s much easier to get laughs out of everybody.”
The writers wouldn’t say too much about it – at first, all they would tell me was that it takes place at the supermarket – but then revealed a couple of details.
Cameo by Yaakov Zada Daniel of Fauda
Amnon (Dov Navon), the world’s fussiest customer, somehow becomes a darling of the Left, and the wealthy life coach, Shuni Stretiner (played by Dorit Lev-Ari), another customer, is running for the Knesset.
They also said Yaakov Zada Daniel of Fauda would make a cameo.
Eretz Nehederet is a sketch comedy show that makes fun of current events, so its Tuesday night content will depend on all the egregious behavior by desperate politicians in the final days of the campaign. The episodes will be posted on the networks’ websites following the broadcasts, so you can watch one live and then stream the other.
While the election results may or may not be a surprise, one genuinely unexpected moment on television recently came with a reference to Hersh Goldberg-Polin on the Netflix series The Diplomat.
Goldberg-Polin was a young man from Jerusalem who was kidnapped from the Nova music festival and killed by Hamas after nearly a year in captivity. He was shot in a tunnel along with his fellow hostages Ori Danino, Alexander Lobanov, Carmel Gat, Almog Sarusi, and Eden Yerushalmi, a group Goldberg-Polin’s mother, Rachel, has dubbed “the beautiful six.”
The scene where Goldberg-Polin is given a tribute comes when the character Frances Munning (Penny Downie), the manager of the residence of the US ambassador to Britain, Kate Wyler (Keri Russell), explains to Stuart Heyford (Ato Essandoh), Wyler’s right-hand man, why she likes Americans.
Her father was a soldier in World War II, she says, and his unit was attached to the US 9th Armored Division. “A gentleman by the name of Hershel Pollen from Richmond, Virginia, watched a live grenade roll right to my father’s feet,” she tells him. “Mr. Pollen snatched it up, tossed it away. It exploded, inches from his hand. He lost the limb. He saved my father’s life.... I am fond of Americans.”
This story references what actually happened to Goldberg-Polin and his friend, Aner Shapiro. Both fled into a bomb shelter crowded with others escaping the music festival, and once they were inside, Hamas terrorists threw grenades at them. Shapiro tossed seven grenades back at the terrorists before he was killed. One exploded near Goldberg-Polin, and his arm was blown off from the elbow down.
Another fact about Goldberg-Polin: He lived in Richmond, Virginia, as a child, before moving to Israel with his parents. Goldberg-Polin’s father, Jon Polin, told Ynet: “Although we have no connection to the writers or the team behind Netflix’s The Diplomat, we appreciate the clear reference to our late son, Hersh, and his childhood in Richmond, Virginia, as well as to the late Aner Shapiro, one of the true heroes of that terrible day, October 7.
“At a time when some are trying to rewrite history or whitewash the October 7 massacre, it is heartwarming to know that so many others refuse to stop talking about Hersh, Aner, and the other victims, and continue to remember them, even through subtle references.”
Not surprisingly, screenwriter/producer Debora Cahn, who created The Diplomat, is a descendant of Holocaust survivors.
The Emmy-winning series is a suitable follow-up for Russell, following her work on the outstanding series The Americans, and features The West Wing alums Bradley Whitford and Allison Janney in key supporting roles.
Netflix series Below features a terrifying sea creature
For those looking for escapist fare to distract from all the political turmoil, there are options. Netflix is offering a series called Below, which may interest those who just saw Whalefall, the new feature film about a latter-day Jonah swallowed by a whale. Below is about a small community in Newfoundland that is menaced by a mysterious giant squid.
It’s kind of like Widow’s Bay meets Jaws, but mostly without the jokes.
Josh Hartnett, who once seemed like the next Brad Pitt and is now having a kind of comeback, has the lead role as Calvin, a widowed father who grew up in a small village. It was once a fishing village, but its inhabitants are now prevented from fishing to protect the environment. He makes a living finding ice chunks for a bespoke vodka company and renting out a small bed-and-breakfast apartment.
The residents are being encouraged to take a government payout to leave, and most think it’s the sensible thing to do, but not Calvin.
Although he has suppressed the memory, he knows that there is something strange and threatening in the local waters, because his father was killed by a sea creature in a strange incident that he witnessed as a child.
When it rears its ugly head again, he is the first one to recognize what is really going on, and he teams up with the prettiest marine biologist since Charlotte Rampling in Orca (one of the best bad movies of all time), played by Mackenzie Davis of the series Halt and Catch Fire and Station Eleven, to catch it.
Below starts off slow, but the atmosphere is compelling, and the suspense builds.
If even Below sounds too serious, try War, a new series running on Hot VOD, Hot Drama, and Next TV. It is a British legal drama, along the lines of The Good Wife, with a lot of sexual scandal and backstabbing.
It stars Dominic West (The Wire) as a tech billionaire and Sienna Miller (Anatomy of a Scandal) as his movie star wife, who are headed for a divorce that, according to one of their lawyers, could be the highest-profile such case in British history.
Their armies of lawyers and spin doctors also have major roles, and it’s fun from start to finish.

Oud across the world, and back: The 27th annual Jerusalem International Oud Festival kicks off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:14:41 UTC
18:14:41 KST

Twenty-six years is a long time by most people’s standards, and much can happen along the way. The Jerusalem International Oud Festival, which takes place for the 27th time, under the aegis of Confederation House, November 5-12, has certainly seen a thing or two over the years.
Back in 2000 it was a modest two-day affair when home venue CEO and artistic director Effie Benaya managed to coax an oud player from Morocco over here. The audiences at Confederation House, quite a few of whom imbibed Arabic music with their mother’s milk back in Iraq, Morocco, and elsewhere around the Arab domain, enjoyed the shows immensely. It was a much-appreciated blast from the past for them.
In the meantime, their offspring – second and third generations – and plenty of Ashkenazi Israelis have jumped on the Arabic music bandwagon, and festival attendees now spread far and wide across the demographic range.
Benaya, naturally, kept tabs on the festival’s growth, and, as in other fields of musical endeavor, the delineating programmatic lines have ebbed and shifted.
Stellar crowd-pullers
The curtain-raiser sets out the crossover stall from the word go. The first thing that springs to mind is that Benaya has gone for star value, with the Jerusalem Theatre show (November 5, 9 p.m.) featuring internationally renowned Iraqi-rooted Israeli rocker Dudu Tassa paired with Jonny Greenwood of famed English rock band Radiohead.
If Benaya was looking to put bums on seats, he has surely hit the jackpot here. Radiohead has been one of the world’s biggest rock acts for over 40 years, and Tassa has been a regular on the global ethnic-leaning rock and festival circuit for well over a decade.
This is something of a supergroup matchup, with the front pair set to play material from their 2023 album Jarak Qaribak, with additional numbers from Tassa’s Al-Kuwaiti projects. They feed off music written and performed by Tassa’s grandfather and great-uncle, Daoud and Salleh Al-Kuwaiti, who were particular favorites of Iraq’s last king, Faisal II, and big shots across the Arab music scene.
The grand production sees Tassa and Greenwood backed by 15 instrumentalists and two vocalists.
With expectations high and tickets hard to come by, Benaya has added another concert to the festival program, with the feted twosome due to strut their stuff for a second time at the same venue, on November 6 (12:45 p.m.).
Happily and, it must be said in the current international political climate, surprisingly, Benaya has managed to work a couple of offshore items into the programmatic fabric, including Greek singers Babis Tsertos, 70, and Areti Ketime, 37.
Their ethnic folk music show features rebetiko, the Greek blues, along with Smyrneika, brought – as the name suggests – to Greek shores by refugees from the Turkish cosmopolitan port city of Smyrna and its hinterland in Asia Minor in the early 20th century.
Lovers of Indian music will, no doubt, be buoyed by the inclusion of the Triveni date at the Jerusalem Theatre on November 10 (9 p.m.).
This is a truly top-notch concert with the stellar trio of bansuri (bamboo flute) player Rakesh Chaurasia, sitar player Purbayan Chatterjee, and tabla player Ojas Adhiya.
This is an Oud Festival reprise for Chaurasia, whose uncle, now 88-year-old iconic bansuri player Hariprasah Chaurasia, also lent his silky skills to the Confederation House-based event, while Chatterjee makes his debut at the festival. This will, however, be his second working trip to Israel, having performed in Tel Aviv and Haifa in 2007 as part of a series of events marking the 15th anniversary of Israeli-Indian diplomatic relations.
Quality Indian music
The Triveni concert looks like a top-class offering to be relished. Chaurasia is hailed as a master of the bansuri, and has several Grammys in his trophy cabinet, while Chatterjee has been dubbed “India’s leading sitar maestro.” He is also gearing up for the 2027 Grammy Award with his new release, Feathered Creatures, in the running for a coveted slot.
The record is a collaborative venture with five-time Grammy-winning American guitarist Mark Lettieri, who plays with celebrated jazz fusion band Snarky Puppy.
After just a few seconds into the opening track of the album, it becomes patently clear that 50-year-old Chatterjee is just as happy delving into such diverse sonic waters as rock, hip-hop, jazz, blues, and even Western classical music as performing more spiritually leaning and ostensibly tranquil ragas from the traditional Indian side of the music tracks.
Watching him do his thing on YouTube, with tabla player Vivek Pandya, or alongside Chaurasia at the 2022 Darbar Festival in London, you cannot fail to discern that Chatterjee is well versed in the intricacies of Hindustani classical material from northern India.
He is a true virtuoso who can reel off white-hot riffs, producing seamless cascading arpeggios at the speed of light, but is not averse to performing more pedestrian, reflective passages. All the above will be rolled out for the Oud Festival attendees.
Chatterjee maintains a balanced eclectic approach to his craft and follows the tenet that anything musical is fair game and can be incorporated into his vast repertoire of sounds and styles.
“I think that in order to truly discover the essence of something, you have to look at it from the external world,” he suggests.
That non-purist ethos got me thinking, and listening to my interviewee even more attentively. “You have to stray. You have to allow yourself to stray and fall in love elsewhere, and come back. That’s exactly the relationship I have with raga music.”
It is, he says, a philosophy borne of experience.
“When I started off this journey – which is now many years old – I was very monogamous,” he chuckles. “I was faithful to this raga music, and I was told it was a sin to stray into anything else. That’s the atmosphere I was brought up in.”
That, presumably, was the line taken by his father, sitar-playing Parthapratim Chatterjee, and Purbayan’s principal source of inspiration, late distinguished sitar player Nikhil Banerjee.
Chatterjee duly put in the requisite shifts to hone his technical skills on the demanding instrument but, over time, also painstakingly developed his own ideas for carving out his niche in his professional timeline. It was time to take a leap of faith.
“I slowly realized that I couldn’t truly love my own kind of music unless I allowed myself to fall in love with every other kind of music; unless I allowed myself to understand every other musical idiom, every other musical language.”
Voyage of discovery
It was a voyage of discovery, and required plenty of sifting and sorting en route to arrive at some kind of distilled – albeit highly varified and generously proportioned – musical sphere in which Chatterjee felt he could explore, imbibe, and eventually present to his audiences.
“There are things that you kind of reject along the way,” he notes. “You think, well, this is not for me. But eventually, when I came back to the [Indian classical] music, I discovered who I was.”
He had arrived at the core of his craft.
“I believe that any form of art is finally about that. It is about getting to a sense of who you are.”
Even so, that hard-earned epiphany isn’t set in stone. “Who you are is constantly changing.”
The go-with-the-flow sensibility is also central to Indian classical music, despite initial appearances.
“Indian ragas are very serene, and a lot of the raga music, and raga-based concerts, is about storytelling,” Chatterjee explains.
But there is a flip side. “Too often, Indian music is described as serene and spiritual and divine, which it is,” he exclaims. “But there is also a sense of ecstasy which lies within that divinity, and a sense of virtuosity and exhilaration, a sense of self-discovery in the moment of exhilaration.”
I came to the unmistakable conclusion that, similar to late modern jazz pioneer drummer Max Roach, who once told me, simply and poignantly, that “music is just music,” Chatterjee does not take a hierarchical route to music appreciation and sonic practice. He calls out a roll of late musical pantheon members.
“It could be [rock guitarist] Jimi Hendrix, [Indian sitar master] Ravi Shankar, [Indian tabla wizard] Zakir Hussain, or [rock guitarist Eddie] Van Halen. That sense of exhilaration, and the pain of not being able to discover and then the exhilaration of being able to discover, are all part of that entire spectrum which you need to explore.”
Chatterjee says he is still finding his way across that rocky, enriching terrain. “I feel there is more to find, but I am at a point in my journey where I am able to at least see the larger picture, as it were.”
Considering his instrumental prowess and his ability to mix it with fellow artists who, seemingly, have little in common with the likes of Chatterjee, who “simply” sit there on the stage and play their music, sometimes for hours on end, his appreciation for ostensibly extraneous art forms is surprising and impressive.
Instruments for all
As the Feathered Creatures venture clearly shows, Chatterjee has no problem with culling sounds from every which place and culture and bringing them into the Indian fold.
Still, he does have a left-field-leaning view of the means employed to put the bottom musical line together. I asked whether, for example, he considers the drum kit or electric guitar acceptable for his line of work.
“I think the drum is a traditional instrument,” he chuckles. “I think the electric guitar is the most traditional instrument there is,” he adds even more surprisingly. That may be because the music business as a whole and musical tastes have changed over the years. “You ask a teenager, they will tell you that is the most traditional instrument.”
That might be challenging for Chatterjee and his ilk. “Nine out of ten Indian teenagers will tell you they are most familiar with the electric guitar. I am not so sure about the sitar.”
Chatterjee adopts a philosophical oxymoronic view of that state of affairs. “It’s a little sad, but, at the same time, it is also cathartic. There is a great deal of influence of Western pop culture [in India today], which I can understand.”
He says, in fact, fusion has been the name of the game almost from the off. “If you look at the sitar itself, it is the result of a collision of two distinct cultures and religions,” he notes, referencing the powerful impact of Persian music and culture that informed the evolution of music across numerous ethnic and cultural demarcation lines.
“I am very proud to be Indian because we’ve allowed for that for many centuries now. We have allowed the culture to slowly percolate, especially in the north of India. The sitar is the result of the setar, which comes from Persia, colliding with the veena, which is the fountainhead of Indian string instruments.”
That broad base has led to a flexibility of musicianship and intent, and the sitar eventually also found its way into Western consciousness, primarily following Shankar’s performance at the seminal 1967 Monterey Pop Festival in California, where he played with Zakir Hussain’s father, peerless tabla player Alla Rakha, with Hendrix happily grooving away in the audience of predominantly hippies and rock and pop fans.
There was also the earlier discovery of the sitar by the Beatles’ George Harrison, who studied with Shankar, and incorporated its captivating textures and otherworldly sounds into such beloved numbers as “Norwegian Wood.”
Chatterjee’s accommodating, free-flowing view of music notwithstanding, the Triveni show will not come with billowing dry ice, strobe lighting, and gigantic video screens. It will be just about the music and, as Chatterjee, puts it, the pure ecstasy of the road to new sonic and emotional vistas, as the trio takes its audience for the best kind of ride.
The rest of the Oud Festival program offers plenty of quality. Percussion player Itamar Doari’s show at the Khan Theater (November 10, 9 p.m.) is also one to look out for, and feted singer-songwriter pianist Shlomi Shaban mixes it, on November 11 at 9 p.m., with internationally renowned kemancha (spike violin) player Mark Eliyahu and the Kadosh Brothers threesome, which colors its Arabic music base with heaping helpings of jazz and rock.
Festival stalwart violinist-oud player Prof. Taiseer Elias will delve into classical Arabic music with mandolin player Shmuel Elbaz (November 7, 9 p.m.), while the confluence of dazzling Andalusian-leaning jazz pianist Omri Mor and 83-year-old, east-west fusion pioneering percussionist-vocalist Shlomo Bar, on November 8 at 9 p.m., promises fireworks aplenty.
Choreographer Orly Portal’s Rite of Spring dance production (November 12, 8:30 p.m.) was inspired by late legendary Syrian-Egyptian singer, oud player and composer Farid al-Atrash, and veteran mizrachi-pop-rock band Teapacks stars in the finale, on November 12 at 9 p.m., supported by the 12-piece The Hafla and Hora Orchestra.
For tickets and more information: *6226, tickets.bimot.co.il, and www.confederationhouse.org
