Why is Israel launching a new military operation in the occupied West Bank?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:14:40 UTC
18:14:40 KST

Why is Israel launching a new military operation in the occupied West Bank?
Netanyahu says ‘we will destroy this place’ as Israeli forces begin days-long operation with raids and demolitions.
Israel’s military has launched another major operation in the occupied West Bank, during which it plans to carry out mass arrests, demolish homes and forcibly displace residents.
The operation comes after an attack at an Israeli military checkpoint near Hebron on Friday in which two Israeli soldiers were killed. The two suspected Palestinian gunmen were shot dead.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who ordered a full lockdown of the West Bank, said Israeli forces would go house-to-house in the Hebron neighbourhood that the suspected attackers came from.
“We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely,” he said.
Israeli rights group B’Tselem warned the Israeli government’s planned offensive amounts to “collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”.
Here’s what we know about the Israeli military operation.
What’s happening in the West Bank?
Israel’s military announced late on Friday that a major “counterterrorism” operation, involving Israeli soldiers, police and other security agents, was under way in the Hebron area of the occupied West Bank.
It said the “targeted” campaign would last “several days”, in addition to operations in “dozens” of other areas across the West Bank.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu earlier said Israeli forces would go “house-to-house” in the Hebron neighbourhood where the suspects involved in Friday’s attack came from, replicating tactics previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank. The operation will involve demolitions and forced displacement, he said.
By Saturday morning, Israeli forces had raided at least 15 towns in the northern West Bank, including Nablus, Jenin, Tubas and Qalqilya, arresting dozens of Palestinians, Al Jazeera correspondents reported.
On Saturday, videos posted on Telegram by Palestinians in the al-Jalda area of Hebron city showed Israeli soldiers standing guard and military vehicles, shopping trolleys and other objects blocking the roads.
Israeli forces in the area had also sent in a bulldozer that could be seen alongside other Israeli military vehicles.
Earlier, Israeli bulldozers wrecked a three-storey building in Hebron, while ordering hundreds of Palestinian families to leave their homes in the Ein Deir Bahha area of the city and its surroundings.
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the West Bank, said there was “a lot of anxiety” in the occupied territory as people largely avoided going into the streets.
Why has Israel locked down the West Bank?
The measure is a response to Friday’s attack at an Israeli checkpoint near Hebron.
But it also takes place just days before Israel’s election on Tuesday, during which Israel had already been planning to lock down the occupied territory, reported The Times of Israel.
During the lockdown, Netanyahu said Israeli troops would conduct “extensive waves of arrests” and pursue Hamas fighters “wherever they are and at all times”.
Is this related to attacks possibly restarting on Iran?
The operation comes amid signs that Israel and its ally the United States are preparing for a potential new wave of attacks on Iran.
According to The New York Times, the US and Israel have drafted plans for a campaign of attacks on Iran that would take place after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Citing unnamed US officials and other informed sources, The New York Times reported that the US and Israel have intensified drills for a “a short but intensive operation” against Iran, with potential targets to include the country’s “energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal”.
US President Donald Trump appeared to confirm on Friday that the US was weighing a new military campaign against Iran. Speaking at a rally, Trump said, “We may do another little epic fury,” using the codename of the US-Israel war against Iran that started with attacks across the country on February 28.
How have attacks on Palestinians escalated in recent weeks?
Israeli settler pogroms against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have been rife in recent weeks, coinciding with the annual olive harvest season.
On Thursday, the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said it had recorded 409 attacks by Israeli forces or settlers against Palestinian farmers, their land, olive trees and agricultural equipment so far during October. It called the attacks part of a pattern of “direct violence to force farmers from their land”.
Visiting Western officials have also found themselves caught up in the violence.
On October 17, Israeli settlers assaulted European diplomats, including a French mayor, near the Palestinian village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank as they visited Palestinian olive farmers. Then on Wednesday, US Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was briefly detained by the Israeli military while volunteering to help Palestinian farmers harvest olives.
What has the response been to Israel’s West Bank operation?
The operation has been cheered on by far-right Israeli officials, but criticised by the United Nations and human rights watchdogs.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position within Israel’s Ministry of Defence where he oversees the administration of the occupied West Bank and its settlements, called for Israel’s large-scale offensive in the West Bank to proceed “exactly like in Gaza”.
Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for the Ramallah-based Palestinian Authority to be “dismantled” and for tighter restrictions on Palestinian movement.
Mustafa Barghouti, secretary-general of the Palestinian National Initiative party, said incitement from far-right Israeli ministers was making the situation worse.
He told Al Jazeera the West Bank lockdown was turning every city and village into “a small prison”, a form of collective punishment that would “lead to explosions”.
Mayy El Sheikh, spokesperson for the UN’s Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory, said Israel’s move to lock down the West Bank marked “yet another episode in a never-ending stream of suffocating measures making life more and more unbearable for Palestinians”.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, through his spokesperson, also expressed concern about West Bank closures that would restrict Palestinians’ “access to basic services and livelihoods”.
B’Tselem sounded the alarm over Israeli “plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”.
“The world cannot stand by as Israel continues its assault on Palestinians, waiting for yet more neighbourhoods to be emptied and erased before intervening, despite what we have already witnessed in Gaza and the northern West Bank,” said the rights group.

====================================================================================================

Trump’s Iran pause is for November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:12:09 UTC
18:12:09 KST

President Trump’s pre-midterm pause on strikes against Iran landed as a claim of diplomatic momentum, not a concession of failure. The pause was framed as proof that negotiations are working. Look closer, and a different mechanism appears. The war meant to project strength has become an electoral liability, and the president’s response is to bury its most visible costs until voters have finished deciding. Then the option can reopen.
The White House insists Washington is negotiating from strength. Military options remain on the table. The blockade stays in force. The administration has not ended the war, only hidden its sharpest edges from the campaign season. That sequence matters. It allows Republican candidates to campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or another energy-price spike, while preserving the argument that renewed action may be warranted later. Nothing has been settled. Everything has been postponed.
Trump’s political identity rested on rejecting costly, open-ended foreign interventions. His appeal to swaths of the MAGA movement included the claim that American leaders had squandered resources and neglected domestic problems chasing overseas conflicts. “America First” was a promise about priorities as much as power.
The Iran war has strained that promise to its breaking point.
Back in February 2026, it looked like a pressure campaign: force Tehran to accept Washington’s terms. Months later, it’s a drawn-out confrontation with no clear settlement. Rising fuel prices, stubborn inflation, and the uncertainty over how long the war will last have turned it into a domestic political problem.
Consumer sentiment has fallen close to a record low, dragged down by rising living costs linked to the conflict.
This creates a tension the Republican coalition cannot easily absorb. Some supporters prioritize nationalist strength and a confrontational stance toward Iran. Others were drawn by pledges to avoid costly wars and focus on economic grievances at home. An extended conflict makes satisfying both impossible. Pausing attacks before the midterms offers a way to postpone the reckoning.
The question is whether this pause is a genuine step toward peace or simply an attempt to protect Republicans from the political costs of an unpopular war. The attacks may have stopped, but the naval blockade remains in place, economic pressure on Iran continues, and neither side appears any closer to a lasting agreement. Trump has ruled out further strikes before 3rd November. What he has not ruled out is a return to military action once the election is over. This sequence allows the administration to present the pause as controlled progress, lets Republican candidates campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or energy-price spikes, and preserves the option of arguing later that renewed action may be warranted.
The reports tell a different story than the public messaging. The Pentagon has been instructed to prepare for a potential resumption of large-scale operations. Discussions involving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have touched on a major new operation before elections in both countries. The White House calls such reports false. But the military remains on alert, and preparations are being finalised.
For many MAGA voters who supported Trump in part because he promised to reject endless wars, a purely electoral pause represents a significant contradiction.
An unpopular foreign war won’t turn MAGA loyalists into Democrats. The real hazard for the GOP is exhaustion: an endless conflict paired with painful pump prices gives frustrated voters every reason to leave their ballots on the kitchen table.
By removing the immediate threat of renewed attacks, Trump can try to prevent the war from becoming the dominant symbol of Republican failure and shift attention toward negotiations. If the conflict remains relatively quiet until November 3, Republican prospects improve. If Democrats gain control of one or both chambers, congressional scrutiny of military spending and presidential war powers would intensify.
This is where the powerless ballot enters the picture. Elections are meant to give citizens influence over decisions made in their name. That relationship weakens when a president can temporarily reduce the visibility of a policy’s costs until after ballots are cast, then resume the same course. Trump’s approach could turn the midterms into a debate over whether he appears willing to pull back from the war, rather than whether his Iran policy has actually changed. Americans are already feeling the strain of higher living costs, and consumer confidence has fallen sharply. A brief pause in the fighting will do little to ease that burden, much less resolve the underlying conflict. What is needed is a lasting diplomatic settlement, not a temporary break that leaves the same problems unresolved.
Neither a Republican nor a Democratic outcome automatically resolves the strategic problem. Iran has its own calculations.
Iranian officials continue to demand sanctions relief and an end to the blockade while Washington insists on further concessions. A pause that leaves these disagreements unresolved may simply delay the next confrontation.
The bigger question is not whether Trump keeps his promise before the election, but what he plans to do once the votes are counted and the political pressure has eased. If the coming weeks bring a verifiable agreement backed by credible safeguards, the pause could be a genuine first step toward ending the war. If instead November 3 is treated as the moment political restraints disappear, then the restraint will have functioned primarily as an electoral maneuver.
In that case the danger is clear. Voters are being asked to endorse the appearance of an ending while the means to continue the conflict remain intact. The ballot becomes a ratification of a decision already made elsewhere.
If the fighting resumes after the votes are counted, the question will no longer be whether Trump delivered peace, but whether his supporters were ever given a genuine choice between peace and a war that had only been postponed.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

Japan introduces historic changes for its 1,500-year-old imperial monarchy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:10:56 EEST
18:10:56 KST

Japan introduces historic changes for its 1,500-year-old imperial monarchy
Kyiv • UNN
The new law allows distant male relatives to be adopted to preserve the monarchy. Princess Aiko will not be able to inherit the throne.
Unpopular amendments to Japan’s Imperial House Law, reinforcing rules for succession exclusively through the male line, took effect on Saturday, October 24. The new rules are expected to bring historic changes to the 1,500-year history of the Japanese monarchy. UNN reports this, citing AP.
Details
The changes include allowing the adoption of distant male relatives raised as commoners so that they can become members of the royal family and fathers of future heirs, as well as allowing princesses to retain their royal status after marrying commoners.
However, the revised law bars the emperor’s extremely popular daughter, 24-year-old Princess Aiko, from becoming his successor, and even bars her future children from becoming members of the royal family.
Critics argue that the amendments discriminate against people on the basis of their family background or sex and place pressure on young members of the royal family to produce male offspring.
The Imperial Household Agency of Japan said that officials are studying ways to implement these measures.
The rule of succession exclusively through the male line means that the line must pass to Emperor Akishino, the emperor’s younger brother, and then to his 20-year-old nephew, Prince Hisahito. Next in line after him is the emperor’s 90-year-old uncle.
The revised law allows the adoption of unmarried male descendants aged 15 and older of distant imperial relatives—but only through the paternal line—into the branch of the royal family.
The plan is to find candidates from families that relinquished their royal status in 1947, which at the time was intended to ease the postwar financial burden on the monarchy. Four of the 11 such families remain, but officials say they have been separated from Naruhito by at least 36 generations since splitting from a common male-line ancestor 600 years ago.
The government’s efforts to ensure that men from royal families produce male emperors have drawn criticism.
Conservative scholars say there are a number of candidates, but so far no one has put themselves forward, and many are skeptical about whether anyone will volunteer. Experts also question the lack of transparency in the selection process.
Princesses may remain members of the royal family after marriage, but with caveats.
Previously, princesses who married commoners had to relinquish their royal status and leave the royal family. The last to do so, albeit voluntarily, was Mako, one of Naruhito’s two nieces, who married her university boyfriend in 2021 and moved to the United States, where he became a lawyer.
The five unmarried princesses, including Aiko and her 31-year-old cousin Kako, can now choose whether to remain members of the royal family after marriage.
The change is intended to prevent women from leaving the royal family by allowing them to continue their work and help carry out official duties as the imperial dynasty ages and declines.
However, experts say the effect will be limited because the law does not grant royal status to their future husbands and children.
Prohibiting the granting of royal status to husbands and children is an explicit attempt to prevent succession through the maternal line, said Hideya Kawanishi, a professor at Nagoya University and an expert on the monarchy.

A new book by the Accademia della Crusca was presented in Warsaw
Italy

18:10:02 KST

The Italian Ambassador to Poland, Luca Franchetti Pardo, presided yesterday over the presentation of the Accademia della Crusca’s book *Lingua gentile, lingua geniale: ideare, progettare, creare con l’italiano* (A Gentle Language, A Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Planning, Creating with Italian), hosted by the Italian Cultural Institute in Warsaw as part of the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World. The event, introduced by the Institute’s acting director, Ilaria Taddeo, featured presentations by Elżbieta Jamrozik, a professor at the University of Warsaw and a foreign corresponding member of the Accademia della Crusca, and Rita Librandi, professor emerita at the University of Naples “L’Orientale” and vice president of the Accademia. The ambassador thanked the speakers for their contribution to the knowledge and dissemination of Italian, emphasizing the Accademia della Crusca’s role in the study and promotion of our language. The book presented, edited by Annalisa Nesi and Raffaella Setti and produced by the Academy in collaboration with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, explores the relationship between language, kindness, and creativity. Through essays dedicated, among other topics, to Leonardo, Galileo, literature, music, cinema, and fashion, it highlights the variety of fields in which the Italian language accompanies the development and transmission of knowledge. This relationship is at the heart of Italian Language Week in the World, scheduled for October 19–25 under the High Patronage of the President of the Republic and dedicated this year to the theme “A Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Designing, and Creating with Italian.” In his remarks, Franchetti Pardo highlighted the link between language promotion, innovation, and Italy’s international presence. “The success of ‘Made in Italy’ is based not only on the quality of its products but also on a heritage of knowledge, sensibility, and traditions that the language helps to express and transmit,” the ambassador observed, highlighting how the spread of Italian fosters a more comprehensive understanding of the skills and excellence of contemporary Italy. According to the diplomat, the creative dimension goes hand in hand with that of dialogue, making language promotion a fundamental component of cultural diplomacy. “Language is not merely a tool for communication: it is a gateway to a culture, a means of understanding a country from within, and an opportunity to build relationships that can stand the test of time,” emphasized Franchetti Pardo, highlighting Italian’s ability to bring people together and foster mutual understanding.

NAIROBI, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Kenyan authorities on Saturday continued to search for seven people still missing after a multi-story building collapsed in a suburb of Nairobi on Friday.
"Search and rescue operations are ongoing at the site of the building collapse in Eastleigh. Two injured people have been taken to Kenyatta National Hospital," the Kenya Red Cross Society said in an update issued late Friday.
Onesimus Kipchumba Murkomen, cabinet secretary for the Ministry of Interior and National Administration, said Friday night that 11 shops on the building's ground floor and in the basement were occupied at the time of the collapse.
"Seven people have been reported missing. The rescue team has made contact with some of them, and efforts are underway to rescue those trapped in the rubble," he said.
All 67 construction workers at the site have been accounted for, Murkomen said, adding that 66 escaped unhurt, while one was hospitalized and is in stable condition.
The seven missing people are believed to have been inside the shops when the building collapsed, he said.
Authorities have yet to determine whether the collapse damaged or compromised the structural integrity of adjacent buildings.
Investigations are underway to establish whether any regulatory or professional violations contributed to the collapse, and local authorities have launched a manhunt for the building's owner. The National Construction Authority said it has identified the developer, contractor and registered professionals associated with the building.
"Details regarding rescue operations, the status of the site, and actions being undertaken by the multi-agency team will be shared in due course," the regulatory body said.
Building collapses have occurred repeatedly in Kenya in recent years, with experts blaming weak enforcement of construction regulations and a lack of routine safety inspections by government officials as among the causes. ■

KAMPALA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Uganda has barred travelers with a history of travel to neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) from transiting through the country to prevent the spread of Ebola, the Health Ministry said Friday.
The move followed a case involving a traveler suspected of having a travel history to the DRC, where Ebola is spreading rapidly, said the ministry in a statement. The traveler transited through Uganda and tested positive upon arrival in Nigeria.
Another traveler with travel history to the DRC also transited through Uganda and turned positive when he reached Kenya in early October.
Under the new measures, all travelers regardless of origin must complete locator forms to facilitate contact tracing, where necessary, the ministry said.
Infection and control measures have been strengthened at all entry and exit points and health facilities, while nationwide surveillance continues, it said.
The ministry warned that people entering Uganda through unauthorized routes would face prosecution for violating public health requirements.
"The ministry requests communities to remain vigilant and report suspected unauthorized border crossings to the relevant authorities to facilitate screening and necessary public health follow-up," the statement said.
It also noted that Uganda remains Ebola-free.
Uganda reported 20 confirmed cases, including two deaths, before the end of the outbreak was officially recognized by the World Health Organization and the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Aug. 27, after 42 consecutive days without a new confirmed case. ■

Expert warns of complex ecological fallout from Mongolia grassland fire linked to Japanese company
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:06:24 CST
18:06:24 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- A large grassland fire in Mongolia reportedly linked to activities by a Japanese company's subsidiary may have caused extensive ecological damage, with its broader environmental impact requiring comprehensive assessment, an expert said.
The fire broke out on Oct. 8 in the Numrug Strictly Protected Area in Mongolia's eastern province of Dornod. The flames were extinguished on Oct. 16, according to Mongolian media reports. Japanese telecommunications operator KDDI said on Oct. 20 that the fire was linked to activities by its Mongolian subsidiary Mobicom.
The fire may have affected not only grasslands but also riverbanks, wetlands and other ecosystems, said Wang Qinxue, a researcher at Japan's National Institute for Environmental Studies who has long studied the region's ecological environment.
A comprehensive assessment is needed to determine whether soil conditions can recover alongside vegetation, whether wildlife can safely survive the winter and whether the fire has caused any transboundary environmental pollution, Wang said.
Preliminary data released by Mongolia's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change showed that the fire had burned about 530,000 hectares of land, including approximately 470,000 hectares within the Numrug Strictly Protected Area, accounting for 79.8 percent of the reserve's total area.
Located in eastern Mongolia near the Chinese border, the reserve features a mix of grasslands, forests, rivers and wetlands. It provides habitats for a variety of wildlife and plays an important role in conserving local biodiversity, Wang said.
Even if vegetation regrows the following year, plant species composition and soil conditions may not recover at the same pace, he said.
Assessing damage to forest ecosystems is particularly complex, requiring an examination of tree survival rates, the availability of seed sources and the growth of new seedlings to determine the extent of damage and the potential for recovery, Wang added.
The fire's potential transboundary ecological effects also warrant further investigation. It remains necessary to determine whether ash and sediment could be carried into rivers and wetlands by surface runoff and whether smoke from the fire had crossed national borders through the atmosphere, Wang said.
Citing research on Mongolia's Dornod Province, Wang said fire occurrence from autumn through the following spring was associated with the number of dust storm days in spring.
Reduced vegetation cover after a fire leaves soil more vulnerable to wind erosion and makes surface materials easier to transport by wind, he said.
Wang called for systematic surveys of the burned areas, categorized by ecosystem type, to scientifically assess the actual damage and determine the scope for ecological recovery. ■

Thirty-three Royal Navy warships have been taken out of operational service since 2010, of which eight have been sold, fifteen recycled and ten are still waiting to be disposed of, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, had asked how many warships had been taken out of service, sold or scrapped in each year since 2010.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Since 2010, 33 Royal Navy warships have been taken out of operational service. Of these, 8 have been sold, 15 have been recycled and 10 are pending disposal.
“As vessels may be withdrawn from service in one year and sold or scrapped in a later year, these categories are not mutually exclusive, and the figures should not be aggregated.
“As set out in the Defence Investment Plan, this Government is investing in new frigates, amphibious ships, new submarines and new standardised vessels alongside a new Hybrid Navy of uncrewed and autonomous systems to increase our Navy’s lethality and deterrence.”
Thirteen new frigates are being built across two classes, eight Type 26 anti-submarine ships on the Clyde and five Type 31 general purpose ships at Rosyth, and Norway has since selected the Type 26 design for its own fleet. Three Fleet Solid Support ships are under construction to resupply the carrier groups, new transport ships are planned to take over from the amphibious and Bay class vessels. The submarine service is completing the Astute class before moving to the four Dreadnought ballistic missile boats and then to SSN-AUKUS attack submarines, which ministers have said will be delivered at a rate of one every eighteen months from the mid-2030s.
The period covered includes the retirement of the Type 42 destroyers, the progressive withdrawal of the Type 23 frigates, and the decision to dispose of the amphibious assault ships Albion and Bulwark, the latter of which is being sold to Brazil.

Inside the Supermassive Debate Over the James Webb Telescope’s ‘Little Red Dots’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
Astronomers built the James Webb Space Telescope to pick up faint light from the first billion years after the Big Bang, a chaotic era when vast swaths of hydrogen and helium gas gathered into the chains of galaxies we see today. Even in the telescope’s first images, astronomers could see a whole zoo of mysterious smears of light.
One batch of objects proved especially difficult to interpret. They glowed blindingly bright, emitting red light with long wavelengths and shining as brilliantly as a whole galaxy. They were tiny, spanning just a pixel. And they were everywhere. A couple appear in almost every image Webb takes. In 2023, researchers started calling them “little red dots.” Astronomers have repeatedly pointed Webb toward the little red dots, wringing precious new information from these pixels of light.
Initially, researchers thought the dots looked kind of like galaxies. Later, they concluded that little red dots look more like the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of most galaxies. These monstrous masses are themselves dark, but their formidable gravity violently vacuums up gas and other nearby matter, generating rings of hot, swirling detritus that completely outshine the stars around them.
Then, in the spring of 2025, two teams of astronomers simultaneously announced observations of a pair of little red dots that were unlike all the rest. In fact, they were unlike any object ever seen.
“In all the millions of [observations] we’ve taken with ground-based telescopes,” said Anna de Graaff, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Heidelberg, Germany, and head of one group, “there’s nothing that looks like these sources.”
The two teams of astronomers propose that they are looking at a new astronomical object: a topsy-turvy lump of hydrogen that shines with the light of billions of suns while hiding a black hole deep in its core. They call it a “black hole star.”
In a paper posted in September, astronomers took this analysis a step further. They argued that the Webb telescope is witnessing the births of supermassive black holes inside the cores of colossal stars. “There is a fundamentally new phenomenon afoot,” said Rohan Naidu, an astronomer at the University of Hawai’i.
But not everyone agrees with this bold interpretation. It has sparked a flurry of follow-up research and reignited a fierce debate over the nature of these peculiar pinpricks of light. “The field has gotten very polarized,” said Anna-Christina Eilers, an astrophysicist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who studies little red dots.
When all you can see is a speck, it’s hard to tell what you’re looking at. All you know about it is its color and brightness. Astronomers first argued that little red dots were distant galaxies on the cosmic horizon, mainly because of their brightness. But galaxies that bright would have to be huge—and there was no known way for them to grow so big in just hundreds of millions of years. Astronomers dubbed them “universe breakers” for the way they seemed to demolish the standard cosmic timeline.
Then they took a closer look. De Graaff led one survey, called Red Unknowns: Bright Infrared Extragalactic Survey (Rubies), and Naidu co-led another survey, called Mirage or Miracle (MOM). These were two of a wave of surveys that trained the Webb telescope on distant objects, including little red dots, for hours at a time. They tabulated precisely what shades of light were coming from each dot and how bright the shades were. This detailed color breakdown, known as a spectrum, told astronomers a far more detailed story than the initial observations had. Different atoms shine in subtly different hues, so the spectrum provided a sense of what the object’s particles were doing.
The bombshell discovery in the little-red-dot spectra was that the colors of hydrogen were smeared out across multiple shades. Usually, seeing such an effect means you’re looking straight at an exposed black hole. Black holes whip hydrogen clouds around them at furious rates, with the clouds emitting slightly different colors depending on their speed. The net effect is that instead of seeing just the hue of hydrogen, you see a range of colors called a broad line. The wider this range, the faster the fastest hydrogen clouds are flying—and the more massive the black hole.
Many astronomers concluded that big black holes dotted the universe, washing out the light of the stars in their host galaxies. As black holes, the little red dots would appear red because dust—grainy stuff much more complicated than gas—was blocking their blue light.
Yet they still seemed weird. Most supermassive black holes flicker as they gulp down chunky streams of gas around them. They also beam powerful x-rays across the universe. Most little red dots seemed to be doing neither of these things.
But that didn’t trouble astronomers much; they expected to see some strangeness during the pandemonium of the early universe. And at least the black holes weren’t breaking any cosmological theories.
Then, in the spring of 2025, de Graaff’s and Naidu’s teams unveiled the two strangest dots yet.
What made these two little red dots exceptional was how red they were. Webb picked up almost no light in the bluer hues of their spectra. And at a particular shade of red, the colors abruptly got much, much brighter. This feature, known as a Balmer break, is something you see when looking at a hot ball of hydrogen gas—typically, certain types of stars or galaxies, which are made of many stars. Deep in a star’s core, nuclear fusion pumps out heat and light, which slowly filters up to the star’s surface. There, hydrogen atoms can become energized in a way that blocks bluer light and lets through only redder light. These red colors have a hump-shaped spectrum that reveals the overall temperature of the star’s surface.
But the new little red dots couldn’t literally be stars—they were way too bright. And they didn’t look much like black holes either. Black holes have an assortment of ringlike structures of different temperatures. They don’t typically produce a Balmer break, or the red, hump-shaped curve indicative of a stellar surface burning at a uniform 5,000 or so degrees Kelvin.
Naidu and de Graaff concluded that they were looking at the first examples of something combining the vigor of a black hole with the outward appearance of a star: a black hole star.
From the outside, a black hole star would appear as a huge agglomeration of hydrogen gas. If our sun were replaced with a black hole star, it would extend a dozen times farther than the orbit of Pluto. Out toward the edge, the star would boil unstably, sloughing off outer layers and explosively ejecting mass. “It’s going to be a very messy system where stuff is being blown out and falling back in,” de Graaff said. “I wouldn’t want to come too close.”
Deep in the center, invisible to the outside world, the star would be powered by a black hole. This black hole would pull gas around it, dramatically heating it and pushing light and energy outward, which would keep the outer layers of hydrogen from collapsing inward. In this way, the black hole would form the “engine” of the star, analogous to the fusion-powered core of our sun. Moving outward, material swirling around the black hole would beam out a range of colors that would slowly make their way toward the surface.
And as with certain stars, the hydrogen near the surface would stop the bluer light while letting the redder light pass through. The end result would be a gassy surface shining as brightly as a more exposed black hole but with the Balmer break and smooth red hump of a 5,000-kelvin star, de Graaff and Naidu theorized. As a bonus, the gas “cocoon” would also block x-rays, and the gas wouldn’t flicker much—which would explain two mysteries surrounding other little red dots.
But what about the broad lines, supposedly caused by hydrogen swirling fast around a black hole? Another group provided a possible explanation.
That group, which included Vadim Rusakov, an astronomer at the University of Manchester, had been scrutinizing the broad lines of the best-observed little red dots. Broad lines take the shape of a sharp mountain peak. But Rusakov and collaborators noticed that in many cases, these mountains sloped slightly more gently than would be expected if they came from fast-moving gas around a black hole. So they suggested that instead of coming from rotating gas, much of the spread of the hydrogen colors could come from light scattering off electrons.
They digitally removed the effect of this electron-induced smudging from their data, Rusakov said. After that, the broad lines stopped looking quite so broad and started looking more like light passing through a sluggishly churning shell of hydrogen gas in a particular state, similar to what you’d expect to see from a black hole star. The three teams—de Graaff’s, Naidu’s, and Rusakov’s — posted their findings on March 20, 2025—“black hole star date,” as some of the researchers called it.
Black hole stars could represent a new stage in the development of a supermassive black hole: First, a black hole would form in the center of a shell of hydrogen, together with a baby galaxy of normal stars around it. Then, over time, the black hole would eat its way out of its cocoon, gaining mass as it cleared the hydrogen gas away.
“We are seeing the seed,” Naidu said. “This is the birth of potentially every massive black hole in the universe.”
The black hole star enthusiasts appeal to Occam’s razor, arguing that their theory gives the simplest accounting of these two little red dots, and perhaps of little red dots in general. But simple is subjective, and astronomers have spent the last year in a lively debate about what’s really going on.
Even years after the discovery of the first little red dot, not much about them is settled. Dale Kocevski, an astrophysicist at Colby College, recalls leading a discussion about them at an April 2026 conference in Aspen, Colorado. He started by recapping what he hoped would be an uncontroversial idea about their trace amounts of blue light. “The group erupted into argument, and we couldn’t even get past the first bullet point,” he said.
Many astronomers still argue that little red dots are traditional black holes—even the new duo. “The data is really compelling,” said Roberto Maiolino of the University of Cambridge. “I’m a little bit more dubious about the interpretation.”
For each point in favor of black hole stars, Maiolino fires off a quick rebuttal. The lack of flicker? In the early universe, black holes may have had a steadier food supply and may therefore have been tidier eaters. The lack of x-rays? Standard galactic black holes are ringed by a thick doughnut of gas and dust, which can block most x-rays. He sees no reason to suspect the little red dots of being anything other than standard supermassive black holes.
The redness of the new objects is striking, he said, and he agrees that it means there must be a ton of gas between the black hole and us. But that gas could come in the form of the doughnut, or as puffy clouds that fill in patches of the black hole’s sky, as opposed to the shell of gas around a black hole star. Maiolino agrees that electron scattering likely contributes to broadening the lines in the spectra of some of the little red dots. But electron scattering also smears hydrogen lines from supermassive black holes, he said.
Maiolino and his collaborator, Piero Madau of the University of California, Santa Cruz, argue that the redness of the dots comes mainly from the angle at which we see them. The reddest dots are those that we happen to see edge on, their gassy doughnuts blocking our view. Webb also sees some “little blue dots.” These could be the same exposed black holes, viewed top-down, Maiolino and Madau pointed out in spring 2026. They also appeal to Occam’s razor—in this case arguing that black holes are a simpler explanation for little dots of all colors.
At this stage either theory—black hole or black hole star—could match what the Webb telescope has seen. “I don’t think that there is a compelling reason to prefer one or the other,” said Mauro Giavalisco, an astronomer at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, who has spent much of his career interpreting the spectra of distant galaxies.
To test their interpretations, astronomers need a clearer picture of how black hole stars might form and how exactly they expect them to look.
Over the last few years, Mitchell Begelman has been teaching a graduate student seminar on little red dots at the University of Colorado, Boulder. It’s kept him reading the firehose of papers coming out on the subject. In these mysterious objects that weren’t quite stars and weren’t quite black holes, he recognized a ghost from his past: the quasi-star. “Suddenly the switch flipped, and I realized that this is what quasi-stars should look like,” Begelman said.
Begelman had proposed the existence of quasi-stars back in 2006, along with Marta Volonteri and Martin Rees, to explain observations of what looked like impossibly massive black holes. Their quasi-star theory offers one way to make a black hole star: The core of a vast gas cloud collapses to directly form a black hole, gathering the remainder of the cloud around it.
In 2025, Begelman and his collaborator Jason Dexter applied the quasi-star model to the little red dots. They estimated that quasi-stars could quickly assemble themselves in a few million years before settling into a more mature form that would look just like little red dots. They would do this for tens of millions of years—lasting long enough for Webb to spot them.
In 2026, Giavalisco worked with a team to flesh out the quasi-star model as an origin for black hole stars, which he finds to be a natural way of explaining how little red dots could mask the signs of a feeding black hole. He points out that our sun performs the same trick, hiding its explosive fusion, just on a much smaller scale. “We have billions and billions of hydrogen bombs exploding every second, and yet we see none of them,” he said.
Giavalisco and his collaborators found that their new model of a quasi-star fit the spectra of de Graaf’s and Naidu’s objects even better than the initial models had. He thinks the quasi-star theory is a plausible explanation for the little red dots but remains open to other ideas. “I just want to know the truth,” he said.
In the meantime, researchers are starting to search for another distinguishing pattern: If little red dots are black hole stars formed in the early universe, then they should grow rarer over time as they each break free from their shells and reveal their inner black holes.
In an August 2026 census of both red and blue dots broken up into different eras, Kocevski of Colby College and his collaborators found exactly that pattern. In the data, as the universe approaches 2 billion to 3 billion years of age, the little red dots seem to vanish—preliminary evidence that little red dots, as black hole stars, might really be a puberty-like phase for many supermassive black holes.
Theorists are already working out what that puberty-like phase might be like. In another analysis, posted on September 8, Naidu, de Graaff, Eilers, and their collaborators tested out an assortment of techniques for deducing the mass of a black hole “seed” inside a black hole star. These hidden black holes seemed to be far less massive than standard, exposed black holes. The scientists propose that Webb is catching supermassive black hole stars—up to 1 million times the mass of the sun—in the act of incubating the universe’s first big black holes.
Some researchers, including Kocevski, still aren’t sure. Kocevski suspects that the universe is a messy place, and that some little red dots are truly as starlike as the black hole star camp is arguing. Others, he thinks, will be more like standard black holes, as the other camp argues. “I have a sneaking suspicion that we’re both right,” he said.

Seven projects by RIBA award-winning Nakshabid Architects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24

18:00:00 KST

Seven projects by RIBA award-winning Nakshabid Architects
Who is RIBA International Prize winner Nakshabid Architects? In this roundup, we get to know the Dhaka-based studio through seven of its key projects spanning Bangladesh.
Founded by Bayejid Khondoker in 2003, Nakshabid Architects’ extensive portfolio is concentrated in Bangladesh and encompasses both public and private projects – from residential blocks to mosques and museums.
Last week saw the studio’s Green Field Factory named the fifth winner of the biennial award, presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) to the world’s best new building outside the UK.
Praised for its focus on passive design principles and the prioritisation of employee wellbeing, the studio considers its latest award to be a recognition of Bangladesh’s architectural contributions at a global scale.
“We see the prize as a recognition of what architecture from Bangladesh can contribute to global conversations on climate and the dignity of labour,” the studio told Dezeen.
Alongside the award-winning Green Field Factory, recent projects undertaken by the 20-person studio include the government-commissioned renovation of the Bangladesh Military Museum in Dhaka, which reached completion in 2022 with a glass geodesic dome.
Central to its architectural approach, the studio said, is forging connections between a building and its “socio-ecological context” in a bid to reframe functional programmes as places of gathering.
“We believe that architecture must respond directly to its socio-ecological context, transforming ordinary programmes into meaningful collective experiences,” the studio said.
“We approach every project as a shared undertaking, listening closely to the people who will use it, the climate it sits in and the building traditions around it before we draw,” it continued.
“In this way even the most functional programmes become places of gathering, where light, air, landscape and everyday social life are woven into the architecture itself.”
Read on for a look at seven of the studio’s key projects:
Green Field Factory, Rangpur, 2017
The Green Field Factory, a rug factory in Rangpur, was designed by Nakshabid Architects to dismantle workplace hierarchies and is the fifth winner of the RIBA International Prize.
Fronted by a monumental green facade, the seven-storey building was informed by the traditional Bengali home, incorporating natural ventilation and biophilic design principles.
Aman Mosque, Narayanganj, 2018
A pair of intersecting arches form an “invisible dome” that frames the interior of Aman Mosque, a cubic prayer hall completed by the studio in Narayanganj.
Set within a sunken circular courtyard, the mosque is defined by its solid concrete volume, which is adorned with triangular perforations that filter light into the space.
Shaptak Insignia, Dhaka, 2021
A concrete facade punctuated with square openings was designed to limit heat gain and control daylight access at the Shaptak Insignia apartment tower in Dhaka.
Comprising two blocks, the residential block contains 18 units on a 670-square-metre plot, with each apartment complete with a balcony and a stepped terrace.
Urban Legacy, Dhaka, 2021
A pair of slender, red-brick residential towers make up the studio’s Urban Legacy project in Dhaka.
Its jagged form is defined by cantilevered balconies, which are enclosed by horizontal louvres and complete with greenery intended to shade and cool the apartment interiors.
“Cascading vines and planters spill from every terrace and the brick-walled garden base, turning the building into a vertical green landscape,” the studio said.
Aman Cement Factory Mosque, Sirajganj, 2022
An arched entrance guides visitors beyond the tiered brick exterior of the Ullapara Mosque, which Nakshabid Architects completed on the grounds of a cement factory for its workers.
Spread across two storeys, the mosque was built using locally-sourced brick, concrete and glass in a bid to blend “tradition with modernity”.
“[The mosque] has become a place where factory workers and neighbours gather for prayer, social events and community life,” the studio said.
Bangladesh Military Museum, Dhaka, 2022
Looking to redefine museum culture in Bangladesh, Nakshabid Architects conceptualised its design for the Bangladesh Military Museum in Dhaka as a “vibrant civic destination”.
Its curving concrete structure contains cafes, galleries, an amphitheatre and an arena, which is sheltered by a 120-feet glass geodesic dome.
Nurpur Graveyard, Rangpur, 2023
Nakshabid Architects intended for the Nurpur Graveyard, a Muslim graveyard in Rangpur, to also offer a place of leisure for the local community.
To do this, the site accommodates a healthcare facility and an education space – or madrasa – with future expansions expected to include a mosque.
“Nurpur Graveyard is a place that diminishes the typical boundaries of graveyards,” the studio said.

New York Archdiocese close to settling sexual abuse claims for over US$800 million

New York Archdiocese close to settling sexual abuse claims for over US$800 million
Maya King and Jeffery C Mays
- The New York Archdiocese is close to a settlement worth more than US$800 million for 1,300 sexual abuse claims, after years of legal pressure and fears of bankruptcy.
- Plaintiffs’ lawyers said all survivors signed the revised deal, though the archdiocese said, “We are not quite there yet,” and a few holdouts delayed final approval.
- The deal would offer at least US$250,000 per person, add US$20 million for holdouts, and force the archdiocese to publish names of credibly accused clergy and lay leaders.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The Archdiocese of New York and plaintiffs’ lawyers were closing in on a settlement on Oct 23 in which the Church would pay more than US$800 million (S$1 billion) to settle claims from 1,300 people who said they had been sexually abused by its clergy members and lay leaders.
The plaintiffs’ lawyers said that they had finalised the settlement with the archdiocese and that all of the plaintiffs had signed off on it.
But Joseph Zwilling, a spokesperson for the archdiocese, said in an interview on the night of Oct 24 that the parties were still working to finalise the agreement.
“We are not quite there yet,” he said.
Terms of the settlement would call for each plaintiff to have the option of receiving a lump-sum payment of at least US$250,000, or a potentially larger payout after a review of the extent of the abuse each plaintiff has claimed, according to the plaintiffs’ lawyers.
The proposal would end a multi-year saga that threatened to bankrupt the United States’ foremost Roman Catholic archdiocese.
The terms of the proposed settlement required that all 1,300 plaintiffs accept it, and there were some holdouts, who argued that the proposal did not do enough to rectify the harms they had experienced. Progress was also stymied by the deaths of some plaintiffs.
“Tonight, we were able to finalise the settlement with the Archdiocese,” Trusha Goffe, an attorney with Jeff Anderson & Associates, wrote on Oct 23 in an e-mail to the firm’s nearly 300 clients who say they were abused.
“All of the survivors agreed to the revised deal. This means that the settlement you agreed to will move forward.”
Lawyers for the plaintiffs said they had repeatedly warned their clients that if they did not accept the proposal, the archdiocese would most likely declare bankruptcy, reducing the size of any eventual payout and extending the length of the already years-long litigation.
To appease the handful of plaintiffs who were resistant to the proposal, the lawyers said, the archdiocese negotiated with one of its insurers to increase the amount of money it would pay the holdouts.
They would now receive a pot of US$20 million to be evenly distributed among them – an uncommon arrangement that hinged largely on the availability of insurance funds.
“The survivors showed an amazing amount of perseverance and patience here,” said Paul Mones, a veteran lawyer whose Los Angeles-based firm represents 33 of the plaintiffs against the archdiocese.
“After a lifetime of pain and struggle, they mustered the energy to push that final mile. And hopefully this deal will give them a degree of solace and healing.”
The Archdiocese of New York, which includes Manhattan, the Bronx, Staten Island and a handful of Hudson Valley communities, would be the latest Catholic institution to pay hundreds of millions of dollars to settle claims of sexual abuse.
In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to pay US$395 million to settle claims from more than 530 people who said clergy members and lay leaders had abused them.
In 2024, the Archdiocese of Los Angeles settled similar claims for more than US$1 billion – one of the largest sexual abuse settlements in church history.
The agreement with the New York Archdiocese also requires it to publish on its website the names of the clergy members and lay leaders who were credibly accused of sexual abuse, and to keep that list updated with any future substantiated claims of abuse.
The accusers and their lawyers said they thought these requirements would not only illuminate past abuses, but also help to prevent future ones. It is unclear what disclosures, if any, the archdiocese would have faced if it had declared bankruptcy.
In her e-mail, Goffe said she would have more details about the settlement process in the next two weeks but wanted to emphasise “what an achievement” the agreement represents. NYTIMES

Data protection officer launches investigation into cyber attack
Following the cyberattack on PK Softech, a software provider for several Swiss pension funds, the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner has launched a formal investigation.
Where there are indications of a possible breach of data protection regulations, the investigation is directed against that company, according to a statement issued today by the commissioner.
PK Softech informed the Federal Data Protection Commissioner on October 8, 2026 of the cyberattack on its IT infrastructure and of possible data security breaches. During the cyberattack, data was stolen from several pension funds to which the company provided software solutions.
As has been known for several days, the Federal Pension Fund Publica is among the organisations affected. The Bernese Pension Fund (BPK) and the Bernese Teachers’ Insurance Fund (BLVK) have also been affected by the attack.

Staff data stolen in cyberattack on Swiss public broadcaster
Consequently, the pension funds concerned have also lodged a complaint over the matter, as has since been reported. On October 14, the Federal Data Protection Commissioner launched an informal preliminary investigation at Publica and, yesterday, finally opened a formal investigation into PK Softech.
The commissioner expects this investigation to provide a comprehensive overview of the personal data that the pension funds concerned made available to the software company. Furthermore, the legal framework governing such data transfers and their actual implementation, as well as the extent of the information stolen, still need to be clarified, it is further stated.

How the Swiss cowbell became political
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

How the Swiss cowbell became political
The Brügger family has been forging bells and cowbells for three generations. But since the Covid pandemic, the objects closely associated with the Swiss rural imagination have also become instruments of protest. This is a problematic appropriation, according to an ethnologist.
You sense the Brügger foundry before you see it: first in your ears, then in your nose. As soon as you get off the bus in Villars-sur-Glâne, a village on the outskirts of Fribourg, you hear the sound of a hammer striking sheet metal. Then, as you step through the door, you’re hit by a smell of smoke, coal and red-hot metal. Alexis Brügger is there to shake your hand. A 26-year-old with powerful arms and a ready laugh. Following the death of his father in 2019, and his grandfather a few months later, he took over the workshop that has been making bells and cowbells for three generations.
“There’s no apprenticeship for this trade,” emphasises Alexis, who immediately addresses us informally. “You learn this craft by forging.” And so, at the age of 22, he gave up his job as a tiler to carry on – initially with his brother Arnaud – the family tradition started some 50 years earlier by his grandfather Marius.
“I had no experience whatsoever,” he says. “My older brother, on the other hand, had worked for about five years with our dad. But he hadn’t learnt how to cast bells. I spent quite a few weekends practising and it took me six months before I managed to make one. A few even flew through the air it was so infuriating,” he laughs.
For a long time, everything he made ended up in the bin, especially the cowbells. But he was able to remelt the bells and reuse the bronze. “It was a long process that required a great deal of patience,” he recalls. “And it did me good because patience isn’t exactly my strong point. This craft has forced me to work on myself as well.”
Today, Alexis knows his trade inside out and has become an expert craftsman. Yet, standing at the forge, he continues to experiment in his constant quest for excellence. “I haven’t finished learning yet,” he says. “There are no shortcuts to perfection: it takes years of experience.”
Four thousand hammer blows
The foundry also tells another story. That of hard, gruelling work that leaves beads of sweat on Alexis’s brow. It takes around 4,000 hammer blows to shape a single cowbell. After being heated in the forge to around 700°C, the sheet of steel is removed with tongs and hammered onto the concave anvil. When it can no longer be shaped, the sheet is returned to the fire. This process is repeated about ten times.
Forging is just one of the many stages in the process. The metal must be brazed, imperfections smoothed out, the two halves welded together, the supports for the clapper and the leather collar fitted, sandblasted, coloured and many other tasks that we won’t list here.
“It takes me about a day to make a cowbell,” says Alexis. “No two are alike because each piece is made entirely by hand.” This is the Paul Morier brand from Morges, a prestigious name taken over by his grandfather Marius. It is a name associated with quality and authenticity, appreciated by herders’ associations, organisers of major folk festivals and players of large cowbells.
>>> A visit to the Brügger foundry:
Political connotation
Once it leaves the foundry, the cowbell can take on different meanings. Its sound can evoke bucolic landscapes, grazing cows and Alpine traditions. In recent years, however, it has taken on a different connotation.
During the pandemic, as part of demonstrations against health measures, the marches of the Freiheitstrychler (freedom bell-ringers – Trychel means cowbell in Swiss German) transformed that chime into a voice of protest, giving a political dimension to an object linked to the rural world.
“The cowbell is neither conservative nor progressive,” emphasises Konrad Kuhn. The expert in popular culture and ethnologist is a lecturer at the University of Basel and an associate professor at the University of Innsbruck in Austria. Kuhn points out that it is, above all, the context that determines its meaning.
“There’s a marked difference between ringing a cowbell to cheer on the national football team and ringing it during a protest march,” he says. Or whether its toll accompanies a local custom, such as the one practised in the Haslital, in the Bernese Oberland, where cowbell ringers drive away evil spirits between Christmas and New Year, or at the Chalandamarz, the custom of bidding farewell to winter in the Engadine, in canton Graubünden. “In these cases, the processions never have a political connotation,” he says.
Kuhn points out that although agriculture has lost some of its economic importance, many of its artefacts continue to hold strong symbolic value.
“In Switzerland, the Swiss People’s Party is seeking to strengthen its ties with the agricultural sector by exploiting its symbols for political ends,” he says, pointing out that, unlike a trade mark, a tradition is not protected.
“In the early 1990s, during the campaign against Switzerland’s accession to the European Economic Area, Christoph Blocher marched at the head of groups of people ringing large cowbells,” Kuhn says. “It would be interesting to see a procession of Trychler marching at a Green Party conference. That would prove that the sound does not convey any political message.”
Traditions belong to everyone
“Traditions evolve,” Kuhn emphasises. “The sound of a cowbell has remained the same over the centuries, but what has changed is the meaning we associate with that ringing. The important thing is not to reduce these symbols to a purely political interpretation.”
According to the ethnologist, this is precisely what happened during the pandemic, when a cultural practice was used to support a very specific stance.
Kuhn regards this appropriation as problematic because it draws a line between those who share that message and those who simply wish to perpetuate a custom.
“Cultural practices belong to everyone and should remain open and inclusive,” Kuhn says. “When they become tools for division, the problem is not merely political. If associated with a protest movement, a tradition risks losing its appeal and, over time, becoming weakened.”
Swiss wrestling, or Schwingen, which enjoys great popularity in German-speaking Switzerland, has taken the opposite approach. “In the past, this sport was reserved almost exclusively for those with Swiss roots going back generations,” Kuhn says. “In recent years, it has opened up to other athletes with a migrant background, making it more appealing.”
It is a process that Kuhn hopes will be replicated in the world of cowbell ringers, thereby freeing them from the label that certain groups have pinned on them.
Politics aside, cowbells remain popular
For the time being, cowbells continue to enjoy great popularity. At the Brügger foundry in Villars-sur-Glâne there is no shortage of work. Alexis is happy about this, despite the heat, the dust, the noise and the long days spent in the workshop.
“I knew from childhood that I would do this job,” says the young man with hands blackened by coal dust. “I don’t want to talk about a calling, but certainly about a great passion passed on to me by my dad.”
It was, however, his father who advised him to learn another trade – that of a tiler. “There are no certainties, and life can play nasty tricks,” he says. Words that, following his father’s sudden death, have taken on a special meaning for him.
As he speaks, Alexis watches out of the corner of his eye the sheet metal he’s left in the forge. When it reaches the right colour, he grips it with tongs, places it on the concave anvil and starts hammering again. He was taught that the more blows the sheet metal receives, the better the sound of the cowbell. Whether this is really the case or merely part of the trade’s folklore, even he doesn’t know for certain. But he carries on doing it. One blow after another. And the hammering follows us even as we leave the foundry.
Edited by Daniele Mariani. Translated from Italian, sub-edited by Thomas Stephens

The ministry advised Israelis to avoid demonstrations, protests, and large gatherings, even when they appear peaceful, warning that such events could escalate suddenly. Luxury stores in France board windows, increase security ahead of fresh protests
Luxury boutiques in France boarded up their normally glitzy windows and added guards ahead of fresh protests on Saturday, with some planning to stay closed after rioters looted shops across the country last weekend.
France, the most visited country in the world, draws large numbers of overseas shoppers seeking Chanel handbags and Hermes scarves, an important source of revenue for brands facing slowing demand.
But some decided staying open was too risky after last week's events, when rioters smashed and looted hundreds of shops in Paris, Marseille, and Bordeaux.
A Rolex retailer and a De Beers store near the capital's famous Place Vendome will remain closed on Saturday, staff said, while managers at stores including Richemont-owned IWC Schaffhausen said they would decide whether to close early depending on the intensity of the protests.
Groups including France's main student union UNEF and the Yellow Vest group, which emerged as a potent anti-establishment movement in 2018, plan to march through central Paris later on Saturday to protest against high living costs and cuts to public services.
Brands increase private security alongside additional police presence
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Friday that his ministry would deploy 70,000 police officers, backed by specialist units, to prevent the violence that occurred last week.
But staff at LVMH brands Louis Vuitton, Dior and Bulgari said they weren't taking any chances and security at their stores near Place Vendome had been increased for the day. Additional private security to supplement the police presence in the neighborhood is also planned.
Nearby department store Printemps also increased its security staff, carried out safety repairs and added security measures to reinforce shop windows and entrances, a spokesperson for the store said.
Hermès finance chief Eric du Halgouet said this week the company had increased security measures at its French stores, adding it was too early to say how much impact recent events would have on business.

Israel's opposition weighs minority coalition as Bennett, Liberman reject Arab support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:58:21 UTC
17:58:21 KST

Israel's anti-Netanyahu bloc is preparing for the possibility of forming a minority government after the upcoming elections, despite opposition from Avigdor Liberman and Naftali Bennett, while a broad agreement is emerging among the parties to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana even before a coalition deal is reached.
In most polls, the anti-Netanyahu camp holds an advantage over the outgoing coalition bloc, but the Zionist parties seeking political change fall short of the majority needed to form a government based on their current agreements.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies are far from securing a majority in many polls, although some surveys give the right-wing bloc enough seats to form a government. The electoral threshold could change the distribution of Knesset seats, and a relatively small number of votes could determine whether Israel forms a new government or enters another round of political turmoil.
There is broad agreement within the camp seeking to replace Netanyahu on the need for a change of government. The disagreement begins over how to form that government if the Zionist parties in the bloc fail to win a combined 61 seats.
Gadi Eisenkot wants to lead the bloc and become its main candidate for forming the next government. He firmly rejects the possibility of serving under Netanyahu, even in a rotation government, and has raised the possibility of establishing a minority government if the parties seeking political change secure 58 or 59 seats.
The idea is to swear in a government that wins a majority in a confidence vote, even without the permanent support of 61 MKs, and subsequently attempt to broaden its parliamentary base.
Eisenkot has made no secret of his ambition to achieve a much stronger electoral result, one that would allow him to form a Zionist government without relying on political actors outside his camp.
Relying on 58 or 59 seats, however, would require detailed agreements with his partners, particularly Bennett and Liberman, who oppose establishing a government dependent on the support or abstention of the Arab parties.
Eisenkot himself has not ruled out the possibility of outside support from Ra'am. In recent discussions and interviews, he has sought to project confidence that progress could be made in stages, but no agreed formula has yet been presented that would allow the plan to be implemented.
From a legal standpoint, swearing in a government does not require 61 votes in favor, but rather a majority in the confidence vote. Abstentions by MKs could allow a government to take office without an absolute majority.
By contrast, a constructive vote of no confidence, intended to replace an incumbent government, requires the support of 61 MKs for an alternative government.
Eisenkot's minority-government scenario could therefore be relevant during the process of forming a government, but it would not allow the anti-Netanyahu bloc to remove an incumbent Netanyahu government through a simple majority vote.
The political difficulty remains: Who would agree to serve in such a government, who would abstain in the vote, and how would the government survive after being sworn in?
Liberman rejects minority government, insists on Zionist majority
Avigdor Liberman categorically rejects this possibility. He has made clear that he would not support a minority government, even for a transitional period, and insists on a government backed by a Zionist majority.
A unity government with Netanyahu is also unacceptable to him. From his perspective, if a suitable majority cannot be found, another election would be preferable to establishing a government that fails to meet the conditions he has set.
Liberman has raised another possibility: bringing Likud MKs into a government without Netanyahu, or creating a Zionist majority through a change in the composition of the political blocs after the elections.
He has even claimed that some Likud MKs would be willing to take such a step. Liberman has not named them, and at this stage there are no public negotiations with Likud MKs about joining such a government.
Eisenkot wants to establish a government even with a partial majority and attempt to expand it later. Liberman is unwilling to join such a government and demands a Zionist majority from the moment it is formed.
Bennett and Yair Lapid, who head the Beyachad list, are also demanding a Zionist government and are unwilling to base its formation on the votes or abstentions of the Arab parties.
By contrast, Democrats chairman Yair Golan has not ruled out cooperation with Ra'am.
The disagreement among the party leaders could intensify when they are required to decide whether to support the swearing-in of a government that lacks a Zionist majority in the Knesset.
The meeting between Eisenkot and Liberman this week ended with a joint statement emphasizing the need to increase voter turnout. It did not resolve their disagreement over a minority government.
Internal competition for leadership also continues. Eisenkot wants to emerge from the elections as the leader of the largest party, believing such a result would strengthen his position during consultations at the President's Residence.
Bennett sees himself as a natural candidate to lead the anti-Netanyahu camp because of his experience as prime minister, while Liberman insists on withholding any commitment that could enable the formation of a government contrary to his positions.
Each party leader is seeking to increase his political strength, even though the transfer of Knesset seats between parties in the same camp does not necessarily increase the bloc's overall representation.
After the elections, they will also need to agree on the identity of the next prime minister, the composition of the coalition, and the conditions for establishing it.
Anti-Netanyahu parties seek agreement on replacing Knesset speaker
Within the anti-Netanyahu bloc, broad agreement is emerging on a step that could be attempted even before the question of forming a government is settled: replacing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana.
The move is intended to give the camp opposing Netanyahu control over the parliamentary agenda, even if Netanyahu remains in office as head of a caretaker government.
Electing the Knesset speaker is among the first steps taken by a newly elected Knesset, and the vote is public.
To replace Ohana, the bloc would need to assemble a majority around an agreed candidate. It could also rely on votes from MKs representing the Arab parties.
The move would not require a prior agreement on the composition of the next government.
Among the names raised as possible candidates are Chili Tropper, Matan Kahana, and Elazar Stern from Eisenkot's list; Meirav Ben-Ari and Eitan Ginzburg from the Bennett-Lapid list; Efrat Rayten from the Democrats; and attorney Oded Forer from Yisrael Beytenu.
No consensus candidate has yet been announced.
Liberman estimated this week that MKs from the outgoing coalition would also support replacing Ohana, suggesting that as many as one-third of them could vote against him.
If such MKs are indeed prepared to take that step, they would have to do so publicly.
Opposition parties prepare legislative agenda for new Knesset
The anti-Netanyahu bloc is seeking to advance a state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7, changes to military conscription legislation, limits on the prime minister's tenure, and the repeal of some of the changes promoted by the outgoing government to the judicial system.
Liberman also wants to advance legislation that would prevent a person facing criminal charges from serving as prime minister.
The parties have not yet reached a binding agreement on all the details of the proposed legislation or the order in which it would be advanced.
Teams representing the parties have already held meetings to coordinate their first steps in the new Knesset.
The idea is to use the first weeks after the elections to advance legislation before coalition negotiations deepen the disagreements between the parties.
The experience of the Bennett-Lapid government also looms in the background. Laws promised when that government was formed were not completed before it collapsed.
This time, the anti-Netanyahu bloc wants to move quickly, but there are concerns that MKs with differing political views will not support every item on the shared agenda.
Replacing the Knesset speaker would not automatically provide a legislative majority, and not all members of the bloc agree on every proposed judicial change.
Legislation effectively targeting Netanyahu would likely encounter constitutional and legal difficulties, including questions of applicability and legislation directed at a specific individual.
Nor would a state commission of inquiry be established automatically simply because the Knesset elected a new speaker.
If the move succeeds, Netanyahu could remain in office as head of a caretaker government while a newly elected Knesset, in which his opponents hold a majority, works to advance an agenda contrary to that of his government.

Şimşek credits reforms for fiscal transparency gains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:48:31 UTC
17:48:31 KST

Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek has credited more than two decades of institutional reform for Türkiye’s gains in fiscal transparency, following an updated International Monetary Fund assessment.
In a social media post on Oct. 24, Şimşek said Türkiye met good or advanced standards on about half the principles in the IMF’s Fiscal Transparency Code in 2015. That share has risen to two-thirds, he said.
The improvement places Türkiye among the leading countries assessed by the fund, according to Şimşek. Around 40 countries have undergone evaluations, including Britain, Finland, Ireland, Austria and Portugal.
“Our work on structural reforms to further improve fiscal transparency continues,” he said.
The IMF’s Fiscal Transparency Evaluation examines government financial reporting, budgeting and the management of fiscal risks. Its latest report credited improvements in fiscal statistics, the introduction of performance-based program budgeting and reforms to implement international public sector accounting standards.
The gains follow a series of changes to public financial management. An IMF review in 2000 found weaknesses in budget preparation and implementation, with reporting largely confined to cash-based budget information. Balance-sheet data were limited, while fiscal risks were insufficiently disclosed.
By the 2015 assessment, the legal framework had strengthened, medium-term budgeting had improved and financial reporting had expanded to cover the general government sector.
In its latest evaluation, the IMF identified fiscal reporting as Türkiye’s strongest area, followed by forecasting and budgeting. It also found scope for further reform in fiscal risk analysis.

Hitler's favorite mountain retreat goes up in flames as 200 firefighters battle blaze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:34:05 UTC
17:34:05 KST

A major fire broke out Friday night at the historic building known as the "Eagle's Nest," a mountaintop retreat once used by Adolf Hitler that has since become a popular tourist destination in Bavaria, southern Germany. Police said no one was injured in the blaze and that one person was arrested on suspicion of involvement in the incident.
About 200 firefighters were dispatched to battle the fire at the building, which stands more than 5,900 feet (1,800 meters) above sea level. Located above the town of Berchtesgaden in the Bavarian Alps, the site is particularly difficult to access.
Footage filmed shortly before dawn showed the building engulfed in flames. The fire later appeared to subside, although smoke could still be seen rising from the structure.
According to law enforcement officials, a smoke detector inside the building triggered the fire alarm at about 9:50 p.m. local time Friday. Firefighters responding to the call could see flames as they approached the scene. When they arrived, they found the building "completely engulfed in flames."
Police spokesperson Lisa Meyer said accessing the site and carrying out firefighting operations posed significant challenges. "The building can only be entered using heavy-duty respiratory protective equipment," she added. The cause of the fire remains unknown, but Meyer said "a criminal investigation is underway." Police also said that shortly after the fire began, "a suspicious individual came to investigators' attention."
Built between 1937 and 1938, the structure was part of the "Führer's restricted area" at Obersalzberg, one of Hitler's favorite retreats. It was intended to serve as a venue for official receptions, although Hitler himself rarely visited. The building, constructed from stone and granite to impress foreign diplomats, became known as the "Eagle's Nest" because of its location on a narrow rocky ridge called Kehlstein.
The building survived World War II undamaged. Since 1952, it has housed an exhibition documenting its Nazi-era history, alongside a restaurant operating on the premises.
