Iran drops four places to sixth at Nagoya Asian Para Games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:33:16 UTC
17:33:16 KST

Iran drops four places to sixth at Nagoya Asian Para Games
TEHRAN - Iran concluded its campaign at the 2026 Asian Para Games in Nagoya in sixth place, suffering a four-position decline from its runner-up finish at the previous edition in Hangzhou, China, in 2023.
The Iranian delegation collected 102 medals, including 26 gold, 36 silver and 40 bronze, compared with 131 medals — 44 gold, 46 silver and 41 bronze — at Hangzhou.
Despite the decline in the overall standings, several Iranian athletes delivered outstanding performances, demonstrating the country's continued strength in para-athletics and swimming.
Among the most successful competitors was Sina Zeighaminejad, who emerged as one of Iran's leading gold medalists in para swimming. He secured three gold medals, underlining his remarkable consistency and establishing himself as a key figure in Iran's medal-winning campaign.
Another standout performer was Elham Salehi, who captured two gold medals in para-athletics. Her achievements provided a significant boost to the Iranian delegation and highlighted the important contribution of female athletes to the country's success.
Alireza Zare also produced an impressive performance, winning two gold medals in para-athletics. His achievements included a record-breaking run in the men's 200-meter T35 event, where he clocked 24.83 seconds to secure the title.
While these individual successes offered encouraging signs, Iran's overall results reflected a noticeable decline compared with Hangzhou. The delegation won 18 fewer gold medals and 29 fewer medals overall, although it also competed with a smaller squad.
Meanwhile, China reaffirmed its dominance of Asian para sports, finishing comfortably at the top of the medal standings with an extraordinary 435 medals, comprising 207 gold, 117 silver and 111 bronze.
Host nation Japan secured second place with 64 gold, 60 silver and 62 bronze medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 45 gold, 49 silver and 51 bronze.
India claimed fourth position with 30 gold medals, followed by South Korea with 29, leaving Iran sixth with 26 gold medals.
China's commanding performance demonstrated its considerable depth across multiple disciplines and reinforced its position as the continent's leading para-sport powerhouse.
For Iran, the Nagoya Games presented a mixed picture of individual excellence and collective disappointment.
Although champions such as Zeighaminejad, Salehi and Zare delivered memorable performances, the four-place drop in the rankings underlined the need for stronger preparation, investment in emerging talent and improved competitive depth.
The challenge now facing Iranian para sports is to build on these individual achievements and regain a place among Asia's leading delegations at future international competitions.

Germany in talks with Ukraine to purchase Bars jet-powered drones – Bloomberg, photo

Germany in talks with Ukraine to purchase Bars jet-powered drones – Bloomberg, photo
Germany plans to replenish its stockpile of precision-guided weapons with several thousand missiles from European arms manufacturers. In particular, the country is in talks with Ukraine regarding Bars jet-powered drones.
Source: Bloomberg
Details: According to Bloomberg, the Ukrainian jet-powered UAVs are among four main options being considered by the German Defence Ministry. In addition to Bars, Germany is discussing a contract worth more than €1 billion to purchase Anthem ground-launched cruise missiles from US company Covenant.
Germany is also considering Ruta missiles from the Dutch company Destinus, which have been used in Ukraine, and the HS1 high-speed missile being developed by German-British defence start-up Hypersonica, the financial news agency's sources said.
"They are also in talks with Ukraine to co-produce and acquire the Bars cruise missile, whose manufacturer has not been made public, people familiar with the negotiations said," Bloomberg reported.
The Bars jet-powered drone has a strike range of up to 1,000 km and can carry a warhead weighing up to 60 kg. The UAV can reach speeds of more than 700 km/h. Bars operates as a modular platform which, depending on its fuel load and warhead weight, can be used for long-range and mid-range strikes as well as strikes near the front line.
The manufacturer of Bars drones is capable of producing around 600 jet-powered drones per month. The company is also working on upgrading the drone to the Bars 2.0 version.
Background: Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that Ukraine and Germany signed an agreement in July 2026 on the joint production of Bars UAVs. During the first stage of the project, Germany will finance drone production, with all the systems produced to be supplied to Ukraine's defence forces.

AI glasses create new growth potential for Taiwan optical industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:32:11 UTC
17:32:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's optical lens makers are expanding into AI glasses as the emerging market creates new business opportunities beyond smartphones, CTEE reported Saturday.
As Meta, Google, and other major technology companies introduce new models, AI glasses are moving closer to everyday consumer use. Research firm IDC estimates global shipments will reach 13.04 million units this year and increase to 16.18 million next year.
Genius Electronic Optical Co. has been developing optical components for AI glasses and augmented and virtual reality (AR and VR) devices in recent years. The company is already working with US clients and is also in talks with Chinese brands.
Although orders for VR lenses have slowed, activity in AI glasses and AR products is picking up. These applications share some of the same technical requirements as smartphone cameras, including compact designs, high resolution, and precise assembly, while also requiring lightweight components, according to Pocket Securities.
Asia Optical Co. has spent years developing metalens technology using nanoimprint lithography, a process that uses a stamp-like mold to transfer nanoscale circuit patterns onto a light-sensitive coating on a wafer. The company holds related manufacturing patents, according to Business Next.
It said the technology could significantly lower the cost of optical waveguide lenses used in AR glasses, potentially making eyewear with built-in displays more affordable. Asia Optical is also exploring the use of metalens technology in sensing modules for AI glasses.
Kinko Optical Co. is focusing its AR, VR, and mixed reality development on optical waveguides and optical engines, which help deliver images to the wearer's eyes. The company expects its investments in AR technology to begin generating returns next year.
Ability Enterprise Co. is starting with specialized applications such as sports glasses. It is participating in a smart sports glasses project under an electronics manufacturing services model, producing devices based on designs provided by clients.
Depending on customer needs, the company may expand into original design manufacturing, which also includes product design.

Taiwan’s NCIST investigates origin of Hsiung Feng III missile part
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:32:00 UTC
17:32:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Kaohsiung-based National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology said Friday that it found a suspected Chinese component in its air-launched Hsiung Feng III missile, CNA reported.
NCSIST is developing Hsiung Feng III missiles for the country's indigenous defense fighter under its Hsiung Chih Project. The institute test-fired the missiles near Pingtung County’s Jiupeng Military Base in July and is still optimizing the design, per the Liberty Times.
Current ship-fired and ground-launched Hsiung Feng III missiles weigh between 1,300 and 1,400 kilograms, Liberty Times said. The missile must be scaled down below 1,000 kg to be safely carried by IDFs, though at the cost of a shorter effective firing range.
Storm Media reported that NCSIST discovered a communication signal filter that may be of Chinese origin during an inspection. The institute said the component has not been installed and it has contacted the supplier for an explanation.
The institute said the metallic filter has no transmission capabilities or embedded electronic components. It added that it conducts routine inspections to weed out Chinese components.

Israel launches major West Bank operation after soldiers killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:31:57 UTC
17:31:57 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel launches major West Bank operation after soldiers killed
Israel's military launched an operation in the occupied West Bank on Friday, which it said would last several days and include searches and building demolitions, after gunmen killed two soldiers days ahead of Israeli elections in which security has been a key focus.
ICC fugitive Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is locked in a tight race to keep his job in Tuesday's vote, having campaigned on promises to keep Israelis safe, and he and his right-wing allies visited the scene of the attack to pledge an even harder line on West Bank militancy.
Security forces were searching targets and questioning suspects to "locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure" in the Hebron area from where they said the attackers had emerged, according to a joint statement from the Israeli military and Shin Bet domestic security agency.
Forces were also "demolishing illegal structures that could pose a security threat at the site of the encounter", they said, adding that "counterterrorism operations" were underway at dozens of locations.
The operation "is expected to continue for several days," the statement said, released late Friday.
Palestinian group Hamas, without claiming responsibility, praised Friday's fatal attack on two Israeli soldiers as a "heroic operation" and called on supporters to carry out more.
A Hebron-based AFP photographer heading to another assignment witnessed the gun battle break out at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint between the soldiers and two men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle.
Israeli forces eventually shot dead the attackers.
Netanyahu credited the soldiers with having "prevented what could have been a major attack", and ordered a lockdown in the West Bank.
Visiting Hebron, the premier said he and Defence Minister Israel Katz were "considering a very extensive IDF operation in Judea and Samaria, such as has not been carried out since" the 1967 war.
The first step would see Israeli forces "enter the neighbourhood from which the terrorists came, evacuate the residents, go from house to house, and destroy the terrorist infrastructure," he said.
The military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank, he said, the scene of a large-scale operation launched in January 2025 that the United Nations said forcibly displaced thousands.
Israeli rights group B'Tselem called for urgent international pressure to prevent Israel from pursuing "plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes".
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, through a spokesman, voiced concern over Israeli closures that affect Palestinian livelihoods and called for a halt to violence on all sides.
'Exactly like Gaza'
Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a large-scale military offensive in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza".
He said authorities were "sending an unequivocal message to our enemies: if you mess with the Jews, you will pay a very painful price."
National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir said the Ramallah-based "Palestinian Authority must be dismantled".
"It is impossible for there to be an authority within Judea and Samaria that incites murder, calls for murder, and works for murder," he told reporters.
No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority, which exercises limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank, was connected to Friday's attack.
Both Ben Gvir and Smotrich are especially vocal champions of illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which have proliferated under Netanyahu's government but are illegal under international law.
Netanyahu vowed to "pursue Hamas terrorists" everywhere, adding: "You have no place to hide."
Israel vowed to obliterate the group in the wake of the 7 October attacks that resulted in 1,221 deaths, according to an AFP tally from official Israeli figures, in what was the deadliest day in the country's history.
Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is Netanyahu's top rival in the upcoming vote, said he was praying for soldiers wounded in Friday's shooting.
The operation comes as tensions soar in the West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters.
According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces and settlers have killed 1,117 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023.

Seoul’s useless placation is a warning for all US trade partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:30:09 UTC
17:30:09 KST

Opinion
Seoul’s useless placation is a warning for all US trade partners
Clearly, appeasement doesn’t work and dependence just feeds leverage. Collective action is the only effective stand that states can take
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Zhou Xiaoming is a senior fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation in Beijing and a former deputy representative of China’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office in Geneva. 
The anxiety gripping Seoul is palpable. Under US pressure, South Korea signed a US$350 billion investment deal last November for a 10-percentage-point tariff reduction, billing it as a strategic alliance. Barely a year on, the facade has crumbled.
Last month, US President Donald Trump announced a US$200 billion tranche of the deal with no South Korean official present. Blindsided, Seoul restated its “commercial viability” clause. Trump’s response was blunt. “If they don’t want to do it, that’s OK with me. I’ll just charge them more,” he told reporters. “Tell them if they don’t sign shortly, I’m going to double it up.”
For South Korea, the numbers are sobering: US$350 billion represents 18 per cent of its annual gross domestic product. Even if much of it is channelled through loans, guarantees and corporate outlays, it risks upward pressure on the won, crowding out domestic investment and political exposure if projects underperform.

Breitling CEO: Business devastated by unrest in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

Breitling CEO: Business devastated by unrest in France
During the serious riots in France, a shop belonging to the Swiss watchmaker Breitling in Marseille was also vandalised. The financial extent of the damage cannot yet be quantified, said CEO Georges Kern in an interview with Tamedia.
The police first had to secure evidence, which is why they had not yet been allowed to enter the shop. “We are insured and have the necessary resources. For small retailers, this is a disaster,” said Kern in the interview published on Saturday. “Fortunately, the riots took place at night, so there were no staff in the shop and nobody was physically harmed.”
The watch manufacturer has stepped up security at its branches. Should there be a threat of further riots, the shops will remain closed. “Staff are free to choose whether to come in, but there is a strong desire to work and to stand up against this trend,” Kern added.
Fears of a hit to Christmas sales
The Breitling CEO also fears a decline in sales during the crucial Christmas period. In Paris, there have already been reports of numerous hotel cancellations. The unrest is having a noticeable economic impact. “I very much hope that the situation calms down quickly,” said the CEO, who has German-French roots.
He said the developments had shocked and pained him. As a private individual, he saw the riots as an expression of an explosive mix of social problems such as the housing crisis, inflation and a lack of prospects for young people. However, he added that the protests had been exploited by extremist groups and anarchists for their own ends.

The Muslims finding belonging in southern Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:28:25 UTC
17:28:25 KST

Alora, Spain - The train chugs steadily out of Malaga station, its rhythmic clatter carrying it inland towards the mountains of the Guadalhorce Valley, where whitewashed villages cling to hillsides.
Beyond the window, pomegranate trees grow close to the tracks. Palms and cypress trees stand alongside young orange saplings planted in neat rows and, farther out, olive groves whose leaves shimmer between green and silver in the breeze. Above the rugged mountains, small white clouds float across an immense blue sky, like pieces of popcorn.
Over the train's rattle, an announcement in Spanish comes through the speakers: “The next station is Aljaima.”
The name derives from the Arabic al-khaima, meaning “the tent”, a small echo of another language, another time.
And then Alora, where the town rises around a rocky hill crowned by the remains of an old fortress. Some etymologists suggest the town's ancient name may derive from the Arabic al-lawra, loosely translated as "the light".
The railway station is quiet in the midday heat.
A large black pick-up truck rumbles into the station car park and stops. Henrietta Szovati, a British-Hungarian Muslim, steps out, having driven down from the mountains to collect provisions.
Dressed in a loose blue shirt and cream trousers, she offers a warm embrace. Silver earrings dangle beside her face, and a sea-blue scarf is wrapped around her hair like a turban. A pair of red-framed spectacles rests on top.
She apologises for the truck’s state. Dust has settled on the dashboard, and bits of dried grass have found their way inside. “It is a working vehicle,” she says, more accustomed to hauling things across farmland than ferrying visitors from railway stations.
For the past two years, she and her husband, Ajmal Masroor, a therapist and imam, have been transforming an old farmhouse and its surrounding land into the House of Andalus. The project aims to bring people closer to southern Spain's Islamic history and the natural world.
Nearly 400 olive trees dot the 14 hectares (35 acres). She wants to plant more and make it a thousand-tree olive grove, she says with a smile, glancing out of the truck's open window.
The road winds higher into the mountains. Wildfires, Henrietta says, swept through parts of the surrounding region at the height of summer, and the landscape still bears the season's harshness. Reddish-brown earth gives way to patches of parched scrub and exposed rock, while slabs of silvery-grey stone jut sharply from the slopes.
"That's slate," Henrietta explains, pointing through the windscreen. The Spanish word is pizarra, she adds, the same name as the neighbouring town.
Oranges flourish here, as do figs and avocados. And mangoes that are better than those from South Asia, Henrietta emphatically declares.
As we drive further into the mountains, Henrietta gestures towards a neighbouring property. “That's my neighbour, Juan Garcia.”
Henrietta buys lemons, avocados and honey from him. Sometimes he comes over to help with the olives. It's this sense of community and neighbourliness she found harder to come by in Britain, where she has lived since 2001, marrying Ajmal a year later.
"I feel like an outsider there. I'm still not ‘one of us’ after more than 20 years."
As a Muslim and as a European, she says, Spain feels familiar in a way no other place does. Hungary was never an option, she adds, describing its government as “racist and right-wing”. And in Britain, she says, being Muslim can feel unavoidably political, her faith viewed through headlines and public arguments about Islam.
In the mountains above Alora, she feels her neighbours meet her first as Henrietta: the woman who lives up the track and joins in village life.
"Practising Islam here is just easier," she adds.
Yet Spain is not immune to the political currents sweeping across Europe. The far-right Vox party has made opposition to immigration and what it calls the "Islamisation" of Spain central to its campaigning, raising questions about how secure that sense of belonging might be.
With a sigh, Henrietta acknowledges that being Muslim can be difficult anywhere in the world today. But she prefers to focus on what she can build, rather than on political circumstances beyond her control. "Circumstances change, but community, connections and faith don’t," she says.
For her, that means building relationships with neighbours, even when they hold different beliefs. A sense of community, she argues, is forged through everyday encounters rather than political rhetoric.
On a visit to Juan Garcia’s home, his 79-year-old mother, Maria, is curious about the scarf wrapped around Henrietta's hair.
The women are standing in Maria's living room, its shutters drawn against the afternoon sun. A portrait of Jesus hangs on the wall.
Henrietta explains that she is Muslim and that covering her hair is part of her faith, a way to feel closer to God. Maria is Catholic. The conversation turns to the Virgin Mary, who also covered her hair.
But Maria insists all that matters is being a good person. If you cannot be good, none of the outward signs of faith means very much.
There is no awkwardness between them, no need to defend or explain their beliefs. The conversation moves on.
It is such ordinary encounters that have made Andalucia feel like home, Henrietta says. But her connection to this part of Spain runs deeper than the friendships she is making. It also stems from a deep respect for a history that stretches back more than 1,000 years.
For British Muslim travel writer and historian Tharik Hussain, author of Muslim Europe, the fascination is understandable. Al-Andalus was the medieval Muslim-ruled territory of modern-day Spain and Portugal. Its heartland lay in the south, in what is now Andalucia, home to cities such as Cordoba, Seville and Granada, where surviving monuments still evoke a period when Muslims helped shape European civilisation.
Its eventual loss, he says, has given it an almost “Atlantis-like aura” in the Muslim imagination, a longing reflected in Muslim literature over the centuries, from the 17th-century historian al-Maqqari to the 20th-century poet Allama Iqbal.
For nearly eight centuries, Muslim dynasties ruled parts of the Iberian Peninsula, leaving behind palaces and fortresses with horseshoe arches, intricate zellij tilework, carved yeseria plasterwork, and curling Arabic calligraphy. Their legacy endured in irrigation channels known as acequias (from the Arabic al-saqiya), scholarship, language and traditions that continued to shape Spain long after the fall of Granada in 1492.
Britons have long headed to Andalucia in search of a place in the sun. But among those putting down roots here are Muslims drawn by something more: The chance to reconnect with a history in which Islam was part of Europe, and to build lives where their faith feels less like a defining difference.
Yet the Andalucia they are entering is not a vanished kingdom waiting to be rediscovered; it is modern Spain, with its own economic pressures, social divisions, and complicated relationship with the past.
What happens when the dream of al-Andalus meets the realities of living here?
The truck turns off the road onto a narrow dirt track, climbing towards a whitewashed farmhouse tucked into the hillside; this is the House of Andalus.
Henrietta and Ajmal bought their whitewashed farmhouse in 2024 after seven years of searching.
It was never intended as a holiday home. They always meant the House of Andalus to be a place to put down roots and invite others in.
But realising that dream meant stretching their finances to the limit. The couple poured much of their savings into the project, then turned to friends and family for loans.
It's early afternoon, and Henrietta leads the way in. The thick stone walls keep the rooms cool in the early autumn sun. Rugs from the local market soften its rustic simplicity, while references to Andalucia's Islamic past give the rooms a sense of place.
But the bookshelves offer perhaps the clearest glimpse into Henrietta's world: Copies of the Quran sit alongside histories of Islam and Spain, novels, and travelogues. There are Dickens and Hardy, V S Naipaul and William Dalrymple, Mark Twain's The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam. A Spanish dictionary is tucked among them.
Then there are the books that seem to speak more directly to the life she has chosen: Peter Mayle’s A Year in Provence, and M Scott Peck's The Road Less Travelled.
On a side table sits a particularly treasured volume: A first edition of Washington Irving's writings on the Alhambra, sent by a former guest who discovered it in a rare-book shop in Inverness and sent it as a thank you for their time in Alora.
“Lunch is ready,” calls Shama Rahman from the terrace. The resident chef has prepared seared tuna steaks topped with a vegetable relish, baked sweet potatoes and a fresh garden salad. Everything is sourced locally and now served on blue crockery Henrietta found in a second-hand shop in a neighbouring village.
There is a loaf of warm bread and olive oil pressed from the trees on the property. Henrietta pours some into a shallow dish, tears off a piece of bread and drags it through the golden oil.
A breeze catches the paper napkins and lifts them off the table, and Henrietta reaches to catch one. Over a slow lunch, she explains what she and her husband hope to create here. They have already begun hosting art and couples' retreats, the latter drawing on Ajmal's work as a therapist.
They plan to build a Quranic garden, dotted throughout with plants mentioned in the holy book. The olive trees were already growing when they arrived, but the couple has since planted pomegranates, figs and mangoes, and plans to add ginger, cucumbers and grapes. Educational programmes exploring the region's Islamic heritage are also in the works, alongside a library that is already taking shape.
But while Islam is at the heart of their vision, Henrietta is eager to emphasise that the doors are open to Muslims and non-Muslims alike. She speaks of “hanifs”, a term the couple uses for those who are “culturally curious and spiritually aligned”, regardless of religious background, reflecting the spirit of coexistence they associate with al-Andalus.
The idea for the House of Andalus, however, began years earlier, with a question from her five-year-old son.
The family packed their car and set off one weekend for a chestnut festival in a village near the town of Ronda. As they drove through the mountains, her son noticed something that made his mother look at the landscape differently.
“Mama, why is there something to do with Islam everywhere we go?” he asked. He’d noticed footprints of Islamic rule in the remains of castles, like the one he was then pointing to, in the zeliji tiles they would spot, and in the names of places.
Henrietta had known about al-Andalus, but now she began seeing traces of it everywhere.
She began wondering how to make that history more accessible, especially to those who had grown up in Europe and had been taught to think of Islam as something that belonged elsewhere.
But she wanted to do more than tell them about al-Andalus. Henrietta wanted to create somewhere they could encounter that history for themselves, where the landscape, food, architecture and traditions of the region might help them see Islam as part of Europe's own story. The House of Andalus became her answer.
And the desire to find a place for Islam within Europe's history extends far beyond Henrietta's family.
Hussain, the author, explains that the surviving traces of al-Andalus offer European Muslims something often missing from conventional accounts of the continent's past: Evidence that their faith is not simply a recent arrival.
“For European Muslims especially, that can help root their identities in a European history from which they have often been excluded,” he says.
But he cautions against making al-Andalus the beginning and end of Europe's Muslim story. Muslim communities have existed elsewhere on the continent for centuries, and remain part of its living cultural landscape, he says.
The following morning, sunlight spills over the jagged mountains as the town wakes to an unusually busy Saturday.
Cars have been stopped from entering Alora centre. Thousands of people are making their way uphill, following the steep cobbled streets towards the Plaza Baja de la Despedia. Some have come from neighbouring villages. Others have travelled much further.
They are all here for a bowl of soup.
It is the first Saturday of October, and Alora is celebrating Dia de las Sopas Perotas, an annual festival devoted to a dish that has sustained generations of agricultural workers in this corner of Andalucia.
The smell reaches the square before the food comes into view: Garlic frying in olive oil, ripe tomatoes, peppers, yesterday’s bread, and fresh mint carried on the warm air.
Spanish guitars compete with the crowd's rising chatter. Beneath the midday sun, cooks stand under a gazebo and tend to enormous vats of sopa perota as steam rises from the pots.
The soup arrives in a disposable plastic bowl, thick and steaming. The bread has absorbed the vegetable broth and olive oil, breaking into soft, irregular pieces, almost like clumps of couscous. It is rich, savoury and surprisingly filling.
Earlier at Maria Garcia’s house, she explained just how to make it.
Dressed in a cobalt-blue sleeveless dress, a mischievous glint in her eye, she says she’ll agree to a photograph, on one condition. She must see it first; she wants to be sure she looks pretty.
At her kitchen table, with the afternoon light falling across her face, Maria talks about the soup as though she were describing an old friend: Dependable, but still capable of causing trouble if not treated properly.
She was 11 or 12 when her mother first began teaching her to make it. Her grandmother had taught her mother, and Maria, in turn, passed the recipe on to her daughter, who now lives in the city.
In those days, people harvested the wheat by hand. "It wasn't that long ago," she says, recalling workers going into the fields with sickles, cutting the wheat and gathering it into great piles.
She gestures as she describes pulling chickpeas from the earth, her hand closing around an imaginary plant and tugging it upwards.
No great machines moved across the fields then. People worked together, and meals had to stretch far enough to feed whoever was helping with the harvest.
Each worker might receive a quarter of a loaf of bread, she recalls, roughly the size of two hands.
For sopa perota, the bread had to be at least three days old. Not the soft, factory-made loaves sold in supermarkets, Maria insists, but the sturdy sourdough traditionally baked in the village. Otherwise, it would disintegrate.
She starts by explaining the bread. "You twist it," she says. ”Don't pull it off, otherwise it will just melt into the soup. The trick is in the twist."
She explains that she places the pieces in a large bowl while the vegetables cook separately. In the old days, people balanced frying pans over three enormous stones, with a fire beneath them.
"You need to calculate measurements with your eyes," Maria says.
Once the vegetables have softened, pour the liquid over the bread. Then comes another rule: Leave it alone. Don't stir. Only when it is ready to eat should everything be mixed.
The bread must be soft enough to yield in the mouth, she says, but not so saturated that it loses its texture.
Could something so thoroughly Spanish have roots in the centuries when Muslims ruled this part of the peninsula?
She shakes her head. "No, never." Nobody has ever suggested such a thing to her.
"It was really well-respected soup, because it was so delicious and nutritious," she says. "It didn't ever matter who made it first, or where it came from."
But Alora's town council points to a possible connection to the region's Muslim past, noting that dishes made with crumbled bread were common then.
Nawal Nasrallah, a food historian and translator of medieval Arabic cookbooks, points to a 13th-century Andalusi one, Fidalat al-Khiwan. In it is a recipe for jinaniyya, an orchard dish prepared with seasonal vegetables, olive oil, garlic and herbs, served as tharid, with bread softened in broth.
Although the medieval recipe uses gourds and aubergines rather than tomatoes, potatoes and peppers, which only reached Europe after voyages to the Americas, the principle is much the same: A filling meal made from what the land provides, with bread to soak up the broth.
"It did indeed descend from the Andalusi jinaniyya," Nasrallah says, suggesting that the introduction of tomatoes, potatoes, and green peppers may explain why people often attribute the soup to 19th-century farmers.
At about 7pm that evening, just more than 100km (60 miles) east of Alora, a taxi winds its way towards the Mirador de San Nicolas, in Granada's Albaicin neighbourhood; the driver reaches for his phone to translate something into English.
"You are about to see the most spectacular sight," he says. "It's even more beautiful at this time, when it's lit up."
The car climbs through a tangle of steep, narrow lanes, past whitewashed houses and little squares where people linger over coffee beneath the trees. Couples wander hand in hand, slowing their steps as though reluctant to let the evening pass.
And then, across the valley, the Alhambra comes into view.
Perched above a wooded hillside, its russet towers and ancient walls are illuminated against the evening sky. Beyond them lies a world of courtyards and palaces, where water murmurs through marble channels and slender columns frame intricately tiled rooms. The words Wa la ghaliba illallah, "There is no victor except Allah," appear again and again in curled Arabic calligraphy across its arches and walls.
This is the Granada most visitors come to see: The extraordinary surviving architecture of a Muslim civilisation whose last kingdom surrendered to the Catholic Monarchs in 1492.
But on the Albaicin hillside, a short walk from the viewpoint, another, rather more modest building tells a different part of the city's Muslim story.
The Mezquita Mayor de Granada, or Great Mosque of Granada, stands among the neighbourhood's old houses, its courtyard facing the Alhambra. Across the valley, the illuminated palaces and towers of the Nasrid rulers rise above the trees.
As the sun sets, the call to maghrib prayer rises from the mosque. It is delivered by the voice of a man, as tradition dictates, without loudspeakers or a recording, the Arabic words carrying into the evening air of a city where the language was once heard in its streets and markets.
After prayers, the courtyard is infused with the sweet scent of night jasmine. Beyond the garden, the Alhambra continues to glow against the darkening sky.
For Granada's modern Muslim community, the mosque's opening in 2003 was a moment of considerable significance. But building it took nearly two decades of fundraising, legal disputes, and determined campaigning.
Among those who remember that struggle is Munira Mendonca.
Reaching her apartment in Granada involves climbing three flights of stairs. There is no lift.
At the top, a petite woman with a thick mane of silver hair, part of it clipped up while the rest falls loosely around her shoulders, opens the door.
Munira is now in her 70s, and although she has spent almost half a century in Spain, the unmistakable Californian drawl has never quite left her voice.
She puts on a fresh pot of coffee and brings out a plate of almond biscuits. As we talk, she occasionally stretches, slipping into a yoga pose without breaking the conversation.
The apartment, which Munira believes is about a century old, glows with colour. Against walls of burned orange and deep terracotta hang magnificent panels of decorated leather, their embossed patterns and calligraphy catching the light. Some are richly gilded, others painted in intricate geometric designs reminiscent of the Alhambra.
They are Munira's own creations.
For decades, she has practised cordoban, a traditional Andalusian art of embossed and painted leatherwork. She learned the craft from Diego Campos Mariscal, a master artisan in Granada, and went on to become a master craftswoman herself, formally recognised by the Andalusian government in 2019.
After coffee, she leads the way to the windows, where the view perhaps says most about the extraordinary path her life has taken.
Beyond the shutters and terracotta-tiled rooftops, the Alhambra's red walls rise above the city.
Munira arrived in Spain in the late 1970s, in a Morris Minor that had doubled as her home during a journey across Europe.
Raised by Catholic parents in Oakland, Munira left behind what she describes as a promising career selling lighting fixtures to construction companies to see the world. Somewhere along the way, she began to question whether she wanted to return to the life she had known.
She eventually found her way into the Alpujarras, the mountains south of Granada, where a small circle of Spaniards and other Europeans had begun gathering, drawn by the prospect of a simpler, more communal way of life.
But these mountains held a darker history. Following the fall of Granada, the last Muslim-ruled kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula, in 1492, Muslims were initially promised religious freedom. Those guarantees were subsequently broken, and Muslims faced forced conversion to Christianity and increasing restrictions on their religious and cultural practices.
By the late 16th century, the Alpujarras had become a centre of Morisco resistance against the Spanish Crown. The movement was brutally crushed. Many were massacred, their villages destroyed, and tens of thousands of survivors driven from their ancestral homes. The persecution culminated in the wider expulsion of the Moriscos from Spain between 1609 and 1614.
Centuries later, in those same mountains, a small group of seekers found its way towards the very faith once so violently suppressed there.
Munira and several others, including the Spaniard she would marry, began exploring Islam. Their changing lives bewildered the villagers.
"We were the best customers in the bar, and overnight we're not drinking," she laughs.
The group eventually moved to Granada, hoping to establish a more permanent community. They were young, idealistic and almost entirely without money.
"We didn't have a bean," Munira says.
New Muslim families also arrived, including Moroccans who came to study at Granada's university and stayed to make homes in the city. The little group of European converts was no longer alone.
Yet the small Muslim community living in its shadow had nowhere permanent to worship.
Their first prayer gatherings took place in borrowed or rented spaces, including a carmen, a traditional Granada house with a garden, in the Albaicin. In time, the idea of constructing a mosque overlooking the Alhambra began to take shape.
Munira remembers years of planning disputes, legal challenges, neighbour objections, and changes in local authorities. Money was a constant problem.
But through fundraising, donations and years of persistence, the community finally opened the doors of the Great Mosque of Granada in 2003.
"I remember feeling overwhelmingly joyful!"
South of Granada, the land rises towards the Alpujarras, a region of steep valleys and terraced hillsides on the southern slopes of the Sierra Nevada. In these mountains, once a stronghold of Muslim resistance, a new generation of Muslims has made its home.
Orgiva, a small town of about 6,000 people, is home to an international mix of Spaniards, Britons, Moroccans, Algerians, West Africans and other Europeans. Artists, retirees, and families are drawn by the landscape, a slower pace of life, and the relatively affordable cost of living. Rooms can be rented for about 300 euros ($340) a month, while small flats start at approximately 500 euros ($560) – prices that help explain the town's appeal to those seeking an alternative to life in Europe's more expensive cities.
On a Sunday afternoon, Orgiva seems to have surrendered to the heat. Shutters are closed, and the streets are quiet. The town seems to sleep through its siesta.
Then, through the stillness, comes the low murmur of Quranic verses. An elderly man is walking alone through a small cobbled side street, reciting, his voice rising and falling, partly to himself and partly, it seems, for anyone who might be listening.
The Arabic words drift into the afternoon air.
Not far away, Medina Tenour Whiteman is watering the plants in her back garden. The leaves are an exuberant green, a small triumph after a summer that seemed capable of scorching almost anything left exposed.
She wears a faded denim shirt and black-rimmed spectacles. Her hair, cut into short, flicked layers, frames a face that seems perpetually on the verge of a smile.
The garden is a fitting place to meet. Medina, an author, singer, and teacher, is writing a book on the sacred ecology of Al-Andalus, exploring the relationship between faith, the natural world, and the lives of the people who once inhabited this region.
Medina was born in Granada in 1982. Her parents, Ian and Tahira Whiteman, were among the British and American converts who came to Andalucia in the late 1970s, drawn by Islam and the hope of building a community here.
But the young family's hopes of making a life in Spain collided with the need to earn a living. Work they had been promised failed to materialise, and money was scarce. With an infant Medina to care for, they eventually returned to Britain, where they raised their growing family in the countryside near Cambridge.
She returned to Andalucia in December 2005, after finishing university, when her parents had moved back. She remembers the weather most clearly. The days were warm enough to sit outside in shirtsleeves. In the evenings, the temperature dropped, and the family lit a wood fire. It reminded her of a crisp English autumn, only with sunshine.
And then there were the oranges. In the mornings, she could step outside, pick fruit cold from the night air and squeeze it straight into a glass. "Why are we not all living like this?" she remembers thinking. "It just felt so sensible." She laughs at its simplicity.
But Medina understands why, for other Muslims, Andalucia's appeal runs deeper than oranges and sunshine.
"Maybe it's to do with the landmarks," she suggests.
Granada's Alhambra and Cordoba's mosque-cathedral offer something tangible: Reminders of a civilisation whose influence still shows in the region's architecture and streets.
"History is one thing, and it's nourishing; it nourishes you in some way, gives you that sense of ancientness and rootedness."
Medina's own attachment to Andalucia has grown through the more ordinary experience of living here.
Granada, she says, pushing her glasses up her nose, is beautiful but intense, particularly with young children. Summers are hotter, winters colder, and daily life can feel exhausting. Orgiva is gentler, remarkably cosmopolitan and sometimes remarkably parochial, too. She laughs. "It is hardly a utopia," she says.
Praying together in a mosque is wonderful, she says, but what matters just as much is whether people genuinely care for one another. "They don't have to be Muslim," she says. "They just have to be warm."
Still, she recognises that not everyone experiences that warmth in quite the same way.
"There is something about me being white that might be different to a brown person walking down the street," she says. "I know that my husband sometimes does not get that treatment because he's Iranian."
She has explored this in her book, The Invisible Muslim: Journeys Through Whiteness and Islam, which examines how race shapes perceptions of Muslim identity.
For Medina, making a home here also means becoming part of the wider community. She insists that learning Spanish is essential, rather than remaining within familiar circles of expatriates or fellow Muslims.
"People are looking for community; that's what they're looking for."
Families like her parents helped establish Muslim communities here decades ago. Their children have grown up, friendships have formed, and others have followed. What began as a search for somewhere to belong has become an ordinary, lived reality.
From inside the house, her son calls out, excited to share a Harry Potter scene. Her daughter needs help with her homework.
Medina excuses herself and goes to see what they need.
Back in the mountains above Alora, the day begins before sunrise.
Henrietta spreads a simple prayer mat on the farmhouse's cold stone floor and performs fajr.
Across the dark Andalusian peaks, the thin white thread of dawn is just separating from the black of night. She makes her way to the terrace, her favourite spot, with a small cup of cortado. Far below lies the Arroyo Jevar, its riverbed dry after the long summer, waiting for the winter rains.
Settling into one of the bamboo-backed chairs, she makes time for dhikr, the remembrance of God, and a few quiet moments of contemplation.
But the tranquillity of these early mornings belies the demands of the life she has chosen.
More olive trees need planting, and an approaching harvest needs preparing.
"We have 15 volunteers coming to stay in the first week of November," she says. Most are travelling from Britain, with others coming from Germany and Malaysia.
Then there are the less predictable challenges. Solar panels ordered for the property have yet to arrive, delayed somewhere between Dubai and the Mediterranean. Water remains a constant concern. Getting it up the mountain is no small undertaking, and every litre must be used thoughtfully. For Henrietta, this honours the land and reflects a faith in which even the water used for ritual washing is not wasted.
“This place humbles you,” she says. “And if that isn’t Islam, what is?”
She wants the House of Andalus to become a place where people can explore an often-overlooked part of Europe's history, reconnect with the natural world, and perhaps even reconsider what gives their own lives meaning.
Among the gatherings Henrietta is organising is a leadership retreat for professional Muslim women, an opportunity to step away from the demands of work and everyday life.
Henrietta asks them to imagine stripping away their job titles, qualifications, achievements, and all the labels they usually use to introduce themselves. “If you were to introduce your soul, what would you say?”
“This place humbles you... and if that isn’t Islam, what is?”
Henrietta has been exploring these ideas for years. In her 2016 book, HeartSmart: One Woman's Journey from Her Head to Her Heart, she considers what happens when we begin to question the lives we've grown accustomed to leading.
That same spirit runs through the House of Andalus. More than a place to explore the past, she hopes it will encourage people to reconsider what matters most, how they live and what they might leave behind.
There is no guarantee that everything she imagines will come to pass. The work is expensive and demanding. “I will never see it finished,” she says. “Not in my lifetime.”

Rubio calls on Cubans to partner with CIA ‘to create positive change’
Washington has increased pressure on Havana following the US military’s capture of Venezuelan then-President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called on those seeking change in Cuba to partner with the CIA and help force an end to the island’s communist government.
US President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have for months openly hinted at military intervention and permanent presence in Cuba to ramp up economic, political, and legal pressure on the country.
On Friday, Rubio seemed to openly confirm this when he wrote on X: “To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba – now is the time.”
Rubio commented on “the disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few” in Cuba, encouraging civilians to “seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discreet partnership with the CIA”.
The call was mocked by Cuban officials, including Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio.
“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA… There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste,” he wrote on X.
This is far from the first time Cuba has been threatened with military intervention by US officials.
Last month, Fernandez de Cossio told the US cable television channel C-SPAN’s flagship programme, Washington Journal, that it would be an “atrocious international crime for the US to use military force against Cuba, which is a peaceful neighbouring country”.
The CIA later uploaded a video on X offering instructions in Spanish for those who believe they have information of interest to the intelligence agency, encouraging them to first and foremost visit an official “US embassy in person” if they can safely travel to one.
These latest developments come as a US-imposed oil blockade on Cuba earlier this year has put civilians in the country under intense economic hardship, as they contend with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.
United Nations rights experts have condemned the oil blockade as a violation of international law, while rights advocates say the Trump administration’s threats have echoed an imperialist approach.
Washington has maintained an embargo on Cuba for more than 60 years, as the Trump administration steps up pressure on Havana following the US military’s capture of Venezuelan then-President Nicolas Maduro in a deadly raid in January.

Fire extinguished in Kyiv’s Obolon district following Russian attack
According to Ukrinform, the Kyiv City Directorate of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine reported this on Facebook.
According to the State Emergency Service, on the morning of October 24, the enemy struck the Obolon district of Kyiv. Two people were injured as a result of the Russian attack on a residential area.
In addition, a single-story residential building was destroyed and a fire broke out after a strike hit a private estate. During the rescue operation, one victim was found and handed over by firefighters to medical personnel for hospitalization. Another victim did not require hospitalization.
“The minor fire caused by the attack was quickly extinguished,” the State Emergency Service reported.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 22, a strike was recorded at a transportation infrastructure facility in the Darnytskyi district.

====================================================================================================

Dan Sullivan vs Dan Sullivan: Why is Trump’s DOJ suing in Alaska?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:11:17 UTC
17:11:17 KST

Dan Sullivan vs Dan Sullivan: Why is Trump’s DOJ suing in Alaska?
US government seeks to delay Alaska Senate result over concerns about two candidates with the same name.
The United States Department of Justice has filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of Alaska’s Senate election result if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses to Democrat Mary Peltola in the November 3 midterms.
The reason? Another candidate named Dan Sullivan is also on the ballot.
In a lawsuit filed on Thursday, the department argued that the second Sullivan, a retired teacher who registered as a Republican, is deliberately trying to confuse voters.
Alaska’s Supreme Court has already ruled that both candidates may remain on the ballot.
So who are the two Dan Sullivans, and what could the lawsuit mean for the election?
What is happening in Alaska’s US Senate race?
Senator Sullivan is seeking a third six-year term in the race against Peltola, a former congresswoman who became the first Alaska Native elected to the US House of Representatives in 2022.
Alaska has traditionally voted Republican in presidential elections. President Donald Trump won the state by roughly 13 percentage points in 2024, but this year’s Senate race appears more competitive.
In August’s primary, Peltola received 49.5 percent of the vote, compared with about 41 percent for Senator Sullivan.
Two other candidates advanced to the November 3 election: Daniel J Sullivan Jr and Gerald Heikes.
Who are the two Dan Sullivans?
Dan S Sullivan was first elected to the US Senate in 2014 and was re-elected in 2020. He previously served as Alaska’s attorney general and commissioner of natural resources.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr is a retired elementary schoolteacher and a former US Forest Service employee from Petersburg in southeastern Alaska.
His entry into the race this year prompted accusations from Republicans that he was trying to confuse voters, something he has denied.
Alaska election officials initially disqualified him, but the state’s courts overturned the decision. In June, the Alaska Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot.
The ballot identifies the incumbent as “Sullivan, Dan S (Registered Republican) Incumbent” and the other candidate as “Sullivan, Daniel J Jr” without a party designation, even though he has registered as a Republican.
Glenn Wright, a political science professor at the University of Alaska Southeast, told Al Jazeera that voters should have no problem recognising each candidate.
“The ballots are super, super, super clear about who the incumbent Dan Sullivan is,” he said.
But Forrest Nabors, chairman of the political science department at the University of Alaska Anchorage, said the similar names could still affect the result.
“It could swing the election if the election is close and the margin of voters who intend to re-elect the senator are confused and accidentally vote for the other candidate named Sullivan,” he told Al Jazeera.
Why has the Justice Department filed a lawsuit?
The Justice Department sued Alaska in federal court on Thursday, arguing that having two candidates with similar names could mislead voters.
It wants the state to be prevented from certifying the result if the Republican senator loses by fewer votes than his namesake receives, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion and whether voters mistakenly supported the wrong Sullivan.
The lawsuit cited the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law governing voter registration.
Nabors described the Justice Department’s intervention as “unusual” but said there could be circumstances in which federal action is justified.
“It’s perhaps not unreasonable,” he said, adding that federal intervention could be justified when an election is administered unfairly.
“Whether voters are confused and erroneously vote or not is a question that is hard to measure,” he added.
Wright questioned the basis of the lawsuit at all, however.
“The legal filing is either, you know, a filing in bad faith, or it’s a filing that misunderstands the way that Alaska’s election system operates,” he said.
How does Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system work?
Unlike most US states, Alaska allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference rather than voting for just one.
The four candidates with the most votes in the primary advance to the general election, regardless of party.
If nobody wins more than 50 percent of the first-choice votes, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated. Their votes are transferred to the next-ranked candidates still in the race. This continues until two candidates remain, and the one with the most votes wins.
Wright said the system helps prevent candidates with a smaller support base from splitting the vote.
“It’s supposed to eliminate the spoiler effect,” he explained.
For example, if a voter mistakenly chooses Daniel J Sullivan Jr but ranks the incumbent second, their vote could eventually transfer to the senator.
“The system is actually designed to cope with this sort of a thing,” Wright said.
However, voters are not required to rank every candidate, meaning some votes may not transfer.
Can the federal government block certification of the results?
The Justice Department may ask a federal court to intervene, but it may not independently stop Alaska from certifying the results.
The lawsuit seeks to delay certification if the Republican incumbent loses and votes cast for the other Dan Sullivan could have changed the outcome.
Derek Muller, an election law professor at the University of Notre Dame, questioned how officials would determine which candidate a voter intended to support.
“The best evidence that voters preferred one Sullivan over another is how they marked their ballots,” he wrote on the Election Law blog.
Muller also questioned the legal basis of the lawsuit.
The Justice Department cited the “findings and purposes” section of the National Voter Registration Act, which lists protecting “the integrity of the electoral process” among the law’s purposes.
But Muller argued that the department was treating that statement as a legal obligation, even though the law says nothing about which candidates may appear on a ballot.
He described the argument as “so absurdly thin” that there was “essentially no likelihood of success”.
He also questioned why the department had waited until days before the election to intervene when the dispute over the two candidates had been known for months.
Nabors said the case could still affect voters even if the courts do not decide it before election day.
“Whether the lawsuit is adjudicated in time, it will at least drive awareness of the problem among voters, which might limit the numbers of those who vote erroneously for the other Sullivan,” he told Al Jazeera.
No federal court has ordered Alaska to suspend certification.
What does this mean for the midterm elections?
Alaska’s Senate race could play a part in deciding which party controls the upper chamber of the US Congress.
Republicans now hold 53 of the Senate’s 100 seats while Democrats and two independents who caucus with them hold 47. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach 51 and secure a majority.
A 50-50 split would allow Vice President JD Vance to cast tie-breaking votes in the chamber.
“The defeat of Senator Sullivan would also take away an important senator from the Republican caucus. He has been influential in foreign policy and energy policy,” Nabors said.
Wright said the competitive race in such a traditionally Republican state reflects wider dissatisfaction with the Trump administration.
“The fact that the Alaska race has come to be competitive is a real indicator of how difficult the road is for a lot of Republican candidates in the current, kind of public opinion environment,” Wright said.
The lawsuit has also raised questions about whether the Trump administration could challenge certification in other states in which Republicans lose.
The Justice Department is already facing criticism over investigations and prosecutions involving Democratic opponents of Trump.
Federal agents have recently searched the home of Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar as part of an immigration fraud investigation. Omar has described the action as politically motivated.
Trump has acknowledged directing the Justice Department to file the Alaska lawsuit while his administration maintains that the action is intended to prevent voter confusion.

Interview: Xi's vision for global governance responds to changing world, says Tajik expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:10:41 CST
17:10:41 KST

DUSHANBE, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- The Global Governance Initiative (GGI) proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping reflects the objective transformation of the world system and responds to the aspirations of most countries for a more just and equitable system of global governance, said Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Ulmasov described the initiative as one of China's most significant initiatives in recent years, saying it came at a time when the existing global governance system was facing serious challenges.
"Geopolitical conflicts, sanctions and trade wars are intensifying, while the gap between developed and developing countries is widening. At the same time, existing international institutions are becoming increasingly inadequate in addressing global problems," Ulmasov said.
Against this backdrop, he said, reforming and improving global governance has become increasingly important to ensure that international institutions can better respond to emerging challenges and reflect the interests and concerns of countries around the world.
Ulmasov noted that the GGI builds on China's previously proposed Global Development Initiative, Global Security Initiative and Global Civilization Initiative.
"Together, they form a coherent Chinese vision for international development, based on the interconnection between development, security, dialogue among civilizations and the improvement of global governance," he said.
He stressed that global governance should be based on equality among countries and decision-making through consultation, which is in line with the core principles of the GGI.
In his view, effective global governance also requires countries with different political systems, civilizational traditions and national interests to strengthen dialogue and seek common ground while respecting their differences.
"The ability to build cooperation despite differences is one of the most important elements of modern multilateral governance," Ulmasov added. ■

====================================================================================================

Trump's foreign policy threatens Republicans in midterms as war, tariffs push costs up - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:07:10 UTC
17:07:10 KST

Foreign policy is rarely the deciding factor in US midterm elections, when economic considerations usually drive voters’ choices.
But this time, with Donald Trump’s war against Iran and his sweeping tariff campaign pushing up costs for Americans, a president’s approach to world affairs has itself become a pocketbook issue.
As the November 3 elections approach, there are growing signs that voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Trump and his fellow Republicans and imperiling their control of Congress.
Those include a Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showing some 78% of Americans blame Trump's policies for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings.
Not since 2006, when President George W. Bush’s Republicans lost both legislative chambers while he was mired in the unpopular Iraq war, has a US leader’s handling of international events appeared so central to shaping the midterms outcome.
The political backlash for Trump could be even bigger, with opinion polls showing that voters feel the economic pain from high gas prices and rising grocery bills in a way that they didn’t two decades ago.
“The bottom line is people are experiencing the impact of Trump’s war and other policies,” said Christopher Preble, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington. “Now voters have a chance to register their discontent with how he’s dealing with all this.”
Politics driving foreign policy
With Trump’s approval ratings touching historic lows, he has left little doubt, despite his public claims to the contrary, that he sees the straight line voters are drawing between his foreign policy and their cost of living.
That has prompted some controversial policy moves in the run-up to the elections.
Chief among them was Trump’s lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports aimed at bringing down fuel prices, a step his critics, including some fellow Republicans, say reinforces the impression that he is increasingly siding with Moscow in its war in Ukraine.
He has also pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian refineries as he tries to shift the blame for high US gasoline prices despite experts saying the surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the war he launched alongside Israel against Iran nearly eight months ago.
At the same time, he has promised not to order any new attack on Iran before the midterms, though the US and Israel are widely reported to be preparing for a possible major escalation after the elections.
Polls have shown that most voters oppose the war initiated by Trump, who had campaigned on avoiding new foreign interventions. He has insisted Americans should accept temporarily higher gas prices so that he can block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
Iran says its nuclear program is for civilian purposes. The UN nuclear watchdog and US intelligence community have assessed that Tehran shuttered a nuclear weapons development program in 2003.
Some Republican candidates have distanced themselves from Trump on matters ranging from the conflict in the Middle East to the trade war with Canada and his pressure campaign against Ukraine.
For its part, Iran has sought to keep oil prices high and hurt Trump in the midterms by deploying new tactics to target ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and deliberately prolonging the diplomatic stalemate, senior Iranian officials have told Reuters.
Defending the administration's approach, White House spokesman Matt Middleton said: "President Trump has always been clear about temporary market disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, but the contrast between President Trump’s economic record and Democrats’ ruinous alternative is clear."
'It's the economy, stupid'
Midterm elections historically have been seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent in the White House.
And in one election after another in recent decades, the conventional wisdom has been that economic concerns - “it’s the economy, stupid,” as the Clinton-era adage goes - dominate voters’ choices.
Opinion polls for this year’s midterms, including the Reuters/Ipsos survey, show that while voters rank foreign policy low on their list of priorities, it is clear that most Americans see some of Trump’s signature moves on the world stage, such as the Iran war and tariffs, feeding into their higher costs.
Other polls have shown that a majority of Americans have also soured more broadly on Trump’s international approach.
The Chicago Council on Global Affairs said its latest nationwide survey “finds that most Americans believe the Trump administration’s foreign policy actions have negatively impacted America’s global standing and hurt national and household economic conditions.”
Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped create from the ashes of World War Two while his relations with allies have steadily worsened and the limits of US power have been increasingly exposed, analysts say.
Legislative balance of power is in play
Against this backdrop, Democrats are widely projected to gain control of the House of Representatives in the midterms, with the Senate also seen as increasingly in play.
For Republicans, losing either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his second term.
But even with a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill on November 3, lawmakers will have a hard time reining in Trump’s capacity to pursue foreign policy as he sees fit.
Once the ballots are counted, a big question will be whether Trump will feel either restricted or emboldened on the world stage as he enters what is traditionally considered a lame-duck phase - when a president is barred from running again and no longer faces electoral consequences for decisions made.
“For many presidents who feel politically constrained (at home), foreign policy is the area where they are able to act with relative freedom,” said Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington.
Analysts say Trump's handling of adversaries such as Iran, Russia, China, and even Cuba, or his approach to allies across the globe could go either way - or he could simply lose interest and double down on his string of construction projects, such as the White House ballroom.
