Will this election end the battle over drafting haredi men into the Israeli army? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:06:48 UTC
17:06:48 KST

Whether to extend military conscription to haredi men, a longstanding question fueling political tensions in Israel, has boiled over since Hamas launched the current war with Israel with its deadly raids on Oct. 7, 2023.
Hundreds of thousands of Israeli soldiers and reservists battled on Israel’s southern and northern fronts and the manpower needs, especially in combat units, increased dramatically. Reservists served for extended periods and many of those serving in the standing army were forced to remain for an extra four months or longer – at an enormous price to soldiers’ families and to Israel’s economy. For the ultra-Orthodox, the Torah study that young men carry out in place of military service provides an important spiritual defense for the Jewish state. Community leaders are extremely fearful that young men will be unable to practice or outright abandon a haredi lifestyle as a result of army service with secular and modern Orthodox Jews.
In some parts of the country, families continue to bury their dead from the battlefield, while in others Haredi protestors block roads and tussle with police to avoid the draft. The preferred political solution of kicking the can down the road on this deeply divisive issue – which has lingered in legislative limbo for decades – might finally come to an end with the Oct. 27 elections.
Which Israelis are currently drafted to the army, and what are their conditions of service?
Most Jewish Israeli men and women are subject to compulsory service at age 18. Men currently serve 32 months, and women generally serve 24, although some roles require longer service. Conscripts are generally allowed to defer service for a year or two in order to attend pre-military programs. Exemptions for service may apply for medical, religious, family or other legally recognized reasons. Druze and Circassian men are generally drafted, while Israeli Arabs are generally not. Conscripts who ignore draft orders are subject to sanctions that can ultimately lead to imprisonment.
Upon completion of compulsory service, most soldiers are placed in reserve units and are called up periodically for training and for active duty in wartime. Reserve duty is generally mandatory until age 40 for non-officers and 45 for officers. Enforcement of a call-up order for reserve duty is traditionally less severe than enforcement of compulsory service; sanctions against reservists who avoid call-ups are rare.
Following the outbreak of war on Oct. 7, hundreds of thousands of reservists were called up for extended periods. Between the outbreak of war and the end of 2025, some 28% of male reservists and 20% of female reservists served for over 150 days. Current IDF policy allows for up to 55 days of reserve duty per year for combat soldiers, compared to a cap of 54 days over three years (18 days per year on average) prior to the war.
Are haredim legally exempt from IDF service?
No. Historically, a small number of full-time haredi yeshiva students were allowed to defer service until they aged out of eligibility, amounting to a de facto exemption. As the share of Haredim in the population grew, so did legal challenges to their exemption, on grounds of inequality. Since June 2023, there are no longer any legal exemptions in place for haredim, and all haredi men face the same legal requirement to enlist as non-haredim.
What is the mainstream haredi approach to IDF service?
Haredim generally oppose IDF service, although recently some small groups of modernizing haredim appear more open to it. Haredi officials and spiritual leaders argue the Torah study that young men carry out in place of military service provides an important spiritual defense for the Jewish state. At the same time, haredi community leaders view the IDF as a bastion of secularism and are fearful that haredi men will not be able to maintain their lifestyle during service.
Historically, how did the draft exemption for haredi men begin?
In 1948, Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion agreed to exempt about 400 yeshiva students so Torah scholarship could be rebuilt after the Holocaust. The arrangement expanded gradually, as the military and political leadership tolerated the arrangement for practical and coalition-building reasons. In 1977, Menachem Begin’s government removed important limits on the haredi exemption. As a result, the number of draft-age haredi men outside the army grew from roughly 7,000 in the late 1970s to tens of thousands by the 2020s.
When did opposition to the exemption first arise?
Opposition grew sharply in the 1980s and 1990s as the haredi IDF exemption grew significantly. Legal challenges to the exemption were initially rebuffed by the court, but were eventually successful, as the Supreme Court in 1998 first deemed the exemption illegal and ruled that such an exemption needed to be anchored in legislation that met constitutional standards of equality.
Following the 1998 ruling, how did ensuing coalitions deal with this issue?
The two decades following the 1998 ruling saw various legislative and policy proposals aimed at increasing haredi enlistment. Two laws passed in 2002 and 2014, but both were eventually struck down by the court on grounds of inequality, as they still enabled widespread haredi exemptions. The second law was struck down in 2017, but the court approved numerous extension requests by the government for the provisions of the law to continue to apply until it could come up with a new law. This left the de-facto exemption in place until the law finally expired in June 2023.
Why did coalitions keep trying to exempt significant numbers of haredim instead of drafting them?
First, haredi parties wield significant political power. In recent decades they have usually occupied 15-20 seats in the 120-member Israeli Knesset, and since 2009 have been part of Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc, save for two years (2013-2015). Governments have been wary of enlisting haredim en masse so as not to lose the support of haredi politicians.
Second, the IDF has not always been keen on drafting haredim. Haredim require special accommodations in terms of Kashrut and mixed-gender military bases. Haredim also go through an autonomous education system, and special efforts are required to instill in them the motivation and sense of duty that are prevalent in general Israeli society.
So have any haredim served in the IDF in recent decades?
Yes, some specific programs have opened up for haredim, mainly in technology-oriented units. The number of annual haredi draftees has fluctuated, but in the years leading up to the expiration of the draft law, the average was slightly over 1,000.
What changed in the IDF’s perspective and the perspective of the general public after Oct. 7?
The mass call-up of reservists for extended periods of time brought many Israelis to experience the inequality between them and the haredi public firsthand. In addition, the expansion of the war to numerous fronts and new security requirements led to a manpower shortage in the IDF, especially of combat soldiers. Officials have described the shortfall as a national-security issue, and the roughly 100,000 Haredi men aged 18 to 29 are viewed as the only large available pool of potential combat recruits. Researchers have also pointed out that without a new policy, the inequality in Israeli society will continue to grow – by 2050 over 40% of the 18-year-old potential male Jewish recruits will be haredi.
What was the outgoing Netanyahu government’s policy after Oct. 7?
The government did not implement significant policy changes to begin drafting haredim in significant numbers, and refrained from instituting sanctions that could have increased the price of draft evasion. The government’s inaction was challenged in court, and the Supreme Court ruled in June 2024 that barring a new law, the continued exemption was illegal. However, the government has continued to push back on attempts by the Attorney General, who leads Israel’s law enforcement apparatus, to abide by the ruling and begin taking measures to increase haredi draft numbers. The government argued in its defense that it was working on a new law, which required time.
Did the government pass a new law?
No. The Netanyahu government attempted to pass a new law that would have incrementally increased haredi draft numbers while enabling the majority of haredim to remain exempt. The attempts failed due to pushback from legal authorities, the political opposition, the general public, and a number of politicians from within the coalition. Instead, in July 2026, in the final weeks of parliamentary activity prior to the election recess, the Netanyahu-led coalition passed a law to freeze enforcement against haredi draft evaders until after the election. On September 3rd, the Supreme Court struck down this law as well.
So haredi draft numbers have remained at pre-war levels?
No. In order to abide by the 2024 Supreme Court ruling and the Attorney General’s interpretation of that ruling, government officials working within the different ministries removed certain subsidies and privileges from draft evaders, and the police and IDF gradually increased their enforcement efforts. The number of haredi draftees rose as a result. Between July 2025 and the end of June 2026, some 4,298 haredim enlisted, as opposed to 2,811 haredim in the parallel period in 2024-25.
How have haredi rabbis, politicians and the general public responded to growing demands that they enlist?
Leading rabbis affiliated with the three main haredi parties – the non-Hasidic Degel Hatorah party, the Hasidic Agudat Yisrael party and the Sephardic Shas party – forcefully opposed IDF service, with some explicitly calling on young haredi men to ignore draft orders should they receive them. Politicians from the three parties also voiced strong opposition to a large increase in haredi draftees, and were willing only to consider minor increases.
A large majority of haredim who received draft orders ignored them, and approximately 90,000 haredi men are legally considered draft evaders, with levels of severity increasing the longer they ignore the orders. Some arrests of draft evaders were met by mass protests and disturbances, including in recent weeks. Some more modernized haredim have increasingly expressed a willingness to serve. These views are represented in two new haredi parties participating in the current election, called Hakahal (roughly translated as “the community”) and Hatzibur Haharedi (“the haredi public”).
Is the haredi draft issue prominent in the election campaigns?
Yes. In a recent poll by the Israel Democracy Institute, a proposition that the next government should draft haredim equally received the most support among a series of propositions. Nearly all of the Zionist opposition parties have made their intention to increase the haredi draft a prominent part of their campaigns. Some opposition party leaders have attempted to frame the election as a choice between the “draft evasion bloc” and the “bloc that serves.” On the other hand, some haredi rabbis and party leaders have expressed their disappointment with Netanyahu’s failure to manufacture a new exemption, and have stated that they no longer view themselves as part of the Netanyahu bloc. However, they have not stated support for any other candidate and are likely to side with Netanyahu again if he is able to form a new government.
What are the most likely scenarios after the next government is formed?
Three outcomes are plausible:
A compromise: full-time Torah scholars receive a narrow exemption, while others perform military or civilian service under threat of sanctions.
Continued stalemate: the government delays enforcement, leading to further court battles and coalition crises.
Broad enforcement: a government less dependent on haredi parties implements substantially wider enlistment.
The first scenario is probably the most politically workable, but the details will determine whether the courts accept it.

Marine from Mykolaiv region returns from Russian captivity after more than four years
The marine’s mother, Hanna Ivanivna, told a Ukrinform correspondent about this.
“When they called me yesterday and told me that Yevhen had returned… We had been waiting for this for so long that I was both overjoyed and in disbelief. I was overwhelmed with emotions that are hard to put into words,” the woman said.
His mother added that she never doubted her son’s return. Just two days ago, she sent him a letter—one she had been putting off writing for some reason, perhaps sensing something on a subconscious level.
Yevhen Uimanov had been held captive since April 12, 2022. In civilian life, he was a construction worker, but on the first day of the full-scale invasion, he went to the military registration and enlistment office, just like three other members of his family—his father, his sister’s husband, and his father-in-law. He was assigned to the 36th Marine Brigade.
“On February 28, he called home and said he was in the Donetsk region, near Volnovakha. Later, we found out that they were defending Mariupol. Then there was another call—on the night of March 17. To call us, he had to climb onto the roof of a high-rise building. That’s when the connection was lost,” said the Marine’s mother.
Lilia, Yevhen’s sister, constantly searched the internet for any news about her family. After all, her husband, Oleksandr Shepelya, and her father, Hennadii Uimanov—who served in the 79th Airborne Assault Brigade and were also defending the Donetsk region—went missing at the same time as her brother. She found a video of our marines who had been taken prisoner near the Ilyich Mariupol Metallurgical Plant and recognized her brother by the backpack that Yevhen had taken from his son when he went to war. Later, Lilia found a photo online of the prisoner holding a tag with his last name and date of birth. Although he looked very gaunt and was wearing dirty clothes, his family was certain it was Yevhenii.
“The first message from him came as early as 2023. We wrote him many letters, but they took 7–9 months to arrive, and not all of them made it. At first, his messages were very short, but lately he’s started writing a little more. He said he missed us very much and wanted chocolate and condensed milk. And in one of his most recent letters, he even wrote that he already had a business plan, and when he returned home, he would need my help to put it into action,” said Anna Ivanivna.
Her son-in-law and husband, as it turned out later, were also taken prisoner in April 2022. Her husband returned home as a result of a prisoner exchange in June 2025; her son-in-law remains in captivity.
The fate of another relative, Arkady, Yevgeny’s father-in-law, remains unknown; he is considered missing in action.
As reported by Ukrinform, 270 Ukrainians returned to Ukraine on October 23 as a result of a prisoner-of-war exchange.

Sonia Gandhi recalls meeting Rajiv Gandhi in Cambridge

Most defence tech firms report a declining market
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:00:52 BST
17:00:52 KST

Seventy-three per cent of defence-oriented technology firms surveyed said the market had declined, eighty-seven per cent had been hit by funding delays and reductions, and ninety-three per cent were reassessing investment or recruitment in the sector, according to evidence given to the Defence Committee.
Julian David, chief executive of techUK, was giving evidence on the implications of the Defence Investment Plan for British industry.
He said: “Last time we were here, we reported on our survey of members, and 73% said that the market has declined; that was in May. Funding delays and reductions have hit 87% of respondents, and 93% of them are now reassessing investment or recruitment of people to focus in this sector.”
David said members had expected the opposite when the plan was published, telling the committee: “From a tech point of view, defence-oriented tech members expected, therefore, that there would be a big uptick in the focus on tech and that orders would flow, particularly to SMEs. We have not found that to be the case.” He added that techUK had checked again with members since the survey and “they have not really seen a lot of progress.”
On the effect on smaller firms he said: “The problem, particularly from an SME point of view, is that they live off the cash flow. If there is no cash flow or no predictable path to cash, they are going to either try to find markets elsewhere or cut back and wait and see.”
David also raised departmental staffing, saying: “I would highlight the fact that, in terms of delivery, the MOD is still not properly staffed in order to deal with procurement, particularly of new things and from smaller companies. Sometimes that is disguised, in that one commercial team’s headcount is 70%, with a gap of 30%, but 40% of the team is filled by contractors who cannot fulfil the whole process of sign-off authority.”
Arnab Dutt of the Federation of Small Businesses gave figures from his own organisation’s research, telling MPs that only thirteen per cent of small businesses use pipeline documentation to find public opportunities, against twenty-eight per cent who use active procurement platforms, and that sixty-two per cent of small businesses looking for public sector contracts report that finding suitable opportunities is difficult.
Dutt said: “Another awful piece of research is that 19% of companies that have already engaged with the MOD said that they will not be doing so again because of the systemic barriers and the level of hard work and engagement. Among that 19%, there could be some brilliant businesses, so that is another issue.”
He told the committee that the Federation had received minimal consultation on the plan, describing it as the organisation’s main bugbear since publication.
David told MPs that of £7.5 billion of small and medium-sized enterprise spend by May 2028, only £2 billion is direct and £5.5 billion indirect, and that the department tracks progress without committing or delivering. He said what is needed is targets and performance indicators for the people doing the procurement, measured as they go, “as opposed to waiting until the end of 2028 and then asking whether it happened.”
He also raised the departmental definition of a small or medium-sized enterprise, which differs from the one in the Procurement Act and the fair payment code, meaning firms used to reporting one way now have to report another.

Spain tests new anti-drone systems at army exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:58:40 UTC
16:58:40 KST

- EM&E Group used remote weapon stations on 4x4 and 6x6 vehicles and a jamming robot to down drones at Spain’s ATLAS 26 exercise.
- The systems were shown as configurations of ARACNE, the counter-drone system EM&E is developing with Indra for the Spanish Armed Forces.
Spanish defense company EM&E Group used remote weapon stations on armored vehicles and a jamming-equipped ground robot to detect and shoot down several drones during the Spanish military’s ATLAS 26 counter-drone exercise this week at the Médano del Loro firing range in Huelva, in southwestern Spain.
The exercise was led by Spain’s Chief of the Defence Staff, organized by the Maneuver Support Command and directed by the Spanish Army’s Anti-Aircraft Artillery Command. EM&E, formerly known as Escribano Mechanical & Engineering, said it took part with several configurations of ARACNE, the counter-drone system it is developing with Indra Group through a joint venture.
Two 4×4 tactical vehicles took part fitted with EM&E’s GUARDIAN 2.0 remote weapon station as a hard-kill option, meaning they physically destroy drones with gunfire instead of disrupting them electronically. The company also fielded its FEROX 6×6 armored vehicle carrying the GUARDIAN L-HIT remote station, which it uses to both detect and engage drones, and deployed its AUNAV LINK robotic vehicle with an integrated electronic warfare package that jams the radio links between a drone and its operator to block or distort its communications.
EM&E said the systems detected and shot down several drones during the exercise, without giving numbers or details of the targets.
ARACNE is one of the Spanish Armed Forces’ main counter-drone programs. The roughly 30.24 million euro ($34 million) effort covers 14 systems for the military, seven fixed and seven mobile, intended to protect critical infrastructure and military convoys, with mobile versions mounted on Vamtac ST5 tactical vehicles. The system pairs Indra’s sensors and command software with EM&E hardware, including a SmartEar radio-frequency scanner that monitors frequencies from 400 MHz to 6 GHz within about 6 km (3.7 miles) and an EM&E electro-optical station that can spot targets more than 14 km (8.7 miles) away with its daylight camera and up to 23.1 km (14.4 miles) with its thermal channel.
Indra and EM&E also demonstrated ARACNE at last year’s ATLAS 25 exercise, held at the same Huelva range from Oct. 20 to 24, 2025, where Indra said the system’s command and control software stood out for its ability to combine data from its own sensors and third-party sensors. A counter-drone system that Indra continues to develop under the ARACNE project also protects the Spanish contingent deployed with NATO in Lithuania, and Indra said in March 2026 that it had drawn interest from several countries on the alliance’s eastern flank.
The ATLAS exercises bring together Spanish military units and industry to test systems for detecting, identifying and defeating drones, and EM&E’s demonstrations this year added ground robotics and electronic warfare to the gun-based options shown on its vehicles.

Typhoon Champi left over 146,000 households without power in Taiwan: Report

Amir Latif Arain
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
More than 146,000 households across Taiwan experienced power outages as Typhoon Champi brought strong winds and heavy rain, local media reported Saturday.
Electricity was restored to over 122,000 households by Friday night, while repair crews began work early Saturday in parts of New Taipei and northern Keelung, which experienced strong gusts overnight, Focus Taiwan reported.
Authorities also dispatched 15 work teams from five regional offices in central and southern Taiwan to support restoration efforts in the north.
At least one person was killed and dozens of others were injured Friday as the typhoon disrupted air traffic.
Authorities ordered schools and offices to close across Taiwan, except in Taitung County and on the outlying islands of Penghu and Matsu, due to the typhoon.
Taiwan's Central Weather Administration said Champi was over waters east of Yilan and was expected to weaken into a mild typhoon Saturday afternoon.
The weather agency also expected to lift land and sea typhoon warnings by Saturday evening.
Rainfall shifted westward Saturday after affecting northern and eastern Taiwan the previous day.
Heavy rain fell in mountainous areas south of Hsinchu early Saturday, with localized torrential rain reported in mountainous areas of Miaoli.
Rainfall is expected to ease gradually in the afternoon, although localized heavy rain remained possible north of Taichung.
The weather agency warned that seas around Taiwan remained rough despite Champi's weakening, with waves reaching 2 to 3 meters (6.6 to 9.8 feet).
Waves exceeding 6 meters (19.7 feet) could still occur in northern and northeastern waters Saturday.

Israel prepares large-scale West Bank operation following deadly Hebron attack
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has announced plans for a major military operation in the occupied West Bank after two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers near Hebron on Friday, days before Israel's general election, a Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
According to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), the attackers opened fire on soldiers stationed at Judea Junction north of Hebron, killing Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman, 23, and Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem, 20. Three other soldiers sustained minor injuries. Both gunmen were killed by Israeli forces, who subsequently discovered a large quantity of weapons and ammunition in their vehicle. The military said the findings suggested the attackers had been preparing a larger assault targeting civilians.
Following the shooting, Netanyahu ordered Israeli forces to cordon off Hebron and prepare for a possible closure of the entire West Bank. Speaking during a visit to the area alongside Defense Minister Israel Katz, he announced plans for an extensive military campaign, describing its potential scale as unprecedented since the Six-Day War of 1967.
"The IDF is ready to carry it out, and we will determine the timing, but it is coming," Netanyahu said.
The prime minister also outlined plans to evacuate Palestinian residents from the Hebron neighborhood where he said the attackers had lived, conduct house-to-house searches and demolish buildings suspected of supporting militant activity. He compared the proposed measures to Israeli military operations in the Jenin and Tulkarm refugee camps in 2025, which displaced tens of thousands of Palestinians. Israeli bulldozers began demolishing buildings near the shooting site on Friday, although residents disputed claims that the properties were connected to the attackers.
Netanyahu identified the gunmen as Hamas militants, although their organizational affiliation has not been independently established. Hamas praised the attack, describing it as a legitimate response to Israeli military operations and settlement activity in Palestinian territories, but did not formally claim responsibility. The group also called for continued armed resistance against Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for a broader military campaign targeting armed Palestinian groups and the Palestinian Authority, advocating measures similar to those employed in Gaza and Lebanon. His remarks came amid increasing tensions in the West Bank, where Israeli settlement expansion and attacks by settlers against Palestinians have intensified in recent months. During his visit, Netanyahu praised Israeli settlers and highlighted the establishment and legalization of more than 100 settlements, alongside the development of additional agricultural outposts. Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are widely considered illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes.
The developments come four days before Israel's October 27 general election, the first since the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023. Netanyahu faces a challenge from former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party has led the ruling Likud party in several recent opinion polls. However, the final surveys published ahead of the election indicate that neither Netanyahu's political bloc nor the main opposition parties have secured a projected majority of 61 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
National security and the future of Israel's military operations in Gaza and the West Bank have featured prominently in the election campaign. On October 15, Eisenkot pledged that, if elected, he would remove Hamas from power in Gaza within 18 months, either through the U.S.-backed peace and reconstruction process or through renewed military action. The latest violence in Hebron has brought the West Bank security situation into sharper focus as Israelis prepare to vote.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Israeli President Isaac Herzog on the sidelines of the Seventh CICA Summit in Baku, where they discussed the situation in the Middle East and the importance of diplomatic efforts to ease regional tensions.

Russian-Indian BrahMos missile is getting future-ready

Russian-Indian BrahMos missile is getting future-ready
The BrahMos corporation is working to add more destructive power and reach to its namesake supersonic cruise missile, following its spectacular combat successes last year.
The operational and functional parameters of the missile are being upgraded, and new versions are in the works, the CEO and managing director of the joint venture between India and Russia, Jaiteerth Joshi, told local media recently.
Named after the Brahmaputra and Moskva rivers, the BrahMos is engineered for high-precision, long-range strikes. The missile offers militaries the versatility to engage threats using land, sea, and underwater platforms.
BrahMos earned its stripes last year when the Indian and Pakistani militaries briefly clashed with missiles and drones, following a terrorist attack on civilians in India’s Jammu and Kashmir state.
As the two militaries tested each other with drones, India fired BrahMos missiles to strike hardened high-value targets, including hangars reportedly housing Pakistan’s US-made F-16 fighter jets.
India has said there was not a single interception of the BrahMos during the clashes, dubbed Operation Sindoor, and buyer interest has risen since.
BrahMos Aerospace is a joint venture between India’s DRDO and Russia’s NPO Mashinostroyeniya.
BrahMos’ trajectory into the future
BrahMos started as a land-launched cruise missile, but its developers have worked to give it more flexibility and lethality as battlefield needs evolved and expanded.
The missile, which flies at nearly three times the speed of sound and carries a 200 to 300 kg warhead, had an initial range of 290 km but continuous upgrades have extended its reach.
In 2023, the Indian Air Force (IAF) successfully tested a version with a 450 km range. Mated to the Su-30MKI fighter, this variant, called the BrahMos-A, offers the IAF a standoff precision strike capability that few air forces in the world can match.
There is also a Block III land-attack variant, which can fly very low and approach targets from unexpected angles – dodging any defenses the enemy may try to throw at it.
The BrahMos corporation is working on a long and ambitious list of upgrades. At the top of the current development efforts sits a lighter, air-launched variant.
Christened the BrahMos-NG, it can be flown on the IAF’s other fighter jets, including the domestically produced Tejas light combat aircraft. The Su-30MKI will be able to sortie armed with three of these missiles.
The BrahMos-NG will feature higher domestically-produced content and advanced materials. The Indo-Russian joint venture expects to unveil this prototype by 2027-28.
The BrahMos corporation is also working on a very long-range missile. This version would be able to strike targets up to 1,500 km away, far more than the 290 km range of the original missile unveiled in the early 2000s.
This long-range version is at the conceptual stage, and the company is discussing further upgrades with its Russian joint venture partner. Joshi has told Indian media outlets in recent interviews that the range-extension program will proceed in phases, with test firings from land, sea, and air to validate the missile’s operational capabilities.
Also, on the missile maker’s drawing board is a hypersonic version – the new frontier of modern warfare – currently called BrahMos II.
The concept aims to integrate advanced technologies, state-of-the-art design, and smart materials to field a hypersonic futuristic weapon that will dominate fast-evolving battlefield technology.
BrahMos II will have an “air-breathing” scramjet engine that would boost it to a top speed of Mach 5.
BrahMos is seeing high global interest
The missile has already been sold to multiple countries, and many others have shown an interest in buying it.
One of the first foreign customers of the Indo-Russian missile was the Philippines, with Manila signing a $375 million contract in 2022. The first batch of BrahMos missiles was delivered to the country in April 2024, and the second in April 2025.
In June this year, India confirmed it had a deal with Vietnam to supply the missiles.
Indonesia, which has also evinced interest, has moved forward with procurement plans.
In addition, over a dozen nations including Malaysia, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Chile, and South Africa have evaluated or expressed a formal interest in the BrahMos missile system.
BrahMos is gearing up for a demand surge
The BrahMos project is a trailblazer in India’s defense industry. It broke the shackles of excessive bureaucratic controls that were once the hallmark of Indian state-owned defense corporations that had forced the country to remain a major arms importer.
Effective management and the synergizing of commercial viability, strike capabilities, and indigenization have helped the missile become the battlefield success it is, whie making inroads into the global arms market.
With a burgeoning order book, BrahMos corporation is prioritizing the fulfillment of orders received from the Indian armed forces, for whom the missile is a primary strike weapon. India recently contracted for more BrahMos launchers and fire-control systems, so more of its warships can be armed with the missile.
The missile maker now has production facilities in four Indian cities: Hyderabad, Nagpur, Pilani and Lucknow. Research and development clusters, nicknamed ‘tech-bricks’ have been set up to work on niche technologies for the next generation missiles.
The supply chain is being expanded to make it more robust and resilient – and to meet an expected surge in demand. For this, the company will expand the industry partners for each system and subsystem to up to 45, from the current one or two partners.
India’s arms export ambitions ride on BrahMos
New Delhi is gradually setting its sights to make a complete transformation from being one of the biggest arms importers to a major defense exporter.
It also simultaneously wants to see more domestically produced components and technology being used in its products. Indian defense exports registered an impressive 67% annual growth to reach $4 billion in the financial year ended March.
The federal government’s annual defense production target is $31 billion by 2029, of which defense exports are pegged at $5.5 billion.
BrahMos will be key to New Delhi’s ambitious goals to emerge as a major global arms exporter.

'Will not sign': AISA chief Neha Bora defies Delhi police peace bond notice after HC setback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:47:15 UTC
16:47:15 KST

NEW DELHI: All India Students' Association president Neha Bora on Saturday said she would not sign a bond to "keep peace" before a special executive magistrate, a day after the Delhi high court dismissed her plea challenging the police notice directing her to furnish a Rs 10,000 bond with a surety."We don't have any conditions. We are not going to sign the bond," Bora said.Bora had moved the high court, arguing that the notice was vague, factually incorrect and unsupported by material establishing the likelihood of a breach of peace.She alleged that the proceedings were a "colourable exercise of preventive powers to suppress peaceful dissent, in violation of Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(b) and 21 of Constitution".During Thursday's hearing, Bora's counsel argued that citizens did not need permission to hoist the national flag, referring to the police notice alleging that she had hoisted it without valid permission.The notice, issued on October 17 under Section 126 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), directed Bora to appear before the magistrate on October 19 and explain why she should not execute a personal bond of Rs 10,000 with one surety "for keeping peace for a period of enquiry".
Bora was taken into preventive detention on October 16 while on her way to participate in the Cockroach Janata Party's (CJP) 'Lehra Do Tiranga' march at Central Park in Connaught Place. She was released the following day.According to her petition, the police initiated proceedings over alleged sloganeering at Mandi House on October 16, repeated protests around Jantar Mantar despite prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, and allegations that she had instigated people to join a demonstration at Connaught Place that day.
"The impugned notice rests on a prima facie incorrect fact, namely that the petitioner instigated people to participate in the demonstration at Central Park, CP on Oct 16. The petitioner's call and the incident alleged were different. The petitioner called for a peaceful gathering at Mandi House at 5.00 pm on Oct 16, and it is a matter of record that she was detained from Mandi House," Bora's petition stated.

His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

The Embassy in Athens celebrates Italian Cuisine Week Around the World
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:46:48 CEST
16:46:48 KST

The Italian Embassy in Athens dedicated the eleventh edition of Italian Cuisine Week in the World to Lombardy’s culinary and wine excellence, celebrating this year’s recognition of Italian cuisine as a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.
                                    
The event, held in collaboration with the ICE Office in Athens and the Lombardy Region—whose delegation was led by the Regional Councilor for Agriculture, Food Sovereignty and Forests—featured fifteen consortia from the region and their wines, cheeses, and cured meats, guardians of traditional excellence and promoters of their local areas.
                                    
Chef Stefano Grandi of the “Il Santa” restaurant in Milan traveled from Italy to showcase the flavors of Lombard cuisine through original menus as part of a comprehensive program of events.
                                    
Ambassador Paolo Cuculi’s residence hosted a gala dinner attended by prominent figures from Greek institutions and the Greek economic and cultural spheres, including Minister of Tourism Kefalogianni, the President of the Greece-Italy Parliamentary Friendship Group, Ypsilantis; the Governor of the Revenue Agency, Pitsilis; and some of Greece’s leading shipowners and entrepreneurs.
                                    
The program continued with an event for industry professionals and media representatives at the Italian restaurant “Sole Giaguaro” in Athens.
                                    
The Ambassador’s Residence then hosted the “Journey to Lombardy Food Excellence” reception, attended by over 300 guests, including Deputy Minister of the Environment and Energy Soukouli Viliali, President of the Council of State Pikrameos, National Security Advisor Dokos, and representatives from institutions, the business community, the cultural sector, and the media, all of whom expressed unanimous appreciation for the variety and quality of the food and wine served.
                                    
Chef Grandi also held a masterclass at the IEK-AKMI School of Gastronomy and Tourism in Athens, demonstrating techniques and recipes from Lombard cuisine to an audience of students.
                                    
As emphasized by Councilor Beduschi and Ambassador Cuculi during the various events,  Italian Cuisine Week in Athens laid the groundwork for raising the profile of Lombard and Italian food and wine products and brands in a market where Italian exports in the agri-food sector already exceed one billion euros annually.
                                    
The event also highlighted other Italian companies of the highest caliber, such as Campari, Ferrero, Lavazza, and Barilla.
                                    
The following organizations participated in the initiative: Provolone Valpadana Protection Consortium; Grana Padano Protection Consortium; Gorgonzola Protection Consortium; Taleggio Protection Consortium; Quartirolo Lombardo Protection Consortium; Salva Cremasco Protection Consortium; the Valtellina Casera and Bitto Protection Consortium; the Bresaola della Valtellina Protection Consortium; the Cacciatore Italiano Protection Consortium; the Lugana DOC Wines Protection Consortium; the Valtènesi Wines Consortium; the Oltrepò Pavese Wines Protection Consortium; Franciacorta Protection Consortium; Mantua Wines Protection Consortium; Valtellina Wines Protection Consortium; AS.CO.VI.LO. – Association of Lombard Wine Consortia; Antoniazzi Pastry Shop; Riserva San Massimo; Menini Pasta Factory.

granite, plaster, and steel define oroco studio’s 40-sqm apartment renovation in madrid
through a restrained palette of granite, plaster and steel, the project explores how simplicity, materiality and spatial continuity can transform a compact home into an open, cohesive and characterful living space.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
OROCO STUDIO RECONFIGURES 40-SQM APARTMENT IN MADRID
RS19 is the renovation of a 40-sqm apartment in Madrid’s Palacio neighborhood, designed by OROCO Studio. Conceived as a first home, the project explores how a limited surface can accommodate everyday life while creating a sense of openness and spatial generosity. The intervention rethinks the existing layout to establish a more fluid relationship between spaces, prioritising continuity, functionality and the perception of depth. Rather than relying on an abundance of partitions or decorative gestures, the design seeks to achieve more with less, allowing the architecture and its material qualities to define the character of the interior.
GRANITE, PLASTER, AND STEEL ANCHOR RESTRAINED MATERIAL PALETTE
A restrained palette of granite, plaster, and steel forms the foundation of the project by Oroco Studio. These materials were selected for their simplicity, durability, and inherent character. Their contrasting textures bring depth to the interior while maintaining a coherent visual language. Plaster provides a quiet, continuous backdrop, while granite introduces a sense of solidity and steel adds precision and contrast. The design approach centers on the idea that a small home does not need to feel constrained by its dimensions.
MATERIAL TRANSITIONS BALANCE AUSTERITY AND WARMTH
Careful attention to proportions, material transitions, and the relationship between individual elements allows the apartment to feel more generous without compromising its practical needs. Each material and architectural decision contributes to a balance between austerity and warmth. Rather than pursuing a predetermined decorative style, RS19 embraces a direct and understated approach to domestic space. The result is a home where materiality, spatial clarity, and everyday functionality come together to create an intimate environment with a distinct identity.
project info:
name: RS19
architect: Oroco | @oroco.studio
location: Madrid, Spain

Second batch of Finnish F-35s arrives in Rovaniemi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:45:32 UTC
16:45:32 KST

- Finnish F-35As JF-509 and JF-511 arrived in Rovaniemi on Oct. 23, 2026, bringing the number of Finnish F-35s in Finland to four.
- JF-511 had stayed in the Azores since September with a minor avionics fault before rejoining the second ferry flight.
Two more F-35A Lightning II stealth fighters arrived in Finland on Oct. 23, 2026, landing at the Lapland Air Wing in Rovaniemi at 5:56 p.m. and bringing the number of Finnish F-35s in the country to four, the Finnish Defence Forces said.
The jets, JF-509 and JF-511, made up Finland’s second F-35 delivery. JF-509 left Lockheed Martin’s plant in Fort Worth, Texas, on Oct. 20 and stopped at Lajes Air Base in the Azores, Portugal, where JF-511 joined the detachment for the final leg. JF-511 had been part of Finland’s first ferry flight in September but stayed behind in the Azores with a minor avionics fault and waited there for the next available ferry flight.
One of the new arrivals carries a nod to Finnish Air Force history. The outer surfaces of JF-511’s vertical stabilizers feature the bison emblem of Fighter Squadron 11, the Rovaniemi-based squadron that flies Finland’s F/A-18 Hornets and is now converting to the F-35.
Finland is buying its jets through the U.S. Foreign Military Sales program, which shapes how they travel. The U.S. government accepts each aircraft at the factory, where ownership passes to Finland, but the jet stays under U.S. control until it reaches Finland, and the United States plans and runs the ferry flights. Those long transatlantic flights need aerial refueling, so the F-35s typically travel in multi-aircraft detachments with tankers and fighters from other nations. Finland’s first two jets, JF-510 and JF-512, were flown by U.S. Air Force pilots and supported by two KC-135 Stratotankers from the 100th Air Refueling Wing at RAF Mildenhall when they arrived on Sept. 18.
Finland has ordered 64 F-35As to replace its fleet of 55 F/A-18C and seven F/A-18D Hornets. Most of the Finnish F-35s built so far remain in the United States to support Finnish pilot and maintainer training at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida and Ebbing Air National Guard Base in Arkansas, which continues until early 2028.
The program is also building an industrial base at home. Finnish defense company Patria assembles F-35 forward fuselage sections in Jämsä and on Sept. 3, 2026, presented the first F135 engine assembled in Finland at its new facility in Nokia.
JF-509 and JF-511 will now go through airworthiness and acceptance inspections carried out by the Finnish Air Force and the Defence Forces Logistics Command, and each jet will receive an individual certificate of airworthiness before it can be used for training. Maintenance training at Rovaniemi is set to begin in late 2026, and pilot training on Finnish soil is planned to start in January 2027.
The Lapland Air Wing is scheduled to fly only F-35s from early 2028, which is also Finland’s initial operational capability milestone, while the Karelia Air Wing near Kuopio is set to receive its first aircraft in 2028 and full operational capability is planned for late 2030.

Elsewhere in his remarks, the head of the Judiciary elaborated on how to strengthen social capital during wartime, stating, "Social capital, and the issue of public trust is of paramount importance. The people are the foundation of the Islamic Establishment, so, the question of how to preserve and bolster this social capital is a critical matter.”
He described enhancing public resilience and resistance during wartime as a highly significant and strategic matter, noting that the enemy, in its hybrid warfare, seeks to infiltrate the social, psychological, and economic structures of society and turn the minds and collective will of Iranian people into a target.
Under such circumstances, increasing the level of public resilience is a critical imperative and must rank among the top priorities for any government, the Judiciary chief underlined.

L3Harris to develop long-range drone killer for U.S. Army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:37:45 UTC
16:37:45 KST

- L3Harris received a three-year contract worth up to $60 million to develop a long-range ramjet-powered drone interceptor for the U.S. Army.
- The company advanced to the Xtended Range Counter-sUAS Missile program’s second phase, which covers flight performance testing of a fully integrated interceptor.
L3Harris Technologies has received a three-year contract worth up to $60 million to develop a long-range, maneuverable missile for the U.S. Army that is designed to shoot down small and medium drones at greater distances than today’s interceptors.
The company announced the award on Oct. 23, 2026, under the Xtended Range Counter-sUAS Missile program run by the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Aviation & Missile Center at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama. L3Harris said it has advanced to the program’s second phase, which involves flight performance testing of a fully integrated interceptor that offers greater range, speed and operational flexibility than current systems, and the missile is meant to engage traditional short-range air defense threats such as aircraft and helicopters as well as drones.
“We are leveraging L3Harris’ deep technical expertise across propulsion, guidance and advanced manufacturing to deliver a next-generation interceptor that meets the Army’s evolving mission requirements,” said Scott Alexander, president of Propulsion Systems at L3Harris Missile Solutions. “This design combines innovative propulsion with advanced seeker technologies to provide a highly capable, modular and cost-effective solution deployable from existing launch platforms.”
The key to the design is an air-breathing ramjet engine. Unlike a conventional rocket motor, which has to carry both fuel and the oxidizer needed to burn it, a ramjet takes oxygen from the air it flies through, freeing space inside the missile for more fuel. L3Harris said its approach improves fuel efficiency and extends engagement range, and the company is also adapting the interceptor to work with existing U.S. military platforms so it can be integrated quickly into current air defense networks.
The Army launched the program, also known as XRC, to find a missile that can be fired from the Stinger Vehicle Universal Launcher with more range than the current Stinger for the counter-drone mission. The service has said it wants the new weapon to reach farther, react faster, hit harder and reload more quickly, with a focus on larger drones that fly higher and from greater standoff distances, while still protecting maneuvering forces carried by systems such as the Maneuver Short Range Air Defense, or M-SHORAD, vehicle.
L3Harris is one of several companies working on the effort. Northrop Grumman received an $18.8 million agreement from the same Army center earlier this fall to develop and integrate solid fuel ramjet propulsion for XRC missile prototypes, with ground and flight testing planned through December 2029 at its Allegany Ballistics Laboratory in West Virginia.
The L3Harris contract runs for three years, and the full $60 million value depends on continued funding as the company moves its interceptor through the second-phase flight tests.

Paris museums close, stores put up barricades as France prepares for more protests
Major museums in Paris closed and authorities deployed a sizable police force for a round of new protests Saturday across France, hoping to prevent a repeat of last week's violent unrest that shocked the country.

Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend. The demonstrations first erupted last month when high school students in southeast of Paris protested for better conditions, but quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.
Protest marches are scheduled in Paris and Marseille, but some other rallies, including in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, have been banned by local authorities. Cities outside Paris were hit hard by the unrest. In Limoges, a suspected arson nearly destroyed the 19th-century city hall.

U.S. Air Force details $20.7B AMRAAM missile contract
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:33:18 UTC
16:33:18 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Raytheon a $20.7 billion sole-source contract for AMRAAM Production Lots 41 through 47, with work in Tucson through June 2033.
- A 2017 justification document found no other company interested in becoming a second source for AMRAAM production.
The U.S. Air Force has published new details of its $20.7 billion contract with Raytheon for AIM-120 AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, confirming that the sole-source deal covers seven production lots and will keep the Tucson, Arizona, production line busy until mid-2033.
An award notice posted on the federal contracting site on Oct. 23, 2026, shows the fixed-price incentive contract was signed on Sept. 25 for AMRAAM Production Lots 41 through 47. It covers AMRAAM missiles, AMRAAM telemetry sets used in testing, initial and field spares and other production components, with all work in Tucson and an expected completion date of June 30, 2033. The notice gives a base and all options value of $20,699,334,581 but does not list how many missiles the contract buys.
RTX announced the deal on Sept. 28 as a multiyear contract worth up to $20.7 billion over five years, with two option years, for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and international customers buying through Foreign Military Sales. The award is more than five times the size of the previous record AMRAAM contract, a $3.5 billion award in July 2025 for Lots 39 and 40, which itself surpassed a $1.19 billion contract for Lot 38 in September 2024.
The AMRAAM is the primary beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile of the United States and many allies, guided by an active radar seeker with mid-course GPS guidance and a two-way datalink. Raytheon says it is fielded by 44 countries on 14 platforms, from fighters such as the F-15, F-16, F/A-18, F-22 and F-35 to the ground-based NASAMS air defense system widely used in Ukraine and across Europe. Recent lots have included the AIM-120D-3 for U.S. services and the AIM-120C-8 for export customers.
The Air Force awarded the contract without competition under federal acquisition rules that allow a sole-source buy when only one responsible source can meet the requirement. A justification notice tied to the award was published the same day, and an earlier class justification signed in 2018 for Lots 34 through 43 lays out the reasoning the service has used for years.
That document traces Raytheon’s position to 1997, when Raytheon and Hughes Missile Systems Company, which the government had funded as competing AMRAAM producers, merged into Raytheon Missile Systems and left a single contractor able to develop, produce and sustain the missile. The program office concluded that qualifying a second source would require buying the technical data package, replicating the factory and requalifying suppliers, at a cost that competition would not recover, and that suppliers below Raytheon would remain sole sources regardless.
“No company has expressed any desire to be a second source for AMRAAM production/sustainment,” the 2017 justification states.
A 2017 market survey drew only limited interest, all of it in managing obsolete parts rather than building missiles, and the interested parties either withdrew or said their services were better suited to a subcontracting role.
The new contract comes as the Department of War pushes to rebuild missile stocks. Under a February 2026 framework agreement, RTX committed to producing at least 1,900 AMRAAMs a year, and the company says it nearly doubled output in 2025 compared with 2024. Work on Lots 41 through 47 is scheduled to run through June 30, 2033.

Labs that design U.S. Navy reactors get $2.4B more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:21:50 UTC
16:21:50 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Fluor Marine Propulsion a $2.4 billion modification for naval nuclear propulsion work at the Naval Nuclear Laboratory.
- The laboratory designs and supports reactors for U.S. Navy submarines and aircraft carriers, with work in Pennsylvania, New York and Idaho.
The U.S. Navy has added $2.4 billion to Fluor Marine Propulsion’s contract to run naval nuclear propulsion work at the Naval Nuclear Laboratory, the network of government labs that designs and supports the reactors powering every U.S. Navy submarine and aircraft carrier.
Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the $2,409,077,590 cost-plus-fixed-fee modification on Sept. 24, 2026, according to a Department of War contract announcement. Work will be split among the laboratory’s main sites near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (47%), Schenectady, New York (45%), and Idaho Falls, Idaho (8%). The announcement lists $582,062 in fiscal 2026 Navy operations and maintenance funds and $15,838 in fiscal 2026 shipbuilding funds obligated at the time of award, with the shipbuilding portion expiring at the end of the fiscal year.
The Naval Nuclear Laboratory is owned by the Department of Energy and overseen by Naval Reactors, a joint Energy Department and Navy program. It includes the Bettis Atomic Power Laboratory in West Mifflin, Pennsylvania, outside Pittsburgh, the Knolls Atomic Power Laboratory in Niskayuna, New York, near Schenectady, the Kenneth A. Kesselring Site in West Milton, New York, where sailors train to operate naval reactors, and the Naval Reactors Facility at the Idaho National Laboratory.
The labs develop new nuclear propulsion systems, provide technical support to keep the fleet’s reactors safe and reliable, and train the sailors who run them at sea. Knolls is the lead design laboratory for the Virginia-class attack submarines and is leading reactor design work for the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarines, while Bettis supports the Nimitz-class aircraft carriers and Seawolf-class submarines. The laboratory employs more than 7,500 engineers, scientists, technicians and support staff.
Fluor Marine Propulsion, a wholly owned subsidiary of Fluor Corporation, took over management of the laboratory from Bechtel Marine Propulsion Corporation on Oct. 1, 2018. The Navy-funded portion of its contract started with a cost-plus-fixed-fee base of about $1.2 billion and options that could bring its total to about $13 billion, alongside a separate Energy Department contract for the same laboratory. Earlier modifications have included a $1.78 billion award in March 2020 and a $1 billion option in 2021.
The new modification covers continued naval nuclear propulsion work across all three regions, and the Department of War contract announcement did not list a completion date for the effort.

Interview: China's clean energy achievements accelerate global energy transition, says IEA chief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:21:06 CST
16:21:06 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's achievements in clean energy technologies are impressive and have accelerated the global energy transition, Fatih Birol, executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), told Xinhua in a recent interview.
The global energy crisis is reshaping energy markets, prompting the adoption of renewable energy and electric vehicles (EVs) as countries seek to reduce their dependence on traditional energy sources, said Birol on the sidelines of the just-concluded Berlin Global Dialogue.
Birol highlighted China's important role in addressing current energy challenges and promoting international energy cooperation, recalling that at the 16th APEC Energy Ministers' Meeting, held in Beijing in September, representatives discussed the current energy crisis and ways for Asia-Pacific economies to work together to address it.
He said that since March this year, the world has faced an unprecedented energy security challenge following disruptions to the two major arteries that had long underpinned global energy flows: energy supplies from western Siberia, Russia, to Europe, and shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to Asia and beyond.
To mitigate disruptions in global oil markets, the IEA announced on March 11 that it would coordinate the release of 400 million barrels of oil reserves by its member countries. The move helped calm market concerns after oil prices initially surged, Birol said. However, he stressed that strategic stock releases could only cushion the impact of supply disruptions, rather than provide a lasting solution.
Beyond their impact on oil and gas prices, supply disruptions are also reshaping global energy trade relations, with some longstanding partnerships giving way to new ones, Birol observed.
He identified key trends emerging in the global energy sector since the outbreak of the war in the Middle East: rapid growth in renewable energy, rising EV sales, a modest increase in coal use, and renewed momentum behind nuclear power.
He said that solar power is the leading source of growth, followed by wind, and that biofuel use was also rising strongly, partly due to higher diesel and gasoline prices.
Birol pointed out that the rapid expansion of renewable energy was driven not only by climate and environmental concerns but also by energy security considerations and countries' efforts to increase domestic energy production.
Noting that EVs are growing rapidly in many markets around the world, Birol said reducing dependence on oil is an important factor driving this trend, which is evident not only in Europe but also in Brazil, Australia and Southeast Asia.
Highlighting China's role in the global energy transition, Birol said that China's electric vehicle market is developing rapidly, with EVs now accounting for about 60 percent of new car sales in the country.
The widespread adoption of EVs is not only fueling a transformation in the automotive industry but also changing the global energy consumption structure and will have a profound impact on the future energy market, he added. ■

Third seed Bublik recovered from a set down to defeat fifth seed Khachanov 4-6, 7-6 (5), 7-6 (5), firing 21 aces and winning two tiebreaks to set up a semifinal clash with defending champion Daniil Medvedev.
No Kazakh player has won the tournament since its inception in 2020, when it was held in Astana. The event moved to Almaty in 2024, with Russian players claiming both titles since then.
Bublik was playing his first match of the tournament after receiving a first-round bye and advancing through the second round without playing when Hungary's Fabian Marozsan withdrew because of illness.
Khachanov, who won the title in 2024, took the opening set after securing a late break, but Bublik held his nerve in the second-set tiebreak to force a decider. Neither player could establish a decisive advantage in the final set, which also went to a tiebreak, with Bublik prevailing to reach the last four.
Top seed Medvedev continued his title defense with a 6-4, 6-4 victory over France's Terence Atmane.
The Russian, who is seeking to successfully defend an ATP singles title for the first time in his career, won 31 of 34 points on his first serve and did not face a break point throughout the contest.
Medvedev has dominated his previous meetings with Bublik, although the Kazakh won their most recent encounter in the final of the Halle grass-court tournament in 2025.
In the other half of the draw, seventh seed Stefanos Tsitsipas of Greece defeated Australia's James Duckworth 6-3, 6-4 to reach his first hard-court semifinal since February 2025.
Tsitsipas controlled much of the contest against Duckworth, whose run in Almaty ended at the quarterfinal stage after he had reached the semifinals of last year's tournament.
The Greek will next face Georgian qualifier Nikoloz Basilashvili, who continued his impressive run with a convincing 6-3, 6-1 victory over France's Adrian Mannarino.
Basilashvili, ranked 128th in the world, needed just 69 minutes to dispatch Mannarino and secure his place in the last four.

TOKYO, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has endorsed Gianni Infantino for re-election as FIFA president, marking a turnaround from two months ago when it criticized him over a controversial World Cup investment plan.

"We affirm our full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president," Sheikh Salman said.

"My feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," he said.
Infantino, who has led FIFA since 2016, is seeking a fourth and final term in the election scheduled for March 2027 in Morocco. The deadline for candidates to register is November 18 this year, and no challenger has announced a bid so far.
Addressing AFC delegates, Infantino acknowledged his mistakes and stressed the importance of learning from them.

The AFC has 47 member associations, 46 of which are FIFA members eligible to vote in the presidential election. While the endorsement does not guarantee unanimous support from its members, it significantly boosts Infantino's re-election bid.

Feature: Global BASE jumpers meet at the world's highest bridge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:20:26 CST
16:20:26 KST

GUIYANG, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Hundreds of meters above a canyon in southwest China, the appeal of BASE jumping from a bridge is obvious: breathtaking height, open air and a few precious seconds of free fall.
But for many international jumpers, the experience extends well beyond the leap itself, encompassing spectacular scenery, cultural encounters and friendships forged through a shared passion.
At the edge of the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge in Guizhou Province, German BASE jumper Hannes Grossmann launched into the air, performing a 360-degree forward somersault, a side flip and another rotation before deploying his parachute and landing smoothly in the designated area.
"The coolest thing about this bridge is that it is super high," Grossmann said. Its open surroundings also give experienced jumpers more room to maneuver.
This is Grossmann's third trip to China for BASE jumping, but his first time leaping from the Huajiang Bridge.
From Oct. 20 to 23, more than 30 BASE jumpers from 19 countries and regions gathered at the bridge for the 2026 International High-bridge Skydiving Invitational, following an earlier competition at Guizhou's Baling River Bridge.
BASE jumping involves parachuting from fixed objects or natural formations rather than aircraft, often leaving participants with only seconds of free fall before they must deploy their parachutes.
Certified by Guinness World Records in April as the world's highest bridge, the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge rises 626.01 meters above the water. The structure has cut travel across the canyon from around two hours to about two minutes. For BASE jumpers, however, its remarkable height offers an entirely different kind of advantage.
Grossmann began BASE jumping in 2019 and has completed more than 2,000 jumps worldwide. His previous trips to China took him to several other jumping sites, including the Nizhuhe Grand Canyon in Yunnan Province.
What distinguishes Huajiang, he said, is the combination of height and open space. With no cliff face immediately beside the exit, jumpers have greater freedom to experiment with different maneuvers.
Grossmann completed three jumps at Huajiang on Wednesday, trying backflips, front flips and other rotations. He gave the site a nine out of 10 for its suitability for practicing new tricks.
For Turkish jumper Ogulcan Geldikaya, who was making his second BASE jumping trip to Guizhou, the extra height offers another benefit: more time to enjoy the free fall.
The additional seconds allow jumpers to perform more maneuvers or attempt two- and three-person jumps with friends. On Friday morning, Geldikaya teamed up with an Australian jumper for a synchronized leap. Wearing their parachutes, the two stood side by side, clasped hands and jumped together. After several seconds in free fall, they let go, deployed their parachutes and landed safely in the designated area.
"The height of the bridge means more time for maneuvers and more fun. But safety is the priority," Geldikaya said.
That priority sometimes means staying on the ground. He had planned to celebrate his birthday on Thursday with another jump from the world's highest bridge, calling it "the perfect gift for myself." Strong winds, however, forced him to postpone the leap.
For Geldikaya, knowing when to wait is just as important as knowing how to jump.
The bridge events have also become a gathering point for athletes from around the world, giving them an opportunity to experience China beyond the competition.
Dutch jumper JP De Kam, who helps bring international athletes to the event, said the bridge initially draws people in, but the local culture is what makes them want to return.
During his visits, he has explored local streets, admired traditional Chinese architecture and taken in Guizhou's mountainous scenery. Just as important, he said, is the chance to see how local people live and discover how their daily lives differ from his own.
On Tuesday evening, the athletes visited Zhenfeng ancient town, where they joined local residents in traditional dances.
"We've been dancing together, doing the Chinese dances," De Kam said. "That's a very big attractive point."
For Portuguese referee Nuno Cunha, the event marked his first visit to China. One aspect of daily life in Guizhou particularly impressed him: the widespread use of digital payments.
"Everywhere I visited, people were prepared to accept digital payments," Cunha said. Even in villages, he saw elderly residents selling local produce to tourists and receiving payments through QR codes.
The event has also helped build friendships among athletes from different countries.
Geldikaya said he had made new friends from around the world during the gathering. He welcomed them to visit Türkiye and jump with him, assuring them, "My house is your house."
Some of these connections have continued long after the competition ended. Athletes who first met at events in Guizhou have since reunited in Türkiye, Japan and Europe, turning a few seconds of free fall into friendships that endure across borders.
De Kam hopes to bring even more athletes to Guizhou in the years ahead. "I would love to be back here for more than 10 years," he said. He wants more jumpers to experience "the culture, the food, the bridge, everything." ■

US President Trump’s defeat turns into a domestic challenge

Nowadays, there is a growing public dissatisfaction with the United States regarding the US war waged against Iran and this issue has been turned into a challenge, a challenge that, in addition to increasing economic pressure on American citizens, could also impact the political standing of the Republicans ahead of the congressional midterm elections. Recent polls indicate that a majority of Americans are unhappy with how the US President has handled this crisis, and skepticism has grown regarding Washington’s ability to achieve its stated objectives.
Within this framework, a Democratic Senator from Connecticut and member of the US Senate Committee on Foreign Relations Chris Murphy has criticized the Trump administration’s policies toward Iran, emphasizing that American people have no desire for this conflict to continue and that the costs to the nation are far from negligible. Murphy, a staunch critic of the Trump administration’s military policies, highlighted the financial burdens, the risks faced by American forces, and the security implications of these policies. Furthermore, he has called for an end to the conflict, asserting that Congress must take responsibility regarding the continuation of this course of action.
Widespread dissatisfaction with Trump's performance
Data from recent polls indicate that opposition to the handling of the conflict with Iran has spread to a significant segment of American society. According to a Pew Research Center poll, the results of which were released on October 8, 2026, 65 percent of Americans are dissatisfied with how Donald Trump has managed US military action against Iran, while only 33 percent approve of his performance. The survey, which included 5,062 American adults, was conducted between September 28 and October 4. The significance of these figures becomes even more apparent when compared to the results of a poll from March; at that time, 61 percent of respondents were dissatisfied with Trump’s handling of the situation, while 37 percent approved of his performance. Consequently, over the course of a few months, the level of dissatisfaction has risen, while support for the President’s performance has declined.
In general, US President Donald Trump's approval rating has tremendously been plummeted which is unique of its kind as compared with the previous presidents of the United States.
Furthermore, only 34 percent of Americans believe that the initial decision to use military force against Iran was the right one—a figure that represents a four-percentage-point decrease compared to March.
These findings suggest that the issue is not limited merely to disagreements over how government policies are implemented; rather, a segment of American society has also developed a more negative assessment of the very decision to employ military force.
Skepticism regarding realization of Washington’s goals
Another sign of public dissatisfaction is the growing skepticism regarding the Trump administration's ability to achieve its stated objectives. According to the same Pew Research Center poll, 52 percent of Americans have little or no confidence that the Trump administration will achieve its goals in the confrontation with Iran. In contrast, 24 percent stated that they have a great deal or a fair amount of confidence that these objectives will be realized.
On the other hand, a large segment of American society does not expect this crisis to end in the short term. According to the survey results, 47 percent of participants predict that U.S. military action against Iran will continue for more than another year, while 30 percent expect the situation to last between six months and a year. Consequently, approximately 77 percent of respondents anticipate that the conflict will persist for at least another six months.
These concerns arise against a backdrop where a prolonged conflict could impose greater financial and military costs on the U.S. government, further straining the nation’s resources. Consequently, the gap between the administration’s promises regarding the achievement of its objectives and public anxiety over the protracted crisis has become a focal point for criticism of the Trump administration’s policies.
Economic costs and concerns regarding American forces
Concerns regarding the economic consequences of a conflict also play a significant role in shaping public opposition. A survey by the Pew Research Center indicates that 73 percent of Americans are very or somewhat concerned about rising gasoline and fuel prices resulting from a conflict with Iran. Furthermore, 71 percent of respondents expressed concern about the injury or death of American troops. Additionally, 58 percent of participants stated that they are very or somewhat concerned about the deployment of U.S. ground forces to Iran.
These statistics indicate that the consequences of the crisis, as perceived by the American public, are not limited solely to military developments. Rising energy costs, the potential for the conflict to spread, and the risk of casualties among U.S. forces all factor into citizens' assessments of the administration's policy.
Under such circumstances, the continuation of the conflict could become a significant factor in U.S. domestic debates—especially if citizens feel that the costs incurred are disproportionate to the outcomes announced by the government.
Murphy’s warning regarding costs of continuing the conflict
Chris Murphy has also highlighted this same set of concerns in his criticisms. In a speech on the floor of the US Senate on September 24, he criticized Republicans for opposing a resolution to end the conflict, noting that public support for this policy has become very limited.
In this speech, Murphy stated that, according to the data he cited, only 18 percent of the American public supports this conflict; he urged Congress to heed the citizens' call to bring it to an end. He also warned of the security and economic repercussions of the crisis, as well as the risks facing American troops. Murphy argues that, in evaluating the outcomes of this policy, the U.S. government must consider not only the stated military objectives but also the costs imposed on American citizens, military personnel, and the nation's security interests.
Political consequences for Trump and the Republicans
Growing public dissatisfaction regarding a conflict with Iran could have significant political consequences for the Trump administration—especially with congressional midterm elections on the horizon, where the administration’s foreign policy performance could emerge as a key point of contention between Republicans and Democrats.
A decline in public support for government policies could pave the way for intensified criticism from opponents and the raising of more serious questions regarding the costs and outcomes of this conflict.
Notably, this erosion of support is not confined solely to Trump’s political adversaries. According to a Pew poll, his approval rating among Republicans and those who lean toward the party has fallen from 69 percent in March to 63 percent in October. While a majority within this group continues to support his performance, a six-percentage-point drop may signal growing reservations among a segment of his political base. Conversely, the negative view Democrats hold of Trump’s performance has remained virtually unchanged—a fact indicating that opposition to his policies remains widespread among his political opponents.
Generally speaking, polling data and criticisms from figures such as Chris Murphy indicate that the conflict with Iran has evolved into an issue that transcends mere US foreign policy. Economic costs, concerns regarding the safety of American troops, skepticism about the realization of stated objectives, and growing public opposition have intensified domestic pressure on the Trump administration.
In this regard, what Trump’s critics characterize as a failure to achieve stated goals could develop into a significant challenge within the realm of US domestic politics. Nevertheless, the extent to which this issue influences the outcome of the midterm elections will depend on future developments, the state of the economy, and how the administration manages the situation in the coming months.
