Canada gets its first two CF-35A stealth fighters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:13:47 UTC
16:13:47 KST

- The Royal Canadian Air Force received its first two CF-35A fighters at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona for pilot training.
- Canada has committed funding for 16 F-35s so far, while a government review of the full 88-jet purchase continues.
The Royal Canadian Air Force has taken delivery of its first two CF-35A stealth fighters, the Canadian version of the Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II, at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona, the service announced.
The jets will stay at Luke, a major U.S. Air Force training base for F-35 pilots from the United States and partner nations, where the RCAF has set up its first CF-35A training squadron. Canada plans to base its first eight F-35s there during 2026 and 2027 to train Canadian pilots, before the first aircraft arrive at 4 Wing Cold Lake in Alberta in 2028, with initial operational capability planned for 2029.
“The future of air and space power is built on more than equipment alone. We are developing the skilled people, integrated capabilities, and modern tools we need to meet future challenges at home and abroad,” the Royal Canadian Air Force wrote.
The deliveries come one month after Canada’s first CF-35A made its maiden flight on Sept. 23, 2026, at Lockheed Martin’s plant in Fort Worth, Texas. That aircraft, production number AR-1, already wore full RCAF markings, including bilingual RCAF-ARC lettering on its air intakes and a roundel matching the one carried by the CF-18 Hornet it will replace. The CF-35A designation is the first two-digit designation for a Canadian military aircraft since the current naming format was introduced in the 1960s.
The F-35 will replace the RCAF’s CF-18s, which Canada has flown since the 1980s and plans to keep in service until the early 2030s while the new fleet builds up. Canada agreed in January 2023 to buy 88 F-35As for about $19 billion, part of a Future Fighter Capability Project valued at C$27.7 billion including training, equipment, sustainment and infrastructure.
How many of those jets Canada will ultimately buy is still undecided. Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered a review of the purchase in March 2025, and Ottawa has so far made a legal funding commitment for the first 16 aircraft, with long-lead payments for 14 more confirmed in February 2026. Defense Minister David McGuinty has said the review is ongoing without setting a timeline, and options under discussion include a mixed fleet that would add Saab Gripen E fighters, which Saab has offered to assemble in Canada.
Preparations for the F-35 have continued in the meantime. On Oct. 7, 2026, McGuinty announced nearly C$4 billion for fighter infrastructure at Cold Lake, the first Canadian base that will fly the jet, while 3 Wing Bagotville in Quebec is the planned second operating base.
With two CF-35As now in Canadian hands at Luke, the RCAF expects to receive the rest of its first eight training aircraft there through 2027.

Displaced West Bank Palestinians face growing hunger after UN cuts food aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:09:55 UTC
16:09:55 KST

Displaced West Bank Palestinians face growing hunger after UN cuts food aid
Already struggling after losing homes to Israeli military operations, Palestinians face hardship as WFP halves aid.
Tulkarem, occupied West Bank – Fawza Awad, a 75-year-old widow, couldn’t hold back her tears as she described the living conditions she has endured since being displaced from the Tulkarem refugee camp in January 2025 – a result of an Israeli military operation that targeted refugee camps in the northern West Bank, forcibly displacing tens of thousands of Palestinians from their homes.
With little money, Fawza and her family found shelter where they could: a small, unfinished house in Tulkarem belonging to her daughter. She currently lives in a portion of the structure alongside her son, his wife, and their child.
The family previously relied on limited financial and food assistance provided by the World Food Programme (WFP), but has not received aid in the past five months.
The UN agency officially announced a 50 percent reduction in the number of food aid recipients in the occupied West Bank in September, citing “critical funding constraints”, the result of reduced funding from international funders. Food needs, conversely, have more than doubled since 2023, when Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza, and increased attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank.
The WFP noted at the time that approximately 900,000 people in the West Bank are currently suffering from food insecurity.
In a statement given to Al Jazeera, the WFP confirmed that some families had stopped receiving aid before the official announcement in September.
Fawza and her family have been left to fend for themselves. There is no prospect of returning to her old home – she says that the Israeli army has completely demolished the structure, replacing it with a wide road to facilitate the movement of its military vehicles.
She added that one of her sons has been detained by Israel since 2024, while her other sons, who previously worked inside Israel, are now all unemployed.
“I suffer from asthma and high blood pressure, requiring monthly medication that costs at least 200 shekels ($64), an expense no one covers for me. We used to receive modest food aid barely enough for two or three people, but now that has stopped completely,” Fawza told Al Jazeera.
‘Not even bread’
Not far away, in the al-Muwahhad School building in the Thannabeh suburb of Tulkarem, more than 1,000 Palestinians displaced from the Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps are sheltering, having found nowhere else to go and unable to pay rent.
Among them are Rabab Qasim, 47, her husband Talib Abu Sarriya, 72, and their three children. For the second consecutive year, they have been living in a small, 30-square-metre (320sq-foot) room on the ground floor of the school, with no source of income and totally reliant on aid.
For the past three months, the family has received no aid whatsoever following the WFP food assistance cut.
“I suffer from a herniated disc in my back, requiring monthly treatment that costs 300 shekels ($96) – an amount I cannot afford,” Rabab said. “I also need physical therapy, which I have never been able to access because I cannot pay for it. I sleep on a worn-out mattress on the floor; all I wish for is to be able to buy a bed.”
Talib told Al Jazeera that the family are often unable to find bread or a meal, and frequently go to sleep hungry. It’s a far cry from their former life in the Tulkarem refugee camp, where he once owned a small vegetable stall. It was a modest livelihood, but one that gave them enough to get by.
Alone in the struggle
The WFP has blamed increasing Israeli pogroms and forced displacements in the West Bank for devastating livelihoods, deepening hunger, and pushing families into even more severe crises. The latest quarterly food security analysis conducted by the WFP indicates that 76 percent of Palestinian households in the West Bank have experienced a significant decline in income.
According to the analysis, 12 percent of the population has poor food consumption, and one-third of households cannot afford a healthy diet due to rapidly deteriorating economic conditions. Rural areas and the governorates in the southern occupied West Bank have been the hardest hit.
Said al-Amour, 61, a resident of Khirbet al-Rakeez in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, told Al Jazeera that he and his 14-person family haven’t received any assistance from the WFP for the past seven months.
In April 2025, while confronting repeated attacks by settlers on the village, Said says he was shot by a settler. The injury resulted in the amputation of his leg and a permanent disability; he continues to face periodic assaults and beatings whenever he encounters the settlers – part of the ongoing pogrom against Palestinians in the West Bank.
“They are trying to steal our land. I refuse to let them take it, and I will continue to defend it, but I am paying a heavy price. Now, they have cut off the aid I used to receive that helped my family remain steadfast here,” he told Al Jazeera.
Due to the amputation of his leg, al-Amour requires monthly medical treatment costing at least 1,200 shekels ($385), an expense that he cannot afford. He has no source of income other than a few olive trees, which settlers frequently attempt to seize.
Collapse of livelihoods
In cooperation with its partners, the WFP still provides assistance to 200,000 Palestinians in the West Bank through cash transfers, food vouchers, direct food supplies, livelihood programmes, and nutritional services.
However, the WFP told Al Jazeera that it simply does not have the resources to cover the needs of all the families in the West Bank requiring assistance.
“The cessation of aid does not imply that a beneficiary is ineligible; rather, it is a broad decision affecting all current beneficiaries, regardless of the outcome of their individual assessment,” the WFP said. “It is possible that changes may occur, and aid could be reinstated for some beneficiaries; in such cases, they would be contacted and notified via text message.”
Economist and human rights activist Ubai Aboudi told Al Jazeera that the West Bank is facing a humanitarian crisis exacerbated by the loss of the WFP food aid, as well as a financial crisis affecting the Palestinian Authority (PA). Israel has completely withheld the customs revenues it collects on behalf of the PA since May 2025, leaving the authority unable to pay public sector salaries.
Aboudi noted other factors, such as the tens of thousands of Palestinians previously employed in Israel and illegal settlements in the West Bank who have been out of work since October 2023, when Israel stopped giving them work permits.
He also added that Israeli restrictions on Palestinian and international NGOs, including the suspension of registration for 37 international organisations and the closure of some local groups, have further limited the ability to provide humanitarian assistance.
“Around half a million Palestinian families need food assistance, while the actual need may be greater,” Aboudi said. “With aid declining from the World Food Programme and other sources, many families are unable to secure food.”

Lockheed gets $115M to update F-35 navigation gear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:07:26 UTC
16:07:26 KST

- Lockheed Martin received a $114.6 million order to redesign the F-35’s GPS electronic unit and NAV100 inertial navigation system with replacement components.
- The work replaces obsolete electronic parts to prevent production disruptions and is expected to be completed in January 2030.
Lockheed Martin has received a $114.6 million order to redesign two key navigation systems on the F-35 Lightning II, the GPS electronic unit and the NAV100 inertial navigation system, replacing electronic parts that are going out of production so the stealth fighter can keep rolling off the line.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee order, announced on Oct. 23, 2026, covers nonrecurring engineering, redesign, integration, qualification and testing of both systems. The new designs will swap in replacements for obsolete components while keeping the same performance and compatibility with the electronics already flying on the jet, so the updated units can be fitted without changes elsewhere on the aircraft. Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, issued the order without competition under an existing basic ordering agreement.
The two systems work together to tell the F-35 where it is. The GPS electronic unit processes signals from navigation satellites, while the inertial navigation system tracks the aircraft’s position, speed and heading using onboard motion sensors and keeps working when satellite signals are jammed or unavailable. Both feed the targeting, flight and mission systems that the pilot and the jet’s weapons rely on.
The problem the order addresses is a common one in long-running aircraft programs, known as diminishing manufacturing sources: suppliers stop making specific chips and electronic parts years before the aircraft that use them are retired. The Department of War said the redesigns are intended to prevent production disruptions and support continued production and sustainment of F-35s for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy, U.S. Marine Corps and the program’s international partners.
Most of the work, 70.1%, will take place in El Segundo, California, with 27.5% in Fort Worth, Texas, where Lockheed Martin builds the F-35, and 2.4% in Clearwater, Florida. The effort is expected to be completed in January 2030.
The U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy are each contributing about $46.4 million from fiscal 2026 aircraft procurement funds, and F-35 cooperative program partners are providing about $21.8 million.
The navigation work comes days after the Department of War and Lockheed Martin unveiled a framework for a 10-year F-35 production and sustainment deal covering 850 aircraft for the United States at a rate of 156 jets a year across all customers. Keeping parts like these available is a precondition for holding that production rate, and the redesigned GPS and inertial navigation units are scheduled to complete testing and qualification by early 2030.

North Korea’s Kim Jong Un arrives in China, South Korean media says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24

North Korea’s Kim Jong Un visits China via newly opened bridge
Kim arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong using the New Yalu River Bridge, officially opened about a week ago, according to South Korean officials.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly opened bridge, according to South Korean officials.
The visit on Saturday comes about a week after the bridge linking the two countries was officially opened, 12 years after its completion, deepening economic ties between the Asian giant and its small, nuclear-armed neighbour.
Kim’s visit also comes a day before the anniversary of China joining the 1950–1953 Korean War.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang met Kim in the border city, the Reuters news agency said, quoting a South Korean official.
China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Kim arrived in Dandong through the New Yalu River Bridge connecting the two countries, the Reuters and AFP news agencies reported, quoting unnamed South Korean government officials. South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency also reported the visit, citing an unidentified government source.
Analysts say the visit represents part of Kim’s increasingly assertive foreign policy, as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a “new Cold War”.
Strengthening ties
Experts said the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, which stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu River, was a key symbol of strengthening ties between the two countries and reflected their intent to expand trade. It is expected to accommodate two-way traffic around the clock, including container shipments and heavy cargo trucks.
The four-lane structure was completed in 2014, but its opening was delayed due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side, according to South Korean news reports.
“The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics,” Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think tank in Shenyang, told Reuters.
“With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further,” Lu said.
China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a vital source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the reclusive state, although ties have not always been smooth.
China, which fought alongside North Korea in the Korean War, is Pyongyang’s main economic and diplomatic backer. However, North Korea has drawn closer to Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which analysts say has reduced Pyongyang’s reliance on Beijing.
Kim’s last known visit to China was in September 2025 to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, where he held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Xi made a state visit to North Korea in June in which he expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.

Investment plan not investable as it stands, MPs told
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:00:41 BST
16:00:41 KST

The Defence Investment Plan is not investable as it stands, because it sets out themes without the contracts, programmes and procurement detail industry needs before it will build factories, according to evidence given to the Defence Committee.
Stephen Phipson, chief executive of MakeUK, was giving evidence alongside Kevin Craven of ADS, Julian David of techUK and Arnab Dutt of the Federation of Small Businesses.
Phipson said: “I have been doing this for a long time, to say the least, and, as Kevin said, there is not sufficient detail. It is nothing like an equipment plan. This is not investable as it stands at the moment. It gives you a thematic direction of travel in many areas, a lot of which is welcome and is great news, and attracts a lot of new companies into the market, but the questions are then around where the contracts, the programme and the procurement are. We do not have that yet, and that is the problem.”
Craven said the plan concentrates on the first four years to 2029, where the old defence equipment plan set out a granular acquisition pipeline over ten years. He said: “We can see that the rough shape of the DIP is around 50% to 55% of the total spend over the 10-year period, so some spend has been brought forward to improve the readiness of what we are doing, but there is not enough granularity to provide certainty to industry. Intent is not the same as a commitment that is suitable for investors in defence.”
Asked whether the plan leaves more questions than answers, Craven said there is a clear shift in strategic direction but that “the lack of certainty over that 10-year period is a real problem. Headlines do not make for good investment.”
Ian Roome, the Liberal Democrat member for North Devon, asked how damaging it would be if the next spending review failed to provide a funded pathway towards three per cent of national income, and whether industry would still invest on the strength of the current plan.
Phipson said: “The answer is that it will not. It is only going to invest when there is certainty on what the programme looks like, and we have seen this for decades in defence. It has to be around a certain programme. The thematics that we have are all good and welcome.”
He added: “To your earlier point, industry welcomes the new technologies and innovation, but, until we see certainty, no one is going to invest a penny. We need to see where those contracts are going to come from. We will play with all the innovation that is happening with the MOD, which is good, but we need to start building factories and capability.”
On the backloading of the funding profile, Craven said: “You cannot switch on industrial capacity and production lines overnight. You need a strong demand signal over a long number of years to be able to do so, so a ramp-up towards the back end of a period is not helpful. It creates a future bottleneck where firms will compete for the necessary skills, monies and other industrial requirements at the same time, so it is not a helpful profile in any way.”
He told the committee that building a new production line from scratch takes between two and four years depending on what is involved.
David said the delay itself carries a cost, telling MPs: “this costs the country money, because delay in an inflationary context and, particularly in tech, an availability crisis of certain components means that what you are going to do costs more when you get around to doing it.”

COP17 puts Armenia’s environmental record in the spotlight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:52:41 UTC
15:52:41 KST

COP17 puts Armenia’s environmental record in the spotlight
As Yerevan hosts the global biodiversity summit, mining interests and weak environmental regulation raise questions about the country’s leadership.
Last weekend, the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) opened in Yerevan with a lavish ceremony. It is the first time the summit has been hosted by a former Soviet republic, an occasion the Armenian government has celebrated as an opportunity to establish the country as a leader in environmental protection. But Armenia’s own ecological record raises serious questions about its suitability for this role.
When Yerevan was awarded the right to host COP17 in 2024, the Armenian authorities celebrated the decision as recognition of the country’s environmental ambitions. Yet Armenia has struggled for decades to develop effective conservation policies, and its record remains poor in several important areas. In Yale University’s 2026 Environmental Performance Index, Armenia ranks 75th out of 177 countries, compared with first place for Estonia, another former Soviet republic.
Its performance is particularly poor on waste management, where it ranks 164th, and wastewater treatment, where it ranks 165th. These figures point to serious shortcomings in basic environmental protection.
The contrast raises an obvious question: why was a country facing such serious environmental challenges chosen to host one of the world’s most important biodiversity conferences? The selection might have offered an opportunity to encourage change, but there is little indication that the Armenian authorities have used the occasion to address the country’s longstanding problems.
A major obstacle is the structure of Armenia’s economy, in which mining plays an important role, alongside ageing industrial facilities and inadequate environmental regulation. The country’s largest mining operations, including the Zangezur, Agarak and Teghut copper-molybdenum mines, extract ore using open-pit methods that generate large quantities of waste and pose serious pollution risks. The World Bank has identified mining as a significant source of environmental pollution in Armenia. Open-pit gold mining has also been licensed at Meghrasar, on land that originally overlapped with Arevik National Park, before the government reduced the park’s boundaries in 2015. The Artsvanik tailings reservoir, which holds millions of tonnes of mining waste, has also been linked to heavy-metal contamination in nearby waterways.
Armenia’s environmental problems extend beyond mining. Forests cover only 11.1 percent of the country, while in Yerevan, levels of harmful fine particle air pollution are about five times the World Health Organization’s recommended limit.
Armenia’s dependence on Russian-linked businesses in some of its most important industrial sectors further complicates efforts to strengthen environmental regulation. These companies are not only major investors and employers, but also important contributors to the state budget, giving the government a powerful economic incentive to protect their operations. Russian-linked investors hold a controlling stake in the Zangezur copper-molybdenum complex, which was Armenia’s largest taxpayer in the first half of 2026.
That conflict between economic interests and environmental protection was on display just days before COP17, when Armenia inaugurated the controversial Amulsar gold mine. Environmental organisations, including the Global Forest Coalition and various Armenian civil society groups, have condemned the move, arguing that it disregards longstanding environmental concerns and recommendations under the Bern Convention.
Human rights organisations have documented intimidation and lawsuits targeting activists campaigning against Amulsar. Armenia’s Economy Minister has defended the project on economic grounds, saying it could contribute between 1.5 and 2 percent of the country’s GDP and generate approximately $130m annually in taxes and other payments to the state budget. The projected revenues expose the contradiction between the government’s determination to expand mining and its ambition to present Armenia as an international leader in biodiversity protection.
These competing priorities are particularly important as Armenia seeks closer relations with the European Union and distances itself from Moscow. The EU–Armenia Strategic Agenda identifies the need for stronger implementation of environmental impact assessment legislation, improvements to waste management, and further action on air quality, water protection and industrial emissions. Progress on these commitments should be central to the EU’s assessment of Armenia’s efforts towards closer integration.
At COP17, governments are reviewing progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which aims to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030. The summit is expected to finalise a “Yerevan Pathway” to accelerate implementation of its targets. The prospects are already bleak. The State of Biodiversity Action report, launched before the summit, found that fewer than half of assessed national targets are on track.
Financing remains a major obstacle. Developed countries have provided about $16bn annually in international biodiversity finance, falling short of the $20bn target for 2025. Meanwhile, the Cali Fund, established with the goal of collecting $1bn in annual contributions from companies profiting from genetic data derived from nature, has received just $6,000. These shortfalls illustrate the difficulties facing governments as they seek to turn their biodiversity commitments into action.
As host of COP17, Armenia should be prepared to demonstrate that the commitments being discussed in Yerevan also apply to its own mining industry, environmental regulations and treatment of conservation activists. Participating governments should use the summit to press the Armenian authorities to strengthen environmental protections, enforce pollution controls, ensure credible environmental impact assessments and address the concerns raised by civil society over projects such as Amulsar.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

====================================================================================================

Using an 800,000-year-old tooth, researchers unlock the secrets of Israel’s ancient elephant haven
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:52:10 UTC
15:52:10 KST

Long before modern history, the Hula Valley’s Gesher Benot Ya’aqov was as close to a Garden of Eden as the ancient world could offer. The site at the “Daughters of Jacob Bridge” is so even today.
Nearly 800,000 years ago, during the Middle Pleistocene Era, giant straight-tusked elephants, hippos, and rhinoceroses roamed a lush sanctuary of woodlands, wetlands, and waterways.
Living alongside these massive creatures were the region’s earliest humans – hominin toolmakers who left behind a remarkable record of survival along the Levantine corridor.
Nestled in northern Israel, the Hula Valley has long served as a vital bridge between Africa and Eurasia. Today, remarkable finds –including a well-preserved ancient elephant tooth and basalt handaxes – provide evidence of giant elephants and early toolmakers that together made the Hula Valley their home.
Saber-tooth tigers, rhinoceroses, hippopotami, giant wild cattle deer, gazelles, wild boars, freshwater turtles, lizards, and snakes shared the lush landscape of woodlands, wetlands, and waterways during the Middle Pleistocene Era that began some 780,000 years ago. But among the most impressive creatures were giant elephants alongside hominids – the Hula Valley’s most ancient humans.
Today, elephants, or other large animals, are kept in Ramat Gan’s Safari or Jerusalem’s Biblical Zoo, but the area remains verdant and bountiful, according to archaeologists from Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and colleagues at the University of Haifa and Tel Aviv University.
They found a remarkably preserved elephant tooth and tusk fragments at the prehistoric site in northern Israel, where early humans made stone tools – basalt handaxes and cleavers that were hallmark tools of the Acheulian tradition, one of the earliest and most widespread stone-tool technologies in human history.
The resource-rich environment that helped sustain both large mammals and early humans along the Levantine land bridge connecting Africa and Eurasia remains.
After studying the area for more than three decades, the archaeologists have just published their latest findings in Quaternary Science Reviews under the title “Elephant dental remains from the Acheulian site at North Bridge Acheulian-Gesher Benot Ya’aqov: hominin behavior and environmental implications.”
The study was led by University of Haifa doctoral student Hannah Farrell, at the site and excavated by Prof. Gonen Sharon of Tel-Hai. The team included Cheryl Makarewicz (isotope studies) and Nimrod Marom (archaeozoology) from the University of Haifa, along with Minji Jin and Dafna Langgut (pollen studies) from Tel Aviv University.
The research focuses on a giant elephant molar and tusk fragments discovered alongside Acheulian stone tools at Gesher Benot Ya’aqov’s northern locality located in the valley in northern Israel. The remains belonged to Palaeoloxodon antiquus, the straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Pleistocene.
Rather than studying the elephant alone, researchers said they used the tooth as a biological archive to reconstruct the broader ecosystem shared by large mammals and early human toolmakers. “We applied high-resolution CT scanning of the tusk and molar recovered from the site,” Sharon noted.
The valley has abundant water, emanating from the Hermon Mountain range (mostly as melted snow), feeding underground springs and accounting for much of the abundant water. Today, the Jordan River with its three main tributaries – the Dan, the Banias and the Hatzbani – is the primary water body of the valley. From as early as the Lower Paleolithic, humans have opted to occupy the Hula Valley.
Today, the bridge is located south of the Hula Valley, probably due to the presence of high basalt there. A stone bridge was built by the Mamluks (an Arabic word that literally means “one who is owned” or “slave”) sometime in the 13th century that was replaced in 1934 by a modern bridge further south during the draining of Lake Hula.
The existing bridge was built almost two decades ago and now forms part of Israeli Highway 91, straddling the boundary between the Galilee and the Golan Heights.
Alongside the broad exposure of archaeological bearing sediments, there are uniquely well-preserved ancient flora specimens – wood, bark, seeds and fruits that provide exclusive data on the environment of the area during the Pleistocene Era and the behavior and diet of early humans in this landscape, Sharon told The Jerusalem Post in an interview. “Understanding how humans and animals responded to environmental change hundreds of thousands of years ago helps us better understand the forces that shaped our species.”
Using CT scanning, 3D reconstruction, microscopic wear analysis, isotope geochemistry, and pollen studies – each field being the expertise of a variety of experts – the team found evidence for a long-lasting landscape of woodlands, grasslands, marshes, rivers, and shallow-water habitats.
Carbon isotope values suggest the elephant lived in a consistently well-watered environment, while pollen recovered from sediments revealed abundant wetland vegetation, including reeds, sedges, willow, tamarisk, and aquatic plants.
Wildlife and human groups both moved via the Levantine Corridor land bridge. “We didn’t actually find human bones because we excavated just 100 square meters, so we would have needed a lot of luck to find them,” he explained. “But we have found tens of thousands of animal bones and tools at the site.”
Conditions for wildlife to survive
The availability of water, vegetation, and animal resources shaped where humans and wildlife could survive, Sharon added. “The wetlands, rivers, and woodlands helped sustain life along one of the world’s earliest migration corridors, offering a rare opportunity to understand the ecological conditions that supported both animals and human populations in that era.
Sharon, who heads the Tel-Hai Prehistory Laboratory, is also curator of the Upper Galilee Museum of Prehistory at Kibbutz Ma’ayan Baruch. He earned his three degrees in archaeology from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and lives at Kibbutz Lehavot Habashan just 15 minutes away from the archeological site.
Asked what the single most important discovery that you could not have made without this particular elephant tooth and that the stone tools, other animal bones or sediments alone could not, he said: “The elephant helped us reconstruct the environment; we didn’t find any human skeletons. We found one elephant’s tooth, out of eight altogether that grow in its jaws, but this is what we do. Quite impressive.
“They eat leaves and other vegetarian food, and this wears down their teeth. When all are worn out, they die of hunger.” The teams were able to establish that both the tooth and the stone tools made by humans were contemporaneous, because they came from the same layer. Humans imported the animal tooth to the site.”
They knew that the environment could support a population of elephants, each of which consumed more than a hundred kilos of food per day. “We have collected bones there from the other animals – wild cows. Boars, bears, and birds. We know that the tooth we found belonged to an elephant species weighing about 10 tons.
“The largest in the Safari Zoo – born in 1974 and named Yossi – is only 6.5 to seven tons. The ancient humans were involved in very sophisticated activities, making stone tools and using nuts, wood, and animals. The ancient elephants couldn’t have been easy to hunt and eat. They apparently killed them with spears.”
The site endured seven or eight ice ages, but even if it got colder in the Hula Valley, the inhabitants survived. Europe was covered by destructive ice, but here, the climate didn’t bother the people and environment much even if the temperature dropped by five degrees.”
The latest findings were a pilot study. “We will study more elephants and animals and combine all the evidence. Dozens of people forming many teams – each with expertise on pollen, seeds, frogs, elephants, fish, isotopes, and much more – worked together since 1989. I joined in 1995. I suppose we have 700 or 800 more years to keep us busy,” Sharon joked.

US Justice Department sues Alaska to preemptively block election of Democrat to Senate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:51:54 UTC
15:51:54 KST

The Trump administration has sued Alaska to preemptively block the state from certifying the results of its US Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses narrowly, saying voters could be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names.
The Justice Department (DOJ)'s lawsuit, filed in federal court in Anchorage on Thursday, signals the willingness of President Donald Trump's administration to contest the results of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers.
The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.
Control of the Senate could come down to Alaska, where incumbent Republican Dan S. Sullivan is running a close race against Democrat Mary Peltola.
The suit, which names the state and local election officials as defendants, takes issue with the presence of another contender in the race, another Republican named Dan J. Sullivan Jr, alleging he is running "with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him."
Officials fear legal challenges will be used to delay results
The DOJ asks a judge to block the certification of an outcome "that may be impacted by voter confusion," so that there can be "an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
Trump told reporters on Friday that he supported the lawsuit, saying, "I'm the one that said do it."
A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement that the agency is taking "necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters.”
Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are preparing for potential federal interference in the elections, including legal challenges and disputes over voting that could disrupt certification of the results.
Trump has a long history of challenging election outcomes and encouraging supporters to contest results he views as unfavorable.
Officials criticize lawsuit as lacking merit
Alaska's other US senator, Senator Lisa Murkowski from Trump's Republican Party, said on Friday the Justice Department "should never have filed this lawsuit."
Election law experts said the lawsuit has no merit and seeks relief not allowed under federal law.
"In short, like many Department letters over the last few years, it is designed to win the press release rather than the litigation," wrote Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller in a blog post, adding that "the legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen."
Trump's administration "has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election," said David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that advises election officials, adding that "this issue has already been fully litigated by Alaska's courts."
Sullivan insists his candidacy is not intended to confuse voters
The unelected Sullivan, a former US Forest Service worker and elementary school teacher, filed to run as a candidate on May 29, seeking to unseat Dan S. Sullivan and "put Alaska first," according to his campaign website, which advertised "Dan Sullivan Challenges Dan Sullivan for US Senate Seat."
Dan J. Sullivan has denied in interviews with US news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan.
The Alaska Supreme Court in June permitted the challenger Sullivan to appear on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent.
Peltola, the Democratic candidate, told MS NOW on Friday that because of how the candidates are displayed on the ballot "there just isn't much room for confusion." The lawsuit is "sending a message that Dan Sullivan does not believe that Alaskans are sophisticated enough to know exactly who they're voting for," she added.
Trump's approval rating has fallen to a record low, hit by rising diesel and gasoline prices during the Iran war, which has proven deeply unpopular with voters.
Public opinion polls suggest Republicans may lose control of one or both chambers of Congress, which would likely limit Trump's ability to enact some of his policy agenda in the final two years of his presidency.

'Not a gradual slide': Menopause can reshape women's bodies in a sudden shift, Israeli study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:51:14 UTC
15:51:14 KST

For decades, women have been told that menopause is a slow, gradual slide into midlife. But groundbreaking research from Rehovot’s Weizmann Institute of Science reveals a dramatically different picture: Menopause isn’t a gentle taper, but an abrupt, body-wide biological overhaul.
Researchers used a novel computational technique inspired by deep-space astronomy to analyze over 300 million lab test results from more than a million women across Israel and the US. The sources were medical records collected over 20 years by Clalit Health Services (Israel’s largest health fund, covering half the population) and the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.
Most women believe that menopause – the end of their fertility – creeps up on them gradually in their late 40s and early 50s, with the average age being 51 to 52. It’s a natural process that occurs when one’s ovaries stop producing reproductive hormones.
Gynecologists define it as the point in time when a woman has gone 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period.
The researchers discovered that the transition triggers sudden shifts across dozens of bodily systems – from liver and kidney function to bone health and cholesterol. The study also showed that the sudden shifts were preceded by escalating changes in the levels of the women’s sex hormone that began more than a decade before menopause – several years earlier than previously thought.
The discovery opens a critical new window for early preventive healthcare.
Prof. Uri Alon and his team identified abrupt changes in dozens of measures of bodily health and function, far beyond the familiar shifts in sex hormone levels and the loss of fertility.
“Menopause reshapes female physiology, yet current understanding has been limited by small longitudinal cohorts that characterize it as a gradual transition,” he asserted.
The changes appeared in 52 of the 90 types of lab tests they studied and included nearly all body systems, including those of liver and kidney function, bone health, and cholesterol levels. Interestingly, no such abrupt changes were observed in men of similar ages, and the changes were less pronounced in women receiving hormone replacement therapy.
The research team included Dr. Glen Pridham and Yoav Hayut from Alon’s lab in Weizmann’s molecular cell biology department; Dr. Noa Lavi-Shoseyov and Prof. Michal Neeman of Weizmann’s immunology and regenerative biology department; Dr. Noa Hovav of Clalit’s Menopause Community Center; and Dr. Yoel Toledano of the Rabin Medical Center in Petah Tikva.
Such large datasets are rarely used in menopause research because they usually lack information about the age at which women had their last period. To overcome this, the researchers developed a computational method inspired by the stars viewed through a telescope. Just as stargazers can sharpen an image by mathematically correcting distortions caused by a telescope, the new method removed the “blur” in medical data caused by differences in the age at which women reach menopause.
The team said that because most of the abrupt changes identified in the study are associated with increased disease risk, the findings could help women take preventive steps, such as exercising and improving their diet, years before menopause.
“Our study extends the window for potential preventive care to almost a decade before menopause,” Alon said. “More broadly, the method we developed may help study other major changes in life, such as puberty, pregnancy, or the onset of disease.”
They published their findings in the prestigious Nature Medicine journal under the title “Population-scale reconstruction of menopause dynamics reveals a physiological cliff at the final menstrual period.”
Asked to comment, Prof. Amnon Brzezinski – a leading expert on menopause at the Women’s Health Center in the obstetrics and gynecology department at Hadassah-University Medical School and former academic faculty chairman of obstetrics & gynecology at the Hebrew University Medical School – sent his congratulations to the Weizmann team.
“The study ratifies (in a very unique technique) that there is a sharp decline in reproductive hormones during the menopause transition and even before. It gives further support to the importance of menopausal hormonal therapy,” he told The Jerusalem Post.
Alon earned his first two degrees from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and his doctoral degree in theoretical physics from Weizmann, going on to Princeton University for his postdoctoral work in experimental biology. He returned to the Weizmann Institute as a professor and in 2021 was named a visiting professor in the bioengineering department of Stanford University.
Asked what the most important physiological finding that would have been missed if they had treated menopause as a gradual process, Alon said: “We were not expecting this result. The Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation (SWAN) study – an ongoing, long-term study that began in 1994 and was funded by the US National Institutes of Health to address a critical lack of diverse, high-quality data regarding how women experience the menopause transition – which followed women every two years and is the gold standard in the field- suggested a gradual transition over about three years. When we saw the data, the hair on the back of our necks stood up. We never saw a cliff like that.”
As menopause is defined as a year after the final menstrual period, many women start hormone replacement therapy (HRT) only then.
Asked what the most striking changes were and which were clinically meaningful rather than merely statistically significant, the Weizmann expert said: “The changes in the body systems are affected by estrogen. Most important is bone mineral density, which drops by about half a standard deviation on average in the population. There is also a jump in liver tests, including markers of liver damage, and in risk factors for heart disease such as lipids and triglycerides.
“The silver lining is an improvement in iron and hemoglobin and less anaemia, because menstrual bleeding stops. However, the most dangerous of these, over decades, are fractures and heart disease. At age 70, about a quarter of women have osteoporosis. A trivial fall that you brush off at 50 can cause a hip fracture at 70, with about 20% mortality within a year and 50% disability.”
When the team members applied the same approach to men, they found that they don’t have a jump.
“They show the gradual changes of aging over decades. Women also have these gradual changes, plus the jump. On average we see gradual changes starting about a decade before menopause, accelerating in the years before the final menstrual period, and then a jump at the final period, which looks like it’s within that year,” Alon explained.
It was an observational study, “so we need randomized clinical trials to be sure. The biology fits, though. Menopause brings a large drop in important hormones, first and foremost estrogen, which has receptors in virtually every cell in the body – muscle, bone, brain, and liver. The hormone generally has protective effects for the vascular system and reduces inflammation. So a large and sudden drop has effects across the body, generally in the direction of increased risk.”
Clinical trials planned
Asked about the benefits of HRT, Alon said: “Our data on this are observational and based on a small minority of women who take it, so they should be taken with a grain of salt. We are planning a clinical trial of hormone therapy before the final menstrual period to test its effect on bone and brain health.”
He stressed that he hoped the new findings don’t cause stress or fear of menopause. The changes don’t mean an immediate health collapse, just increased risk. They emphasize taking care of exercise, nutrition, and other healthy habits before the final menstrual period, and consulting a physician, especially if you have risk factors for bone, heart, or liver disease.
“For some women, physicians may advise bone density tests earlier than usual. HRT is now given for symptoms; future clinical trials will show whether it can be given before menopause for prevention. Of course, we don’t want to overtreat, so this has to be done on the advice of a physician.”

One arrested after fire at Hitler's Eagle Nest mountain retreat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:46:59 UTC
15:46:59 KST

Suspect arrested after fire "completely engulfed" Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat in Germany
A suspect has been detained in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.
Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.
The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and there were no injuries reported.
Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added.
"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.
At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist attraction, which also operates as a restaurant and beer garden. According to its website, the Eagle's Nest is "one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hilter era" and it "stands for the insanity of the regime."

Türkiye’s energy ambitions, Eurasian financial links dominate Verona Economic Forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:45:50 UTC
15:45:50 KST

Energy security, investment, and the financial infrastructure needed to support greater economic connectivity across Eurasia took centre stage on Friday, the second and final day of the Verona Eurasian Economic Forum in Istanbul.
Speaking at the forum, Turkish Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said a world facing geopolitical tensions, supply disruptions, and rising energy demand needs greater diversification, investment, and international cooperation.
Bayraktar said Türkiye imports almost 70 percent of its energy needs, making reducing external dependence a strategic economic and national security priority.
Renewable sources account for more than 62 percent of Türkiye's installed electricity generation capacity, while combined wind and solar capacity has exceeded 43 gigawatts, he said.
Türkiye eyes major energy investments
Bayraktar said Türkiye will need significant investment in its electricity networks in the coming years as it seeks to integrate more renewable capacity, improve grid resilience, and expand cross-border electricity trade.
Türkiye is also preparing to hold its first offshore wind tenders in the first half of 2027, while its Renewable Energy Resource Area program aims to allocate 2 GW of new capacity annually.
On nuclear energy, Bayraktar said it is continuing work with Russia's Rosatom to commission the first reactor at the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant in the coming months. Once all four reactors are operational, the 4.8-GW plant is expected to meet around 10 percent of Türkiye's electricity demand.
The country aims to reach 20 GW of nuclear capacity by 2050, including conventional reactors and small modular reactors.
Bayraktar also pointed to Türkiye's position between energy-producing and consuming regions, saying Ankara wants to strengthen its role as a reliable partner connecting regional energy markets.
COP31 presidency to focus on implementation
With Türkiye set to host next month’s COP31 UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Bayraktar said the Turkish presidency will put implementation at the center of the climate agenda, focusing on turning commitments into investment, technology deployment, and concrete results.
He stressed that countries have different energy systems and development needs, arguing against a one-size-fits-all approach to the energy transition.
Bayraktar said Türkiye would also advance a voluntary "35 by 35" global electrification pledge to boost electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035.
Mobilising private capital, international financial institutions, and technology partnerships would be critical to delivering the investments required for the transition, he added.
Eurasia looks to deepen financial links
The broader question of strengthening financial connectivity was also taken up in the "Financial markets in the heart of Eurasia: Resilience, Infrastructure, Undervalued Opportunities" panel, where officials and financial executives discussed how regional capital markets could become more connected.
Russian Deputy Finance Minister Ivan Chebeskov said deeper and more liquid capital markets would become more attractive and efficient, arguing that Eurasian economies still have considerable room for financial integration.
He said the Eurasian Economic Union has already begun introducing mechanisms to facilitate cross-border market access for investors and issuers, while a mechanism to provide access for professional market participants is nearing completion.
Chebeskov said another priority is integrating market infrastructure, including exchanges and depositories. Within the BRICS group – also including Brazil, India, China, and several other nations – he said pilots involving the Moscow Exchange and Russia's National Settlement Depository are testing links between the capital markets of interested member countries.
He also pointed to national currencies as an area likely to play a growing role in financial markets.
Russian capital markets shift toward domestic financing
Moscow Exchange Chairman Viktor Zhidkov said activity in Russian equities is now concentrated in the domestic market, with stock and bond placements taking place locally and domestic demand sufficient to absorb them.
He said retail investors' stock market assets had nearly doubled over five years to 16 trillion rubles ($199 billion), while private investors had put more than 4 trillion rubles ($50 billion) into corporate bonds on the Moscow Exchange since 2022.
Corporate bond placements reached 7.2 trillion rubles ($89.6 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, up 20 percent from the same period last year, according to Zhidkov.
Gazprom's First Deputy Head of Department Ignat Dirks described a similar shift at the corporate level, saying the share of foreign markets in the company's financing portfolio had fallen from 77 percent in 2022 to 13 percent by mid-2026.
Dirks said Gazprom had raised more than $14 billion on the domestic market in the last four years for refinancing and around $20 billion to finance new projects. He said the restructuring of the company's financing portfolio had been made possible by the growing maturity of Russia's domestic financial market.
Common standards seen as key to integration
Gazprombank Deputy Chairperson Elena Borisenko highlighted the importance of greater complementarity and specialisation among financial centres.
She said common standards, compliance rules, and approaches would help build greater financial compatibility, while the quality of settlement systems, capital flows, trade finance, and investment products would determine the resilience and effectiveness of Eurasia's financial architecture.
The 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum, held at Istanbul's Ciragan Palace on Thursday and Friday, was organised by Italy's Associazione Conoscere Eurasia with the support of Türkiye's MUSIAD and Ibn Haldun University, bringing together political, diplomatic, academic and business representatives from more than 30 countries.

Keeping the world safe when no one is in charge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:45:18 UTC
15:45:18 KST

Keeping the world safe when no one is in charge
As AI creates new global threats and power becomes increasingly fragmented, international cooperation is more vital than ever.
International politics today feels like a collective sleepwalk into the abyss. Three trends are particularly alarming. Artificial intelligence is globalising and turbocharging old and new threats. Meanwhile, no state is strong enough to impose order. And, as in earlier periods of global crisis, geopolitical blocs are hardening, with international cooperation increasingly portrayed as weakness. Alas, there is ample reason to fear a repetition of the worst of history.
Much attention has focused on the risk of war between the US and China, as shifts in hegemonic power historically produce conflict. That is not, however, what is happening. Instead, we are approaching an international order with no hegemon, with several states and regional blocs competing for influence. Using the jargon of international relations theory, we are on the cusp of genuine global multipolarity.
Artificial intelligence is adding further stress to existing power structures. On the one hand, we are all being transformed into godlike figures — soon no innovation or information is beyond our reach. But it is also disempowering everyone, creating new threats and making old ones harder to contain.
Larger states are finding it increasingly difficult to convert power into control. This is already evident in the military domain, where inexpensive drones and AI-assisted targeting have changed traditional hierarchies. The US, with its vast military arsenal, is unable to force an isolated and bankrupt theocracy in Iran to bend the knee; Russia’s failed attempt at subjugating Ukraine is another example of a much more powerful state not getting its way.
New technology is making the loss of control even more evident in other domains. The next pandemic could originate in a hidden laboratory and prove far deadlier than COVID-19. Devastating cyberattacks could be launched from someone’s garage. Frontier AI systems could spiral beyond human control. AI could lower the barriers to developing nuclear weapons, while biological weapons could proliferate without anyone noticing.
Such threats recognise no borders. If one state establishes effective safety measures, nefarious actors will simply move somewhere else and deploy from there. A state can possess overwhelming military and economic capabilities and still be unable to stop a pathogen, prevent a cyberattack or contain the spread of dangerous technologies. Strategies based on peace through strength, regional primacy and zero-sum power dynamics will be like fighting mosquitoes with heavy weaponry — costly and unworkable.
Yet much of the world is doubling down on precisely these strategies. Some state leaders are focusing on winning AI and achieving digital supremacy. Negotiating mutual constraints through international law and institutions is seen as naive or self-defeating. Such approaches are at best ineffective. As global policy, they can destroy humanity. It is as though one can hear the voices of earlier wartime generations: “Do not fall for it again.”
And we really shouldn’t, given how unfettered national ambition coupled with weak international rules and institutions has hurt us in the past. Yet many seem incapable of rising to the occasion. One reason is surely our tendency to underestimate risks that accumulate over time. A 1 percent annual probability of a global catastrophe may sound reassuringly small. Yet, over a century that translates into roughly a 63 percent chance of catastrophe—an intolerable level of risk.
Military strength will remain necessary. But the only way to ensure real security in this new paradigm of multipolarity and artificial intelligence is through powerful international institutions and laws. Global standards must be developed and enforced. International organisations must be allowed to monitor, inspect and report on activities within countries’ borders. Governments will regularly have to share sensitive information. Peace through cooperation must be the new global slogan; not out of altruism but because it is the only way to achieve real security.
Fortunately, we don’t have to start from scratch. Institutions such as the United Nations, the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the World Health Organization (WHO) still retain unparalleled authority and legitimacy. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has shown that international monitoring can effectively verify compliance even in highly sensitive areas.
Recent events offer some grounds for optimism. Last year, the WHO adopted a Pandemic Agreement, which will improve the world’s collective readiness to prevent and mitigate future health emergencies. The UN General Assembly recently adopted the BBNJ Agreement to protect biodiversity on the high seas, the first global treaty of consequence in at least a decade. The Security Council has shown that it’s serious about addressing the security challenges posed by AI; during a high-profile debate in September this year, most governments and leading AI developers alike called for stronger global governance and more robust international oversight mechanisms.
These are encouraging signs. But overall, states are investing too little in such global frameworks at a time when the opposite is needed.
Norway has made it a priority to break the curve. We have defined respect for international law and effective multilateral institutions as a core national security interest. We’re investing heavily in UN reform; as one of the UN’s largest financial contributors, we have leverage which we will use to push for greater effectiveness. Alone, Norway is too small to change the course of international politics. But through cross-regional coalitions with like-minded countries, we can make a real difference.
One recent example came in September when Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb launched a joint Call for Action to establish global oversight and control over advanced AI models. Countries from all over the globe have joined the initiative. Hopefully, it can serve as a springboard for concrete international action in this field.
No one is in charge in a multipolar world. This new reality is taking shape precisely as technology is making threats harder to contain. The defining challenge of our time will therefore be to couple multipolarity with multilateralism. Building effective institutions when no one can impose order is inherently difficult. But just as previous generations were able to overcome profound challenges, so can we.
It was only after the lived catastrophes of the first and second World Wars that nations united around shared legal principles and institutions. I am convinced that, in time, states will once again realise that this is the only way. What remains to be seen, however, is whether we can muster the necessary resolve without first experiencing another global crisis of world-war-like proportions.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Moonshot tweaks the hack out of latest AI model
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:43:15 UTC
15:43:15 KST

Moonshot AI has reduced the cyber-offensive capabilities of its newest model, the Chinese startup said on Saturday, as fears grow that increasingly autonomous artificial intelligence could turbocharge hacking.
Beijing-based Moonshot announced the curbs while introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, which it describes as its most capable three-trillion-parameter-class open-weight model. The company plans to publish the model's weights –  files allowing outside developers to run and modify it on their own systems – by November 4.
Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model while retaining general coding skills.
"We aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability," the company said.
Governments, technology companies and security researchers are growing increasingly concerned that AI could make sophisticated hacking easier and cheaper. Models that can write code, operate software tools and complete long, multi-step tasks may help users identify weaknesses in programs and automate parts of cyberattacks.
China proposed export controls last week that would ban exports of AI-driven malware-generation and mutation technology and restrict AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery tools. 
The draft measures, which remain open for public comment, cite the risk that such capabilities could be used against critical infrastructure, defence-industrial and core government systems, or to bypass security protections.
Moonshot said open-weight models can improve security by helping more organisations inspect and secure their own software, including older systems that receive little attention.
Unlike proprietary, closed-weight AI systems, however, open-weight releases make central oversight more difficult. Once the files are widely distributed, the original developer has less ability to restrict access, monitor use or update safeguards than with a hosted service.
K3.1 Pro scored 81 percent on its internal cyber benchmark, compared with 90.5 percent for a similar version without the risk-reduction measures, the company said. The test involved finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. 
Moonshot said the comparison showed that filtering cyber-related data reduced the model's offensive cyber performance, although it still outperformed its predecessor. The results have not been independently verified.
K3.1 Pro has a one-million-token context window, allowing it to process very large amounts of text at once. Moonshot also released a faster version, K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which it said runs at two to three times the speed of the standard model. (Reuters)
