491 days in the grey zone: exclusive details of the first-ever aerial evacuation aboard a Heavy Shot drone
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:34:00 EEST
15:34:00 KST

491 days in the grey zone and losing both feet: exclusive details of the first-ever aerial evacuation aboard a Heavy Shot drone
In October, Ukraine's defence forces carried out the first-ever medical evacuation of a wounded soldier using a heavy unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). The soldier, a member of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade who goes by the alias Magura, was airlifted from the grey zone aboard a Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 drone. No evacuation vehicle had been able to get to the area for over a year.
The roads are heavily mined, and FPV drones prowl the skies, destroying anything that moves within tens of kilometres. The brigade spent over six months preparing the daring rescue operation, which brought together heavy and light quadcopters, ground robots, electronic warfare units and even artillery.
"I realised there was a person down there: I wanted to get him to safety as quickly and safely as possible," a drone pilot recalls.
Ukrainska Pravda has interviewed the soldiers behind the operation, the drone's developers and the wounded serviceman. Find out how troops from the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, named after Kostiantyn Ostrozkyi, teamed up with neighbouring units to pull off the evacuation and make history.
The operation was made possible by the coordinated efforts of the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, the 14th and 30th Separate Mechanised Brigades, and the 10th Army Corps.
491 days
Sadly, this story began quite some time ago. On 2 June 2025, Kostiantyn "Magura" Vlasenko, an infantryman with the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, set off from the rear with a fellow soldier for their positions on the Kupiansk front, which were on the left bank of the Oskil River. In the grey zone, Magura initially took shelter in one spot. But when it flooded, he had to move into an abandoned building.
His brother-in-arms was killed while making his way to a fallback position. Then, on 14 February 2026, a Russian drone dropped a munition that wounded Magura in both legs. Faced with a fight for survival and having lost one of his feet, he amputated the other foot himself, leaving him unable to get out of his position on his own.
There was no way to drag him out overland: the Oskil River, dense minefields and relentless Russian drone patrols made the approaches impassable. The battalion tried to use a ground robotic system to evacuate him, but Russian forces spotted and destroyed it while it was still on its way. Infantry groups also failed to reach him. Russian drones filled the skies, and Russian infantry had infiltrated the area around his position, effectively sealing it off.
All this is further evidence that the "golden hour" – the crucial first 60 minutes after an injury, when prompt medical treatment can mean the difference between life and death – is becoming increasingly difficult to meet on the modern battlefield. Evacuating wounded soldiers is a dangerous mission in its own right, and one that becomes harder with every passing year.
Every four to five days, drones brought Kostiantyn food, cigarettes and sweets. He kept in touch with his brothers-in-arms by walkie-talkie. He held out in his position until his evacuation on 4 October.
It was Alex, the reconnaissance chief overseeing UAV operations for the 2nd Mechanised Battalion, who came up with the idea of evacuating the soldier by air. It took around six months to move from the initial concept to the flight itself. The military had conventional Heavy Shot bomber drones, but these were not up to the task. The soldiers instead turned to the newly developed Heavy Shot Ayudag-6, a heavy-lift drone that can carry up to 130 kg and is equipped with a cargo winch.
"We'd been using Heavy Shot bomber drones for a long time and had an established line of communication with Gurzuf Defence," Alex said. "When I found out they were testing the new Ayudag-6 heavy-lift drone, I went to them immediately with this unconventional task. The drone was still a work in progress, but the developers were immediately fired up by the idea."
Gurzuf Defence designed the drone primarily for frontline logistics, as a heavy-lift modular platform. However, the engineers ensured from the very beginning that it had enough thrust to lift a person. The drone underwent two years of testing, during which the company's chief developer, Oleh Hynda, became the first person to fly aboard the test model.
"We never intended this drone to be just for evacuations – it's a heavy-duty logistics platform," Pavlo Feldblium, co-founder of Gurzuf Defence, told Ukrainska Pravda. "But we always knew it might have to be used for a rescue mission in certain circumstances. To prepare for this operation, we brought in units with experience of evacuating people using ground robotic systems. It was their experts who configured the winch and the mounting systems."
The company spent several months fine-tuning the platform at the unit's request. Experts from the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade's unmanned ground systems company then fitted the aircraft with additional equipment, and the 2nd Battalion's headquarters spent two months planning the operation. Around 15 military personnel were involved in preparing and planning the mission.
Pre-flight preparations took seven days. The military personnel worked out the flight routes, planned cover corridors and identified alternative emergency landing sites in case of a technical failure.
The evacuation drone was operated by Chornyi ("Black"), a squad leader in a mortar battery at the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Mechanised Brigade. "I first got to know the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 a week before the mission, when I took part in special training exercises. Until then, I'd only worked with standard Heavy Shot drones," he says.
The most dangerous part was hoisting the soldier, who had to attach himself to the cable on his own. The day before the flight, the drone delivered off-the-shelf mountaineering equipment and a phone loaded with a video explaining how to put on and secure the harness.
According to the plan, the soldier had to attach himself to the drone's winch with carabiners, sitting in a semi-reclined position. Any mistake when securing himself, or losing consciousness during the flight, could have sent him falling to the ground.
16 kilometres
Russian FPV anti-aircraft drones meant the cargo drone could not fly alone. Slow and bulky, with a payload suspended beneath it, it would be immediately spotted by Russian reconnaissance. The headquarters planned a diversionary manoeuvre to draw attention away from it.
Several formations helped provide cover for the operation. Alongside the 2nd Battalion of the 30th Mechanised Brigade, units from the 14th and 43rd Separate Mechanised Brigades took part, as did personnel and equipment from the 10th Army Corps. The day before the flight, the neighbouring units involved suggested putting it off because there was no fog. But the forecast showed no fog was expected any time soon, so the command decided to go ahead.
"We studied enemy drone activity to find the time when it was at its lowest. We decided to fly at first light, as night gave way to day," explains Alex, the battalion's reconnaissance chief.
The main diversion was carried out by Vampire heavy bomber drones, which flew into neighbouring sectors simultaneously to draw the attention of Russian anti-aircraft drone operators. The Russians shot down one Vampire, but the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 carrying out the evacuation went unnoticed.
Alex spent 48 hours studying data on Russian assets around the planned mission area. Experts from the 3rd Army Corps also helped prepare the Ayudag's electronic warfare system for the flight.
An Autel quadcopter operated by the battalion provided visual cover for the Ayudag-6, giving the crew a pair of eyes in the sky. However, it struggled to keep pace with the faster evacuation drone. A Ukrainian Lucky Strike drone waited nearby, ready to ram any Russian reconnaissance or strike UAVs that appeared. As the aircraft carrying Magura returned, artillery from the 10th Army Corps delivered concentrated suppressive fire against the identified launch points used by Russian drone operators.
Headquarters had a backup plan in case the drone malfunctioned or was shot down over the left bank of the Oskil River. Reconnaissance teams and ground robot crews were standing by near the designated emergency landing sites, ready to respond.
The Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 relied on Starlink for communications, which kept Russian electronic warfare systems from jamming it. No interference was detected on the control links. The drone's altitude was adjusted to suit the terrain, and it took a different route back to prevent the Russians from identifying its outbound flight path.
The drone was in the air for less than an hour and a half. The operator spoke to the wounded soldier through the drone's onboard camera and microphone.
The drone could not cover the full 16 km on a single charge: carrying a person drained its batteries too quickly. Two ground support teams were deployed along the route in advance to provide the necessary support.
"On command, I flew to a waypoint, where the team changed the batteries. Then I continued to the evacuation point, picked up the wounded soldier and flew him back," says Chornyi, who piloted the evacuation drone.
At the transfer point, the wounded soldier was detached from the winch. The next leg of the evacuation was carried out by a Peacemaker ground robotic system, as using vehicles would have risked exposing the operation to the enemy.
The troops camouflaged the platform and laid mattresses in its cargo compartment. The remotely controlled Peacemaker then covered another 8 km off-road. Once in a safe area, the team transferred Kostiantyn to a vehicle and took him to a frontline stabilisation point for emergency surgery. The Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 returned to base intact after a battery change at a stop along the route.
Kostiantyn told Ukrainska Pravda: "The flight went smoothly. I spent most of the time looking at the terrain below. When I landed, I felt safe and relieved – I'd finally be able to see my family soon. A special thank you to my unit clerk, Livsha, for keeping me well supplied with treats."
Despite the soldier's calm assessment, the actual flight revealed issues that had been difficult to anticipate during training with a dummy load. He had not been given protective goggles, so the powerful airflow beneath the rotors and the headwind caused discomfort. However, this did not detract from the mission's overall success.
Alex also credited Kostiantyn's calmness during boarding with helping make the mission a success. He had to get onto the drone in an open area while its rotors were spinning above him.
"The soldier was exceptionally quick-thinking and determined to survive," he said. "We had already dropped off his equipment and instructions. When the quadcopter approached, he did everything exactly as instructed, as quickly as possible. There was no panic or hesitation – the whole thing took just seconds and went exactly to plan."
The future of aerial evacuation
One successful operation does not make aerial evacuation a regular option, nor can it replace ground-based evacuation. Missions like this require extensive preparation and coordinated support from multiple units. This operation involved reconnaissance, artillery, decoy-drone crews and ground teams. Without them, the aircraft carrying the wounded soldier would have been shot down by the first Russian interceptor drone on its way.
The drone's developers take a similar view. Gurzuf Defence says the risks to a casualty's life during flight are simply too high for aerial medical evacuation to become standard practice.
"We don't see aerial evacuation becoming routine," says Pavlo Feldblium, co-founder of Gurzuf Defence. "When people talk about thousands of such missions or suggest that drones could help meet the 'golden hour', I think of the science fiction of Ray Bradbury or Stanisław Lem. You can't launch an operation like this on the spur of the moment. Every mission is unique and has to be planned around the specific conditions on that section of the front line. It's important to understand that this is always a last resort."
The experience of rescuing Magura, however, has prompted changes to drone development. Gurzuf Defence has decided to equip its mass-produced Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 logistics drones with the technical modifications and mounting kits needed for emergency evacuations, enabling them to be used for rescue missions when necessary.
The company stresses, however, that the evacuation equipment will not necessarily be used on every flight: the drone remains primarily a logistics platform. The developers are also working on entirely new variants of the platform with a substantially higher payload capacity.
The operation has shown that wounded soldiers can be evacuated by air even if they cannot walk and are stranded in remote positions. Other manufacturers are also exploring this capability. SkyFall recently unveiled its StarGate evacuation drone.
This evacuation, carried out by the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade and the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, has proved the viability of the concept and highlighted the urgent need for an evacuation method that can be used when all other options fail. Magura's rescue has set a precedent for saving lives in situations where conventional evacuation is impossible.
Kostiantyn "Magura" Vlasenko, who held a position on the left bank of the Oskil River for 491 days despite losing both feet, has been nominated for the title of Hero of Ukraine.
After Magura was evacuated to the rear, the commander of the 10th Army Corps visited him in hospital and personally presented him with the Order of Bohdan Khmelnytskyi, 3rd Class. The infantryman had been awarded the order in May, while still holding his position. Soldiers from the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, who planned and carried out the aerial evacuation, have also been nominated for state awards.
Representatives of Gurzuf Defence – the manufacturer of the very Ayudag-6 that flew him out of hell – also visited Magura in hospital.
Yurii Denysiuk

Salvador Dalí’s surreal universe unfolds in Istanbul through digital art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:33:42 UTC
15:33:42 KST

The exhibition explores Salvador Dalí’s art and his fascination with DNA, geometry, the fourth dimension and nuclear physics. (AA Photo)
Melting clocks, shifting dimensions and the strange logic of dreams take on a new dimension in Istanbul, where an immersive exhibition invites visitors into the mind of Salvador Dalí, the Spanish surrealist whose art blurred the boundaries between reality, illusion and scientific possibility.
“Into a Genius Mind: Dalí Cybernetics” opened on Oct. 22 at Istanbul Municipality’s Digital Experience Center. First presented in Barcelona in 2022, the exhibition has welcomed hundreds of thousands of visitors across 14 cities, including London, Berlin, Copenhagen, Lisbon and Athens, making Istanbul its 15th stop.
Developed by Barcelona-based Layers of Reality with support from the Gala-Salvador Dalí Foundation, the exhibition explores how Dalí transformed scientific ideas into surrealist imagery. His fascination with DNA, nuclear physics, geometry, optical illusions and the fourth dimension reveals an artist who drew inspiration not only from dreams and the subconscious but also from humanity’s expanding understanding of the universe.
Across approximately 2,000 square meters, large-scale projections, interactive installations, augmented reality and virtual reality reconstruct Dalí’s imaginative world.
In “Dalívers,” visitors board a virtual ship and navigate dreamlike landscapes inspired by his art. Up to 20 people can explore the virtual reality space simultaneously.
An immersive room equipped with 30 4K projectors envelops visitors in 360-degree images, while an installation inspired by Dalí’s fascination with DNA brings the meeting of scientific discovery and artistic imagination into focus.
A particularly intimate section offers a rare glimpse of Dalí through the lens of Ara Güler, Türkiye’s internationally acclaimed photojournalist, whose photographs capture the artist beyond his iconic imagery.
Güler first met Dalí in 1971 at the Hôtel Meurice in Paris, after a long-standing desire to photograph the surrealist was fulfilled through a mutual acquaintance. The encounter led to further visits during which Güler photographed Dalí’s daily life and working environment, producing hundreds of frames. The exhibition presents just four photographs from this body of work — three in black and white and one in color — selected from the extensive archive preserved by the Ara Güler Archives and Research Center.
The collection also holds slides, negatives and contact prints of Dalí portraits, as well as a portrait signed by Dalí himself. Güler later included the artist among seven prominent figures of the 20th century in his book “Seven Personalities on Earth,” first published in 2002, recording his memories of their encounters.
The exhibition also features a cinema room drawing on Jack Bond’s 1965 documentary “Dalí in New York” and Albert and David Maysles’ 1966 film “Dalí’s Fantastic Dream.”
Layers of Reality Managing Partner Jordi Sellas i Ferrés said the exhibition asks what Dalí might have created had he possessed today’s technological tools, using immersive environments to turn his artistic universe into an experience visitors can explore from within.

When a restaurant becomes the journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:33:30 UTC
15:33:30 KST

At three-Michelin-starred Azurmendi, you become part of the story long before you ever take your seat. Chef Eneko Atxa has woven the landscape, memory and produce of the Basque Country not only into his dishes but into every aspect of the restaurant. For me, Azurmendi was one of the most compelling dining experiences I have had in recent years. And the story continued when I returned to Bilbao, seven floors above the hotel where I was staying.
The moment you walk through the door, you feel less as though you have entered a three-Michelin-starred dining room than arrived at a picnic. A small basket is placed before you, its contents intended to be eaten with your hands. From there, instead of being shown to your table, you are invited into the kitchen. Across the counter are heirloom tomatoes in different colors and shapes, alongside a series of tomato-based bites. Leaving the kitchen, you still do not head for the dining room. Instead, you move through another space, created with recycled materials and resembling a contemporary art installation, discovering a succession of small bites as you go. Only then are you taken to your table in the main dining room. Beyond the floor-to-ceiling glass are trees, and the boundary between inside and out seems almost to disappear.
I have been eating in exceptional restaurants around the world for many years. At some point, three Michelin stars, flawless service and dazzling technique no longer impress quite as easily as they once did. There are even moments when I find myself wondering whether fine dining is beginning to look increasingly alike wherever you go. Here, however, I never felt I was watching a spectacle engineered simply to surprise me. I felt I had stepped inside the world of a chef who knows exactly what he wants to say.
That chef is Eneko Atxa, one of the defining figures of contemporary Basque cuisine. Alongside its three Michelin stars, Azurmendi has twice been named the World’s Most Sustainable Restaurant by The World’s 50 Best Restaurants.
The restaurant preserves the seeds of more than 400 local vegetable varieties, conducts research into hydroponic cultivation, produces its own compost, harvests produce daily and works with a network of small local producers. When the building was designed in 2012, locally sourced and recycled materials, together with renewable-energy technologies, were already integral to the project.
Azurmendi is an extraordinarily refined, beautiful and at times theatrical experience. Yet it redefines luxury not through the quantity of expensive ingredients on the plate, but through the quality of the relationship between an ingredient and its journey from seed to table. The tomatoes I encountered in the kitchen are a perfect example. Atxa takes this most everyday of ingredients and explores its skin, flesh, pulp and liquid in different forms. Within minutes, the same tomato appears in different textures, temperatures and intensities of flavor.
An oyster arrives topped with an icy preparation made from more than 30 marine ingredients, shoots and seaweeds. The first sensation is of an icy, saline, iodine-rich sea; seconds later, the natural sweetness of the oyster emerges. Recently singled out by Michelin inspectors as one of their most memorable dishes, it does not so much represent the sea as allow you to taste the Cantabrian coast in a few mouthfuls.
Another dish brings together charcoal-roasted pepper, fermented pepper juice and txistorra, the characteristic Basque sausage. For me, this dish is every bit as important as the others in understanding Atxa’s relationship with tradition. Here, tradition is a living memory, rearticulated through contemporary technique. The pepper is still unmistakably pepper, the txistorra still txistorra, yet familiar flavors acquire a clarity, intensity and contemporary language of their own.
The lobster takes a different approach. Removed from its shell, it is cooked over charcoal and served with vegetable jus and a butter made from its own shell. There is intensity rather than ostentation. It feels less like transforming an ingredient into something else than making it somehow more itself. To me, this is one of the great strengths of Atxa’s cooking. However sophisticated the technique, what you remember in the end is not the technique itself, but the ingredient — and the flavor it leaves on your palate.
The name of one dessert sums up Atxa’s entire approach more eloquently than any technical explanation could: “Honey and a Thousand Flowers.” The menu describes it as the representation of a landscape. And at Azurmendi, everything ultimately leads you back to the same place: Geography. The tomato speaks of the soil, the oyster of the sea, the pepper of Basque culinary memory and the honey of the landscape. Behind the dishes are farmers, fishermen, beekeepers and small producers; beyond the windows is the green world to which those dishes belong. The landscape outside ceases to be scenery and becomes an extension of what you are eating inside.
If Azurmendi was one of the most compelling dining experiences I have had in recent years, I think it was not simply because I ate exceptionally well. It was because, for a few hours, I was allowed to see the world through Eneko Atxa’s eyes.
On the way back from Azurmendi to my hotel in Bilbao, I found myself thinking about an article I had written a few months earlier: “Now the Restaurant Chooses the Hotel.” Fittingly, on the top floor of the Radisson Collection Hotel Gran Vía Bilbao, where I was staying, is Azurmendi’s sister restaurant, Eneko Basque. Here we encounter a more relaxed, urban expression of Atxa’s cooking. Basque cuisine, grilling, cured meats, dishes designed for sharing and wines from the region take center stage. One of the most appealing features of the restaurant, which is also included in the Michelin Guide, is its terrace. Bilbao’s urban landscape on one side, a strong expression of Basque cooking on the other: In a city you have travelled to for its gastronomy, your hotel can keep you connected to the story of the destination without even having to step outside for dinner.
Once, a good restaurant was simply an added advantage of staying at a five-star hotel. Today, as gastronomy increasingly becomes a reason to travel in its own right, some restaurants have developed identities strong enough to influence the choice of where we stay. In a city such as Bilbao, already a destination for food lovers, that relationship becomes even more meaningful. You stay in the heart of the city, spend the day exploring Bilbao’s food culture, travel out to Larrabetzu for Azurmendi, and when you return to your hotel in the evening, the gastronomic journey continues.
When I left Bilbao, it was not the most expensive ingredient or the most spectacular plate that stayed with me. It was those tomatoes in the kitchen. A chef pursuing every possibility of an ingredient, from its skin to its liquid; a restaurant preserving hundreds of local seeds; and the idea that a meal can begin long before you ever sit down at the table… A few months ago, I wrote that restaurants were beginning to determine the hotels we choose. Returning from Bilbao, I found myself wanting to add one more line: Sometimes a restaurant determines not only the hotel, but the entire journey.

Türkiye’s brain drain rate reaches highest level since 2015: Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:33:19 UTC
15:33:19 KST

Germany is the top destination for Turkish university graduates moving abroad, followed by the United States and the United Kingdom.
Türkiye’s brain drain rate among university graduates rose to 2.2 percent in 2025, marking its highest level since the data series began in 2015, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK).
The rate stood at 2.7 percent for men and 1.8 percent for women.
According to TÜİK’s higher education brain drain statistics for 2025, Istanbul recorded the highest rate among Turkish provinces, at 4 percent, followed by Izmir, Ankara, Eskişehir and Yalova. The lowest rate was recorded in Siirt, at 0.2 percent, followed by Hakkari, Kilis, Van and Bitlis.
The rate was higher among graduates of foundation universities, which are privately established higher education institutions in Türkiye, than among public university graduates. It reached 4.4 percent for foundation university graduates, compared with 1.9 percent for those graduating from state universities.
By field of study, information and communication technologies recorded the highest brain drain rate at 7 percent, followed by engineering, manufacturing and construction at 4.8 percent and natural sciences, mathematics and statistics at 3 percent.
Molecular biology and genetics topped the list of undergraduate programs, with a brain drain rate of 13.1 percent, followed by business engineering at 13 percent, mathematics engineering at 11 percent, electronics engineering at 10.9 percent and physics engineering at 10.2 percent.
Graduates whose programs were taught in French had the highest brain drain rate by language of instruction, at 10.5 percent, followed by German at 7.5 percent, English at 6.8 percent and Russian at 5 percent.
Germany was the most popular destination for Turkish university graduates who moved abroad, followed by the United States at 16.9 percent, the United Kingdom at 10.5 percent, the Netherlands at 8.3 percent and Canada at 5.2 percent.
Computer engineering graduates accounted for the largest share of those moving to Germany, the United Kingdom and the Netherlands. Electrical and electronics engineering graduates made up the largest share of those moving to the United States, while business graduates were the leading group among those relocating to Canada.

Istanbul sees seasonal rise in respiratory infections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

06:33:09 UTC

Seasonal changes are driving up the risk of respiratory infections. (AA Photo)
Istanbul is experiencing a seasonal surge in upper respiratory infections, with roughly 559,000 patients seeking hospital care for related symptoms over the past month, according to a health official.
Abdullah Emre Güner, Istanbul’s provincial health director, said that seasonal changes and the reopening of schools have increased the risk of infections spreading, particularly among children.
Güner noted that fluctuating temperatures, reliance on heating and air conditioning, and poor sleep or dietary routines could further contribute to the spike in cases.
He advised the public to eat well, get adequate rest, and keep living areas well-ventilated, emphasizing that symptomatic children — those with fever, sore throat, or a runny nose — must stay home until recovery.
While infections are generally mild among children and middle-aged adults, they can become life-threatening for older people who are bedridden or have chronic illnesses. Güner encouraged older adults and other at-risk groups to receive flu vaccinations.
Hospital bed capacity remains stable and infections are tracking within normal seasonal expectations, with no major increase over last year’s figures, according to Güner.

Aegean castle awaits UNESCO World Heritage listing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:32:58 UTC
15:32:58 KST

Güvercinada Castle sits gracefully off the scenic coast of Kuşadası.
Güvercinada Castle in Kuşadası, in Türkiye’s Aegean province of Aydın, remains on UNESCO’s Tentative List six years after its inclusion, with the coastal landmark still seeking World Heritage recognition.
The castle was added in 2020 to a wider grouping of fortifications and walled settlements along Genoese trade routes from the Mediterranean to the Black Sea. Kuşadası Municipality prepared the submission with support from the Aydın Governor’s Office.
Built to defend the entrance to Kuşadası Gulf, the castle has an inner fortress commissioned by Ottoman Grand Admiral Barbaros Hayrettin Paşa. İlyas Ağa later commissioned the surrounding walls during the Morea Rebellion to protect the island site against pirate attacks.
The restored inner fortress now serves as a thematic open-air museum. Its Maritime Trade History Exhibition Area presents maritime heritage spanning the Roman and Ottoman periods, welcoming hundreds of domestic and international visitors each year.
UNESCO’s Tentative List is an inventory of sites countries could nominate for World Heritage status. Inclusion is a prerequisite for nomination, but does not guarantee inscription. The World Heritage Committee decides which sites enter the World Heritage List.

Quake survivors train kindergartners in eastern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:32:46 UTC
15:32:46 KST

Children wearing red helmets gather around AFAD teams and an emergency vehicle at Simya Kindergarten in Van’s Edremit district.
University students who survived the 2011 earthquakes in the eastern province of Van have been teaching kindergartners disaster preparedness since the start of the school year, aiming to build regional resilience.
Trained by academics and experts under the Disaster and Emergency Management Presidency (AFAD), these volunteers have been conducting outreach across the region. Having already reached three kindergartens and two facilities, the group recently taught the “drop, cover, and hold on” method at Edremit’s Simya Kindergarten, where AFAD officers also showcased specialized emergency equipment.
Van Yüzüncü Yıl University (YYÜ) Security Vocational School Director Eda Gökırmak Söğüt said she established the Emergency Management Student Club following her own experiences during the Oct. 23 and Nov. 9, 2011 earthquakes. Marking the 15th anniversary of the disasters, the initiative aims to create awareness for everyone from ages 7 to 70, she said.
“The foundational steps of creating a resilient society pass through here. Our buildings, children and society must be prepared,” Söğüt said. They aim to reach all provincial institutions to maintain this resilience, keep the memories alive and ensure communities are prepared, she said.
Preschool teacher Nisa Ebinç said the pain remains fresh 15 years later, describing early childhood as a crucial period for acquiring basic life skills. “We must prepare our children for the future with knowledge, not fear,” she said.
YYÜ Emergency and Disaster Management student Hiranur Güzem said she was forgotten at her home with her sibling due to panic during the initial 2011 tremor. “We experienced great fear inside. If we knew what to do, we could have gone under a table. Now we want children to learn these,” she said.
Fellow survivor and student Merve Çelik said she was caught unprepared as a child, remaining directly under damaged buildings out of ignorance. “We distribute brochures across university faculties to explain how they can protect themselves. We showed the students here how to drop under a desk,” Çelik said.
Kindergarten student Narin Hena Ekinci said she learned how to act during a disaster. “We protect our heads, go under a desk and hold onto a sturdy item tightly. After the earthquake ends, we move to a pre-determined safe area,” Ekinci said. Another young student, Sena Kavin Balka, said she will share the information with her family.
A 7.2-magnitude earthquake struck Van on Oct. 23, 2011, causing widespread destruction. A subsequent 5.6-magnitude tremor hit the region on Nov. 9, 2011, exacerbating the severe damage across the province.

Turkish car market holds sixth place despite sales decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:28:08 UTC
15:28:08 KST

Türkiye remained Europe’s sixth-largest passenger car market in the first nine months of 2026 despite a 15.45 percent decline in sales, while also retaining sixth place in battery-electric car sales.
Sales totaled 627,977 units, placing Türkiye behind Germany, Britain, Italy, France and Spain, according to data compiled from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) and the Automotive Distributors and Mobility Association (ODMD).
ACEA’s figures, released on Oct. 22, showed registrations across the EU, European Free Trade Association countries and Britain rising 6.3 percent to 10.56 million. All five markets ahead of Türkiye grew, while Türkiye recorded the steepest percentage decline among the 10 largest markets.
Battery-electric car sales in Türkiye fell 9.1 percent to 120,329 units. Germany, Britain and France led that market, followed by Belgium and Denmark.
Türkiye was the only country among the 10 largest battery-electric markets to record a decline. Sales rose 58.1 percent in Germany, 79.1 percent in France and 30.2 percent in Britain.
Despite the decline in volume, battery-electric cars increased their share of Türkiye’s shrinking market to 19.2 percent from 17.8 percent a year earlier.
Within the EU, battery-electric cars accounted for 22.7 percent of registrations, up from 16.1 percent. Hybrids remained the largest category with a 36.3 percent share, while plug-in hybrids accounted for 10.1 percent.
The combined share of gasoline and diesel cars fell to 28.2 percent from 36.9 percent.
Türkiye’s inclusion in the EU’s proposed “Made in EU” rules remains uncertain following a Franco-German compromise on the plan, which aims to support European production against Chinese competition.
Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius told the Berlin Global Dialogue this week that modern cars relied on thousands of parts sourced worldwide. Local production requirements could make supply chains more resilient but would also raise costs, he warned.

IMF cites gains in Türkiye’s fiscal transparency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:26:31 UTC
15:26:31 KST

Türkiye has made significant progress in fiscal transparency over the past decade, placing it among the leading countries assessed by the International Monetary Fund, according to an updated report.
The IMF’s Fiscal Transparency Evaluation examines government financial reporting, budgeting and the management of fiscal risks. Around 40 countries have undergone assessments, including Britain, Finland, Ireland, Austria and Portugal.
The report credited improvements in fiscal statistics, the introduction of performance-based program budgeting and reforms to implement international public sector accounting standards.
Türkiye now meets good or advanced practice in nearly two-thirds of the principles in the IMF’s Fiscal Transparency Code, the fund said.
The gains reflect more than two decades of institutional reform. An IMF review in 2000 found weaknesses in budget preparation and implementation, with public financial reporting largely confined to cash-based budget information. Balance-sheet data were limited, while fiscal risks were insufficiently disclosed.
By the 2015 assessment, the legal framework had strengthened, medium-term budgeting had improved and financial reporting had expanded to cover the general government sector.
In its latest evaluation, the IMF identified fiscal reporting as Türkiye’s strongest area, followed by forecasting and budgeting. It also found scope for further reform in fiscal risk analysis.

The pact seeks to strengthen collective deterrence and defense, treating an external armed attack on any signatory as an attack on all three. It also provides for defense industry cooperation, including technology sharing, joint development and production.

Lower inflation helps Turkish banks withstand shocks: S&P
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:23:36 UTC
15:23:36 KST

Progress in reducing inflation is helping Türkiye’s banks withstand global and regional shocks, keeping the risks manageable despite pressure from high financing costs, an S&P Global Ratings director said.
Regina Argenio, a director and lead analyst for financial institutions at S&P, told Anadolu at the Türkiye Capital Markets Conference in Istanbul on Oct. 22 that the economy was performing better than the agency had expected at the start of the Middle East war.
S&P is monitoring banks’ ability to refinance their substantial external debt, she said, warning that disruptions could cause difficulties. She also welcomed the removal of regulatory relief measures introduced over the past year.
High real interest rates were constraining lending and making financing harder to afford for small and medium-sized businesses and retail borrowers, creating risks to banks’ asset quality, Argenio said.
Lending could improve in 2027 if interest rate cuts feed through to loan pricing. She also expects net interest margins to improve as lower rates reduce lira funding costs, although foreign-currency funding could become more expensive.
The outlook depends on the timing and pace of rate cuts and the success of the disinflation program. Sustained reductions in inflation and greater economic stability could improve asset quality and returns on capital in real terms, even if nominal profitability weakens, she added.
On the recent investment fund investigations, Argenio said the impact should remain limited if the problems stay isolated. She described the policy response as strong, with liquidity support to banks helping contain the effects.
It was still too early to assess the impact on external borrowing costs, she said. Turkish borrowers could face a small increase in risk premiums, depending on how effectively and quickly the situation is contained.

Has Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad against Amy Acton backfired?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:21:11 UTC
15:21:11 KST

Has Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad against Amy Acton backfired?
Ramaswamy’s ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother draws Republican criticism as Ohio governor’s race heats up.
An attack advertisement by Republican Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy targeting his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, has sparked criticism within his own party, less than two weeks before November 3 midterm elections in the United States.
The ad features Acton’s estranged mother accusing Acton of being a liar.
Ramaswamy has refused to withdraw the ad, even as senior Republicans have called for its removal.
So what does the ad show, why has it sparked controversy and could it affect Ohio’s governor’s race?
Here is what we know:
What does Vivek Ramaswamy’s advert show?
The ad, which began circulating online on Monday, features Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying about her childhood and suggesting she has a mental illness.
“It’s not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy has a serious problem. She is a liar. She lies about her past,” Arthur said in the video.
Arthur also disputed Acton’s account of experiencing homelessness and living in a tent as a child as she urged Ohioans not to vote for her daughter.
However, the ad does not mention that the two have been estranged since 1978 when Acton was 12 and was removed from her mother’s custody after her stepfather was charged with raping her.
Her stepfather pleaded not guilty but failed to appear in court and was never tried. Acton and her brother have publicly described the abuse they experienced as children.
Court records and news reports from the time support key elements of Acton’s account of her childhood. FactCheck.org also found records linking her stepfather to the campground where Acton said her family lived in a tent, contradicting Arthur’s claim that the family never lived there.
Arthur remained married to Acton’s stepfather until his death.
On Tuesday, Ramaswamy’s campaign confirmed it was behind the advertisement and announced plans to spend $4m promoting it.
Why has the advertisement sparked controversy?
On Tuesday, Acton’s campaign released a statement recounting her childhood and a response ad featuring her brother, Phil Stearns.
“I received a lot of abuse, but Amy always got the worst of it,” Stearns said. “She continued to receive that abuse because she knew she had to protect me.”
The use of Acton’s family history has raised questions about how far political campaigns should go in attacking opponents.
David Niven, a political science professor at Ohio’s University of Cincinnati, told Al Jazeera that while campaigns have used relatives to criticise candidates before, this advertisement was particularly unusual.
“We’ve seen family members used before but not in such a deeply personal way,” Niven said.
“So we occasionally see a family member who’s talking about disagreements, you know, talking about a different kind of political outlook, but not this degree of just personal destruction. That’s what’s unprecedented here.”
How have Trump and other Republicans responded?
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended Ramaswamy while other senior Republicans have called for the ad to be withdrawn.
On Thursday, Trump described the ad as “very powerful” and said he had encouraged Ramaswamy to continue running it. Vance told Republicans to “stop whining” about the controversy and focus on winning the elections.
Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, who has endorsed Ramaswamy, called the advertisement “deeply, deeply troubling” and urged its withdrawal although he maintained his endorsement.
Ohio Senator Jon Husted has also distanced himself from the ad.
Niven said the disagreement reflected a broader divide between traditional Republicans and the party’s Trump-aligned wing.
“So there’s a real divide between the Republican Party as it kind of traditionally was, that had something of a standard, and the Republican Party of Trump and Vance that will say anything at any time, regardless of the, you know, propriety of it.”
Ramaswamy has refused to withdraw the ad.
Who are Vivek Ramaswamy and Amy Acton?
Vivek Ramaswamy, 41, is a Republican businessman and former biotechnology executive who unsuccessfully sought the party’s presidential nomination in 2024 before endorsing Trump.
Born and raised in Ohio, he is running for governor with the president’s endorsement.
Amy Acton, 60, is a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health who became nationally known for leading the state’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic under DeWine.
Raised in Youngstown, she has spoken publicly about experiencing poverty, homelessness and abuse during childhood.
Neither candidate has previously held elected office.
Could the ad backfire?
The ad could generate sympathy for Acton, particularly among survivors of sexual abuse and their families, according to political analysts.
“Every negative attack carries the risk of backfiring,” Jerry Miller, a professor of communication studies and a political advertising expert at Ohio University, told Al Jazeera.
He explained that campaigns sometimes use controversial advertisements to energise their supporters, even at the risk of alienating other voters.
“I do believe that this ad will generate a degree of empathy, particularly from sexual assault survivors and their families who have had to confront these issues,” he added.
Trump has survived numerous political controversies without losing the support of his base, but Niven said Ramaswamy may find it harder to move past this one.
“The thing that Trump has mastered is he’s always involved in a hundred controversies at a time,” he said. “So you kind of lose track of one controversy because it’s replaced by another one so quickly after.”
But Ramaswamy may not have that advantage.
“The problem for Ramaswamy is this is the only thing people are going to be seeing and hearing. He’s not going to be able to achieve the sort of Trump controversy distraction game,” Niven added.
Why does the controversy matter for Ohio’s governor’s race?
The controversy comes with Acton leading in several recent polls although some surveys suggested a closer contest.
On Friday, the Cook Political Report shifted the race from being a toss-up to leaning towards Acton. It cited the fallout from the advertisement. Its analysts said the race had already been moving towards Acton and the controversy had reinforced their assessment.
The backlash has also generated financial support for Acton, including a $500,000 donation from MK Pritzker, wife of Illinois Governor JB Pritzker.
Hundreds of Ohioans have already cast early ballots, and it remained unclear whether the controversy would influence undecided voters.
“What is already clear is that the controversy has taken on a life of its own, becoming a major factor in this campaign, independent of the ad that sparked it,” Miller told Al Jazeera.
Ohio is an important battleground in the November 3 elections. Once considered a swing state, it has voted for Trump in the past three presidential elections, and Republicans have held the governorship since 2011. A victory for Acton would make her the state’s first Democratic governor in 20 years.

Permanent secretary pressed five times on backloading
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:00:43 BST
15:00:43 KST

The Permanent Secretary at the Ministry of Defence was asked five times by a member of the Defence Committee whether the Defence Investment Plan settlement is backloaded, telling MPs at one point that he was not sure he understood the definition and finally that there was not more he could give the committee.
Jeremy Pocklington was giving evidence alongside Wes Streeting, the Secretary of State for Defence.
Derek Twigg, the Labour member for Widnes and Halewood, put it to Streeting that John Healey’s resignation letter had said the funding settlement was insufficient, and that the extra support was backloaded when the pressure of operations and the imperative to speed up readiness falls in the first two years.
Streeting said extra funding was won by Dan Jarvis during the Defence Investment Plan process and brought in the Permanent Secretary, who had been party to those discussions.
Twigg asked: “Is it backloaded or not?” Pocklington began: “Additional resource DEL was given to the Department between the time of John Healey’s resignation and Dan Jarvis settling the DIP.”
Twigg interrupted to say he wanted a straight answer for the committee and repeated the question. Pocklington said: “The overall departmental spending is on a rising profile, so by the end of this Parliament it will be 27% higher in real terms than at the start.”
The chair, Tan Dhesi, intervened twice to ask for an answer, and Pocklington said: “I am keen to help the Committee. I can read out what our spending totals are for each year.” Asked again, he said: “I am not sure I understand the definition.”
He then said: “We received additional support between the time between the time of John Healey’s resignation and Dan Jarvis that meant that the spending power of the Department has actually increased by £15 billion. It was a lower amount at the time that John Healey resigned. We do have additional support, including, in particular, additional support for RDEL for readiness.”
Asked a final time whether he agreed with the previous Secretary of State on the point, Pocklington said: “I think the settlement had changed. There is not more that I can give to the Committee.”
On the trajectory of spending, Streeting told the committee that defence spending was 2.3 per cent of national income when Labour came to office and will be 2.7 per cent in 2027-28, and that the Chancellor has said he will plug a £4.7 billion gap at the Budget with more to come at the spending review.
Twigg pressed him on whether there is any commitment to reach three per cent by 2030. Streeting said: “But we would not normally, and we do not normally, set out ahead of spending reviews what the control totals will be.”
Dhesi told him: “It seems palpable to many of us that we are not meeting the moment, and that is why there is a sense of exasperation.” He noted the committee had visited Denmark, which has gone from spending 1.3 per cent of national income on defence to 4.99 per cent within four years.
Streeting said: “And in those cases, Chair, look at the cost of borrowing in those countries. We are not comparing like with like.” He said the debt-to-GDP ratio is around a hundred per cent and that roughly one in every ten taxpayer pounds goes on servicing debt interest.

====================================================================================================

How Ukrainians in US advocate for Ukraine’s interests
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:00:00 EEST
15:00:00 KST

How Ukrainians in US advocate for Ukraine’s interests
For decades, the Ukrainian community in the U.S. has been working to ensure that relations between Ukraine and the U.S. remain strong and that Ukraine has reliable partners in Washington.
The Ukrainian Congress Committee of America (UCCA), a nonpartisan organization of Ukrainian Americans, has represented the community's interests since 1940. Our position does not depend on which party is in power; our mission is to defend Ukraine's interests. In our work and communications, we consistently explain to the American public that supporting Ukrainian sovereignty is important for America itself.
One focus of our advocacy is increasing economic pressure on Russia. As part of this effort, we have supported legislative initiatives by Senators Lindsey Graham and Richard Blumenthal to strengthen sanctions against the Kremlin.
The latest decisions by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration – in particular, regarding the return of Russian diesel fuel to the global market and the easing of sanctions against Russia – contradict our position on the need to increase economic pressure on the Kremlin, as they provide Russia with additional resources to continue the war.
While the U.S. Administration might couch the rationale for the diesel deal to 'lower fuel prices' for American consumers, the easing of sanctions should be evaluated in light of their consequences. A decision that claims to offer only minor benefits for U.S. citizens but simultaneously increases Russia's revenues – which it uses to finance the war – runs counter to the long-term security interests of the U.S., and most importantly to worldwide democratic values and principles.
Similarly, we disagree with the U.S. government's criticism of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure as an argument in favor of making concessions to the Kremlin. Ukraine is defending itself against a state that launched a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and still shows no willingness to end its aggression. Unilateral concessions by partners do not, in and of themselves, guarantee peace.
Moreover, the experience of recent years shows that Vladimir Putin is not seeking a compromise for the sake of a just peace, but rather the opportunity to continue the war on terms favorable to himself. Therefore, in its communications with the American audience, the UCCA strives to clearly explain Russia's true intentions and outline the real mechanisms for deterring the aggressor.
At the same time, we see that concerns about such decisions are shared not only by Democrats but also by Republicans in Congress. This is important because support for Ukraine must not become a pawn in intra-party struggles.
Not just protests
When talking about the influence of the Ukrainian community in the U.S., it is important to understand the unique characteristics of the American political system. American democracy has its own mechanisms for influencing the government, and mass street protests are just one of them. They can draw attention to an issue, but they do not guarantee a change in political course.
Large-scale demonstrations on various domestic and foreign policy issues take place regularly in the U.S.. However, our experience shows that if we want to achieve concrete results for Ukraine, we must work simultaneously on many levels – in Congress, in the media, with civil society organizations, business representatives, and various ethnic communities.
The UCCA's activities are not limited to public events; we also maintain regular contact with members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, convey our position to political circles in both parties, collaborate with journalists, and strive to ensure that Ukrainian issues remain on the American public agenda.
We have developed partnerships with other communities, including Polish, Baltic, Georgian, Jewish, and Cuban. For example, in 1994, the UCCA was instrumental in founding the Central and East European Coalition (CEEC), which unites the concerns of over 20 million Americans citizens of Central and East European descent. Many of them have their own historical reasons to take a close interest in Russian aggression, authoritarianism, and international security issues. Working together helps us better explain to the American public why supporting Ukraine is in the interests not only of Ukrainians, but also of the U.S. and its allies.
We also work with business leaders. When influential businesspeople publicly support decisions that could weaken Ukraine's ability to defend itself, it is important for Americans to understand the consequences of such decisions, especially in bringing attention to the American businesses that have been targeted by Russian attacks in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022. We view public communication and peaceful protests near commercial facilities as one way to draw attention to the responsibility businesses have for their influence on societal processes.
Our task is not simply to express disagreement, but to convey our arguments to as broad an audience as possible and to translate public support for Ukraine into concrete policy decisions.
We see a basis for this work. According to the sociological studies on which we rely, the majority of Americans supports aid to Ukraine and views Russia as an existential threat to American interests. At the same time, this support cannot be taken for granted – it must be constantly reinforced by explaining to Americans what is at stake.
Strength lies in unity
The Ukrainian community in the U.S. is not homogeneous; among Ukrainian Americans, there are supporters of both Democrats and Republicans, representatives of different generations of immigrants, and people with diverse experiences and views on US domestic policy.
From the very beginning, the UCCA has been an organization that unites the community around shared national interests, rather than party affiliation. We have contacts with people who have worked in both Republican and Democratic administrations, and we collaborate with representatives of both parties. This allows us to convey the Ukrainian position to various political circles, regardless of who is in the White House or leading Congress.
The diversity of our community is not a weakness but a strength. It enables us to speak to different audiences in the language of their values and interests. For some, the main argument is the defense of democracy; for others, it is national security; and for still others, it is the need to prevent aggressive authoritarian regimes from changing international borders by force.
Ukrainians who arrived in the U.S. after the start of the full-scale invasion deserve special attention. The issue of their future and immigration status remains critical, and we are working with our partners in Congress and other government officials to advocate for their interests.
At the same time, their contribution to supporting Ukraine is already extremely significant. The Ukrainian community in America is raising funds, organizing humanitarian aid shipments, and assisting hospitals and the civilian population. Since the start of the full-scale war, tens and hundreds of millions of dollars in aid have been sent to Ukraine through various community initiatives and charitable projects.
Not everyone can attend a demonstration or speak out publicly against a particular political decision. But helping Ukraine takes many forms, and each one is important. Our goal is to create opportunities for everyone who wants to get involved, regardless of their background, political beliefs, or life circumstances.
One area of our work is direct humanitarian support for Ukraine. I recently joined the Ukraine Focus mission to deliver ambulances that were collected in Europe and transported to Ukraine. This time, there were about fifty vehicles intended for the needs of Ukraine's territorial defense forces and other units requiring medical transport.
Another important area is political advocacy. As early as 2000, the UCCA launched Ukrainian Days in Washington so that representatives of Ukrainian communities from across the country could meet with their congressmen and senators, representatives of research centers, diplomats, and other influential figures. Following Russia's aggression in 2014, we stepped up this work.
We also collaborate with other initiatives to strengthen U.S. support for Ukraine. Overall, our guiding principle is that the voice of the Ukrainian community must be heard consistently, not just when another crisis arises.
Ukraine's security is America's security
For decades, American leadership and cooperation with European allies have been key factors in the stability of the democratic world. If the U.S. distances itself from its partners in Europe or gives the impression that aggression can be rewarded with concessions, the consequences will be felt not only by Ukrainians. This will affect allies' confidence in American commitments, the ability to deter future conflicts, and the international system, in which the sovereignty of states should not depend on the strength of their neighbors.
We work earnestly to ensure that cooperation between the White House and Congress will pave the way for a more consistent policy toward Ukraine. It is important that our security issues not be turned into a tool for domestic political struggles, and that support for Ukraine remain a shared strategic interest of the U.S.
I often recall the words of American pastor Mark Burns, who, after visiting Ukraine and seeing things with his own eyes, said: "Ukraine is America First". These words are particularly telling in the context of the "America First" slogan frequently used by President Trump. Their meaning is that defending Ukraine does not conflict with American interests. On the contrary, Ukraine is part of the democratic world, and the outcome of this war will affect security, stability, and the future far beyond its borders.
That is why we will continue to explain to Americans that aid to Ukraine is not just a matter of solidarity, but an investment in international security and the protection of the principles of American democracy.
To the people in Ukraine, I want to say that we are constantly working for victory for Ukraine. Ukraine remains in our thoughts, in our humanitarian work, in our meetings with politicians, and in every effort to convince the American public that our struggle matters to the entire democratic world.
Having been to Ukraine several times since Russia's full-scale invasion, I, and my organisation, understand how difficult it is to live under constant rocket and drone attacks and how much depends on the support of our partners, so we will continue to work – in the humanitarian sphere, in political advocacy, and in building partnerships that help Ukraine endure.
I would like to thank Ukrainian Americans for their tireless work. Regardless of when they or their families arrived in the U.S., what political views they hold, or how they choose to help, their contribution is of great importance.
We must remain united around a common goal. We don't have to agree on every issue of the American domestic policy to understand that a free, democratic, and sovereign Ukraine is in the interests of both Ukraine and the U.S.
Our task is to continue our work, expand our circle of partners, find new ways to convey our position, and turn support into concrete actions. I am convinced that a strong, democratic, and sovereign Ukraine will remain an important strategic partner of the United States for infinity. And that is precisely what we are working toward.
Michael Sawkiw, President of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America (UCCA) and Director of its Washington, DC bureau – the Ukrainian National Information Service (UNIS), Chair of the Ukrainian World Congress (UWC) Foreign Policy Council, and recipient of the Order of Merit II degree.

US has asked Musk to change Starlink services in Ukraine, Middle East for years, fears misuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:58:26 UTC
14:58:26 KST

Well before the throttling this month of Ukraine's military access to Elon Musk's satellite communications system, the Biden and Trump administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn its Starlink service on or off in various countries, according to six former senior US officials familiar with the matter.
During the presidency of Joe Biden, the requests included switching off the service to prevent Iranian proxy militias in Yemen and Lebanon from using Starlink to communicate, and activating the service to provide internet access inside Iran and in Ukraine to support its military, said four of the former officials.
Similarly, President Donald Trump's administration asked Musk, who is CEO of SpaceX, to make the service available in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in 2025 and 2026, in hopes it would bolster internet access and communications for anti-government protesters, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters.
All of the people spoke on condition of anonymity. The previous US requests about Starlink access are being reported here for the first time.
The recent blowup over restrictions to Ukraine's use of SpaceX satellite services has raised questions about the ties between the US government and Musk, whose company owns systems vital to the US military and to US allies.
The Biden-era and Trump requests to Musk show a close relationship in which US administrations rely to an unprecedented degree on a private-sector company to help implement foreign policy.
The recent limits on Ukraine, despite being a US ally, have also rattled officials in Europe, some of whom argue that Europe must develop its own military satellite communications capabilities because no viable short-term alternative currently exists.
Starshield restrictions hobble Ukrainian military
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that his country's access to Starshield, the military version of the Starlink system, had been intentionally limited, interfering with the performance of the country’s military drones. He also said the speeds were reduced for Starlink, which Ukraine uses for some military activities including defense against Russian missile attacks.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. The Trump administration has acknowledged the slowdown but has not said whether it gave the order.
The White House, contacted for comment, referred Reuters to Trump's remarks on Friday, when he said he had not spoken with Musk about Starlink access issues for Ukraine and that "if there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out."
Halyna Yusypiuk, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Ukraine's priority is "to have the service restored to normal speed as soon as possible, as the lives of our people depend on it."
SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment, although Musk said in a social media post earlier this week: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States).”
Democratic US Representative Jason Crow called on Friday for clarity about the recent changes to Ukraine's satellite service, saying there are risks to the US dependence on SpaceX.
"Unelected billionaires and private corporations should not decide what is in the best interest of America's national security," Crow said.
For Ukraine, the Starlink internet service has become the lifeblood of frontline communication between units, who say there is currently no rival to the capabilities of SpaceX's products.
Starshield receivers, largely impervious to radio jamming, are used as onboard guidance systems and to provide links to a remote pilot for Ukrainian drones, including deep behind Russian lines inside Ukraine.
Musk's influence raises uncertainty
Musk's role as the strong-willed CEO of a company with outsized influence over US national security has at times raised questions over who is making decisions about SpaceX's satellite services.
The SpaceX CEO is "supposed to be a business executive, with government contracts, and he's essentially making huge foreign policy decisions," said Armand Musey, president of Summit Ridge Group, a satellite industry consultancy.
"He's sufficiently ambiguous of a person that you don't know if his decisions are sort of his personal quirks, or it's because there's an influence elsewhere that's impacting him," Musey said.
In previous years, Musk has moved to limit Ukraine’s access to Starlink. In 2022, according to Reuters reporting, Musk ordered SpaceX personnel to cut Starlink coverage in areas Ukraine was trying to retake, a move that surprised White House officials.
Musk has said publicly that he refused a 2022 Ukrainian request to activate his satellite network in Crimea's port city of Sevastopol to aid an attack on Russia's fleet there, saying he feared complicity in a major act of war.
The Biden administration at times relied on Musk to help implement policy, five of the former officials said.
Concerns that Houthis, Hezbollah use diverted Starlink terminals
Biden officials coordinated with SpaceX to thwart US adversaries by cutting the service, and to help allies by expanding Starlink’s availability, they said.
They added that discussions between the government and SpaceX, which usually included Pentagon and White House officials, often focused on preventing groups such as the Iranian-linked Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon from using Starlink terminals.
Biden officials several times shared intelligence with SpaceX that indicated that the Houthis and Hezbollah were using diverted Starlink terminals - hardware that made its way to the militants through intermediaries.
In October 2023, during fighting between Israel and Hezbollah militants in southern Lebanon, intelligence officials told the White House that individuals linked to Hezbollah could have gained access to Starlink terminals. Officials had similar concerns about the Houthis in Yemen in 2024 during a US air campaign against the Iran-linked group, five of the officials said.
In both cases, the administration contacted SpaceX and asked it to identify the terminals and shut them off. At least some of the terminals were deactivated, said two of the officials.
In a 2024 submission to the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, SpaceX said it works closely with US government agencies to secure export authorizations where required and to safeguard technology in support of US national security objectives and foreign policy goals.
Soon after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Biden officials pushed SpaceX to expand Starlink use for the Ukrainian military, said two of the former officials.
In a separate instance, the Biden administration asked SpaceX to turn on Starlink in Iran during a protest movement launched in September 2022 after the death of Mahsa Amini, an Iranian arrested for not wearing her hijab properly, according to one of the former officials.
Starlink terminals were moved into the country with the help of the administration, said the official, who declined to say how many were transferred.
The Trump administration took a similar step earlier this year and discussed with Musk and SpaceX getting Starlink terminals into Iran and activated following US-Israeli strikes in the country in June 2025 and again in February 2026, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Neither the Trump administration nor SpaceX has publicly confirmed that those terminals were turned on. The Wall Street Journal reported in February that the US government had sent thousands of Starlink terminals into Iran.
Iran's delegation to the UN did not respond to a request for comment.

Türkiye’s innovation ecosystem grows with state support as active R&D centres top 1,300
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:46:22 UTC
14:46:22 KST

Türkiye’s innovation ecosystem grew significantly over the years, driven by state support, with the number of active research and development (R&D) centres reaching 1,365 and design centers totaling 348 by the end of September.
Data from the Turkish Ministry of Industry and Technology showed that R&D hubs employ nearly 94,000 workers nationwide, including nearly 57,700 with bachelor’s degrees, over 18,500 with master’s degrees, and over 2,100 with a doctorate or higher.
Türkiye’s academically well-equipped R&D workforce has completed more than 80,400 projects to date, with nearly 16,000 still underway.
The robust innovation hubs have generated almost 49,000 patents so far, with over 17,500 registered and about 31,300 awaiting examination results.
Türkiye’s R&D network spans the country and many sectors, from energy, agriculture, and healthcare to transportation, logistics, and aviation.
The machinery and equipment manufacturing sector led with 160 centres, followed by the auto supply industry with 136 and the software sector with 128, the data showed.
The drivers of R&D innovation also included the computer and communications technologies sector with 86 centres, chemicals with 82 hubs, textiles and electrical sectors with 77 facilities each, food and the defence industry (excluding weapons and ammunition) with 65 each, and the general manufacturing industry with 43 centres.
The facilities are spread nationwide, but Istanbul has the highest concentration of R&D hubs with 428 centres, Ankara with 168, Kocaeli with 137, Bursa with 134, Izmir with 105, Tekirdag with 54, Manisa with 34, Konya with 26, Sakarya with 25, and Antalya with 21.
Meanwhile, Türkiye’s 348 design centres employ 8,481 workers, 5,540 of them with bachelor’s degrees, 820 with master’s degrees, and 50 with doctorates or higher degrees.
While the design centres operate across a myriad of sectors, they are heavily focused on industrial and structural sectors, with the textile industry ranking first, boasting 54 centres, followed by engineering and architecture with 51, general manufacturing with 45, and machinery and equipment manufacturing with 43.
The design ecosystem also included 23 design centres for the auto supply industry, 17 for media and communications, 15 for the furniture sector, 12 each for construction and auto manufacturing, and eight for the defence sector.
Istanbul is home to most of the design centres, with 154, followed by the capital Ankara with 39, Bursa with 31, Izmir with 28, and Kocaeli and Tekirdag with 15 each, according to ministry data.

Japan's energy vulnerabilities exposed by Mideast crisis: white paper
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:41:16 CST
14:41:16 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Japan's vulnerability in energy supply and demand has once again come to the fore as tensions in the Middle East escalate, according to the Japanese government's energy white paper for fiscal 2025, released Friday.
The white paper said Japan has long relied on the Middle East for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports. Following U.S. and Israeli military strikes on Iran in late February this year, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key global energy transit route, was disrupted, creating uncertainty over supplies of crude oil and petroleum products.
The disruption also hindered the distribution of some petroleum-related products, including naphtha, the report said.
To secure domestic energy supplies, the government has released oil reserves and stepped up efforts to procure alternative supplies from regions outside the Middle East since March. These measures helped ensure crude oil supplies to Japan, according to the white paper.
However, concerns over the supply outlook prompted stockpiling of certain petroleum-related products, disrupting distribution and leading to uneven supplies across the country, it said.
The white paper noted that the energy crisis response mechanisms Japan had developed over decades following the oil crises of the 1970s are no longer adequate to address emerging risks to energy supplies.
The annual energy white paper is usually adopted by the cabinet around June each year, but its compilation was delayed this year until October to incorporate developments in the Middle East and the government's responses to the situation. ■
