How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:29:07 UTC
14:29:07 KST

How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutions
As Israel heads to the polls on October 27, its polarising and longest-serving prime minister is seeking re-election.
To his supporters, he is known as “King Bibi”; but to his opponents, he is the king of security failures and corruption.
Disputes over names aside, what is not in question is that Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has left his mark on the country’s institutions, politics and social attitudes during a decades-long career that has been defined by Israel’s lurch to the right.
As he seeks re-election in Israel’s October 27 polls, analysts say his most enduring domestic legacy may be the right-wing, militaristic opposition that he has helped create and now faces.
Born in 1949, Netanyahu entered Israel’s central political stage in the early 1990s by fuelling anger at possible peace deals with the Palestinians and Syria.
Israeli political leaders have accused him of leading incitement that motivated the 1995 assassination of then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, who was leading negotiations with the Palestine Liberation Organization, by an ultranationalist Israeli. Netanyahu had led rallies in which participants depicted Rabin in a Nazi SS uniform and held signs of him in the crosshairs of a gun, while others shouted “traitor”.
The Likud Party leader denies any responsibility, but former security officials have said they warned Netanyahu before the assassination and asked him to dial down his rhetoric, only for him to refuse, according to Israeli media reports.
In 1996, Netanyahu’s populist tactics succeeded at the ballot box, making him Israel’s youngest prime minister. Netanyahu’s transactional leadership style gave prominence to extreme-right and religious parties that are now an indispensable part of his right-wing alliance.
Under him, religious courts have expanded powers, including over civil and business disputes. State institutions accommodate religious agendas and allocate record levels of funding to ultra-Orthodox schools and institutions.
Netanyahu inscribed his political ideology, especially on the identity of the state and the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel, into law. In 2018, the Knesset passed the so-called Nation-State Basic Law, which states – among other things – that Israel is the exclusive state of the Jewish people and also makes advancing illegal settlements a national priority.
Human rights organisations in Israel petitioned the High Court to stop the legislation from going into effect, but the petition was rejected. International experts and rights groups cite this law, among others, as evidence of Israel committing the crime of apartheid in its treatment of Palestinians.
Netanyahu also re-engineered state institutions, including Israel’s security structures, appointing loyalists and political allies to senior positions. He also clashed with security chiefs that he deemed antagonistic. And in the aftermath of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack, which triggered Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, Netanyahu deflected blame and responsibility on the security establishment, prompting Ronen Bar, who was the Shin Bet chief in 2023, to sue him for defamation.
A major change to Israeli institutions that was spearheaded by Netanyahu during his 19 on-and-off years in power affected the judiciary, which is examining lingering corruption charges that could see him serve time in prison if he is convicted. Netanyahu, who is up against three separate cases of corruption filed in 2019, denies any wrongdoing.
Under his leadership, the Knesset adopted legislation that changed the composition of the Judicial Selection Committee to ensure greater political influence for the governing coalition.
Netanyahu called it “judicial reform” to stop what he often calls a “judicial dictatorship” ruling over elected officials.
Opponents called it a “coup” that sparked wide-scale protests: a push to curtail the independence of the High Court and give politicians influence over the courts and ministerial legal advisers.
In line with his efforts to subvert independent oversight, Netanyahu tried repeatedly, but unsuccessfully, to fire the attorney general.
But he succeeded in dismissing the military’s advocate general for leaking a video of Israeli soldiers gang-raping a Palestinian detainee. The soldiers were also released and cleared of charges.
At the same time, Netanyahu is dogged by corruption cases dating back to 2019, which could see him serve time in prison if convicted
The prime minister, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza, says his work is not over. He promises his supporters he will complete the overhaul of judicial review and press on with other highly controversial policies.
Netanyahu’s supporters and allies view him as a leader who delivers, and one who achieved what others could not. His opponents pledge to undo the damage Netanyahu caused over the past decades, pointing to corruption, social divisions and increasing international isolation as outcomes of his rule.
But undoing such formative changes, many of which are now law, may be easier said than done.

Addressing the UN General Assembly, Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi pushed back against Western pressure, asserting that Article IV of the NPT (Non-Proliferation Treaty) guarantees all state parties the right to develop peaceful nuclear energy, including the full nuclear fuel cycle.
The following is the full text of the statement which is read:
Mr. President,
The Agency’s reporting must remain professional, objective, factual, and free from political influence. Its credibility depends on impartiality and technical integrity.
Nuclear energy is indispensable to development and energy security. Article IV of the NPT affirms the inalienable right of all States Parties to develop research, production, and use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, without discrimination and in conformity with Articles I and II. Yet certain States systematically demonize this right and weaponize proliferation concerns to pressure States into abandoning their national nuclear fuel cycles.
The United States, an NPT depositary, openly questions the very existence of States Parties’ right to pursue the full nuclear fuel cycle, including uranium enrichment. Denying States access to this essential technology while claiming to uphold their right to peaceful nuclear energy violates Article IV. No State can unilaterally rewrite the Treaty or impose its own political veto on the legitimate rights of other States Parties.
In response to Iran’s resolute defense of its inalienable rights under the NPT, the United States and the nuclear-armed Israeli regime launched two wars of aggression against Iran in 2025 and 2026, massively targeting its peaceful nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards.
These aggressions caused immense destruction and killed thousands, including our martyred Leader, whose well-known fatwa rejects nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction. They also violated international law, the UN Charter, the IAEA Statute, relevant IAEA General Conference resolutions, and Security Council resolution 487 (1981).
Neither the IAEA General Conference, the IAEA Board of Governors, nor the Director General has condemned these attacks. The Security Council has likewise failed to do so. The Director General has once again failed to condemn these attacks in his statements delivered today under this agenda item. Instead, pressure is directed against the victim while the aggressors escape accountability.
Certain Western delegations continue to invoke so-called proliferation concerns while refusing to condemn attacks against safeguarded peaceful nuclear facilities. This is not a consistent commitment to non-proliferation; it is the weaponization of non-proliferation for political purposes.
The hypocrisy of this approach is blatant. Iran, an NPT State Party since 1970, has consistently affirmed its commitment to its international obligations and diplomacy. Yet its peaceful nuclear program and safeguarded facilities have been subjected to political pressure and military attacks, while the Secretariat’s withholding of technical cooperation deprives Iran of the benefits of peaceful nuclear development that the Agency is mandated to promote. Meanwhile, the Israeli regime—the region’s sole possessor of nuclear weapons, with unsafeguarded nuclear facilities—continues to enjoy impunity. This selective application of non-proliferation standards exposes the political motives behind the pressure on Iran and undermines the credibility of the international non-proliferation regime.
These same delegations demand access for inspectors while military threats persist, disregarding the extraordinary circumstances created by aggression. Let us be clear: Iran has neither abandoned nor formally suspended its safeguards obligations. However, aggression has fundamentally altered the physical and security conditions for their implementation. The Agency’s own reports acknowledge that verification activities ceased and inspectors were withdrawn for safety reasons. Those same safety concerns cannot be ignored when their return is demanded.
The continued existence of safeguards obligations does not eliminate the need to assess whether verification can be performed safely and effectively. No country can reasonably be expected to provide access amid military operations and persistent threats without adequate safety guarantees. Responsibility for creating these circumstances lies with the aggressors, not their victim.
Iran will continue to cooperate with the Agency to the extent circumstances permit. However, such cooperation cannot come at the expense of the safety of its people, facilities, or IAEA inspectors.
Thank you.

Paris shuts museums as France braces for new nationwide protests with massive security deployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:22:01 UTC
14:22:01 KST

Major museums in Paris closed and authorities deployed a sizable police force for a round of new protests on Saturday across France, hoping to prevent a repeat of last week’s violent unrest that shocked the country.
Scenes of looting, burned-out cars and attacks on public buildings left the impression that the government had lost control, as groups of masked vandals targeted businesses in Paris and other city centres.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannons.
A massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.
Museums are closed and shopkeepers are worried
Major museums including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organisers to cancel the weekend program.
Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République in Paris, one of last weekend’s hot spots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters.
Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged Parisian shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments is the responsibility of the government.
Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend.
Some protests have been banned
Protest marches are scheduled in Paris and Marseille, but some other rallies, including in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, have been banned by local authorities. Cities outside Paris were hit hard by the unrest. In Limoges, a suspected arson nearly destroyed the 19th-century city hall.
Trade unions have criticised the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
President Emmanuel Macron, a centrist, entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term, with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings.
Saturday’s demonstration in the city of Orléans, about 110 kilometres (70 miles) south of Paris, will also be closely watched.
About 50 organisations have called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of the two-day congress of Marine Le Pen’s nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring’s presidential election. Organisers include labour unions, left-wing parties, student and anti-racism groups.
Students and workers are angry
The demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school southeast of Paris over a lack of staff.
From there, class boycotts and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and nationwide, including smaller towns. High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as unfair.
With the government seemingly unable to respond to students’ demands, the movement has morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before the vote to choose Macron’s successor.
“The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people," said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. “And it’s not possible anymore.”

Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:20:35 UTC
14:20:35 KST

Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege
Dialysis patients face shorter treatment sessions as severe shortages of fuel, medicines, and oxygen threaten hospitals in besieged Yemeni city.
Taiz, Yemen – It was approaching 10:30am in the dialysis centre of the Republican Hospital in Taiz when a machine began filtering excess fluids, toxins and salts from the blood of Omar Mukhtar Hammoud.
The 16-year-old suffers from kidney failure and is one of 270 patients who regularly receive dialysis at the centre in the government-held city in southwest Yemen. But with essential medical supplies and fuel running critically low under the renewed Houthi siege, doctors fear they may soon be unable to provide the treatment that keeps their patients alive.
Dr Essam Mahyoub Dahan, the centre’s director, warned that a complete shutdown could happen within days.
“Because of the siege and the shortage of diesel and medical solutions, we have recently been forced to reduce dialysis sessions from four hours to just two and a half,” Dahan told Al Jazeera. “We know this is not adequate, but we have no choice if we are to keep the centre operating for as long as possible before it shuts down completely.”
Dahan said the centre’s remaining stocks of specialised dialysis solutions were also close to running out.
The supplies, which are expensive, are normally provided by the Yemeni Ministry of Health every three months. But the latest delivery which was due earlier this month failed to arrive because of the Houthi siege on Taiz city. It began in the first week of October after Houthi advances in the Taiz countryside.
The city was previously under complete Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, in the early years of Yemen’s ongoing war.
Across Taiz governorate, where battles are raging between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iranian-allied Houthi fighters, the number of patients at risk is far greater.
In an October 12 statement, the governorate’s health office warned that the continued siege and obstruction of essential supplies could endanger the lives of 1,110 patients with kidney failure. They depend on dialysis services in the governorate’s hospitals, which collectively provide about 210 dialysis sessions a day.
International humanitarian and health organisations have issued similar warnings about the impact of the siege on the already fragile healthcare system in Taiz.
On Thursday, Amnesty International called on the Houthis to immediately reopen vital roads into and around the city, warning that the closure of the main road between Taiz and the southern port city of Aden threatened hundreds of thousands of civilians with losing access to food, water and healthcare.
Fuel: A lifeline for hospitals
Taiz’s hospitals depend heavily on diesel-powered generators because much of the city’s electricity infrastructure was destroyed during the war that began 11 years ago and has not been restored.
The renewed Houthi siege has severely disrupted the entry of fuel, including the diesel needed to run hospital generators and lifesaving medical equipment.
Dr Shaheed al-Ameri, deputy director-general for technical affairs at the Republican Hospital, said the shortages have had a devastating impact on medical services.
“A very large part of this suffering is because of the shortage of diesel,” he told Al Jazeera. “We have no reserve diesel supplies. Our stocks ran out early in the siege and we are now buying it on the black market almost every day, at prices that have reached five times what they were before the siege.”
Al-Ameri warned that the longer the siege continues, the more prices will rise and the further medical services will deteriorate.
The hospital has already suspended operations in some departments, including essential units, he said.
“If this situation continues much longer, we fear we will reach a complete and comprehensive collapse of healthcare services,” he said.
The shortages are not confined to the Republican Hospital. On October 22, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned that critical shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies were threatening lifesaving healthcare throughout Taiz governorate, with some hospital services already disrupted.
According to the WHO, 42 health facilities in Taiz city had reported severe shortages of essential supplies. Hospitals and ambulances require at least 156,000 litres of fuel a month to continue functioning.
The organisation also warned that diesel shortages threaten to disrupt oxygen production, water pumping, vaccine refrigeration and sanitation services, increasing the risks of disease outbreaks, particularly among displaced families and other vulnerable groups.
The United Nations has separately warned that the restrictions on supplies are bringing Taiz’s health system close to collapse and urged the Houthis to allow humanitarian assistance and essential goods to enter without obstruction.
Oxygen shortages deepen crisis
In its October 12 statement, Taiz’s health office warned that continued restrictions on fuel deliveries could lead to the shutdown of medical oxygen production plants, further endangering patients.
Taysir al-Samei, the health office’s media officer, said that would dramatically worsen the crisis.
“Many medical departments depend on oxygen, particularly operating theatres, inpatient wards, intensive care units and incubators for premature babies,” al-Samei said.
“Most hospitals have already suspended services in some units because of the shortage of diesel and the lack of necessary medical solutions, as well as shortages of medical staff who are struggling to get to work because of the lack of transport,” he added.
He warned that if conditions continued to deteriorate at the same pace, some hospitals could stop providing services in the coming days.
At the Republican Hospital, al-Ameri said that shortages were also affecting diagnostics and treatment. The availability of laboratory reagents had fallen to just 10 to 15 percent of previous levels, he said, while approximately half of the medicines normally available were now out of stock.
Prices for the remaining medicines had doubled, he said, placing them further out of reach for patients already struggling with Yemen’s worsening economic crisis.
The continued fighting and shelling around Taiz have increased the number of wounded people requiring emergency care – placing additional pressure on facilities already struggling with shortages of surgical supplies, anaesthetics and intravenous fluids.
Abdul Badi Abdulwuhab, 53, is another dialysis patient in the Republican Hospital, struggling to cope with the shorter dialysis sessions.
His voice was filled with desperation.
“Because of these measures, I suffer from weakness and I cannot bear the pain,” Abdul Badi told Al Jazeera. “Two and a half hours is not enough to remove all the fluids and toxins from my body.”
Dr Dahan said that the patient’s condition had deteriorated since his sessions were shortened.
“These measures are not effective for many patients,” Dahan said. “The only solution is to end the siege and return things to the way they were.”

Lebanese sceptical Israeli polls will bring change, end occupation of south
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

05:04:32 UTC
14:04:32 KST

Lebanese sceptical Israeli polls will bring change, end occupation of south
Residents and analysts express doubt that October 27 election will bring any meaningful shift in Israel’s policy towards their country.
Beirut, Lebanon – As Israel’s October 27 election nears, so does the possibility that the government that has overseen the invasion and reoccupation of southern Lebanon could be deposed.
But for people in Lebanon, optimism that a change in the Israeli government will bode well for Israel’s neighbours is low.
“I don’t think anything major – or at all – will change for Lebanon even if there’s a change in [Israeli] leadership,” said Beirut resident Fouad Debs.
“Any internal change might lead to small, insignificant changes just to show the outside world that Israeli society and politics are not messed up or evil,” added the lawyer.
For many in Lebanon, Israel’s history of airspace violations, ground invasions and occupation has led to a general atmosphere of distrust, regardless of who is in charge of the country.
“Proof is what people [in Israel] are saying as the elections [approach],” said Karim Safieddine, a Beirut-based nonresident fellow at the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy.
“No one is promising withdrawal, and no one is addressing south Lebanon as a crisis or a mistake,” he added, noting that the “general Israeli establishment looks at Lebanon as its prize”.
Israel and the Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah have been fighting, with different levels of intensity, since October 2023 in the wake of the Hamas-led attack in southern Israel and Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip that followed it. Israel has twice escalated the conflict – first in September 2024 and then in March this year, following the start of the United States-Israeli war on Iran.
In June, following direct negotations that were rejected by Hezbollah, Israel and the Lebanese government signed a US-brokered framework agreement that included the goal of securing the phased withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon. Still, Israel continues to occupy large parts of its neighbour’s south, where it has systematically demolished homes and infrastructure in dozens of villages, forcing more than one million people from their homes.
Lebanese generally disagree on how to deal with Israel, as shown by a June 2026 survey by Lebanese American University professor Jad Melki and his team.
In the study, 54 percent of Lebanese polled said they supported diplomacy with Israel, while 35 percent preferred armed resistance. But the poll also found that regardless of the tactic, Lebanese views of Israel were overwhelmingly negative, with 87 percent of those polled considering it “as their enemy”.
Netanyahu vs Dahiyeh Doctrine inventor
In next week’s polls, the primary challenge to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – the man who has overseen Israel’s war on Lebanon that has killed almost 9,000 people since October 2023, including journalists, first responders and children – appears to be Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party.
Many Israelis see Eisenkot as a break from Netanyahu, who has been inundated with corruption trials, accusations of failure to prevent a Hamas-led attack in October 2023 and of prioritising attacking Gaza over releasing Israeli captives.
But in Lebanon, the general feeling is that whoever replaces Netanyahu is unlikely to deviate from the current policy of occupation and destruction.
Eisenkot, in particular, is a former general and chief of staff in the Israeli army with a historical impact on Lebanon. He acted as northern front commander in Israel’s 2006 war on Lebanon and is the architect of the Dahiyeh Doctrine, an Israeli military strategy of using disproportionate damage and destruction currently being used by Israel in Gaza and Lebanon.
More recently, he has accused Netanyahu of giving in to US pressure by stopping attacks on Beirut since April, arguing that the Israeli military should attack Hezbollah targets anywhere in Lebanon.
‘Normalised dehumanisation’
Lebanese analysts said that, although Netanyahu is wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza, Eisenkot and other challengers have mostly attacked him on domestic issues and from the right, calling him soft on issues of security.
“Those that have come forward as candidates in Israeli elections criticise Netanyahu and his handling of the war,” Elia Ayoub, a Lebanese researcher and podcaster, told Al Jazeera. “They’re not criticising him based on any kind of humanitarianism or anything [related to] human rights.”
Ayoub said the attitude towards Lebanon and other peoples and countries in the region goes beyond the Netanyahu government. He pointed out the governmental and societal backlash to the recent release of NAZA, a documentary made by Israeli journalists in which Israeli soldiers speak about the calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza.
“There’s a profoundly dehumanising discourse that is completely normalised in Israeli society, and the backlash against any pushback is drastic,” said Ayoub. “I don’t necessarily believe that it’s going to change Israeli policy towards Lebanon.”
Since the June trilateral framework agreement, Lebanon appears stuck in a limbo. While active fighting between the two sides has largely stopped, Israel continues its demolition campaign with little opposition. As the occupation becomes increasingly entrenched, many Lebanese fear it could last another generation.
“Definitely, it’s a prolonged situation of neither war nor peace,” said Safieddine. “We’re going to be living in this grey area for a very long time.”
With next week’s election unlikely to bring any meaningful change to Israel’s policies towards Lebanon and the wider region, Ayoub stressed the importance of the midterm polls in the US on November 3.
“The US elections are just as important, if not more important,” he said, “because they tend to determine how much the Israelis feel emboldened toward Palestinians first and foremost, but of course, towards Lebanon as well, and Syria to a large extent.”

14:00:46 KST

More than a billion pounds was moved out of the defence housing budget during the Defence Investment Plan process, and the Secretary of State for Defence has told MPs he is not comfortable with the choice and will not pretend rephasing allows the department to deliver as much as before.
Wes Streeting was giving evidence to the Defence Committee alongside Jeremy Pocklington, the Permanent Secretary at the Ministry of Defence.
Ian Roome, the Liberal Democrat member for North Devon, asked whether a decision had recently been taken to move over a billion pounds from the defence housing budget. Streeting said: “My predecessor took that decision. The amount being spent on defence housing is unchanged, but I concede that the profile of that spend—back to Mr Twigg’s earlier question—is more backloaded than it would have been. That is not stopping us from making a big difference on defence housing. Is it as fast as we would all like to see? No. You cannot pretend that, by backloading, you are still able to deliver the same as you would have done earlier on. It will improve year on year, but a choice was made to focus on capability over housing at that point in the process.”
Roome told him that personnel are the best capability the armed forces have, said he has a large garrison in his constituency with poor housing in some areas, and that without personnel to operate it there is no capability.
Streeting said: “I absolutely take that on the chin. I think a lot about the responsibility that I personally, and we as the state, have to people who serve, their families and people who have served previously. When I see the condition of some of our defence housing, it is up there with some of my worst constituency casework. I expect a lot better for those families who make enormous sacrifices and experience a lot of disruption for what they do. I am not comfortable with that choice, and I am not going to add insult to injury by pretending that rephasing does not mean that we will not be able to do as much as we would otherwise have done on the previous phasing.”
He said: “There will be year-on-year improvement, and already, since coming in, we have brought 36,000 military homes back into public ownership, delivering significant upgrades. I am keen to see what more we can do to leverage in investment in that area, because I understand the choice, but I do not think any of us ought to be comfortable with it.”
Pocklington said: “It was a very difficult decision in the final stages of the defence investment plan that the Secretary of State’s predecessor had to take. I would emphasise that we are still getting on and delivering. We are going to refurbish 1,000 homes this year and move another 1,000 homes from void unavailable to void available. It is a technical change, but it will release more homes through the hard work of the Defence Infrastructure Organisation.”
The department bought back 36,000 service family homes from Annington Homes and has committed to a programme of repair and renewal across the estate. The condition of service family accommodation has been the subject of sustained complaint and featured in the work of the Armed Forces Commissioner.
Dan Jarvis held the defence post before Streeting and settled the Defence Investment Plan, which was published in June.

13:51:03 KST

HEFEI, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- While his family set out for holiday adventures earlier this month, Wang Libing, 74, chose to stay behind as a persistent leg ailment made walking tough. But he was determined not to spend the holiday alone at home.
He checked into a care center, where he was looked after by caregivers and could socialize with other older residents in Xinyuan community in Hefei, capital of eastern Anhui Province.
"I fear loneliness more than anything else," Wang said. His children are busy with work and his wife sometimes goes back to her hometown to care for her mother.
Wang has used the center for short stays each year since 2017, enjoying the companionship and meals planned by professional dietitians.
Families can bring their elders to the center for a short-term stay when they are away for work or travel, said Feng Jinjin, Party chief of Xinyuan community.
Each eligible elderly resident is entitled to 15 days of free care per quarter and unused days can be accumulated for a stay of up to two months at a time, Feng said.
Xinyuan, a residential area of high-rise apartment buildings, has about 26,000 permanent residents. People aged 60 and over account for 30 percent of the population, including 352 aged 80 and above.
Wang's experience reflects efforts across China to meet the needs of an aging population through short-term community elderly care, health services and volunteer support.
Community service centers in Hefei provide a range of activities and basic health services. In the mornings, teachers from seniors' universities offer free classes, and medical workers conduct basic checks such as blood pressure and blood glucose measurements.
Community canteens serve nutritionally tailored meals at noon, with home delivery for those with limited mobility. Afternoons feature performances and sports activities.
"Our goal is to ensure that the elderly are looked after properly, have access to medical care, and can enjoy their later years," Feng said.
Two floors of the four-story Xinyuan community service center are dedicated to elderly care, and the center also offers 27 courses for elders, including dance, fine arts, table tennis and choir.
Communities in Hefei are also adopting simple ways to check on elderly people living alone.
At Binhu Shiji community, seniors switch on red balcony light bulbs between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. and turn them off before bed. If a light is not switched on or off as scheduled, volunteers will come to check on their situation, said Lang Ping, a community official.
Similar arrangements in Taiyuan, capital of Shanxi Province, and Qinhuangdao in Hebei Province, both in northern China, use balcony lights or curtains as signals to help confirm residents are safe.
Volunteers also help elderly residents with daily chores. Ma Menglan, 86, lives alone in Xinyuan community, where Ye Qinghua, a 64-year-old community social worker, and other volunteers regularly visit to clean Ma's home and wash clothes.
"I retired not long ago and am in good health, so I wanted to do some volunteer work to help other much older people," Ye said.
Two years ago, Ye joined a community initiative pairing younger seniors with older residents who live alone.
The program helps ease pressure on community services. Xinyuan's service center has only about a dozen staff members and social workers, making it hard to meet growing demand, Feng said.
The community now has more than 10 small teams of social workers pairing with younger seniors to support community elderly care. Feng said the community hopes to attract more young people and students in the future.
Elsewhere in China, other cities are developing services tailored to local needs. In Ningbo, Zhejiang Province, in China's eastern coastal region, programs offer free help with medical appointments, medicine collection, health follow-ups, and household tasks. In Xi'an, capital of northwestern Shaanxi Province, retired residents with specialized skills volunteer as teachers for the elderly.
Researchers are also exploring ways to make residential areas safer for aging residents.
Li Lianjun, a research associate professor at the School of Public Policy and Management at the University of Science and Technology of China, is leading a study on fall-risk perception and prevention behavior among older adults. She hopes the findings will help improve age-friendly renovations.
"China has a huge elderly population with diverse care needs. This poses new challenges for grassroots public services while also testing the sophistication of grassroots governance," Li said.
Official data shows that China's population aged 60 and above exceeded 323 million by the end of 2025, accounting for about 23 percent of the country's total population.
Meeting those needs requires government support, professional services, and help from residents, volunteers, and researchers, which can make community-based care more targeted, diverse, and sustainable, Li said. ■

Türkiye’s innovation ecosystem grows with state support as active R&D centers top 1,300
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
04:47:31 UTC
13:47:31 KST

Ayşe Böcüoğlu Bodur
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Türkiye’s innovation ecosystem grew significantly over the years, driven by state support, with the number of active research and development (R&D) centers reaching 1,365 and design centers totaling 348 by the end of September.
Turkish Industry and Technology Ministry data showed that R&D hubs provide employment to nearly 94,000 workers nationwide, made up of a highly educated workforce that includes nearly 57,700 employees with bachelor’s degrees, over 18,500 with master’s, and over 2,100 with a doctorate or higher.
Türkiye’s academically well-equipped R&D workforce has completed more than 80,400 projects to date, with nearly 16,000 still underway.
The robust innovation hubs have generated almost 49,000 patents so far, over 17,500 of which have been registered, while some 31,300 await examination results.
Türkiye’s R&D network spans the country and many sectors, from energy, agriculture, and healthcare to transportation, logistics, and aviation.
The machinery and equipment manufacturing sector led with 160 centers, followed by the auto supply industry with 136 and the software sector with 128, the data showed.
The drivers of the R&D innovation also included the computer and communications technologies sector with 86 centers, chemicals with 82 hubs, textiles, and electrical sectors with 77 facilities each, food and the defense industry (excluding weapons and ammunition) with 65 each, and the general manufacturing industry with 43 centers.
The facilities are spread nationwide, but Istanbul has the highest concentration of R&D hubs with 428 centers, Ankara with 168, Kocaeli with 137, Bursa with 134, Izmir with 105, Tekirdag with 54, Manisa with 34, Konya with 26, Sakarya with 25, and Antalya with 21.
Meanwhile, Türkiye’s 348 design centers employ 8,481 workers, 5,540 of them with bachelor’s degrees, 820 with master’s, and 50 with doctorates or higher degrees.
While the design centers operate across a myriad of sectors, they are heavily focused on industrial and structural sectors, with the textile industry ranking first, boasting 54 centers, followed by engineering and architecture with 51, general manufacturing with 45, and machinery and equipment manufacturing with 43.
The design ecosystem also included 23 design centers for the auto supply industry, 17 for media and communications, 15 for the furniture sector, 12 each for construction and auto manufacturing, and eight for the defense sector.
Istanbul is home to most of the design centers, with 154, followed by the capital Ankara with 39, Bursa with 31, Izmir with 28, and Kocaeli and Tekirdag with 15 each, according to ministry data.

Reading Xi's vision for global governance through metaphors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
04:45:21 UTC
13:45:21 KST

The 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an) is set to open on Friday in the Xiong'an New Area, north China's Hebei Province, bringing into world focus a pressing question: How can countries work together to address shared challenges in an interconnected world amid growing protectionism and unilateralism?
In speeches and meetings on multiple occasions, Chinese President Xi Jinping has used vivid metaphors to articulate his vision for global governance. These metaphors offer insights into his approach to building a more just, equitable and inclusive global governance system.
IN SAME BOAT
"I was looking at the vast ocean when I boarded the ship, and it struck me that we are all indeed fellow passengers in the same boat," Xi said while addressing the 2018 APEC CEO Summit hosted at a unique setting -- onboard the giant cruise Pacific Explorer in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea.
The metaphor embodies the essence of Xi's vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity, highlighting the interconnectedness of countries and the need for solidarity and cooperation in addressing common challenges.
Today, the interconnected world is grappling with four mounting deficits: a peace deficit that exacerbates geopolitical conflicts, a development deficit that widens the North-South divide, a security deficit that erodes mutual trust, and a governance deficit that undermines the effectiveness of multilateralism.
In 2019, at the China-France Global Governance Forum held in Paris, Xi proposed a four-pronged approach to addressing the four deficits. First and foremost, he called for fairness and reasonableness to address the governance deficit.
"It is advisable to uphold a vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefits," Xi said, calling for actively advancing the democratization of global governance rules.
As the world has found itself in a new period of turbulence and transformation, global governance has come to a new crossroads. Against this backdrop, Xi put forward the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in September 2025 in China's coastal city of Tianjin.
"I look forward to working with all countries for a more just and equitable global governance system and advancing toward a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said, stressing sovereign equality and genuine multilateralism.
TRAFFIC LIGHTS
"A world without rules is like a crossroads without traffic lights, where chaos and disorder are all but guaranteed," Xi said at the 2026 BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India.
This metaphor highlights the importance of rules in maintaining the international order. While having rules in place matters, how they are made and who gets to make them matter even more. International rules must be written and upheld jointly by all countries based on the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, rather than dictated by those with the strongest muscles or the loudest voice, Xi once stressed.
He has also called for the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and other universally recognized basic norms of international relations to be observed comprehensively, fully and in their entirety.
"There should be no double standards, and the house rules of a few countries must not be imposed upon others," he said.
The GGI proposed by President Xi reflects the objective transformation of the world system and responds to the aspirations of most countries for a fairer and more representative system of global governance, said Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University.
MAKING THE PIE BIGGER
Xi has repeatedly used the metaphor of a pie to describe the gains of international cooperation. "We should make the pie of win-win cooperation bigger, and ensure that more development gains will be shared more fairly by people across the world," he said at the 23rd meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization in 2023.
The pie metaphor reflects the people-centered and action-oriented vision of the GGI: making the gains of cooperation bigger while ensuring that they are shared more widely and fairly. When proposing the GGI, Xi emphasized the importance of "ensuring that the people of every nation are the actors in and beneficiaries of global governance."The SCO, the platform where Xi proposed the GGI, provides an example. Within the grouping, China has announced the establishment of cooperation platforms in energy, green industries and the digital economy, as well as centers for scientific and technological innovation, higher education, and vocational and technical education.
The expanding scope of cooperation shows how the "pie" can be made bigger in practice: by opening up new areas of cooperation, creating more opportunities for development and ensuring that the benefits reach more people.
Beyond making the pie bigger, Xi has also called for sharing the pie fairly to ensure justice and equity. For him, the ultimate purpose of better global governance is to promote common development and improve people's well-being across the globe.
At the G20 summit held in Brazil in 2024, Xi called for building a just world of common development, saying "prosperity and stability would not be possible in a world where the rich become richer while the poor are made poorer, and countries should make global development more inclusive, beneficial to all, and more resilient."
To build such a world, Xi said, there should be more bridges of cooperation, and less "small yard, high fences," so that more and more developing countries will be better off and achieve modernization.
Source: Xinhua

Those who docked at Lantau Yacht Club could use their craft as accommodation, Chan said, but they would still go on shore to spend.
“Some of them visited Stanley, some even headed to Central,” she said.
“Apart from sightseeing at sea, they would also go on shore to shop and head to theme parks.”
Yacht owners and masters have to register an account with the SAR’s Marine Department as part of the procedure for them to travel here, with Chan saying 32 accounts have already been set up so far.
She also said that, ahead of the end of the application period for platform companies to apply for ride-hailing service licences on October 30, the government is considering allowing applicants who are, for instance, particularly able to meet Hong Kong's needs, to have a higher chance of securing a permit.
A lottery will be carried out if the number of applications exceeds the 10,000-permit cap.
“I think that some of the main considerations include whether they are able to provide transport capacity or if they are really committed – this is very important," Chan said.
"We will also take into consideration how long they have owned the vehicles.”
Since a new combined written test for taxis and ride-hailing vehicles was launched in early August as part of the new regulatory framework for ride-hailing services, Chan said around 16,000 people have registered for the exam so far.
The government was, she stressed, pleased to see the enthusiastic response to the test, which has seen a passing rate of more than 60 percent.

Iraq says no US troops left in the country, not even advisers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
03:58:45 UTC
12:58:45 KST

Şahin Demir
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Iraq’s prime minister said Friday that no US troops are left in the country, including in advisory roles, as Baghdad moves to bring all weapons under state control by next June.
Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that the absence of foreign forces had removed the justification armed factions previously cited for retaining their weapons.
He stressed that the government’s decision to restrict weapons to state institutions was final and irreversible.
“By June 30, 2027, there will be no weapons outside the framework of the state,” he said.
Al-Zaidi said the government reached agreements concerning weapons held by three armed factions and is negotiating with four others to complete the process.
“Iraq is a state that has factions, not factions that own a state,” he added.
Al-Zaidi said Iraq once was only days awa from facing international isolation, including the possible departure of foreign embassies and the imposition of restrictions.
He said Western countries had believed that certain armed groups had effectively taken control of the Iraqi state, but his government had managed to overcome the threat. 
Strategic partnership with US
Despite the withdrawal of US troops, Al-Zaidi stressed that Baghdad remains committed to strengthening its strategic partnership with Washington.
He said Iraq chose the US as a strategic partner for its technological and economic capabilities.
The prime minister said US companies had already begun operating in Iraq and implementing projects in areas of bilateral cooperation.
He added that the partnership with Washington, alongside the development of Iraq’s energy sector, would significantly enhance the country’s regional and international influence compared with previous years. 
US troop withdrawal
Baghdad and Washington agreed in September 2024 on a phased withdrawal of US-led coalition forces from Iraq, with the military mission scheduled to conclude by this September.
On Sept. 30, Iraq announced the end of the US-led coalition’s military mission in the country, while the Pentagon confirmed the departure of coalition forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base.
The withdrawal marked a transition from the coalition’s military mission against the terror group ISIS (Daesh) to security cooperation, including training and intelligence sharing, according to Anadolu reports. 
Regional tensions
Turning to regional developments, Al-Zaidi stressed that Iraq would not take part in any war and would remain a meeting point for opposing parties.
He said the regional crisis would ultimately have to end with an agreement, regardless of how events unfolded.
The prime minister rejected the possibility of closing Iraq’s border with Iran, warning that such a move would harm both countries.
“Closing the border with Iran means economically besieging ourselves,” he said. 
Oil exports, Strait of Hormuz
Al-Zaidi said Iraq is working to establish a network of oil export pipelines to reduce its dependence on the Strait of Hormuz amid disruptions to maritime navigation in the strategic waterway.
He said the government is seeking to reactivate the oil export route through Türkiye’s Ceyhan port and diversify its export outlets.
“The Hormuz crisis has deprived Iraq of benefiting from rising oil prices,” he said, noting that Iraqi oil exports had fluctuated between suspension and resumption due to regional conditions.
The prime minister also announced plans to boost Iraq’s oil production capacity to 10 million barrels per day by 2032.
Describing the Development Road project with Türkiye as Iraq’s “third river,” he said construction would begin following parliamentary approval of the budget.
The project aims to establish a major transportation corridor linking Iraq’s southern ports to Türkiye and onward to European markets.

US lawmakers urge Pentagon to expand Starshield contract for Ukraine
Members of the US Congress have called on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Pentagon to expand its contract under the Starshield programme and restore Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite communications following recent disruptions.
Source: a letter from US lawmakers
Details: In a bipartisan, bicameral appeal, US lawmakers insist that services be restored without speed restrictions to ensure Ukraine has the technical capabilities it needs.
Quote: "Ukrainian forces depend on these services for command and control, intelligence sharing, battlefield communications, and the operation of unmanned systems. Any degradation in service, including reduced connection speeds, restricted geographic coverage, or interruptions in access, undermines Ukraine's military effectiveness and provides Russian forces with an operational advantage that will extend the conflict and put more civilians in harm's way."
Details: The lawmakers urged the US Department of Defense to maintain the coverage Ukraine needs to conduct legitimate military operations, including over Russian territory, and to ensure that the transition from the commercial Starlink service to the government-run Starshield programme takes place without any interruption to service.
"Decisions regarding service availability, coverage, and performance should not be left solely to the discretion of a private provider when they have direct consequences for Ukraine's ability to defend itself," the lawmakers added.
They also called on the Department of Defense to consider using its powers under the relevant provision of the Defense Production Act, which allows the federal government to require companies to prioritise government orders.
"The United States and Europe have made significant investments in Ukraine's defence because of how a Russian victory would put our security at risk. Those investments should not be undermined by preventable disruptions to the communications infrastructure on which Ukrainian forces depend," the lawmakers concluded.
Previously: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on 23 October that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.
The New York Times reported that US senators had warned the White House they would withhold votes on nominees until President Donald Trump's administration ensured the restoration of the communications capabilities used by Ukrainian troops.
A bipartisan group of nearly 20 members of the US House of Representatives called on Trump to ask Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink systems to target missile launchers on Russian territory.
US Democratic Senator Chris Coons had previously contacted Elon Musk's SpaceX, asking the company to explain who had decided to restrict Starlink's operation in Ukraine and why.
Background:
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk had ordered Starlink services to be slowed down. It is unclear to what extent Trump was involved in discussions about the slowdown.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- US House of Representatives member Joe Wilson and nearly two dozen of his colleagues prepared a letter calling for Ukraine to be permitted to use Starlink for strikes on launch sites within Russian territory.
- The Wall Street Journal, citing US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
- On the evening of 22 October, Trump said Musk had already lifted speed restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine but declined to say whether he had personally called him about the issue.
- Ukraine's Defence Ministry said it was recording disruptions to Starlink and Starshield services on the line of contact.

Israel raids towns, detains dozens of Palestinians in occupied West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24

Israel raids towns, detains dozens of Palestinians in occupied West Bank
Israeli military raid targets at least 15 towns in the northern West Bank, including Nablus and Jenin.
Israeli forces have raided towns, detaining dozens of Palestinians, after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a full lockdown of the occupied West Bank following an attack in the city of Hebron that killed two Israeli soldiers.
At least 15 towns in the north have been targeted, Al Jazeera correspondents reported on Saturday, with military raids targeting several northern cities and towns, including Nablus, Jenin, Tubas and Qalqilya.
Meanwhile, in the southern occupied West Bank, clashes broke out Saturday morning between Israelis and Palestinians in the Dura area of Hebron, Israel’s Walla news outlet reported.
This comes after Israeli bulldozers demolished a three-storey building in the city, with families given five minutes to collect their belongings. Israeli forces also ordered hundreds of Palestinian families to forcibly evacuate their homes in the Ein Deir Bahha area of Hebron and its surroundings.
Israeli troops also surrounded the home of one of the suspects in the shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers in Hebron.
‘Widespread fears’
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Birzeit in the occupied West Bank, described “a very tough night” for residents of al-Jalda neighbourhood in Hebron, where 200 families were forcibly displaced from their homes.
“They carried small bags of clothes with them but did not have time to take any other belongings,” she said.
“The municipality of Hebron has set up temporary shelters, but it remains unclear how long the families will be displaced.”
The Israeli army said late on Friday that its operation in Hebron would last “for several days”, but Palestinians fear it could continue much longer.
Odeh said the Israeli prime minister’s pledge to replicate what he described as the successful model in Tulkarem and Jenin refugee camps has fuelled fears of months of displacement and the possible loss of homes to large-scale demolitions.
In Nablus, Israeli forces carried out arrests and raided Palestinian homes in the villages of Jalud and Qaryut. Arrests were also reported in Arrabeh and Burqin, near Jenin, while Israeli forces entered Tubas and the nearby town of Aqqaba.
Further east, Israeli forces entered Jericho and the nearby Aqabat Jabr refugee camp.
“Across the wider occupied West Bank, villages and towns are completely isolated because roads and checkpoints between Palestinian communities have been closed,” Odeh said.
With the lockdown, nearly 1,000 checkpoints and gates across the West Bank will be closed, affecting millions of Palestinians.
The Palestinian Authority warned of the danger of the “ongoing Israeli escalation” and called on the “international community to intervene urgently”.
Meanwhile, Hamas said in a statement that the “campaigns and escalations carried out by the occupation and its criminal settlers against our people will only fuel further outrage”.
‘A small prison’
Netanyahu gave the order on Friday, shortly after the Israeli military said it had killed two Palestinian gunmen who attacked a reserve battalion near the Israeli settlement of Telem, killing two soldiers.
Israel’s ambulance service initially reported that at least five Israeli soldiers were injured, two of whom later died. All Israeli settlements, including Telem, are illegal under international law.
The attack and clampdown came amid heightened tensions across the Palestinian territory as Israeli settlers and soldiers engage in violent pogroms. Attacks on olive harvesters have been rife as aggression has been on the rise before the coming Israeli elections on Tuesday.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir responded to the killing of the Israeli soldiers by calling for Israel to take full control of the West Bank, in which the Israeli government is encouraging the construction of numerous settlements.
Mustafa Barghouti, secretary-general of the Palestinian National Initiative political party, said incitement from far-right Israeli ministers is making the situation worse.
The closure turns every city and village into “a small prison”, with checkpoints and gates blocking healthcare, the economy and education, he told Al Jazeera. He warned that collective punishment “will lead to explosions”.

The aliyah that took a century shows what olim can bring to Israel - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
03:39:59 UTC
12:39:59 KST

This Shabbat, Parashat Lech Lecha, 42 communities across Israel will mark Shabbat Aliyah.
The timing is apt: the Torah portion opens with God’s command to Abraham, “Lech lecha me’artzecha ... el ha’aretz asher ar’eka,” leave your land for the land that I will show you.
Abraham’s was the first aliyah; every journey since echoes that departure from the familiar towards an uncertain future in our ancestral land.
Young Israel of Ramat Poleg in Netanya is among the participating communities. Our honored guest is Dr. Norman Goldwasser, a clinical psychologist who recently left Miami Beach for Israel. His aliyah began not at Ben-Gurion Airport, but over a century ago.
In 1919, Norman’s grandfather left the Galician town of Chrzanow by boat for the Holy Land.
His family’s dry-goods business brought contact with the town’s non-Jewish population, and he sensed danger in the antisemitism that followed Germany’s defeat in World War I.
He intended to establish himself here and then bring his wife and children. He never had the chance.
He died of malaria in 1920 and was buried on the Mount of Olives. Of the seven children and their descendants whom he had hoped to bring to safety, almost all were murdered by the Nazis. Only Norman’s father and one brother survived.
When Norman first visited the grave in 1968, he found words that would shape his life. His father had inscribed the words, “Hassid vehalutz,” a hassid and a pioneer.
Norman’s family belonged to the Zalishitzer branch of Bobover hassidim, a community almost obliterated in the Holocaust. The inscription united deep hassidic loyalty with passionate love of the Land of Israel.
Norman calls his pull towards Israel an “epigenetic yerusha,” an inheritance embedded in his being. His grandfather had passed on the mission he could not complete.
That was not the family’s only interrupted aliyah. More than 25 years later, Norman’s father met his mother in a displaced persons camp. He had endured years in concentration camps; she had survived two years hiding in the forests of Ukraine.
After more than two years in the camp, they married and prepared to emigrate to British Mandate Palestine.
British restrictions on Jewish immigration blocked them, so they went instead to the United States and settled in Newport News, Virginia, where Norman was born and raised.
America gave the family safety and opportunity, and Norman built a distinguished career there. Yet he never entirely belonged. He grew up in the Baptist Belt as one of relatively few children of Holocaust survivors.
At camp and yeshiva, he was the boy with the southern accent. In Spanish-speaking Miami, where he never learned Spanish, he again felt like an outsider.
A sense of belonging in a time of war
Then came October 7, 2023.
Norman was staying at a hotel about 20 kilometers west of Jerusalem. While guests prayed in the hotel synagogue that morning, a missile was intercepted directly above the building. The explosion shook the hotel.
In the protected room, people screamed and cried as earlier traumas broke into the present.
One woman had survived the 2001 Sbarro bombing in Jerusalem. More than two decades later, its terror returned so forcefully that she again felt the pain of the glass that had pierced her body.
Norman had spent decades treating trauma, particularly with eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, or EMDR. He stepped forward and helped her return to the present and regain control.
Two days later, another young woman was too frightened to leave the protected room for the airport while missiles were falling. Her father’s urgent pleas deepened her panic. Norman asked him to wait in the lobby and worked quietly with her.
After a short period of EMDR, she calmed, assessed the danger, and walked out to her anxious family. They caught their flight.
When her mother thanked him in tears, Norman understood that his place was here, where Israel needed the expertise he had spent a lifetime acquiring.
He returned six times to volunteer with soldiers, families, and other trauma victims, and to train Israeli clinicians in EMDR. He made aliyah earlier this year.
There is something moving about finding one’s place in Israel by helping Israelis through one of our darkest mornings. Norman arrived with the skills this wounded country needed.
That is one reason Shabbat Aliyah matters. Olim are often discussed chiefly in terms of what they need: Hebrew, housing, employment, schools, and help with the bewildering bureaucracy.
Those needs are real. Anyone who has stood in the wrong government queue with the wrong form knows that.
Yet olim also bring experience, knowledge, traditions, and a fierce desire to contribute. They become doctors, teachers, soldiers, volunteers, and neighbors who strengthen our communities.
In Norman’s case, expertise forged over decades reached Israel when it was needed most.
Answering the call
Shabbat Aliyah recognizes both sides of the journey: the courage to begin again and our duty to welcome olim, not as permanent guests but as members of the household. We must hear their stories, help them find their place, and allow them to shape Israel rather than merely fit into it.
Norman now sits in his Jerusalem apartment looking at the Knesset, illuminated in cobalt blue. To him, it represents Jewish self-determination and the promise that Jews from the four corners of the earth will always have somewhere to seek shelter.
He does not romanticize Israel. He wrote: “And despite all of the confusing political turmoil, ridiculous traffic, outrageous prices of groceries, and bureaucratic madness, I still feel I belong.”
That sentence alone suggests he has already become thoroughly Israeli.
Aliyah should never become a slogan or a means of judging Jews whose responsibilities keep them elsewhere. It is a deeply personal decision, complicated by family, health, work, and circumstances outsiders cannot see.
Shabbat Aliyah honors those who made the journey; it does not diminish those who have not.
Yet Lech Lecha reminds us that Jewish history is advanced by people willing to answer a call whose consequences they cannot know.
Norman ends his account with another verse from the Torah portion: “For all the land that you see, to you I will give it and to your descendants, forever” (Genesis 13:15).
His grandfather answered that call in 1919. His parents prepared to answer it after the Holocaust. History stopped both journeys. Over a century later, their grandson completed them.
Between his grandfather’s grave and his Jerusalem window lies a century of Jewish tragedy, survival, and return. When Norman described what aliyah has finally given him, he used the simplest and most powerful word of all: “Home.”
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman

====================================================================================================

Large share of Israelis prefer holding new elections if no coalition formed, IDI survey shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
03:39:44 UTC
12:39:44 KST

Israelis would prefer to hold new elections if a coalition is unable to be formed after the upcoming Knesset election, according to recent survey data released by the Israel Democracy Institute on Friday.
Over a third of Jewish Israelis, 37%, and 46% of Arab Israelis surveyed preferred new elections over the alternative options of forming a minority government or forming a unity government with rotation.
Only 25% of Jews and 23% of Arabs stated that forming a minority government was the best option, with 23% of Jews and 9% of Arabs favoring the formation of a unity government with rotation.
If a coalition were to be successfully formed, the largest share of Jewish respondents, 37%, said that they would like to see a broad coalition of Jewish Zionist parties form without Haredi parties.
A majority of all Arab Israelis surveyed, 71%, however, favored a coalition of Center and Left parties, with the support or participation of Arab parties.
Only 14% of Jewish respondents shared the sentiment, making it the least preferable coalition for the demographic, according to IDI’s data.
The smallest share of Arab respondents, 2.5%, chose a coalition of the Right parties and Haredim as the preferred coalition, sharing the same view as 23% of Jewish participants.
No clear consensus on which bloc has highest chance of forming next government
When asked if the Right-Haredi bloc or the opposition bloc has a higher chance of forming the next government, there was no clear consensus among the total sample.
The Right-Haredi bloc was perceived as having a higher chance by 27.5% of individuals surveyed. There was a large discrepancy between demographics on this prediction, with 7.5% of Arabs and 32% of Jews agreeing.
The opposition bloc was seen as having the most promising chance of forming a coalition among 31% of total respondents, with 29% of Jews and the majority of Arabs, 42%, sharing that view.
The majority of all respondents agreed that to increase the political stability of Israel’s government, the head of the party that receives the largest number of votes should automatically be appointed prime minister, with both Jewish Israelis, 63%, and Arab Israelis, 51%, agreeing.
Yashar's Eisenkot seen as easiest to accept option for prime minister
When it comes to specific candidates, IDI found that the largest share of both Jewish and Arab Israelis said it would be very or somewhat easy to accept Yashar party head Gadi Eisenkot as Israel’s next prime minister.
Among Jewish respondents, 56% said they would find it easy to accept Eisenkot and 40% said it would be very or somewhat hard to accept. Similarly, 55% of Arab respondents said it would be easy and only 29% said it would be hard.
B’Yachad head and former prime minister Naftali Bennett was the second most acceptable to both Jewish and Arab Israelis surveyed, being labeled so by 51.5% and 48% of each demographic, respectively. Bennett was seen as difficult to accept by 46% of Jews and 41.5% of Arabs.
Current Prime Minister and Likud party head Benjamin Netanyahu maintaining his office was the third easiest for Jewish Israelis to accept, with 44% of Jewish individuals surveyed holding that view. More than half of Jews, however, viewed Netanyahu as hard to accept.
For Arab Israelis, Netanyahu was seen as the least favorable option, with 84% of the demographic saying it would be very or somewhat hard to accept. Only 12.5% of Arab Israelis said they would find Netanyahu securing another term easy to accept.
Yisrael Beytenu head Avigdor Liberman was seen as the most difficult to tolerate option for prime minister, with 60% of Jews and 66.5% of Arabs viewing him as hard to accept. Only 35% and 20% of each demographic, respectively, said it would be easy to accept Liberman assuming the office.
Across demographics, however, Israelis are approaching October 27 with cautious optimism, according to IDI.
Only 19% of total respondents agreed that Israel’s current situation would not change regardless of who one votes for, as opposed to previous years, when 29%-49% agreed with that sentiment.

03:39:43 UTC
12:39:43 KST

Less than 24 hours after he was stabbed in midtown Manhattan, Yosef, a Chabad-Lubavitch man from Crown Heights, was back on the same street where he’d been assaulted, popping into Diamond District businesses as usual to help employees wrap tefillin.
Yosef, 26, who did not share his last name to maintain his privacy, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that he was back on 47th Street on Thursday afternoon, the day after the stabbing, without missing a beat in his Monday-through-Thursday rounds even as police investigate the incident as a possible hate crime.
A number of the people he visited pieced together that the widely circulated footage of a man being stabbed the previous night was of him.
“They were in shock. They were obviously scared for me,” said Yosef, who has been wrapping tefillin and distributing Shabbat candles to Jewish Diamond District employees for about three years. He started that routine when his father, a Chabad Jew who works in the jewelry business, realized he needed his son’s help to handle the demand for those acts. Yosef told Chabad.org that he was “still shaken” by the attack a day later.
'We can't allow hate to stop us,' Yosef urges
Still, he told JTA, “We can’t allow some hate to stop us.”
Yosef said he felt it was important to communicate that message because “we need more mitzvahs in the world, we need more light in the world.”
Yosef was taken to Bellevue Hospital on Wednesday evening around 6 p.m., where medical staff assessed that he had no internal bleeding and would not need stitches. No arrests have been made, but the assailant has been described as a woman in her 40s.
The attack has renewed concerns about security that have faced Chabad adherents and institutions, which often host public events and maintain a visible street presence. But the threat didn’t diminish their presence in midtown Manhattan on Friday.
Multiple Chabad men stood under a bright yellow tent on the sidewalk wrapping tefillin for a steady stream of workers in the heavily Jewish Diamond District.
“The Rebbe says that the way to defeat darkness is only through the addition of light,” said Shmuel Cohen, who was handing out small photographs of the movement’s late leader, the Lubavitcher Rebbe Menachem Mendel Schneerson.
Cohen told JTA that he had not heard about the attack that took place just down the block two days earlier, though his partner under the sidewalk tent had. Cohen said that the best way to respond is through “the observance of Torah and mitzvot without being ashamed of our Judaism but presenting it to everyone.”
Chabad officials meet with NYPD to discuss security amid rise in attacks
Also on Friday, Chabad officials met with New York Police Department representatives for their annual meeting about security ahead of Chabad’s international conference in Crown Heights, the Brooklyn neighborhood where the movement is headquartered. The conference begins on November 5.
Chabad has been targeted in multiple high-profile attacks in the past year, including the deadly Bondi Beach shooting in Australia in December. The following month, a man rammed a car into the doors of the Chabad-Lubavitch headquarters in Brooklyn, raising further questions over how the movement should balance its commitment to making its events accessible with security.
Meanwhile, Jews have been targeted in more than half of hate crimes committed in New York City in 2026, despite making up about 12% of the city’s population.
“Security is our top priority. Our goal is to provide an environment where every participant feels safe and can fully experience the purpose and spirit of the gathering,” said Rabbi Mendy Kotlarsky, a top organizer of the upcoming conference.
In the wake of the attack, Yosef said he is not concerned about going out in public as a visibly Jewish person and doesn’t plan to change how he approaches the world.
“I was wearing the same clothes on Tuesday and Wednesday and Thursday,” he said. “I didn’t change my routine.”
