Shabbat Aliyah: Israeli communities that make aliyah possible come together to honor new olim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
03:39:38 UTC
12:39:38 KST

When Abraham, Sarah, and Lot arrived in the land of Canaan after a grueling trek from Haran, no aliyah representati or government officials met them.
The story of their journey, their travails in the Holy Land, and the divine promise to give the land to Abraham’s descendants is the subject of this week’s Torah portion, Lech Lecha.
Because of its proximity to the Shabbat Torah reading of Lech Lecha, Israel’s official Aliyah Day is observed on the seventh day of the Hebrew month of Heshvan, which this year corresponded to October 18.
While the day usually passes with little official fanfare or celebration, Young Israel in Israel and the Mizrachi-Young Israel Shuls Network will mark this coming Shabbat, when Parashat Lech Lecha is read, as a national moment to recognize those who have made aliyah.
Forty-two communities throughout the country will mark the day with special celebrations, such as a communal kiddush, oneg shabbat, or seuda shlishit in honor of their olim; an aliyah-themed sermon; personal reflections from olim about their aliyah journey; or classes by a Scholar-in-Residence on the theme of aliyah.
The participating communities range from Zichron Ya’acov and Mitzpe Netofa in the North to Karmei Gat and Beersheba in the South. They include Israeli communities with a small proportion of olim, as well as communities with large olim populations, such as Beit Shemesh, Gush Etzion, and Jerusalem.
Katie Matanky, one of the local organizers in the Karmei Zion community
THE KARMEI ZION community in Karmei Gat will observe its Shabbat Aliyah with guest speakers sharing personal stories and historical perspectives from ancient to modern times.
Elementary school-aged children will participate in an activity to discuss the story of Abraham and their own experiences of aliyah and becoming Israeli. The community is also distributing prompt cards for Shabbat table conversations to bring the themes of aliyah and “Lech Lecha” into members’ homes.
Katie Matanky, one of the local organizers, explains: “Taking one Shabbat a year to really appreciate the significance of our presence in Israel, and the vast contributions of a broad spectrum of Jews to the land and the state, is of critical importance – especially in today’s social climate.
“Personally, this Shabbat is a time for me to reflect with my family on our choice and privilege to be in this land and the opportunities it provides to my children and one day to their children, grandchildren, and generations to come.”
Rabbi Matanya Kaplan, rabbi of Mitzpe Netofa
Rabbi Matanya Kaplan, rabbi of Mitzpe Netofa, a community made up largely of native-born Israeli families, says, “The great step these families have taken, the price they have been willing to pay to move to Israel, and the strength they project are all felt and talked about in our community.
“That is why, among the yishuv’s various committees, there is one called the Olim Support Committee, and every year it is important to everyone to mark a Shabbat in honor of the olim. On this Shabbat we celebrate together with them, engage with the subject through Torah study and speeches related to it, and, above all, salute them.”
Rabbi Yossi Goldin, director of Young Israel in Israel
Rabbi Yossi Goldin, director of Young Israel in Israel, explains that celebrating aliyah as a community gives the concept greater significance.
“It encourages those who have gone through this experience and have either found there to be challenges or have certain doubts about some of the decisions they made,” he says.
“When the community rallies around them and celebrates with them, it becomes much more meaningful. Also, when people who have gone through similar experiences share them, people feel validated.”
Goldin, who himself made aliyah in 2007, says that one of the most valuable commodities that olim bring to Israel is idealism.
“People who have changed their lives and uprooted their lives to come here are doing that because of a certain vision and a certain dream that they have. That’s something that people who have been living here all their lives might not fully see and might not fully appreciate. But there’s a real excitement that olim come with, and an idealism that they bring when they come.”
While this year’s celebrations focus on English-speaking congregations, Goldin hopes to add olim communities from other countries to next year’s observance so that the Shabbat of Parashat Lech Lecha will become an annual aliyah celebration for Israeli communities.
BEYOND THIS WEEKEND’S communal celebration of Shabbat Aliyah, the event points to a unique component of synagogue observance not always found in Israeli synagogues: a community structure centered on the synagogue itself.
Many Israelis see their synagogue simply as a place to attend prayer services, without any special communal significance.
By contrast, many synagogues in the Diaspora, particularly in North America, view the synagogue as the focal point of communal observance. Many olim have brought this concept to the synagogues they attend here in Israel.
“In America, the frame of mind is that the synagogue is the center of one’s religious life,” says Goldin. “In Israel, that’s not necessarily needed, but creating that sense of community, support, and companionship through the Beit Knesset is a great benefit, and it isn’t necessarily taken for granted here.”
Rabbi Shlomo Sobol of Kehillat Shaarei Yonah Menachem Congregation, Modi'in
RABBI SHLOMO SOBOL, spiritual leader of Kehillat Shaarei Yonah Menachem Congregation in Modi’in, which is participating in the Shabbat Aliyah, is the co-founder of Barkai, a rabbinic association that certifies Israeli rabbis in counseling, abuse recognition, sensitivity training, mediation, and other pastoral skills.
A 10th-generation Jerusalemite, Sobol spent four years leading the Torah MiTzion kollel in the Detroit area. Torah MiTzion’s kollels in the United States are religious Zionist learning centers where Israeli emissaries study and teach Torah while strengthening local Jewish communities’ ties to Israel.
Before coming to Detroit, Sobol had never left Israel. Adjusting to life in the US brought its own difficulties, but what surprised him most was the concept of a synagogue-based community.
“I arrived in Southfield, Michigan, and for the first time in my life I saw what a community could be. I also saw what it meant to have a community rabbi. I suddenly saw this whole structure: a community with a rabbi, committees, and activities.
“I saw a form of communal rabbinic leadership I hadn’t known before. I knew heads of yeshivot, yeshiva teachers, and city rabbis [in Israel], but I hadn’t encountered this concept of the community rabbinate. It impressed me enormously.
“The other thing that impressed me – I’m not sure exactly how to define it – was the mutual responsibility and the resilience. You could feel it in the air: there was a community here, and it had strength. I knew synagogues and Torah classes, but I had never encountered this power of community.”
Four years later, Sobol and his family returned to Israel, determined to adapt the Diaspora synagogue model in this country. He suggests that the establishment of the state led many Israelis to see less of a need for a synagogue-based community.
“Precisely because we had gathered together and established a Jewish state, the communal structure that had sustained the Jewish people through thousands of years of exile gradually faded.
“The state was now providing services, including religious services. But I felt that wasn’t enough. It’s wonderful, and thank God that the state provides eruvin, kashrut supervision, and so on. But we still need the strength that a community provides.”
SOBOL HARBORS great admiration for olim and the sacrifices they made to come to Israel. “As an Israeli, I admire new immigrants. I’m not just saying that – I truly admire them.
“Part of that comes from being Israeli, and part comes from having spent four years abroad and discovering how difficult it was for me to live within American culture. Then I see people moving to Israel. Generally speaking, life in the United States is more comfortable than life here in many respects.
“People come here and struggle. A child comes home from second grade with homework, and the mother or father who used to help with everything suddenly can’t understand the wording of a math question in a second-grade workbook.
“It requires tremendous dedication and sacrifice. People need to help one another and offer encouragement.
“Every year, when Parashat Lech Lecha is read, we speak about how the people in our community heard the divine call that first came to Abraham – a call that continues to echo through the world, asking the Jewish people to return home.
“They chose to leave successful countries – the United States, Britain, Australia, South Africa. We have many immigrants from all those English-speaking countries. They chose to make aliyah.
“I think immigrants both deserve encouragement and need it. They absolutely deserve to have their aliyah recognized. They also bring enormous blessings. They deserve support, they need support, and they contribute so much. Look at how they run a community.”
Sobol says that the Israelis in Modi’in learn from the example set by olim, simply by observing how they act.
“In our neighborhood, for example, the immigrants’ influence extends beyond their congregation. You see Israelis learning from them. Not through a formal class, but simply by observing.
“People throughout the neighborhood see that our community is warm and welcoming. It has a chesed committee and other committees. During the war, it organized extensive support for soldiers. Israelis learn from that.”
Shabbat Aliyah is an opportunity to present aliyah as a positive accomplishment and encourage Jewish communities living in the US, Goldin adds.
“The approach here is to recognize and take those who have made aliyah and celebrate them and celebrate what they’ve done and celebrate their accomplishment. I think it can have an effect largely on aliyah in general.
“By creating a movement, an initiative where communities across the country celebrate olim and aliyah, it creates a conversation around aliyah that I think raises the bar for how we look at it and how people feel about it.”
Abraham, Sarah, and Lot had no welcoming committee waiting when they reached Canaan. Thousands of years later, those following in their footsteps can hope for a warmer reception – or at least a communal kiddush.
Whether you come from Haran or the Five Towns, the journey still takes courage, a little luck, and some divine help – and a welcoming community makes it easier to call your destination home.■

UK teachers could be barred from wearing pro-Palestine badges amid antisemitism concerns - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
03:39:34 UTC
12:39:34 KST

Teachers in the United Kingdom could face bans on wearing pro-Palestinian badges following a government-commissioned review into antisemitism in schools, The Telegraph reported Tuesday.
The review, commissioned in March by the Department for Education (DfE), was conducted by Sir David Bell, the current vice-chancellor and chief executive of the University of Sunderland and a former chief inspector of Ofsted. It details the extent of antisemitic abuse experienced by Jewish students, with three in five reporting that they had been targeted.
The review follows reports of teachers wearing pro-Palestinian badges in classrooms, including those featuring the watermelon symbol, which has become associated with Palestinian solidarity.
Review calls for stronger guidance on political impartiality
The review outlines 27 recommendations to tackle antisemitism in schools and colleges across England, including stronger guidance on political impartiality, particularly when addressing geopolitical issues.
Under existing UK regulations, schools are legally required to prevent teachers from promoting partisan political views. However, school administrators decide whether expressions of political support, such as wearing pro-Palestinian badges, violate those rules.
No blanket ban currently exists on teachers wearing pro-Palestinian badges in schools.
Speaking to Sky News, Bell called for clearer guidance on political impartiality to ensure students could “debate topical and difficult issues without feeling that teachers are imposing their own views on students."
Bell emphasizes importance of recognizing antisemitism
In a video posted to X/Twitter by the Department for Education, Bell emphasized the importance of recognizing antisemitism as a distinct form of prejudice.
"Calling out antisemitism as a specific kind of prejudice and harm is an essential aim of this report," Bell said.
Education Secretary Lucy Powell also addressed the need to tackle antisemitism in schools, saying, "I want to make a real impact. This has to be a point where we draw a line in the sand, and we can begin that clear roadmap for change."
Bell calls for antisemitism to be recognized as a distinct form of prejudice
Bell also argued that broader efforts to combat discrimination have not adequately addressed antisemitism as a distinct form of prejudice.
“I think what this review has demonstrated is that a general commitment to tackling racism or prejudice or hate has not properly identified antiSemitism as a particular kind of hate, and certainly that’s one of the themes of this report.
“We do need to name antiSemitism as a particular kind of prejudice and hate, because I think if you don’t name it, you don’t actually know what you’re tackling.”
Bell further urged schools to ensure that staff conduct policies explicitly prohibit antisemitism and that effective procedures are in place for students to report incidents and receive an appropriate response.
The recommendations place emphasis on establishing clearer expectations for teachers while ensuring that schools have the necessary measures to identify and address antisemitism when it occurs.

Pentagon designates Confucius Institutes a national security threat

Pentagon designates Confucius Institutes a national security threat
Pete Hegseth says the Pentagon dismantled 80 ‘propaganda cells’ operating under new names at 30 universities.
The United States Department of Defense has designated Confucius Institutes, Chinese-funded cultural centres on university campuses, as a threat to US national security.
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the move on Friday in a video posted on social media, saying the Pentagon added the organisations to its list of institutions that threaten national security.
Washington has long accused the centres of serving as Chinese propaganda tools and has taken steps to crack down on them.
Hegseth said Confucius Institutes had operated in disguise after being restricted by Congress, calling them “sleeper organisations”.
“It turns out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds of American students,” he said.
In the video, Hegseth said that Chinese government-backed cultural programmes had infiltrated universities and reappeared in new guises despite congressional restrictions.
Over the past two months, the Pentagon has “systematically dismantled every single one of these organisations”, he said.
The Chinese embassy in Washington did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment.

UN Day: How an exhibition in Astana tells stories of change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
03:34:29 UTC
12:34:29 KST

UN Day: How an exhibition in Astana tells stories of change
Zeenat Muznabi was a child when her family fled conflict in Afghanistan. In Kazakhstan, she received an education and now helps raise funds for people in need. Her portrait features in the GLOCAL exhibition at Kazakhstan’s National Museum. It brings together photographs and stories of 30 people connected to UN-supported programs. Ahead of United Nations Day on October 24, Qazinform News Agency correspondent introduces several participants.
The name GLOCAL combines the words “global” and “local.” The exhibition shows how international goals become part of everyday life. For one person, that means the chance to learn a profession. For another, it means protecting women from violence or sharing family responsibilities differently.
Passing help on
In 2024, Zeenat graduated in Information Technology from Al-Farabi Kazakh National University. A government scholarship supported her studies. Kazakhstan provided it as part of its commitments at the Global Refugee Forum.
Today, Zeenat coordinates fundraising at the Kazakhstan Red Crescent. Its Direct Dialogue program helps provide regular humanitarian support. She trains staff, works with donors and partners, and keeps donation records.
“I had the chance to study, work and grow. Now I can help others support people in need.”
Another exhibition participant, Armin Talebi, followed a similar path. He also arrived in Kazakhstan from Afghanistan as a child. Two decades later, he is studying plastic and reconstructive surgery.
He wants to help people recover their health and return to everyday life. The DAFI scholarship program supports his education. It is backed by the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees.
Armin has also contributed to the UN Youth Advisory Board and advocates for refugee inclusion.
His portrait carries the words “Together for Inclusion.” He explains that his profession helps him feel safe and part of society.
One button
For Aruzhan Mede, working on safety began with a specific problem. Women facing domestic violence needed a way to call for help quickly.
Her startup, AMAN, initially offered an emergency alert activated with one press of a button. The team later expanded the project. AMAN now uses artificial intelligence to identify potentially dangerous situations. The system works with security cameras in schools, workplaces and other public spaces.
Aruzhan trained through UN Women’s entrepreneurship program. She studied investment, sales and ways to enter new markets.
In 2026, she presented AMAN to international investors at GITEX AI EUROPE in Berlin. She now also helps other women turn their ideas into businesses.
“Every woman, every child, every person has the right to feel safe.”
These stories connect international programs with decisions people make every day.
Kazakhstan’s First Deputy Foreign Minister Yerzhan Ashikbayev discussed that connection at the exhibition’s opening.
“The theme of today’s exhibition underscores the importance of connecting this global agenda with national priorities and actions in our regions, cities, and rural communities,” he said.
Equality begins at home
In another portrait, Didar Smagulov holds a smiling child in his arms. He is a lawyer, head of the Adildik Zholy Public Association and father of three.
His story focuses on men’s participation in family life. As a United Nations Population Fund trainer, Didar works on responsible fatherhood. He helps civil society organizations promote shared household responsibilities and equal partnerships between spouses.
He follows the same principle in his own family: parents share responsibility equally. In the exhibition text, Didar connects this with children’s futures. What they see at home today will shape the families they build themselves.
For 17-year-old Konstantin Tsoy, equality also begins with someone close to him. He wants his younger sister to know her rights and freely choose her future.
At fourteen, Konstantin joined the Y-PEER youth network in Kyzylorda. The United Nations Population Fund supports the network. He now helps coordinate volunteers across 18 cities in Kazakhstan.
They teach their peers about reproductive health, rights and gender equality. For Konstantin, the network has become a community where young people support one another.
“Y-PEER showed me that being young, or coming from a small city, should never stop me from taking responsibility and changing society.”
At the opening, UN Resident Coordinator in Kazakhstan Sarangoo Radnaragchaa discussed growing inequality and other shared challenges.
“These challenges know no borders, they affect us all and they remind us of a simple truth, no country can address them alone,” she said.
For the exhibition’s participants, this shared work continues beyond the museum. Zeenat raises donations. Armin studies surgery. Aruzhan develops her safety system. Didar raises his children, while Konstantin works with his peers. Each of their stories is still unfolding.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that 63-year-old Danna from Kazakhstan and 17-year-old Venera from Kyrgyzstan. They help people in need, join environmental activities and encourage others to volunteer.

Russia launched 2,597 drones at Ukraine over past week, air defenses neutralized over 87%
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces reported this on Facebook.
"Russia continues its massive air attacks against Ukraine, using attack drones to strike critical infrastructure and terrorize the civilian population. Over the past week, the enemy deployed 2,597 Shahed-131/136/238, Parodiya and Gerbera UAVs. Ukraine's Defense Forces neutralized 2,282 of them. Every aerial target neutralized reduces the risk of fatalities, damage to residential buildings, and damage to energy facilities and other critical infrastructure. At the same time, the General Staff added, even highly effective Ukrainian air defense cannot eliminate the threat entirely.
"We therefore continue to urge citizens not to ignore air raid alerts and not to share information about air defense operations," the General Staff said.
Ukraine's Defense Forces continue to strengthen the country's multilayered air defense system and improve methods for detecting and neutralizing enemy aerial targets.

Israeli cyber authorities deactivated social media accounts connected to foreign actors suspected of attempting to influence the upcoming election, the Shin Bet security agency said on Thursday, though many accounts remain active.
The agency said the joint operation, conducted with the State Prosecutor's Office's cyber department and the Central Elections Committee, was aimed at preventing foreign interference in the election, preserving its integrity and ensuring that efforts to thwart such attempts would continue.
One Facebook page still active, named "All of Our Sons," spreads anti-government content focusing on the Netanyahu government's responsibility for the October 7 massacre. Indications suggest the page is partly operated from the United Arab Emirates.
The world is watching: The global stakes of Israel's election
Israel's elections, now only six days away, will be decided by whatever proportion of its 7.3 million eligible voters turn up at the polling stations – and the signs are that turnout will be high. These elections are momentous for Israel – the repercussions will be felt way beyond the 120 politicians who will win places in the Knesset. Yet they will also resonate far beyond even the country itself: its elections will affect millions who aren't even voting.
In the past, hasbara advocates liked to boast that diminutive Israel punched above its weight. These days, the fact that Israel is a pivotal factor in the domestic debates on campus, in the streets and corporate offices of so many other countries is more often a curse, self-inflicted or not, rather than a blessing.
Whether this election sees the end of the decades-long Netanyahu era or its continuation will have far reaching effects across the globe on day-to-day lives, from members of the Jewish and Palestinian diasporas to investors, publishers and human rights activists.
Election panel orders Likud to pull signs of Eisenkot bloc party leaders with Arab MKs
Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg ordered the Likud party to remove billboards featuring Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and other party leaders from the Jewish opposition alongside Arab lawmakers Ahmad Tibi of the Joint List and Mansour Abbas of the United Arab List.
Sohlberg said the signage could create a misleading impression about a possible political connection between the Yashar slate and the Arab parties, with which Eisenkot has ruled out forming a coalition.
The signs, displayed across the country, include Arabic text stating that they were put up on behalf of Likud. However, Solberg ruled that the Arabic text did not adequately identify the party responsible, as the signs were placed in areas where most residents do not speak Arabic.

Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people, including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

"It's no use, Lula, giving with one hand and taking away with your nine fingers."

'Who governs Brazil?'
Bolsonaro apologised to Lula, but not without asking him to "apologise to the Brazilian people who suffer from insecurity."
Lula questioned the senator's experience, insisting that "he doesn't know Brazil."
His challenger doubled down on presenting himself as a capable candidate who represented change for the country.
Lula repeatedly asked viewers to "Google" Bolsonaro's claims, to which the senator shot back: "Who governs Brazil, you or Google?"
A Datafolha institute survey published on Thursday shows the pair tied with 50 percent of voting intentions each, compared to Bolsonaro's four-point lead in polls published two weeks ago.

====================================================================================================

Report: Iran advancing sophisticated plots to assassinate senior US officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
02:47:41 UTC
11:47:41 KST

U.S. intelligence has warned that Iran has significantly intensified efforts to assassinate American diplomats and senior officials in the Middle East and beyond, with some plots reportedly reaching advanced stages, as Washington reduces its diplomatic presence across the region amid fears of a wider military confrontation.
The warning appears in a one-page intelligence memorandum dated October 23 and sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The document was first reported by Axios and subsequently obtained by the Associated Press, while CNN reported on the related diplomatic staffing reductions and the disruption facing American diplomatic families. 
In the memo, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran had "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" and that potentially lethal plots had reached "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The document does not identify specific targets, disclose which countries outside the Middle East may be involved or provide details about how the alleged assassination attempts would be carried out. It indicates, however, that the underlying intelligence has already been shared with senior State Department officials.
Clayton also expressed concern that the information was not reaching enough American personnel who could be exposed to the threats. He offered to lower the classification level of as much of the intelligence as possible, allowing Rubio to distribute the warnings more widely.
US quietly moves diplomats and families across Middle East
The intelligence warnings come as Washington has begun scaling back its diplomatic presence across several Middle Eastern countries, with personnel and family members being relocated amid growing security concerns.
Earlier this week, the State Department ordered nonessential personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, including the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh and consulates in Jeddah and Dhahran. Officials cited the intensifying attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels as the immediate reason for the decision.
On Friday, the department moved to further reduce diplomatic and government staffing at embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. Unlike the mandatory departure order issued for Saudi Arabia, personnel at these four missions have not been formally ordered to leave.
The embassies remain open under restricted operations, a designation that allows Washington to maintain essential diplomatic functions while limiting the number of personnel stationed there.
Staffing adjustments have also been taking place more quietly at American diplomatic posts in Bahrain and Kuwait, with no publicly announced change in their operational status.
For many American diplomats and their families, the latest moves have brought back memories of the earlier stages of the war with Iran. Some had only recently returned to their assignments after being evacuated during the height of the fighting, forcing them to find temporary accommodation and arrange new schooling for their children.
Now, those same families face another round of disruption, with some reporting that the financial assistance available to them is more limited than during their previous departures.
The American Foreign Service Association, which represents U.S. foreign service officers, has raised concerns about confusion surrounding the arrangements, particularly at embassies that have not formally changed their operational status.
Some families have reportedly been directed to leave without receiving confirmation that the State Department will cover temporary housing or daily living expenses in the United States. Those allowances can be especially important when a diplomat must remain at an overseas post while their spouse and children relocate.
Nikki Gamer, a spokesperson for the association, criticized the uncertainty facing diplomatic households.
"Families deserve to know how they will pay for a place to live before they board a plane," she said.
Diplomatic personnel have also complained about inadequate communication between State Department headquarters in Washington and staff serving abroad. Some said they learned about the departures through news reports rather than directly from their embassy leadership.
The State Department has acknowledged the difficulties facing its personnel and said it is working to help families manage additional expenses and disruptions to their children's education.
Fears of broader conflict with Iran
The diplomatic reductions come amid an increasingly volatile security situation in the Middle East, with Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia raising concerns that the fighting could spread to neighboring countries.
U.S. officials fear that the Houthis could expand their missile and drone attacks beyond Saudi Arabia, potentially threatening American personnel, military facilities and critical infrastructure elsewhere in the region.
At the same time, the prospect of renewed American and Israeli military operations against Iran has added to the uncertainty. U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly suggested that Washington could resume strikes against Tehran, potentially after the upcoming U.S. midterm elections.
Israel has also reportedly pressed Washington to take military action against Iran sooner, although those efforts have so far been unsuccessful.
U.S. officials, however, have denied that the diplomatic staffing reductions are connected to preparations for possible new American or Israeli strikes. They maintain that the measures are driven by immediate security concerns, including the threat of Iranian assassination plots and further Houthi attacks.
The intelligence warning and the simultaneous reduction in diplomatic staffing underscore Washington's concern about the risks facing American personnel as tensions with Tehran intensify. With the alleged assassination plots still undisclosed and the threat of wider regional hostilities unresolved, U.S. diplomats and their families face renewed uncertainty over when they will be able to return to normal assignments.

11:45:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Western countries may temporarily ease sanctions against Russia in their own interests, but they are unlikely to completely abandon them, Federation Council Vice Speaker Konstantin Kosachev said in an interview with TASS.
But Moscow should not worry, because it has proven its self-sufficiency.
"It can be assumed that we will live to see the moment when sanctions are lifted legally, but, in my view, their inclusion in US legislation and in the relevant directives of the European Union is, if not an eternal phenomenon, then at least an extremely long·term one, because lifting sanctions requires consensus — a convincing majority, in case of US Congress, or consensus, unanimity, in case of the European Union," the senator said.
According to Kosachev, temporary exceptions to the sanctions regime are possible thanks to the interests of the Western countries.
"My prediction is that the sanctions regime will be eased over time, because maintaining it at its current maximum level clearly runs counter to the interests of those who came up with and are using these sanctions," he explained.
However, the parliamentarian continued, the Westerners will certainly retain the ability to reinstate the sanctions at any time if "Russia behaves, in their view, in a way they do not like."
"I am convinced that this is not the issue we should be focusing on, because over these decades -- if we look at the period starting from 2008, when sanctions related to the Georgian issue first appeared -- we have proven that Russia cannot be isolated, that Russia cannot be broken even by the most severe sanctions, and that we are able to maintain our self·sufficiency and our ability to develop regardless of what is happening around us," the senator believes.
He added that the maintenance or lifting of anti-Russian sanctions in one form or another is "a headache for those who imposed these sanctions," not for Russia.
Sanctions and Russian diesel fuel
The White House is exempting Russian diesel fuel supplies to global markets from sanctions until April 7. On October 9, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump discussed over the phone the supply of petroleum products. Later, the Russian president confirmed Moscow’s readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak previously told TASS that Russia is beginning to lift the ban on diesel fuel exports early and is ready to supply 100,000 tons of diesel in October, 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons in December, with the potential to increase this volume to 3 million tons per month.

James Tasamba

Health officials in the Democratic Republic of Congo have launched a trial of a new Ebola vaccine as the struggle to contain the fast-spreading epidemic continues, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Friday.
The first participants in a new vaccine trial, known as Tumaini, which means hope in Swahili, were vaccinated in Ituri’s provincial capital Bunia, the WHO Africa regional office said.
The WHO called the launch “a major step in the fight against Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus strain,” which is spreading rapidly across geographic boundaries.
The trial will evaluate candidate vaccines against Ebola strains caused by the Bundibugyo virus among contacts of confirmed cases.
No vaccine against the Bundibugyo virus strain has been approved, which was first declared in Congo in May.
The trial is being guided by scientific rigor, transparency, ethical principles, informed consent, as well as community engagement, according to the WHO.
“This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work,” WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a post on US social media company X.
In August, Congo received 70,000 Ervebo vaccines from the global Ebola virus disease vaccine stockpile for use in the outbreak, which was approved for use against the Zaire Ebola virus.
The vaccine trial is coordinated by the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) and supported by WHO, the Congolese Health Ministry, and partners.
The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Congo since the outbreak has surpassed 9,700, including more than 4,690 deaths, according to the latest data by Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
The disease has affected eight provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo, South-Ubangi, and North Ubangi.
Health officials said the spread to other countries in the region is complicating efforts to contain the outbreak.
Kenya has reported nine confirmed cases, including two deaths. Nigeria confirmed its first case earlier this week, believed to be imported from Congo.

Three men allege late Lindsey Graham paid for sex; one says he was 17 and filmed without consent

11:40:54 KST

A new documentary featuring three men who allege that the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham paid them for sexual encounters has sparked a political controversy in the United States, nearly three months after the death of one of President Donald Trump's closest congressional allies.
One of the men claims he was just 17 when he met Graham in 2001 and alleges that the senator secretly recorded their encounter without his knowledge. The accusations emerged Thursday, less than two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, in which Graham's sister is running to retain his Senate seat in South Carolina.
The approximately 30-minute documentary, titled The CLOSETocracy, was released by The Young Turks, a U.S. progressive news network. The New York Times, which reported on the film, emphasized that it had not independently verified the identities of the three men or the accuracy of their allegations.
Graham, who served in the Senate for 23 years, died suddenly in July at the age of 71. His death means he cannot respond to the accusations, which have prompted sharply contrasting reactions within the Republican Party.
One man claims he was 17 and secretly filmed
One of the men featured in the documentary, identified only as Kelvin, alleges that Graham paid him for sex in 2001, when he was 17 years old.
According to Kelvin's account, the encounter took place at a residence in Arizona, where Graham allegedly paid him $120 and secretly recorded the sexual encounter.
No independently verified evidence has been presented establishing that the encounter occurred or that any such recording was made.
Another man, identified as Cory, described being collected by a chauffeured vehicle and driven to the Mayflower Hotel, an upscale hotel in Washington, D.C. He alleges that he was paid to spend the night and have sex with a man whose identity he did not recognize at the time.
Cory claims he realized the man was Graham only months later, when he saw the Republican senator on television during the 2016 presidential election campaign.
A third man appearing in the documentary also alleges that Graham paid him for sexual encounters.
A website created to promote the film, called the Lindsey Graham Files, displays documents and travel receipts that its creators say support the men's accounts. However, those materials have not independently established the truth of the allegations.
Allegations first surfaced in 2020
According to The New York Times, Cory previously appeared in adult entertainment productions under the name Sean Harding. In 2020, he published a social media post alleging that an unnamed Republican senator who opposed LGBTQ+ rights regularly paid men for sex.
In that post, he criticized the senator for supporting legislation he said harmed LGBTQ+ people and minority communities, and suggested that several sex workers could publicly identify the politician.
Although he did not explicitly name Graham, he hinted that the senator's initials were LG.
Only after Graham's death did Cory and the two other men publicly identify him in the documentary.
The timing has become a central element of the controversy, particularly because the former senator is no longer alive to challenge the allegations or respond to the accounts.
Graham repeatedly denied rumors about his sexuality
Graham, one of Washington's most influential Republicans and a longtime ally of Trump, never married. Throughout his political career, he faced recurring speculation about his sexual orientation, which he repeatedly denied.
In a 2010 interview with The New York Times, Graham dismissed the rumors with a sarcastic remark about disappointing gay men who might have been interested in him. He concluded: "I ain't gay. Sorry."
The documentary focuses heavily on what its creators portray as a contradiction between Graham's alleged private conduct and his public positions on LGBTQ+ rights.
During his political career, Graham was a prominent opponent of same-sex marriage. He voted against repealing the U.S. military's "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" policy, which barred openly gay and lesbian Americans from serving in the armed forces.
He also opposed legislation aimed at expanding federal hate crime protections to include sexual orientation and gender identity.
The filmmakers argue that the allegations, if true, would expose a disparity between Graham's personal life and the conservative social policies he championed. The allegations themselves, however, remain unverified.
‘Everyone knew’: Marjorie Taylor Greene backs documentary's claims
The film's release triggered a wave of reactions from prominent conservative figures, though not all were critical of its creators.
Former Republican congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, who was once among Trump's most outspoken allies before falling out with him and leaving Congress earlier this year, publicly expressed support for the three men.
Greene described the allegations as one of Washington's worst-kept secrets and praised the men for coming forward with their accounts.
"We all knew Lindsey Graham was gay. Everyone did," she wrote on X. Her statement was an assertion about Graham's sexuality, not independent verification of the documentary's allegations.
Greene argued that the central issue was not Graham's sexual orientation but the possibility that powerful political figures might conceal information about their personal lives that could leave them vulnerable to pressure or manipulation.
She warned that such secrecy, in her view, could have implications for U.S. national security and the public's trust in its leaders.
Republicans dismiss claims as political attack
Andrew Kolvet, a spokesperson for the conservative organization Turning Point USA, also weighed in on the controversy, suggesting that speculation about Graham's sexuality was hardly new.
Referring to a derogatory nickname that had circulated about the senator online, Kolvet wrote that conservatives had been discussing the rumors for years.
"This isn't an October surprise," he said, arguing that the documentary was unlikely to damage the election prospects of Graham's sister. He also dismissed the controversy over the senator's private life as politically irrelevant.
Other Republicans were far more critical of the filmmakers.
Republican Rep. William Timmons of South Carolina, who regarded Graham as a longtime mentor and friend, condemned the release of the documentary and accused its creators of spreading "disgraceful lies" about someone who could no longer defend himself.
Timmons argued that Graham's decades of public service deserved greater respect and accused the filmmakers of resorting to homophobic attacks for political advantage.
He did not directly address the allegations about Graham's sexual orientation but said the effort to use claims about his private life against his family reflected poorly on those promoting the documentary.
Documentary released as Graham's sister fights for Senate seat
The documentary's publication has also raised questions about its political timing.
Graham died on July 11 after suffering an aortic dissection, a potentially fatal condition involving a tear in the wall of the body's main artery. Following his death, South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed his sister, Darline Graham, to serve the remainder of his Senate term.
Darline Graham subsequently secured the Republican nomination for the November 3 election and is facing Democratic candidate Annie Andrews in a closely contested race for the seat.
Her campaign has received the endorsement of President Trump, who maintained a close relationship with her late brother.
A spokesperson for Darline Graham's campaign declined to comment on the documentary.
Timmons predicted that Darline would win by a margin of 10 percentage points and argued that attempts to damage her campaign by publicizing allegations against her brother would ultimately prove counterproductive.
The late senator had been one of the Republican Party's most prominent foreign policy voices. Initially a fierce critic of Trump, he later became one of the president's closest allies in Congress.
Graham was also a strong supporter of Israel, advocated a confrontational approach toward Iran and was among the leading congressional supporters of U.S. assistance to Ukraine.
The film's release, so close to the midterm elections, has brought renewed scrutiny to Graham's political legacy and the unresolved allegations about his personal life. With the claims still uncorroborated and Graham no longer alive to answer them, the controversy now extends beyond the documentary itself to the political battle over the Senate seat he left behind.

====================================================================================================

Three years after October 7, 75% of Israel's border-area Jews say war will shape their vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
02:28:31 UTC
11:28:31 KST

For nearly three years, Israelis living along the Gaza border and Israel's northern frontier with Lebanon have experienced the war more directly than most. What began on the morning of October 7, 2023, transformed their communities into front lines, bringing fighting, prolonged evacuations and an often difficult return to homes and neighborhoods.
Now, as Israel approaches its October 27 election, a new survey reveals how the war has shaped the political priorities of residents in these areas, their assessment of the government's performance and the issues likely to influence their votes.
A survey conducted for ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth by the Dialog polling institute, part of the Amanat Pro Group, questioned 498 Jewish residents of communities affected by the war. Respondents came primarily from kibbutzim, agricultural villages and small communities, alongside several towns and cities in the north and south.
The results show that approximately 75% believe the war that began on October 7 will influence their vote to a great or very great extent. Nearly half, 48%, say it will have a very significant impact on their decision.
But the findings also reveal a distinction between how these residents judge the government's initial response to the Hamas-led October 7 massacre and how they assess its subsequent management of the war.
Only 31% satisfied with government's response to October 7
Asked about the government's response to the October 7 attack, 48% of respondents expressed low satisfaction, compared with 31% who reported high satisfaction.
The divide is particularly pronounced along party lines. Among voters supporting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party, 30% said they were very satisfied with the government's response. Among supporters of National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir's far-right Otzma Yehudit party, however, only 9% expressed the same level of satisfaction.
The criticism extends to voters backing parties within Netanyahu's governing coalition. Among Otzma Yehudit supporters, 23% said they were not at all satisfied with the government's response, compared with just 7% of Likud supporters.
Among voters supporting former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party and former prime minister Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad party, 47% and 48%, respectively, said they were not at all satisfied with the response to the attack.
The government's handling of international public opinion received even lower marks. A majority of respondents, 54%, expressed low satisfaction with Israel's wartime public diplomacy and international messaging, while only 23% reported high satisfaction.
Among Likud voters, 45% said they were satisfied or very satisfied with the government's performance in this area. By contrast, 85% of Yashar supporters said they were either not at all satisfied or only slightly satisfied.
Otzma Yehudit voters were also critical. Some 42% expressed dissatisfaction with the government's international messaging, compared with 22% of Likud supporters.
Age also played a significant role. Respondents aged 65 and older were the most critical, with 52% saying they were not at all satisfied and only 11% expressing satisfaction. Among respondents aged 18 to 24, just 16% said they were not at all satisfied.
War management receives better marks than initial response
Although many respondents expressed dissatisfaction with the government's immediate reaction to the October 7 massacre, their assessment of its subsequent wartime management was somewhat more favorable.
Overall, 43% expressed high satisfaction with the government's conduct of the war after the attack, compared with 36% who reported low satisfaction.
Likud supporters were the most positive, with 78% saying they were satisfied or very satisfied with the government's management of the fighting.
Otzma Yehudit voters, despite their criticism of the government's initial response, also gave its later wartime performance relatively high marks, with 61% expressing high satisfaction.
The picture was markedly different among supporters of Ofer Winter's People of Israel party. Only 4% reported being very satisfied with the government's conduct of the war, while another 60% expressed little or no satisfaction.
Among supporters of Yair Golan's Democrats party, 87% said they were not at all satisfied with the government's handling of the war. Half of Bennett's B'Yachad supporters gave the same response.
Northern residents less satisfied with reconstruction efforts
The survey also examined how residents assessed government assistance during the fighting and efforts to rehabilitate communities damaged or disrupted by the war.
Only 34% expressed high satisfaction with the assistance provided to residents during the fighting, while 32% gave similarly positive assessments of the reconstruction and recovery of affected communities.
Once again, supporters of coalition parties generally expressed greater satisfaction than opposition voters. Among Likud supporters, 58% said they were satisfied or very satisfied with reconstruction efforts.
Among Eisenkot's Yashar supporters, none reported being very satisfied, and only 7% said they were satisfied to a great extent.
Among supporters of the Democrats, 90% said they were not at all satisfied with reconstruction efforts, while 7% expressed moderate satisfaction. The remaining respondents said they did not know.
A geographic divide also emerged. Only 27% of respondents living in northern communities expressed high satisfaction with the government's reconstruction efforts, compared with 38% of respondents in the south.
The findings suggest that perceptions of postwar recovery differ not only according to political affiliation but also between communities near the Lebanese border and those surrounding Gaza.
Cost of living and security top election priorities
Despite the war's profound impact, the survey found that economic concerns remain central to voters' decisions.
Asked to identify the single most important issue from a list of options, 32% of respondents selected the cost of living, narrowly ahead of the security situation at 31%.
Another 17% identified establishing a commission of inquiry into the failures surrounding October 7 as their top priority, while 13% selected equality in military service obligations and the conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, many of whom currently receive exemptions from mandatory military service.
The differences between political parties were substantial.
Among Likud supporters, 50% identified national security as their most important election issue. The corresponding figure among Otzma Yehudit supporters was 49%.
Among Shas voters, 34% prioritized the cost of living, while 66% said none of the issues presented in the survey was their most significant concern.
Supporters of Winter's People of Israel party, whose leader has pledged to join only a Netanyahu-led government, also emphasized security, with 40% identifying it as their leading concern. Another 35% prioritized equality in military service and ultra-Orthodox conscription.
Among Eisenkot's Yashar supporters, the leading issue was establishing a commission of inquiry into October 7, selected by 39%. Military service equality and ultra-Orthodox conscription followed at 21%, while only 20% identified the security situation as their top priority.
For Bennett's B'Yachad supporters, the cost of living was the dominant concern, cited by 41%, followed by an October 7 inquiry at 25%.
Among supporters of Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu, 42% prioritized the cost of living, while 28% chose equality in military service and ultra-Orthodox conscription.
Undecided voters focus on their wallets
Respondents who had not yet decided which party to support were particularly critical of the government's performance.
Among these undecided voters, 74% expressed dissatisfaction with the government's response to the October 7 massacre, while 57% were dissatisfied with its international messaging.
Nevertheless, their most pressing concern was economic rather than security-related. Half of undecided respondents, 50%, identified the cost of living as the most important issue influencing their vote.
Regional differences reinforced the importance of economic pressures. In southern communities, 37% of respondents chose the cost of living as their leading election concern, compared with 27% in the north.
The issue of equality in military service and ultra-Orthodox conscription was more prominent in the north, where 17% selected it as their top priority, compared with 9% in the south.
National security received nearly identical levels of support in both regions, with approximately 31% identifying it as the most important issue.
Younger voters focus on prices, older residents on security and accountability
Age emerged as another important factor shaping election priorities.
Among respondents aged 18 to 44, 40% identified the cost of living as their primary concern. That figure fell to just 17% among those aged 55 to 64, a group in which national security was the leading priority at 39%.
Respondents aged 65 and older stood out for their emphasis on accountability and military service obligations. In this age group, 23% prioritized a commission of inquiry into October 7, while 22% selected ultra-Orthodox conscription and equality in military service.
This was the only age group in which both issues approached a quarter of respondents, highlighting differences in how generations view the questions facing Israel after three years of war.
Women more critical of government's performance than men
The survey results were weighted by gender to give men and women equal representation in the findings. The responses revealed a consistent gender gap in assessments of the government's wartime performance.
Among women, 57% expressed low satisfaction with the government's response to the October 7 attack, compared with 39% of men.
The divide was also evident in evaluations of the government's subsequent management of the war. Only 33% of women reported high satisfaction, compared with 52% of men.
On the reconstruction of communities affected by the fighting, 23% of women expressed high satisfaction, compared with 42% of men.
Taken together, the findings paint a complex picture of attitudes in communities that have borne some of the heaviest consequences of the war. While three in four Jewish respondents say October 7 and the ensuing conflict will influence their vote, their assessments of the government's performance differ sharply depending on political affiliation, age, gender and location.
For some, the overriding concern is national security. For others, it is the rising cost of living, the reconstruction of their communities, the demand for accountability over October 7 or the unequal burden of military service.
Three years after the massacre, the war remains central to the political considerations of these residents, but the survey shows that their experiences have produced sharply different judgments about what the next government should address first.

MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. The loss of Ukraine’s foreign exchange earnings from the downtime of the ports of Greater Odessa, which has been going on for more than three months, amounted to about $6 billion, according to TASS calculations.
Commercial merchant ships continue to boycott the ports of Odessa, Chernomorsk, and Yuzhnoye; only vessels associated with the Ukrainian army enter them. Maritime trade is conducted through the Danube ports — Ukraine’s Izmail and Romania’s Constan·a, which together can potentially account for no more than a third of the exports that previously passed through the ports of Greater Odessa.
As a result, in September, Ukraine was able to export only 44% of the agricultural products planned for exports that month. Exports of metallurgical products ceased completely by the end of September. Together, these items accounted for about 65% of Ukraine’s exports and about $26 billion in foreign exchange earnings per year.
By using the railway network and the Danube ports for exports, Ukraine managed to partially reduce losses, but only slightly -- from about $70 million per day in August to about $60 million in September-October.
The idle time of Greater Odessa has been ongoing since July 22.

Two opinion polls published Friday in Israel – the last legally allowed as elections loom – projected 50 seats for incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 52 for the opposition camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, ahead of Tuesday’s parliamentary elections.
Public broadcaster KAN and private Channel 12 released the surveys four days before the vote. Both showed identical totals for the two main camps, but differed on how seats were distributed among parties.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party would win 22 seats, followed by Netanyahu’s Likud with 20, and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett’s Together party with 14, according to Channel 12’s poll.
Jewish Power, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir; Yisrael Beiteinu, led by Avigdor Lieberman; and the Democrats, led by Yair Golan, were each projected to win eight seats.
The Religious Zionism–Zehut alliance was projected to get nine seats, Shas seven, United Torah Judaism eight, and the United Arab List five.
The poll gave Hadash–Ta’al eight projected seats and the Hendel–Zelekha alliance four.
According to Channel 12’s bloc breakdown, Eisenkot’s camp would get 52 seats, Netanyahu’s bloc 50, Arab parties 14, and the Hendel–Zelekha alliance four.
KAN’s poll also projected 22 seats for Eisenkot’s party, 20 for Likud, and 14 for Bennett’s party, matching Channel 12’s findings for the three largest parties.
The Democrats, Yisrael Beiteinu, Jewish Power, and United Torah Judaism would each get eight seats, with Shas and the Religious Zionism–Zehut alliance seven apiece.
The joint slate of Hadash, Ta’al, and Balad would get nine seats, with the United Arab List at five. The Reservists party and the Economic Party would each get four.
KAN likewise put Netanyahu’s bloc at 50 seats and Eisenkot’s camp at 52. 
Prominent difference
The most prominent difference between the surveys concerned the Religious Zionism–Zehut alliance, which would get seven seats in KAN’s poll compared with nine in Channel 12’s.
KAN also projected nine seats for the joint Arab slate, compared with eight for Hadash–Ta’al in Channel 12’s survey.
In KAN’s poll, Netanyahu’s bloc fell one seat from 51 the previous week, while Eisenkot’s camp remained unchanged at 52.
Likud and Yashar each lost one seat, while Bennett’s party gained two, reaching 14.
On suitability for prime minister, KAN found Netanyahu and Bennett tied at 38% for the first time since late August. Netanyahu had led Bennett 38% to 34% in the previous survey.
In a separate matchup, Eisenkot got 44% support compared with Netanyahu’s 38%.
Against Bennett, Eisenkot got 35%, compared with Bennett's 22%, while 43% considered neither suitable to lead the government.
On turnout, 71% of respondents said they were certain they would vote. The figure reached 80% among opposition supporters and 75% among supporters of governing coalition parties.
The survey also found that 36% of voters had not definitively decided which party to support, up from 30% in the previous poll.
Security perception
On security, 58% rated Israel’s situation as poor, compared with 37% who described it as good.
The proportion describing the security situation as poor reached 73% among opposition supporters and 28% among governing coalition supporters.
Asked about their preferred outcome if Eisenkot’s camp finished ahead of Netanyahu’s without reaching 61 seats, 27% favored a unity government and another 27% preferred fresh elections.
A further 26% supported a minority government formed by the change camp, with Arab parties abstaining from voting against it.
Among supporters of the governing coalition, 47% preferred another election, while 45% of opposition supporters backed a minority government.
The polls indicated that neither main camp would secure the 61-seat parliamentary majority needed to form a government on its own.
Under Israeli law, publishing new election poll results is prohibited from the end of the Friday preceding Election Day until polling stations close.
The Israel Democracy Institute says the restriction was adopted in 2007 to prevent misleading information and manipulating public opinion through polls shortly before elections.

youtaro sakamoto’s kinetic thread column transforms human presence into shifting shadows
a delicate column formed from fine threads moves in response to nearby visitors, casting constantly changing shadows.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
KINETIC THREAD COLUMN installation draws from SUDARE SCREENS
Created by Japanese artist, engineer, and researcher Youtaro Sakamoto, Schattenrequisit: Column is a kinetic installation formed from fine threads that explores the relationship between architectural permanence, human presence, and shifting shadow projections. Drawing conceptual inspiration from the light-filtering properties of sudare (traditional Japanese slatted screens), the project treats physical material and immaterial shadows as unified components of a single sculptural composition.
ANIMATING STATIC ARCHITECTURAL FORMS THROUGH HUMAN MOVEMENT
The installation takes the form of an architectural column constructed from closely spaced fine threads. Integrated millimeter-wave sensors detect the proximity of visitors, triggering a stepper motor developed through computational design and physical prototyping. In response to movement within the space, the motor slowly rotates and shifts the thread assembly, altering the overlap of the linear strands and continuously transforming the shadow silhouettes cast across surrounding walls and floors. By animating a typically static structural archetype, the installation by artist Youtaro Sakamoto mirrors the interaction between fixed urban infrastructure and transient human circulation.
project info:
name: Schattenrequisit: Column
artist: Youtaro Sakamoto | @youtarosakamoto
location: Hibiya OKUROJI, Tokyo, Japan
exhibition: DESIGNART TOKYO 2026
dates: October 30th – November 8th, 2026

Cattle prices hit 'a new gear' as rain tumbles down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
02:06:02 UTC
11:06:02 KST

analysis
Cattle prices hit 'a new gear' this week as rain tumbled down
Cattle prices jumped this week as heavy rain fell across key production areas in Queensland and northern New South Wales.
Meat and Livestock Australia's (MLA) benchmark Eastern Young Cattle Indicator (EYCI) surged beyond 1,000 cents a kilogram, as restockers and backgrounders competed for numbers.
"The cattle market shifted to a new gear off the back of this rain," Stuart Bull, MLA's market information manager said.
"Some of these regions were in need of a good drink and this rain has really helped pushed prices, along with fewer cattle coming to market."
At Roma on Tuesday, some weaner steers from the Winton region sold for an incredible $7 a kilogram, which equated to more than $1,900 a head.
At Dubbo, the local saleyard report said restocker demand "sparked a market boom".
"Restocker demand was a stand-out, with young cattle selling up to an impressive 80 cents per kilo dearer [than last week]," the report said.
"Young steers reached a top of $7.40/kg, while young restocker heifers sold to $6.50/kg, showcasing the strength of competition and confidence among buyers looking to replenish their herds."
Loading...
Scott Loughnan, who runs a mixed farming operation west of Roma, had received more than 160 millimetres of rain when he spoke to ABC News.
"We'd organised to feed cattle all summer with forecasts of a super El Niño,"
he said.
"It was apparently never going to rain again, but this will definitely make it easier."
Mr Loughnan was in the middle of harvesting wheat, barley and chickpeas, and said for winter crops in the area, the rain was "not very good".
"I looked at some chickpeas this morning and they might not be much good, but I'm trying to look at the positives that this rain will grow us some grass and give us moisture for the next planting."
Record cow and heavy steers
Meanwhile, MLA's national processor cow indicator has cracked $4 a kilogram for the first time on record, and the national heavy steer indicator has also reached a new high of $4.77 a kilogram.
Global AgriTrends livestock analyst Simon Quilty said the supply of heavy steers was tight and processors were competing against feedlots to secure numbers.
"Once upon a time, feedlot operators wanted 450 kilogram to 500 kilogram steers, that was the preferred weight," he said.
"But that's now been lifted because of the lack of supply and they're taking 550 kilograms to almost 630 kilograms, creating an overlap [in demand] between processors and their needs for slaughter-ready cattle and the feedlotters who have extended the requirements of their cattle.
"So there's competition for numbers between the north and the south of Australia, plus processors versus feedlots [and] the net effect is this incredible demand for heavy steers that I think will continue."
Mr Quilty believes Australia's cattle industry is at the start of a herd rebuild and is forecasting cattle prices to increase next year.
He is forecasting heavy steer prices to rise by about 20 per cent to about $5.70/kg next year.

US intel memo flags 'advanced' Iranian plots to target American diplomats abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
02:00:51 UTC
11:00:51 KST

The State Department is reducing staffing at four US embassies in the Middle East after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel in the region and elsewhere.
In a memo sent on Friday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said his teams "have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel."
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo was obtained by The Associated Press and reported earlier by Axios.
There was no immediate reaction from Tehran.
"These materials have been provided to appropriately-cleared senior staff on your team and we are available to brief you at your convenience. We will make every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so you can share it with State Department personnel at your discretion," Clayton added.
Three US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, confirmed that the memo was sent to Rubio in his capacity as secretary of state and national security adviser.
The memo emerged shortly after the State Department announced it is reducing staff at the US embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.
The three officials said the threats from Iran and Yemen's Houthi militia are related to the staffing changes.
Houthi threat
The embassies involved are all under what is known as "restricted operations" status that has already reduced the size of their personnel footprints. The embassies will remain open.
However, unlike in Saudi Arabia, where nonessential US personnel and their families were ordered Wednesday to leave the country, staff in the other four countries are not compelled to depart.
In announcing the staffing drawdowns this week, the State Department pointed specifically to increased threats from Houthi militias and did not mention threats to US personnel directly from Iran.
US officials have adamantly denied they are tied to any potential new US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

US senators threaten to block Trump's nominees over Starlink restrictions in Ukraine – NYT
US senators have warned the White House they will withhold their votes to confirm nominees until US President Donald Trump's administration secures the restoration of communications systems used by Ukrainian forces, The New York Times reports.
Source: The New York Times, citing sources
Details: According to three people familiar with the discussions, Republicans and Democrats in the Senate have told senior White House officials that they will block confirmation of Trump's nominees awaiting congressional approval until the administration restores critically important satellite communications capabilities used by the Ukrainian military.
The move, disclosed to the NYT by sources speaking on condition of anonymity because it has not yet been officially announced, will intensify bipartisan tensions over the White House's ever-more conciliatory approach towards Russia.
This will take place during the remaining congressional session scheduled for after the midterm elections, when Republicans are expected to try to confirm dozens of Trump's nominees before the current Congress's term ends.
The stance highlights growing divisions between the White House and Congress over Russia, with even senior Republicans showing increasing willingness to challenge Trump's policy positions. It also points to a possible shift after the midterm elections, when control of Congress could pass to the Democrats and lawmakers from both parties may be more resolute in using their leverage and oversight powers on the issue.
Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican from Pennsylvania who is fighting to retain his seat in a highly contested district, has threatened to seek the dismissal of US officials responsible for the network disruptions as well as cuts to their departments' budgets. He said he doubts the problems were accidental.
A US Senate staff member told the NYT on condition of anonymity that the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations had approved several shipments of critical air defence interceptors that had still not been delivered to Ukraine, raising concerns about delays in aid already authorised by Congress.
Staff are also considering launching investigations into SpaceX in connection with the satellite disruptions and have asked companies involved in Russian diesel fuel transactions to retain documents in the event of possible congressional investigations, the source added.
Previously: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on 23 October that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.
A bipartisan group of nearly 20 members of the US House of Representatives called on President Donald Trump to ask Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink systems to target missile launchers on Russian territory.
US Democratic Senator Chris Coons had previously contacted Elon Musk's SpaceX, asking the company to explain who had decided to restrict Starlink's operation in Ukraine and why.
Background:
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk had ordered Starlink services to be slowed down. It is unclear to what extent Trump was involved in discussions about the slowdown.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- US House of Representatives member Joe Wilson and nearly two dozen of his colleagues prepared a letter calling for Ukraine to be permitted to use Starlink for strikes on launch sites within Russian territory.
- The Wall Street Journal, citing US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
- On the evening of 22 October, Trump said Musk had already lifted speed restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine but declined to say whether he had personally called him about the issue.
- Ukraine's Defence Ministry said it was recording disruptions to Starlink and Starshield services on the line of contact.

Argentinian judge drops fraud investigation into Milei over crypto scandal
