Argentinian judge drops fraud investigation into Milei over crypto scandal
President Javier Milei’s role in cryptocurrency launch does not translate into a fraudulent scheme, judge says.
An Argentinian federal judge has dropped a criminal investigation into President Javier Milei and his sister Karina Milei over the collapse of a cryptocurrency he promoted online.
Judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi issued the decision on Friday, according to court records, ending an inquiry into Milei’s role in the launch of the $Libra token, which crashed after a brief rally.
“The reported events do not constitute a criminal offence,” the judge said in a ruling. He also wrote that investor losses and the rise and fall in the currency’s price were insufficient to establish fraud.
In his ruling, Martinez de Giorgi said that Milei’s institutional standing could have given the launch “greater impact” when he posted about it, but that does not translate into a fraudulent scheme.
Javier Milei recommended the little-known meme coin in a post on X in February 2025. He later deleted the post and denied any link to the cryptocurrency, whose value soon plunged.
The judge also dismissed an investigation into US businessman Hayden Davis, who described himself as a “launch adviser” for the token. Davis has acknowledged that he held close to $100m after the crash and denies any wrongdoing.
“For the first time in history, a President of the Nation was investigated with complete freedom, resulting in absolute proof of his innocence,” read a post shared on X by the official presidential office.
“The question that remains is this: Who will take responsibility for having wasted Argentine taxpayers’ money and the President of the Nation’s time in a failed attempt at an institutional coup?”
Milei’s friendship with Trump
Milei is one of US President Donald Trump’s closest allies. Trump firmly backed him a year ago and has called him his “favourite president”.
Trump made clear the support hinged on a victory for Milei’s party.
“I’m with this man because his philosophy is correct,” he said ahead of a White House lunch with the Argentinian leader last year. “If he wins, we’re staying with him. And if he doesn’t win, we’re gone.”
Earlier this month, Milei urged Trump to emerge stronger from the US midterm elections, saying the vote mattered for the West as a whole.
Austerity at home
Since taking office in 2023, Milei has laid off thousands of state employees, shut ministries, cut subsidies and reduced government-funded programmes. The measures were meant to fight high inflation, which has fallen to about 2 percent a month.
Milei says his plan is working, claiming that Argentina has grown for 27 consecutive months and is expanding at four times its historical rate.
When the coin crashed, Milei said he had acted “in good faith” and accused his political rivals of trying to exploit the situation.

OPINION - The collective, international merits of Badr memorandum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
00:59:33 UTC
09:59:33 KST

Hannan Hussain is a senior expert at Initiate Futures and leads the West Asia Program at the Institute of Regional Studies, both based in the Pakistani capital, Islamabad.
On Oct. 21, Türkiye, Qatar, Pakistan, and Indonesia signed the Badr Memorandum of Understanding in Doha [1], aiming to strengthen their defense industrial cooperation and lay the groundwork for technical military training [2].
The agreement should be seen as a continuation of existing defense engagements that have consolidated in the lead-up to the pact [3]. Its signing makes a range of collective as well as regional merits abundantly clear.
The agreement provides a critical gateway to further coordinate complementary strengths in the high-value defense industry space. Qatar alone has been a trusted procurer [4] of state-of-the-art Turkish defense equipment, ranging from armored vehicles to multipurpose Bayraktar TB2 armed drones [5]. These have made important capacity-building contributions to the Qatari Armed Forces.
By entering the four-way agreement, Qatar can acquire stronger and more coordinated support from Türkiye on scaling up existing projects and joint defense initiatives. Areas of focus span internationally competitive defense assets, such as SARP remote-controlled weapon systems and defense surveillance support [6]. Prior experience in expanding local assembly and joint production of these systems generates greater optimism for four-way complementarity. Look to Qatar’s BARQ joint venture: it continues to thrive at a time when Qatari defense manufacturers enjoy growing traction with Turkish defense giants Aselsan, STM, and MKE – entities increasingly integrated into the global defense market [7].
The significance of this channel for overseas defense outreach cannot be overstated. Pakistan [8] and Indonesia [9] have been leading efforts to localize a share of their defense production on home territory, with Qatar building on its well-established investment ties with the Turkish defense industry. Its push to sustain over a decade of investments across various spheres of Türkiye's multipronged defense sector puts those interests into perspective [10]. With the Turkish defense procurement push expected to increase by over 200% in the medium-term program [11], the four-way deal can serve as a gateway for overseas markets and help consolidate Qatar’s latest indigenization drive [12].
The Badr pact also succeeds in bringing Ankara’s robust defense indigenization drive into further sync with Qatar’s capital investment niche. Türkiye has sealed $15 billion in fresh defense contracts this year and is in the process of streamlining billions in domestic orders [13], underlining space for targeted Qatari investments in value-added defense exports. Given Doha’s stated resolve to invest more deeply in companies that can undergird its domestic defense manufacturing base [14], the Badr pact can help advance Qatari defense indigenization ambitions in line with Türkiye’s multipronged defense export strategy. A recent track record of linking together targeted defense enterprises highlights that potential [15].
The strength of the Badr pact lies in looping in the comparative advantages of Pakistan and Indonesia’s ongoing joint defense production initiatives with Ankara, including robust technology transfers, to inform the trajectory of well-integrated defense procurement supply chains as well.
Pakistan, for its part, brings a strong track record of high-quality technical training and capacity-building support for defense industrial upgrades [16]. Islamabad’s record of involvement in Turkish defense projects says it all: it has been a recurring candidate for prospective engagement in Ankara’s KAAN fighter jet program [17], alongside strong cooperation in naval warship procurement and joint production [18]. This experience can serve as a value addition to Qatar, as Pakistan brings in a depth of future human capital accustomed to new offerings in the defense industrial space. Ankara fills the void with cutting-edge drone supplies [19], which can be further streamlined under the agreement. This year alone, Ankara and Jakarta partnered on developing next-generation autonomous combat drones [20], with operational production likely to take off in 2028. Bringing these complementary strengths under one umbrella is part and parcel of the utility of this pact.
On regional contributions, the pact also arrives at a critical time. There is a deep understanding among partner states that they need to bolster their future defense posture by partnering closely with nations on enduring defense supply chains [21]. That understanding was put into action at October’s Global Security Forum, when Doha called for non-aggression and cultivating cooperative security solutions for enduring peace [22]. The Badr memorandum's emphasis on advancing cooperation across research and development qualifies as a qualitative strength to see these cooperative security ambitions through. Indonesia is a proof point: it is in the process of building two high-tier submarines on the back of French technology transfers, and is focusing billions on defense spanning maintenance [23], domestic self-sufficiency, and cutting-edge industrial infrastructure – elements at the heart of the Badr defense pact.
Interestingly, the Badr memorandum also provides a rare opening to cultivate “strategic partnerships” that can help each partner foster the integration of defensive capabilities. Qatar’s multiyear involvement in Türkiye’s defense industry, Pakistan’s bid to scale up indigenously manufactured drones, and Indonesia’s growing potential to advance jointly produced tanks make these future prospects abundantly clear.
Ultimately, the Badr memorandum's utility for defense industrial integration in four critical economies, emphasis on technical defense training, and industry-ready solutions for indigenous manufacturing make it a novel blueprint for cooperative security at a time when the region needs it most.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has slammed the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.
The Magpies slumped to a new low on Friday night after failing to kick a single goal against Port Adelaide.
The 48-point defeat to the Power was the club's 10th loss this season out of 11 games. Under head coach Sam Wright, the Magpies have won just five games since the start of 2024.
"Overall, it was not the best standard of AFLW football that we would expect to see at this point of season 11," Arnell said on ABC Radio.
"Ash Centra was one of the first to walk off the ground in tears right in front of us. Totally fair. I would probably be about the same level."
The pioneer of women's football and former captain of Carlton said while the AFLW continued to play 16 a side in venues open to conditions, unlike protected stadiums the MCG, Perth Stadium and Docklands in the men's game, if teams did not have high skill levels or offensive systems, they would not be able to put goals on the board.
"If you're Sam Wright, you've made some clear decisions where you want to play plus two behind the ball for a lot of the game. And my personal belief is that if you do that in AFLW, you're giving up score, and that's what we saw again tonight," Arnell said.
"And having coached against Collingwood in 2024, we beat them here at Alberton, and it was quite frustrating as a coach and someone who's been invested in women's sport and AFLW for a period of time, [as] you know that broadcast relies on high scoring.
"People who forever criticise AFLW as a sport, or a league, will always point to the lack of score and short quarters … and I'm a firm non-believer in heavy defensive systems for all of those reasons, not just because you can't score, but because we have a responsibility if you're coaching to grow the game and put on a show."
Last week, Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly fronted the AFLW playing group after media reports of player unrest and concerns with the operation of the women's program.
Kelly told News Corp that when AFLW was to be introduced in 2017, Collingwood put its hand up to be an inaugural club, but now he often wondered if the Magpies would have been better off waiting to enter the women's competition at a later date.
He conceded being a foundation AFLW club might have been a mistake, while ruling out any prospect of an independent review into the women's program, which other struggling clubs have done, such as Carlton in 2023, Richmond in 2025 and St Kilda following this season.
To Arnell, those remarks from Kelly screamed a lack of understanding between the executive and the playing cohort.
"That statement just immediately tells me you have never sat down with enough of your women's players and even asked them questions of their perspective and where they've come from," Arnell said.
"Like you've got no understanding of your playing group and potentially your coaching group."
Despite being one of the biggest sporting clubs in Victoria, Collingwood players are reported to feel behind local rivals in Melbourne, North Melbourne and Carlton, and are unhappy with multiple aspects of the program, including coaching, high performance and list management.
Collingwood is not alone down the bottom of the ladder, with St Kilda and Essendon also entering round 11 having won only one game this season.
"And I'll guarantee you, off the back of that, there's going to be a lot of movement in the trade period coming up in the next month and a half," Arnell said.
There is an expected player exodus from Collingwood at the season's end, with captain Ruby Schleicher already announcing she'll be leaving to head back to Western Australia. It is reported the West Coast Eagles offered her a four-year deal, while the Magpies' initial offer was a one-year contract extension, then upped to two.
On top of Schleicher, the high-profile players such as Tarni White, Brianna Davey, Sarah Rowe and Lauren Butler are all out of contract at season's end. Vice-captain Jordy Allen tried to exit last trade period for Brisbane but Collingwood blocked her attempts.
"I think the washout of this whole storyline will be well beyond Collingwood, and we're going to see evidence of it across the trade period coming in December, and it will be really clear which players feel like their club's not invested in the environment," Arnell said.

A US official confirmed to The Jerusalem Post on Friday that US Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio received an intelligence memorandum warning that Iran has significantly increased its efforts to target American officials and citizens, with plots to carry out lethal attacks reaching advanced stages.
The confirmation follows a report by Axios, which obtained the October 23 memorandum sent to Rubio by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, with a copy to CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
According to the document, US intelligence agencies have received information through multiple channels indicating that Iran has substantially intensified its efforts to target American personnel.
“The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries,” Clayton wrote.
The intelligence chief warned that information concerning Iranian plots to target American government personnel was relevant to a wider group of individuals than those currently authorized to receive it.
Clayton said the underlying intelligence had already been shared with appropriately cleared senior members of Rubio’s team and offered to provide the secretary with an additional briefing.
He also pledged to make every effort to downgrade the classification of as much intelligence as possible, allowing Rubio to share the information more broadly with State Department personnel who could potentially be at risk.
The memorandum, marked unclassified, did not identify specific targets, attack methods, or countries outside the Middle East where the alleged plots were being developed.
US reduces diplomatic presence amid regional tensions
The warning comes as the State Department moves to reduce its diplomatic presence across several Middle Eastern countries, amid concerns about Iranian retaliation and the possibility of renewed US military operations against Tehran.
Earlier this week, Washington ordered nonessential government employees and family members to depart Saudi Arabia following an escalation in attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis.
According to Axios, additional reductions in US diplomatic personnel were ordered at embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon, Qatar, and Jordan.
CNN also reported on Friday that the United States was accelerating the departure of diplomats and their families from several regional posts, with some personnel having only recently returned following evacuations earlier in the Iran war.
The network further reported that Israel had pressed Washington to launch renewed strikes against Iran sooner, but those efforts had so far been unsuccessful.
Washington weighing renewed military action
The intelligence warning emerged as US President Donald Trump continued to leave open the possibility of additional military action against Iran.
Speaking on Friday, Trump said the United States could launch another operation similar to Operation Epic Fury if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
“We may do another little Epic Fury. Or they’ll agree,” Trump said.
The latest warning underscores mounting US concerns about the security of American diplomatic personnel as Washington weighs further military action and continues diplomatic efforts to reach an agreement with Iran.

Prehistoric hunter-gatherers stayed connected across 200 kilometers, Israeli study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
00:44:14 UTC
09:44:14 KST

Ancient social networks may have been key to the resilience of prehistoric hunter-gatherer communities in the Southern Caucasus, according to June study published in Quaternary Science Reviews.
Led by Dr. Ariel Malinsky-Buller of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, the study challenges long-held assumptions of how prehistoric hunter-gatherers survived between 57,000 and 27,000 years ago.
By combining archaeological, geological, and paleoenvironmental evidence, researchers were able to reconstruct how such small, wide-spread populations were able to navigate the diverse landscape spanning what is now Armenia, Georgia, and other neighboring regions.
The findings revealed a surprising paradox: Even though the hunter-gatherer communities were relatively small and sparsely located, they were not isolated.
Evidence found in stone tools and obsidian artifacts from the time showed that members of these communities routinely traveled between 40 and 200 kilometers, maintaining connections with other hunter-gatherers across vast territories.
Prehistoric communities, culture changed over a gradual period of time
Similar traditions found across the Southern Caucasus and the Armenian Highlands further suggest that prehistoric communities exchanged knowledge and maintained social ties over long distances.
Malinsky-Buller’s research provides a new perspective on on of the most important periods of human prehistory, the transition from the Middle Paleolithic age to the Upper Paleolithic age.
It shows that instead of a rapid replacement of one population or culture by another, evidence points to a more gradual process, where different cultures and traditions successfully coexisted for thousands of years.
Researchers argue that the mobility of these communities, their environmental conditions, population size, and social networks must all be considered when reconstructing how ancient communities reacted to wider change.
"Our findings suggest that mobility alone does not tell the full story of prehistoric survival," said Dr. Ariel Malinsky-Buller. "Even in regions with small and dispersed populations, people remained connected through networks of knowledge, technology, and social interaction.”
“These connections may have been just as important as environmental adaptation in helping communities endure periods of profound change."
The study was conducted by an international team of researchers from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, the National Academy of Sciences of Armenia, Yerevan University, the University of Castilla-La Mancha, the University of Algarve, the American School of Classical Studies at Athens, the University of Seville, the University of California Berkeley, Yale University, the University of Liverpool, the Technical University Bergakademie Freiberg, and the Royal Holloway University of London.

In short:
WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament when it resumes next week.
Senator Steele-John is facing allegations of inappropriate conduct towards women, which he has denied.
What's next?
An independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens is expected to get underway imminently.
WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has reiterated he won't be attending parliament next week, after releasing and then deleting a copy of a letter detailing allegations of misconduct against him.
On Friday night the senator took to social media to publish the letter which is addressed to Greens leader David Shoebridge and signed by seven current and former Greens staff or party office bearers.
The writers, who are not named, state they have been made aware of "multiple allegations of serious misconduct" being made against Senator Steele-John "spanning almost a decade (2017-2025)".
"These allegations all concern his behaviour in the presence of women. We are aware of multiple women who have taken up roles or volunteered in the party, who because of these allegations, have been warned not to be alone with him."
The letter, dated October 13, goes on to state the accusations have come from both inside and outside the party, and urges Senator Shoebridge to commission an independent investigation into the allegations, and review and update gendered violence protocols.
Senator Steele-John has repeatedly and strenuously denied the allegations.
On Saturday the 32-year-old senator said a copy of the letter was sent to him by Chief Political Commentator for the Nine papers, James Massola, who then broke the story on October 15.
The senator said he had initially chosen to post the letter on his own social media accounts because he "did not want to be seen as hiding from it".
"I'm now not sure that was the right call and I've taken it down. I'm really sorry for any additional distress it caused," he said, and reiterated his absence from parliament next week.
The WA branch of the Greens has commissioned an independent investigation into the allegations.
'Growing chorus'
In the days after the allegations became public, Senator Shoebridge initially said he understood Senator Steele-John was taking leave from parliament.
But last Sunday the WA senator denied that was the case in a lengthy open letter, prompting the federal Greens leader to encourage his colleague to take leave.
"I think the community assumptions are that he step aside for the extent of this inquiry and I've communicated that to Jordon," Senator Shoebridge told ABC Radio National Breakfast on Thursday.
In a statement on Saturday, Senator Shoebridge reiterated his view that Senator Steele-John take leave.
"This is in no way a prejudgement of any of these matters," he said.
Senator Steele-John reflected in his post on Friday that there had been a "growing chorus" calling on him to not attend parliament next week, when senate estimates will take place.
"I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable," he said.
"The precedent has now been set: any MP can be kept out of parliament by allegations of allegations."

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The United States has reported 4,588 confirmed measles cases so far in 2026, more than twice the total for all of 2025, according to the latest data released Friday by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Of the confirmed cases, 4,570 were reported by 47 jurisdictions, while 18 involved international visitors to the United States, the CDC said.
Children and adolescents aged 5 to 19 accounted for the largest share of cases, with 1,914 infections, or 42 percent of the total.

In Pennsylvania, the measles outbreak continued to expand, with 78 new cases reported over the past seven days, according to data released Friday by the state's Department of Health. The state has recorded 1,338 cases across 44 counties, accounting for nearly 30 percent of the U.S. total.
Pennsylvania reported only 16 measles cases in 2025, according to the CDC. ■

WHO announces start of Ebola vaccine clinical trial in DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
00:27:21 UTC
09:27:21 KST

WHO announces start of Ebola vaccine clinical trial in DR Congo
The World Health Organization (WHO) has announced the beginning of the first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak that started in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
WHO’s director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said in a social media post on Friday that participants in the trial were vaccinated with the Ervebo vaccine in Bunia, the capital of the DRC’s northeastern Ituri province, which is the epicentre of the Ebola outbreak.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial to see if it offers any cross-protection against the Bundibugyo species of Ebola that is behind the epidemic.
“This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work,” the WHO chief said on X.
“WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives,” he added.
The DRC declared its 17th and worst-ever Ebola outbreak in May and has since reported more than 9,700 cases, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600.
The WHO, in response, triggered a public health emergency of international concern, its second-highest alert level.
The current outbreak has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central and western Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
Vaccines in the pipeline
The so-called Tumaini trial is a single trial framework that can test the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of multiple vaccines.
The trial will use a ring vaccination approach: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection.
The trial is set to incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are currently advancing through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.
Both have received funding from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations and are expected to enter the trial “shortly”, CEPI said in a statement.
The trial will include pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials.
WHO emergencies director Chikwe Ihekweazu said the trial was set up to generate the rigorous evidence needed to determine whether the participating vaccines could protect people at risk.

Bill Gates warns of 20 years of turmoil from artificial intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
00:12:05 UTC
09:12:05 KST

Halis Sünnetci
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Bill Gates warned that artificial intelligence could trigger two decades of economic and social upheaval, disrupting jobs and life even if the technology is managed successfully.
In an interview with the Decoder podcast posted Thursday, the Microsoft co-founder said the transition to an AI-driven economy would create winners and losers, potentially reshaping employment and raising questions about people's roles in society.
"My big concern is this 20-year transition period, where they'll have winners and losers and a lot of disruption," said Gates, 70, adding that society would have to navigate the upheaval before potentially entering an era of abundance.
He described the timeframe as an estimate rather than a firm prediction, acknowledging that the transition could be shorter or longer depending on technological advances and decisions about slowing development.
Gates said advances in AI and humanoid robotics could eventually allow machines to perform much of the physical labor carried out by humans, including building homes, growing food, and even performing surgery.
While the advances could reduce shortages of goods and services, he suggested societies might deliberately reserve certain activities for humans, including childcare, food preparation, arts, and sports.
The billionaire philanthropist also highlighted AI's potential benefits in healthcare and agriculture but warned that governments and society are not adequately prepared for its rapid development.
He urged stronger government oversight and technical safeguards against cyberattacks and biological threats, arguing that AI companies alone cannot be responsible for managing the risks.
Gates also warned that even under the most favorable circumstances, AI's development could bring one of the most tumultuous periods in human history.
"I hate being the bearer of concerning news on this, but it's even worse not to tell people that this is coming. We have choices as humans to make about how we shape it," he said.

Andrew Wasike 
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Deadly fighting between ethnic communities in southern Ethiopia has driven more than 2,000 people to seek refuge in neighboring Kenya, with at least nine deaths reported as violence continued, officials said Friday.
Stanley Kamande, the commissioner for Kenya’s Marsabit County, told reporters that thousands of Ethiopians had crossed the border into the town of Moyale after armed confrontations erupted on the Ethiopian side of the frontier on Wednesday.
Reports from Ethiopia indicated that at least nine people had died and dozens were wounded during the fighting. The casualty figures have not been independently verified.
The violence involves ethnic Oromo and Somali communities following tensions about the display of the Somali Regional State flag in an area administered by Ethiopia's Oromia region. Both are federal regions of Ethiopia, as distinct from the country of Somalia, which borders both Ethiopia and Kenya.
A woman in Moyale was also reportedly injured by a bullet fired from across the border and received medical treatment. 
Kenya mobilizes humanitarian assistance
The Kenya Red Cross said Thursday it was providing emergency assistance to displaced families, initially targeting 1,000 households.
It said it was working with government authorities to provide temporary shelter, food, clean water, and other essential supplies.
Moyale, a major crossing between the two East African countries, lies 780 kilometers (485 miles) north of Nairobi, Kenya's capital, and 775 kilometers (482 miles) south of Addis Ababa, Ethiopia's capital.
The unrest has raised concerns about further displacement and disruption of cross-border trade.

Netanyahu says end of US military support to Israel is 'only a matter of time'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
00:00:34 UTC
09:00:34 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed that his country must prepare for the end of US military assistance worth tens of billions of dollars, calling the prospect "only a matter of time", adding Israel may need to develop an alternative digital economy to circumvent rising international sanctions. 
Speaking just days before hard-fought elections, Netanyahu, who faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant and ongoing corruption proceedings, told Israel's business broadcaster Channel 10 that he had ordered preparations for potential economic and banking sanctions, including exploring alternative financial technologies.
"If you think we're going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that's tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defence budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won't happen, because America has changed," he said, apparently referring to growing opposition in the US to such support in light of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, brutal occupation of West Bank, and almost daily killings of Palestinians.
"This is over, and it will end. It is only a matter of time."
Netanyahu gave no date for an end to the assistance and announced no formal US decision, instead calling for preparations for a possible future halt.
On potential sanctions, he said Israel must develop alternative economic and financial mechanisms.
"You have to understand that there could be sanctions, including banking sanctions. You need to prepare an economy that can get around them," he said.
Asked whether blockchain technology could offer an alternative for dealing with economic sanctions, Netanyahu replied: "Yes, that's one of the ways. And I've already asked for a plan to be prepared."
Netanyahu did not specify from which country he expected sanctions.
But his remarks come after UK and several other countries imposed sanctions targeting goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank in response to a wave of settler attacks on Palestinians and settlement construction approved by Netanyahu's extremist government.
Netanyahu still has a close alliance with US administration but criticism in the US has been rising, especially within the young Americans, since Israel's genocide in Gaza.
Combating 'Jewish terrorism'
Yair Lapid, a centrist former prime minister who is part of the opposition bloc challenging Netanyahu, seized on the remarks.
"Netanyahu now admits, in his own words: if his government is reelected, American security aid will come to an end and Israel will face sanctions that would devastate our economy, lead to runaway price hikes, and cause irreparable damage," Lapid said.
Netanyahu's remarks come as he threatens to resume war on Iran, which under heavy international sanctions has embraced cryptocurrency and other alternative economic measures.
Opposition Democrats party leader Yair Golan also slammed Netanyahu’s remarks, accusing him of being detached from reality.
He argued that preventing economic sanctions requires combating "Jewish terrorism" that damages Israel’s international standing, preserving strategic alliances, and replacing the government in next week’s election.
Golan called for a new government "without Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Deri," referring to extremist politicians Itamar Ben-Gvir and Shas party leader Aryeh Deri.
The remarks came four days before Israel’s Tuesday parliamentary elections, amid debate about relations with Western allies and the potential consequences of economic sanctions.
Under a pact signed with Washington in 2016, Israel receives $38 billion in military assistance over a 10-year period set to end in 2028.

Arab nations condemn deadly funeral attack at church in Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:57:40 UTC
08:57:40 KST

Rania R.a. Abushamala
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Officials, institutions, and factions from 11 Arab countries condemned Friday’s terror attack on mourners attending a funeral at a church in southern Jordan, expressing solidarity with the kingdom and rejecting attempts to sow division.
Condemnations came from Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Palestine, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Bahrain, as well as the Arab League and the Arab Interior Ministers Council.
The attack killed seven people and injured 27, according to Jordan’s Public Security Directorate.
Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy denounced attacks on places of worship as “an unacceptable terrorist act and a crime condemned by every standard,” pledging support for Jordan’s measures to protect its security and stability.
He urged national unity against attempts to spread discord, division, and chaos.
The Arab Interior Ministers Council expressed “full solidarity” with Jordan and confidence in its security agencies’ ability to apprehend the perpetrators. 
Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Palestine
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said the attack violated the sanctity of places of worship, the deceased, and mourners.
“Terrorism has neither a religion nor a homeland,” he said, warning that it seeks to undermine coexistence and sow discord.
The Syrian Foreign Ministry expressed support for Jordan’s security, stability, and national unity.
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein conveyed Baghdad’s solidarity in a call with his Jordanian counterpart Ayman Safadi.
The Palestinian presidency said targeting innocent people and places of worship is a crime that cannot be justified under any pretext, stressing that the attack will not undermine Jordanians’ unity.
Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh, Hamas, and Palestine’s Higher Presidential Committee for Church Affairs also condemned the attack.
The committee urged Palestinian churches to ring their bells at 9 pm Friday and urged Muslims and Christians to join a solidarity gathering Sunday at 11 am in Bethlehem’s Manger Square. 
Egypt, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi pledged support for Jordan against “all forms of violence and terrorism.” The Foreign Ministry and Al-Azhar Grand Imam Ahmed al-Tayeb also condemned the attack.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE rejected terrorism aimed at undermining Jordan’s security, while Oman condemned violence against places of worship and the terrorizing of civilians.
Kuwait and Qatar backed Jordan’s measures to preserve its security and stability. Bahrain also expressed support for efforts to pursue the perpetrators and bring them to justice.
Jordanian authorities said unidentified gunmen opened fire on St. George Greek Orthodox Church in Hamoud, Karak. Citing an unnamed source, public broadcaster Al-Mamlaka TV reported that two assailants stepped out of a vehicle and opened fire during a funeral.
Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said security agencies are working around the clock to find the attackers, stressing that it is too “early to discuss the perpetrators and their affiliations.”
King Abdullah II pledged the harshest punishment for those responsible.

China
Unknown Publisher

Staff members of the Nainang ecological and cultural protection center walk on the way to collect the infrared cameras in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Oct. 22, 2026.
Snow leopards are under China's highest national-level protection and are listed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. World Snow Leopard Day falls on October 23 annually.
Nainang Valley, which is only 38 kilometers away from the urban area of Lhasa in a straight line, is a rare stable habitat for snow leopards located in the suburb of a city in Xizang.
The Nainang ecological and cultural protection center in Doilungdeqen District was established in May 2023. To date, 40 snow leopards have been identified and named within the 200-square-kilometer monitoring area of Nainang Valley. (Xinhua/Jigme Dorje)

Cuban FM denounces Trump's new military threat
China

Two vintage cars run on a street in Havana, Cuba, Oct. 23, 2026. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Friday denounced a new threat of military intervention against the Caribbean nation by U.S. President Donald Trump. In a post on X, Rodriguez rejected "any threat regarding U.S. ambitions toward Cuba" in response to remarks by Trump, who said Friday that U.S. ships "will pass" Cuba on their way back from Iran. (Photo by Joaquin Hernandez/Xinhua)
HAVANA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Friday denounced a new threat of military intervention against the Caribbean nation by U.S. President Donald Trump.
In a post on X, Rodriguez rejected "any threat regarding U.S. ambitions toward Cuba" in response to remarks by Trump, who said Friday that U.S. ships "will pass" Cuba on their way back from Iran.
"They'll raise up their hands. And then we're going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal," Trump said at a campaign rally in Fort Myers, in the southern U.S. state of Florida. He said one of the ships would stop about 50 yards (about 46 meters) off the coast.
"On our shores there are beautiful beaches, but also diente de perro (a jagged coastal coral formation), inhospitable to those who arrive with hostile aims and a thirst for domination," Rodriguez wrote.
Rodriguez, Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel and other officials have denounced U.S. threats of military intervention, which have escalated since early 2026, and have defended the island's sovereignty and its right to self-defense.
In May, Trump said in Florida that the United States would be taking over Cuba "almost immediately." ■

BRASILIA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) has asked social media companies Meta and X to provide, within 24 hours, technical explanations of their use of artificial intelligence, the distribution of political content, the publication of electoral ads and the removal of posts ahead of the presidential runoff on Sunday, Oct. 25.
The decision, announced Friday, was made Thursday night by the court's inspector general Ricardo Villas Boas Cueva, who set a daily fine of 500,000 reais (about 100,000 U.S. dollars) for each company in case of unjustified noncompliance.
The measure responds to an electoral investigation brought by a political coalition supporting incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking reelection against opposition candidate Flavio Bolsonaro.
With the runoff approaching, Cueva demanded that the companies explain the criteria for content distribution and any differences in treatment between the candidates competing for the presidency.
United Nations experts sent a letter to Meta earlier this week seeking an explanation of alleged unequal treatment of the presidential candidates in Brazil. ■

Trump modifies scope of 50-pct tariffs on Canadian products
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:38:12 CST
08:38:12 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday signed a proclamation modifying the scope of 50-percent additional tariffs on certain Canadian products, removing some goods from the tariff list and adding others, with the changes set to take effect on Oct. 30.
According to the proclamation posted on the White House website, products including plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes imported into the United States from Canada will no longer be subject to the additional 50-percent ad valorem duty.
Instead, certain valves, carpets, waste products and other items imported into the United States shall be subject to the additional 50-percent ad valorem duty.
The changes will apply to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouses for consumption, on or after Oct. 30, according to the proclamation.
"The modification in this proclamation will offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce, is consistent with the public interests and the interests of the United States, is required by the public interests, and will better serve the public interest," the proclamation states. It describes the duties as a response to what it calls Canada's "discrimination or unreasonable and unequal imposition" on U.S. auto and auto parts exports.
Trump imposed 50-percent tariffs on about 20 billion U.S. dollars worth of Canadian goods on Aug. 22, prompting Canada to retaliate with tariffs on an equivalent value of U.S. imports, which took effect on Sept. 8. ■

Ex-ESPN reporter Britt McHenry resigns from State Department after incident at Wizards game

Ex-ESPN reporter Britt McHenry resigns from State Department after incident at Wizards game
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Britt McHenry is no longer a press advisor at the State Department, reportedly resigning days after videos of a confrontation at a Washington Wizards game went viral.
- Footage appears to show a drink thrown toward the ex-ESPN reporter before she throws one back.
- The altercation reportedly began after she defended Bucks forward Kyle Kuzma’s fiancée, Winnie Harlow.
Former ESPN reporter and Fox News personality Britt McHenry is no longer a press advisor for the U.S. Department of State, multiple media outlets are reporting. The development comes after viral videos appeared to show her throwing a drink at someone (after one was thrown at her) during an altercation in the stands at an NBA game.
Page Six reported Friday that McHenry was “forced to resign” on Thursday, the day after the alleged incident at the Washington Wizards’ home opener against the Milwaukee Bucks at Capital One Arena. McHenry then told Front Office Sports that she signed a resignation letter.
The State Department told both publications that it does not comment on internal personnel matters.
As president of White House Correspondents Assn., Jacqui Heinrich goes to bat for the 1st Amendment rights of her competitors.
The incident reportedly started after a group sitting behind McHenry started shouting insults toward Bucks forward Kyle Kuzma about his fiancée, Winnie Harlow. McHenry is said to have spoken up in Harlow’s defense.
Video footage posted by TMZ appears to start a bit later. It shows McHenry talking to a male companion and an usher from her seat while fans seated around her can be heard making negative comments about her, with some chanting, “Kick her out!”
As McHenry and her companion eventually start to leave on their own, a clear liquid can be seen hitting or coming close to hitting her on the back of the head. She responds by throwing a drink in that person’s direction. As she makes her way up the stairs in the aisle, McHenry is seen giving the middle finger and blowing kisses to the crowd as some people heckle and throw towels at her.
The Atlanta Falcons briefly used a profile image inspired by their throwback helmet ahead of Sunday’s game against the 49ers, but many social media users saw a resemblance to Nazi-era imagery.
Later in one of the videos, McHenry appears to argue with a security worker near at one of the venue’s entrances. As he gestures toward the exit, she appears stunned and asks, “What did I do?”
Monumental Sports & Entertainment, which owns and operates the Wizards and Capital One Arena, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
McHenry worked at ESPN from 2014 to 2017. In 2015, she was suspended for a week after a video surfaced of her yelling at and belittling a towing company employee. McHenry later apologized for the incident.
She announced her State Department job on social media last month.

Chabad rabbi arrested on suspicion of murder after fatal Costco collision in California
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:27:59 UTC
08:27:59 KST

A Chabad rabbi in Southern California has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a 28-year-old man was fatally struck by a vehicle in the parking lot of a Costco store near Los Angeles.
The suspect, Rabbi Abba Bryski, 35, of Agoura Hills, is the son of Rabbi Moshe Bryski, a prominent Chabad leader in Southern California and a well-known figure in the Los Angeles Jewish community.
The incident occurred Tuesday evening near the gas pumps of a Costco location in Camarillo, northwest of Los Angeles. According to the Ventura County Sheriff's Office, deputies were dispatched to the scene after receiving a report that a pedestrian had been struck by a vehicle.
When deputies arrived, witnesses directed them to Bryski, identifying him as the driver involved in the collision. Officers located him sitting inside his vehicle in the parking lot, detained him and subsequently placed him under arrest.
The victim, a 28-year-old resident of Modesto, California, was taken to a nearby hospital in critical condition, where he was later pronounced dead. Authorities have not released his identity.
Bryski was booked into the Ventura County Jail on suspicion of murder. He also faces an allegation of resisting or obstructing a law enforcement officer. His bail was set at $3 million.
Investigators have not revealed whether the collision was deliberate
The circumstances surrounding the fatal incident remain unclear. Investigators have not disclosed what happened in the moments before the collision, whether an altercation occurred between Bryski and the victim, or whether the vehicle strike was intentional.
Authorities have also not explained what evidence led them to investigate the death as a homicide rather than a fatal traffic accident.
Under California law, a murder conviction does not necessarily require proof that a defendant specifically intended to kill. In some circumstances, conduct carried out with knowledge of a serious danger to human life and conscious disregard for that danger can support a murder charge. Ordinary driving negligence, however, is not sufficient on its own.
The investigation is being led by the Ventura County Sheriff's Office Major Crimes Bureau, which has appealed to the public and potential witnesses for information that could help establish the circumstances of the incident. The county medical examiner is responsible for determining the cause and manner of death.
Son of a prominent Chabad leader
Bryski's father, Rabbi Moshe Bryski, is a leading figure in the Chabad-Lubavitch movement in Southern California and oversees the organization's activities in the Conejo Valley region.
He serves as executive director of Chabad of the Conejo and dean of the Conejo Jewish Academy, a Jewish educational institution in Agoura Hills. Over several decades, he has played a central role in establishing Jewish educational programs, synagogues and community institutions throughout the area.
His influence extends beyond the local community. He was previously named among the region's 25 most influential figures by a local weekly publication and was selected to deliver the keynote address at Chabad's international gathering of emissaries, one of the movement's most prominent annual events.
Authorities have not disclosed a possible motive in the case, and investigators have yet to establish publicly what led to the fatal encounter in the Costco parking lot.

Netanyahu says end to US military aid to Israel ‘only a matter of time’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:17:21 UTC
08:17:21 KST

Said Amori, Rania Abushamala
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that Israel must prepare for the end of US military assistance worth tens of billions of dollars, calling the prospect “only a matter of time.”
Speaking just days before hard-fought elections, Netanyahu told Israel’s business broadcaster Channel 10 that he had ordered preparations for potential economic and banking sanctions, including exploring alternative financial technologies.
“If you think we're going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that's tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defense budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won't happen, because America has changed,” he said, apparently referring to growing opposition in the US to such aid in light of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and mistreatment of the Palestinians.
“This is over, and it will end. It is only a matter of time.”
Netanyahu gave no date for an end to the assistance and announced no formal US decision, instead calling for preparations for a possible future halt.
On potential sanctions, he said Israel must develop alternative economic and financial mechanisms.
“You have to understand that there could be sanctions, including banking sanctions. You need to prepare an economy that can get around them,” he said.
Asked whether blockchain technology could offer an alternative for dealing with economic sanctions, Netanyahu replied: “Yes, that's one of the ways. And I've already asked for a plan to be prepared.” 
Opposition pushes to replace Netanyahu’s government
Opposition Democrats party leader Yair Golan criticized Netanyahu’s remarks on US social media company X, accusing him of being detached from reality.
He argued that preventing economic sanctions requires combating “Jewish terrorism” that damages Israel’s international standing, preserving strategic alliances, and replacing the government in next week’s election.
Golan called for a new government “without Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Deri,” referring to National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Shas party leader Aryeh Deri.
The remarks came four days before Israel’s Tuesday parliamentary elections, amid debate about relations with Western allies and the potential consequences of economic sanctions.
Under a pact signed with Washington in 2016, Israel receives $38 billion in military assistance over a 10-year period set to end in 2028.
Netanyahu has previously called for reducing Israel’s dependence on US military aid and strengthening its domestic defense industry.

Wallaroos send retiring pair out with win over Scotland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:16:33 UTC
08:16:33 KST

Former Wallaroos skipper Emily Chancellor and teammate Cecilia Smith signed off with a win as Australia beat Scotland 38-31 in Canberra.
Chancellor and Smith, who was sent off after a second yellow card, were both chaired off by teammates at the end of the game.
What's next?
The Wallaroos have no more games until their new full-time program next year under new coach Sione Fukofuka.
The Wallaroos have completed their three-game Scottish sweep in a spicy Canberra contest that featured biting accusations and a string of yellow cards.
Australia produced plenty of classy moments in Friday night's 38-31 win but again lacked discipline in tackles and around the ruck to keep the tourists in it.
The hosts copped four yellow cards, retiring centre Cecilia Smith earning two of those to finish her 34-Test career on a red.
Scotland had two players sin-binned and it could have been far uglier if Wallaroos centre Georgina Friedrichs's accusations of biting had been verified on review.
But the officials saw no evidence and there were no bite marks on Friedrich's forearm, so the referee waved the complaints away.
Fifty-game prop Eva Karpani was yellow-carded for a high shot in her milestone game, while impressive flyhalf Waiaria Ellis was marched for slowing down a Scottish charge late in the first half.
The win came as a relief for retiring pair Emily Chancellor and Smith, with the latter smiling as she received a standing ovation after being sent off.
"I'm really sorry about that, just wanted to go out with a bang I guess," Smith said as she embraced her daughter Ruby post-match.
Loading Twitter content
"She's been there since day one [of Smith's Wallaroos career].
"Having her there at trainings, camps, on the sideline, means so much and I just want to be that role model and show you can do anything if you put your mind to it and the hard work in."
A teary Chancellor, former captain and two-time World Cup member, signed off with a win in her 42nd Test after debuting in 2018.
"It's created so much opportunity for me, so much purpose in my life. I love these girls and what we play for," she said.
"I love what this game has given us: travel the world with great people and create opportunity. You can't be what you can't see."
Victory for Australia followed wins in Sydney and Edinburgh against the same opponents, the side now out of action until the Wallaroos program transitions to a full-time operation next year under new coach Sione Fukofuka.
The hosts led 14-0 early but trailed 17-14 at half-time after a string of penalties led to three successive Scottish tries.
The Wallaroos regained the ascendancy and surged back ahead 38-24 when captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona finished a long-range effort.
But Karpani and then Smith were marched, keeping Scotland interested until the final play, but they were unable to find the match-tying converted try.

Typhoon Champi hits Taiwan, killing one and injuring hundreds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:10:54 UTC
08:10:54 KST

Typhoon Champi hits Taiwan, killing one and injuring hundreds
Authorities warn of ‘destructive winds’ and urge residents to shelter as the storm passes the island’s northeast.
Typhoon Champi has struck Taiwan, killing one person and injuring more than 500 others, as authorities warned of “destructive winds” and instructed people to stay indoors.
The storm swept past the island’s northeast on Friday, toppling trees, triggering brief flooding, disrupting power lines and forcing more than 5,000 people to evacuate from their homes.
Emergency crews were sent on Saturday to restore power to about 56,000 households still without electricity, authorities said. Most shops in northern and central Taiwan stayed shut for a second day as the storm edged away from the northeast and headed north.
Champi is heading towards China and Japan, forcing flight cancellations in the region.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Transportation and Communications said 259 flights were cancelled, an improvement from Friday, when the number was almost 1,000.
Champi was briefly a super typhoon with winds of nearly 300 kilometres per hour (186 miles per hour) but has since weakened. The US Joint Typhoon Warning Center on Friday reported maximum winds of 185km/h (115mph).
Worse is still expected to come on Saturday. Champi could drop up to 900mm (35 inches) of rain between Thursday and Saturday, with the northeast hit hardest, Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA) said. More than 400mm fell in Yilan County on Friday.
The forecaster also said the storm weakened overnight as it looped off the city of Yilan, which has received 650mm of rain since Thursday.
CWA forecaster Lu Kuo-chen said the typhoon could slow near the island’s northeastern tip, prolonging its impact.
Residents reacted differently.
“It was most terrifying around midnight,” a retired teacher surnamed Lin told the Reuters news agency as he inspected downed banana trees in his garden in Yilan. “It was a sleepless night. I haven’t seen anything like this in many years.”
Taipei resident Thomas Wang, 70, said the storm felt like something out of the horror film “Poltergeist”.
Martha Wang, a 55-year-old secretary, told the AFP news agency that she feared being “blown away” as her scooter shook on a bridge in New Taipei City.
While William Yu, a 55-year-old librarian, told AFP that the storm “wasn’t any stronger than other typhoons”.
About 8,400 households in Japan’s Okinawa islands were without power on Friday afternoon, according to the Okinawa Electric Power Company. The government said two people were injured in the typhoon in Japan’s southernmost prefecture.
Champi is forecast to hover near Okinawa and then China’s eastern coast before turning northeast, towards mainland Japan.
Chinese authorities warned of “strong winds and heavy rain” as the typhoon approaches mainland China’s east coast, the state-run broadcaster reported. It said parts of Jiangsu, Shanghai and Zhejiang could see heavy to torrential rain.
Some train services were suspended and tens of thousands of people evacuated in Shanghai.
El Nino weather event
Champi is the latest storm in a Pacific season supercharged by El Nino.
The United Nations said on Wednesday that El Nino, a natural cycle that warms the tropical Pacific, is heading off the charts.
“The current El Nino event could be unprecedented in strength. Literally off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades,” said Celeste Saulo, secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization.
It is expected to peak in December, with its impact lasting into 2027 and beyond.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

Saadet Gökce
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Pakistan has completed the ratification processes for the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told a news conference on Friday.
The defense agreement reflects Pakistan, Türkiye, and Saudi Arabia’s shared commitment to strengthening collective defense and cooperation for regional security and stability, he said, according to a transcript.
"Matters related to the agreement, its ratification, and operationalization remain under discussion by the three parties including in the Strategic Political and Defense Committee whose recent meeting was held on 5 October," said Khan, adding that each country follows its own constitutional and legal procedures for the approval and ratification of international agreements.
Saudi Arabia has also completed its ratification processes, he said.
Islamabad "remains fully committed to the letter and spirit of the agreement, which is defensive in nature, consistent with the UN Charter, and aimed at promoting regional peace, security and stability," Khan added.
The agreement reflects Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia's commitments to developing regional solutions to regional problems and their shared strategic vision focused on regional security and stability.
It aims to strengthen the three countries' security through collective deterrence and defense.
On Aug. 7, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman signed the agreement in Mecca.

US quietly moves diplomats and families across Middle East as fears of wider war grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:04:54 UTC
08:04:54 KST

The United States is quietly relocating some diplomats and their family members from posts across the Middle East amid growing concerns that the escalating conflict involving Iran-backed Houthi rebels could spread across the region, CNN reported, citing multiple sources familiar with the moves.
The State Department this week ordered non-emergency personnel and all family members to leave Saudi Arabia, citing the recent escalation in Houthi attacks. At the same time, Washington has been making less-publicized staffing adjustments at embassies in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Lebanon.
Unlike the formal departure order issued for Saudi Arabia, the changes at those six embassies have not been publicly announced. The State Department maintains that their operational designations remain unchanged and that they continue to operate under "restricted operations" status, which allows staffing adjustments without a formal change in embassy status.
The moves come as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensify, prompting repeated State Department warnings that the hostilities "have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area."
Tensions have also risen following President Donald Trump's suggestions that the United States could resume military strikes against Iran after the November midterm elections. Israel, meanwhile, has reportedly pressed Washington to take military action sooner, although those efforts have so far been unsuccessful, according to sources familiar with the discussions.
Diplomats describe chaotic departures and mounting frustration
For many American diplomatic families, the latest relocation instructions have brought back painful memories of the earlier stages of the war with Iran. Some had only recently returned to their overseas assignments after being evacuated earlier this year, forcing them to find temporary housing and arrange schooling for their children.
Now, those families face another round of upheaval, with some reporting that the financial assistance available to them is less generous than during their previous departures.
"To say it has been chaotic is an understatement," one U.S. diplomat said, explaining that the assistance offered so far does not cover the full cost of relocating an entire family.
Nikki Gamer, spokesperson for the American Foreign Service Association (AFSA), which represents U.S. foreign service officers, said the repeated disruptions were taking a significant toll.
"This echoes the chaos families experienced earlier this year. Some had barely settled back in before being told to leave again," Gamer said. "They are understandably upset, confused, and angry."
Not every embassy had permitted children to return following the earlier evacuations, although most had allowed spouses to rejoin personnel stationed abroad. Now, even those family members who recently returned are being told to leave again.
One source in the Jordanian capital described the atmosphere as eerily familiar. "There’s a very Groundhog Day vibe," the source said, referring to personnel being asked to leave Amman once more.
Families uncertain whether Washington will cover relocation costs
The latest departures have also prompted complaints about poor coordination between State Department headquarters in Washington and diplomatic personnel serving abroad.
One person familiar with the arrangements described communication between officials in Washington and embassies overseas as "just as much of a shit show" as during the early stages of the Iran war.
Some personnel have expressed concern that the department may not provide their families with daily living allowances, commonly known as per diem, to cover accommodation and other expenses after returning to the United States.
The source said several embassies had not held the planning meetings or staff briefings that would normally precede such departures, leaving employees and their families uncertain about the next steps.
"A lot of people are hearing about it through the news instead of their leadership at post," the source added.
AFSA has also raised concerns about the handling of the process, describing reports "of bureaucratic ping-pong."
In a statement Thursday, the association criticized the lack of clarity surrounding financial assistance for families being asked to leave their posts for a second time.
"Families that had barely returned to their posts and re-enrolled their children in school are being told to prepare to evacuate again without being advised as to what level of financial support they can count on," the association said.
According to Gamer, the uncertainty is particularly acute at embassies where no formal change in operating status has been announced.
"families outside Saudi Arabia have told AFSA they are being directed to leave without confirmed housing assistance or per diem."
She said families had been told that the uncertainty surrounding their benefits was linked to the fact that their embassies remained under the existing restricted-operations designation.
For diplomatic households suddenly forced to relocate, such allowances can be essential to securing temporary accommodation, especially when the employee must remain behind to carry out critical embassy duties.
"Families deserve to know how they will pay for a place to live before they board a plane," Gamer said.
