====================================================================================================

American Jews fly to West Bank to help Palestinian olive harvesters amid settler attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:43:43 UTC
07:43:43 KST

The thud of a body hitting the ground startled the group. "Oh, Jerry, what happened?" the volunteers called out in English as they rushed toward an elderly man sprawled across a black plastic sheet, trying to assess the damage after falling from a ladder.
"I'm fine," he groaned, also in English, before getting to his feet with a smile and some help from his companions. "An accident while picking olives. That's a first for me." Satisfied that he was unharmed, the others picked up their small plastic rakes and returned to work.
The scene unfolded in a modest olive grove of just a few dozen trees in Jalud, a Palestinian village near Nablus in the northern West Bank. The village is surrounded by 13 Israeli settlement outposts. Its residents own approximately 23,000 dunams, or 5,700 acres, of agricultural land, most of it planted with olive trees. But fear of attacks by violent settlers prevents them from reaching much of it.
"Because of the fear, we only harvest the olives inside the village, between the houses," said Riyad Haj Mohammed Abu Amr, head of the village council. "Even inside the village, we're not safe. Just yesterday, settlers came and threw stones at our elementary school. The children were terrified and crying. You can't imagine how frightening it was."
Standing in the grove, less than 100 meters from the school building, with nearby settlement outposts visible in the distance, Rabbi Toba Spitzer described the fear she and her fellow volunteers experienced when they first arrived.
"It was our second day picking olives," said Spitzer, 63, who leads Congregation Dorshei Tzedek in Newton, Massachusetts, outside Boston. "We had only arrived in Israel on Friday, and before Shabbat our families back home started sending worried messages asking whether we were all right."
The concern followed the attack on Heidi Levine, a photographer working for The Washington Post, who was beaten by Israeli settlers while covering the Palestinian olive harvest. Footage of the assault circulated widely across American news outlets.
"Our families thought that if someone could attack a Washington Post photographer who had come to document Palestinians harvesting olives, who knew what might have happened to us?" Spitzer said. "We weren't there to take photographs. We had actually come to harvest. We reassured them that we hadn't gone into the fields yet and wouldn't begin until Sunday."
The following day, around noon, the group heard screams from the village.
"People were shouting, 'The settlers are attacking the school,' and we didn't know what to do. We were in the middle of our work and, of course, we were very frightened. We know that if settlers come into the village and see us, they won't spare us."
Then she offered a dose of humor.
"They say we're anarchists who came here to provoke people. Look at me. I'm 63. Another woman in our group, Sue, is 82, and Jo is 80. We're very, very frightening. I wouldn't advise anyone to cross our path," she laughed. "I'm joking, of course. Heaven forbid someone takes that seriously."
Hundreds of Jews travel to the West Bank to help Palestinian farmers
Every day during the current olive harvest, Israeli volunteers travel to Palestinian communities to help residents pick their crops. Their presence does not necessarily prevent violent settler attacks, and sometimes the volunteers themselves become targets. Still, for farmers who are afraid to enter their fields alone, even a small sense of security can make a difference.
The Israeli human rights organization Yesh Din documented 640 incidents of violence involving settlers and soldiers against Palestinian residents during the first 24 days of the harvest, an average of 26.7 incidents a day, across 189 West Bank communities. Of those, 316 were directly connected to the olive harvest, averaging 13.2 incidents daily.
Against that backdrop, it is hardly surprising that many Palestinian farmers are reluctant to harvest their trees without accompaniment.
Alongside the Israelis are several hundred volunteers from abroad, most of them Jews from communities in the United States and Britain. Like Spitzer, many say they could no longer remain at home watching the disturbing images emerging from the West Bank.
Their motivation goes beyond the basic humanitarian desire to help people in distress. For many, including committed Zionists, it reflects a profound concern about Israel's future and the direction in which the country is heading.
Under the olive trees, with the possibility of another settler attack never far from their minds, the volunteers explained why they felt compelled to come now, just days before Israel's October 27 election. Its outcome, they believe, will affect not only Jews living in Israel but Jewish communities around the world.
Newton, where Spitzer lives, is a prosperous Boston suburb known for its expensive homes, strong schools, parks and gardens. For its residents, there is little obvious reason to leave the comfort of their surroundings to spend days harvesting olives in one of the West Bank's most volatile areas.
"It's a place with many different Jewish communities," Spitzer explained. "Our congregation, for example, has 270 households. These are people for whom Israel is a meaningful part of their Jewish identity. Israel matters to them in the deepest, most fundamental way. We have family and friends here."
"Our community follows the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. We understand the fears of Israelis living here. Those fears aren't imaginary. They are real and justified. But we also care about human rights, whoever the person may be."
She said the images emerging from the West Bank convinced the group that they needed to witness the situation firsthand.
"This is the first time any of us has harvested olives in a Palestinian village in the West Bank. After just two days here, I can tell you that I don't think American Jews understand the scale of settler violence, how widespread it is, how it happens every day and how severe it has become."
"And it's not just American Jews who don't understand what's happening. I think most Israelis don't know what's going on here either, barely an hour from Tel Aviv."
‘We're here for the soul of the Jewish people’
Some members of the group asked that the location of their accommodation in Israel not be published. Others agreed to speak only if their names were withheld. Their concern was not about criticism from their communities back home, but about possible action by Israeli authorities.
Since the beginning of 2026, Israel has deported 54 foreign nationals, many of them Jews, who came to participate in solidarity activities with Palestinians in the West Bank. The authorities have also halted the immigration processes of two young people following their participation in protective-presence activities in Palestinian communities.
Spitzer, however, refuses to be intimidated.
"I would be deeply saddened if they decided to deport me or take away my right to visit Israel in the future because of this activity," she said. "What we're doing here isn't against the Israeli establishment. It's not against anyone or anything. It's an act of human solidarity. We're here for the soul of the Jewish people."
She pointed to the case of Lila Stillman-Utterback, the daughter of her friend Danielle, who was detained and had her passport confiscated before being deported.
"She was banned from entering Israel for 10 years. She grew up in America loving Israel. She came here to promote coexistence, to show Palestinians that there is also a Judaism that brings goodness into the world, that cares about basic human rights. She paid a heavy price for it."
By lunchtime, the volunteers had settled beneath the olive trees in Jalud to eat. One of them agreed to speak on the condition that only his first name be published.
"The reason is simple. I want to be able to return to Israel in the near future," he said. "My wife has relatives here, and I have friends here. We're both retired, and we love visiting Israel."
His name is Mitchell. At 78, he is a retired philosophy professor from a major university in Massachusetts, and he is deeply troubled by what he sees happening in Israel.
"We didn't have to come here," he said. "But when you see the horrors taking place here, you can't just sit at home and do nothing, even when you live across the ocean."
"I care about Israel. I care about the Jewish people. I'm part of that people. That's why I came here and not to Sudan, where terrible things are also happening."
What frightens him most, he said, is the damage Israel may be inflicting on itself.
"I'm very afraid because it seems you've set a mechanism of self-destruction in motion without understanding the disastrous consequences it could bring."
"How do you think what's happening here looks in the United States? It's shameful, truly shameful. American media outlets can't understand how something like this can happen, how the Israeli military and government allow masked Jewish extremists to attack women and elderly people with clubs, burn Palestinian homes and property, without being arrested or anyone trying to stop them."
He said the violence and the response of the authorities were beginning to shape how Americans viewed Israel.
"In mainstream American media, they ask, 'How can this happen?' And commentators answer, 'Because this is the policy of the Israeli government.'"
"That makes me deeply anxious about Israel's future. You're approaching a crucial election. But it's not crucial only for Israelis. It's crucial for me as an American Jew, too."
"If the outcome is that the same government remains in power, more and more Americans will ask whether Israel is truly an ally of the United States, whether we share the same values and whether maintaining such strong ties with Israel is really in America's interest."
His concern, he stressed, goes far beyond politics.
"Israel is an idea. Every Jew in the world has a meaningful and profound connection to this place."
When helping farmers is treated as a provocation
As the school day ended in Jalud, children ran into the olive grove and wandered among the elderly volunteers.
"They're not used to seeing Jews coming here to help us," one village resident said. "There have been four attacks on our village in the past week alone."
One of the most striking aspects of the situation is the way humanitarian activities of this kind are increasingly portrayed as provocations intended to disturb public order.
Against the backdrop of violence by extremist settlers, the foreign Jews and Israelis helping Palestinian farmers are sometimes treated as anarchists and lawbreakers who should be detained and removed. It represents a profound reversal of how acts of solidarity are understood.
The only Israeli lawmaker encountered in the fields on Tuesday was Gilad Kariv of the Democrats, an opposition party.
While fellow Knesset member Zvi Sukkot has visited Palestinian villages under military and parliamentary security escort, including during incidents in which he smashed memorials, Kariv was moving around the West Bank alone, without protection.
"Two days ago, I informed the Knesset Guard that I intended to visit Sinjil and Suwaya to see how the olive harvest was going," Kariv said.
"A few hours later, my contacts in those villages called and begged me not to come. One of them told me, 'The army came to us and said that if an Israeli Knesset member visits, we won't allow you to harvest anymore.'"
"So today, I went into the area without informing anyone."
Anton Goodman, acting CEO of Rabbis for Human Rights, said his organization was in contact with Jewish communities around the world and repeatedly encountered the same questions.
"People ask us, 'What's happened to you over there? Have you lost your minds? What kind of Judaism is this?'"
"What they see in the photographs and videos are Jews wearing ritual fringes, sidelocks and large skullcaps doing terrible things. On Shabbat and religious holidays, they're driving vehicles, filming on their phones, burning homes and attacking people with clubs. They're imposing terror based on an ideology of Jewish supremacy."
Goodman said these images were prompting a growing number of Diaspora Jews to take action.
"We're seeing an awakening among Jews abroad who simply cannot bear to watch these scenes any longer and stand aside. They're willing to buy plane tickets with their own money, come here and put themselves at risk to help Palestinians."
Kariv described the volunteers' work as a Jewish and Zionist act reflecting deep concern for Israel, its future and its character.
"I hope more and more Israelis and Jews from around the world join activities like these," he said.
He also promised that if an alternative government emerged from the coming election, it would do everything possible to stop violence by Jewish extremists.
‘Iran isn't Israel's greatest danger’
The visit ended beneath Spitzer's olive tree. We held the ladder as she stood above us, working a small plastic rake through the branches to knock the olives loose.
After several days in the West Bank, she said, her understanding of the threats facing Israel had changed.
"I've come to realize that Iran isn't Israel's greatest danger," she said. "It's the brutal violence of settlers against Palestinians in the West Bank. That's the greatest danger facing Israel today."
"If you don't put an end to it, if you don't make a determined effort to stop it through real action, Israel will become internationally isolated. It will turn into a Jewish ghetto."
Dozens detained during olive harvest, including US congressional candidate
The following day, Wednesday, Israeli security forces detained 42 American and Canadian Jews who had joined 28 Israeli activists from Rabbis for Human Rights to harvest olives in Nahalin, a Palestinian village south of Bethlehem.
The official explanation was that the group had entered agricultural land for harvesting without prior coordination or authorization from the IDF.
The volunteers were taken by bus to a police station in the Israeli settlement of Beitar Illit. Among those detained was Brad Lander, the Democratic nominee for New York's 10th Congressional District in the U.S. midterm elections scheduled for early November.
After a lengthy day at the police station, the 28 Israeli activists were barred from entering the West Bank for periods ranging from 15 to 30 days.
Thirty-eight foreign nationals, most of them Americans, were released without conditions. Four Americans were questioned on suspicion of supporting a terrorist organization before being released under orders prohibiting them from entering the West Bank for 15 days.
For the activists, the incident underscored the risks of an effort they regard as a basic expression of Jewish solidarity and a moral obligation toward Palestinian farmers.
"What happened in Nahalin was simply madness," Goodman said. "We are determined to continue showing solidarity with Palestinian farmers throughout the olive harvest."

Kenya announces second Ebola death, says ‘no evidence’ of community spread
Kenya has announced its second Ebola death, as the virus outbreak spreads from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to several parts of Africa.
The Kenyan Ministry of Health said on Friday that the latest death was that of a 65-year-old woman who had developed symptoms during quarantine and was a close relative of a Kenyan man who died of Ebola earlier this month.
The ministry added that Kenya currently has seven Ebola cases receiving treatment at two isolation facilities.
All the cases are within “one cluster, with no evidence of community spread”, it added.
Kenya’s first Ebola case was identified this month in a man who travelled from DRC to Kenya and died at a Nairobi hospital on October 5.
Since then, Kenyan authorities have traced 135 contacts, all of whom were placed in quarantine, with nine cases confirmed, including the two patients who died.
African outbreak
The DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak in May and has since reported more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,600 deaths. The deadly disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
The current outbreak has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central and western Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
On Tuesday, Nigeria became the fourth African country to report an Ebola case. Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said on Friday that an analysis showed the case was closely related to the virus detected in the index case in Kenya.
Uganda announced on Saturday that travellers with a history of travel to DRC would not be permitted to transit through the East African nation.
Uganda had recorded 20 people infected, almost all of whom had travelled from DRC, and two deaths before being declared Ebola-free in August.

Final Israel election polls put Eisenkot's Yashar ahead of Likud, but neither bloc wins a majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:29:16 UTC
07:29:16 KST

Israel's final television election polls have delivered a clear but politically complicated verdict: former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party is ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud, yet neither the opposition nor Netanyahu's allies are projected to secure the 61 seats needed to form a government.
The three surveys, published Friday by Kan 11, Channel 12 and Channel 13 ahead of Tuesday's October 27 election, give the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu a lead of between two and six seats. With about 7.3 million Israelis eligible to vote, the results point to another potentially difficult round of coalition negotiations, and possibly even another election if no governing majority emerges.
All three networks project Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc winning exactly 50 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the opposition's so-called change bloc receives between 52 and 56 seats. The Arab parties, which are not counted as part of either bloc, are projected to win between 14 and 16 seats.
How the political blocs are divided
Kan 11 projects 52 seats for the opposition bloc and 50 for Netanyahu's allies. The Arab parties receive another 14 seats, while the Reservists-Economic Party, led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, wins four seats that are not assigned to either major bloc.
Channel 12 gives the opposition its strongest showing, with 56 seats compared with 50 for Netanyahu's bloc. The Arab parties receive 14 seats.
Channel 13 predicts a narrower opposition advantage of 54 seats to 50, with the Arab parties winning 16 seats.
The figures highlight the central challenge facing both camps. While the opposition leads in all three surveys, it remains short of a majority without additional parliamentary support. The Arab parties could therefore become pivotal, although their projected strength does not automatically translate into support for an opposition-led government.
Eisenkot, a former IDF chief of staff, emerges as the leader of the largest party in all three polls. Yashar wins 22 seats in the Kan 11 survey, 23 in Channel 12 and 22 in Channel 13.
Likud follows with 20, 21 and 19 seats, respectively, while former prime minister Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad, or Together, comes third with 14, 15 and 14 seats.
The electoral threshold could decide the outcome
Beyond the rivalry between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, one of the biggest uncertainties concerns smaller parties struggling to cross Israel's 3.25% electoral threshold, the minimum share of valid votes required to enter the Knesset.
Former IDF general Ofer Winter's People of Israel party, known in Hebrew as Amcha Yisrael, falls below the threshold in all three surveys. It receives 2.9% in Kan 11's poll, 2.5% in Channel 12's and 3.1% in Channel 13's, coming closest to entering parliament in the latter survey.
The joint Reservists-Economic Party, headed by former minister Yoaz Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha, faces a similarly uncertain future. While Kan 11 projects it winning four seats, Channel 12 puts its support at just 2.4% and Channel 13 at 3.0%, both below the threshold.
The Haredi Public party, led by Moti Leitner and seeking support among ultra-Orthodox voters, also remains well below the cutoff, receiving between 0.5% and 1.3% across the three polls.
The consequences could be substantial. Votes cast for parties that fail to cross the threshold do not translate into parliamentary representation. Depending on which parties fall short, the resulting redistribution of seats among those that qualify could alter the balance between the rival political camps.
The poll of polls: Eisenkot leads with 22 seats
A combined picture based on the three television polls places Eisenkot's Yashar first with 22 seats, followed by Netanyahu's Likud with 20 and Bennett's B'Yachad with 15.
The Democrats, led by Yair Golan, and the Arab-majority Joint List, headed by Yousef Jabareen, each receive nine seats in the published composite.
Three parties receive eight seats apiece: Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu, Itamar Ben Gvir's Otzma Yehudit and United Torah Judaism, led by Yaakov Asher.
Aryeh Deri's Shas and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism-Zehut alliance each receive seven seats, while Ra'am, the Arab party led by Mansour Abbas, receives six.
Winter's People of Israel and Hendel and Zelekha's Reservists-Economic Party both fall below the threshold in the overall assessment, although the latter retains a residual average of approximately one seat because it crosses the threshold in one of the three surveys. That statistical remainder does not mean the party is projected to enter parliament.
The complete results from the three television polls
Kan 11 poll
Yashar: 22 seats; Likud: 20; B'Yachad: 14; Joint List: 9; Democrats: 8; Otzma Yehudit: 8; Yisrael Beytenu: 8; United Torah Judaism: 8; Shas: 7; Religious Zionism-Zehut: 7; Ra'am: 5; Reservists-Economic Party: 4.
Below the electoral threshold: People of Israel, 2.9%; Black Color, 0.8%; Haredi Public, 0.7%.
The survey was conducted by Kantar, headed by Dudi Hasid, among 1,006 respondents, with a reported sampling margin of error of 3 percentage points.
Channel 12 poll
Yashar: 23 seats; Likud: 21; B'Yachad: 15; Democrats: 10; Joint List: 9; Shas: 8; Yisrael Beytenu: 8; Otzma Yehudit: 8; United Torah Judaism: 7; Religious Zionism-Zehut: 6; Ra'am: 5.
Below the electoral threshold: People of Israel, 2.5%; Reservists-Economic Party, 2.4%; Haredi Public, 0.5%.
The survey was conducted by the Midgam polling institute, headed by Mano Geva, in cooperation with iPanel. It included 1,018 respondents and had a reported sampling margin of error of 4.4 percentage points.
Channel 13 poll
Yashar: 22 seats; Likud: 19; B'Yachad: 14; Democrats: 10; Joint List: 9; United Torah Judaism: 8; Yisrael Beytenu: 8; Religious Zionism-Zehut: 8; Otzma Yehudit: 8; Shas: 7; Ra'am: 7.
Below the electoral threshold: People of Israel, 3.1%; Reservists-Economic Party, 3.0%; Haredi Public, 1.3%.
The survey was conducted by HaMadad, headed by Shmuel Rosner and Noah Slepkov, together with Stat-Net, the Midgam Project and Asakria, with additional data from Hive and statistical advice from Professor David Steinberg. It included 1,875 respondents and had a reported sampling margin of error of 2.3 percentage points.
Could Israel face another election?
The final surveys leave considerable uncertainty over Israel's next government, with both political camps facing obstacles to building a workable parliamentary majority.
The outcome could change significantly depending on voter turnout, particularly among supporters of smaller parties, and on how many votes ultimately go to lists that fail to enter parliament.
Last-minute shifts in voter preferences could also reshape the final distribution of seats, while party leaders may find themselves under pressure to reconsider commitments made during the campaign if coalition negotiations reach a deadlock.
For now, the three television polls show Eisenkot's party leading the race, but winning the largest number of seats is not the same as securing the premiership. The decisive question on October 27 will be not only which party finishes first, but which political leader can assemble the 61 lawmakers needed to govern.

Intervision was a song contest organized by the International Organization of Television and Radio Broadcasting (OIRT), which existed from 1946 to 1993. It was held in the 1960s-1980s, following the same model as "Eurovision," a music award of the European Broadcasting Union, which broke away from OIRT. The contest involved not only socialist countries close to the USSR, but also Austria, Belgium, Spain, Canada, the Netherlands, Portugal, and Finland.
The Intervision was revived in 2025 in Moscow. Russia was represented by Honored Artist of the Russian Federation Yaroslav Dronov (Shaman). More than 20 countries, including all BRICS states, took part.

Barack Obama’s Belfast speech was a shameful, distorted rewrite of Israel's history - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:14:01 UTC
07:14:01 KST

Barack Obama has apparently discovered a new historical crime: the Jewish people stole their own homeland.
That, at least, is the impression left by his latest attempt to rewrite Middle Eastern history.
Speaking in Belfast on October 13, the former American president managed to turn the Jewish people’s return to the Land of Israel into a story of persecuted European Jews who sought refuge, took Palestinian land, and provoked an understandable demand to get it back.
Never mind 3,000 years of Jewish history, two Temples in Jerusalem, or centuries of Jewish longing for Zion. In Obama’s telling, the Jews somehow became interlopers in the very land where their national story began.
“The Jewish people, for millennia, were oppressed, discriminated against, killed,” he said. They “understandably sought a refuge” but “took land off people, and they were excessive.” Palestinians, he added, “understandably said, ‘This is injustice, and I want my land back.’”
Former president Obama barely made an effort to explain the Jewish people’s ancient connection to the land
Obama made little effort to explain the Jewish people’s ancient connection to the land. Instead, he presented their return to their ancestral patrimony primarily as an act of injustice.
Let’s start with the most basic fact that Obama chose to downplay: the Jewish people are indigenous to the Land of Israel.
More than 3,000 years ago, the Israelites had already established themselves in the Land. By the 10th century BCE, they had formed a kingdom, developed their own language, and centered their national and religious life on Jerusalem. According to the biblical account, King David made the city his capital, and his son King Solomon built the First Temple there.
That is not a late European invention. It is a starting point of Jewish history.
The archaeological record provides striking evidence. The Tel Dan Stele, a ninth-century BCE stone monument discovered in northern Israel in 1993, contains an ancient Aramaic inscription referring to the “House of David.” It is the earliest known reference to David’s royal dynasty outside the Bible.
Hebrew inscriptions, Israelite seals, and the remains of ancient fortifications and settlements appear throughout the land.
After the Babylonian exile ended in 516 BCE, Jews returned and rebuilt the Temple.
Roman ruins, the Western Wall, coins from the Jewish revolts against Rome, and the Dead Sea Scrolls all attest to the Jewish people’s deep historical roots in the Land of Israel.
Even after the Romans destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE and suppressed the Bar-Kochba revolt, Jews never severed their connection to the land. Communities persisted in Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed, and Tiberias – the four holy cities. Jewish legal and religious life continued there.
For centuries, Jews prayed facing Jerusalem, invoked Zion in their daily prayers, and ended the Passover Seder with the words “Next year in Jerusalem.” The connection was not a modern recovery of ancient memory. It was never broken.
Nor did Zionism begin as a desperate European response to Hitler. The First Aliyah began in 1882, bringing thousands of Jewish pioneers back to the Land of Israel. And in 1897, Theodor Herzl convened the First Zionist Congress, decades before the Holocaust.
Jewish pioneers purchased land from Arab owners and built farms, towns, and thriving agricultural communities. To reduce this remarkable enterprise to simple theft, as the former president effectively did, is a gross distortion of history.
OBAMA SKIPPED the diplomatic record, too.
In 1917, Britain issued the Balfour Declaration endorsing a Jewish national home. Five years later, the League of Nations Mandate explicitly recognized “the historical connection of the Jewish people with Palestine” and the grounds for “reconstituting their national home” there.
The word “reconstituting” is important. The League of Nations was acknowledging the Jewish people’s preexisting connection to the land, not creating a new one.
Then came November 29, 1947.
The UN voted to partition British Mandatory Palestine into two states, one Jewish and one Arab. Jewish leaders accepted the plan. Arab leaders rejected it.
That refusal was hardly new. In 1937, Britain’s Peel Commission had also proposed partition. Zionist leaders accepted partition as a basis for further negotiations, while Arab leaders rejected it outright. A decade later, another chance for two states met much the same fate.
Violence followed, and when Israel declared independence on May 14, 1948, neighboring Arab armies invaded. The nascent Jewish state fought for its survival.
Israel’s Declaration of Independence even appealed to its Arab inhabitants to help build the new state as equal citizens and extended a hand of peace to neighboring countries. That hardly fits Obama’s account of a nation conceived simply as an instrument of dispossession.
The fact is that there was no sovereign Palestinian state that Israel overthrew in 1948. There was, however, an internationally proposed Arab state that the Arab leadership refused to accept.
Israel also absorbed hundreds of thousands of Jewish refugees driven from Arab lands after 1948. Yet while Israel integrated these refugees into its society, most Arab states refused to grant Palestinian refugees citizenship, leaving generations in a state of uncertainty.
And the rejection did not end in 1948. For nearly two decades, Jordan controlled Judea and Samaria and eastern Jerusalem, while Egypt administered Gaza. Neither established a Palestinian state.
Obama would have his audience believe that Palestinian rejectionism was simply a response to Jewish dispossession. But the historical record clearly tells a very different story.
Obama’s treatment of Palestinian violence
MORE DISTURBING still was Obama’s treatment of Palestinian violence.
Speaking about Hamas’s Oct. 7 massacre, Obama declared that “you could not have designed something that was less likely to produce meaningful change.”
Think about that.
When terrorists murder approximately 1,200 people and kidnap 251, the principal issue is not whether their actions will produce meaningful political change. It is that they committed an act of unimaginable barbarity.
By discussing the massacre in terms of its political effectiveness, Obama risks reducing a moral atrocity to a tactical mistake. Would the slaughter have been any less reprehensible had Hamas managed to advance its political objectives?
Indeed, no political claim, no matter how loudly asserted, confers a license to murder families in their homes or drag hostages into Gaza.
And terrorism did not begin with Israel’s founding, let alone the 1967 war. In 1929, Arab rioters murdered 67 Jews in Hebron, destroying an ancient Jewish community nearly two decades before independence.
WHAT OBAMA did in Belfast was more than distort Israel’s history. He turned the descendants of ancient Israel into trespassers in their own homeland, while treating the massacre of Jews as a failed political strategy.
Obama is, of course, entitled to his own opinions. But he is not entitled to his own version of history.
The Jewish people lived in the Land of Israel long before Barack Obama entered the world stage. And they will still be there long after his shameful revisionism has been forgotten.■
The writer served as deputy communications director under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The operation is focused on the area out of which the terrorists operated and is expected to last several days.
Residents living within the operational area will be permitted to leave through three designated exit points after undergoing questioning and security checks. Anyone who raises suspicion during the screening process will be taken for further questioning by security forces.

Security forces were also operating in Kafr Aqab in east Jerusalem and the West Bank town of Tamun, according to the report.
The operation follows a series of counterterrorism measures carried out since Friday morning, including mapping the terrorists' homes, sealing off the Hebron and Halhul areas, establishing roadblocks, and conducting operations in nearby villages. Security forces are also removing illegal infrastructure that could pose a security threat near the site of the attack.
Security forces are currently operating at dozens of locations throughout Judea and Samaria as part of ongoing efforts to prevent terrorist attacks, protect Israeli civilians, and eliminate security threats, the statement added.
Terrorists attacked IDF soldiers at Judea Junction
The attack took place at Judea Junction, where two terrorists traveling in a car opened fire on four soldiers stationed at the junction. IDF sources estimated that the attackers had originally intended to continue past the junction and carry out a larger attack on the heavily traveled Route 35, but opened fire after realizing they would be unable to proceed.
Staff Sergeant Ron Yonatan Roytman, 23, from Ashkelon, and Sergeant Yuval Shai Svilem, 20, from Hod Hasharon, were killed in the attack, while three others were lightly wounded.
Both terrorists were killed during the confrontation, and the IDF said no additional terrorists were involved.
Netanyahu orders closure of Hebron following attack
Following the attack, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered security forces to seal off Hebron and prepare for a broader lockdown across the West Bank.
"I have instructed the IDF and security forces to immediately impose a closure on the city of Hebron and prepare for a full lockdown of all of Judea and Samaria, beginning today," Netanyahu said, adding that the IDF would carry out extensive waves of arrests.

====================================================================================================

American Catholics reported a greater sense of meaning in life after Pope Leo XIV’s election, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:00:05 UTC
07:00:05 KST

The election of Pope Leo XIV in May 2025 was followed by a modest rise in the sense of meaning in life among a sample of practicing Roman Catholics in the United States, according to a study published in The Journal of Positive Psychology. Through the end of the study’s 10-day post-election window, participants reported a stronger sense that their lives had meaning, along with a gradual decline in their search for meaning. The pattern held after the researchers accounted for participants’ religious commitment and their feelings about the new pope sharing their American nationality.
In psychology, meaning in life refers to the subjective judgment that one’s existence is worthwhile, makes sense, and is guided by an overarching purpose. Psychologists break this concept down into three parts: having a motivational goal or purpose, feeling that life is coherent, and believing that one’s life matters. Rather than treating meaning as a single feeling, researchers distinguish between the presence of meaning and the search for meaning. As a 2006 validation study demonstrated, already feeling that one’s life has purpose is distinct from actively looking for something that makes life feel meaningful.
Religion is a major source of this sense of purpose for many people. For example, a 2005 study found that religious people tend to report greater well-being, largely because they feel their lives have purpose and direction. Similarly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2022 indicated that religious individuals tend to experience a stronger sense of meaning largely through feeling that they matter on a grand, cosmic scale.
Most psychological research on religion and meaning has examined steady, long-term beliefs rather than specific religious events. One of the most prominent rituals in the Roman Catholic tradition is the papal conclave, the secluded meeting of cardinals inside the Sistine Chapel to elect a new pope. Filled with symbolic traditions like burning ballots to send black or white smoke from a chimney and the Latin announcement of “Habemus Papam” (“We have a Pope”), the conclave is framed by the Church as a moment of divine guidance.
The research, led by Stefan Stieger of Karl Landsteiner University of Health Sciences in Austria, examined whether living through this major religious transition alters how Catholics experience meaning from day to day. The authors drew on three psychological frameworks to explain how a papal election might affect believers. Under the meaning-making model, the death of a pope may create a temporary spiritual void that disrupts a believer’s worldview, and electing a successor may help restore a sense of order and coherence.
Social identity theory offers a second perspective, suggesting that people derive self-worth from belonging to social groups; losing a leader can threaten that shared identity, whereas choosing a new leader may restore group unity. A third possibility involves emotional contagion, the tendency for feelings to spread rapidly across a crowd or through global media coverage. For instance, a 2024 field study of a public Hindu ritual found that participants who stood close to one another during the ceremony experienced synchronized emotional arousal, showing how collective religious practices can align feelings across a group.
To capture how the 2025 papal transition affected believers in real time, the researchers used an experience sampling method. Instead of asking people to recall their feelings weeks later, this technique prompts participants to answer short smartphone surveys during their normal daily routines, reducing memory biases. Beginning on May 3, 2025, four full days before the conclave started, the team tracked participants across 14 consecutive days covering the pre-conclave, conclave, and post-conclave phases.
The researchers recruited English-speaking United States citizens through the online platform Prolific who identified as practicing Roman Catholics. After excluding 17 individuals who did not identify as Roman Catholic, dropped out early, or provided inconsistent demographic data, the final sample consisted of 117 American Roman Catholics. Participants ranged in age from 19 to 76 years, with an average age of about 45, and were split nearly evenly between men (52.1 percent) and women (47.9 percent).
At the start of the study, participants installed an open-source smartphone app called ESMira and completed a baseline survey. On 1-to-100 scales, the group reported being fairly religious on average (72.7) and relatively balanced between conservative and progressive views in both their theological orientation (46.1) and political views (47.4). They also completed a 10-item questionnaire measuring both their private religious devotion and their involvement in their church community.
Every evening at 8:00 p.m. local time, the app prompted participants to complete an end-of-day survey assessing their current sense of meaning in life. Using a 7-point scale from 1 (absolutely untrue) to 7 (absolutely true), participants rated five statements about the presence of meaning (such as “At this moment, I understand my life’s meaning”) and five statements about the search for meaning (such as “At this moment, I am looking for something that makes my life feel meaningful”). Across the two-week window, the 117 participants completed 1,470 daily questionnaires.
When the cardinals elected Pope Leo XIV, an unexpected factor emerged: the new head of the Catholic Church was also from the United States. To help account for the possibility that any boost in meaning among the American participants was a byproduct of national pride, the researchers added a question to the final survey. Participants rated how much Pope Leo XIV’s American background influenced their feelings toward him on a scale from -4 (much more negative) to +4 (much more positive).
To analyze the daily ratings, the researchers divided the timeline into a four-day pre-conclave baseline, the conclave phase (from the first black smoke signal until the day before the election), and 10 post-conclave days starting with the day of the papal announcement. Using multilevel statistical models, they tracked daily changes within each individual while controlling for age, gender, personal and social religious commitment, and feelings about the pope’s American nationality.
Across the four pre-conclave baseline days, participants averaged 5.16 out of 7 on the presence of meaning and 4.34 out of 7 on the search for meaning. During the conclave itself and on the first day of the post-conclave phase (the day Pope Leo XIV was announced), neither dimension showed a notable shift from baseline, possibly because not all participants had heard the news before completing that first evening survey. Starting the day after the election, however, the presence of meaning rose above the pre-conclave baseline and stayed elevated through the final day of tracking.
On the 7-point scale, daily presence-of-meaning scores increased by 0.14 to 0.20 points above the 5.16 baseline on every day from Day 2 through Day 10, except for Day 8, when a 0.09-point increase was not statistically significant. Standardized effect sizes during this period ranged from 0.09 to 0.14, which the authors describe as small to medium; in raw terms, the increases amounted to roughly 3 to 4 percent of the baseline score.
At the same time, participants reported a gradual decline in their search for meaning, with statistically significant drops on Days 2, 7, 9, and 10. Compared to the 4.34 baseline, search-for-meaning scores fell by 0.23 points on Day 7, 0.34 points on Day 9, and 0.30 points on Day 10, with standardized effect sizes reaching -0.19 on Day 9 and -0.17 on Day 10. This pattern suggests that participants felt more settled in their sense of purpose and less driven to look for missing meaning.
These shifts held after the researchers accounted for age, gender, religious commitment, and feelings about the pope’s nationality. On average, participants viewed the pope’s American nationality positively (averaging 2.03 on the -4 to +4 scale), and those more active in church communities tended to feel warmer about it. However, the analysis adjusted for these factors rather than testing whether the post-election boost was larger or smaller for particular groups, so it cannot show whether less devout Catholics, or those less enthusiastic about an American pope, experienced the same shift.
The authors noted that their findings are compatible with all three psychological frameworks they examined. They suggest that emotional contagion from widespread media coverage may have contributed, and that because media excitement typically fades, the persistence of the effect, with the drop in searching for meaning strongest on Days 9 and 10, points to deeper social identity and meaning-making processes as well. They also acknowledge, however, that emotional contagion can sometimes last several days, so the line between these explanations is not sharp.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study does not appear to have been preregistered. Because it began just four days before the conclave, after the death of Pope Francis had already occurred, there is no way to know what the participants’ sense of meaning looked like before the papal vacancy began. The post-election increase in meaning might represent a genuine rise above their typical everyday levels, or a rebound back to normal after a temporary dip caused by the previous pope’s death.
In addition, the tracking period ended 10 days after the election, leaving open the question of how long the heightened sense of purpose lasted before leveling off. The study also focused solely on Roman Catholics in the United States and had no comparison group tracked over the same days, so it cannot rule out that scores would have drifted for other reasons, such as participants growing accustomed to answering the same questions each evening.
Because the new pope’s American nationality became known at the same moment as his election, the study also cannot fully separate a religious response from a patriotic one. Including people from other religious backgrounds exposed to the same news coverage would help future researchers separate media-driven emotional contagion from the spiritual effects of welcoming a new religious leader.
The study, “The election of Pope Leo XIV and its impact on the meaning of life for Roman Catholic Christians: A longitudinal experience sampling method study in the USA before, during, and after the pope’s election,” was authored by Stefan Stieger, Selina Volsa, and David Willinger.

Organized by China's Xinhua News Agency Africa Regional Bureau in partnership with several organizations, the event was held under the theme of "Remembering Taiwan's Restoration, Advancing National Reunification." The one-week exhibition features four thematic sections and more than 30 photos.
Guo Haiyan, Chinese Ambassador to Kenya, said the historical fact of Taiwan's restoration, together with international legal instruments, including the Cairo Declaration, the Potsdam Proclamation and the Japanese Instrument of Surrender, constitutes a key link in the historical and legal chain underwriting the one-China principle.
On Oct. 25, 1945, a ceremony to accept Japan's surrender in the Taiwan Province of the China war theater of the Allied powers was held in Taipei, and Taiwan, which had been under Japanese colonial rule for 50 years, was finally restored to China and returned to the embrace of the motherland, she said.
In 2025, the Standing Committee of China's National People's Congress designated Oct. 25 of each year as the "Commemoration Day of Taiwan's Restoration," she added.
Guo said that since the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries, Kenya has always abided by the one-China principle and properly handled Taiwan-related issues.
She noted that in the joint statement issued during Kenyan President William Ruto's state visit to China in April 2025, the Kenyan side "resolutely opposes any form of 'Taiwan independence' and supports all efforts by the Chinese government to achieve national reunification."
Erastus Mwencha, former deputy chairperson of the African Union Commission, said the restoration of Taiwan in 1945 marked the end of the Treaty of Shimonoseki of 1895 and a monumental moment of restored integrity for the Chinese nation. History is a living reminder of the sacrifices nations make in defense of their identity, freedom and dignity, he said.
Mwencha recalled that when the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758 in 1971, restoring the lawful rights of the People's Republic of China, 26 African nations voted in favor.
"Our relationship was not born out of mere commercial interest or diplomatic convenience; it was forged in the crucible of a common struggle against colonialism and foreign domination," he said, citing China's support for African liberation movements from the 1955 Bandung Conference to the construction of the TAZARA Railway.
Ying Qiang, director of Xinhua News Agency Africa Regional Bureau, said the exhibition is being held in five African countries -- Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa, Nigeria and Mozambique.
"It is a look back at an important chapter of history, an act of remembrance for the fruits of victory in the World Anti-Fascist War, and above all an affirmation of peace, justice and historical fact," said Ying.
Ying said that the photographs on display capture the historical moments of Taiwan's restoration and the course of the Chinese nation's resistance to foreign aggression, alongside the struggle for national liberation.
"Through these images, we hope our African friends will gain a more vivid understanding of the historical background, the historical facts and the historical significance of Taiwan's restoration, and a deeper appreciation of the firm position of the Chinese people in safeguarding national sovereignty and territorial integrity," Ying added. ■

Feature: More than a sweet -- Türkiye's lokma tradition offers comfort in grief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:56:00 CST
06:56:00 KST

ANKARA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Outside the historic Haci Bayram Mosque in Ankara, the capital of Türkiye, strangers reached for golden pieces of lokma, a traditional fried dough sweet soaked in syrup. For Adnan Kirbas, the treats carried a meaning far beyond their sweetness.
The retired Ankara resident had arranged for the sweets to be distributed to the public to mark the second anniversary of his mother's death. Each serving he handed to a stranger was a small tribute to the mother he still deeply missed.
"This is part of our tradition," Kirbas told Xinhua.
As the pastries passed from hand to hand, strangers became part of a family's act of remembrance. They offered prayers and blessings. Their kind words brought comfort to a son still seeking ways to honor his mother's memory.
Their prayers, Kirbas said, helped ease the grief of those mourning a loved one, reminding them that they did not have to bear their sorrow alone.
Fried dough sweets are enjoyed across the Mediterranean and the Middle East, while charitable food-sharing traditions take different forms across cultures. In Türkiye, this practice takes a distinctive form known as hayir lokmasi, or charity lokma, in which freshly prepared sweets are distributed free of charge to the public to honor deceased loved ones or mark joyful occasions, such as births and personal achievements.
Families typically hire a mobile lokma van, where a specialist prepares and fries batches of yeast-based dough on site, coats the golden pieces in light sugar syrup, and serves them on small disposable plates with toothpicks.
For Ankara shopkeeper Serkan Erdogan, the tradition carries a similar personal significance. The previous week, he had arranged for lokma to be distributed in memory of both his late father and his wife's late father.
Erdogan learned the custom from older generations and hopes his children will carry it on. Yet he worries that younger people are gradually drifting away from such traditions in an increasingly digital age.
"We are trying to pass certain things on to the younger generation, but we have not been very successful," he said.
His concern points to what is at stake beyond lokma itself: a tradition that draws people out of their private lives and encourages them to share with others.
Ismail Kadir Aran, a lokma maker who began learning the family trade at the age of 13, summed it up simply: "People want to share their happiness and their sadness with others. That is why they offer these treats."
The sweets soon disappear. But the remembrance, shared among hundreds of strangers, lingers a little longer. ■

Palestinian sources said Israeli forces demolished a building containing three apartments in the Farsh al-Hawa area west of Hebron, each covering about 200 square meters.
Local sources said Israeli forces closed Hebron and its main entrances, preventing residents and vehicles from entering or leaving. Roads linking the city to nearby areas were also closed.
Palestinian security sources said Israeli forces tightened restrictions at entrances and exits to cities across the West Bank, and closed many checkpoints and iron gates in the southern, central and northern areas.
Hebron is a major economic center in the West Bank. The closure of its entrances has disrupted daily life in the area, which is home to more than one million Palestinians, according to Israeli reports. ■

The UK and Oman agreed to deepen cooperation in defense, trade, investment, green industries, and emerging technologies during Omani Sultan Haitham bin Tarik’s state visit to the UK, according to a joint statement on Friday.
It said Britain and the Gulf state reaffirmed their longstanding friendship and committed to building an “ambitious, forward-looking partnership” during the sultan’s three-day visit this week as a guest of King Charles III.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Sultan Haitham on Wednesday discussed cooperation priorities at 10 Downing Street, including modernizing defense and security ties, expanding investment in advanced industries, addressing regional and global challenges, and strengthening institutional and people-to-people relations.

A new Sovereign Partnership for Cooperation and Promotion of Investment will support cooperation in green growth, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, space, advanced technologies, and industrial development, while strengthening links between the UK’s Office for Investment and the Oman Investment Authority.
Both countries also reaffirmed their commitment to decarbonization and sustainable economic growth.

UK Export Finance increased its country limit for Oman by £1.6 billion ($2.1 billion), bringing its capacity to £7 billion to support British exports to the sultanate.
The statement also welcomed an agreement between the UK Space Agency and Oman’s National Space Program to share expertise, explore potential cooperation on space launches, and promote commercial partnerships.
The two countries pledged to monitor progress on agreed priorities, aligning cooperation with Oman’s Vision 2040 and the UK’s growth agenda, while pursuing shared goals of security, prosperity, and resilience.

Israeli army announces drills simulating surprise attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:38:36 UTC
06:38:36 KST

Said Amori, Rania Abushamala
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
The Israeli army announced Friday that it will hold large-scale military exercises in northern and central Israel on Sunday and Monday, simulating surprise attacks and aerial and ground infiltrations ahead of Tuesday’s parliamentary elections.
The army said in a statement that the drills aim to test and improve its readiness to defend multiple fronts and prepare for possible military escalation along the borders.
The exercises will involve the air force and several military divisions, including the Northern Command’s 210th Division, the West Bank Division and the Central Command’s 98th and 96th divisions, according to the statement.
Troops will practice scenarios, including surprise attacks and infiltrations into Israeli territory by air and land. Increased movements of security forces and aircraft are expected in the areas involved.
The army said the exercises are part of its annual training plan for 2026 and an ongoing effort to improve military proficiency and readiness, stressing that there were no concerns about a security incident.
Although the drills will take place immediately before the elections, the army did not link the two events.
Israeli Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir announced Monday that military readiness would be raised to its highest level, soldiers’ leave restricted starting Thursday and troop deployments in the West Bank reinforced to ensure the elections take place safely and on schedule.
Despite the army’s assurances that the exercises were scheduled in advance, warnings about possible attacks, heightened military readiness and restrictions on soldiers’ leave could give security greater prominence in public debate ahead of the vote. The statements announced no specific imminent threat.
A poll published Friday by the Maariv newspaper projected that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc would win 48 seats, down three from the newspaper’s poll a week earlier, compared with 54 for the Jewish opposition bloc.
Neither bloc would secure the 61 seats required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
The poll projected 19 seats for Netanyahu’s Likud, seven for Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power, seven for United Torah Judaism, eight for Shas and seven for Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party.
Within the Jewish opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party was projected to win 21 seats, followed by Naftali Bennett’s Together party with 15, Yair Golan’s Democrats with 10 and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu with eight.

French opposition challenges protest restrictions as 70,000 officers mobilized for Saturday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:33:32 UTC
06:33:32 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
French left-wing and green parties filed an emergency appeal on Friday against restrictions on demonstrations, as authorities prepared to deploy 70,000 police officers and gendarmes nationwide Saturday, according to media reports.
The Ecologists, France Unbowed (LFI), the Socialist Party, the Communist Party, and several other political groups filed the joint challenge with the Council of State, Le Parisien daily reported.
The parties challenged President Emmanuel Macron’s instructions concerning bans on demonstrations organized by groups he considers illegitimate and changes to union march routes without individual assessments.
The appeal comes amid mounting tensions about security measures introduced after violence and looting during last weekend’s demonstrations.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said Saturday’s deployment would include local police and mobile units, supported by helicopters, armored vehicles, and water cannons. Some officers have been recalled from leave.
Nunez said authorities had identified online calls for looting and attacks on public buildings, including from radical far-left groups, and pledged firm action against those responsible for violence. 
Up to half a million could take part in demonstrations
Some 400,000-500,000 people are expected to demonstrate, according to a territorial intelligence assessment cited by the newspaper.
High school student representatives urged continued protests after meeting Macron at the Elysee Palace on Friday.
“We are calling for continued mobilization,” said Nathanael Combary, the head of Renouveau Lyceen.
He said the meeting created an opening that protesters needed to seize to achieve concrete progress. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is scheduled to meet student organizations on Monday.
In Paris, unions rejected a police proposal to move Saturday’s procession from the previously agreed Bastille-Nation route to one between Porte de Vincennes and Porte d’Italie.
Organizers said they would gather at the Bastille as planned, arguing they could not secure the alternative route.
Authorities also approved aerial surveillance in Paris and prohibited leaving furniture or materials on public roads that could be used as weapons or barricades. The overnight curfew around Place de la Republique and Les Halles was extended until Monday morning. 
Restrictions
In Limoges, restrictions set to last through Monday include a curfew in designated areas and a ban on gatherings of more than 10 people within a specified perimeter.
Other restrictions affect central areas of Lyon – France’s third-largest city by population – as well as Besancon, Clermont-Ferrand, and Laval. In Marseille – the second-largest – authorities approved a union-organized march as an exception to broader restrictions.
Several museums and cultural venues in Paris and Lyon announced closures for Saturday. A Paris Saint-Germain-Lyon football match was postponed from Sunday to Monday due to demands on police resources.
In Orleans, 3,000 police officers and gendarmes will be deployed during the weekend as the far-right National Rally holds its congress and opponents stage a counter-demonstration.
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said 232 people had been incarcerated following last weekend’s violence, while more than 1,000 were brought before judicial authorities.

China unveils space governance paper prioritizing preventing arms race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:29:45 UTC
06:29:45 KST

Saadet Gökce
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
China on Friday unveiled a position paper on strengthening outer space governance, prioritizing efforts to prevent an arms race in space.
"The achievements of outer space exploration should benefit all countries," said the paper, warning that the existing international legal framework for outer space lags behind rapid advances in space science and technology and their widespread applications.
"The risk of an arms race in outer space and the trend of turning outer space into a new theater of conflict have become the gravest threat and challenge to space security," it said. "Strengthening global space governance is an urgent issue for humanity and the shared responsibility of all States."
China advocates that countries take the common values of humanity as their fundamental guide, uphold sovereign equality, abide by international law, practice multilateralism, and pursue a people-centered, action-oriented approach, said the paper.
It also urged a balanced approach to outer space development and security, as well as stability and sustainability, with the aim of building a community with a shared future in space for the benefit of all humanity.
The paper’s release comes after US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told a defense conference last month that the US Space Force has "on-orbit space control weapons" capable of defending American forces against hostile action.
China urged countries to commit to openness and shared benefit, ensure equitable access to outer space, promote space research and technological innovation, respect all states’ rights and security interests, oppose offensive military policies, and prevent an arms race.
It also called for abiding by the international rule of law, safeguarding common security, greater transparency to reduce misunderstandings, the regulation of commercial space activities, deeper international cooperation, and the UN remaining the main channel for global space governance.
The paper called for equitable, non-discriminatory access to outer space and opposed activities threatening other states' sovereignty, security, and development, adding that the principle of refraining from the threat or use of force in international relations and preventing the threat or use of force against outer space objects should be reaffirmed to avoid armed conflict in outer space.
Separately, China on Friday also launched a remote sensing satellite from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in north China's Shanxi Province, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency.
It will mainly be used for land survey and estimating crop yields, as well as disaster prevention and relief.

====================================================================================================

One-time minnows Tonga and Samoa now star World Cup attractions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:22:36 UTC
06:22:36 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Once seen as minnows, Tonga and Samoa are now Rugby League World Cup drawcards
At Western Sydney Stadium last week, Toa Samoa had a moment of pure elation, a crushing 78-4 victory over France at the men's Rugby League World Cup.
It was capped off with an extraordinary final play that saw a penalty goal attempt from Stephen Crichton ricochet off the post.
The ball bounced towards Benaiah Ioelu who scored a try after the full-time siren had sounded, delivering Samoa's largest-ever victory.
What was more extraordinary was that a game with a kick-off time of 5:45pm on Friday, playing out what was likely and ultimately proved to be a walkover, still drew a crowd of 13,000.
It was a horror slot to play in: a workday, outside school holidays, in a busy part of Sydney where traffic was banking up across the many arterial roads that led to it.
Yet the crowd, largely comprising Western Sydney's large Samoan population, bellowed Ua fa'afetai — a traditional song of thanks and gratitude.
Fiji and the Cook Islands played each other on Sunday in Newcastle; there was a tick over 10,000 in the stands and another 1.7 million watching on television across Australia, outrating several flagship current affairs shows, news bulletins and reality programs.
These are just two examples that show this is a World Cup transformed by Pasifika passion.
The growing strength of Samoa and Tonga's men's teams has been no secret, but now more than ever the iron grip of dominance largely held by Australia on international rugby league, occasionally disrupted by New Zealand, could be under threat.
What has also been clear to those at the grounds or watching from home is that this World Cup in Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea is one where diaspora communities have breathed life into a tournament that has previously lacked the same level of excitement or prestige compared to other international sporting events.
Australia's migration story tracks with this
The shift will be most obvious on November 1, when Samoa and Tonga play each other in Sydney, in a game that was the first to sell out despite being in the third week of the tournament.
Already a series of ex-players and pundits have raised the call to move the game to the larger Stadium Australia to accommodate a crowd beyond the 30,000 that Western Sydney Stadium holds.
The interest should come as no surprise though, as the Pasifika population in Australia has been steadily increasing.
In 2011, 165,000 Australians identified as being from Pasifika communities; by 2021, that number had almost tripled to 415,033.
Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics shows outer suburban areas of Sydney and Brisbane have burgeoning communities.
Sierra Keung, a senior lecturer in sports leadership and management at Auckland University of Technology, said she was not surprised by the fan turnout.
"The pride for our cultures, for our people, it's more than just a jersey for our Pasifika communities," Dr Keung told ABC Sport.
She cited a distinctive moment on the field that set this explosion in motion.
In 2017, the International Rugby League changed the rules to allow players with cultural ties to multiple nations to play for the country of their choosing.
The most famous change in allegiance was Jason Taumalolo.
That rule change is on full display at this tournament.
Of the listed starting line-up for Tonga's match against Lebanon last night at Western Sydney Stadium, none of the players were born in Tonga, but all have deep familial ties to the island nation.
Tonga beat Lebanon 36-0 to keep its campaign on track.
"This is years in the making, and it's come down to people making bold decisions, like Jason Taumalolo to be the first to say, 'I'm going to go home and represent my people,'" Dr Keung said.
Salesi Foketi is one of a number of Tongan players that chose to represent his familial roots over his country of birth, New Zealand.
"Right from when I was a boy, it was always Tonga," he said.
Winger Jojo Fifita made his debut last weekend for Tonga and it was a moment to acknowledge his forebears.
"Being able to represent my dad's side was something I'd always wanted to do when I was older and I finally got that opportunity," he said.
Extension beyond Pasifika diaspora may be the future
There is another team outside the South Pacific that is relying on heritage and cultural ties as the bind for players to represent it.
Lebanon's winger Jason Saab has potentially the most unique ties to the country.
His stepfather, whose name he took, is Lebanese, and Saab is now lining up for the Cedars.
Saab told ABC Sport in September of the sincere ties to Lebanese culture through his stepdad Pierre.
"That's the culture that raised me ultimately, that whole community of people. That's kind of where I found my identity to be," he said.
While all players in the Cedars squad were born in Australia, Lebanon coach Michael Cheika, who is also Lebanese Australian, said the small but dedicated rugby league community in Lebanon was driving the entire playing group, especially for those with family in Lebanon where strikes from Israel continued amid a broader conflict in the region.
"With everything that's going on over there … you've got to understand that they may not have enough petrol to get to the games, let alone field markings, fields that are available," he said.
As Samoa and Tonga have brought a genuine competitiveness to the tournament, there are other countries with large populations in Australia, such as Fiji and the Cook Islands, that could also challenge the Kangaroos, who have won 12 world titles, including six of the last seven.
"The talent is just through the roof right now, both men's and women's," Dr Keung said.
"So I'm really excited for this World Cup, but also for future World Cups too, because it's just going to get better and better each time it comes around."
There is no doubt rugby league has cottoned on to its international life blood, and it seems the public is following suit.

An Ecuadorian judge ordered pretrial detention for opposition politician Luisa Gonzalez and two other people investigated for alleged money laundering linked to campaign financing, the Attorney General’s Office said Friday.
The ruling stems from the Laberinto case, which investigates alleged irregularities in the financing of the Citizens’ Revolution’s 2023 presidential campaign.

The investigation focuses on the suspected use of funds linked to illegal fuel trading to finance electoral advertising and other campaign expenses.

When a business suddenly collapses, how can customers get money back?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:07:49 UTC
06:07:49 KST

Can paying a deposit by credit card help you claw back losses when a company suddenly goes bankrupt?
The spate of caravan companies going bust has led to hundreds of customers losing tens of thousands of dollars in deposits.
From Sunshine Coast based Zone RV last December to Australian Off Road just last month, there is a long list of manufacturers going bust after trading while insolvent.
But buyers being caught up in business insolvencies is not a new issue.
Building companies and tech giant Dick Smith in 2016 have left customers out of pocket, while the collapse of whitegoods company Kleenmaid saw a former director jailed.
When it comes to getting back money you have forked out for a deposit, Deloitte senior liquidator Richard Hughes said there are no guarantees.
"There is no risk-free way of doing anything these days,"
he said.
"You have to be really careful."
And if possible, he warns, do not pay by cash.
Is paying by credit card the answer?
Mr Hughes helped creditors fight over the carcass of Kleenmaid, which collapsed owing $100 million, and says credit card payments can be good insurance.
His forensic examination of the company's books found customers were set to lose $25 million in deposits.
But when he realised half of those had been paid on credit card, he was able to help get $12.5 million back into disillusioned customers' bank accounts.
This was through charge back requests, which is when customers have paid for good or services they did not receive, like a cancelled flight or a brand new caravan.
How does a charge back request work?
The Australian Banking Association describes it this way.
"When someone pays for goods or services by card that they never receive, they can ask their bank to dispute the transaction," a spokesperson said.
"The rules are set and administered by the card schemes, such as Visa and Mastercard — time limits apply, so customers should contact their bank as soon as possible."
The customer's bank lodges the claim through the scheme with the business's bank.
"If the claim succeeds, the money goes back to the customer and is taken from the business's bank," the spokesperson said.
"Payments by cash don't carry charge back rights."
The Office of Fair Trading said financial institutions may be able to assist customers who have paid "by credit card, debit card, or through a secure payment provider such as PayPal".
Will changes to card fees make it hard to pay by credit?
From October 1, the reserve bank banned credit and debit card surcharges across major card networks.
Some customers may be concerned about whether these changes will impact their ability to pay a deposit, and whether companies may stop accepting credit card payments.
But Mr Hughes said he believed businesses would still be happy to take credit card deposits, with card fees most likely added into their quotes.
If a small business insists on only cash, it could be seen as a red flag.
Customers are also encouraged to do a financial health check on the business they are putting their faith in.
It is also important to remember that unlike real estate companies, which are legally bound to hold deposits in a protected trust account, small businesses are not.
How to check if a business is struggling
ASIC says warning signs customers can watch out for include:
- bad reviews
- ongoing losses
- board disputes and director resignations, or loss of management personnel
- suppliers placing the company on cash-on-delivery terms
- a sudden change of name
- movement of a business or its assets to another company
ASIC encourages customers to check whether a company has entered liquidation or external administration through ASIC Connect or ASIC's Published Notices website.
Will creditors get money back?
When a company goes into liquidation, the question every creditor wants answered is simple: am I going to get my money back?
According to ASIC, the data is stark.
In most small to medium-sized corporate insolvencies, 97 per cent of creditors received between 0–11 cents in the dollar.
In the recent cases of collapsed caravan companies, majority of customers have not been able to get their money back, and have seen their savings vanish.
Caravanning Queensland Trade advised any customers who have purchased a product they haven't received to contact the appointed administrator or liquidator as soon as possible, and bring their contract, receipts and proof of payment.
"For anyone considering buying a caravan, Caravanning Queensland recommends a deposit of 10 per cent of the purchase price, with the balance paid when the completed van is ready for inspection and handover," chief executive Jason Plant said.
"We remain committed to promoting responsible business practice, transparency and consumer confidence across the caravan and RV industry."

Kadena Implements Curfew, Alcohol Restrictions for Junior Troops After Japanese Civilian Dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:59:50 UTC
05:59:50 KST

The top Air Force commander on the Japanese island of Okinawa has clamped down alcohol and issued a curfew for junior enlisted Airmen and Guardians at Kadena Air Base for the next month. The order came roughly two weeks after a U.S. Marine was arrested for allegedly robbing and murdering a Japanese woman on the island.
Brig. Gen. John B. Gallemore, commander of the 18th Wing at Kadena, issued the Oct. 22 memo, ordering the “Curtailment of Liberty and the Consumption of Alcohol,” according to a memo posted on the popular unofficial Air Force amn/nco/snco Facebook page.
A PACAF spokesperson confirmed the memo’s authenticity. The order went into effect Oct. 22 and will last “throughout the 30-day period of reflection,” concluding on Nov. 8, according to the memo:
- All personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4 are not to consume alcohol.
- Off-base liberty between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. local time is curtailed for all personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4.
- Possession of alcohol is banned in all dormitories within Kadena Air Base, to include dormitory common areas.
During the period, “commanders at all levels are authorized to conduct unannounced, systematic health and welfare inspections of dormitory rooms to ensure compliance of this order,” the memo states.
The memo follows an Oct. 6 memo from United States Forces Japan that ordered similar liberty restrictions and personal conduct training as part of a “period of reflection” following the Marine’s arrest in connection with the alleged murder of an Okinawan woman in Naha.
Japanese police arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, on Oct. 4 for allegedly killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi and stealing her wallet, Marine Corps Times reported.
“Incidents like this demand we pause for reflection,” Benjamin T. Watson, area coordinator for U.S. Forces Japan, wrote in the memo. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will continue to ensure full cooperation with Japanese authorities throughout the investigation.”
Watson added that serving on Okinawa “comes with responsibility.”
“We live, work, and socialize alongside the people of Okinawa; their home is our home,” Watson wrote. “Every interaction with our neighbors either builds or undermines the trust that is essential to our team. When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region.”
The USFJ memo prohibited alcohol consumption for 48 hours from Oct. 7-9 but stopped short of restricting consumption during the 30-day period of reflection. In a statement, PACAF Gallemore’s Oct. 22 memo contains extra restrictions.
“The 18th Wing continually assesses measures to reinforce good order and discipline and maintain positive relationships with our host community,” the PACAF statement read. “As part of the ongoing 30-day period of reflection on Okinawa, Japan, [Gallemore] determined that additional preventive measures were appropriate to reinforce expectations for responsible conduct among service members.”
Periods of reflection and associated restrictions have been used by commanders on Okinawa in the past to reinforce discipline after violent, criminal incidents involving U.S. personnel and Japanese residents. In 2024, USFJ prohibited all American troops in the country from publicly consuming alcohol from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. every day after a string of alleged sexual assaults. In 2017, the command prohibited all drinking and cut off-base liberty for troops on Okinawa after a fatal car crash involving a drunk Marine. In 2010, then-Brig. Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach—now the Chief of Staff—instituted a brief period of reflection restricting alcohol and off-base liberty at Kadena after a string of alcohol-related arrests. In 2008, commanders imposed the measure to calm an uproar in the surrounding community over allegations that a Marine raped a 14-year-old girl on the island, The Guardian reported.
Kadena is the closest U.S. air base to Taiwan, making it a strategically vital location should China ever launch an invasion.
