How a Fake Pollster May Have Hurt Real Candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:21:19 UTC
03:21:19 KST

A pollster admitted this week to using fabricated data in its surveys that were picked up by leading publications across the U.S., claiming the stunt was an “experimental project” intended to showcase the “vulnerabilities” of the polling industry. The announcement has shaken trust in polling infrastructure ahead of the midterms, especially as some candidates say their campaigns were directly harmed by the fake numbers.
After election analysis website FiftyPlusOne submitted an inquiry to Wedgewood Polls regarding the authenticity of its data and methodologies, the pollster put out a statement across social media on Tuesday, saying it had been conducting a test to show "how easy is it for an entirely fabricated polling firm to gain traction, be taken seriously, and expose how little scrutinization exists in media and public commentary?" In the statement, which has since been deleted, the group claimed it had been “far too easy” to distribute false data and insisted it "highlights a systemic breakdown in media vetting and data aggregation.”
Wedgewood's polls had been used by multiple national outlets for their midterm reporting, including the New York Times, Newsweek, MS NOW, and POLITICO. The Times, which cited around 15 Wedgewood polls between June and October, has since removed the data from its stories. In an accompanying editor’s note, the publication detailed its checking process for polls and said Wedgewood had answered several of their inquiries prior to the data being published, including questions on the identities of the group’s pollsters, the methods used to draw their samples, and the source of their funding.
TIME's email to Wedgewood Polls bounced back.
In another fraudulent polling operation uncovered in August, a company called Median Strategies fabricated polls for races in Wisconsin, Nevada, and California and similarly called the ploy a “social experiment” in a statement to the Los Angeles Times.
“It's very troubling that we've had two examples of this within a very short period of time during election campaigns, creating a lot of problems for legitimate polling,” says Michael Traugott, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of Michigan, who previously served as president of the American Association for Public Opinion Research (AAPOR).
Here’s what to know about the Wedgewood scandal, and what it says about polling ahead of the pivotal midterm elections.
What do we know about Wedgewood Polls?
The polling group called itself a “fictional entity run by a small group of industry veterans” in its statement. Its X account, which contained many of its polls, no longer exists.
G. Elliot Morris, a pollster and journalist who works at FiftyPlusOne, tells TIME that he and his colleagues had been suspicious about a “crop of new polling firms” that have emerged and released anonymous data. An individual eventually tipped off FiftyPlusOne to Wedgewood's polling, which was “the straw that broke the camel's back for us,” he says.
FiftyPlusOne said in a public statement that Wedgewood “operated as if it were a legitimate polling firm” by collecting money from donors to carry out crowd-funded polls and share its survey data.
The poll analysis group said Wedgewood disclosed two names in connection to the company: Jack Sims and Andrew Prater. According to FiftyPlusOne, Sims had prior experience in the polling industry. SoCal Strategies, another polling firm, this week acknowledged in an email to an NPR affiliate in Michigan that Sims had worked there, but is not currently employed by the company and “has not been for a year.”
“It is not atypical for a pollster to leave an existing firm, form their own, and self-fund some surveys to build reputation; we had no reason at the time to believe this case was any different,” FiftyPlusOne said regarding Sims.
“This event does not help what is a decades-long trend of declining confidence in the polling industry,” Morris added, when asked about Sims’ involvement with Wedgewood. TIME has been unable to reach Sims for comment.
Senate candidate in Michigan says fake polling damaged her campaign
The polling scandal has sparked a flurry of reactions within the politics and government sector, with one former Senate hopeful claiming the numbers circulated by Wedgewood contributed to the collapse of her campaign.
Democratic Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow recalled how a poll from Wedgewood had shown her “plummeting into single digits.”
Wedgewood released polling on June 29 that placed McMorrow as having the support of only 9% of registered voters, leaving her trailing behind Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed. Other polls also showed McMorrow in third place with single digits. A Susquehanna Polling survey conducted June 9 to 14 put McMorrow at 9%, although 49% of Democratic primary voters surveyed were undecided. A July 1 Quantus Insights poll put her at under 8%. McMorrow suspended her campaign on July 5, just one month before the primaries.  
In a statement posted to social media on Oct. 20, McMorrow said donations “dried up” and she was “hounded” with calls to exit the race after the circulation of the “infamous” Wedgewood poll numbers. 
Advising others not to trust the polls, McMorrow said she hoped Democrats are ready to “blow up the system with campaign finance and transparency reforms.”
Jennifer Holdsworth, a Democratic strategist who ran a SuperPAC that supported McMorrow, claimed the fake poll had been “used by several donors to pull back funding at a time we were being outspent by $80 million.”
Amid widespread discussions over fabricated data, Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr said, without naming any specific instance, that there has been a “significant surge” in fake polls and blamed news outlets for “amplifying or airing” them “without regard to basic journalistic ethics.”
Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez quipped back and shifted the onus onto fraudulent pollsters themselves.
“Pollsters who intentionally mislead the public should answer for it, but broadcasters who report publicly available polling data should never be punished when a poll is wrong,” she said in response to Carr. “FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith.”
What impact can polls have on elections?
While documented fake polls are rare, according to experts, polling in general often plays a large role in shaping the narrative of hotly contested races.
Traugott tells TIME that polls can affect voting behavior and support for campaigns “because by and large, the average citizen is interested in backing the winner, and backing means not just votes; it also means financial contributions, contributing time and effort to the campaign, and the like.”
Research has demonstrated what is known as the “bandwagon effect,” in which voters become more likely to vote for candidates or issues that are more favored in polls. A 2023 study from the Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties showed that polls discouraged support for less popular ballot items, or as the paper’s authors put it: “polls demobilize the minority and mobilize the majority.”
It also found that moderate voters, who often represent a crucial demographic of voters and can swing tight elections, were the most impressionable when it comes to being influenced by polling. “Social conformity is strongest among ideological moderates,” the study said.
This effect has been documented going back decades.
A 1996 experiment showed that participants who were shown a fabricated poll ahead of that year’s primary had a “significantly greater tendency” to vote for the candidates favored by the poll.
This phenomenon has similarly been demonstrated in prediction markets, which have been shown to sway voters almost as much as polls. A study released on Oct 20 by policy think-tank the Brennan Center showed that voters were 10% more likely to say that a candidate would win in an election if that person had higher odds of winning based on a prediction market.
Likewise, voters were less likely to believe that a candidate would win if their odds were predicted to be lower. These prediction market odds, the study said, had a similar effect on perceived electability as traditional polls.
Traugott says that generally speaking, voters who identify with a specific party are unlikely to change their vote as a result of polling, but that they might not show up to the polls at all if they see their party’s nominee is disfavored to win.
“It's often the case in the general election that the polls have an influence in terms of turnout,” he says.
Should you trust polls?
Michael Dimock, the president of the Pew Research Center, says that in tight races, of which there are many in the upcoming midterms, “it's very easy for polls to ‘pick the wrong winner.’”
“I do think that people should be very cautious in over-interpreting pre-election polls' ability to project an election outcome, whether it's at a national level, state level, a district level, [or] local level,” he tells TIME.
One of the main reasons for this, Dimock contends, is that even if participants in a survey say who they would vote for, they still might not show up to cast their ballot. He refers to this immeasurable but important factor as “enthusiasm differences.”
“What polls are really bad at capturing is who's going to actually show up and cast a ballot. It's really hard,” Dimock adds. “Human beings are bad at predicting their [own] future behaviors.”

Restaurant holding !Fest is preparing to open the first location of its Piana Vyshnia (Drunken Cherry) chain in Germany in December, the holding's CEO and co-owner Andriy Khudo said.
"We are preparing to open the first Piana Vyshnia location in Germany... It is at 5 Rathausstraße, next to the TV tower, where lots of people walk around. And, of course, there are many Ukrainians in Germany, and in Berlin in particular, these days. Future customers come up to the door and try to open it by pulling the handle... So it is already a little 'tired'... But winter will come, and we plan to open our first business in Germany in December 2026, and the handle will work!" he said on LinkedIn.
The first Piana Vyshnia location opened in Lviv's Rynok Square in 2015. The chain currently has more than 70 locations in Ukraine and abroad, including in the United Kingdom, France, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Hungary, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Moldova.
The !Fest holding was founded in 2007. It develops a chain of creative restaurants, coffee shops and stores in Ukraine. Its owners are Andriy Khudo, Yuriy Nazaruk and Dmytro Herasymov.

PrivatBank launches Open Banking for retail and small business users

03:18:47 KST

PrivatBank has launched an open banking service in its Privat24 app for individual customers and in the web version of Privat24 for Business for individual entrepreneurs, the financial institution's press service reported.
"For individuals, this will change the experience of using financial apps, since all accounts and personal finances will be brought together in one Privat24 app. For individual entrepreneurs, it offers an opportunity to simplify the tracking of operating expenses in Privat24 for Business," said Dmytro Musienko, a member of PrivatBank's management board responsible for retail banking.
With the service, users can, with their consent, add accounts from other banks, view balances and transaction histories, top up cards and make transfers. Individual entrepreneurs using Privat24 for Business can monitor transactions on their business accounts at other banks and make payments.
Currently, individual customers can link accounts from Universal Bank, including monobank, as well as FUIB, A-Bank and Globus Bank, to Privat24. In Privat24 for Business, users can link accounts from Universal Bank, including monobank.
The bank said the list of participating institutions would gradually expand as they integrate with open banking technology.
As reported, National Bank of Ukraine Resolution No. 80, which provides for authorized third-party service providers to access customer account information only with the customers' consent, took effect on August 1, 2025.
For the following 12 months, the regulator did not impose enforcement measures for violations of requirements concerning continuous access to accounts and the configuration of dedicated interfaces.
PrivatBank is Ukraine's largest bank. According to the National Bank of Ukraine, the financial institution's total assets stood at UAH 983.82 billion as of September 1, 2026, accounting for 22.8% of the banking sector's total assets.
At the end of the first half of 2026, the bank had 18 million active individual customers, 13.7 million Privat24 users and 950,000 business customers.

US Announces Russia-Ukraine Ceasefire Deal for Civilian Evacuations in Temporarily Occupied Oleshky

- Category

US Announces Russia-Ukraine Ceasefire Deal for Civilian Evacuations in Temporarily Occupied Oleshky
UPD: Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced on October 23 that Russian forces would introduce a ceasefire in the Kherson sector starting at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 27 to facilitate a humanitarian operation in the temporarily Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. On the Ukrainian side, senior negotiator Davyd Arakhamia confirmed preparations for an operation to unblock Oleshky and establish humanitarian corridors.
US First Lady Melania Trump secured an agreement between Ukraine and Russia for a localized ceasefire in Oleshky, Kherson region, scheduled to begin October 29.
The White House announced the agreement on October 23, stating that both countries had agreed to temporarily suspend military operations in the city to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations through a designated safe corridor.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
However, Ukraine has not officially confirmed the ceasefire agreement announced by the White House. On October 23, Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets indicated that negotiations with Russia over civilian evacuations from Oleshky were still underway, although they were nearing completion.
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," Melania Trump stated. She emphasized that the remaining residents, predominantly elderly people, urgently need food, clean water, medicine, and medical assistance.
According to the White House, Melania Trump and her representative negotiated directly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership, coordinating the agreement's timing, technical procedures, and implementation. The first lady acted as an "Exclusive Intermediary" between the two sides.
Under the arrangement, civilian representatives from both countries will visit residents in their homes to assess their humanitarian needs. Those wishing to evacuate will receive transportation and assistance in reaching their preferred destinations, whether in Ukrainian-controlled territory or Russia.
Melania Trump also announced that an independent American media organization would accompany the Ukrainian and Russian teams to document the evacuation process and help ensure residents' preferences are respected.
The agreement includes coordination on demining operations, as roads around Oleshky remain contaminated with explosives. The White House did not specify how long the ceasefire would last or how compliance with the temporary suspension of hostilities would be monitored.
Oleshky lies on the temporarily Russian-occupied eastern bank of the Dnipro River, opposite the city of Kherson. Before Russia's full-scale invasion, approximately 24,000 people lived there.
The White House estimates that between 1,700 and 2,000 residents remain, primarily elderly civilians, alongside approximately 50 children. No comprehensive population census has been conducted since 2022.
The city also suffered extensive destruction following the collapse of the Kakhovka Dam in June 2023, when approximately 90% of its territory was flooded, according to the White House.
The ceasefire agreement builds on earlier humanitarian contacts established by Melania Trump's office to reunite Ukrainian children separated from their families during Russia's invasion.
On April 2, 2026, the White House announced arrangements for seven Ukrainian children taken by Russia to return home. On July 30, she facilitated another reunion, helping five children return to their families in the fifth such operation. Her office maintained direct communication with Ukrainian and Russian officials throughout these efforts, establishing channels later used in the Oleshky ceasefire negotiations.
The agreement capped weeks of diplomatic pressure over the humanitarian crisis in the temporarily occupied city. On October 16, Pope Leo XIV urged the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, in a phone call to accept a ceasefire around Oleshky so food and medical aid could reach civilians.
By October 19, Kyiv and Moscow were moving to finalize an evacuation from Oleshky and six nearby settlements, where around 6,000 civilians, including up to 200 children, were believed to remain.

Israel’s election campaign lacks substance, fresh leadership, and vision - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:11:46 UTC
03:11:46 KST

Looking back at the coming-to-a-close Israeli election campaign, it can be summarized as sleepy and disappointing.
Sleepy, because the tough-it-out and raucous campaigning that characterized previous Israeli election rounds has been absent.
Almost no party has sought to block roads or spark physical clashes with rivals. There are none of the drum-beating demonstrations and die-hard, overwrought rhetoric that Israel suffered in the heydays of the judicial reform and haredi (ultra-Orthodox) military draft debates; and thinking farther back, during struggles over the Oslo Accords and disengagement from Gaza.
I had feared that this year’s election campaign would be marked by violence, so such sleepiness is good.
Perhaps it’s exhaustion in a society still under the shadow of war; perhaps this is evidence of maturity and restraint. Perhaps it’s a function of social media as a central political battle zone, where discourse is indeed vitriolic and scary. Whatever the case, this election campaign has not boiled over, and that is a blessed reality.
It’s also probable that this election campaign has not ignited or excited the masses because the candidates are, well, boring.
Election fails to offer anything new
The Likud is once again offering the Israeli public a chance to vote for Benjamin Netanyahu. He may be successful and still indispensable; he may be a failure and past his sell-by date, but he is nothing new.
The so-called “change camp” is not offering much fresher produce either, only some more Oslo-era military generals like Gadi Eisenkot (who are as responsible for the failures of October 7 as is Netanyahu), as well as cynical politicians that have hung around Israeli politics for too long like Avigdor Liberman and Yair Lapid.
Anybody who hoped that the long wars Israel has fought over the past three years would kindle a revolution in Israeli politics, a renaissance in which a fresh crop of brave and ideologically motivated leaders would breathe hope and inspiration into Israeli politics – well, this election is not that moment.
Neither is this election the People of Israel’s moment, the “coming together” centrist-nationalist moment, which might have been hoped for. None of the middle-of-the-road leaders promising national unity who threw their hats into the ring this time have skyrocketed in the polls. Ofer Winter, Yoaz Hendel, and others remain in the doldrums.
WHAT DISAPPOINTS me about this election campaign is that nobody is discussing policy; not national security and foreign affairs policy, not economic and social policy, nothing of substance.
Instead, the campaign has been personal and superficial, nasty and negative. We are told only that Netanyahu is strong while Eisenkot is weak. Netanyahu is experienced, while Eisenkot is untutored. Conversely, we are told that Netanyahu is a dictator, while Eisenkot is a democrat. Netanyahu is corrupt, while Eisenkot is honest, etc.
But what about real policies on core, critical issues of our day? Yes, we know that Netanyahu hopes to dismantle the regime in Tehran and work with US President Donald Trump to finish off Iran’s nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs. He is right that Israel needs strategic continuity in confronting Iran, and this is a pivotal point in his favor.
Gadi Eisenkot said that he too will work with the US to confront Iran, and that he will eliminate Hamas in Gaza within 18 months – unlike Netanyahu, who has not done so over three years. Nice and correct aspirations.
Beyond this, however, neither leader has offered specificity on a broad range of issues that will hit Israel in the coming months.
Will Netanyahu and/or Eisenkot mistakenly withdraw under American and international pressures from the security zones in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria that the IDF has established; or might they maintain Israel’s newly declared forward strategic posture without flinching and hew to Israel’s aggressive military approach of constantly interdicting emerging threats over the borders?
Well, we don’t know, because neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot nor any of the wannabe candidates for prime minister of Israel have spoken on these matters during the current election campaign.
Again, all we are told by the candidates is that their rival is crooked or weak, while actual or potential policy is blurred under the piles of mutual delegitimization and denigration.
Will Netanyahu and/or Eisenkot strengthen Israeli settlement in critical parts of Judea and Samaria, including strategic hills in Areas A and B, and continue to develop the E1 area on the eastern edge of Jerusalem; or unilaterally withdraw Israeli settlers from significant sections of Judea and Samaria? How are they going to handle threatened sanctions from European and other countries relating to Israeli settlement policy?
Again, we don’t know. Aside from radicals like Yair Golan (who would tear all settlements down) and Itamar Ben-Gvir (who would expel all Palestinians and resettle Jews in Gaza), none of the main candidates for prime minister have clear policies here.
Will Netanyahu and/or Eisenkot seek new ways of strengthening Mahmoud Abbas and his Palestinian Authority and allow the PA to assume responsibility for Gaza; or prepare the IDF for escalated confrontation with hostile armies including PA troops and terrorist groups in the West Bank, ensuring that Israel is not caught off-guard again by an October 7-scale surprise assault?
Will either Israeli leader be stupid enough to bend to international pressures for Palestinian elections in Judea and Samaria, which would bring Hamas and other bad actors into power, whitewashed under the rubric of a supposedly fresh technocratic Palestinian government?
What about the defense budget and keeping Israel’s economy solvent? How is Israel going to afford development of an independent defense-industrial base with indigenous manufacturing of weapons and munitions to the tune of NIS 500 billion or more over the next decade?
Just how high will the Israeli income tax rate spike in 2027, and how deep will the cuts need to be in government spending on education, health, and social services?
Well, we don’t know. The Israeli election campaign has sidestepped discussion of these important matters.
Netanyahu’s outgoing government has staked out pathways forward regarding military buildup, but the consequent economic picture ain’t pretty, and Netanyahu’s approach toward the PA is unclear.
Eisenkot has avoided taking a position on these matters or any other key strategic-economic issue. Again, all we are told is that he is “yashar” (honest) – which is the name of his party.
How about tackling the Gaza-ification of the Negev, where Bedouin mafia gangs basically run their own country, where every house is flush with weapons and drugs, and where smuggling using airborne drones of dangerous contraband to/from Gaza, Egypt, and Jordan (including military strike drones) is the principal driver of the economy?
How come the outgoing nationalist government of Netanyahu made so little progress in curbing this escalating disaster, and what might Eisenkot do differently?
And how about countering the hegemonic advances of the radical Islamist Turkish dictator Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his Syrian satrap, the former ISIS terrorist Ahmed al-Sharaa? Does Israel have a strategy here? Netanyahu/Eisenkot, hello?
Does Israel have a real strategy for bringing about significant haredi military draft, or just wild rhetorical commitments to bending the haredi Israeli community into submission?
What would Netanyahu do differently in this regard in a next term in office – given his umbilical cord connection to the old, retrograde haredi parties, and what realistic alternative approach might Eisenkot adopt? I have not heard any serious discussion of how to crack this oh-so-painful and central issue.
Too bad none of the leading Israeli candidates for prime minister have commented on the wise and brave, solid proposals for the combination of Torah study and national/military service put forward by the new Haredi Public party – a party which I hope will be the surprise success of this election.
All in all, this election campaign has been substandard. I certainly do not view it as the big inflexion point in Israeli life and politics that many were expecting or hoping for.
That moment, I believe, will soon come, and Israel will be blessed with dramatic recovery and redemption.
Israel will yet elect a new, younger generation of bright and believing, capable and courageous, leaders to take the reins of state – some of them the fearless heroes of Israel’s recent wars and the equally heroic civil society leaders of the past three years.
I eagerly await the day when the current crop of politicians will have passed – and that means everybody from Netanyahu to Eisenkot, and Naftali Bennett to Yitzhak Goldknopf. Wait for the 2028 or 2030 elections.
The writer is managing senior fellow at the Jerusalem-based Misgav Institute for National Security & Zionist Strategy. The views expressed here are his own. His diplomatic, defense, political, and Jewish world columns over the past 30 years are at davidmweinberg.com

First Russian diesel from Putin-Trump deal heading for US, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:11:34 UTC
03:11:34 KST

The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday.
Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November 3 US midterm elections.
Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.
The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel in Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7.
Buyer, seller unknown
The identities of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022.
Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere.
"As far as I'm aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call.
The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports.
Russia resumes global exports
Since the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries.
It also supplies Central Asia by rail.
Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signaling trips to Turkey and Brazil.
It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signaling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port Said, LSEG data showed.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts.
Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia's sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement.
That account was not accurate, a source familiar with the matter said.
Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by year-end.

Israel’s ballot box or Pandora’s box? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:11:20 UTC
03:11:20 KST

In Greek mythology, Pandora opened a mysterious box, unleashing suffering and misfortune upon humanity. Horrified, she slammed it shut. But the forces had escaped. Only hope remained inside.
As Israelis approach the ballot box, I wonder whether we are about to open our own Pandora’s box. Or whether it has already been opened.
Israel is not entering an ordinary election. We are a nation confronting eight interconnected fronts of conflict: military, diplomatic, political, and cognitive. We face Iran and its proxies, international delegitimization, uncertain alliances, and profound internal divisions.
Yet the greatest danger may lie in our diminishing ability to distinguish truth from lies, disagreement from hatred, and political competition from a struggle against our own brothers and sisters.
What happens when a democracy must make decisions essential to its survival while the cognitive faculties required to make them are under sustained assault?
The intoxicated electorate
In my Jerusalem Post column, “When journalism fails, democracy fails,” I described a family awaiting news of a loved one undergoing lifesaving surgery. The surgeon emerges needing an urgent decision. But the family, overwhelmed by anxiety, has become intoxicated. Nobody is capable of sound judgment.
The patient is Israel.
Millions of Israelis are being asked to make consequential decisions while immersed in accusations, selective reporting, propaganda, outrage, and increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence.
We consume information constantly. But are we better informed?
In “The biggest threat to Israel is mass cognitive warfare,” I explored how dopamine-driven digital platforms exploit our appetite for stimulation, rewarding emotional reactions over understanding.
Outrage attracts engagement. Certainty is rewarded. Nuance struggles to survive.
Not every social media user is addicted, nor is every voter incapable of independent thought. But the architecture of our information environment can reinforce vulnerabilities that make careful political judgment harder.
AI adds fabricated voices, synthetic images, and manipulated videos, enabling deception at extraordinary speed. Traditional journalism, once expected to distinguish fact from opinion, increasingly competes in the same attention economy.
When citizens cannot agree on what happened yesterday, how can they intelligently decide what should happen tomorrow?
The eighth front comes home
Israel possesses formidable military capabilities. Yet tanks, fighter jets, and missile defenses cannot protect a society against every form of cognitive manipulation.
Iran, Russia, China, Qatar, and other actors have differing interests and methods. Their influence activities must be assessed individually, not assumed to be a single coordinated conspiracy, but rather a global ecosystem focused against Israel. Nevertheless, hostile information operations are exploiting these same internal divisions.
An adversary need not persuade Israelis to embrace its ideology. It may be enough to deepen mistrust, weaken institutional credibility and encourage Israelis to regard one another as enemies.
This is the eighth front.
Unlike a conventional battlefield, it has no clear border. It reaches our homes, smartphones, schools, newsrooms and political conversations.
A nation can prevail militarily while undermining the cohesion needed to sustain that victory.
Brothers and sisters, not enemies
Our disagreements are real. Israelis differ over leadership, accountability, judicial authority, religion and state, military service, national security and relations with the world.
These questions deserve serious debate. But something dangerous happens when disagreement becomes delegitimization: every opponent becomes a traitor and electoral defeat is portrayed as national extinction.
The people voting differently from us are not foreign armies.
They are our brothers and sisters, even though this is not always an easy pill to swallow.
Our children go to the same hospitals and confront the same emergencies, may serve in the same military, may attend the same universities, may work in the same companies, but for sure all of our children are dependent on a strong, united Israel.
Whatever government emerges, Israelis will still need one another.
We cannot defend our country against external enemies while treating half our population as an internal enemy.
That does not mean excusing wrongdoing or abandoning convictions. It means recognizing that democratic legitimacy cannot depend on our preferred candidate winning.
The enormous ship called Israel
Another illusion poisons our political discourse: that replacing or retaining a government can immediately transform the country’s strategic circumstances.
Israel is not a speedboat capable of turning sharply with one movement of the wheel.
It is an enormous ship carrying millions of people through dangerous waters, subject to powerful currents, accumulated momentum and forces beyond its captain’s control.
Consider ultra-Orthodox conscription. No campaign promise can instantly resolve generations of religious, educational and institutional realities. Meaningful change demands military capacity, enforceable policies, accommodations and time.
A new government cannot instantly eliminate Iran’s capabilities or ambitions. A different foreign minister cannot reverse decades of international narratives. Exceptional access to one American president cannot guarantee bipartisan support for the next generation.
Some turns may take months, others years or decades. Some may prove impossible without changes beyond our shores.
This is not an argument for paralysis or the status quo. It is an argument for strategic realism.
Ask candidates not merely where they would steer the ship, but how they would execute the turn, what resistance they expect, what sacrifices it requires, and how long it will take.
A captain promising an impossible turn may be more dangerous than one acknowledging the difficult navigation ahead.
Finding our why
Viktor Frankl, the Holocaust survivor and psychiatrist, repeatedly invoked Nietzsche’s observation that a person with a compelling why can endure almost any how.
Frankl understood that resilience depends not simply on surviving hardship but on preserving meaning and purpose.
Israel needs to rediscover its collective why.
Not the why of Netanyahu or his opponents. Not of religious versus secular, Right versus Left, coalition vs opposition.
The why that allows a diverse people to remain a nation despite profound disagreements. The why that recognizes Israel as a shared home whose citizens must determine its direction peacefully.
Without that common purpose, every election risks becoming an existential confrontation. With it, even bitter political defeats remain survivable, because the nation is larger than any government.
Before entering the voting booth
Perhaps Israelis should approach this election as soldiers preparing for a consequential mission.
Not a battle against one another, but a struggle against fear, anger, exhaustion, manipulation, and overconfidence.
Do not enter the voting booth drunk on hatred.
Do not enter intoxicated by propaganda, selective journalism, viral outrage, or the false certainty that your side possesses every answer.
Question what you believe. Examine competing evidence. Distinguish promises from executable plans. Consider consequences beyond the next electoral cycle.
Ask not merely whom you want to win, but what kind of country your children will inherit.
And remember: even the most decisive electoral victory cannot eliminate the need to live together afterward.
Is hope still inside the Box?
Pandora’s tragedy was that once the evil forces escaped, they could not simply be returned to their box.
Israel’s tragedy would be to allow political divisions and cognitive vulnerabilities to become more dangerous than the election itself.
But unlike Pandora, we still possess the capacity to choose our response.
The ballot box cannot defeat Iran, repair journalism, reverse polarization, or instantly redirect the enormous ship called Israel.
It can, however, affirm our commitment to resolve differences through democratic institutions rather than hatred, intimidation, or violence.
Israel’s democracy is not simply another front to defend. Our ability to manage disagreement peacefully is part of the national strength on which every other front depends.
The question is no longer simply who emerges victorious when Israel opens its ballot box.
The question is whether, after all the hate and fears, we have allowed to escape that ballot box before election day, we will still find hope inside, that our collective why is still strong and our democracy is stable.
The writer is a global strategist and a strategic adviser at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs. Follow him on X: @jeffkahn2020

Beyond the polls: What are Israelis really thinking as they head to the ballot box?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:11:10 UTC
03:11:10 KST

Polls only go so far in predicting election winners. With only a few days left before Israelis vote on Tuesday, the country has plenty of them. KAN, Channel 12, Channel 13, and Maariv publish surveys from various sources, while i24NEWS and Channel 14 run their own polls.
Each new poll produces a headline that often disagrees with other outlets. Israelis follow polls like a tennis match, their heads swiveling from side to side, following the ball in play.
Polls are often constructed to reinforce the media sources that conduct them, giving the public a clear picture of who the news outlet may endorse, but not an accurate snapshot of what people are really thinking.
The Magazine therefore sought people from various parts of the country and asked who they supported and why. There were a few surprises.
For instance, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has attracted supporters from left-leaning places like Rosh Hayin, to haredi enclaves such as Tel Stone. We also uncovered new voting approaches, such as “splitting the vote,” and picking two options, then choosing one blindly.
Do these represent trends? Perhaps. But they are certainly reflections of the turmoil that Israel faces, both domestically and when dealing with world powers. Here are the people we interviewed, speaking for themselves.
In their own words
Mike | Ra’anana
I’m still not sure who I’m voting for, but I think it will be either Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist Party or Likud.
Smotrich has done an excellent job, and he’s a straight guy. They haven’t come up with any shmutz against him, like putting his hand in the cookie jar or anything like that. I want to see how the situation develops over the next week.
I’m much more concerned about the situation in Israel than I am about America. Because in America, I don’t believe there’s much anyone can do anymore. Here, there’s a strong likelihood we’ll have to go to another election.
I have a lot of issues with B’Yachad leader Naftali Bennett. I just don’t think he’s good for the Jewish people or the State of Israel.
Reggie | Jerusalem
My husband and I are splitting the ticket: he’s voting for Netanyahu, and I’m voting for Ben-Gvir.
We’re voting right-wing, because we feel like the world is on fire with antisemitism, and all our enemies want Netanyahu out. For me, that is the best reason he should stay.
In the past, Netanyahu has aligned himself with the Center, or even the slightly Left, so I’m leaning toward voting for Ben-Gvir, all the way to the Right.
Yori | Ra’anana
I live in Ra’anana, less than 10 km. from Kalkilya [in the West Bank]. If Kalkilya becomes part of a Palestinian state, then I expect there will be white pickup trucks full of Hamas supporters on the streets of Ra’anana in no time. That’s why the ultimate goal for me, never mind all the other issues, is to prevent a Palestinian state.
The person most proactive in this area is Smotrich. He has done more to secure the future of Israel than anyone, including Netanyahu. His closeness to Netanyahu has kept Bibi from making major mistakes, such as considering Ra’am (United Arab List) [in a coalition].

Iran threatens to sever Gulf internet cables in retaliation if US, Israel renew attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:11:03 UTC
03:11:03 KST

Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel attack Iran again, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters.
Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington collapses.
The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections.
"If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one of the officials said.
The official warned Washington not to "play with fire," and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.
Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.
Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency. But the global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited, as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography.
The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.
The US Department of State and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Iranian security officials' remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.
Iran expects war to resume soon
The plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran's leadership that a renewed US military campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.
Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centers and AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.
Washington's Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they "should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables," the second Iranian security official said.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and US companies fear for their investments in the region.
"Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (US President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans," said Vatanka.
Cable cuts could slow down internet, disrupt global networks
Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.
Restoring connections during wartime could be difficult, experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.
The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.
The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia, with capacity routed through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic traveling between regions, Mauldin said.
Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with US technology firms.
Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain. The IRGC named US tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the height of the war in March.
Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and US technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.
Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.

US leads JPPI database of measures against Israel
According to a survey by the Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI), the country with the highest number of recorded measures against Israel is its close ally, the United States.
According to JPPI's new database, which tracks sanctions, restrictions, and diplomatic measures against Israel worldwide, 15 measures were recorded in the US. Spain follows with 10 measures, the UK with eight, Turkey with seven, and Belgium with five. Ireland, with just three recorded sanctions, does not even make the top 10.
This finding does not, of course, mean that the US is more hostile toward Israel than Turkey or Ireland. On the contrary, it also reflects the depth of relations between the two countries.
Israel and the US maintain security, trade, investment, academic, and political ties on a far greater scale than Israel has with most other countries. As a result, there are also more areas in which sanctions, boycotts, or restrictions can be pursued.
The measures documented in the US illustrate this complexity. Some are not sweeping government decisions but rather legislative initiatives or proposed resolutions in Congress, including efforts to restrict the sale of weapons, ammunition, or defense equipment to Israel.
The database also includes academic measures, such as calls by student associations, faculty organizations, or academic institutions to boycott Israel, divest from Israeli investments, or restrict ties with the country.

daft punk enters the LEGO universe with a brick-built version of its alive tour stage
nearly two decades after the alive tour, daft punk’s glowing pyramid stage is making an unexpected return as a LEGO building set.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
LEGO brings daft punk’s alive stage into brick form
The illuminated pyramid at the center of Daft Punk’s 2007 Alive tour is on its way to becoming an official LEGO set. Announced on October 22nd, the collaboration between the Danish toymaker and the French electronic duo begins with a fan-designed concert model, bringing one of electronic music’s most recognizable stage designs down to tabletop scale.
The pyramid became a defining image of the Alive shows, placing the helmeted musicians within a glowing geometric structure. In the LEGO Ideas concept, a miniature version of the triangular stage sits between two wide, gridded structures, with colorful lighting recreated across its faceted surfaces. The model shows an early look at the proposed set, while the final product design is still in development.
a father-and-son LEGO project becomes an official set
The design began during lockdown, when Luxembourg-based LEGO enthusiast Patrick Harboun and his son started building their own version of the famous concert stage. Their proposal won the LEGO Ideas Music to Our Ears challenge in 2020 and later gathered 10,000 supporters on the platform. Six years after its initial success, the father-and-son project has been approved for official development.
The stage is a particularly fitting subject for a construction set. Its triangular silhouette and illuminated surfaces translate naturally into the language of LEGO bricks, while the surrounding stage structures give the miniature model a sense of scale. Daft Punk creative director Cédric Hervet describes the pyramid as one of the most recognizable elements of the duo’s visual world, and sees the fan-created design as a fitting starting point for the partnership.
an upcoming LEGO Ideas set will recreate the pyramid stage from daft punk’s 2007 alive tour
daft punk’s robots enter the LEGO universe
The announcement follows a brief teaser broadcast on Daft Punk’s WDPK 83.7 channel on October 21st. A familiar red 2×4 LEGO brick appeared with its underside facing outward, its three circular tubes resembling the woofers of a speaker. The 30-second transmission offered an early clue to the collaboration, leaving viewers to connect the two worlds.
A new promotional film develops the idea further. Minifigure versions of the helmeted musicians follow a holographic red brick through a dark environment, where glowing architectural forms assemble around them in time with the music. The sequence ends with the pair operating a brick-built console, accompanied by ‘Voyager’ from the 2001 album Discovery and ‘Human After All,’ the title track of their 2005 album.
more LEGO and daft punk collaborations to come in 2027
The upcoming concert set marks the first announced product of a wider partnership between the LEGO Group and Daft Punk. Beyond just the building model, the collaboration will extend into new content and events which will draw from the duo’s visual identity and the creative community that has continued to reinterpret their work.
For now, the image released by LEGO depicts the original fan submission, with the finished design still to be determined. Pricing and a release date have yet to be announced, although the companies have indicated that further details about the partnership will arrive in 2027. The miniature Alive pyramid brings an intriguing first glimpse of how Daft Punk’s concert architecture might take on a second life in bricks.
project info:
name: LEGO x Daft Punk, Alive Concert LEGO Ideas set
collaboration: LEGO Group, Daft Punk
original fan design: Patrick Harboun and his son

Ukrainian customs automates processing of intl express mail
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:09:22 EEST
03:09:22 KST

Ukraine's State Customs Service has introduced a mechanism for the automatic customs clearance of imported and exported international postal and express shipments without physically presenting them to customs authorities and without the involvement of customs officials.
According to a statement posted by the agency on its Telegram channel on Thursday, the new system is designed to speed up the processing of large volumes of parcels and optimize logistics processes, particularly under martial law. The mechanism combines an automated risk management system, including the use of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, with the processing of advance information by customs specialists. Additional criteria and stricter requirements have been established for automatic clearance.
Clearance decisions are made automatically after electronic data are submitted. This allows customs officers to focus on analyzing information and handling cases that require additional checks or professional intervention.
The State Customs Service added that the new approach was developed and implemented with the participation of the Kyiv and Lviv customs offices. In particular, Kyiv customs specialists submitted proposals on organizing the processes, while the first cases of automatic shipment clearance have already been recorded in the area of responsibility of the Lviv customs office.
As reported, on October 15, the Verkhovna Rada, on its third attempt, adopted at second reading and in its entirety bill No. 16051-1 amending the Tax Code regarding VAT taxation of e-commerce transactions. The amendments abolish the exemption from tax for international postal shipments valued at up to EUR 150.
Implementation of the law, together with amendments to the Customs Code adopted on the same day under bill No. 15460, is a condition for Ukraine to receive the next tranche of approximately $0.7 billion under its program with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the second tranche of EUR 3.7 billion in macro-financial assistance from the European Union under a EUR 90 billion loan to support Ukraine. Under the updated memorandum with the IMF, Ukraine was required to adopt this law by July 2026. The original deadline had been the end of March, alongside other tax provisions, but this structural benchmark was not met.
The law provides for special VAT rules for distance sales of goods, excluding excisable goods, imported in international postal and express shipments addressed to individuals and valued at up to EUR 150. Electronic interface operators or their intermediaries are designated as responsible for calculating and paying the tax.
At the same time, the VAT exemption remains in place for small noncommercial consignments valued at up to EUR 45, sent free of charge between individuals, as well as for goods in unaccompanied baggage valued at up to EUR 150 and goods intended for security and defense purposes, including energy equipment and goods for the defense forces.
During consideration of the legislation, Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko said the provisions would begin to apply on July 1, 2027, following the technical implementation of automated tax payments by international online marketplaces.

The deaths of 19,349 Ukrainian civilians have been confirmed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, including 762 children, Ukraine's acting Prosecutor General Anton Kovalsky said on Facebook on Friday.
According to him, more than 55,000 people have been wounded. More than 19,000 Ukrainian children have been forcibly displaced by the aggressor state.
Since the beginning of 2026, some 2,960 civilian deaths have been confirmed, including 87 children. Another 16,316 civilians were wounded, including 668 children, which accounts for nearly 30% of the total number of wounded civilians recorded throughout the entire period of full-scale armed aggression.
"In 2026, 84 individuals were sentenced for committing war crimes. Among those convicted this year are 54 Russian military personnel, including eight commanders. Another 261 individuals have been notified of suspicion… In total, over 266,000 war crimes have been registered in Ukraine. A total of 317 people have been convicted," Kovalsky said, noting that the scale of Russia's aggression cannot be measured by the number of criminal cases.
He reported on a meeting with Ukrainian and international partners who are assisting in bringing the perpetrators to justice and discussed joint efforts for further work with them.
"It is important to me that accountability for these crimes not be postponed until the end of the war. We must simultaneously document new crimes, bring already investigated cases to trial, and ensure that those who are currently beyond the reach of Ukrainian justice can be held accountable. This is a task that will take years," the acting Prosecutor General said.
The meeting was also attended by coordinators and representatives of the Advisory Group on the Most Serious International Crimes (ACA) – Clint Williamson (ICJI), Wayne Jordash (GRC), Claudio Pala (EUAM), Tinna Goletiani (PravoJustice4EU), Serhiy Drozach (IDLO), as well as experts from Global Rights Compliance, Project Expedite Justice, Justice Rapid Response, Truth Hounds, the Ukrainian Legal Advisory Group, and The Reckoning Project.
Kovalsky said uniform standards for investigating torture, unlawful deprivation of liberty, deportation, and forced displacement have already been implemented, a model indictment regarding attacks on the civilian population has been developed, and this week, joint guidelines on investigating sexual violence related to armed conflict came into effect.
"The next step is the implementation of the Strategy for the Prosecution of International Crimes for 2026-2028. Our priorities also include creating a Registry of Victims of War Crimes, establishing clear criteria for prioritizing criminal proceedings, introducing digital tools for analyzing large volumes of evidence, and developing a support system for victims and witnesses," he said.

Clean Energy Has a Lot Riding on the AI Data Center Boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:06:36 UTC
03:06:36 KST

Recent weeks have brought red flag after red flag for investment in AI and the related data center boom. Bond yields soared for AI infrastructure giant CoreWeave, a sign that investors view the buildout as increasingly risky. And Meta’s reporting of negative free cash flow for the quarter to fund its infrastructure buildout while saying it might need to raise even more capital to fund its AI buildout not only hit its own stock but contributed to a price decline across the big tech companies.
These developments raised questions across Wall Street about whether too much is being spent too quickly on data center expansion. How questions over data center investment play out has big implications for how companies and investors approach the future of energy and, by extension, climate. A pullback in the pace of new data centers could ease pressure to build fossil generation, but it would also weaken the commercial case for clean energy technologies that need big, reliable buyers who are willing to pay a premium for power.
Most obviously, a dent in the AI buildout would translate directly into a slowdown in related electricity demand growth. In advanced economies like the U.S., data centers will account for 20% of that growth through 2030. By then, data centers are expected to account for 3% of global electricity demand, according to data from the International Energy Agency.
Future Proof
Weekly
Making sense of the climate and energy economy.
Some climate advocates may initially rejoice at slowing electricity demand. Even as renewable energy expands, grids around the world still rely on fossil fuels. In the U.S. in particular, AI demand has sparked a wave of building new natural gas infrastructure. In the short term, slowing demand would mean lower emissions from the existing system than today’s baseline assumptions and less investment in new natural gas infrastructure.
But a slowing data center build out leaves less mature technologies at risk. From advanced geothermal to new ways of producing nuclear power, big tech companies have been willing to pay more to lock in reliable power sources, thereby accelerating the market for these new efforts. Even unproven technologies like nuclear fusion have received a big financial boost from tech firms speculating that they might help solve their power challenges and give them a competitive leg up in the AI race. In a tighter financial environment with lower projected electricity demand, both the incentive and the financial capacity to make bold bets diminish.
To be clear, data centers are not the only source of growing electricity demand. New manufacturing continues to create the need for power. The need for air conditioning has ramped up in many emerging markets, particularly in the Global South, creating new grid pressures. And electric vehicles continue to take off in many markets outside the U.S.
Even as gas remains resilient, much of the power built to meet demand will come from clean sources, including and especially solar and battery storage. Solar is increasingly cost competitive. And this year’s spike in fuel prices—particularly natural gas—has made local power more appealing. But the companies behind growing sectors like air conditioning and EVs are less involved in local power systems and lack the capital to really shape them like the world’s wealthiest tech companies have. In short, clean energy will take a hit without the backing of big tech.
It’s too soon to tell whether, in the long run, this week’s AI infrastructure recalibration will be a blip in time or part of a much broader realignment. But it’s something that anyone invested in clean energy and climate should be watching closely.

South Korea’s Ruling Democratic Party Is Tumbling in the Polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:05:00 UTC
03:05:00 KST

On October 19, Gyeonggi, South Korea’s most populous province, held a post-funeral ceremony ahead of a firefighter’s internment. More than 2,700 people filled the indoor stadium. Choo Mi-ae, the provincial governor, stood on the green sports surfacing, tears streaming down her face. File after file of uniformed firefighters weaved around her amid dirgeful tributes.
Of course, the firefighter’s burial signified the loss and sacrifice of a serviceman who braved a conflagration to save lives. Yet, it also rang the death knell for the ruling Democratic Party’s approval ratings.
The same day, Realmeter, an authoritative pollster, released a poll. The DP’s approval rating, at 36.2 percent, was lower than the opposition People Power Party’s 40.9 percent. It was the first time since the June local elections that the PPP had outpolled than the DP.
The alienation of DP supporters happened fast. Less than five months ago, the June local elections handed the DP a resounding victory. Since then, the DP has registered a double-digit plunge in approval ratings.
The party’s fall was particularly steep in Seoul, with the DP polling at 26.7 percent as opposed to the PPP’s 45.7 percent. One-fifth of South Koreans live in Seoul; track records in the capital thus tend to reflect where the swing voters stand. Oh Se-hoon, its current mayor, may lose the post should the Supreme Court uphold the special counsel’s charge that Oh allegedly paid a pollster to rig polls in his favor. (On October 23, the appellate court overturned his guilty verdict. The Supreme Court will rule on the case early next year.) The DP hopes to retake Seoul in a potential by-election, but with these poll numbers success is far from assured.
The DP’s popularity may still crater further. Given the touchy nature of the reform agenda still ahead for the Lee Jae-myung administration, the rest of this year and next year may not really be a rosy picture for the party. And then it will already be time for the 2028 general elections.
The party’s poor polling performance is of its own making, though. Choo, the governor of Gyeonggi-do, dealt the most immediate damage in a controversy that preceded the firefighter’s funeral
On October 13, during a parliamentary audit, Choo said that “firefighting is like a financial straw, causing the biggest headache.” She then elaborated on how much firefighters are setting back the province’s coffers. Firefighters’ unions went up in arms, wondering how the sacrifice of constantly putting their lives in jeopardy could be reduced to a budgetary complaint.
Choo ignored their calls for an apology. The province explained that her remark was in reference to the ballooning budgetary burden on the local government due to decreasing financial contributions from the central government – even though the firefighters are directly employed by the central government. Despite her true intention, Choo’s phrasing was no doubt inappropriate and hurtful. She was already facing steep criticism. Then October 16 changed everything.
A fire erupted in a metal printing factory in a town in Gyeonggi. Flames engulfed firefighter Kim Jin-seok, who passed away in the line of duty. The nation became even more infuriated with Choo’s callous analogy earlier.
The next day, Choo attended Kim’s funeral, where she finally apologized: “Since you want an apology, I wholeheartedly apologize.” You have to want to apologize for an apology to feel sincere. But she made it clear she was forced. Her apology duly backfired, to the point where she might have been better off not apologizing at all.
Making matters worse, when Kim Min-seok, the DP’s leader, arrived at the funeral his car parked in a spot reserved for emergency patients. It was a collective PR disaster for the party.
Choo has also been stirring the pot within the DP. She openly clashed with President Lee Jae-myung on the latter’s choice for head of the Serious Crime Investigation Agency (SCIA). It’s a new institution born out of abolishing the prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor’s office used to wield unchecked political powers through its dual authority to investigate and indict. Lee’s criminal justice reform and the DP’s legislation kiboshed this practice by distributing investigatory powers to the police and the SCIA, and indictment authority to the Prosecution Service, also a new body.
In September, when Lee picked Kim Ji-yong, a former prosecutor, to lead the SCIA, Choo maligned Lee by wondering out loud, “Why is he shivering before the insurrection forces?” Kim Yong-min, a popular hard-line DP legislator, joined forces with Choo. They believe Kim Ji-yong huddled around former President Yoon Suk-yeol when Yoon was chief prosecutor and that appointing Kim means giving in to the prosecutors and insurrection forces that aided and protected Yoon for his authoritarian practices and failed self-coup. For his part, Lee maintains that Kim was anti-Yoon.
Their public disagreement continued into this month. “Why appoint someone who can turn their back to the people and justice as the captain of our reform ship?” Choo wrote on October 2. On the same day, Kim Yong-min held a press conference publicly denouncing Kim Ji-yong for having always opposed prosecutorial reform. Meanwhile, Lee made repeated social media posts and a parliamentary submission arguing that the nominee had appropriate qualities needed to establish a trustworthy criminal justice system.
Voices in and out of the DP expressed concerns that such open defiance seemed to challenge Lee’s authority over personnel. The spat peaked in rhetoric on October 9, when Lee made a social media post maligning “those incompetents … who stage internal attacks purportedly for radical reform as a noble cause” when in fact they were complaining because “personnel and national policy didn’t go the way they wanted.”
Separately, the president’s online spat with Cho Kuk, a former justice minister who founded the Rebuilding Korea Party (RKP), further fractured the support for the DP. With 12 legislators in the National Assembly, Cho’s RKP is the third largest party after the DP and the PPP. Cho is also frequently mentioned as a strong contender for the next presidency. The RKP collaborated with the DP to boost liberal voters’ turnout during the 2024 April general elections.
The DP-RKP alliance became uncomfortable in June, however. When Cho ran for a parliamentary by-election, the DP fielded a candidate of its own – a choice many questioned. Liberal votes naturally split, and the PPP easily nabbed the seat.
Ever since, talk of merging the two parties has become fraught with grudges. Cho and Lee have also exchanged criticisms over each other’s stance on the extent of prosecutorial reform. Lee must have targeted Cho as well when he wrote on October 5 that his detractors “shouldn’t try to influence personnel choices and specific affairs of investigation and indictment in the name of prosecutorial reform and for selfish reasons.” (Cho and his wife served prison time after the prosecutors dug every dirt on them to stem former President Moon Jae-in’s and Cho’s effort to curtail the prosecutor’s office’s undue investigative and political powers.) Cho retorted that “the sense of crisis over the dissolution of our alliance has reached the boiling point.”
The past couple of months has seen Lee devoting a large portion of his time and energy to putting in place vociferous elements within the liberal camp. There are two reasons the president rolled up his sleeves to personally engage with critics.
First, Lee must be feeling isolated and betrayed. In September, he shared someone else’s post: “What hurts more are words from within than foes from without … In this chess game, we need to protect the queen that is Lee Jae-myung.” Second, Kim Min-seok, the DP leader who had Lee’s support in the August chair election, has failed to set the party’s house in order. He is kind and voluble but ineffective in quelling the internal unrest. His frequent warnings against those critical of Lee have fallen flat.
While the DP’s big shots are preoccupied with aggrandizing their own presence, the RPK’s support rating reached 9 percent, its highest since the onset of the Lee administration, according to the October 22 figures released by Media Tomato, another major pollster. On the one hand, it indicates the degree to which the DP let down even its core supporters. On the other hand, at least the overall support for the liberal bloc is still more robust than for the PPP. The most pressing thing would be learning how to coalesce at critical moments.

Why did humans’ brains surpass chimps’? A tiny foe might help explain it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:02:09 UTC
03:02:09 KST

Why did humans’ brains surpass chimps’? A tiny foe might help explain it
Ancient viral DNA bits are still in chimp genomes, possibly affecting brain genes
Viruses may be minuscule, but one could have influenced major differences between human and chimpanzee brains.
Millions of years ago, a virus left DNA behind in an African ape’s genome, and the genetic material stuck around in modern day chimps. Those ghosts of infections past appear to influence genes involved in neuron development, which may help explain how human and chimp brains ended up so different, researchers report October 23 in Science Advances.
Compared with the brains of their chimpanzee kin, human brains are three times larger and more cognitively powerful. Yet “most of their protein-making genes are very similar,” says Johan Jakobsson, a neuroscientist at Lund University in Sweden. In the absence of large differences in the genetic code, Jakobsson and his colleagues decided to look at the parts of the human and chimp genome that control when and where genes are turned on or off.
Changes in gene regulation can come from viruses. Some viruses called retroviruses insert their own DNA into their hosts’ genomes to command host cells to build more viruses. But those parasitic bits of DNA can linger long after an infection. If this happens in reproductive cells, the viral DNA gets passed down with the host’s DNA.
These leftover bits, called endogenous retroviruses, no longer code for the production of infectious viruses, but they can have a big impact on the host’s biology — especially if they make copies of themselves across the genome. And they have. Such viral remnants make up at least 8 percent of the genomes of humans and chimps alike. More generally, these DNA leftovers have been linked with some major evolutionary events, such as the evolution of the mammalian placenta.
Jakobsson and his colleagues focused on a particular viral vestige in chimps. The holdover came from an infection in an ancestral African ape somewhere between 5 million and 7 million years ago. In chimpanzees, the viral DNA had stuck itself into the genome at 158 different locations. However, it is curiously absent in humans. It’s still unknown why.
The researchers wanted to know how that exact pathogen footprint might affect chimpanzees’ brains compared with those of humans. Working with chimpanzee stem cells, they removed the viral DNA using CRISPR, a gene editing technology that allows for precise, targeted cuts in DNA. Once the viral DNA was gone, a nearby gene called LINC00662 — normally silenced in chimpanzees — turned on, making RNA the team could detect. This matches the normal condition in human brain cells, in which LINC00662 is active. The team also used CRISPR to shut off LINC00662 in the human cells, matching the silenced condition seen in chimpanzees.
When LINC00662 was active in chimp or human cells, the researchers noticed activity boosts to other genes that may be important to brain development — such as genes involved in the development and maturation of neurons and in making new neural connections. It’s not yet clear exactly how the viral DNA’s shutdown of this brain gene network affected the biology of chimpanzee brains. However, this genetic difference may have contributed to a divergence in how human and chimpanzee brains evolved, Jakobsson says. “Our findings show one way an ancient viral [DNA] insertion could create a lasting difference in how a gene is regulated in humans and chimpanzees,” Jakobsson says. Other genetic and environmental changes could be involved in the puzzle as well, he says.
Researchers have previously looked to single letter swaps in DNA to help explain how humans and chimp brains drifted apart in their evolution. But the new study highlights that creatures can rack up genome changes in other ways, says Giorgia Modenini, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Padua in Italy who was not involved with this research.
The researchers do a convincing job of showing that these particular viral leftovers influence developmental differences between human and chimp neurons, says Ravinder Kanda, an evolutionary geneticist at Oxford Brookes University in Oxford, England. “They’ve proved that absolutely. How far that goes, I don’t think we can quite say yet.”
It could be that other controls on genes’ activity are also involved or that this particular ancient lever-puller may represent just a sliver of the viral holdovers that have shaped brain development, Kanda says. “I think there are many, many more retroviruses to be discovered, and at the moment we’ve only touched the tip of the iceberg.”

Defence equipment spending in the year to March 2026 was £5 billion lower than in the previous year, which industry witnesses described as an indication of the Ministry of Defence working to stay within its budget, according to evidence given to the Defence Committee.
Kevin Craven, chief executive of ADS, gave the figure during a session on the implications of the Defence Investment Plan for British industry.
He said: “In terms of orders, what is probably interesting to note is that the equipment spend to the year ending March 2026 was £5 billion less than in the previous year, which is an indication of the MOD looking to remain within its budget or live within its means. We are hearing all of this language. The lived experience on the ground is that it is still hard to get orders.”
Craven said there have been procurement announcements since the plan was published, including the Royal Oak programme for the mobile docks on the Clyde and rapid procurement processes covering £1.4 billion around defence artificial intelligence.
He also told MPs that it was unclear whether around a third of the £298 billion announced in the plan is unfunded or simply not articulated in the right way.
On the additional £15 billion provided to defence, Craven said: “We are concerned. The MOD has a long history of baking in efficiency savings to its plans and then not necessarily being able to deliver them. The commitment to deliver those is not the same thing as doing so.”
He pointed the committee to a change in the department’s own provisions, saying: “One of the interesting things about the DIP was that the central contingencies held by the MOD were increased from 1.2% to 2% over the spending period, which is perhaps indicative of some of their own cynicism around the ability to deliver those efficiencies and savings.”
Craven said the difficulty of transforming the department while implementing a major shift in capability makes the savings harder to realise.
Julian David of techUK told the committee that nearly £5 billion is dependent on the Budget, and that there was potential confusion over whether the Budget would deliver it or whether it would wait for the spending review. He said waiting would be a very big mistake and would compound delays already identified.
Wes Streeting, the Secretary of State for Defence, told the committee the previous week that the Chancellor has said he will plug a £4.7 billion gap at the Budget, with more to come at the spending review. Jeremy Pocklington, the Permanent Secretary, told MPs that additional support received between John Healey’s resignation and Dan Jarvis settling the plan increased the department’s spending power by £15 billion.
Craven told the committee that the National Armaments Director group, the aggregation of departments now reporting to Rupert Pearce, numbers some 25,000 people, and that transforming the department while implementing a strategic shift is causing large amounts of pain within it.
