Since Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by imposing speed limits on Starshield, the military-grade Starlink offering. Any drone traveling above 100 mph lost its connection, disrupting some missions, officials said.
Despite recent comments from President Donald Trump that indicated service was restored, Ukraine's Starshield terminals continued to experience problems on Friday, said Dmitri Alperovitch, chairman of the Silverado Policy Accelerator, a Washington, D.C., think tank focused on energy, defense tech and global trade.
"They are losing drones," Alperovitch, who is also a co-founder and former chief technology officer of cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike, told CNBC. "Ability to do mid strike to hit Russian logistics is now limited."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Friday post on X that the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield "are still there," and added, "The speed has not been restored." He noted that the country is also waiting for the U.S. to deliver missile interceptors "that were already agreed on."
"Things have become harder — partly because of the Starlink and Starshield policies and speed limits," Zelenskyy wrote. "But our frontline is still holding and I am proud of how strong our people are."
Zelenskyy's defense tech advisor, Serhii Beskrestnov, also confirmed the restrictions were in place in a post on his Telegram channel.
"While there are isolated cases where Starlink may operate somewhat beyond the established limits, this is likely a result of SpaceX's algorithms or specific usage conditions, rather than an actual removal of restrictions," Beskrestnov said in a post translated by Google.
Elon Musk and representatives from SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Who is ultimately responsible for the decision to limit Ukraine's service remains unclear.
Democratic lawmakers have since called for an investigation into Musk and the Starshield throttling. A group of bipartisan lawmakers penned a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday urging the agency to "act expeditiously to expand its Starshield arrangements and ensure uninterrupted satellite communications support for Ukraine."
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump spoke to Musk by phone about lifting the restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield terminals. Trump said Thursday he didn't "want to comment one way or the other" about whether he made the call to Musk, and added, "The bottom line, he put it back."
But on Friday, Trump insisted that he hadn't spoken with Musk, and reiterated that Starshield service had been restored.
"I've heard it was fixed," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "But if it's not, I'll speak to him."
Amid the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy and other Ukrainian officials have floated the possibility of adopting additional satellite internet communications systems. Experts previously told CNBC that it could prove challenging for Ukraine or other countries to secure alternatives to Starlink since other options are not yet comparable to the service.
Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday in a post on X that he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors."
On Thursday, Ukraine's Ministry of Defense signed a letter of intent with Nokia and ICEYE, a Finnish space intelligence firm, to "explore cooperation in space" and "support Ukraine's defense capabilities, particularly in building sovereign satellite communications," the companies said in a release.
"Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security," Zelenskyy said in a statement. "We must all rely on capabilities that we can control."

Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security with 19.5 million people experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, the UK and 31 international partners have warned in a joint statement.
The statement on Friday called for urgent action to avert famine in the coming months, citing warnings from the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC).
An estimated 41 percent of Sudan’s population is facing acute food insecurity, including 5 million people experiencing emergency levels of hunger, according to the statement.
Without immediate intervention, the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000, while the number of food-insecure areas, initially assessed at 14, is expected to double.
“Conflict is the key driver of Sudan’s hunger crisis,” the statement said, noting that fighting has displaced millions, damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted health care, food production, supply chains and markets.
The crisis has been further aggravated by systematic obstruction of humanitarian aid and the effects of El Nino, which has reduced rainfall and increased drought across more than half of the country, it added.
Unimpeded humanitarian access
The civil war between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces erupted in April 2023.
It has since displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The partners urged the warring parties to remove all obstacles to humanitarian assistance and ensure “full, safe, rapid, and unimpeded humanitarian access,” while protecting aid workers.
They called for humanitarian operations to be authorised through all cross-line and cross-border routes, including air access into Darfur, and urged measures to reduce bureaucratic delays affecting aid delivery.
The statement also called on the parties to refrain from attacks on civilian infrastructure, including agricultural and food systems, and strengthen coordination to protect humanitarian personnel and sites.
Urging the international community to scale up funding, the partners stressed the need to support the winter cropping season and strengthen locally led responses.
“Together we must act without delay to avert famine,” the statement said, expressing solidarity with Sudanese people and humanitarian organisations working to deliver life-saving assistance under extremely challenging conditions.

DOJ sues to block Alaska from certifying Senate race winner if Republican narrowly loses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:04:10 UTC
02:04:10 KST

The Department of Justice filed an extraordinary lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying the winner of its upcoming U.S. Senate election if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses the contest.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 election, cites what it argues is likely voter confusion from the name of another candidate appearing on the ballot, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan.
The DOJ says that could help Democratic nominee Mary Peltola defeat the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, in what is expected to be a close contest.
The Alaska race is among several closely watched Senate races that could determine control of the chamber. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority.
The suit asks a federal judge in Alaska to bar the state from certifying "any result that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
The DOJ did not say how anyone could determine a voter's intent. Doing so might be impossible, given the anonymity of ballots.
"The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska," says the suit filed Thursday in U.S. District Court in Alaska. In addition to the state, the complaint names Alaska Elections Division Director Carol Beecher, the state's election boards and the state Ballot Counting Review Board as defendants.
President Donald Trump on Friday told reporters that he had set the lawsuit in motion.
"I'm the one that said 'do it,'" Trump said in Fort Myers, Florida while traveling for a political rally. "They have two guys ... named Dan Sullivan, so the Democrats put up a guy."
Before the suit was filed Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that the DOJ had no plans to "improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process."
"There's no circumstances that we would ever do that," he said at a press conference. "Of course I'm not going to say that. But am I planning my days around the election to be somewhere to not certify? Of course not, no, not at all."
The DOJ's suit alleges that Daniel J. Sullivan's "sole purpose" of running for the Senate "is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan." Sullivan first registered as a Republican earlier this year. He previously was a member of the Alaska Independence Party.
The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the Alaska Senate race as one of seven "toss-up" contests for that chamber. The election tracking site FiftyPlusOne's average of polling shows Peltola, a former U.S. House member from Alaska, with just a 2-percentage-point lead over Sullivan.
The suit came hours after Trump, in a Truth Social post, wrote, "I am very concerned about the Dan S. Sullivan Race for the U.S. Senate in Alaska in that it is totally confusing, with the Dumocrats putting up another man, totally unrelated to Politics, named Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr."
"It's ridiculous that the Court didn't stop this SCAM. Even 1, 2, or 3% could make the difference," Trump said.
"We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness."
Alaska's general election for the Senate uses ranked-choice voting. Voters rank their candidates in order of preference. If no candidate gets more than 50% in round one, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated in the second round, and that process continues until there are just two candidates and the winner is the one with the most votes.
"Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot threatens to mislead Alaskan citizens who want to vote for Senator Sullivan," the suit says. "For example, some supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan."
"Other supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will be confused as to how to rank the three Republican candidates as to defeat Peltola," the suit says. "They might not rank Senator Sullivan at all, resulting in votes for Daniel J. Sullivan to be transferred to Peltola after Daniel J. Sullivan's all-but-guaranteed elimination in the first or second round of tabulations."
In a statement to CNBC, a DOJ spokesperson said, "Alaska's Division of Elections determined that Mr. Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot."
"Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters," the spokesperson said.
Nate Adams, the campaign spokesman for Sen. Sullivan, said, "We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course."
"Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska, a record he'll keep building on for the next six years," Adams said.
Harry Child, a spokesman for Peltola's campaign, said, "This is a despicable political threat to overturn an election, designed by Senator Dan Sullivan's allies to suppress the voices of Alaskans because Sullivan is terrified he'll lose the seat that has allowed him to enrich himself at Alaskans' expense for over a decade."
"We will fight to ensure every single eligible voter in Alaska can make their voice heard and that no bureaucrat or politician from the Lower 48 can interfere with our lawful, secure elections," Child said.
CNBC has requested comment from Daniel J. Sullivan, Alaska's attorney general, and state election officials.
Daniel J. Sullivan, in a social media post in June, said, "I entered this race because I am unhappy with the 12 year record of the current Senator and I feel we need a change. It's that simple."
Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, in a statement to CNBC said, "Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses."
Daniel J. Sullivan originally was blocked from the state's primary ballot in June, after the Alaska Division of Elections said his declaration of candidacy was not properly filed, and because of a finding that the candidacy was aimed at duping voters who planned to vote for Sen. Sullivan.
The division cited his request to appear on the ballot as 'Dan Sullivan,' his recent switch to the Republican Party and his work with a political consultant described as a longtime supporter of Democratic candidates, including Peltola, according to the DOJ complaint.
Daniel J. Sullivan was added to the ballot after challenging the division's decision in state court. The Alaska Supreme Court later upheld that decision.
Daniel J. Sullivan received just 2.5% of the vote in Alaska's open primary on Aug. 28, but that was enough to win him one of four spots on the Senate general election ballot.
Peltola got 49.5% in the primary, and Sen. Sullivan received 41.4%. Another Republican, Gerald Heikes, received just 1.1% of the primary vote, earning him the fourth spot on the ballot.
Although Daniel J. Sullivan sought to run as a Republican, the Division of Elections decided not to list that party next to his name on the general election ballot. His name is spelled out, "Daniel J. Sullivan," and there are no other words on that line.
Both Sen. Sullivan, who has been in the Senate since 2015, and Heikes have the words "registered Republican" in parentheses next to their names.
And Sen. Sullivan, listed on the ballot as Dan S. Sullivan, also has the word "incumbent" next to his name.
— CNBC's Justin Papp contributed to this article.

The 3.5% Rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:01:15 UTC
02:01:15 KST

Hello everybody,
This week we’re looking at what’s needed for change. And to do that, we’ve partnered with the team rereleasing V for Vendetta, a film I enjoy, and whose Guy Fawkes mask has arguably become one of this century’s most iconic political symbols of change.
V for Vendetta hits theaters on November 1 & 5 in the U.S. Click here to get your tickets.
I increasingly like Threads.
Threads is Meta’s version of Twitter, and I find myself pressing its squiggly little logo more and more often. There’s the usual AI slop and bilious nonsense, but I find these few are outweighed by genuinely funny jokes and mostly interesting people.
Every so often, though, my Threads is overwhelmed by a pile-on. Disney+ has upped its prices, Netflix is cracking down on account-sharing, YouTube is changing its payouts, and Meta has updated its TOS to the disadvantage of the everyday user.
“It’s time to go!”
“So, where are we heading then?”
“This is the last straw,” says John from Inverness.
People angrily, vocally, performatively declare they’ve had enough. They’re going to leave. They’re going to join this new app. They post screenshots of a canceled subscription.
And yet, these apps get bigger and richer. Disney keeps raising its streaming prices. YouTube brought in more than $60 billion last year, and Americans now spend more of their TV time on it than on Netflix — or the whole of Disney. Meta’s apps are used by 3.6 billion people a day, and Threads alone passed 500 million monthly users in June. And when Netflix told password-sharers to pay up, more people signed up.
The thing is, these companies have spent decades and billions creating what the business lot call a “moat.” A moat is when your audience essentially has to stay with you because there’s nowhere else to go. It might be OneDrive hoarding all your family photos. It might be a Facebook page you need for your company’s visibility. It might be that no other company has all the Pixar, Marvel, and Star Wars movies all together.
And so, when you are trapped behind a moat, it can feel like you’re trapped. John from Inverness wants to let Netflix know he’s unhappy, but he’s small fry. “Let’s boycott Meta,” people say on Threads, owned by Meta, which also owns WhatsApp. And thousands download a new app created by an exciting new startup alternative, only to return within days after finding it glitchy, boring, or empty.
This feeling of trapped hopelessness is not unique to capitalism. It’s in politics too. So this week I want to explore the question: Just how far can any of us actually change things? How far can we shake up the world?
Go well,
Jonny
The need of a hero
The problem with any “what would you do?” scenario is that hardly any of us actually know.
“What would you do in 1930s Germany?”
“What would you do if you had to kill five people to save your family?”
“Would you sacrifice yourself to save ten strangers?”
When we answer these questions, we do so in the calm and rational light of day. But if you ever found yourself in a war zone or in any life-or-death situation, there is very little that is rational. What we think we’ll do now and what we would actually do are worlds apart.
In 2025, I spoke with Paul Lynch about his Booker Prize-winning novel, Prophet Song. The book explores the messy reality of what life would be like for those caught up in things. The novel is set in a dystopian Ireland turning toward totalitarianism. And, like many in 1930s Germany, the main character, Eilish, has opportunities to leave. Go to Britain. Go to America. Go somewhere else. But life is complex. Eilish has kids in school, a job that pays for her life, and family to look after. Totalitarianism doesn’t plop down with a swastika or a Stalin; it creeps. It edges in. And as with all creep, it’s hard to know when things go too far. It’s apparently false that frogs will stay in warming water until they boil. What’s true, though, is that humans will often stay around and do nothing until it’s “too late.” But then, when was it the right time?
The writer Susan Sontag supposedly said that “10 percent of any population is cruel, no matter what, and 10 percent is merciful, no matter what, and the remaining 80 percent can be moved in either direction.” And if you’ve spent any time looking at the bystander effect — either in formal publications or in real-life examples — you will likely agree. People tend to go along with things. Charitably, we could call this evolutionary wiring — we’re built to get along and fit in. Less charitably, you could say we’re mostly selfish. We care only for our own skin. So long as I’m okay, what does it matter?
There is both hope and dread in those minority fringes. In any society, it often takes a surprisingly small number of people to pull everyone this way or that. In the 2010s, the Harvard professor Erica Chenoweth popularized the 3.5% rule. Chenoweth analyzed 323 resistance campaigns from 1900 to 2006 and found that every campaign in her dataset succeeded or partially succeeded after achieving active participation of 3.5% of the population at the movement’s peak. (She’s since noted that the 3.5% figure is a tendency, not a law.) In Moral Ambition, the historian Rutger Bregman points out the disproportionate power a few determined individuals can have in changing things.
And this is where we find the idea of the hero.
In movies, a hero will often have special powers. Magic hammers, superintelligence, laser eyes. In real life, a hero is someone who rallies the forces of good in the world. I’m sorry if that sounds a bit like Lord of the Rings, but sometimes a cliché does the job. A hero catalyzes people. They remind us what the right thing is, and they become an emblem.
This is something explored well in the movie and graphic novel V for Vendetta.
V for Vendetta is set in a dystopian future where a totalitarian government called Norsefire runs the country with fear, propaganda, and brutality. Into this comes V, a freedom-fighting antihero in a Guy Fawkes mask. Near the end of the movie, V says, “Beneath this mask there is more than flesh.” He follows this with, “Beneath this mask, there is an idea, and ideas are bulletproof.”
Yes, V for Vendetta is a superhero movie of sorts. A superantihero movie, really. But it also explores something brilliantly philosophical — something morally gray. Because the main character, V, is not a Socratic model of heroism. He hasn’t reflected on justice to Do The Right Thing™.
While V might object to Norsefire, he was also radicalized. He was tortured and abused by the system. As V tells Evey, “What was done to me was monstrous.” Her reply: “And they created a monster.” V fits my Tolkienesque definition of hero not because of his motivation — ultimately, a vendetta — but because of what he represents. He is an idea incarnate. He is a Guy Fawkes mask, and it’s vitally important to the movie and the message that the man underneath is not seen.
So, should we feel hopeless? Probably not. It takes only a small minority of good people — 3.5% if Chenoweth is right. And 3.5% will often just need to follow someone. John from Inverness was never going to bankrupt Netflix on his own. But if John’s message took off, if John became a symbol, then he might well start the process. Just look at Spain to see the power one person — one tragic story — can have.
What history shows is that you don’t need everyone. You need a few people who mean it, and who stay fighting for long enough for others to join in. Beneath the canceled subscription, there has to be an idea. And an idea is bulletproof.
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

Energy costs driving manufacturers abroad, MPs told
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:00:46 BST
02:00:46 KST

Britain has seen an enormous flight of businesses this year because it has become uncompetitive to manufacture goods here, with larger companies finding the arithmetic works better in France and Germany, according to evidence given to the Defence Committee.
Stephen Phipson, chief executive of MakeUK, raised the point during a session on the implications of the Defence Investment Plan for British industry.
He said: “There is a wider point that I would like to make about manufacturing in this country, which is something that we have been talking to the Chancellor about. In fact, Julian and I were with the Chancellor this morning on this very subject. We are now losing a lot of companies because it is uncompetitive to manufacture goods here. That is because of energy costs in the UK.”
He continued: “This year, we have had an enormous flight of businesses out of the UK. In particular, larger companies are finding it hard to allocate capital to UK capability because the maths works better if you do it in France and Germany than it does in the UK. It is very difficult to isolate that just to the MOD, but there is a wider issue about the competitiveness of manufacturing in this country, which, to be fair, the Chancellor recognised this morning as a key issue for growth.”
Kevin Craven of ADS told MPs that price is not the only problem, saying grid connections are “now running at eight to 10 years versus an average of about four years anywhere else”, and that the same pressures show in skills and the supply of componentry. He said a broader economic focus is needed to secure the defence technology and wider defence sector.
Craven said government can help through enablement in areas such as skills and by considering the general business context, and named the carbon border adjustment mechanism as another measure coming down the track that makes it expensive to do business in Britain.
On firms leaving, Craven told the committee the numbers are low, that companies are nonetheless going, and that the United States and Europe represent more attractive defence markets at present. Julian David of techUK said the number saying they will no longer be in Britain is low, but that firms are shifting emphasis and investment money.
David also told MPs that international members who came to Britain to invest are not seeing a resulting pathway to growth and business, and are asking whether they made the wrong decision to expand here.
Arnab Dutt of the Federation of Small Businesses said British firms are finding opportunities abroad, particularly in the Baltics and northern Europe where countries see the threat as imminent. He said that if their capacity is taken up elsewhere, even though they would rather be working in Britain, the country will lose out, and described the risk to capability over the next few years as potentially very dangerous.
Phipson told the committee that Britain does not lack industrial capacity, pointing to thousands of smaller firms already exporting defence technology to other nations and to the automotive sector, which employs six hundred thousand people and has capacity available. He said those companies would rather be doing the work with their own Ministry of Defence.

Why we fear death and how to live with it: Prof. Yoram Yovell explains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:59:52 UTC
01:59:52 KST

In The Epic of Gilgamesh, written some 4,000 years ago, the king of the city of Uruk is portrayed as a hero who battles monsters and accomplishes seemingly impossible feats. But when his friend Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh realizes something that even his greatest victories had not prepared him for: One day, he too will die. For the first time, Gilgamesh confronts a truth he cannot bear. He leaves his city and sets out in search of the one thing he lacks. Yet after a long and dangerous journey, he returns home defeated, having failed to discover a way to live forever.
Gilgamesh or no Gilgamesh, several thousand years later, we're still in much the same place. Running away. Somewhere in a hidden corner of our minds, we know that life will eventually end, whether we like it or not, but we struggle to truly grasp what that means. After all, there are still things to do: visit the Galápagos Islands, go to that concert we've always promised ourselves we'd attend, make peace with an old friend after a falling-out over something utterly trivial.
Death appears in the news, in conversations and in announcements about people we once knew, certainly here in our little corner of the world. But most of the time, we manage to carry on. Until, at some point, that abstract knowledge becomes intensely personal. Throughout history, humanity has searched for almost every imaginable way to live with that thought, or somehow escape it.
"When we exist, death has not yet arrived, and when death arrives, we no longer exist," wrote the ancient Greek philosopher Epicurus, attempting to soften the blow by pointing out that we will never actually be there to experience the thing that frightens us so much.
Nearly 2,000 years later, the 16th-century French writer and philosopher Michel de Montaigne offered a different, more practical solution. "I want death to find me planting my cabbages," he wrote. If we must die, we might as well be productive until the final moment. Two very different ways of coping with the same knowledge.
Woody Allen managed to compress the entire debate into a single joke: "I'm not afraid of death. I just don't want to be there when it happens." Television host Larry King was equally reluctant to accept that the life he had already lived would be enough.
"My biggest fear is death," King said in 2011, explaining that he wanted his body frozen in the hope that future technology might bring him back to life. Asked what would happen if he returned 200 years later and no longer knew anyone, he had a ready answer: "I'll meet new people."
Meanwhile, as Israeli singer Yuval Banai sang in Mashina's song "The Society for the Study of Mortality," everyone must die eventually. The question is what we do with that knowledge until then. How do we keep making plans, getting angry, swearing in traffic and thinking about what to cook for dinner when somewhere in the back of our minds sits the thought that one day, all of this will end?
What will the last day of your life look like?
"When human beings ate from the Tree of Knowledge, something terrible happened to them," says Prof. Yoram Yovell, a psychiatrist and brain researcher at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. "After all, their choice was between eating from the Tree of Knowledge and eating from the Tree of Life. They lost the possibility of living forever and understood, for the first time, something that apparently only human beings understand in the entire animal kingdom: that our lives will end."
Animals are familiar with death too, he emphasizes. "Social animals, both mammals and birds, are not indifferent to it. We know of elephants that remain beside the bodies of dead members of their herds. We know that animals can recognize when death is approaching. But there's a difference between that and an understanding that, as far as we know, no other creature in the history of the Earth shares with us: that we ourselves are going to die and will no longer exist."
Now try making plans for next year with that realization hanging over your head. According to Yovell, the effort to live with this knowledge explains far more than the moments when we consciously think about death.
"A great deal of human behavior can be explained by our attempts to cope with this terrible fact, which we understand, which makes us feel awful, and which we somehow have to live with," he says.
The problem is that we invest considerable effort, and suffer considerable anguish, in finding that "somehow."
"There are some very famous experiments in which ordinary people are asked to imagine the final moments of their lives: What will the last day of your life look like? Write a few sentences about it," Yovell explains.
"What we see is that many measures of distress increase. When you ask people to perform this small mental exercise, you see some interesting patterns that repeat themselves. Their anxiety levels rise, their hostility toward people outside their social group increases, and they develop a stronger sense of closeness to the people nearest to them.
"We're extremely sensitive to this issue. Usually, we manage to repress it successfully. I don't wake up in the morning thinking about the fact that I'm going to die either. But when it enters our consciousness, it doesn't make us feel good."
What are we actually afraid of? The pain, the separation, the loss of consciousness, or the life we won't get to live?
"I think that, as is often the case in psychology, all of the answers are correct. Many of us are afraid of pain, but the fact is that today, the possibility of a painless death is within reach through a few simple internet searches, and yet most of us don't choose it. We keep living, and we keep living even when things are difficult and painful. To do that, we need something that gives us hope. Something that provides motivation or comfort, so we can go on."
Today there are many biohackers, people who try to improve their health, brains and longevity through self-experimentation and technology, as well as people who declare that they will achieve immortality. Do you think this comes from that fear?
"Of course. Absolutely. And by the way, it won't work. That's completely clear. Let's say, for the sake of argument, that somebody manages to extend their life by a thousand years. So what? Eventually, it will still end. You're postponing the problem, which isn't such a bad thing either."
The immense power of religion
Human beings know how to draw conclusions, but we also know how to avoid them when necessary. When it comes to death, we have good reason to want to look away. And so, being the sophisticated creatures we are, we have developed our own ways of living alongside the deeply unpleasant knowledge that one day, someone will switch off the lights on this whole celebration we call life. Most of the time, it works.
"When a particular fact is unbearable for us, the most basic psychological mechanism is to deny its existence," Yovell says. "When small children hear or see something frightening, they often close their eyes. You can tell them, 'Wait a minute, you do understand that closing your eyes doesn't mean the monster stops existing, or that whatever is frightening you disappears.' But at a very basic level, that's a psychological mechanism.
"As we grow older, we develop more sophisticated and less harmful mechanisms for doing this, because ignoring danger is not a good thing."
But denial also has a disadvantage: Reality is under no obligation to cooperate. And when it insists on reminding us how fragile everything is, as it did on October 7, we also need a story that allows us to keep going. Preferably one in which separation is not final, and there is still a chance of seeing the people we love again.
"Our ability to tell ourselves stories that bring us comfort is important and powerful, and that is the immense power of religions," Yovell says. "Religion tells us that the end of life is not the end of the story. Something continues after death. And that knowledge, or that thought, or what some people might call that illusion, is tremendously comforting. We mustn't dismiss it. It's something very important."
And not only does it offer comfort, but this is apparently not an invention exclusive to our species.
"We, Homo sapiens, aren't the only ones who had this form of consolation," Yovell explains. "We share it with the Neanderthals. How do we know? Archaeological findings, some of them discovered in the Land of Israel, show that Neanderthals buried their dead with provisions for the journey: food, weapons, things they would need in the world beyond.
"It's clear that the Neanderthals believed they could do something to make life easier for the people they loved in the world awaiting them after death."
And yet, Yovell himself finds it difficult to accept the promise of an existence beyond death. "Religion is important, and it gives strength to many people, but I'll tell you my personal opinion: It doesn't stand up to the test of reality," he explains.
"Nobody has ever come back from the afterlife and said, 'Yes, yes, it's true. This is only the beginning.' There are all those cases of people who nearly died and then came back saying they saw a great light. With all due respect, they didn't actually die.
"When I look at things through the scientific lens, we don't have even a shred of evidence that consciousness continues after death. The impression is that it doesn't."
Doing the right thing
Not exactly the answer most of us would want to hear, if we're being truthful. But Yovell offers another solution. Instead of asking, "Will we still be here?" he suggests beginning with the question, "What will we do while we're here?"
It may be less exciting than a promise of eternal life, but at least it's something we can get up tomorrow morning and act on, rather than clinging to things that may or may not exist. Quite practical, really.
"I think that religions, and not only religions, also offer an approach that says: Given that your life is going to end, what are you doing with the life you've been given, here and now, today, to do the right thing, to feel that you've contributed, to feel that you've accomplished something?" he asks. From there, he outlines two different approaches.
"You can see it in Maimonides' Guide for the Perplexed, in the great distinction between faith for its own sake and faith that is not for its own sake," he explains.
"Faith that is not for its own sake says: I believe in God and observe the commandments because I hope that if I do so, God will look after me. We mustn't dismiss that. Maimonides didn't dismiss it, and neither do I.
"If you want to see it in our own society, think of the words, 'God always loves me, and everything will always be good for me.' That is the essence of faith that is not for its own sake. You believe in God, and you believe that God will take care of you, protect you and make sure everything turns out well for you.
"But Maimonides says there is another kind of faith, one practiced by only a few, and that is faith for its own sake. It says: I believe in God not because of what God will do for me, but because of what I will do to make this world a better place.
"My faith moves from the bottom upward. I do something for the God I believe in, something I think God wants from me. I don't sit around wondering how God will pamper me, save me or what he will do for me."
Meaning?
"Come, let me tell you a story about my grandfather," Yovell says, referring to the late Prof. Yeshayahu Leibowitz, the religious scientist and philosopher known for his sharp tongue.
"My grandfather wrote extensively about these matters and, of course, thought about them very much like Maimonides," he says.
"He told me about a conversation he had with a very senior figure in Israel's legal world, a Supreme Court justice. He was a moral and decent man who had thought deeply about these questions.
"The man told him that after Auschwitz and World War II, he had lost the ability to believe in God.
"And then my grandfather said to him, 'You know, I think that if that's the case, then before Auschwitz you didn't believe in God. You believed in God's help. You believed that God was watching over us and would help us, and at Auschwitz God neither watched over us nor helped us.
"'But if you don't expect that in the first place, if your faith is such that you don't ask what God will do for me, but instead ask what my duty is in this world, what I need to do and how I should behave, given that my life is so short and will end, what am I supposed to do right now? If that's the question you're asking, then that is faith for its own sake.'"
We can continue arguing about what awaits us in the next world. In this one, meanwhile, there is more than enough work to do. And the sense of meaning Yovell finds in that work is something he also offers to people who have no religious faith to rely on.
"I think this idea is very important," he says. "It's what Albert Camus proposed, and what Viktor Frankl, who was also in Auschwitz, proposes in Man's Search for Meaning. It's also what the Buddha taught, if you look at Buddhism not as a religion, but at what the Buddha told his followers:
"Use this life to leave the world a slightly better place than you found it. That's the challenge. I think that's the answer. And especially now, for us here, during these difficult days we're all going through, that's what should guide us."

Thailand revokes Israeli woman's visa over 'bad behaviour'
Unknown

2026-10-23
16:58:55 UTC
01:58:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Thailand revokes Israeli woman's visa over 'threats, bad behaviour'
Authorities on the Thai island of Koh Phangan have revoked an Israeli woman’s visa following reports of alleged misconduct and aggressive behaviour on several occasions while she was working there.
The woman, identified as 33-year-old Ensav Ashual, was accused of directing abusive remarks and using offensive language towards authorities, according to The Bangkok Post, which cited a committee reportedly established to monitor the behaviour of foreigners on the island of Koh Samui.
Ashual also allegedly refused to pay for accommodation and entrance fees at Than Sadet Ko Phangan National Park, known for its wildlife, the newspaper reported.
The committee responsible for her case did not explicitly identify the type of visa Ashual held.
She is reported to have worked on Koh Phangan as an art therapist and breathwork guide, although it has not been independently confirmed whether she held a work visa.
Israeli nationals can visit Thailand visa-free for tourism for up to 30 days, but this exemption does not permit them to work.
Ashual is the third Israeli national on Koh Phangan to have had her visa revoked. Ten foreign nationals on the island have had their visas withdrawn since January this year.
The latest incident comes amid growing anger in Thailand over a series of incidents involving Israeli tourists since the outbreak of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza on 7 October 2023.
Thailand, along with other Southeast Asian countries, has become a popular destination for Israeli travellers, including many former soldiers.
Reports have documented Israeli military veterans travelling in the region after their service, including individuals who took part in Israel's onslaught on Gaza, where more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since 2023.
Critics in Thailand have raised concerns about alleged illegal land acquisition, breaches of local laws and behaviour perceived as disrespectful towards local communities.
Despite maintaining warm relations with Israel, the Thai government has raised concerns with Israeli officials, stressing that Israeli nationals must respect the country’s laws and culture.
In September, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said he had held a “frank discussion” with Israeli Ambassador Alona Fisher-Kamm about concerns involving some Israeli nationals.
These included businesspeople suspected of using Thai nominees to circumvent foreign ownership restrictions, as well as tourists accused of causing friction with local communities on Koh Phangan, Koh Samui and Phuket.
“Thailand is a country that welcomes tourists, but at the same time, that doesn’t mean tourists, regardless of nationality, can do whatever they want,” Sihasak told reporters at a press briefing in Bangkok following the meeting.
He stressed that visitors must “respect Thai traditions, culture and local ways of life”, adding that Thailand would enforce its laws against foreign nationals regardless of nationality.
Fisher-Kamm acknowledged the concerns and agreed to step up efforts to inform Israeli visitors about appropriate conduct in Thailand, Sihasak said.
The New Arab contacted the Israeli embassy in Thailand and the Department of South Asian, Middle East and African Affairs under Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment, but did not receive a response by the time of publication.
Israeli arrivals in Thailand have increased in recent years, with more than 277,000 recorded in the first eight months of 2026 - a 7% rise compared with the same period last year. This followed a reported 45% increase in 2024.
Growing criticism has also fuelled local protests, with members of the Thai public condemning recent incidents.
The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement in Thailand has called on the government to stop sending Thai migrant workers to Israel, to screen Israeli tourists, and arrest those suspected of war crimes.
It has also urged Thailand to end arms trading and military agreements with Israel, impose sanctions, and ultimately sever diplomatic relations.
Late last month, Thai authorities announced an investigation into as many as nine Jewish centres, known as Chabad houses, across the country.
The investigation has brought renewed attention to the Chabad-Lubavitch movement, a global Jewish religious movement headquartered in the United States.

Fewer people are flying as airfare soars. Here's why airlines aren't worried
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:51:21 UTC
01:51:21 KST

Fewer people are flying this year, but with airfare this high and climbing, airline executives say that's just fine.
The number of people screened at U.S. checkpoints is on track for its first annual decline since 2020. Major U.S. carriers have said capturing higher fares is more important than fully filling their planes or flying record numbers of travelers.
"We're actively prioritizing yield versus load factor and really happy as we see it. It fits right in with the premium investments that we're making," American Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said on the company's earnings call Thursday.
American's load factor, a gauge of how full planes are flying, fell to 83.4% in the third quarter from 86% in the same quarter of 2025.
Fares keep climbing
The price of plane tickets has skyrocketed as airlines grapple with a spike in jet fuel prices, their biggest expense after labor, and pass more of those costs on to customers.
Fares in September were up more than 22% from a year earlier, according to the latest inflation read. Fare tracker Hopper said it expects this holiday season to come with the most expensive ticket prices in years.
The average Southwest Airlines fare in the third quarter, for example, was $231.69, up close to $50 from a year earlier. That doesn't include Southwest's new fees, like its extra charges for checked bags or a seat closer to the front of the plane.
The airline's count of revenue passengers, however, fell 3.2% from a year ago, to about 33.5 million people.
Still, both fares and the passenger counts exceeded Southwest's expectations.
"Passenger fares came in about $3 above what our forecast was and the more important thing is that passenger volumes also exceeded our expectations," Southwest CEO Bob Jordan said on an earnings call Thursday.
Since April — when airlines began warning in earnest about profits taking a hit from the spike in jet fuel — through Thursday, about 9.3 million fewer people were screened at airport checkpoints compared with the same period of 2025, according to the Transportation Security Administration. While that's down less than 2% from last year, it follows years of growth.
With jet fuel prices more than double year-ago levels — as seen in U.S. Gulf Coast spot prices going for $4.63 a gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration — airlines have been focused on recovering as much of the fuel spike as possible.
Even despite some drops, airline executives said during their earnings calls that travel demand overall is robust, especially for profitable premium cabins like business class.
And not every carrier is seeing a decline. United Airlines flew 2.4% more passengers in the third quarter than it did a year ago, and said its unit revenue rose by 16%, the biggest increase since the pandemic.
"I've been pleasantly surprised at the industry's ability this year to raise yields and pass through much of the increase in fuel prices," CEO Scott Kirby said on the company's earnings call Wednesday. "So it's possible that airlines will continue to focus on yields at the expense of load factor and that alone could get us to double-digit margins next year."
Profit hit
Most airlines are anticipating that fuel costs will continue to bite, but executives say they're confident in their pricing power.
United, for example, said it expects to pay an average of $4.80 a gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from an average price of $3.90 a gallon in the third.
American, United, Delta Air Lines and Southwest all cut their profit forecasts for 2026 this month when they reported earnings. American is the only one of the four that expects to post a loss this year.
American and others have also reduced growth plans or warned the industry could dial back on its goals for expanding capacity, which could keep fares elevated. Reduced capacity can make bookable seats scarcer, driving up prices even more if demand holds.
The carriers said demand has been particularly strong for premium seats, which command hundreds, if not thousands of dollars, more than coach tickets.
Smaller airlines set to report results in the coming weeks, including Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air, have traditionally focused on more price-sensitive customers, which could show if those travelers are pulling back at all.
One factor that could also affect air travel is the demise of Spirit Airlines, which went out of business in early May.
"Some of its customers have likely stopped flying," Bank of America said in a research note Thursday.

Protests, clashes erupt in Tunisia over recent deaths and deteriorating living conditions

PRESS RELEASE 159
Albares strengthens bilateral relations between Spain and Switzerland with counterpart
- The ministers have signed an agreement on political consultations that consolidates the dialogue between the two countries
The Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, met on Friday with his Swiss counterpart, Federal Councillor for Foreign Affairs Ignazio Cassis, with whom he discussed the good bilateral relations between Spain and Switzerland, as well as the main issues on the EU and international agenda. During the meeting, the ministers also signed an agreement to establish a mechanism for regular consultations that will consolidate and expand bilateral political dialogue between the two countries.
Spain and Switzerland enjoy good bilateral relations across all areas. There is a large community of Spanish residents in Switzerland – more than 149,000 – and, in terms of trade and investment, the situation is positive, with tourism being the main item in the balance of services: 2.25 million Swiss citizens visited our country last year.
The potential for bilateral scientific cooperation is particularly noteworthy, with a large number of Spanish researchers and scientists in Switzerland working in sectors such as health, artificial intelligence and quantum technologies.
Politically speaking, the relationship is also strong, and the agreement signed this Friday is proof of this. The aim is to hold annual consultations – and whenever deemed necessary – on thematic and geographical areas of mutual interest.
EU agenda
The ministers also discussed relations between Switzerland and the European Union, and Switzerland’s prospects for closer ties with EU institutions through the so-called ‘Bilaterals III’ package, which is currently under consideration.
This package of agreements governs, amongst other matters, the conditions for Switzerland’s access to the EU’s internal market, as well as the alignment of its legislation with EU regulations and case law. Switzerland’s contribution to European peace and security in the current international geopolitical context was also discussed.
International agenda
Finally, on the international agenda, the ministers discussed security, the Russian aggression against Ukraine, the war in the Middle East and the defence of multilateralism. Switzerland hosts several international organisations and is the depositary and guarantor of the Geneva Conventions on international humanitarian law.
On this last point, both countries reaffirmed their support for the work of the International Criminal Court.

Govt finalizes changes to reservation system – Koretsky
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:43:32 EEST
01:43:32 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has finalized changes to the mobilization system – a company's critical importance is now separated from its economic performance, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said.
"The main goal is to establish fair and clear rules for everyone working on the home front, and above all for those fighting on the front lines. Every month, the number of reservations increases by tens of thousands. And the people who have been defending the country for five years must be able to return home from service. That is why we are making difficult but necessary decisions," Koretsky said on his Telegram channel.
According to him, the first change involves separating a company's criticality from its economic performance.
"Sectors that actually contribute to defense and the economy – such as the defense industry, energy, communications, logistics, housing and communal services, and others – should be designated as critical. Nothing will change for them. At the same time, sectoral and regional criteria for criticality will be updated and monitored for abuse," he said.
The second change is that the maximum level of reservation – particularly for the energy sector and the defense industry – will no longer be 100%.
"Unconditional full exemption is unfair to those who serve and opens the door to abuse. There were companies created specifically to take advantage of the exemption, and it became a business," the prime minister said.
At the same time, Koretsky said the government will not relax the requirements for those who manufacture weapons or maintain critical infrastructure. Specifically, if a company needs to reserve more personnel to ensure uninterrupted operations, it will be able to submit a substantiated request to the Coordination Center.
The third change is that the Ministry of Defense is increasing penalties for evading military service.
"Fourth, we are developing a mechanism for 100% exemption from military service, provided that mobilization obligations are fulfilled. A company will be able to fully reserve its employees if it regularly and voluntarily enlists some of them for military service. It is essential that the individual knows where they are going and for how long. Their job and salary will be preserved," Koretsky said.
He said the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Economy will work out the details together with the business community.
"The government's goal is to approve a transparent and effective mechanism by December 1. This will give confidence to those on the front lines: rotation is possible, and others will take their place. And for those who are going to serve, it means they are going for a clearly defined period," the prime minister said.
He said the ultimate goal is to ensure that no one is left searching for anyone on the streets.
"These decisions do not mean that mobilization will be intensified tomorrow. They are needed first and foremost to bring order to the conscription process and root out abuses. At the same time, as a state and a society, we must be prepared for any turn of events, including an intensification of mobilization in Russia. We are waging a war for the survival of the state and our people. These decisions are not easy, but they must be made," the prime minister said.

Breadcrumb
Netanyahu vows collective punishment against Palestinian neighbourhood after Hebron shooting
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to carry out collective punishment against a Palestinian neighbourhood in the city of Hebron after an attack on an Israeli army checkpoint in the occupied West Bank killed two soldiers.
Speaking during a visit to the city with Defence Minister Israel Katz, Netanyahu said: "First of all, we will act to destroy this place, to change it completely."
"But we are going to do something that has not been done until now: We will implement the successful and aggressive model we used in the refugee camps, which are essentially terrorist strongholds," he added, according to the Times of Israel.
Netanyahu's comments refer to Israel's policy of forcibly expelling thousands of Palestinians from several northern West Bank refugee camps, including Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams, that occurred in early 2025, with around 33,000 being expelled.
Laying out the plan for the neighbourhood, Netanyahu said: "We will evacuate the residents, we will go house to house, we will remove the weapons there as well, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed."
He added that the Israeli military would carry out a major operation in the occupied West Bank, the largest since it first occupied the area following the 1967 war when it first took control of the area.
The announcement comes in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers and wounding three others at an Israeli army checkpoint in the occupied West Bank, with two Palestinian gunmen also killed in the incident.
Israel Katz confirmed Netanyahu's comments, saying "the Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron."
The attack comes days before Israel's Knesset elections that could see the formation of a new government, with polling suggesting that both the pro-Netanyahu and opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot are both under the threshold to form a majority government, with many politicians putting out statements on the incident.
Zizette Darkazally, an Associate Fellow at Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, told The New Arab that the reactions from Israel's politicians confirm the preexisting positions that they already held.
This includes Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right finance minister who also oversees Israel's military occupation in the West Bank, who announced he had already ordered the destruction of several buildings near the site of the shooting, and approved new farms in the area of Masafer Yatta, where Palestinian residents have long fought against Israeli attempts to destroy Palestinian homes.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also weighed in, again calling for the government to dismantle the Palestinian Authority that governs parts of the West Bank, while opposition politicians Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, and Yair Golan praised the Israeli military's response.
Darkazally said that Netanyahu's announced policies were an attempt to exploit the attack to gain more votes and further his self-proclaimed image as 'Mr Security', but that it's unlikely to change the base of voters between the two blocs.
"I don't think the attack will change votes of the base in any of the two blocs," she said, adding, "most of the 'undecided' at this stage are undecided within the same camp, meaning that they are undecided between parties in the same bloc", Darkazally said.
‘Restrictions on top of restrictions’
Restrictions announced by Netanyahu have immediately come into effect, according to Amir Daoud, Director of Publishing and Documentation at the Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission, who told The New Arab that the city has been cordoned off, with preparations for wider closures occurring across the West Bank.
Hebron is the largest city in the occupied West Bank, with 250,000 Palestinians calling it home.
Daoud noted that these restrictions come on top of the plethora of restrictions, checkpoints, and barriers that are already in place across the area that impede freedom of movement for its three million Palestinian residents.
"According to the latest figures documented by the Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission, there were 942 movement obstacles across the West Bank as of September 2026," he said, adding that "these restrictions have transformed Palestinian movement between cities, villages and communities into a process controlled by Israeli military decisions."
Israel's ever-tightening policies in the occupied West Bank have occurred in conjunction with its expansion of settlements and parallel infrastructure allowing them freedom of movement across the territory.
The policy, which rights groups have labelled apartheid, comes alongside an uptick in settler terror attacks against Palestinians that have escalated dramatically since the start of Israel's genocide in Gaza.
Daoud said that the restrictions mean Palestinians will be unable to reach their jobs or get medical treatment, with farmers losing access to land and markets to sell produce. This is set to impact the olive harvest season, already disrupted by widespread settler violence.
Medical Aid for Palestinians warned on Friday that, following announced restrictions and an Israeli military escalation in the occupied West Bank, its staff are reporting increased obstacles to reaching Palestinians in need of care.
The aid group noted that settler attacks in the village of Umm Safa, north of Ramallah, illustrate the risks posed to Palestinians amid the heightened security.
Aseel Baidoun, the group's Deputy Director of Advocacy and Communications in the West Bank, warned that both settler attacks and ministerial threats of collective punishment and forcible displacement meant "the risk of atrocity crimes is acute."
There is also a risk of these measures becoming permanent, adding to the layers of restrictions that already impact life in the occupied West Bank.
"Our concern is that measures initially introduced as temporary security responses frequently become prolonged restrictions or are incorporated into the existing system of military control," Daoud told The New Arab.
“From our perspective, the fundamental issue is the cumulative effect of these measures,” he said, adding, “what we are witnessing is not merely a temporary interruption of movement, but the continued consolidation of a system in which freedom of movement is increasingly treated as an exception rather than a basic right.”

Brazil’s right has already changed the balance of power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:41:09 UTC
01:41:09 KST

Brazil’s right has already changed the balance of power
Bolsonaro’s party has strengthened its position in Congress, posing a formidable challenge to another Lula presidency.
In a televised presidential debate in Sao Paulo on October 18, Flavio Bolsonaro brought a number from Brazil’s prisons into an argument over crime. “Seventy-three percent”. The 45-year-old senator claimed that was the share of prisoners who had voted for his opponent, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, 80. The figure came from polling stations inside detention facilities, where staff and eligible detainees awaiting trial could cast ballots. Convicted prisoners serving final sentences could not vote. Lula paused. “I want 100 percent,” he replied. “Even your father.”
Jair Bolsonaro, the absent father, had spent 28 years in Congress, where he repeatedly praised the 1964 military coup that ushered in more than two decades of dictatorship. He went on to become president, lost re-election to Lula in 2022 and was later convicted of plotting to overturn the result. He is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest. A week after Lula’s inauguration, thousands of Bolsonaro supporters invaded and vandalised the presidential palace, Congress and Supreme Court in Brasilia, claiming without evidence that the election had been stolen.
Back in the studio, Flavio was promising to “redemocratise” Brazil. He demanded respect for the 56 million Brazilians who had voted for him and said he would send Lula into retirement.
On October 4, Brazil held the first round of its presidential election, alongside elections for the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate. Flavio received 56.1 million votes, or 47.03 percent of valid ballots, against Lula’s 53.9 million and 45.16 percent. Since then, Bolsonaro’s lead in the polls has narrowed, with several surveys placing the candidates within the margin of error. The latest readings suggest Lula is gaining ground, although just days before the October 25 run-off, it remains uncertain whether the president can overcome Flavio’s first-round lead.
The October 18 debate had begun with a discussion of armed groups spreading through Brazilian neighbourhoods. Nearly 69 million Brazilians say they perceive the presence of criminal gangs or militias in their neighbourhoods, even as the country’s murder rate falls. Flavio called for treating those organisations as narcoterrorists and for Brazil to join United States President Donald Trump’s Shield of the Americas alongside Javier Milei’s Argentina. He promised 500,000 additional prison places, easier civilian access to firearms and a reduction in the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16, and to 14 for certain serious crimes.
For residents of poorer neighbourhoods, Flavio proposed a Ministry of Prosperity, promising vocational training and credit to help families receiving government assistance to start businesses of their own. The word “prosperity” had a history of its own in Brazil’s influential evangelical churches, where sermons sometimes link material advancement to faith and individual endeavour.
Taken together, the promises linked the prospect of safer streets to a particular idea of prosperity, in which government assistance would become a starting point for vocational training, credit and small businesses.
Lula spoke of the social gains of his governments and of restoring democratic institutions after the Bolsonaro years. A former union leader who helped found the centre-left Workers’ Party (PT), he proposed stronger federal coordination of public security. The tougher approach to crime was not confined to Flavio’s campaign. Lula, too, supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 16 for certain serious offences.
Two days before the debate, Lula had stood among congressional leaders to celebrate a reform that would gradually bring Brazil’s six-day working week to an end, reducing hours from 44 to 40 without cutting wages. After initially criticising the reform as opportunistic, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro changed his position and voted for it, saying he had listened to workers on the campaign trail.
Lula had other economic gains to highlight. Unemployment in Brazil has fallen from 7.8 percent in 2023 to 5.3 percent this year, while real wages have risen. For many households, however, expensive credit and debt repayments have dampened the impact of any improvements. Flavio has sought to capitalise on the resulting economic frustration, as well as concerns about public security.
If re-elected, Lula would have to address those frustrations while dealing with a Congress reshaped by the October 4 legislative elections. In the 513-seat lower house, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) won 121 seats, up from 97. The PT-led bloc moved from 82 to 88, while the largest alliance of traditional centre-right parties lost 18 seats. The sharpest rearrangement had taken place within the right, leaving the parliamentary left’s numbers largely intact.
The right’s gains raise a question about the kind of change the Bolsonaro movement represents. In an October Datafolha survey, 48 percent of Lula’s supporters mentioned social protection, while 41 percent of Flavio’s supporters expressed a desire for change. Yet the PL’s new deputies were hardly political novices. Of the 121 elected, 111 had held office before and 93 had belonged to other parties.
In 2002, the same party had placed Jose Alencar, a conservative textile magnate, next to Lula on the presidential ticket that first brought the former union leader to power. Alencar remained vice president until 2010, though he left the PL in 2005 amid a corruption scandal involving its leadership. Jair Bolsonaro joined only in 2021. The party now housed his family’s ambitions alongside politicians whose careers had begun under very different banners.
In a country where presidents rarely command a parliamentary majority of their own party, politicians of such experience are seldom without work. Governments change, and parties move between coalitions to negotiate cabinet appointments and influence over the funds that reach their constituencies. Established centre-right parties have served administrations of widely differing orientations. Jair Bolsonaro eventually relied on them after campaigning against the political establishment. His movement’s gains had not made those alliances obsolete.
Lula has spent much of his political career constructing governments with former adversaries. His current vice president and running mate, Geraldo Alckmin, once challenged him for the presidency as the candidate of the centre-right opposition. A fourth term would demand more of that experience, with the right holding greater power in Congress. Lula’s successor, Dilma Rousseff, was impeached in 2016 amid a deep recession and the collapse of her governing coalition, circumstances quite different from those Lula faces today.
The new balance of power would be particularly consequential for the Supreme Court. Alexandre de Moraes had overseen the case that sent Jair Bolsonaro to prison. As the Bolsonaro family accused him of political persecution, Lula’s party defended his authority as part of its defence of democracy. But the court has become a major target of the right’s parliamentary ambitions.
Moraes’s name had travelled through the October 4 Senate elections, in which 54 of the chamber’s 81 seats were contested. Candidates allied with the Bolsonaros promised to impeach him and curb the court’s powers. Some wanted its jurisdiction narrowed, while others sought to limit the authority of individual justices to act alone. The collapse of Banco Master, a private bank that had a lucrative contract with the law firm of Moraes’s wife, raised questions about possible conflicts of interest. The firm has denied wrongdoing.
A fourth Lula term would face 28 Liberal Party senators in an 81-seat chamber empowered to approve Supreme Court appointments and remove justices through impeachment. A survey by Folha de S. Paulo identified at least 49 members of the next Senate who had expressed support for impeaching Supreme Court justices in some circumstances. That was five short of the two-thirds required for removal, even before agreement on a particular case. Support for restricting the court’s powers extended beyond the Bolsonaro movement.
Congress’s growing power could also constrain Lula’s ability to deliver the economic and social improvements on which he has based much of his political appeal. Control over public money had been moving towards Congress. In 2025, parliamentary allocations for local projects reached about 47 billion reais ($9.3bn) in committed funds, more than four times their level 11 years earlier. Legislators increasingly choose where that money goes. A president can secure their votes for a particular measure without recovering control over the funds they distribute.
On Wednesday, Lula sent Congress a proposal to make public transport free on weekends and public holidays, allowing some workers who would soon have two days off to travel without paying fares. He suggested using money politicians had set aside for projects in their constituencies. The Speaker of the lower house welcomed the idea. He wanted the money to come from somewhere else.

Ukraine Brings Home 270 People From Russian Captivity, Including 86 Convicted by Russian Courts

Ukraine Brings Home 270 People From Russian Captivity, Including 86 Convicted by Russian Courts
Ukraine has brought home 270 people from Russian captivity, including service members from multiple branches of the military and nine civilians, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on October 23.
Those released include National Guard troops, including Azov fighters, border guards, territorial defense personnel, Navy service members, Ground Forces troops, Air Assault Forces personnel, and members of the State Special Transport Service.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets described the exchange as historic because it returned the largest number of Ukrainian service members who had been convicted by Russian courts. Among those released were 86 such prisoners, as well as one service member who had been facing criminal prosecution in Russia.
Most had been held in Russian captivity since 2022, Zelenskyy noted. The majority of those released were Ukrainian troops who defended Mariupol, while others fought on the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, and Chernihiv fronts.
Many of those returning had also been illegally sentenced in Russia, according to Zelenskyy.
Two of the released Ukrainian defenders had been in captivity since before Russia’s full-scale invasion, having been captured in 2018 and 2020. They spent eight and six years in captivity, respectively, Lubinets stated.
The exchange also included seriously ill and severely wounded Ukrainian service members. Lubinets noted that several were in critical condition and that he had repeatedly appealed to the Russian side for their release. The youngest person released was 24, while the oldest was 63.
Lubinets stated that the exchange followed several months of negotiations by the working group of Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, which includes the Ombudsman’s Office.
“We remember every single person and continue searching for everyone,” Zelenskyy wrote.
“I am grateful to our soldiers on the front lines who are replenishing the exchange fund for Ukraine so that we can bring our people home,” he continued.
The exchange comes as hundreds of Ukrainians remain in Russian captivity. In July, Dmytro Lubinets reported that 494 Ukrainian women, including civilians and service members, were still being held by Russia, while Moscow had largely stopped including women in prisoner exchanges.
