How the upcoming U.S. and Israeli elections could lead to the third round of the Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:38:19 UTC
01:38:19 KST

There is little doubt that the United States and Israel are about to renew the war on Iran that they started without provocation, or any real planning, back in February. The question is only about the timing.
In fact, by the time you read this, the war may have resumed in full force. More likely, though, it will be delayed until after the U.S. midterm elections. That will put it after Israel’s elections as well.
Israel may find itself with an entirely new leadership after its upcoming elections on October 27, which, while still seeing Iran as a hated enemy, might have different ideas about how to attack that enemy.
The United States is even more uncertain following the midterm elections on November 3. Donald Trump will remain president and free of electoral concerns, as he will not be allowed to run in the next election. But a Congress hostile to this war can make it harder for him to continue his current course. Conversely, an indecisive Congress unwilling to confront Trump on the war could unleash his worst tendencies.
Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu both have personal interests that the war might serve. Both could seek to undermine their country’s election results, and a war that escalates into a global economic crisis could give them the cover they need.
Iran and the Israeli election
Netanyahu has been pushing hard for a renewed war. In a public phone call with Trump, Netanyahu told him, “We have a job to finish.”
Beyond the bombast, there have been concrete actions. The United States and Israel have been busy drawing up plans for another attack on Iran even if it seems that Netanyahu is not content to wait as long as Trump wants him to.
Trump has repeatedly said that the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. Given his history, there is no reason to take Trump at his word. To the contrary, Trump has repeatedly broken such promises, sometimes due to impulsiveness, sometimes because he lied intentionally to try to get Iran to drop its guard. Moreover, Trump has not said that he would continue to block Israel from attacking before the midterms.
But in this case, there is good reason to believe that Trump is telling the truth. Nothing is certain, but the United States is moving a considerable number of troops and a third aircraft carrier to the Gulf. By most accounts, they are slated to arrive in late November.
That works for Trump, but less well for Netanyahu.
For Trump, an escalation against Iran will be useful for months, from the election until the beginning of January, when the new Congress would be seated.
Netanyahu has less time.
The Israeli election will take place next week. Many analyses in the United States have misunderstood how a renewal of war affects Netanyahu’s position.
Had it happened a few weeks before the election, Netanyahu might have been able to postpone the election (which would require approval from 80 of 120 members of the Knesset), or sway some voters toward his camp. Now, with only a few days left, those prospects are very dim.
But an Israeli election is not like an American one where votes are cast, someone wins, and that’s supposed to settle the matter. Israel’s unstable coalition politics mean the real intrigue happens after the votes are counted, as the leaders of the top parties jockey for the right to form a coalition government.
Netanyahu is not going to win this election, according to almost every poll that has been conducted recently and since the beginning of the year. The parties that would join with his Likud coalition simply won’t have enough seats to form a majority unless a real miracle happens.
But the opposition, although in a better position, also doesn’t have a good chance of forming a majority coalition. Their only hope, which is not available to Netanyahu, is support from the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up around 20% of the population.
But that is complicated. The opposition leader, Gadi Eisenkot, has vowed not to form a government with Arab parties. But he could form a government with less than a majority of seats by getting support from Arab parties outside the governing coalition.
That’s a fraught path in as racist a society as Israel’s. Even the non-nationalist, conservative United Arab List (called Ra’am) would trouble some of Eisenkot’s other coalition partners. And it is hard to imagine parties led by right-wing figures like Avigdor Lieberman or Naftali Bennett agreeing to a coalition that gets any support from the Joint List, which is much more representative of Palestinian national sentiment than Ra’am.
And even with Ra’am’s support outside the coalition, the opposition could still fall short of the 61 votes needed to form a government.
Netanyahu is counting on the opposition’s inability to form a coalition. If that should happen, Netanyahu can try to poach parties or even individual Knesset members from the opposition to reach a majority. That would be difficult, but possible.
Or he could simply ride the impasse to another round of elections, leaving him in charge of a caretaker government, the most likely scenario at present.
In either case, a hot war with Iran is a significant boon to Netanyahu.
Under the threat of Iranian missile attack, Netanyahu can make the case that Israel needs continuity to win the war, to stop Iran’s nuclear program, and all the other accusations Netanyahu will make. If polls don’t show he is gaining ground, he can also propose a national unity government, and a hot war will absolutely bolster that case.
Netanyahu needs the stalemate that comes with the opposition failing to form a government. Yet, if he gets it, and there are no Iranian or Hezbollah missiles raining down on Israel, his failings will only come under even more scrutiny, and he will stand even less chance in the next round of elections. So he needs a war even more than usual.
Netanyahu’s push for an early resumption of the war, against Trump’s preferences, was motivated by several factors.
First, given Trump’s indecisiveness and strong tendency to flip-flop, he wanted to lock in American support for renewing the war. Second, he wanted to refocus the war’s guiding principle on regime change, an idea he has been banging on in recent days but that has largely fallen out of favor in Washington, even among the most hawkish voices.
Finally, Netanyahu knows that the U.S. is planning a quick, impactful strike. He also knows this is almost certainly not going to happen, and he wouldn’t want it to. He wants prolonged engagement to maximize both his own political gains and the chances of stressing Iran to the point of threatening the Islamic Republic’s continued existence. Time is not on his side, as he knows that this may be his last chance to defeat Iran.
So, Netanyahu pushed to rekindle the war earlier this month, knowing that it would almost certainly last until well after Israel’s election.
Iran and the U.S. midterms
Trump is probably sincere about his desire to hold off the attack on Iran until after the midterms, but this is just another indication of how little he grasps the depths of his own failure.
The damage to the Republican chances in the midterms is done, and resuming the war on Iran won’t make things much worse. But, even more than with Netanyahu in Israel, the Republicans are about to take a beating at the ballot box. The only question is how bad it will be.
It is overwhelmingly likely that the Democrats will take back the House of Representatives, and they stand a good chance of taking the Senate as well. For Trump, even though he is not on the ballot, this will be a humiliating loss, and we have already seen how he reacts to such things.
This is where a renewed war on Iran comes in for him. Trump is sure to do all he can to throw the results of the election into doubt, and to stir up suspicions as he did in 2020. With a smaller base of support now than before, and no pandemic, he will need to sow even more chaos than he did then.
A war with Iran will do that for several reasons.
First, the war itself will be intense and will immediately send shock waves through the global economy.
But that will only be the start. Iran has been clear that it is going to respond more forcefully than before and that it will calibrate that response to the intensity of the American and Israeli attack.
Iran has warned that they will target data centers, which they know are important to Trump, as well as underwater fiber networks that are key to the internet. That will cause disruption across many different industries.
And that will be added to Iran’s targeting of Gulf energy infrastructure if the U.S. and Israel target theirs. They could also target civilian infrastructure, including desalination plants, which would devastate the entire region.
None of this will matter to Israel, which will see it as pressure on the Gulf Arab states to join in the war effort. Israel wants to see as much chaos as possible, because that is the road to the regime change in Iran they crave.
But Trump should be concerned about the potential crash of Gulf economies and the massive impact this will have on the entire world.
Crippling Gulf infrastructure will send oil prices soaring much higher than they already are. It will greatly expand the fertilizer-export crisis from the region and could further devastate the liquefied natural gas market. Global inflation could surge, and the measures used to date to keep prices from that kind of massive inflation are unlikely to be sufficient.
Yet the chaos it will cause in the United States might offer Trump an advantage in forestalling the seating of a new Congress, or increasing his opportunities to once again cast doubt on the election results.
These efforts are unlikely to get Trump what he wants. His base is too small, the country is more aware of this potential, and many of the foot soldiers Trump had six years ago now recognize that he betrayed and used them.
But an attack on Iran will succeed in causing global devastation, beginning in Iran itself, and quickly expanding outward.
Israel, too, is much more vulnerable than it was last time around. The protective ring of American installations and support from places like Saudi Arabia and Jordan in intercepting Iranian missiles and drones is severely diminished. Many American bases are gone, and the Americans stationed in the region have few interceptors left.
Israel has managed to save many interceptors of its own, having relied on American missiles against Iran. But even they had to use quite a few to defend against attacks from Lebanon. More to the point, because Iranian missiles will have a much clearer path to Israel than they did before, more missiles will be shot down above Israeli space, meaning more debris will fall on Israel, while more Iranian missiles are likely to get through Israel’s defenses since so many more will get into range.
Perhaps Trump is not thinking about how to use a war to undermine elections in the U.S. Maybe he is tired of losing the war and is desperately grasping at the idea that this time the bloodshed and destruction that have repeatedly failed will work.
That sad fact is the very definition of murderous insanity.

Israeli roadblocks disrupt schools and medical care in West Bank village
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:37:59 UTC
01:37:59 KST

Israeli roadblocks disrupt schools and medical care in West Bank village
Residents of Madama describe being cut off from hospitals, schools, and olive groves as Israeli forces blockade village.
Wail Qut, 42, usually commutes to work in Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank. But for more than two weeks he has been stuck at home in the village of Madama, south of Nablus, due to a tight Israeli siege.
On October 11, the Israeli army blocked the village’s four entrances with earthen barriers, citing “security reasons”. Qut says that the Israeli military has told residents that the restrictions would remain until Palestinian farmers stopped trying to access their land, particularly in the northern part of the village, where an illegal settler outpost is located.
The decision has completely restricted the movement of more than 2,500 residents. On October 20, the army briefly opened the northern entrance for a few hours before closing it once again.
Qut works as a legal consultant for the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center in Ramallah. Three days into the siege, he needed to reach his office in the city to deal with urgent case files.
“The residents managed to clear a rough, unpaved dirt track between Madama and Asira, which I used to reach Ramallah. It was a dangerous gamble, though the area is swarming with settlers, and the path is not even passable for most vehicles,” he told Al Jazeera.
Whenever Palestinian residents attempted to leave Madama via this makeshift route, the Israeli army deployed a drone to monitor them. Soldiers have also attacked the residents and fired sound grenades and tear gas canisters to force them back.
The soldiers have subsequently blocked the dirt track, cutting off the only small opening that had allowed some residents to leave the village. As a result, Qut was forced to spend days away in Ramallah, only returning home once he learned that the northern entrance had been briefly reopened.
“I returned to the village and found settlers everywhere, monitoring the tight siege. Shortly afterwards, the army closed the entrance once again. Some residents who had left were unable to return and had to leave their vehicles outside the village,” he added.
Uprooting trees
The restrictions have coincided with Israeli bulldozing operations that residents say have destroyed agricultural land and uprooted hundreds of olive trees.
Locals in Madama have described the scenes as “horrific”, particularly as they came during the annual olive harvest season, a vital source of income for local farmers already struggling to access their land because of Israeli restrictions.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the Israeli military for comment, but has yet to receive a response.
Rami Nassar, head of the Madama Village Council, told Al Jazeera that the village spans about 340 hectares (840 acres). He said Israel had seized village land in the 1980s for the establishment of the illegal Yitzhar settlement, while another portion was taken in the 1990s to construct a settler-only road – Route 60 – which now restricts residents’ access to their agricultural land.
Last April, Nassar said, Israeli settlers established an illegal pastoral settlement northwest of the village, near the al-Murabbaa checkpoint. Since then, he said, settlers have been siphoning electricity and water from the village’s utility networks and destroying agricultural crops.
Last July, the council leader added, under the protection of the Israeli army, settler bulldozers levelled what he estimated to have been about 57 hectares (140 acres) of land in the northwest of the village, and uprooted hundreds of mature, fruit-bearing olive trees.
During the current olive harvest season, according to Nassar, Israeli soldiers have chased Palestinian farmers away from their fields, while settlers have stolen both harvested olives and farming equipment from those who managed to reach their land.
“The olive harvest season has come to an end for the people of Madama, a season they rely on entirely, especially given their harsh living conditions. Every year, the harvest felt like a celebration; now, all we see is them bulldozing and uprooting our trees,” Nassar said sorrowfully.
The closures have disrupted daily life in Madama, preventing residents from reaching work, schools and hospitals, while blocking the delivery of essential supplies, including cooking gas, Nassar said.
“A few days ago, a resident suffered a heart attack and needed to be taken to a hospital,” he recalled. “As the village doctor, I had to transport him carrying him over earthen berms and navigate through olive groves and steep slopes in a private vehicle travelling between various villages to reach a nearby hospital. It took over two hours to get him there; under normal circumstances, this journey would take no more than 15 minutes.”
The plight of students
The siege has also disrupted schooling across Madama and neighbouring villages, preventing teachers from reaching classrooms.
Samer al-Jamal, director general of education for the southern Nablus district, said that the closure of roads and gates, combined with the restrictions on the movement of educational staff, had deprived thousands of students of their education.
Three schools in Madama, Burin, and Asira were forced to switch to remote learning for three days following the imposition of the blockade. As the closure continued, students and teachers were eventually compelled to cross earthen barriers on foot to reach their schools.
Maryam Rayan, 48, the principal of al-Fayha Kindergarten in Asira, told Al Jazeera that the simple task of ensuring children could arrive at and leave the kindergarten safely was increasingly dangerous, as 35 of the school’s enrolled children live in Madama.
She explained that she lives in the neighbouring village of Burin. The journey from there, passing through Madama to reach Asira, should typically take no more than eight minutes; however, due to the blockade of Madama, the trip now takes more than an hour and a half.
“The kindergarten bus would have to stop near the earthen barrier after we verified that no soldiers or settlers were present, and we would wait for the children to arrive on a local shuttle from within the village. I would then cross the barrier on foot to help them get over it, one by one. It was a tragic scene, but we had no other choice,” she added.
On the return journey, Rayan would again help the children cross the barrier, boarding the shuttle with them to ensure they all reached their homes safely. Afterwards, she would cross the barrier alone to return to the kindergarten bus, which would then take her back to Burin.
“I have been working in education for 25 years, yet I have never encountered circumstances as difficult as those we have lived through due to the blockade of Madama. From the moment I left my home until I returned, I felt tense, fearful, and anxious, all because I am responsible for the lives of 135 children at the kindergarten, while the streets are filled with soldiers or settlers,” she explained.
On Thursday, Israel reopened the northern entrance to Madama, though Palestinians expect it could be closed again at any moment, especially since the other entrances to the village remain shut. And on Friday, Israel began imposing widespread restrictions on movement throughout the West Bank after an attack in Hebron killed two soldiers, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordering preparations for a complete lockdown and a large-scale operation throughout the occupied territory.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said it had identified 925 physical obstacles restricting the movement of Palestinians in the West Bank by December 2025, including 167 earth mounds, which collectively affect the movement of approximately 3.4 million Palestinians.
The agency noted that these obstacles sever connections between villages, towns, and main roads, forcing residents to take longer, alternative routes and limiting their access to workplaces, essential services, and agricultural land.

New York City to phase out Central Park horse-drawn carriages by Jun 1, 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

New York City to phase out Central Park horse-drawn carriages by Jun 1, 2028
The New York City Council has approved historic legislation to phase out the city’s horse-drawn carriage industry by June 1, 2028, following decades of concerns about animal welfare and public safety, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The bill, known as Romanch’s Law, was passed after the death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who was killed this summer after being thrown from a horse-drawn carriage in Central Park.
Horse-drawn carriages have been operating in Central Park since 1858, originally serving as a mode of transportation and evolving into a popular tourist attraction.
The legislation prohibits the issuance or renewal of licenses for carriage horses, carriages, and horse-drawn cab drivers on or after June 1, 2028. It also requires the city to develop a transition plan by April 1, 2027, to support carriage owners, drivers, and other industry workers, including stable employees. The plan will include employment assistance and consider programs to help horse owners rehome their animals and dispose of equipment, as well as provide compensation to carriage owners for their businesses, licenses and equipment.
The law also establishes protections to ensure the humane treatment of horses and prohibits their sale or transfer for slaughter or use in other horse-drawn carriage businesses.
Council Speaker Julie Menin said: "Today, the City Council made history. Our landmark vote to pass Romanch’s Law is a demonstration of this Council’s commitment to animal welfare, public safety, and worker protection."
Earlier, Qazinform reported that a snow leopard named Altai became the first in Kazakhstan's Southern Altai to be fitted with a satellite tracking collar. The satellite collar will allow researchers to track the snow leopard's movements, study its travel routes, and identify key areas of its habitat.

Dozens feared trapped as high-rise collapses in Kenya’s Nairobi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:36:00 UTC
01:36:00 KST

A multistory building collapsed in Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, on Friday, leaving many people feared trapped beneath massive piles of concrete as more than a dozen floors crumbled on top of one another.
The building was under construction when it collapsed at about 1 p.m. along a busy commercial street in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, which is often crowded with thousands of traders and residents.
Nairobi police chief Issa Mohamud said the building had more than 10 upper floors under construction. Rescue operations were complicated, with police firing tear gas at people who had begun looting neighboring shops, as officers sought to clear the area and provide access to emergency response teams.
Joseph Kaula made it out just in time. A plasterer working on the fifth floor, he said he heard screams and spotted other workers rushing outside, shouting that the building was collapsing.
"I was the last person to walk out before it collapsed and the whole area was filled with dust,” Kaula said.
Kaula suspects a few of his colleagues were trapped in the basement.
One injured woman was rescued and hospitalized, and another person who was crying for help had gone silent, the police chief said.
Mohamud also warned of a possible secondary collapse, as the collapsed building was leaning on its neighbor.
There was little in the way of heavy equipment immediately available. Hours later, a group of rescuers in hard hats were using poles stripped from trees to poke at the huge pile of rubble. One excavator began to move concrete bound with steel away. By evening, at least two more back shovels arrived.
Rescuers were hoping to reach into any spaces left in the basement and the ground level, which had been rented out for an electronics shop, a butchery and a grocery while construction continued on the upper floors.
Residents said some of their loved ones who were trapped had made phone calls calling for help immediately after the collapse, but that their phones later became unreachable. A tent was set up where people could report the missing. How many might be inside the wreckage wasn't known.
Building collapses are a recurring problem in Nairobi . County officials responsible for issuing building permits have been accused of failing to conduct adequate inspections to ensure developers comply with safety guidelines and construction standards.
"Investigations will be carried out,” Mohamud said. "We’ll make sure people face the law for any negligence.”
Nairobi Gov. Johnson Sakaja said the building had been approved for construction, but did not have a certificate of occupation, so opening shops on the ground floor was against the law. Kenya's county governments need stronger enforcement powers, he said, arguing that lenient penalties for non-compliance are just a "slap on the wrist” for developers that violate regulations.

Two ex-FBI officials charged with allegedly lying about Hunter Biden probe: DOJ

Two former senior FBI officials were taken into custody on Friday after being charged with lying to Congress about their roles in investigations into Hunter Biden, top Department of Justice officials announced.
The former officials, 46-year-old Nikki Floris and 56-year-old Bradley Benavides, surrendered on arrest warrants Friday morning, the DOJ said in a press release.
The charges were filed less than two weeks before the midterm election, breaking with longstanding DOJ guidance discouraging actions that could affect upcoming political races.
The announcement also comes amid growing concerns that President Donald Trump — who refused to accept his 2020 election loss and tried repeatedly to overturn those results — is looking for ways to challenge potential Republican midterm losses.
On Thursday, the DOJ filed an unusual lawsuit against Alaska seeking to preemptively challenge the results of that state's Senate race if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowly loses.
The charges unveiled Friday morning accuse the two ex-FBI agents of lying in 2023 testimony before the House Judiciary Committee about their agency's probe of Hunter Biden, the now-56-year-old son of former President Joe Biden.
The agents were "actively involved" in federal investigations of Hunter Biden, which began in 2019 on tax- and money-laundering-related matters, but said otherwise in separate interviews before the House panel, according to an FBI special agent's affidavit in support of the charges.
"Floris and Benavides allegedly lied to Congress about their roles in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations, with one claiming they only learned about it from Wikipedia — despite evidence showing their involvement in helping shape the public narrative about Hunter Biden's laptop right before the election," U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said in an X post.
FBI Director Kash Patel said on X that the charges "stem from an ongoing investigation into the since-dissolved FBI Foreign Influence Task Force."
Floris and Benavides, who both worked on that task force, testified that it "was not involved in the Hunter Biden investigations," Patel wrote. "Documentary evidence, contemporaneous communications, and witness accounts contradict their testimony."
Attorneys for Floris called the charges "nonsense," and accused the Trump administration of deliberately filing them just before the Nov. 3 midterm election in hopes of gaining political advantage.
"Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts," read a statement from her counsel, including Margaret Donovan, Chris Mattei, Mary Dohrmann and Kyle Freeny.
"It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," they wrote.
"The government's reasons for charging Nikki are as transparent as they are unjust: to push a false narrative for a shot at political points," their statement added. "It's another sad day for the DOJ, but we look forward to Nikki's day in court."

01:32:25 KST

The US administration has filed a lawsuit to block certification of the US state of Alaska's Senate race if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses while another candidate with the same name is on the ballot.
Many in both parties believe the fight over Senate control could come down to Alaska, where Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman.
Also on the Alaska ballot is a Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg. He has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate.
The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit on Thursday in federal court in Alaska, asking the court to block the state from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. remains on the ballot.
“The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” the lawsuit says, contending that federal law requires states to protect the integrity of federal elections.
The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot.
He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent.
Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system will also let voters select both men if they're confused.
Election certification process
Democrats have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that GOP loses.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said that was unlikely outside of extreme circumstances. “It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process,” he told reporters in Virginia before the lawsuit was filed.
Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lost the Alaska Senate race.
“The statute simply doesn’t let the Department of Justice enjoin certification,” he said. “The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month.”
The US Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Elections for federal office like the Senate must comply with standards Congress sets.
Trump has complained about Daniel J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot, referencing it at a rally in Alaska this month and in repeated social media posts, including one this week in which he called it “CHEATING.”
“We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” the president wrote on Wednesday.

London shoppers face facial scans as Oxford Street gets new cameras
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:31:00 UTC
01:31:00 KST

London's busiest shopping district is set for heightened surveillance this December, as live facial recognition cameras are scheduled to be introduced along Oxford Street, potentially scanning thousands of visitors during the Christmas shopping season
Oxford Street is one of the world’s busiest shopping areas, with about half a million visitors each day.
It would be among the first areas in the country to have permanent, live facial recognition (LFR) infrastructure scanning the faces of people passing through and comparing them with a watchlist of wanted suspects.
LFR has been widely criticized by human rights groups, with one organization describing the technology as "unregulated.”
The cameras will likely be installed in December, it is understood, and could be attached to street furniture such as lampposts.
It comes as a stretch of Oxford Street is due to be pedestrianized next week, with plans for the whole street to eventually become traffic-free.
The Metropolitan Police plans to use static, live, facial recognition cameras in London’s West End and Soho, which have some of the highest crime rates in London.
The U.K. government launched a public consultation in December 2025 to develop a legal framework for law enforcement use of biometrics, facial recognition and similar technologies.
The Home Office is expected to publish its response to the public consultation later this Parliamentary session.
Akiko Hart, director of human rights organization Liberty, told the Press Association: "The introduction of fixed, live, facial recognition cameras on Oxford Street will mean thousands of Christmas shoppers will have their faces scanned by this unregulated surveillance technology without being given a choice.
"Despite a public consultation on facial recognition closing in February, the government has yet to publish its response. Yet permanent, facial recognition cameras are set to be installed in one of the country’s busiest destinations without a legal framework to protect the public’s rights.
"This lack of transparency damages public trust and, until clear laws, proper safeguards and independent oversight are in place, this significant rollout should be paused.”
A Met spokesperson said: "Live, facial recognition is an important tool which is helping us keep London safe.
"Static cameras have already been piloted in Croydon for six months and contributed to a 10% reduction in crime and led to 173 arrests - one every 35 minutes. Considering this success, the public would rightly expect us to look at how we can use technology to keep the busiest parts of our capital safe.
"It is important to note that static systems are only turned on when officers are present on the ground, and signs will make it clear to the public that a deployment is taking place.
"Conversations remain ongoing with our partners on where we will place the cameras.”
Commissioner Mark Rowley, of the Met, has described LFR as "one of the most revolutionary technology advances in policing in recent years”, with the force arresting more than 2,000 people using facial recognition since the start of 2024.
The technology has also started to be deployed at London’s Tube stations.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has backed the expansion of LFR.
Speaking at the Police Federation annual conference on Thursday, she said: "We will expand live, facial recognition so that instead of spending hours and hours crawling through CCTV, you’ll get a match in seconds.”

491 days in the grey zone and losing both feet: exclusive details of the first-ever aerial evacuation aboard a Heavy Shot drone
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:30:00 EEST
01:30:00 KST

491 days in the grey zone and losing both feet: exclusive details of the first-ever aerial evacuation aboard a Heavy Shot drone
In October, Ukraine's defence forces carried out the first-ever medical evacuation of a wounded soldier using a heavy unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). The soldier, a member of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade who goes by the alias Magura, was airlifted from the grey zone aboard a Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 drone. No evacuation vehicle had been able to get to the area for over a year.
The roads are heavily mined, and FPV drones prowl the skies, destroying anything that moves within tens of kilometres. The brigade spent over six months preparing the daring rescue operation, which brought together heavy and light quadcopters, ground robots, electronic warfare units and even artillery.
"I realised there was a person down there: I wanted to get him to safety as quickly and safely as possible," a drone pilot recalls.
Ukrainska Pravda has interviewed the soldiers behind the operation, the drone's developers and the wounded serviceman. Find out how troops from the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, named after Kostiantyn Ostrozkyi, teamed up with neighbouring units to pull off the evacuation and make history.
The operation was made possible by the coordinated efforts of the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, the 14th and 30th Separate Mechanised Brigades, and the 10th Army Corps.
491 days
Sadly, this story began quite some time ago. On 2 June 2025, Kostiantyn "Magura" Vlasenko, an infantryman with the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, set off from the rear with a fellow soldier for their positions on the Kupiansk front, which were on the left bank of the Oskil River. In the grey zone, Magura initially took shelter in one spot. But when it flooded, he had to move into an abandoned building.
His brother-in-arms was killed while making his way to a fallback position. Then, on 14 February 2026, a Russian drone dropped a munition that wounded Magura in both legs. Faced with a fight for survival and having lost one of his feet, he amputated the other foot himself, leaving him unable to get out of his position on his own.
There was no way to drag him out overland: the Oskil River, dense minefields and relentless Russian drone patrols made the approaches impassable. The battalion tried to use a ground robotic system to evacuate him, but Russian forces spotted and destroyed it while it was still on its way. Infantry groups also failed to reach him. Russian drones filled the skies, and Russian infantry had infiltrated the area around his position, effectively sealing it off.
All this is further evidence that the "golden hour" – the crucial first 60 minutes after an injury, when prompt medical treatment can mean the difference between life and death – is becoming increasingly difficult to meet on the modern battlefield. Evacuating wounded soldiers is a dangerous mission in its own right, and one that becomes harder with every passing year.
Every four to five days, drones brought Kostiantyn food, cigarettes and sweets. He kept in touch with his brothers-in-arms by walkie-talkie. He held out in his position until his evacuation on 4 October.
It was Alex, the reconnaissance chief overseeing UAV operations for the 2nd Mechanised Battalion, who came up with the idea of evacuating the soldier by air. It took around six months to move from the initial concept to the flight itself. The military had conventional Heavy Shot bomber drones, but these were not up to the task. The soldiers instead turned to the newly developed Heavy Shot Ayudag-6, a heavy-lift drone that can carry up to 130 kg and is equipped with a cargo winch.
"We'd been using Heavy Shot bomber drones for a long time and had an established line of communication with Gurzuf Defence," Alex said. "When I found out they were testing the new Ayudag-6 heavy-lift drone, I went to them immediately with this unconventional task. The drone was still a work in progress, but the developers were immediately fired up by the idea."
Gurzuf Defence designed the drone primarily for frontline logistics, as a heavy-lift modular platform. However, the engineers ensured from the very beginning that it had enough thrust to lift a person. The drone underwent two years of testing, during which the company's chief developer, Oleh Hynda, became the first person to fly aboard the test model.
"We never intended this drone to be just for evacuations – it's a heavy-duty logistics platform," Pavlo Feldblium, co-founder of Gurzuf Defence, told Ukrainska Pravda. "But we always knew it might have to be used for a rescue mission in certain circumstances. To prepare for this operation, we brought in units with experience of evacuating people using ground robotic systems. It was their experts who configured the winch and the mounting systems."
The company spent several months fine-tuning the platform at the unit's request. Experts from the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade's unmanned ground systems company then fitted the aircraft with additional equipment, and the 2nd Battalion's headquarters spent two months planning the operation. Around 15 military personnel were involved in preparing and planning the mission.
Pre-flight preparations took seven days. The military personnel worked out the flight routes, planned cover corridors and identified alternative emergency landing sites in case of a technical failure.
The evacuation drone was operated by Chornyi ("Black"), a squad leader in a mortar battery at the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Mechanised Brigade. "I first got to know the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 a week before the mission, when I took part in special training exercises. Until then, I'd only worked with standard Heavy Shot drones," he says.
The most dangerous part was hoisting the soldier, who had to attach himself to the cable on his own. The day before the flight, the drone delivered off-the-shelf mountaineering equipment and a phone loaded with a video explaining how to put on and secure the harness.
According to the plan, the soldier had to attach himself to the drone's winch with carabiners, sitting in a semi-reclined position. Any mistake when securing himself, or losing consciousness during the flight, could have sent him falling to the ground.
16 kilometres
Russian FPV anti-aircraft drones meant the cargo drone could not fly alone. Slow and bulky, with a payload suspended beneath it, it would be immediately spotted by Russian reconnaissance. The headquarters planned a diversionary manoeuvre to draw attention away from it.
Several formations helped provide cover for the operation. Alongside the 2nd Battalion of the 30th Mechanised Brigade, units from the 14th and 43rd Separate Mechanised Brigades took part, as did personnel and equipment from the 10th Army Corps. The day before the flight, the neighbouring units involved suggested putting it off because there was no fog. But the forecast showed no fog was expected any time soon, so the command decided to go ahead.
"We studied enemy drone activity to find the time when it was at its lowest. We decided to fly at first light, as night gave way to day," explains Alex, the battalion's reconnaissance chief.
The main diversion was carried out by Vampire heavy bomber drones, which flew into neighbouring sectors simultaneously to draw the attention of Russian anti-aircraft drone operators. The Russians shot down one Vampire, but the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 carrying out the evacuation went unnoticed.
Alex spent 48 hours studying data on Russian assets around the planned mission area. Experts from the 3rd Army Corps also helped prepare the Ayudag's electronic warfare system for the flight.
An Autel quadcopter operated by the battalion provided visual cover for the Ayudag-6, giving the crew a pair of eyes in the sky. However, it struggled to keep pace with the faster evacuation drone. A Ukrainian Lucky Strike drone waited nearby, ready to ram any Russian reconnaissance or strike UAVs that appeared. As the aircraft carrying Magura returned, artillery from the 10th Army Corps delivered concentrated suppressive fire against the identified launch points used by Russian drone operators.
Headquarters had a backup plan in case the drone malfunctioned or was shot down over the left bank of the Oskil River. Reconnaissance teams and ground robot crews were standing by near the designated emergency landing sites, ready to respond.
The Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 relied on Starlink for communications, which kept Russian electronic warfare systems from jamming it. No interference was detected on the control links. The drone's altitude was adjusted to suit the terrain, and it took a different route back to prevent the Russians from identifying its outbound flight path.
The drone was in the air for less than an hour and a half. The operator spoke to the wounded soldier through the drone's onboard camera and microphone.
The drone could not cover the full 16 km on a single charge: carrying a person drained its batteries too quickly. Two ground support teams were deployed along the route in advance to provide the necessary support.
"On command, I flew to a waypoint, where the team changed the batteries. Then I continued to the evacuation point, picked up the wounded soldier and flew him back," says Chornyi, who piloted the evacuation drone.
At the transfer point, the wounded soldier was detached from the winch. The next leg of the evacuation was carried out by a Peacemaker ground robotic system, as using vehicles would have risked exposing the operation to the enemy.
The troops camouflaged the platform and laid mattresses in its cargo compartment. The remotely controlled Peacemaker then covered another 8 km off-road. Once in a safe area, the team transferred Kostiantyn to a vehicle and took him to a frontline stabilisation point for emergency surgery. The Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 returned to base intact after a battery change at a stop along the route.
Kostiantyn told Ukrainska Pravda: "The flight went smoothly. I spent most of the time looking at the terrain below. When I landed, I felt safe and relieved – I'd finally be able to see my family soon. A special thank you to my unit clerk, Livsha, for keeping me well supplied with treats."
Despite the soldier's calm assessment, the actual flight revealed issues that had been difficult to anticipate during training with a dummy load. He had not been given protective goggles, so the powerful airflow beneath the rotors and the headwind caused discomfort. However, this did not detract from the mission's overall success.
Alex also credited Kostiantyn's calmness during boarding with helping make the mission a success. He had to get onto the drone in an open area while its rotors were spinning above him.
"The soldier was exceptionally quick-thinking and determined to survive," he said. "We had already dropped off his equipment and instructions. When the quadcopter approached, he did everything exactly as instructed, as quickly as possible. There was no panic or hesitation – the whole thing took just seconds and went exactly to plan."
The future of aerial evacuation
One successful operation does not make aerial evacuation a regular option, nor can it replace ground-based evacuation. Missions like this require extensive preparation and coordinated support from multiple units. This operation involved reconnaissance, artillery, decoy-drone crews and ground teams. Without them, the aircraft carrying the wounded soldier would have been shot down by the first Russian interceptor drone on its way.
The drone's developers take a similar view. Gurzuf Defence says the risks to a casualty's life during flight are simply too high for aerial medical evacuation to become standard practice.
"We don't see aerial evacuation becoming routine," says Pavlo Feldblium, co-founder of Gurzuf Defence. "When people talk about thousands of such missions or suggest that drones could help meet the 'golden hour', I think of the science fiction of Ray Bradbury or Stanisław Lem. You can't launch an operation like this on the spur of the moment. Every mission is unique and has to be planned around the specific conditions on that section of the front line. It's important to understand that this is always a last resort."
The experience of rescuing Magura, however, has prompted changes to drone development. Gurzuf Defence has decided to equip its mass-produced Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 logistics drones with the technical modifications and mounting kits needed for emergency evacuations, enabling them to be used for rescue missions when necessary.
The company stresses, however, that the evacuation equipment will not necessarily be used on every flight: the drone remains primarily a logistics platform. The developers are also working on entirely new variants of the platform with a substantially higher payload capacity.
The operation has shown that wounded soldiers can be evacuated by air even if they cannot walk and are stranded in remote positions. Other manufacturers are also exploring this capability. SkyFall recently unveiled its StarGate evacuation drone.
This evacuation, carried out by the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade and the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, has proved the viability of the concept and highlighted the urgent need for an evacuation method that can be used when all other options fail. Magura's rescue has set a precedent for saving lives in situations where conventional evacuation is impossible.
Kostiantyn "Magura" Vlasenko, who held a position on the left bank of the Oskil River for 491 days despite losing both feet, has been nominated for the title of Hero of Ukraine.
After Magura was evacuated to the rear, the commander of the 10th Army Corps visited him in hospital and personally presented him with the Order of Bohdan Khmelnytskyi, 3rd Class. The infantryman had been awarded the order in May, while still holding his position. Soldiers from the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, who planned and carried out the aerial evacuation, have also been nominated for state awards.
Representatives of Gurzuf Defence – the manufacturer of the very Ayudag-6 that flew him out of hell – also visited Magura in hospital.

European, Middle East ministers urge US-Iran diplomacy, not new attacks
An escalation would ‘create nothing but losers’, French foreign minister says as US official warns of possible strike.
Foreign ministers from eight countries are cautioning the United States against further attacks on Iran after meeting in Turkiye to discuss the Strait of Hormuz and other regional developments.
Ministers from the United Kingdom, France and Germany, known as the E3, convened with counterparts from the R4 group of Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt on Friday, along with Italy.
Speaking after the meeting in Istanbul, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that none of the countries participating in the meeting approved of another military intervention or attack on Iran.
Such a move would only exacerbate tensions and further expand the conflict, he said, adding that diplomacy and dialogue were the only way to end the war.
A further escalation between Iran and the US “would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told reporters.
“And so the first thing this group of eight countries … will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region,” he added.
Italy’s Antonio Tajani said the aim was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he said, noting that “we must promote dialogue” in order to reopen Hormuz.
The warnings came as the US ambassador to Turkiye, Tom Barrack, said Washington could “absolutely” strike Iran this weekend.
Speaking to X podcast host Mario Nawfal, Barrack said that although US President Donald Trump is “open and available and accessible to a deal … he’s also been very clear about what he wants”.
Barrack claimed that any potential US military action against Iran would not be aimed at regime change, saying Trump is “interested in rebalancing so that there’s no hostages, no threats, and the world can calm down”.
‘First of its kind’
The eight ministers discussed Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, escalating fighting in Yemen and prospects for ending the Russia-Ukraine war.
Reporting from Istanbul, Al Jazeera’s Sinem Koseoglu said the eight-nation summit was a “first-of-its-kind” attempt to discuss the parameters of regional conflicts and possible solutions.
Although participating countries “all have different national interests, especially when it comes to the crisis in the Gulf”, the Turkish foreign minister “underlined that what is happening in the Gulf … is affecting the other parts of the world”, Koseoglu added.
Foreign ministers of the R4 group issued a joint statement after a separate group meeting on Friday, saying that Israeli occupation “constitutes the fundamental source of instability in the region and beyond”.
The group urged Israel to “bring an end to further destruction and humanitarian tragedy in Palestine”.
The ministers also “condemned in the strongest terms the unacceptable escalation by the Houthi militia”, expressing full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government. They also called on the Houthis to cease all military actions and return to the political process.
The ministers underlined the urgent need for dialogue and diplomacy concerning the US-Israel war on Iran. They rejected any measures that restrict lawful navigation and called for the full resumption of secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
Turkiye’s regional efforts
The meeting at an Istanbul hotel came as Turkiye seeks to bolster its role in the region, including through the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, the trilateral pact launched with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August.
Turkiye has said that the pact is not aimed at any specific country and remains open to others joining, including Egypt.
Referring to the diplomatic platform, Fidan said it has “several advantages, particularly because it is informal and flexible and focuses specifically on the issues we face”.
“We are not aware of any other platform that brings together countries with such different geographical and political backgrounds,” he said, noting that Ankara “is well placed to play a constructive role in this process”.
Cairo has yet to decide whether to join the agreement. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi recently said that Egypt would “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia.
The Iran-backed Houthis are fighting Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces, who are backed by Saudi Arabia, and have launched a series of deadly attacks on the kingdom.

A cable across contested waters: The great sea interconnector’s promise and risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:28:37 UTC
01:28:37 KST

A seabed survey is usually an engineering step. For the Great Sea Interconnector (GSI), it has become a test of how far Greece, Cyprus and Türkiye can manage their maritime dispute without letting it derail a major infrastructure project.
In mid-October 2026, the GSI developer applied to resume surveys for the planned undersea electricity cable linking Greece and Cyprus, with a possible extension to Israel. Türkiye says the survey area overlaps with claims set out in its 2019 maritime agreement with Libya. Greece says it can proceed. The application has brought that agreement back into focus because someone must map the seabed before the cable route can be finalized and the parties disagree over who has the right to do so.
The project has a clear purpose for Cyprus. It is the only EU member state without an electricity connection to the continental grid. The first phase would link Greece, via Crete, to Cyprus along an 898-kilometre route, with a planned capacity of up to 1,000 megawatts. If completed, the connection could give Cyprus another source of electricity, allow it to export surplus power and make it easier to integrate renewable generation into its isolated grid. The EU has committed €657 million through its Connecting Europe Facility.
Greece would gain a stronger position in regional electricity trade. A later extension to Israel could widen the network, although that is not part of the immediate Greece–Cyprus link. US officials have backed the project as a way to diversify energy connections amid the war in Ukraine and instability around the Strait of Hormuz.
That case for diversification needs a clear boundary. The GSI is an electricity interconnector; it will not carry oil or gas, and it cannot bypass Hormuz. It could give Cyprus another way to access electricity from a connected market. It cannot replace hydrocarbon supplies or guarantee that power will be available during a regional crisis. Its value will depend on how much electricity is available to exchange, how well the grids are connected and whether the cable remains operational.
Building digital resilience: Qatar, Iraq and the new Gulf–Europe fibre corridor
The route is where engineering meets diplomacy
Greece’s Independent Power Transmission Operator, IPTO/ADMIE, is developing the roughly 1,200-kilometre project. French contractor Nexans has applied for permission to resume seabed surveys on the developer’s behalf. Greek approvals and a maritime notice are still required. Around 60 percent of the survey work has been completed; the outstanding section lies in disputed waters. The completion estimate has moved from around 2030 to early 2031.
Greece and Cyprus say the route is within their maritime rights and that Türkiye has no legal basis to stop the work. The EU supports the project and maintains that the Türkiye–Libya memorandum infringes the rights of third states and does not comply with the law of the sea. Türkiye rejects the EU’s assessment.
It argues that parts of the proposed route overlap with its continental-shelf claims and the 2019 agreement. These are competing legal positions; the survey application does not settle them.
There may, however, be room for a practical arrangement. On 22nd October, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Türkiye did not oppose the surveys if it received written notice, including the coordinates of the planned work. That could help prevent a misunderstanding at sea. Whether it will be enough for Greece and the project’s other partners to proceed remains uncertain, and notification would not resolve the underlying claims.
Libya’s recent move has complicated the picture. The 2019 agreement was signed by Türkiye and Libya’s then Government of National Accord in Tripoli. On 20th October, Libya’s eastern-based House of Representatives approved it, reversing its earlier opposition.
Greece rejected the decision as legally ineffective, while Türkiye welcomed it. The vote gives the agreement broader political backing within Libya, but it does not settle its international legal status or remove the objections of Greece, Cyprus, Egypt and the EU.
This shift matters because it makes it harder to dismiss the memorandum as an arrangement supported only by Libya’s western authorities. At the same time, Libya’s divided political institutions and the disagreement among regional states make it harder to see a quick diplomatic settlement. The EU is both a major funder of the cable and an outspoken critic of the maritime agreement. Its support gives the project weight, but also places it squarely within the wider political dispute.
Overland lifelines under pressure: Iran’s trade with its neighbours
War adds urgency and another layer of risk
The war in the Middle East has made the GSI’s diversification argument more compelling. Shipping disruptions and tension around Hormuz have reminded governments that energy markets remain vulnerable to events far beyond their borders. A connection between Cyprus and the European electricity system could offer more flexibility. It would not shield the project or the connected countries from conflict.
The war can affect construction through practical channels. Reuters has reported sharp increases in maritime insurance premiums and shipping costs since the conflict widened. Those reports concern vessels operating in the region; they do not establish that GSI survey or cable-laying vessels have already faced higher premiums. But if insurers judge those operations riskier, coverage could become more expensive or restrictive. Extra security measures could add costs, while an incident or prolonged delay could push the project further behind schedule.
Even without conflict, a subsea cable of this length is technically demanding. The route must be mapped in detail, installation requires specialist vessels, and converter stations must connect the cable to the grids at each end.
Once the link is operating, maintenance and repair capacity will matter: an interconnector improves resilience only if faults can be addressed promptly. Delayed surveys can hold up design decisions and construction planning as well as the cable itself.
The financing plan will face a harder test
The EU’s €657 million grant is substantial, but it covers only part of the investment. The remaining costs are expected to be shared through national contributions, private investment and regulated cost recovery. Under the current allocation, Cyprus would bear about 63 percent of capital costs and Greece 37 percent. French investor Meridiam has taken a 66 percent stake in the project company; IPTO holds the remaining 34 percent. That brings in a private partner, but it does not guarantee that investors will pay for overruns.
The €1.9 billion estimate is already in question. Cyprus’s finance minister has warned that the final cost could be significantly higher and that additional funding may be needed. He has also questioned whether the project will reduce electricity costs enough to justify the investment. If the total rises, governments will need to identify who pays the difference through new financing, public contributions, borrowing or higher regulated charges.
Cyprus has made some payments conditional on progress. Its commitment includes annual payments of €25 million for five years, capped at €125 million, and officials have linked the first payment to a notice confirming that surveys are resuming. Consumers are expected to pay through regulated charges once electricity begins flowing. That delays the impact on bills, but it does not mean the project will lower prices. If construction costs rise, consumers in Cyprus and Greece may ultimately shoulder part of the increase. The surveys should help clarify technical requirements, but until they are complete, €1.9 billion should be treated as a working estimate rather than a final bill.
Beyond shared identity: Military cooperation across the Turkic states
A narrow path forward
The GSI could give Cyprus a valuable link to Europe and create new opportunities for electricity exchange. But the project’s benefits are not automatic: they depend on completing the cable, keeping it reliable and paying for it on terms governments and consumers can sustain.
The next step is to make the surveys possible without turning them into a contest of resolve. Advance notice, clear coordinates and direct communication could reduce the risk of a confrontation while leaving the legal dispute for diplomacy. The project’s sponsors also need to publish credible cost updates and make clear how overruns would be shared.
If survey work resumes safely and the funding plan holds up under scrutiny, the GSI could become a useful addition to Eastern Mediterranean electricity infrastructure. If the route remains a recurring flashpoint or the final cost rises without a transparent plan, political support may weaken. The cable’s prospects rest on engineering and finance but also on whether the states involved can manage their disagreement without letting it block the work.

Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

19:24:11 EEST
01:24:11 KST

As of October 21, Ukrainian farmers had sown 3.9279 million hectares of winter grain crops, or 75.4% of the projected area, and 1.1207 million hectares of winter rapeseed, or 101.4% of the forecast area, the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food reported on its website.
In particular, 3.5134 million hectares had been sown with wheat and triticale (a hybrid of wheat and rye), representing 77.4% of the forecast area; barley covered 343,800 hectares (57.9%), and rye 70,700 hectares (92.1%).
Grain crop sowings increased by 536,800 hectares over the past week, compared with an increase of 870,900 hectares the previous week and 925,700 hectares in the week before that.
Compared with the area sown with grain crops by the same date last year, at 3.8039 million hectares, this year's total is 3.3% higher. The area sown with wheat is up 2.0%, barley 14.5% and rye 17.8%.
As for winter rapeseed, the area sown this year is 8.8%, or 90,700 hectares, larger than last year's.
The Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food specified that the leading regions in terms of winter grain crop sowing area are Mykolaiv region, with 462,000 hectares; Dnipropetrovsk region, with 399,000 hectares; and Kirovohrad region, with 348,000 hectares.

R4, E3 mechanisms

The E3 mechanism, comprising Germany, the UK and France, emerged in 2003 as part of trilateral diplomatic cooperation concerning Iran's nuclear programme.
Over time, it evolved into a framework for joint diplomatic initiatives on various regional and international issues.

Iran calls for nationwide oral history program across all 31 provinces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:24:01 UTC
01:24:01 KST

Iran calls for nationwide oral history program across all 31 provinces
TEHRAN - Iran’s minister of cultural heritage, tourism and handicrafts has called for a national program to record and document oral history across all 31 provinces, saying the initiative is essential to preserving the country’s historical and cultural memory.
Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri made the remarks in a message issued to mark the opening of the ministry’s first practical training workshop on oral history. The message was read by Gholamreza Zarifian, head of the council for oral history policy, at the workshop’s opening ceremony, Mehr news agency reported on Thursday.
Salehi-Amiri described oral history as a means of documenting, analyzing and safeguarding a nation’s collective memory, stressing the importance of systematically recording experiences, knowledge, accounts and developments related to cultural heritage, tourism and handicrafts.
“Future generations will build Iran’s tomorrow based on recording the developments of today,” he said in the message.
He said expanding oral history projects to all 31 provinces was a strategic necessity for protecting Iran’s historical, cultural and social heritage and developing a more complete national account of changes in the three sectors.
Much of the knowledge and experience associated with these fields, he noted, has developed within local and regional communities. Failure to document such material could result in the loss of an important part of the country’s historical wealth.
The minister stressed that oral history should not be confined to the ministry’s central administration, a handful of provinces or widely known historical accounts. Instead, he called for a nationwide program implemented in stages and tailored to the capacities and characteristics of each province.
Achieving this goal would require a common scientific methodology and a coordinated national framework, allowing provinces to document their distinctive experiences and narratives while following shared research standards, the message said.
Key measures would include developing national oral history guidelines, identifying research priorities, selecting significant interviewees, establishing appropriate sampling methods and using standardized interview guides.
The process should also include accurate recording and transcription of interviews, verification of information, documentation of sources, expert review, preservation of original files and the creation of standardized metadata, according to the message.
Salehi-Amiri also highlighted the need to train provincial researchers and interviewers and strengthen cooperation among provincial offices, universities, research centers, professional associations and local cultural institutions.
He said ethical research practices must be observed throughout the process, including obtaining informed consent from interviewees, protecting their intellectual and material rights, and establishing clear rules governing the storage, access and publication of their accounts.
The proposed program should reflect Iran’s historical, cultural, linguistic, social and geographical diversity, ensuring that the experiences of different social groups are represented in the national oral history collection.
These groups could include veterans and experienced professionals, former and current managers, handicrafts masters and practitioners, tourism professionals, cultural heritage workers and local communities.
Salehi-Amiri stressed that the initiative should go beyond collecting interviews and lead to the production of useful, credible materials, including books, documentaries, audio and video programs, portraits, exhibitions and educational content.
Such outputs could help integrate local accounts into a broader understanding of Iran’s national history, strengthen cultural identity, document developments in tourism and handicrafts, and provide information to support future policymaking, he said.

The Netherlands confronts Israel while hiding from its own Jewish history - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:23:45 UTC
01:23:45 KST

On September 22 the Netherlands began enforcing a decree that makes it a crime, punishable by up to six years in prison, to buy or sell Israeli goods produced beyond the 1967 armistice line. Customs officers at Schiphol Airport are reportedly searching luggage from Tel Aviv for wine and dates. The government says it is meeting its obligations under international law.
No Dutch decree threatens prison for a bottle of Turkish wine from occupied Northern Cyprus, Moroccan phosphate from Western Sahara, or a cotton shirt from Xinjiang. China, Turkey, Morocco, and many other governments with disputed territory can sell freely in Amsterdam. Of all the countries in the world, the Netherlands wrote a criminal statute for exactly one, and it is the Jewish state.
From most European countries that would be ordinary bias or hypocrisy. From the Netherlands, it is something else. To explain why, we are compelled to share our own families' experience in the country we grew up in, and about what Anne Frank's diary left out.
Many know the Dutch from cheese, herring and Anne Frank. Two of those are accurate. The diary gave the world an image of ordinary Dutch people risking everything to hide a Jewish family. That story is true, but as a portrait of the nation it is almost exactly backwards. The helpers were real, but they were rare. The diary turned these singular saviors into the whole country, and the Dutch were happy to let that be the narrative.
Here is the rest. The Dutch Nazi party had over 75,000 active members during World War 2, several times the few tens of thousands who ever joined the resistance. After the war, 425,000 Dutch individuals were accused of active collaboration with the Nazis, which is nearly 5% of the wartime population.
The machinery of persecution in the Netherlands was Dutch
The Germans did not even bother with a military administration. Unlike France or Belgium, the Netherlands got a civilian one, and the machinery of persecution was Dutch. The municipal registry handed over every Jewish address. Local police carried out the raids. The Amsterdam tram company drove Jews to the collection points and billed the occupier for the fare. In 1943, Dutch civilians formed a unit to collect a German bounty for every Jew in hiding they turned in. The Frank family was discovered, likely on a Dutch tip, and sent through that machinery to Westerbork and then east.
Of about 140,000 Jews in the Netherlands, roughly 102,000 were murdered, three in four, the highest rate in Western Europe. Dutch authorities often implemented the anti-Jewish orders with zeal. Fortunately for our families, that was not the whole population: thousands of Dutch citizens disobeyed their authorities and risked their lives for their Jewish neighbors. But they were the exception. Survivors, our grandparents among them, came home to find neighbors occupying their houses, and in 1946 the city sent them back tax bills covering the years they had spent in concentration camps. Amsterdam's tram company was still chasing the German government in 1947 for payment on its final deportation run. The Dutch government did not apologize for the treatment of its Jews until 2020.
None of this obliges the Dutch to admire Israel's government or policies towards the Palestinians, and we don't doubt that the images from the war in Gaza produced real revulsion. But something else happened underneath it. The Israeli psychoanalyst Zvi Rex once put it in a sentence: the Germans will never forgive the Jews for Auschwitz. If the Jewish state can be cast as the perpetrator of the age, then the descendants of the people it was built for are owed nothing, and the tax bills and the tram fares and the bounties are finally paid off. The Dutch found a way to liberate themselves from feeling guilty.
When NOS, the Dutch public broadcaster, began describing Israel's conduct as "genocidal violence," following a report about Gazan casualties that turned out to be incorrect, leaked emails published online showed the editor-in-chief applauding the decision and justifying it by the lack of complaint emails it received. True, there aren't many Dutch Jews left to write them.
Dutch Jews hunted
You can see how liberated the Dutch feel from their history in how the country now treats the Jews who still live there. In March 2024 the Netherlands opened its National Holocaust Museum, twenty years behind schedule, partly because residents petitioned to keep such memorials out of their streets. At the opening, broadcast live, a survivor named Rudie Cortissos fixed a mezuzah to the doorpost with his great-granddaughter beside him. A few dozen feet away, with the mayor's permission, a crowd whistled, shouted and hurled slurs about “Zionists” and Jews.
On the first anniversary of October 7, Jews and their supporters gathered on the main square in Amsterdam to mourn the victims while protesters were again permitted to station themselves nearby, assaulting and harassing dozens on their way in. A month later, Israeli soccer fans and Dutch Jews were hunted through the same streets by hundreds of young men who had planned the night in group chats. They called it a Jodenjacht, a “Jew hunt”. That was their own word for it.
Under international pressure, prosecutors moved. Courts gave the men they caught sentences measured in weeks; the heaviest was six months, and several were cut on appeal. Through Dutch media, however, a false narrative was promoted that put the blame on the Maccabi Tel Aviv fans.
Now put the numbers side by side. Beating a Jew on an Amsterdam street: six months. A Dutch Jew bringing back wine from the wrong side of a line: six years. That is the moral ranking the Netherlands has written into law, for Israel alone, and it is the same country that delivered over three quarters of its Jews to the Germans and then billed the survivors for taxes.
None of this is the 1940s, and we will not pretend it is. It is something smaller and, to Dutch Jews, quite familiar: a country that has decided its history entitles it to judge rather than obliges it to remember. Shame is not a punishment. It is what a decent country feels when it looks at its own record. The Dutch did look. Then they hid behind a young Jewish girl's diary and those rare exceptions to the Dutch record of shameful compliance, and decided to move on.
Richard Priem and David de Bruijn grew up in Amsterdam and The Hague respectively and now live in the United States. Richard is the CEO of the Community Security Service, a nonprofit that works to secure the American Jewish community. David is Senior Lecturer at Auburn University.

UAE reports oil spill from tanker as ships attacked during war

Breadcrumb
UAE reports oil spill from tanker as ships attacked during war
The United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill from a tanker off its coast on Friday, as vessels in Gulf waters come under attack during the Middle East war.
Frequent attacks on ships have been reported in recent weeks near the Strait of Hormuz, at the heart of the conflict between Iran and the United States.
The authorities "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement, referring to an emirate north of Dubai.
It said "teams immediately began containment, cordoning, clean-up and remediation... to limit environmental impacts," adding that the emirate's beaches had been closed.
Access to the area in Umm Al Quwain was restricted by police, AFP journalists who went there said.
The neighbouring emirate of Sharjah also closed one beach, Al Hamriyah, "as a proactive precautionary measure", the local government said.
Satellite images analysed by AFP showed a hydrocarbon slick on October 19 surrounding a vessel, likely the tanker GEM NO.2, located about 20 kilometres (12 miles) off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.
Images from October 21, analysed by Wim Zwijnenburg from Dutch NGO PAX, revealed a slick about 40 kilometres long and covering an area of 190 square kilometres, stretching to just six kilometres from shore.
The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on October 9 that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control.
Maritime security company Vanguard also identified the vessel as the oil tanker GEM NO.2, sailing under a Panamanian flag.
Owned by Taiwan's Global Energy Maritime, the ship loaded 2 million barrels of oil in early March from a Saudi port.
Since then, it has been regularly transferring cargo with other ships along the Emirati and Omani coasts near the Strait of Hormuz, according to tracking data from maritime company Kpler.
The images do not make it possible to determine whether it is thick crude oil or "a thin light oil sheen," Zwijnenburg said.
"If it is crude oil, then it is a serious pollution risk as this will end up on the beaches, affect marine ecosystems, including birds and turtles that can get stuck," he said.
"If it is a light oil sheen and mostly diluted oil, the hope is that it evaporates fast, and (you) only have short-term risks," Zwijnenburg added.
Foul odours
Many residents in the north of the country have reported chemical smells on social media in recent days, including residents in northern districts of Dubai, the largest city in the UAE.
"For the past two days it smelled like 10 gas stations spilled their gas everywhere," a Sharjah resident told AFP, asking to remain anonymous.
"I was on my balcony and panicked thinking gas was leaking in my house and I will blow up everyone."
The UAE says the odours "pose no health risks to residents".
Beyond efforts to contain the oil spill, "monitoring and assessing its environmental impact will also be essential to protecting marine ecosystems and the communities that depend on them," Inesaf Benzaki, campaigns lead at Greenpeace MENA, told AFP.
Since the start of the Middle East war in February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz and regularly targets ships that transit there without its authorisation.
Washington, in response, has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and escorts tankers through the passageway.
