The role of defense R&D in strengthening Israel’s capabilities, technological superiority - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:23:11 UTC
01:23:11 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu presented in a press conference a “lean,” concise document setting out his view of Israel's national security doctrine. It was drafted under his direct guidance by his National Security Advisor Shmuel Ben-Ezra. As expected, in the run-up to an election, the document drew torrents of criticism and scorn from his opponents, regardless of its contents and its role.
The last time the prime minister published a national security doctrine was in 2018. I had the honor of helping launch that effort in 2017 when I was the NSA. The final drafting and refinement were led by the Military Secretary, Maj. Gen. (res.), at the time, Brig. Gen. Eliezer Toledano and his team, with assistance from the National Security Council people.
The 2018 document included about ten unclassified pages, plus roughly eight classified pages. It contained several significant and new principles, among them: punishing those who send the attackers against Israel, not only those who attack us directly, a clear reference to Iran, and adding “civilian” infrastructure targets in the country from which Israel is being attacked to the list of legitimate targets, an obvious reference to Lebanon.
Some of the doctrine’s principles did not hold up on October 7. In the "Nagel Committee on the Defense Budget", which I have already discussed in several articles, we recommended several substantial changes to what we called Israel's “operational concept”, at the request of then Defense Minister Yoav Gallant. He insisted the committee will not develop a new “National Security Strategy”, before the Ministry of Defense had formulated its position. In practice, some of our recommendations clearly fall within the scope of NSS. They all feature prominently in the short document published this week. For example, the shift from a policy of "containment and defense" to one of "prevention and offense", and the principle that maintaining calm is very important, but not at any price.
Another principle we emphasized in our committee report is that an NSS cannot and should not be approved by the cabinet or the full government, as it is in many other places in the world, like the US, for example. The reason is very simple. The ministers understand that adding budgets to the MOD, as a result of the new NSS, will come on their ministry's behalf, so they will not vote for it, even when they accept it completely. This didn’t stop the comptroller and some anti-PM reporters from brutally attacking the fact that the old and new papers were not approved by someone other than the PM, as it should be.
The current document is much shorter than the one published in 2018, which was itself relatively brief compared with a traditional NSS paper. Despite its considerable importance, I don’t think the name "NSS document" is the right definition for such a paper. A full NSS doctrine should be broader and partly classified. I would instead describe it as a set of lighthouse guidelines and principles for Israel’s NSS. This description would not diminish the document’s value and might have defused some of the unjustified criticism.
In this article, I want to address one point in the new document and explain why it is critically important, as we claimed in the Nagel Committee: Technology and independence in force development.
The paper calls for:
Reducing dependence on external sources.
Strengthening Israel’s ability to develop its own forces through research, development, and domestic production.
Building world-leading capabilities in critical technologies such as quantum technology, artificial intelligence, and space.
Achieving all of these ambitions, and some more that are not mentioned probably because of classification, will require a substantial increase in the defense budget.
These principles rely first and foremost on sustained investment in defense and civilian R&D. The rest of this article will focus mainly on defense R&D.
As the committee’s recommendations stated, the IDF’s technological and operational strength, as successfully demonstrated in the Iron Swords War, despite some faults and gaps that emerged, is the result of sustained, long-term investment in defense R&D. This work has been led mainly by the Directorate of Defense Research and Development (MAFAT) and carried out by universities, research institutes, large and small defense companies, and startups.
R&D is conducted primarily through the central R&D budget, which funds basic research, technology incubation, feasibility studies, and demonstrations, as well as through government-to-government cooperation. The R&D budget must match the capacity to advance technologies and developments at the global frontier, keeping them relevant and attractive worldwide while preserving Israel’s technological superiority and independence where needed, and the qualitative edge (QME) of the IDF and the defense establishment.
In addition to advancing military technologies, the R&D budget also acts as a force multiplier for the defense industry, a phenomenon known as the “R&D multiplier”. Several independent studies have found that every shekel invested in research and development generates a return of at least seven times that amount, and sometimes considerably more, in future sales. Most of those sales come from defense export deals by the relevant defense companies. Recently, the trend has become reciprocal: defense R&D is also benefiting from spillovers from the civilian sector.
In recent years, especially in light of wars and the threats perceived by countries around the world, global demand for Israeli military technologies has risen dramatically. At the same time, competition is increasing, including from some countries that were not previously in the field. The rapid pace of change, input costs, technological developments, and other macroeconomic shifts led the committee to recommend increasing the budget allocated to the central R&D at MAFAT and to some specific huge projects, like space. This is in addition to the funding MAFAT directs toward R&D in the industry through government-to-government deals that it leads.
Recently, the boundaries between civilian and military technologies have become increasingly blurred. This creates intense competition for the technological workforce between the military sector and the civilian technology companies, even though some civilian technologies later find their way into military use. One example is autonomous robotic systems, including all types of drones, which have become a decisive factor in the Russia-Ukraine war and in our region. Similar competition exists in other technological fields, including AI, quantum technology, energy, advanced computing, advanced optics, and space. It is expected to intensify in the coming years.
Key elements in achieving technological superiority through R&D investment
The committee recommended focusing a significant part of R&D and force-development efforts on several key areas, with the goal of creating a complete system: a concept, an organizational framework, and the required weapons and equipment.
Israel must continue strengthening important areas that have received funding in recent years, including artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, space technologies, directed energy, with an emphasis on HPEM, and deep technologies. These fields will be essential to establishing Israel’s technological superiority over the coming decade.
At the same time, the defense establishment must continue identifying "disruptive technologies", particularly low-end capabilities. Some of these are based on “good enough” solutions that would allow the acquisition of large numbers of inexpensive systems. For example, a drone capable of flying 2,000 kilometers, carrying 50 kilograms of explosives, for less than $100,000 per unit.
The following is a partial list of key areas, without further detail. More information can be found in the unclassified version of the committee’s report:
Long-range missiles and munitions launched from the ground.
AI-based analysis and decision-making systems, leaving the final decision in human hands.
Robotics and autonomy for the battlefield.
Advanced space technologies.
Deep technologies.
Directed energy, with an emphasis on HPEM.
Hypersonic capabilities and high-speed flight.
New approaches to unmanned systems in the air, land, sea, underground, and underwater.
Scientific and technological workforce
The main resource needed to advance research and development in the IDF and the defense industries is technological talent. In recent years, the shortage of technological personnel in the IDF has become more severe. I will address this problem in a separate article, including the immediate recommendations the committee underlined that should be implemented. Some of them were already ordered for immediate implementation by the prime minister in 2025. We must act before we reach the point of no return.
Academia and high-tech as engines of defense innovation
Academia provides an essential foundation for many areas of science and technology that serve Israel’s security. Israeli academic institutions, including the Technion, the Weizmann Institute of Science, and the country’s other universities, are major sources of knowledge in fields such as artificial intelligence, cyber, nanotechnology, quantum, and nuclear physics. Israeli researchers develop groundbreaking solutions for the defense establishment, from missile-defense systems such as Iron Dome to advanced cyber technologies used by the intelligence services.
In Israel’s challenging security environment, where threats are constantly evolving, technological superiority is not a luxury; it is essential to survival. Countries and terrorist organizations are investing more in advanced technologies, and this threat requires Israel to maintain a significant technological edge.
Investing in academic research and development, dual-use civilian infrastructure, and startups, and accelerating and strengthening these efforts alongside the traditional defense industry, will enable Israel to stay one step ahead of its enemies. Technologies such as autonomous drone swarms, AI systems for intelligence analysis, and machine-learning-based information security solutions are all products of academic research that have been integrated into the defense industry, alongside significant advances in the private sector. It is essential to make full use of these assets as part of a comprehensive national vision and to invest in programs that can generate substantial progress in science and the economy.
Brig. Gen. (Res.) Prof. Jacob Nagel is a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD) in Washington. He served as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s national security adviser and as acting head of Israel’s National Security Council.

Lebanese people want Israel ties, stronger government to oust Hezbollah, AMCD head says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:23:10 UTC
01:23:10 KST

The Lebanese people want “full diplomatic ties” with Israel and to enjoy the benefits of tourism and trade with their neighboring state, but are being held captive by both Hezbollah and a government unwilling to confront the Iran-backed group, President of the American Mideast Coalition for Democracy John Hajjar told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday night.
Hajjar, who visited Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, and Haifa several years ago, said he grew up hearing stories from his Lebanese grandparents about Jewish holidaymakers who would visit the Lebanese mountains for rest and relaxation when his grandmother was young. He said Israel and Lebanon had much to offer each other’s citizens, arguing that the misapplication of Lebanon’s 1955 anti-boycott law had created unnecessary barriers to engagement between the neighboring countries.
The law was originally intended to prevent trade and financial dealings with Israel as part of the Arab League’s efforts to economically isolate the Jewish state, but has since been used to prevent even the most basic forms of communication, benefiting Hezbollah and Hamas, Hajjar said.
When the boycott law was first introduced, Article 7 stipulated that violations could be punished with three to 10 years of temporary hard labor, alongside financial fines, asset seizures, and product confiscation. However, Hajjar said, members of the Lebanese diaspora have since faced sentences of up to 15 years in absentia simply for expressing the view that Lebanon would benefit from pursuing peace with its neighbor.
More recently, there were efforts to have Lebanon's Ambassador to Washington, Nada Hamadeh Moawad, prosecuted over her message of support to Israeli Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter, whose son was wounded in a terror attack.
The Lebanese people demand peace
“The Lebanese people demand peace. They want to grow their economy. The infrastructure in Lebanon is in shambles. Lebanon is still a beautiful place, and a lot of economic activity still goes on, but it could be so much better if there were strong ties with Israel,” Hajjar argued. “... It would be mutually beneficial for both Lebanese and Israelis if peace is established.”
Earlier this week, Hajjar and his co-chair, Tom Harb, wrote an open letter urging Washington to use its influence with Lebanon to push for the repeal of the boycott law, which would allow religious groups in Lebanon to finally visit the many holy sites in Jerusalem. They also called on the US to sanction members of the Lebanese judiciary involved in prosecuting violations of the law.
“You see it in poll after poll among the Lebanese. They're trying to break the wall of silence imposed by Hezbollah and other terrorist organizations, and by their proxies in the Lebanese government. But I believe that day is fast approaching when people will finally break free and say, ‘That's it. We're not going to tolerate these laws that forbid us from speaking with Israelis, and we want full diplomatic ties.” he continued.
Nostalgic for the years Lebanon was the “Paris of the Middle East,” Hajjar shared it had been disheartening to see a country he feels so connected with struggle to bear the weight of sectarian violence, terrorism and wars.
He argued that, given Lebanon’s own experience with Palestinian terrorism, many Lebanese could empathize with Israel following the October 7 attacks even as the war touched their own country following Hezbollah’s attacks a day after the invasion.
“I think the Lebanese diaspora in the United States understands the persecution of minorities, and they feel a natural affinity to the State of Israel and what Israelis have endured, because the Lebanese themselves have endured the same things in Lebanon for hundreds of years,” he said. “The horrible terrorist acts of October 7 were happening to the Lebanese in 1976 in Damour and Aishi, another Christian village, which was savagely attacked by the Palestinians. The same methods were used on October 7 in Israel, and I think a lot of Lebanese understand the suffering and feel a natural affinity for Israeli citizens because of what they are going through.”
Palestinian armed groups, including Fatah and other PLO-aligned factions, attacked the predominantly Christian town of Damour in January 1976, killing hundreds of people and forcing its inhabitants to flee. In October that year, Palestinian factions, including Fatah and As-Sa'iqa, attacked the southern Christian village of Aishiyeh, killing dozens of civilians and displacing its population. Palestinian refugees displaced from the Tal al-Zaatar camp were later resettled in Damour, while Aishiyeh was used as a PLO base. In total, more than 600 were killed in both attacks.
Asked how to deal with Hezbollah, particularly as AMCD advocates sanctions that critics argue could push Beirut closer to Tehran, Hajjar said Lebanon’s government needed to be refreshed if it could not end the “double game” of promising to disarm Hezbollah while turning a blind eye to it.
Hajjar calls for stronger government capable of getting rid of Hezbollah
Softer in his stance for Lebanon’s Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, Hajjar didn’t mince his words on the corruption in Beirut. He argued Nabih Beri has grown rich while pushing the boycott laws that deny opportunity to Lebanon’s struggling economy
“It's time for him to go, and if President Aoun and Prime Minister Salem can't get Hezbollah disarmed, then it's time for them to go,” he insisted.
Hajjar said that while the Lebanese people were often seen as eternally patient with a government unable to fulfill its promises, as demonstrated by the lack of justice over the Beirut port explosion and now the arms laws, that patience was waning, as was their willingness to remain “captive by Hezbollah.”
“Hezbollah has, despite its claims to the contrary, carried out wave after wave of assassinations against prominent Lebanese officials. It has infiltrated every segment of the government and civil society. It has operatives throughout the country, even in Druze and Christian areas, and the Lebanese have strong reasons to be very fearful. They also lack strong political leaders, and that is a direct result of the fact that those who have been outspoken and principled have paid with their lives,” he said, acknowledging how hard it has been for the Lebanese to push for any kind of change.
Asked about the war with Israel and the collateral damage that has wreaked havoc across multiple sects in southern Lebanon, Hajjar blamed the Lebanese government, saying that some people were too emotionally affected by the tragic losses to understand its responsibility.
“Some people have paid with their lives, unfortunately, because the Lebanese government is really a failed state. When you don't have a government that can protect its people and is strong enough to negotiate peace, the consequences can be very disastrous, and that's what has happened,” he shared. “I understand why Israel is conducting this war against Hezbollah, and I just wish the Lebanese government would realize that they have a common enemy in Hezbollah and other terrorist groups, including Palestinian groups that are still armed in the camps and Hamas, to the extent that it has any operations in Lebanon.”
“When all those terrorist organizations are defeated and held accountable, and their leaders are held accountable, either paying the ultimate price or serving long prison terms, maybe for life, then you're going to have more of this,” Hajjar concluded. “Hopefully, justice will be served, and the Lebanese government will stand up and look out for the interests of the Lebanese, not terrorists and foreigners who don't even hold Lebanese citizenship and are not patriotic Lebanese.”

Saudi missile plant expansion may produce more powerful missiles, study says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:23:00 UTC
01:23:00 KST

Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its ballistic missile factory to build larger solid-fuel missiles that could fly farther or carry heavier payloads, according to two US researchers who analyzed more than a year of commercial satellite images.
More capable missiles could help Saudi Arabia to deter attacks by Iran and make its military more self-reliant, while possibly strengthening its position in a deadly conflict with Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthi fighters.
But they risk fueling a regional missile race and could deepen opposition in the US Congress to a US-Saudi civilian nuclear agreement that has already raised concerns about proliferation.
Satellite company Planet Labs, based in the US, took images of the al-Duwadimi complex about 125 miles (200 km) west of Riyadh between April 2025 and September 2026.
The two researchers, Sam Lair and Michael Duitsman of the Foreign Policy Research Institute, assessed that those images show a new building that houses casting pits — wells in which a mixture of fuel ingredients is poured into missile motor casings and allowed to harden.
The Saudi embassy and Information Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
The building, flanked by what appear to be walls to protect nearby structures from accidental explosions, is at least twice as large as the one believed to house the plant’s existing casting pits, Lair and Duitsman said in their assessment. The Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI) is a non-partisan research organization in Philadelphia.
A second new building could be used to store fuel ingredients or finished missile components, they said.
The imagery "suggests that Saudi Arabia is expanding the infrastructure at the missile production complex, likely to produce larger missiles which could deliver larger payloads or reach longer ranges," they wrote.
Militaries favor solid-fuel missiles because they can be stored for long periods and launched more quickly than liquid-fuel systems.
Lair and Duitsman and experts from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) and the CNA research and analysis organization told Reuters that the makeup of Saudi Arabia's missile force suggests that the al-Duwadimi complex relies on Chinese technology. Lair and Duitsman said that its characteristics also are similar to Chinese missile plants.
Saudi Arabia secretly acquired about 40 liquid-fuel DF-3 ballistic missiles from China in 1987, according to a 1991 declassified CIA estimate. It displayed two of them for the first time in an April 2014 military parade, according to a Youtube video and photographs of the event.
The FPRI team also recently identified from social media videos and photos what they assessed was the wreckage in Yemen of a Saudi-fired Chinese-designed DF-15 missile.
Lair said the kingdom may now be producing the solid-fuel DF-15, and that the expansion of a1-Dumadimi is likely for the production of the longer-range DF-21 or a similar missile.
Riyadh is believed to have turned to Beijing because Washington has long restricted exports of longer-range missile systems.
The Chinese embassy and defense ministry did not respond to requests for comment. The CIA declined to comment. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Missiles would alter the balance of power
Sascha Bruchmann, a research fellow at IISS, said longer-range missiles would allow Saudi Arabia to strike Iran without risking its US-supplied F-15 jet fighters against Iranian air defenses.
“You’d want a system to threaten whatever is holy to Tehran ... if you don’t have the political will to send an F-15 with JDAMs over Tehran,” said Bruchmann, referring to US-made satellite-guided bombs. “Iran has a lead because its missiles and drones can strike Saudi wherever it wants. The Saudis could close that capability gap a bit.”
Bruchmann, who reviewed the FPRI analysis at Reuters request, concurred that the expansion of al-Duwadimi could be for producing more powerful solid-fuel missiles. Janes, the defense intelligence company, also reviewed it and said the buildings “may suggest an effort to expand production capability or support the development of longer-range missiles.”
Saudi Arabia's apparent pursuit of more powerful missiles comes as other Gulf powers are also seeking to expand their offensive and defensive arsenals, said Decker Eveleth, a CNA analyst who has been tracking the al-Duwadimi construction with commercial satellite imagery and concurred with the FPRI assessment.
“This is being replicated across the Middle East,” he said. “You see exactly the same thing happening in the UAE. You see the exact same thing happening in Turkey. Everybody is doing this now.”
The expansion of al-Duwadimi could have political consequences in the US by stiffening bipartisan congressional opposition to a US-Saudi agreement under which the US would help Riyadh establish uranium enrichment for power generation.
Opponents say that the deal lacks sufficient safeguards to prevent Riyadh from secretly building a nuclear weapon. The kingdom has denied any such plan.
Work began last year
The FPRI assessment said the Planet Labs imagery showed that the expansion at al-Duwadimi began in April 2025 with ground-clearing and digging for the suspected storage building. Work on the suspected casting-pit building began later that month or in early May, it said.
A December 12, 2025, photo showed what researchers assessed were two deep pits inside the building that had no roof yet.
A September 18, 2026, photo shows the roof still partly missing and "heavy duty blast diverting walls" on either side to prevent accidental explosions from damaging adjacent structures.
The walls, the researchers said, are somewhat similar to those depicted in imagery of US and Iranian missile plants and "further evidence the building is for casting solid propellant motors."
Finishing the roofs would not take long, the FPRI said, but installing casting equipment may take several months. The facility could be ready to start producing missiles as early as the end of the year.

Joint statement on famine risk in Sudan
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:22:42 CEST
01:22:42 KST

Joint statement on famine risk in Sudan Sudan Humanitarian action Joint statement On : October 23rd 2026 Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security. The risk of famine in the coming months, as warned by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, needs urgent action. There is no time to lose to save lives and prevent famine. An estimated 19.5 million people (41% of the country’s population) are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, including 5 million facing emergency levels of food insecurity. Without immediate action to reverse the current trajectory, the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000. The number of food insecure areas, initially assessed at 14, is expected to double. Conflict is the key driver of Sudan's hunger crisis, displacing millions of people, damaging critical infrastructure and disrupting healthcare provision, food production, supply chains and markets. The situation is being exacerbated by systematic obstruction of aid and the effects of El Niño, which has resulted in reduced rainfall and increased drought across over half of Sudan. The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people. We urge the parties to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance, allow and facilitate full, safe, rapid, and unimpeded humanitarian access, and protect humanitarian personnel. Left unchecked, these impediments will hamper the ability of the humanitarian response to address famine risk. In practice, we call on the parties to: Authorise humanitarian operations through all crossline and cross-border routes, including air access into Darfur which will allow for the rapid deployment of aid operations and timely aid worker medical evacuations; Sustain presence and protection of humanitarian personnel throughout Sudan, including reducing delays for visas and customs clearance, increasing the duration of visas and travel permits and removing additional permits, taxations and other bureaucratic requirements slowing aid delivery; Refrain from strikes on civilian infrastructure, including agriculture and food systems, which are critical to the delivery of essential services to the civilian population. Strengthen civil-military coordination to ensure the safety of humanitarians and humanitarian sites. In the face of a potential famine, we call on all members of the international community to urgently scale up funding in response to increased needs and support efforts to ensure assistance reaches those most in need. We further encourage development and financial institutions to adapt their ongoing programmes to the food security situation and focus on the areas of greatest need. Together we must act without delay to avert famine by supporting the winter cropping season and strengthening locally led responses. We stand with the people of Sudan and humanitarian organisations who are working tirelessly and under extremely challenging conditions to provide life-saving assistance. Israel's Gaza ceasefire violations erode trust in international system: Turkish FM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:17:07 UTC
01:17:07 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said that Israel’s daily violations of the ceasefire in Gaza undermine trust in the international system and create an atmosphere of distrust.
Speaking at the opening of the 9th Istanbul Mediation Conference on Friday, Fidan said occupation in Gaza and the occupied West Bank continues and is met with impunity.
He stressed that ensuring humanitarian aid access and protecting children in particular must be priorities, reiterating that the Israel-Palestine conflict can only be resolved through a “just political solution.”
Dialogue and mutual trust
Fidan said Türkiye’s mediation efforts rest on the consent of the parties, mutual trust and inclusiveness, citing Ankara’s engagement in Libya.
“Türkiye's efforts in Libya, for instance, show how consent, mutual trust, and inclusiveness can build confidence,” he said.
“We engage in a result-oriented dialogue in Libya with all parties, both in the West and the East, as well as international partners,” the foreign minister said.
A Libyan-owned process based on sincere dialogue is the only path to a lasting solution, he said.
Fidan stressed that communication channels must remain open even when progress is slow and fragile. That approach, he said, has guided Türkiye’s efforts in Russia-Ukraine talks, the Black Sea grain initiative, as well as the Ankara process between Somalia and Ethiopia.
Regional ownership
Turning to the recently signed Mecca defence agreement between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, Fidan said the alliance “aims to secure the region's peace, prosperity and future”.
“Its foundation in regional ownership gives these efforts a stronger chance of success,” he noted.
He also highlighted the Balkans Peace Platform as a mechanism rooted in regional ownership that could turn dialogue among Balkan nations into practical results.
Fidan stressed that Türkiye has consistently worked to elevate mediation from a diplomatic instrument into a strategic discipline, and built the institutional architecture to match that ambition.
“We do not seek to impose outcomes, but to create the conditions in which parties can reach their own,” he said.
“Because mediation is not about deciding who wins, who loses, or who makes concessions. It is about finding common ground and working towards a win-win solution for all parties.”
Türkiye's experience, based on sincere dialogue, sustained engagement, and regional ownership, demonstrated how this approach can contribute to regional and global security, Fidan added.

Ukraine's electricity exports halve due to Russian strikes – Energy Map
Ukraine's electricity exports have halved, falling to 83,600 MWh, while imports have increased by 49% to 19,400 MWh.
Source: Energy Map portal
Details: Significant changes in electricity exports and imports occurred in the middle of this week. On 12-14 October, daily exports amounted to 19,900-25,200 MWh, but after yet another massive Russian attack on 15-17 October, they dropped to 4,200-6,600 MWh.
On 18 October, exports amounted to just 500 MWh. Imports remained stable throughout the week at 2,600-3,100 MWh per day.
Structure of imports by country:
- Hungary – 12,300 MWh (63.3%)
- Romania – 5,600 MWh (29.0%)
- Poland – 1,500 MWh (7.5%)
- Moldova – 30 MWh (0.2%)
The volume of purchases from Poland has increased by 103%, from Romania by 56% and from Hungary by 41%, while the volume bought from Moldova has decreased by 30% (insignificant volumes). There have been no supplies from Slovakia for six consecutive weeks.
Structure of exports by country:
- Hungary – 42,000 MWh (50.2%)
- Moldova – 24,400 MWh (29.2%)
- Romania – 16,600 MWh (19.9%)
- Poland – 600 MWh (0.7%)
Exports have decreased across all destinations: to Poland by 66% (insignificant volumes), to Moldova by 57% and to Hungary and Romania by half. There were no sales of electricity to Slovakia.
Background: At the beginning of October, the Ministry of Energy reported that Russian attacks had caused several elements of the power grid supplying Kyiv to shut down, leaving a significant number of consumers in some areas of the capital without a stable power supply.

Experts highlight Lut Desert geopark bid, Kerman’s geological and natural attractions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:16:42 UTC
01:16:42 KST

Experts highlight Lut Desert geopark bid, Kerman’s geological and natural attractions
TEHRAN - Experts have highlighted the potential benefits of establishing a UNESCO Global Geopark in Iran’s Lut Desert, saying the initiative could promote sustainable tourism, create local jobs and strengthen protection of the region’s unique geological heritage.
The issue was discussed at a specialized meeting on the Lut Desert, part of a series of seminars on Kerman studies held at Shahid Bahonar University of Kerman.
Speaking at the meeting on Thursday, Ebrahim Mohammadi, a faculty member at the The Graduate University of Advanced Technology (GUAT) in Kerman, discussed the province’s tourism potential, with a particular focus on the Kaluts of Shahdad, a striking landscape of eroded earth formations in the Lut Desert.
Mohammadi said Kerman province is home to 10 properties inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List and covers an area larger than the combined territories of 115 countries. He didn’t, however, mention that some of those UNESCO sites are shared with other nearby provinces.
Despite its vast size and exceptional range of natural, geological, historical, cultural, religious and spiritual attractions, the province attracts only about 0.7% of Iran’s tourists, although it accounts for around 11% of the country’s territory, he said.
Mohammadi, who holds a doctorate in paleontology, outlined several potential benefits of securing Global Geopark status for the Lut Desert.
He said the designation could strengthen the desert’s international profile and bring its important geological sites under a more integrated management framework.
It could also encourage sustainable geotourism, support the development of scientific and nature-based tourism routes, and persuade visitors to spend more time in the region by offering a wider range of experiences.
According to Mohammadi, the initiative could generate employment and strengthen the local economy by creating opportunities for tour guides, traditional accommodation providers, transport services, handicraft producers and other local businesses.
He also emphasized the importance of expanding scientific research and education, particularly in geology and geomorphology, while increasing local communities’ participation in protecting the region’s natural heritage and benefiting from tourism.
Elsewhere in his remarks, Mohammadi suggested that a geopark could help improve conservation across the Lut Desert by establishing stronger management links among its prominent geological sites and reducing damage caused by uncontrolled tourism and inappropriate use of natural resources.
Developing a unified tourism destination would also help promote the Kaluts of Shahdad alongside other geological attractions through complementary routes and visitor experiences, he added.
The initiative could further strengthen Kerman’s international tourism brand, raise awareness of its natural and geological assets, and expand scientific and international cooperation.
Mohammadi also stressed that sustainable development in the region would depend on directing tourism toward environmental protection, distributing its economic benefits among local communities and adopting scientific and participatory management practices.
He also highlighted the need for a comprehensive conservation and tourism plan, systematic documentation of geological sites, public education and cooperation between responsible institutions and local residents.
The meeting also addressed the historical importance of traditional water-management systems in Shahdad, a settlement on the edge of the Lut Desert.
Mohammad Barshan, director of Kerman province’s Qanat Center, discussed the origins and age of Shahdad’s qanats and their role in supplying water for agriculture and sustaining human settlement in the arid region.
Qanats are traditional underground water channels that transport groundwater to the surface, allowing communities to obtain water in areas where rainfall is scarce.
Drawing on years of research and practical experience with qanats, Barshan emphasized their significance in the development of settlements and civilizations.
“Digging a qanat is an epic, a great epic of replacing death with life,” he said, describing the ancient water systems as closely linked to the development of civilization among communities across Iran.
Barshan also discussed the qanats of Shahdad, stressing the central role of water in the rise and decline of civilizations.
“Civilizations are formed with water and disappear with water,” he said.
The discussions highlighted the potential for combining geological conservation, scientific research and the preservation of traditional water-management heritage to support sustainable tourism and local development in Kerman province.

Spouses of six countries’ ambassadors named honorary tourism envoys of Hamadan

Spouses of six countries’ ambassadors named honorary tourism envoys of Hamadan
TEHRAN - The spouses of ambassadors from Denmark, Romania, Mexico, Uruguay, Nicaragua and Armenia, along with Romania’s ambassador to Iran, have been named honorary ambassadors for cultural heritage, tourism and handicrafts in Iran’s western province of Hamadan.
The initiative, held in cooperation with Iran’s Foreign Ministry, aims to introduce Hamadan’s historical and cultural attractions to international audiences and strengthen cultural ties and tourism cooperation between Iran and other countries.
Speaking at the ceremony on Wednesday, Mohammadreza Akbari, head of the Hamadan Department of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts, said cultural heritage could transcend geographical borders, linguistic differences and national identities, serving as a common language that brings nations closer together.
He described Hamadan as a province with thousands of years of history, valuable historical monuments, rich cultural traditions and considerable potential in tourism and handicrafts.
Akbari said these assets form part of Iran’s civilizational identity and the shared heritage of humanity, adding that introducing them to international audiences could improve mutual understanding and pave the way for greater cultural and tourism cooperation.
According to Akbari, cooperation with diplomatic figures could help introduce foreign audiences to the province’s historical landmarks, local arts, handicrafts and cultural traditions.
He also emphasized that developing international tourism requires more than historical monuments and natural attractions, noting that effective promotion, sustained international engagement and cooperation between cultural and tourism institutions are equally important.
Akbari expressed hope that the initiative would mark the beginning of lasting cooperation between Hamadan and the six countries, contributing to cultural understanding, friendly relations and the preservation of shared human heritage.
Hamadan, often described as the historical and civilizational capital of Iran, is home to a range of archaeological, historical and natural attractions.
Among its best-known sites are the ancient city of Ecbatana, the Ganjnameh inscriptions and waterfall, Ali Sadr Cave, the mausoleums of Avicenna and Baba Taher, and the Alavian Dome, to name a few.
The province is also home to Lalejin, internationally recognized for its pottery-making tradition, which has made it one of Iran’s leading handicrafts centers.

Gokhan Ergocun
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Gold prices fell below the $4,000 level for the first time since July 2026 as a selloff in technology stocks and inflation concerns fueled by rising oil prices weighed on demand.
Gold traded at $3,998 an ounce, down 0.5% as of 1600GMT. The precious metal has fallen 6.3% over the past month and 2.63% over the past year.
Silver prices also fell 0.75% to $54.2 per ounce.
The decline came as losses in technology and artificial intelligence (AI) stocks prompted investors to sell precious metals to cover losses elsewhere in their portfolios.
Concerns over the cost of AI investment intensified after Meta Platforms outlined plans to increase capital expenditure, raising fears that technology companies could take on additional debt to finance their expansion.
Rising oil prices also pressured gold by heightening inflation concerns and reinforcing expectations that interest rates could remain elevated for longer.
Higher interest rates typically reduce the appeal of gold, which pays no interest, relative to interest-bearing assets.
However, uncertainty over the sustainability of AI investment, a key contributor to US economic growth, prompted markets to pare back expectations for further Federal Reserve rate increases, offering some support to precious metals.

Elon Musk Just Dumped Another $76 Million Into the Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:12:49 UTC
01:12:49 KST

Elon Musk gave his personal political committee, America PAC, more than $76 million in the first two weeks of October to boost Republicans in the final stretch of the midterms, according to a pre-election report the PAC filed Thursday evening with the Federal Election Commission.
The group spent nearly $43 million in the first two weeks of October, and entered the campaign’s last leg holding nearly $47 million in cash.
The Texas Senate race dominated the new spending. It drew $15.2 million, double what the PAC spent there all summer. That spending included $12.4 million to attack Democratic candidate James Talarico and $2.8 million to promote Republican Ken Paxton.
Daily filings since then show $9.1 million more against Talarico, bringing the PAC’s spending against him this cycle to nearly $28 million, about 40 percent of everything it has spent supporting or opposing candidates. The PAC also shifted toward online ads, spending $11.4 million on digital ads in the same two weeks, which is close to what it spent on mail and texting combined.
All told, Musk has given more than $445 million to Republican political groups this election cycle, according to WIRED’s analysis of FEC filings, making him the biggest known individual donor in the midterms. More than $165 million of that has gone to America PAC since July alone.
America PAC declined to comment.
Musk—who has several companies, including Tesla and SpaceX, based in Texas—has also been posting online about the race. On Wednesday, Musk posted on X that “there is something deeply wrong with Talarico,” then called him “a creep” and claimed, without evidence, that he “would vote to take away your kids and transition them.” Earlier this month, Musk amplified a false claim that Talarico had been treated at a mental health facility. Talarico shot back the same day: “There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator.”
The Texas race remains a toss-up. An Emerson College poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters, conducted October 17 to 19, found Talarico at 48 percent and Paxton at 46 percent, within the poll’s 3-point margin of error.
The stakes for Musk reach well beyond Texas. If Democrats win the House, the lawmakers in line to lead its committees have signaled they will investigate his role in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), his companies’ federal contracts, and what Zoe Lofgren, a California Democrat, called an “astounding” number of conflicts of interest. Unified Democratic control of Congress would pose even more problems for him.
Silicon Valley Democrats added another target on Friday: restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service in Ukraine. In a letter to the White House demanding an investigation, Representatives Sam Liccardo, Jimmy Panetta, and Ro Khanna vowed that the next Congress “will closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk’s businesses.”

Ukraine customs, WTO launch joint audit in Lviv region to fight corruption
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:12:23 EEST
01:12:23 KST

The State Customs Service of Ukraine, together with experts from the World Customs Organization (WCO), has begun reviewing internal goods-clearance procedures and is introducing the European practice of process mapping to eliminate corruption risks.
According to a statement on the State Customs Service's Telegram channel, the mapping method involves a detailed analysis of every stage of a work process, from the sequence of actions and decision-making to the allocation of powers and responsibilities among participants. This makes it possible to identify vulnerable stages and develop mechanisms to minimize the associated risks.
The practical stage of risk assessment and analysis of the actual movement of cargo took place directly at Lviv Customs facilities. During the review, WCO experts and Ukrainian customs officers assessed each stage of export and import clearance operations, as well as the use of scanners and other technical customs control equipment to eliminate the human factor.
In addition, the State Customs Service is working with WCO specialists to develop a Code of Ethics establishing standards of professional conduct and integrity for customs officers in line with international approaches.
Earlier, the State Customs Service announced the introduction of a mechanism for the automatic customs clearance of imported and exported international postal and express shipments without physically presenting them to customs authorities and without the involvement of officials.

ICE agents tackle and injure U.S. citizen student with disabilities, local officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:08:06 UTC
01:08:06 KST

ICE agents tackle and injure U.S. citizen student with disabilities, local officials say
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A Santa Maria High School student, who is a U.S. citizen, was detained by immigration agents on Wednesday, according to school and city officials.
- The student, a 20-year-old with limited verbal communication, was hospitalized for wrist injuries afterward.
Federal immigration agents violently detained a 20-year-old U.S. citizen and Santa Maria (Calif.) High School student with special needs on Wednesday morning, according to school and city officials.
The student, who has limited verbal communication and is on an individualized education program, was walking to school around 7 a.m. when two agents tackled him from behind, questioned him about his citizenship and restrained him in their vehicle. He was eventually released in the area where he was picked up and walked to school, where officials called for an ambulance to take him to the hospital, said Santa Maria City Councilmember Gloria Soto.
The student underwent surgery for injuries to his wrist, she said, and was left with bruises and lacerations.
Soto said a school resource officer obtained security footage from a nearby grocery store and confirmed that the people who had detained the student are agents with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
In an emailed statement, an unidentified ICE spokesperson wrote that agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation in Santa Maria “when they encountered an individual they believed matched the description of the criminal illegal alien target.”
“When the individual resisted officers, refused lawful commands, and assumed a fighting stance with clenched fists, they relied on their training to safely control the situation until they could confirm his identity, whereupon he was released,” the spokesperson wrote.
The spokesperson added that claims that the student suffered broken bones are false because “he never requested medical assistance.”
Glenn Goldin, a retired special education teacher at Santa Maria High who still mentors the student who was detained, said he worked for a long time to build the confidence to walk by himself to school. Now he’s wary of returning to school.
The student told Goldin that he saw a black car pull up and kept walking. The agents were masked and didn’t announce who they were, but he noticed they wore vests that said “POLICE ICE.” The student told Goldin that he had his Real ID in his wallet, but the agents didn’t ask to see it.
“He told them repeatedly that the handcuffs were too tight and they were hurting him,” Goldin said.
Goldin said the student has no family and lives in a group home for adults with developmental disabilities.
After the agents released him, the student walked to school, crying and in pain. His teacher saw him and dialed 911, Goldin said.
“He was so scared,” Goldin recalled the student telling him. “He thought they were going to kill him. He thought he was going to die.”
Soto said it appears the student was racially profiled. She called for an independent investigation into how a case of mistaken identity by ICE agents ended with the student being hurt.
“Our community is living in terror right now and this needs to stop,” she said, referencing a recent uptick in immigration arrests across central California. “I’m a mother, and the thought of my child not being safe walking to school is frightening.”
The Santa Maria Police Department declined to comment and referred questions to ICE.
Alma Hernandez, board president of Santa Maria Joint Union High School District, said she was horrified by ICE’s actions.
“Our district remains committed to protecting our students and families,” she said.
Kenny Klein, the school district’s spokesperson, said the student was detained by ICE about a half-mile from campus.
“The student then proceeded to walk to school. School administration called an ambulance, and the student was taken to the hospital to receive medical care,” Klein wrote in a statement, adding that parents, guardians, students and staff were notified of the incident.
Santa Maria police responded to the situation and notified appropriate agencies, including the local district attorney and the California attorney general, he added.
805 UndocuFund, an advocacy group, wrote in an Instagram post that volunteers witnessed several more community members stopped and questioned by ICE on Wednesday. The group organized a rally and protest this Saturday in support of the student.

One person killed in suspected ‘Islamophobic’ shooting near Paris

One killed as Elysee calls Paris area shooting ‘racist, terrorist attack’
Antiterrorism prosecutors investigating motive of attack that seriously wounded five, including a 12-year-old girl.
A gunman has killed one person and wounded five others, including a 12-year-old girl, in a possible Islamophobic “terrorist crime” in the Paris suburbs, authorities said.
An unidentified 39-year-old male suspect was taken into custody shortly after the attacks in the towns of Trappes and nearby La Verriere outside the capital on Friday.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the suspect fired at a children’s playground, a fuel station and a medical centre, the Reuters news agency reported. Three of the victims, including the 12-year-old girl, suffered life-threatening injuries, he said.
Nunez said the attack lasted less than 15 minutes and that the gunman appeared to have used “a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon”. Prosecutors were treating it as a “terrorist crime” and investigating whether it was racially or religiously motivated, he said.
The Elysee presidential palace described the shooting as a “racist, terrorist attack” as French President Emanuel Macron visited Trappes, a working-class town about 20km (13 miles) west of Paris, after the shooting on Friday.
Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh said the gunman “appeared to be firing at random and seemed intent on carrying out a massacre”.
“This was a terrorist attack with racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones,” he said.
Rabeh said the person killed was “of African origin” and that one of the wounded, who was in critical condition, was “of North African origin”.
La Verriere Mayor Nicolas Dainville said the girl, who was shot eight times, was seriously wounded but in stable condition.
“I’m North African and it’s frightening for everyone who has the same background,” Adel, a 50-year-old resident of Trappes, told the AFP news agency, saying his “heart was broken” at learning the victims might have been targeted for their race.
Two of the wounded in his town, cleaners working at a school on Friday morning when the gunman got out of his car to open fire, were of African origin, he said.
Macron said national antiterrorism prosecutors had taken over the case, opening an investigation for “murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise” and examining whether the attack targeted the “real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion” of the victims.
They said the suspect had also booby-trapped his flat with three gas canisters and electric wires “connected to a timer”.
“Our thoughts go out to the victims, their families, and all the residents of Yvelines. In this terrible ordeal, the Nation stands by their side,” Macron posted on X.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said in a post on X that the case was “very serious” and that “all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised”.
Tensions ahead of Saturday protests
Separately, security was tightened ahead of planned nationwide protests this weekend. Many of the demonstrations have been banned following burning and looting at protests last weekend.
Nunez said France would deploy 70,000 officers across the country on Saturday, along with helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannon. In addition, elite police units will help secure public buildings, such as city halls, in a “highly mobile” security operation, he said.
Protests last week caused chaos, with people setting fires, storming public buildings, smashing shop windows, looting and clashing with police, in France’s most violent unrest in years.
France has been on edge since the riots, and overnight curfews were put in place in cities across the country for a week.
Far-right politicians say the government has not cracked down hard enough on protesters, while left-wing groups say the security around demonstrations violates rights.
Demonstrators plan to take to the streets again on Saturday to denounce the high cost of living. Students, members of the Confederation of Labour, a national trade union and activists from the “yellow vest” movement, whose demonstrations against social injustice shook France in 2018 and 2019, are all set to join.

Israel’s olive harvest attacks demand full UK sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:02:16 UTC
01:02:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel’s olive harvest attacks demand full UK sanctions
Some fifteen years ago, I was lucky enough to be in Palestine during the olive harvest season. So much about what I saw on that visit was overwhelmingly sad and infuriating. The ugly infrastructure of apartheid was everywhere—the huge concrete apartheid wall with the looming Israeli sniper towers, checkpoints seemingly at every turn, menacing armed soldiers and hilltops dotted with settlements. But a visit with farmers in a village outside Jenin felt like stepping into an alternate universe, full of joy and beauty.
Multiple generations of Palestinian families all gathered together in varying degrees of work and play. Teenagers, usually glued to their mobile phones, were getting gentle lessons from their elders on the best way to shake the tree branches to loosen the crop. Joyful toddlers waddled around their grandmothers and mothers, who made tea while chatting and preparing the freshest, most delicious bread I’ve ever eaten, filled with fresh cheese and za’atar.
If you could train your eyes on this scene, you could imagine, for a moment, what a free Palestine might look and sound like.
The olive harvest season is not just a time for Palestinians families to gather and celebrate their heritage. It is traditionally the economic lifeblood of Palestine, already under significant pressure because of decades of Israel’s land grabs, not to mention restrictions on exports which benefit Israeli settlers and harm Palestine’s indigenous olive economy under occupation.
The olive harvest used to be a significant part of the economy in the Gaza Strip, where olive trees are now largely a memory of a time past, before endless expanses of rubble dominated the terrain.
A site of existential threat
In recent years, on top of the ordinary hardship of occupation, the olive harvest in the West Bank has increasingly been hit with violence and danger. Gone are the days when the olive groves could offer a glimpse of a possible future life — now they are a site of existential threat and fear.
The UN reported that last week, the official week starting the olive harvest, saw nearly 200 settler attacks across the expanse of the West Bank, with casualties, property damage or both, including damage to 2,500 trees and saplings. This is already more than the 185 comparable incidents recorded during the entire olive harvest season last year in 2025, which was already the worst many could remember.
These settler attacks don’t come out of nowhere. UN human rights experts raised alarm that the Israeli military had issued orders in September for the removal of vegetation, including provisions to uproot olive trees, from approximately 339,000 square metres (84 acres) of Palestinian agricultural land in the West Bank.
In what has now become a predictable pattern, the Israeli military provided a blueprint for settler attacks on the olive harvest through its policies. It is the same military, of course, which provides armed cover for the settlers when they wage their violent attacks.
When Palestinians report that the settlers and the army are working hand in hand, this is what they mean.
News footage from Palestine this week shows this starkly. Farmers work as quickly as possible before the mobs of settlers arrive, armed with clubs or worse. For Palestinian farmers, the thought of bringing family members who aren’t able to work quickly is unimaginable now, because of the looming danger in every minute.
The settler attacks are ruthless and don’t spare any man, woman or child. Mainstream news outlets globally showed videos last weekend of settlers beating and attacking a Washington Post journalist covering the West Bank, as well as European diplomats who had been on an official visit. One journalist who tried to help his colleague reported the difficulty of reaching her. This was not only because of the settlers, but also because the Israeli military was firing tear gas and live ammunition into the area, forcing the Palestinian farmers to flee their own fields.
You don’t need much more information to guess that if that is how white Americans and Europeans are being treated, Palestinians are confronted with violence that is ten times worse.
Weaknesses in the UK government’s response
Here in Britain, Israel’s colonial settlements have had more media exposure in the past few months than possibly ever before, as the British government announced new measures last month to ban the import of settlement goods and some limited sanctions, along with other measures designed to curb the actions of what Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband called “settler terrorists”.
Whilst these measures are certainly a step in the right direction, they don’t go nearly as far as they should. This month’s spike in attacks on Palestinians harvesting their olives shows both the weaknesses of the British sanctions as they are currently formulated, but also the possibilities that could be pushed if the government is serious about tackling settler violence.
The weakness of the British government’s position is that it has rhetoric that is tough on settler violence but treats that phenomenon as its own isolated problem. Understanding the inextricable link between the settler movement, the colonial settlements already established for decades, and Israel’s military occupation itself is key to intervening in the violence.
The settlers couldn’t function as they do without the full-throated support they enjoy from the Israeli military. And despite commitments to curb the flow of arms that enable the occupation, no additional arms exports to Israel have been halted since Miliband’s announcement last month.
The problem goes even further if one understands the link between the settler movement and the Israeli government itself. The British government seems to be still entertaining the fantasy that the settler movement can be isolated and treated separately from the Israeli state.
Of course it is the Israeli state itself which, over decades and across parties, has enacted policy and funded the settlements. Nowadays top Israeli government ministers come directly from the far-right settler movement, but this is a result of decades of normalisation of settlements, rather than the start of it.
Even if you could magically remove the far-right settler movement in isolation, many of Israel’s earliest West Bank settlements are now major hubs of the Israeli agricultural industry. They profit from land grabs from Palestinians, enriching themselves from Palestinian land and water, and dominating the exports of produce abroad, whilst Palestinian olive farmers struggle, and still would even without the violent settler attacks.
In order to really tackle settler violence, the British government must extend its sanctions proposal to be state sanctions on Israel. There is no separating out the settlements from the state, and there is no legitimate trade with a state committing apartheid and genocide.
These sanctions must include, but not be limited to, a full two-way arms embargo on Israel.
Stemming from this, the tasks of the solidarity movement are clear. We must continue to push the British government to strengthen its sanctions on Israel, through lobbying and protesting, but also by exposing the contradictions in what is currently in place.
None of these actions will stop the horror of settler attacks during this olive harvest season. The coming month will be a painful time for Palestinians who are being forced to defend themselves, their families, their livelihoods and their lands.
Whilst political debates within our solidarity movement rage on, certainly we can all agree that we absolutely cannot lose sight of the stakes for Palestinians, and the horrible costs they are paying every day. But this urgency must compel our solidarity forward to push our government to enact full sanctions on Israel now.
Ryvka Barnard is the Deputy Director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign UK.

The conflict has killed tens of thousands and displaced around 13 million people, fueling one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

Personalized cancer vaccine cuts risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% in trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:01:36 UTC
01:01:36 KST

Aysu Bicer
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
A personalized cancer vaccine administered alongside an immunotherapy drug reduced the risk of death or melanoma recurrence by 42%, according to results from a major clinical trial involving more than 1,000 patients.
The phase three trial found that the combination of the vaccine and Keytruda, an immunotherapy drug widely used in cancer treatment, also reduced the risk of melanoma spreading by 38% over two years compared with treatment with Keytruda alone.
The international trial involved patients with high-risk melanoma, an aggressive form of skin cancer. Participants received either the personalized vaccine alongside Keytruda or Keytruda with a placebo for approximately one year.
The study was double-blind, meaning neither the patients nor the researchers knew who received the vaccine or the placebo.
Researchers said the findings could represent a significant step toward personalized cancer treatment, which aims to stimulate the body's immune system to identify and attack cancer cells remaining after surgery.
“The personalized cancer vaccine uses exciting technology to stimulate the patient’s own immune system to recognise and attack any tumour cells remaining after surgery,” said Professor Pippa Corrie, a consultant medical oncologist in a statement on Friday.
“It is a whole new approach to cancer treatment which is designed to improve outcomes compared with standard anticancer drug treatments that don't take into account individual differences, and this trial was the first proof of principle,” she added.
Tony Chapman, 75, from North Northamptonshire, who participated in the trial at Addenbrooke’s Hospital, described the findings as “groundbreaking.”
Chapman was diagnosed with stage three melanoma in 2019 and underwent surgery to remove a tumour from his chest. Four years later, he discovered a lump under his armpit and required surgery to remove lymph nodes.
After completing treatment at the NIHR Cambridge Clinical Research Facility last year, Chapman remains cancer-free. However, it is not known whether he received the personalized vaccine or the placebo.
Drugmakers MSD and Moderna said the same approach is also being tested against other cancers, including kidney, bladder and lung cancers.
Independent cancer experts welcomed the results but stressed that longer-term studies are needed to determine whether the treatment improves overall survival for most patients.
The findings offer encouraging evidence for personalized cancer vaccines, although further research will be needed to establish their long-term benefits.

UN says 90% of women's organizations report unsafe conditions, distress among displaced from Sudan's El Fasher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:01:33 UTC
01:01:33 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Nine in 10 women's organizations assisting people displaced from Sudan's El Fasher report unsafe living conditions and persistent psychological distress a year after the city's fall, the UN Women said on Friday.
Anna Mutavati, UN Women's regional director for East and Southern Africa, told reporters in Geneva that a survey of 50 organizations found 45 reporting continued psychological distress among displaced women and girls, while 49 observed signs of distress.
"One year on, the scars of the violence in El Fasher have not faded," Mutavati said, citing sexual violence, missing relatives, killings and the destruction of homes and livelihoods.
She said 48 organizations reported that women were struggling to sleep because of traumatic experiences, while nine in 10 described unsafe living conditions.
Around two-thirds of the groups were aware of women or girls who had disappeared during or after the city's fall.
Mutavati said 43 organizations had encountered women or girls who received no mental health, psychosocial or legal assistance after fleeing.
She also warned of increasing drone attacks across Sudan, including in Blue Nile, Khartoum, West Kordofan, Gedaref and Kassala states, with women and children accounting for most of those killed or injured.
According to a separate assessment, 84% of 117 households surveyed in El Fasher reported that women avoided marketplaces.
Mutavati called for stronger civilian protection, accountability for abuses and improved access to essential services, while emphasizing the role of women-led organizations in supporting affected communities.
The civil war between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces erupted in April 2023. It has since displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

France to deploy 70,000 police ahead of new protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:01:18 UTC
01:01:18 KST

Breadcrumb
France to deploy 70,000 police ahead of new protests
France will deploy some 70,000 police nationwide as it braces for new protests this weekend after some of the worst urban violence in years erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations a week ago, the government said Friday.
President Emmanuel Macron, who according to aides is postponing a visit later this month to Nigeria and Senegal amid the crisis, held a meeting of his defence council of top ministers and officials and was to meet security forces.
He also hosted for the first time representatives of high school pupils, whose protests over conditions at their schools sparked the movement that has broadened into a nationwide show of anger against the government at the rising cost of living.
Some 70,000 security personnel will be deployed on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at a press conference in Paris, warning that calls for violence and looting were circulating on social media.
The protests have come at a critical moment for France six months ahead of elections to replace Macron, with a new poll underlining far-right candidate Marine Le Pen as the frontrunner and showing her position has been strengthened by the latest events.
Adding to tensions, Le Pen is at the weekend due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orleans, with thousands of supporters expected but local authorities fearing clashes as opponents head to the city.
Nunez was expected to visit the city Friday to "inspect the security arrangements" at the request of the prime minister's office, it said.
At Macron's meeting with students, "we will present our demands to him -- which remain the same: the state of school infrastructure and an overhaul of the Parcoursup (university admissions) system," Nathanael Combary, president of Renouveau Lyceen (High School Renewal) told AFP ahead of the talks.
Macron's government has sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of protests last Saturday.
In a judicial response of unprecedented firmness, courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said.
On Thursday, Macron called for "the utmost severity" against "acts of delinquency", accusing "ultra-left" groups of having sought to "bring down the republic" last weekend.
'Police have a responsibility'
A fresh wave of demonstrations is expected across France on Saturday, with authorities stepping up security measures and imposing restrictions on protests.
In Orleans, between 20,000 and 30,000 people were expected to come out against Le Pen's National Rally party, but the gathering will be barred from the city centre, the prefecture said.
In the southeastern city of Lyon, central areas will also be off-limits to demonstrators this weekend, while in Paris protesters will only be allowed to march a limited route between Bastille and Nation squares.
Authorities in Marseille had also banned protests but announced Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an "exceptional basis" -- the only one authorised in the southern Bouches-du-Rhone department.
They also reversed a decision to suspend all public transport in the city on Saturday. But in the capital, leading museums including the Louvre will be closed on Saturday while the Art Basel art fair is being cut short.
Some 20 percent more members of the security forces will be deployed this weekend after heavy criticism of the anticipation and intelligence gathering of police last week.
"In a country governed by the rule of law, the police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder," said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressing alarm over reports of children being severely injured by crowd-control weapons.
The violence has tarnished the image of France ahead of elections that could be a turning point in its modern history, with the government's debt pile also troubling investors.
A new poll by Harris Interactive for M6/RTL made after the violence showed Le Pen soaring ahead on 33-35 percent in the first round of voting for the presidential elections.
It predicted that hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon was on course to face her in the run-off where Le Pen would emerge as an easy winner on some 70 percent of the vote.
