Speaking at a press conference, Major General Abdallah al-Maaytah said most of those wounded in the shooting at the Hamoud Church in Karak governorate were still receiving treatment, and that the hunt for the attackers was ongoing. Jordan's health minister said 40 people were wounded.
Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said the attack had been carried out by "extremists", but that it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups inside or outside Jordan.
Khaled Burqan, a man who had been attending the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people had been attending the funeral and at least two men - one carrying a rifle and another carrying a pistol - opened fire on them for several minutes.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack and Jordanian authorities did not say who was responsible.
Jordan's King Abdullah said those behind the attack would be punished "with an iron fist."
"The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," he said in a statement.
Reuters footage from the church after the attack showed blood smeared on the floor near its entrance, where security forces were deployed.
Such attacks are extremely rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable, though Jordanian authorities say they have repeatedly foiled attempted attacks by terrorists in recent years.
Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.
Jordan's Minister of Endowments and Islamic Affairs Mohammad Khalayleh and several members of Jordan's parliament condemned the attack in comments to Al-Mamlaka.
In a post on X, United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the violence and said attacks against civilians and places of worship are unacceptable.
People who gathered at a Karak government hospital to support the wounded expressed shock.
"What happened today has left people unable to speak or raise our voices. But our only reproach to the state is that it must investigate these dark ideas - where they come from and how they enter the minds of our children," said one of them, Hani Al-Mbaydeen.

Microsoft says AI system outperforms doctors in simulated disease diagnosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:53:15 UTC
23:53:15 KST

Halis Sunnetci
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Microsoft said Thursday that its artificial intelligence system diagnosed complex medical conditions more than twice as accurately as physicians in simulated tests, citing research published in the journal Science.
The company’s AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO) achieved 83% diagnostic accuracy on complex medical cases, compared with 36% for physicians using textbooks and online resources, according to a Microsoft statement.
Physicians working without external reference materials achieved 22% accuracy.
Researchers evaluated 304 complex cases drawn from The New England Journal of Medicine, using a system in which multiple AI agents work together to assess symptoms, select diagnostic tests and reach conclusions.
The system also achieved 80% accuracy on more typical emergency department cases, compared with 47% for physicians, Microsoft said.
The company said MAI-DxO could also reduce diagnostic testing costs by selecting fewer or less expensive procedures while maintaining high accuracy.
In one cost-optimized configuration, the system achieved 81% accuracy on complex cases at less than half the estimated cost of comparative systems.
Microsoft described the findings as progress toward “medical superintelligence,” its vision of AI systems capable of surpassing leading clinical teams in medical reasoning and care coordination.
However, the results were based on simulated cases rather than real-world clinical practice, and the physician comparison did not include specialist teams.
The company said further evaluation in clinical environments is necessary to establish how the technology performs in actual patient care.
Microsoft plans to evaluate the system through a prospective study with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, comparing its diagnostic assessments with those of physicians in hospital settings.

Kneecap, Hozier urge Ireland to act over Gaza student visa refusals
A number of prominent Irish figures from film, television and music, including Kneecap, Hozier, Aisling Bea, Siobhán McSweeney and Christy Moore, have urged Taoiseach Micheal Martin to intervene on behalf of 55 Gazan students who have been refused study visas.
The appeal comes amid ongoing legal challenges to the visa refusals, with a High Court hearing examining the government's handling of applications from Palestinian students who secured fully funded scholarships at Irish universities.
In an open letter published by the Irish Examiner on Friday, the artists joined other signatories in urging Martin to “do the decent thing” by the students.
The letter cited Martin’s remarks to the United Nations last month, when he said the international community had failed Palestine, and called on him to intervene on the students’ behalf.
“You have the power to act, to stay true to our principles and promises, and grant these young Palestinians the opportunity of an education far from the rubble of Gaza,” the signatories said.
They added that the students were not taking places away from anyone else and had undergone rigorous vetting.
“They provided every document available to them in a warzone, and yet the minister for justice is refusing to grant them study visas. They are caught in a breakdown of co-ordination between Government departments that they did nothing to cause.”
The open letter follows similar appeals earlier this month from academics and the Ireland-Palestine Alliance Sadaka, who urged Martin, also Ireland’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, to intervene to resolve what they described as an “appalling injustice”.
They called for the applications of all affected students to be reconsidered properly and in time for the students to be evacuated from Gaza.
High Court challenges visa refusals
The continuing appeals come as legal proceedings challenge the Irish government's refusal of study visas to Palestinian students from Gaza.
During a High Court hearing on Tuesday, lawyers representing the students argued that the decisions were unlawful and irrational, highlighting the difficulties applicants faced in obtaining documentation amid the destruction caused by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
The government argued that the refusals were based on applicants’ inability to provide documentary evidence required for the visas.
The case centred on Shaymaa Abudalu, a survivor of the Gaza genocide who reportedly lost several family members, including her mother and siblings.
She had secured a fully funded place on a four-year engineering degree programme at University College Cork (UCC), but was refused a visa.
During the hearing, the court heard that documents confirming Abudalu’s English-language proficiency had been received by the Department of Justice but had not been considered by the official who rejected her application.
Judge Anthony Barr described this as a “substantial hole” in the government’s case.
However, the proceedings were ongoing, and the court had not yet issued a final ruling that the visa refusal was unlawful or ordered it to be set aside.
Following the hearing, Abudalu’s lawyer, Sarah Jane Hillery, said she hoped the case would clarify the issues affecting all the students.
The Irish Examiner reported that the Irish embassy in Tel Aviv processed Palestinian study visa applications last year, rejecting 13 per cent of them.
This year, the Department of Justice has reportedly refused 114 of 138 applications- a rejection rate of 83 per cent- including 55 applications from students in the Gaza Strip.

====================================================================================================

With Strict Agendas and Silent Corridors Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Is Muzzling the Press
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:50:00 UTC
23:50:00 KST

When Kazakhstan’s Kurultai convened in late August for the first time, there were new rules for the media. Journalists in the Kazakh capital’s parliament building were no longer able to question deputies in the corridors. The new rules set firm boundaries not only on where, but what, they could ask members of the country’s new unicameral parliament.
At the opening of the Kurultai’s first session on August 28, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proclaimed the body would “radically modernize the system of government and provide a powerful impetus to the work of the entire state apparatus.” Later in his speech he urged the Kutultai to become “a platform for national dialogue to develop solutions to key issues in society.”
The boundaries of that dialogue, however, are to be set by the Kurultai itself.
As explained by the Kurultai’s Deputy Chief of Staff Bolat Kalyanbekov in a September 2 Facebook post, “All interactions between journalists and deputies – as well as invited members of the Government – will now take place exclusively within the press center and strictly in relation to the Kurultai’s agenda.”
Kalyanbekov stated that briefings would be held on a regular basis and laid out the rationale behind the decision to bar off-topic questions.
“Our goal is to communicate the substance of the draft laws under consideration by the Kurultai to the public as clearly and comprehensively as possible – explaining the significance of each new legal provision and how the decisions being made may impact the lives of citizens,” he wrote.
Kalyanbekov also argued that the new rules were consistent both with Kazakh law and “established global practices.”
That’s not quite how Fiona O’Brien, the Europe and Central Asia regional director for the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), sees it. “Allowing journalists to informally approach and question deputies in the halls of parliament, and to ask questions not strictly related to the agenda of press conferences, are standard practices of established democracies,” O’Brien told The Diplomat.
Although Kazakhstan deems itself a democratic state, human rights organizations such as Freedom House, classify the country as “Not Free.”
“The kinds of restrictions on movement and questions implemented in Kazakhstan are more common in authoritarian or hybrid environments, where the authorities try to maintain an appearance of democracy while retaining strict control of the information sphere,” O’Brien explained.
***
On October 20, Otkir Kurek – an independent media outlet headed by Nazymgul Kumyspayeva, who also runs a YouTube channel – reported that a group of around 40 journalists accredited to the Kurultai had sent an appeal to Aibek Dadebay, chair of the body, demanding revision of the new media rules.
Otkir Kurek means “sharp shovel” in Kazakh.
Dadebay is also leader of the Adilet party, into which the former ruling party Amanat (née Nur-Otan) merged earlier this year in the runup to the Kurultai elections on August 23. Until May 5, Dadebay headed Tokayev’s presidential administration.
In the recent appeal, as reported by KazTAG, the Kazakh journalists took particular issue with the restriction of questions to agenda-items only.
Under the present rules, “For a question that the moderator deems off-topic, the journalist receives a warning. Two violations mean the loss of accreditation for six months… For a journalist who covers parliament, this is effectively a six-month ban from the profession.”
The appeal noted that the purpose of accreditation is to enable journalists “to inform the public broadly and promptly.”
“Kazakhstan’s parliament and other state organs have long tried to stop journalists asking ‘off-topic’ questions during press conferences,” CPJ’s O’Brien explained. “Introducing sanctions for doing so and preventing journalists from mixing freely with deputies in the halls of parliament essentially closes down the last avenues for journalists to freely question parliamentarians on issues not decided in advance by the authorities themselves.”
“A briefing that repeats what has already been said at the meeting provides no new information,” the journalists argued in their appeal, seeking a revision to the existing regulations to allow journalists to ask questions outside the strict agenda but within the purview of the featured speakers.
“A minister or deputy can always refuse to answer a question, respond later, or respond in writing,” the appeal noted. The journalists characterized the existing policy as unjustified. Journalists, they argued, need to be free to question ministers, deputies, and other officials – who, the appeal pointed out, “rarely appear in public and for whom the public has many questions.”
Kazakh journalists have already run afoul of these rules.
In early October, in the wake of a tragic accident on the Caspian Sea in which 14 servicemembers drowned during a military drill, journalist Asem Gumarova of Ulysmedia.kz asked questions related to the incident during a briefing with a member of parliament, Unzila Shapak, and Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs Sanjar Adilov. The brief was to cover a draft cybercrime law.
Gumarova asked Shapak when the 146 million tenge that had been reportedly collected by Kurultai members would be transferred to the families of the fallen servicemen. She also asked Adilov about reports of pressure being exerted by mysterious callers masquerading as police demanding that the authors of critical posts related to the Caspian accident take their posts down.
Ulysmedia said it received a warning letter threatening to strip Gumarova of her accreditation. The publication cited the “extraordinary nature of the incident and public demand” as justifying Gumarova’s questions.
The recent appeal to Dadebay cited the incident directly, noting that “[t]he question concerned police work online or crimes carried out under the guise of police – that is, the very topic of the briefing.”
***
Accreditation procedures vary country to country. But broadly speaking accreditation confers a degree of legitimacy on a journalist and their outlet and, importantly, provides access to official spaces and proceedings. In Kazakhstan, the Foreign Ministry handles foreign media and individual state bodies, like the Kurultai, as well as the Ministry of Culture and Information, deal with the domestic media.
Kumyspayeva, the editor-in-chief and founder of Otkir Kurek, was earlier this month denied accreditation by the Kurultai. Kalyanbekov provided an official response, which The Diplomat has reviewed, stating that the reason was a mismatch in email addresses on her application materials.
“The official reason given for the denial was that I had provided my professional email address in the accreditation application rather than the email address listed on our media outlet’s website,” Kumyspaeva told The Diplomat. “In my view, this was merely a technicality used as a pretext to deny me accreditation. I suspect the real reason lies in my independent journalism.”
Kumyspayeva takes no government funding, and told The Diplomat that the outlet does not participate in government-funded media contracts.
“As a result, government institutions have no leverage to dictate our editorial policy, determine what subjects we cover, or tell us which questions we are allowed to ask,” she said.
Kumyspayeva has lodged a formal complaint with the Kurultai’s leadership and she intends to pursue the matter in court, if needed. “I believe my professional rights as a journalist have been violated,” she said.
Kumyspayeva also signed the appeal sent to Dadebay regarding the media rules. She told The Diplomat her concerns stretch far beyond her own case.
“In my opinion, these restrictions constitute a form of censorship and contradict Kazakhstan’s constitutional guarantees of freedom of expression and the prohibition of censorship,” she said. “For me, this is not simply a dispute over accreditation for my media outlet. It is about something much more fundamental: the public’s right to information, the freedom of independent journalism, and the accountability of those in power.”
***
The tension here – between the Kutultai leadership and the journalists who cover the Kazakhstan’s legislature – is rooted in diametrically opposed perspectives on the purpose and role of the media.
In the Kazakh government’s view, as implied by Kalyanbekov and the new rules, the media’s role is to disseminate information provided by the government. Based on that, anything not on the agenda just shouldn’t be on the agenda. The government believes that it has the authority to decide what is newsworthy, and pestering officials with questions they’d rather not answer is rank insubordination.
“What concerns me most is that the leadership of the legislative body is effectively assuming the power to decide which journalists and media outlets are allowed to cover its activities and which are not,” Kumyspayeva explained. “In practice, this means access to elected representatives may depend not on a journalist’s professional status, but on how acceptable their reporting and questions are to the authorities.”
The Kutultai’s media rules merely add to a host of challenges faced by independent journalists in Kazakhstan.
“These restrictions are part of a severe constriction of the media sphere in Kazakhstan since the start of this year,” O’Brien argued, noting the cases of Gulnara Bazhkenova and the heads of KazTAG Aset Matayev and Amir Kasenov. Bazhkenova, former editor-in-chief of Orda, was sentenced to eight years in prison in August. Matayev and Kasenov were each given 15-months of “restricted freedom” and banned from journalistic activity for five years in July. The CPJ and other media watchdogs have characterized these cases as politically motivated.
Kazakh courts have increasingly banned convicted journalists from engaging in journalism or engaging in other forms of public activity. The real goal, O’Brien told The Diplomat, “is to ensure that prominent journalists are silenced for years ahead.”
The larger political context is unmistakable.
“This repression appears designed to instill a chilling effect and strengthen control over the press as President Tokayev navigates the final years of his constitutionally mandated single term,” O’Brien told The Diplomat.
Tokayev was first elected in a snap presidential poll in the summer of 2019, following Nursultan Nazarbayev’s surprise resignation that spring. At the time, Kazakhstan’s presidency was limited to two five-year terms. Not even three years into his first term, however, in the wake of Qandy Qantar – Bloody January – Tokayev saw through a wide-ranging constitutional referendum. Later that year, and 18 months early, Tokayev announced another snap presidential election. He paired that announcement with a proposal to limit the presidency to a single seven-year term. In November 2022, Tokayev was elected to his second term, confirming his grip on power until 2029.
The tinkering did not end there. Six months after commenting that haste in changing the constitution again was “completely inappropriate,” Tokayev saw through another constitutional referendum that touched almost every aspect of the document.
As the new constitution went into effect on July 1, Tokayev asked the Constitutional Court to clarify what it meant for re-election, or re-appointment, of term-limited officials, as well as the implications for the timeline on elections. The court replied that the president is eligible to run for another single seven-year term – which would technically be his third. But who’s counting?
Tokayev “is widely thought to be either preparing to run again or attempting to maintain strict control of the succession process,” O’Brien told The Diplomat. “The passing of a new constitution earlier this year and Kurultai elections, which coincided with major waves of pressure on the press, appear to be part of this process. With key journalists in jail or banned from working, the people of Kazakhstan will be less informed as this political process plays out.”
Dadebay has not yet responded officially to the Kazakh Kurultai press corps’ appeal.
“Freedom of the press is not a privilege granted by the authorities,” Kumyspayeva stressed to The Diplomat. “It is a fundamental right, and it is the public – not the government – that ultimately pays the price when that right is restricted.”

Many in Serbia’s Youth Movement Fear a Rigged Election on Sunday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:48:00 UTC
23:48:00 KST

Riding an extraordinary wave of public mobilization, Serbia’s student-led opposition heads into Sunday’s snap parliamentary election genuinely believing it can break President Aleksandar Vučić’s 14-year grip on power.
Yet beneath the euphoria of this week’s mass rallies lies a pervasive conviction among its supporters that the contest will be anything but fair—and that the ruling party will resort to outright ballot theft rather than concede defeat.
On Thursday night, that tension was on full display as hundreds of thousands of people flooded into Belgrade’s central Slavija Square, filling the surrounding boulevards in a buoyant, flag-waving display of collective defiance. The assembly marked the movement's final campaign rally ahead of an early vote that serves as the culmination of nearly two years of youth-led unrest against Vučić’s rule.
What began in November 2024 as grief and outrage following the collapse of a newly renovated railway station canopy in the northern city of Novi Sad—a disaster that killed 16 people and was turned by the protesting youth into a lethal symbol of state corruption and crony contracting—has since metastasized into a nationwide rebellion.
Now polling in a dead heat with the governing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), the youth movement’s “Students’ List” has mounted the most formidable electoral challenge Vučić has faced in over a decade. But across the sea of demonstrators in the capital, few harbored illusions about how the ruling machine will be handling the vote.
“I believe he will do anything he can to steal the votes and remain in power,” said Katarina Zajić, 45, a food technologist who works as an administrative clerk in the Belgrade municipality of Zemun.
That skepticism is informed by years of documented electoral abuse. International election observers, led by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) and backed by European Union institutions, have consistently found that while Serbian elections offer voters a nominal choice of candidates, the playing field is fundamentally compromised. In report after report, monitors have cited pervasive state capture of broadcast media, intense pressure on public-sector workers to mobilize for the ruling coalition, the routine abuse of public resources for partisan gain, and deep-seated anomalies in the voter register.
Domestic watchdogs have leveled even harsher verdicts. The Center for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA), Serbia’s prominent independent election observation group, concluded that recent election cycles—including the disputed parliamentary and municipal votes in 2023 and 2024—were “not free and fair.” The watchdog documented organized voter migration schemes, the mass registration of “phantom voters,” and the wholesale erasure of the boundary between state institutions and the ruling party.
Vučić and his party have vehemently denied any wrongdoing, routinely dismissing allegations of electoral manipulation as the reflexive excuses of “sore losers” fabricating an alibi for their own political weakness.
“These were by far the cleanest and fairest elections to date, and everyone knows it,” Vučić declared following the 2023 ballot, even as opposition leaders launched hunger strikes and thousands took to the streets to protest organized cross-border voter bussing.
For many of those who massed in Belgrade on Thursday, however, the gap between the government’s assurances and the documented reality on the ground has left them preparing for a confrontation that will not end at the ballot box.
“Vučić never organized fair elections. He never won the elections he didn’t organize, and there won’t be any difference this time,” said David, 45, who attended Thursday’s rally. “The more people come out for the elections, the bigger the chance to win against him. But if he still tries to steal, well, I don’t know... the streets.”
He paused, measuring the consequences of what might follow Sunday night.
“Violence is the last answer,” he said. “But if that’s the answer, we’re probably going to have to go that way.”

IMF sees $50–55 bln Ukraine gap for 2027–28, Russian assets key – Alternate Executive Director Rashkovan
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:47:49 EEST
23:47:49 KST

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates Ukraine's uncovered external financing needs for budget expenditures in 2027–2028 at $50 billion–$55 billion: $30 billion–$35 billion next year and another $20 billion in 2028. Instruments linked to frozen Russian assets are being considered among the key sources for covering these needs, Vladyslav Rashkovan, Ukraine's Alternate Executive Director at the IMF, said.
"I am confident that Russian assets will remain our key issue both now and in the future. It seems to me that over the next two months, the range of options available to us for financing 2027 will lie somewhere between ERA-2 and Ukraine Support Loan-2," he said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group, held in Bangkok on October 12–18.
Rashkovan clarified that IMF assistance with financing would cover nonmilitary budget expenditures, while additional defense financing needs would remain. Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko estimates Ukraine's defense financing needs for next year at EUR 40 billion. That is why Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced Ukraine's total need for additional financing next year at EUR 70 billion during a European Council meeting in Brussels on October 14.
The IMF Alternate Executive Director said that Ukraine's international partners are currently more focused on covering financing needs for 2026–2027, although the Fund's Extended Fund Facility (EFF) with Ukraine runs through 2029, and there is an understanding that financing needs in 2028 will also be substantial.
He referred to the Ex-Post Assessment of the previous "wartime" EFF program for 2023–2025, which contained an important conclusion: even if the war ends, for example, in 2027, this does not mean that public finances will return to normal as early as 2028, partly because demobilization cannot happen immediately and social spending will need to increase to support veterans and their families.
"Therefore, even if the war ends in 2028, almost the same amount will be needed. Expenditures will begin to decline only later. This is the model the IMF is working with today... This figure will not come as a surprise to our partners," Rashkovan explained.
As for the main sources of financing other than frozen Russian assets, he pointed to the EU's multiannual budget for 2028–2034, which is being discussed by the European Council.
"European officials assure us that support for Ukraine will be included in it. The current draft allocates EUR 100 billion for Ukraine. We will see what the final structure of the document looks like after the political discussions within the EU. I think it should be agreed by the end of the year," Ukraine's representative at the IMF said, describing the current status of this funding source.
Regarding frozen Russian assets, Rashkovan recalled that most of them are held in Belgium at the international depository Euroclear. They are invested in various instruments of the European Central Bank and the National Bank of Belgium and generate income. In 2024, the G7 established the ERA mechanism, based on discounting future cash flows generated by the continued investment of these assets. Through this mechanism, Ukraine received $50 billion. These are nominally loans serviced using revenues from Russian assets, but for Ukraine they are effectively grants with no repayment obligations or conditions.
After the failure to introduce a EUR 140 billion reparations loan, which European countries lacked the courage to implement at the end of 2025, the EU developed the Ukraine Support Loan mechanism, worth EUR 90 billion for 2026–2027, to provide military and nonmilitary support to Ukraine, Rashkovan added. He clarified that this is also nonrepayable assistance to Ukraine, but it is financed by EU taxpayers.
"I think that over the next two months, discussions within the G7 will revolve around these two instruments (ERA-2 and Ukraine Support Loan-2). Another option would be to look for unused funds in European Union budget programs. I do not have full access to this information, but I am afraid that EUR 70 billion will not be available there," the expert said.
He explained that ERA-2 would again be a financial engineering instrument built around the valuation of future cash flows. While ERA covered a 30-year period, a longer-term model is now being considered, for example, one spanning 50 years. Last December, the European Council decided that the EU would not return Russia's assets until reparations had been paid, significantly reducing the risk associated with this mechanism, Rashkovan said.
According to him, the amount of assistance to Ukraine could also be increased by raising the expected return on investments of Russian assets from the current average of 2.8% annually to, for example, 4% annually, given that yields on U.S. and European government securities are currently around 5%.
"Finally, we know that the assets are not held exclusively at Euroclear. Around EUR 30 billion is held in private French banks. It would be worth provisionally factoring in these funds when developing the model as well," Ukraine's representative at the IMF added.
Summing up, he said that such planning and financial engineering could mobilize around $20 billion for Ukraine, but this would not solve all its problems, particularly given military spending.
"Ultimately, we will still have to turn to G7 finance ministers to cover those costs, because their countries are the ones financing them. (Therefore,) the second option is the Ukraine Support Loan," Rashkovan said.
In his view, it would be possible to increase the size of this instrument beyond the initial EUR 90 billion, the amount determined by the IMF last year.
"If the Fund had identified a need for EUR 140 billion, our partners would have looked for EUR 140 billion. Therefore, it is important now to agree on a common understanding of the total amount: $30–35 billion in nonmilitary needs plus EUR 40 billion in military expenditures, for a total of approximately EUR 70 billion. Accordingly, the ceiling for the Ukraine Support Loan needs to be increased. The instrument and its legal framework already exist; the only thing needed is to raise the lending limit," Ukraine's representative at the IMF said, outlining a possible course of events.
He clarified that in this case, the European Union would have to raise the funds on the market before providing them to Ukraine. At an interest rate of 4%–5%, this would cost approximately EUR 3 billion annually in interest, which European countries would like to cover through assistance from non-European G7 countries. In that case, the mechanism would be almost cost-free for both the European Union and Ukraine.
Among less realistic sources of financing, Rashkovan also mentioned the $5 billion frozen in the United States and the REPO Act (Rebuilding Economic Prosperity and Opportunity for Ukrainians Act), adopted in April 2024. The law allows the U.S. president to confiscate Russian sovereign assets under U.S. jurisdiction and direct them toward assistance to Ukraine.
"Unfortunately, it was not applied even under the Biden administration, and this has still not been done. That is why another initiative, called the PEACE Act, has emerged. It effectively requires the U.S. Treasury secretary, within 90 days after the law enters into force, to seize the relevant assets and transfer the funds to the Ukraine Support Fund. These funds could also be used to purchase defense equipment for Ukraine. The bill has not yet become law, but it is important that discussions on sanctions are continuing," the expert said, describing the current situation.
Another option he mentioned was a levy on Russian oil, similar to the one that existed for Iraq. It could also become a source of funding for the International Claims Commission, established in The Hague.
As for the confiscation of Russian assets, Rashkovan believes it may become possible in the future and that work on the issue should therefore continue.
"Some people propose returning Russia's assets as part of the price of peace. I categorically oppose this: the idea is fundamentally misguided... We know that Russia has no intention of stopping. Therefore, returning the assets would not be the price of peace for Russia, but a prize: it would simply say 'thank you' and carry on," Ukraine's representative said.

In Syria, Israel’s female field intelligence soldiers power the IDF's covert operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:43:00 UTC
23:43:00 KST

The Jerusalem Post recently interviewed female field intelligence soldiers on the Syrian border, overlooking areas where they routinely conduct surveillance and penetration operations.
Meeting at the former Syrian intelligence building, captured during the 1967 Six Day War, near Merom Golan in the Golan Heights, and traveling along the border to the Quneitra lookout, the Post interviewed IDF Capt. ‘O.’ and female intelligence collection soldiers ‘N.’ and ‘R.’ of Battalion 595.
They discussed what it means to be part of a new generation of women who operate inside Syria, monitor increased Iranian activity in the area, and navigate growing tensions with local Syrian residents who were once grateful for the IDF’s presence. They also discussed breaking the glass ceiling for women in combat roles in the IDF. Women now make up more than 50% of their unit.
‘N.’ and ‘R.’ specialize in a combination of direct visual surveillance and drone-based field intelligence collection.
The Post visited Battalion 595 about a year ago in a more southerly part of Israel’s buffer zone in Syria. During both visits, female intelligence soldiers described their efforts to locate and track a range of hostile groups, from Iranian operatives to Hamas members and regime-linked HTS jihadists.
In late 2025, a different group of female soldiers revealed that they had penetrated as far as 18 kilometers beyond the buffer zone into Syria. The operation included providing field guidance for the 890th Paratroopers Battalion.
During one operation, the soldiers studied four individuals who were working for, or associated with, Iran or Iranian agents. Each individual had to be analyzed separately, including their movements, schedules, and habits, one soldier, identified as ‘S.’, said at the time.
By October of this year, however, the soldiers could no longer disclose how far they were penetrating into Syria.
This came amid repeated public pressure from the Trump administration for Israel to scale back its activities in Syria and begin partial withdrawals from its buffer zone.
Nevertheless, all three interviewees, ‘N.’, ‘R.’, and ‘O.’, emphasized that they continued to carry out missions throughout southern Syria, quietly but aggressively.
The IDF has also issued several updates in recent weeks, including an announcement that it killed Iranian-linked Syrian terrorist Yusef Ali al-Hasan on October 9.
According to the IDF, al-Hasan was killed because of his involvement in a series of terrorist activities against Israeli forces, including drone operations and previous rocket fire from southern Syria.
In two separate incidents on October 4 and 5, the IDF also opened fire on three other suspects in Syria.
In the first incident, an IDF reservist from the Carmeli Brigade spotted a suspect attempting to infiltrate an IDF position and shot him dead. The suspect was found to be unarmed, and the incident is under review.
In the second incident, two suspects approached an IDF position in Syria on a motorcycle. IDF soldiers opened fire, wounding one of them, and arrested both for questioning.
These announcements followed a period in which the IDF had been relatively quiet about its activities in Syria, apart from an August 18 attack on a Turkish position. The relative silence came amid pressure from the Trump administration and growing reports of tensions with local Syrian civilians, some of whom have become increasingly frustrated with the IDF’s presence as it approaches its second anniversary.
What do these developments mean for future Israeli-Syrian security relations and intelligence collection along the border?
How female intelligence soldiers track threats in Syria
According to ‘N.’, who has served for two years and eight months, “our job is to guard the civilians, to secure this front, and to collect as much intelligence as possible.”
Asked how she and her unit determine where to focus their intelligence collection efforts within Israel’s extensive security zone in Syria and beyond, she said: “We have technological tools, and we do not work alone. We work with other intelligence partners, there are other IDF forces, and we get intelligence also from higher-ranking headquarters officers.”
Asked how long she had spent in the field on a single deployment, ‘N.’ explained that it varied according to the situation.
“It changes all the time, according to the [character of a specific] period. It could be a few days, or it could be a few hours. The longest was probably around a week, or a bit longer,” she said.
‘N.’ said she had spent longer periods in the field during the June 2025 war with Iran.
“The whole environment was hotter and more unstable, and there was a need for higher readiness, so we did what was required of us,” she said.
While international attention was focused on Israeli airstrikes against Iran and Iranian missiles launched at Israel, activity in Syria also increased.
“Whenever the situation is more tense, there are more incidents, so you need to be more ready in the field,” ‘N.’ said.
She also described an operation in which the unit gathered intelligence on several hostile individuals over a period of days.
“We collected intelligence on multiple hostiles over a period of days. We returned to the same area multiple times – and then an operation was carried out,” she said.
The process involves determining who a target is, whom they meet, and when and how those meetings take place.
“You try to find out who this is, who he meets with, when, and how,” she said, explaining that the soldiers also monitor the times of day or night when a target carries out activities or holds meetings.
‘N.’ emphasized that her unit’s role is to gather the information needed to help other forces carry out operations safely and effectively.
“[Our role is] to collect as much relevant intelligence as possible, so that the [IDF] forces which carry out the operation afterward will be able to do so in the most secure and optimal manner possible,” she said.
The soldiers collect intelligence both during the day and at night, ‘N.’ added, noting that “a lot of activities happen at night,” when people are harder to observe.
Combining drones, surveillance, and field intelligence
‘R.’, who has served for more than two years, described her experience leading teams and managing the unit’s operational readiness.
“I have commanded a few different units, including responsibilities for equipment and technology. I was a team leader [for a small unit] for running the operational activities regarding intelligence and regarding the readiness of the unit, working on their professionalism and their combat knowledge,” she said.
“We carried out many operations to get as much information as the brigade needed. We kept our eyes peeled for [collecting intelligence for] them. Sometimes they also ask for very specific intelligence, and we get as much as we can for them,” she added.
‘R.’ said soldiers must look beyond the immediate target during an operation to understand the broader context.
“Sometimes when you go out to perform an operation, it is easy to just focus on the main mission-target itself, but you can miss some of the important [secondary] things going on around the mission-focus,” she said.
She stressed the importance of connecting the unit’s observations to the overall situation in the area being monitored.
‘R.’ explained that the soldiers do not always know how an operation ultimately unfolds. They therefore try to learn what happened afterward, allowing them to understand how their work contributed to the mission.
The feedback is also important for morale, she said, helping soldiers feel that their work has made a difference even when they do not see the final outcome.
Regarding the choice between direct visual surveillance and drones, ‘R.’ said the decision depends on the mission and the target’s location.
“It depends on the mission. Where is the target? What do you need to do to get [close enough to observe the target] there?” she said.
“We have lots of different tools, and our job is to be skilled enough to choose each time what is the right tool to accomplish the mission in the best way possible,” she added.
Asked whether direct observation was preferable, with drones used when approaching a target would risk exposing the soldiers, ‘R.’ said the priority was to get as close as possible without compromising their safety.
“We want to be as close to the target as possible, without endangering ourselves. We are a clandestine unit. So we do need to keep our distance sometimes, but each time is different,” she said.
Asked about situations in which she and her fellow soldiers had faced danger, ‘R.’ said they could sense when a front was becoming more volatile, whether because of Iranian activity or threats from other groups.
Part of what helped them cope, she said, was the close-knit nature of the unit.
“We are always together, and each of us is there for the next-door soldier. So even if there is a bit more fear or official threat warnings, we have each other's backs, and this is one of the best things [about the unit],” she said.
‘R.’ added that the soldiers supported one another through conversations, body language, and eye signals, particularly when operations required them to remain silent.
“There is a dynamic between the [female] soldiers [in the unit] that they can do this [communicate] even without speaking – this is awesome, and it shows true sisterhood between the women. It is inspiring to see this, and even fun,” she said. “But sometimes with these matters which can cause stress, we need to focus and perform our operations. Then later we get to celebrate it.”
Asked how the unit determines whether a target is linked to Iran, Hamas, HTS, the Syrian regime, or another group, ‘R.’ said the process relies on cooperation with intelligence headquarters.
“These are matters that come to us from intelligence [headquarters]. We also help each other in both directions. They give me guidance in a direction about what I need to search for and look for, and I can help them in another direction, including signs relating to HTS or another group,” she said.
She added that surveillance operations are often repeated to build a more complete intelligence picture of a potential threat.
‘R.’ agreed that activity in Syria had intensified recently, saying that the soldiers could feel the change through sudden mission call-ups and other indications.
“It is felt. It is felt. Whether due to sudden mission call-ups of the unit [or other signs], but we are always ready, whether it [a threat] plays out or not, we are ready to stay here and we are not afraid,” she said.
IDF commander says threats persist despite US pressure
Capt. ‘O.’ commands the larger company to which ‘N.’ and ‘R.’ belong.
He has spent his entire five-and-a-half-year military service in the Golan Heights, including operating in Syria since December 2024, when the IDF established its buffer zone following the fall of the Assad regime.
“Once we understood what was happening with the revolution [against the Assad regime], we saw this was an amazing opportunity,” he said.
‘O.’ said the decision to establish the buffer zone was driven by the opportunity to strengthen Israel’s security by moving its defensive position forward.
“We were ready. It was not a question of whether to go in [to set up a Syrian buffer zone]. It was [only a question of] when do we go in so we can defend from a forward position. Our job is to prevent enemies from getting into Jewish towns which are right next to us here,” he said, gesturing toward nearby residential areas.
Asked about the elevated threat from Iran, including the recent incidents publicized by the IDF, ‘O.’ said the situation involved increased friction.
“There is more friction. There is more ongoing friction. We have no problem with some friction. It is a good thing as it makes us readier for anything and everything [appearing] at any place,” he said.
The Post noted that the IDF spokesperson had issued more updates about Iranian activity and other threats after a period in which IDF sources said Iranian associates had largely left Syria.
‘O.’ responded that attempts to establish terrorist infrastructure in Syria continued.
“There is always an attempt to establish [a terror] apparatus. And they will always remain [at some level]. They want to destroy us, and they will [try to] do this however they can,” he said.
He added that hostile groups would continue to look for different ways to threaten Israel, but said the IDF was prepared to defend residents and visitors to the Golan Heights.
“So sometimes they will try one way, and sometimes they will try another way, but we are ready for everything, ready to defend the civilians and tourists who live in and tour the Golan,” he said.
During the summer, he added, the area attracted many tourists, requiring the soldiers to work harder to protect them. With winter approaching, visitors would again come to see the snow on Mount Hermon, and the IDF would need to protect them as well.
Asked about diplomatic pressure to reduce Israeli operations in Syria and eventually withdraw partially from the buffer zone, ‘O.’ said those decisions were outside his remit.
“I am not part of the political echelon. I am at the tactical level…I receive orders, and I carry them out,” he said.
“What they order me to do, I do. Where they tell me to be, I will be there. If there is an operation which is approved or not, [when it is approved] we will do it as best as possible,” he added. “Whoever decides what the missions will be, that is way over my head. I am not part of these debates…I deal with the here and now.”
Asked whether he had noticed a freeze in operations following US demands, ‘O.’ said such decisions were made at higher levels and that he had not necessarily observed a change in his daily work.
“This is a decision made at the higher levels. I don’t know if I feel this [change]. We have lots of missions every day. I don’t necessarily feel there are more or fewer missions,” he said.
‘O.’ also described the difficulty of distinguishing between hostile operatives and civilians in Syria.
“The people who want to harm us are not fools. They know where to be, when to be there, how to present themselves,” he said, explaining that they also know how to observe others without attracting attention.
He added that hostile operatives can conceal themselves within the civilian population, making it difficult to distinguish between terrorists and civilians.
‘O.’ said the IDF draws on a wide range of capabilities to identify and neutralize threats, with his unit contributing intelligence gathered through clandestine observation and drones.
“The IDF is a very powerful military in all of its sections and on all of the platforms that one can use. We all do this together. In the end, I provide another perspective to complement the broader IDF picture,” he said.
He added that he was part of a larger intelligence apparatus that combines different sources and methods to address specific threats.
“In the end, there is an integration of various kinds of intelligence which collectively provide an answer to more specific issues,” he said.
Syrian civilians grow less patient with the IDF presence
The Post received independent confirmation of increased rock-throwing incidents and tensions between some Syrian civilians and IDF soldiers.
However, neither ‘N.’ nor ‘R.’ believed the situation had deteriorated dramatically. They said the soldiers were still generally received warmly.
“We receive more cherries than rocks,” ‘R.’ said, although she acknowledged that tense encounters sometimes occurred and that the soldiers had to remain prepared for any eventuality.
Field intelligence lessons from Lebanon and Jordan
‘N.’ has also been involved in field intelligence operations relating to Lebanon and Jordan.
‘R.’ described the challenges of gathering intelligence on Hezbollah in Lebanon, noting that the group operates differently from other adversaries.
“Hezbollah is a different organization and it uses different tools and methods. We use different tools and methods [against them],” she said.
‘R.’ added that her unit had been heavily involved in Lebanon during the IDF’s early 2026 invasion, describing the work as more intense in some respects than intelligence collection along a relatively quiet border.
Female combat soldiers still face resistance in the IDF
Asked about serving as a woman in a combat role, ‘N.’ said she had wanted to become a combat soldier since childhood.
“Even as a child, I always wanted to be a combat fighter, so no one was surprised that I went into combat,” she said. “Now I think that the biggest contribution female combat fighters can make is in intelligence collection. I really believe in what I and we are doing.”
‘N.’ said that while her own company was supportive, she had encountered resistance outside the unit.
“My company knows how to deal with this, but I had experiences outside my unit which were not the nicest,” she said.
“There are still both men and women who do not accept this, especially reservists who do not love it. I explained it to them, but we still have a long way to go,” she added.
In some cases, she said, she had managed to reach a “tie” with people who were initially opposed to women serving in combat roles, even if they had not fully changed their views.
‘N.’ said she had generally been admitted to the IDF bases she visited, but there had been occasions when soldiers refused to let her and her fellow soldiers stay overnight because the bases lacked separate sleeping quarters or bathrooms for women.
“It depends on who is the commander and what kind of unit is there at the time,” she said.
‘R.’ said women could perform some tasks as well as men, and in some cases better, pointing to their attention to detail and patience.
“Some things are the same and some things we can do better [than men]. The day-to-day work is less physical,” she said.
Like ‘N.’, ‘R.’ said she generally received cooperation from other IDF bases, although acceptance from male counterparts sometimes depended on the commander in charge.
At higher levels, including the battalion and brigade commands, she said, the unit enjoyed full support because senior officers understood its contribution.
“They understand what we bring to the table,” she said.
‘R.’ recalled an instance in which someone who had initially been skeptical of her role later recognized its value when he needed her help.
“Hopefully, once someone was not excited about me [being a female soldier], but then a week later, he needed me to find something,” she said, describing how their relationship improved.
Such experiences, she added, motivated the soldiers to work harder and demonstrate their capabilities.
“It just motivates us to work harder and in the end we get results,” she said.
The two female soldiers were divided on whether they were ready to see a woman become IDF chief of staff.
‘O.’, meanwhile, said he judged soldiers by their ability to carry out their missions, regardless of gender.
“I expect the same thing from female and male combat soldiers. I do not say a mission is for men or for women. It can be either one for any given mission,” he said.
“We need to remember we are all working toward the same goal: to defend the citizenry – whether a man or a woman doesn’t matter,” he concluded.

jean prouvé’s 1944 demountable house becomes japanese tea pavilion in paris
presented in the garden of the hôtel de maisons, the 1944 prefabricated structure brings together postwar architectural experimentation and a new interpretation of japanese tea culture.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
galerie patrick seguin brings prouvé’s 6×6 house to paris
For this year’s Design Miami.Paris, Galerie Patrick Seguin presents Jean Prouvé’s 6×6 Demountable House (1944) in the garden of the Hôtel de Maisons, as part of Design at Large. Originally conceived as emergency housing for families displaced by World War II, the prefabricated structure reflects Prouvé’s approach to industrialized construction and combines a lightweight steel frame with standardized wooden panels. For the Paris presentation, the gallery reinterprets the interior of the residence as a space inspired by the chashitsu, the traditional Japanese tea pavilion, bringing Prouvé’s architectural principles into dialogue with Japanese culture.
a demountable house designed for postwar reconstruction
Prouvé developed the 6×6 Demountable House in response to an urgent housing shortage in France at the end of World War II. Commissioned to design temporary homes for displaced families in Lorraine and Franche-Comté, he sought a construction system that could be manufactured economically, assembled quickly, and dismantled for relocation when necessary. The house measures six by six meters, a compact footprint intended to accommodate three rooms. Its design allowed families to move in as soon as assembly was complete, without having to wait for permanent reconstruction to finish. The structure builds on his patented axial portal frame, which organizes the house around a bent steel skeleton. Standardized wooden panels fit into the frame, while a roof of bitumen-coated building paper completes the enclosure. With steel subject to strict quotas in postwar France, reserving the material for the primary structure responded to the practical constraints of reconstruction.
Prouvé designed the house to provide shelter quickly, but he also saw potential in the construction method beyond the immediate postwar crisis. The steel frame and wooden panels could be assembled and taken apart with ease, and he hoped the same approach would eventually be used to build permanent homes. At Design Miami.Paris, the presentation by Galerie Patrick Seguin offers an opportunity to revisit these ideas in the setting of the Hôtel de Maisons’s garden. A structure developed for postwar housing is brought into the context of a design event, while the new interior concept introduces another layer to its interpretation.
project info:
 name: 6×6 Demountable House
architect and designer: Jean Prouvé
year: 1944
presentation: Design Miami.Paris | @designmiami, Design at Large
gallery: Galerie Patrick Seguin | @galeriepatrickseguin
location: Hôtel de Maisons, Paris, France

What States Make of Military Exercises: Ulchi and Beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:42:00 UTC
23:42:00 KST

Just before the South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise began in mid-August, U.S. President Donald Trump ordered a substantial reduction in its scale. Describing the drills as “costly” and an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea – a state he termed “unthreatening and respectful” – Trump also criticized what he described as Seoul’s lack of support for U.S. operations against Iran.
Trump’s sudden decision raised concerns about South Korea-U.S. defense readiness, alliance reliability, and Washington’s wider commitment to Asia. Several analysts warned that reducing exercises could weaken deterrence and alliance coordination, while others questioned whether the move would secure reciprocal restraint from Pyongyang. Such concerns are understandable: joint military exercises are a visible manifestation of the South Korea-U.S. defense commitment, while North Korea routinely denounces them as rehearsals for war.
The reduction alone, however, does not carry a single, self-evident political meaning. U.S. commanders have since emphasized that other combined training continues and proposed changes to its frequency and geographic distribution. How audiences interpret these changes depends on the wider pattern of cooperation, established relationships, and political context.
Scale, Scope, and Strategic Meaning
Joint military exercises can serve two different but complementary strategic functions. They demonstrate capability and resolve to deter adversaries, but exercises also facilitate defense diplomacy. Repeated military cooperation can help build predictability, trust, interoperability, and institutionalized relationships among participants.
Our research suggests that an exercise’s scale and scope alone cannot reliably distinguish between these functions. Deterrence and defense diplomacy often generate the same observable characteristics, making it difficult to determine where one ends and the other begins simply by examining an exercise’s material features.
Larger and more complex exercises – featuring tens of thousands of troops, sophisticated command-and-control systems, live-fire maneuvers, and complex scenarios – can demonstrate greater warfighting capability and resolve to deter. At the same time, however, those same characteristics may instead reflect years of accumulated defense cooperation and deeper levels of trust and institutional integration between the participating militaries. Their material features reveal what militaries practice and provide evidence of their capabilities but cannot by themselves establish the political messages governments intend or how different audiences will interpret them. Rather, as a political signal, joint military exercises ultimately depend on what participating states and other audiences make of them.
Different audiences will not necessarily derive the same meaning from the same exercise. Washington might intend a reduction in Ulchi as restraint toward Pyongyang, while North Korea might interpret it as a concession, Seoul as uncertainty over U.S. commitment to the bilateral alliance, and Beijing as evidence of Washington’s transactional approach to alliance management. Established relationships and political contexts are therefore essential to interpreting an exercise’s strategic meaning.
Instead, established relationships and political contexts are more important in determining the strategic meaning of exercises than scale and scope alone. The history of Ulchi itself illustrates this.
Ulchi’s scale and scope have seldom increased in tandem with the danger from North Korea. This divergence is significant. If Ulchi’s scale simply tracked the North Korean military threat, as one would expect for greater deterrence, participation should have risen relatively consistently alongside Pyongyang’s expanding nuclear and missile capabilities. Instead, exercise participation has repeatedly risen and fallen according to changes in the diplomatic environment. Participation declined during periods associated with the Six-Party Talks and suspended altogether to facilitate diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Trump’s first term.
The scale of South Korean participation also reflects domestic politics. According to publicly available data, South Korean troop numbers were generally lower under the progressive administrations of Kim Dae-jung and Roh Moo-hyun, increased substantially under conservative presidents Lee Myung-bak and Park Geun-hye, and were again affected by diplomatic engagement under Moon Jae-in. These patterns are consistent with progressive administrations’ greater emphasis on creating diplomatic space for negotiations with the North and conservative administrations’ stronger emphasis on deterrence and alliance cohesion.
Trump’s decision should therefore be understood within this broader political context. Indeed, his own explanations identified several purposes for the same reduction: reducing costs, signaling restraint toward North Korea, and expressing dissatisfaction with Seoul over Iran. The reduction’s material features cannot establish which purpose predominates or how different audiences will interpret it.
Interpreting the Wider Exercise Program
Recent developments illustrate why Ulchi’s reduction should also be understood within the wider pattern of South Korea-U.S. military cooperation. In an interview with the Financial Times, U.S. Army Pacific commander General Ronald Clark emphasized both displaying military capabilities to influence adversaries’ calculations and strengthening military partnerships. His account illustrates how the two functions can reinforce one another: military partnerships help sustain the access and cooperation through which forces demonstrate capability and resolve.
South Korea-U.S. cooperation has continued despite the reduction in Ulchi. Eighth Army commander Lieutenant General Joe Hilbert clarified that other combined training continued, although some activities affected by Trump’s order were conducted by South Korean forces alone. Continued trilateral training through Freedom Edge and South Korea’s observer participation in Keen Sword also demonstrate different forms of military engagement. Observation offers opportunities for familiarity and relationship building without active participation in training. These activities do not cancel out Ulchi’s reduction, but they complicate its interpretation as a broader withdrawal from military cooperation.
Exercise design can also change in response to operational requirements. U.S. Forces Korea commander General Xavier Brunson has proposed more frequent training and geographically dispersed operations, drawing lessons from Ukraine about the vulnerability of concentrated command posts. He suggested the possibility of expanding the scope of exercises from Jeju Island to Gyeonggi Province, while also adjusting the training schedule to include additional smaller-scale drills between the two large annual exercises, Freedom Shield and Ulchi Freedom Shield. Frequency, geographic reach, and the concentration of forces need not change together. Thus, the size of a single exercise therefore provides an incomplete picture of the training program. Whether audiences interpret such changes as reinforcing alliance commitments or altering priorities depends on their political context.
Reducing Ulchi or cancelling a single amphibious exercise does not erase South Korea-U.S. warfighting capability. The institutional defense relationship between the two militaries established over decades – combined command structures, joint planning, interoperability, established procedures, and accumulated experience and “muscle memory” – remains in place. None of this is to suggest that exercises are irrelevant to preparedness; repeated reductions or cancellations over an extended period could eventually erode South Korea-U.S. interoperability and combined warfighting effectiveness. The effects, however, would be cumulative rather than instantaneous. A reduction or cancellation of a single iteration should not be conflated with the disappearance of capabilities built through decades of combined training.
Exercise scale and scope matter, but their strategic meaning is neither fixed nor self-evident. Rather than asking simply whether the United States is exercising more or less and with whom, the more pertinent questions are what particular exercises are intended to accomplish and how Seoul, Tokyo, Washington, Pyongyang, Beijing and other regional audiences interpret them. The deterrent or diplomatic value of an exercise ultimately lies not simply in how many troops participate, but in the political meaning that states attach to their participation – or absence.

Discussing grain initiatives without Russia is pointless, Global South nations agree — MFA

ROME, October 23. /TASS/. International partners within UN forums acknowledge that Black Sea grain initiatives are futile without Russia’s participation and the resolution of the root causes of the conflict in Ukraine, Kirill Logvinov, Director of the Department of International Organizations at the Russian Foreign Ministry, has told the media.
"Our partners from the Global South recognize that discussing any Black Sea Grain Initiative 2.0 without Russia’s participation and without addressing the root causes of the conflict in Ukraine is a dead end," he said after attending a meeting of the Committee on World Food Security at the Rome headquarters of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
Logvinov pointed out that the current situation in the Black Sea is a consequence of actions taken by Kiev, as well as the large-scale military and financial support that the Kiev regime receives from the West. "What is happening must be viewed in a broader historical context, rather than plucking individual events out of the overall picture to use them for yet another political campaign involving sweeping accusations against Russia," he noted.
The Russian Foreign Ministry hopes that the FAO is capable of providing an objective assessment; the organization "should not turn into a platform for issuing 'political verdicts' or become involved in any political games."
"Its task is to provide an objective assessment of the state of food systems and to foster international cooperation in the development of sustainable agriculture. Therefore, Russia has an interest in seeing the FAO remain guided by the goals and objectives enshrined in its founding documents, and in ensuring it acts impartially and objectively. Only through such an approach can the Organization remain effective," Logvinov concluded.
The Russian side holds Ukraine and the UN responsible for the collapse of the "grain deal" - which remained in effect until July 2023 - stating that they failed to fulfill their respective obligations. Meanwhile, Russia continues to meet its own commitments, accounting for 26% of global wheat exports alone and supplying agricultural products to 160 countries.
FAO assessment
As FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero noted during an event on the impact of the situation in the Black Sea on global food security - held as part of the World Food Forum - the challenges in the Black Sea region represent only one, and not necessarily the most significant, factor threatening food security. He pointed out that the observed price increases and instability are driven by geopolitical conflicts, funding cuts, and extreme weather events.
"In countries dependent on wheat from the Black Sea, there has been no deterioration in the food situation beyond average levels; however, a number of food-importing nations remain potentially vulnerable and require close monitoring," he said.
Earlier, Russian President Vladimir Putin explained that the Russian strikes on Ukrainian ports and export routes were a response to Ukraine’s attempts - beginning in the summer of this year - to target Russian oil refineries and vessels in the Black and Azov Seas. He emphasized that the Ukrainian armed forces of Ukraine had attempted to organize a naval blockade of the Black Sea coast, damaging over 100 Russian and foreign vessels.

Deadly France shooting a 'racist, probably Islamophobic' attack: mayor
A gunman firing from his car killed one person and wounded five -- including a 12-year-old girl shot eight times -- in the Paris suburbs Friday, with prosecutors investigating a potential "terrorist" act.
The man was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through the southwestern working-class towns of Trappes and neighbouring La Verriere, Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh said.
Most of the victims were from foreign backgrounds and prosecutors are investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims.
The 12-year-old girl shot eight times was "seriously wounded" but in a stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told AFP.
The alleged shooter -- a 39-year-old man, according to a source familiar with the case -- was arrested in nearby Coignieres.
Police found him in possession of a submachine gun and tear-gas grenades, according to a police source.
Prosecutors said they had opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise."
Rabeh said the man was firing sporadically from his car and that the person killed was "of African origin."
One of the wounded, "in critical condition, is of north African origin," he added.
It was "objectively a racist, probably Islamophobic attack," the mayor said, calling for national unity as the toll rose from an earlier count of four wounded.
Dainville said that two of the wounded in his town -- cleaners attending a school Friday morning when the shooter got out of his car to open fire -- were of African origin.
Laurent Nunez, France's interior minister, travelled to the two affected towns. He called the shooting "clearly a terrorist crime."
Bursts of gunfire
A police source told AFP that the man had fired in bursts from his vehicle around 10:30 am (0830 GMT).
Adel, a resident of Trappes, about 20 kilometres (13 miles) west of Paris, said his "heart was broken" as he learned the victims might have been targeted for their race.
"I'm north African and it's frightening for everyone who has the same background," the 50-year-old told AFP.
Samy, another resident, told AFP he had seen a body on the ground from his window.
His mother, he said, saw a grey Renault Clio car speeding by and heard "loud bangs."
Writing on X, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the case was "very serious" and that "all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised."
President Emmanuel Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."
The shooting came with France on edge following last weekend's riots on the sidelines of mass protests over the cost of living, some of the worst street violence in recent years.
More protests are expected this weekend, but police will be out in force after a week of overnight curfews put in place in cities throughout the country.

UN rights chief 'strongly' condemns surge in drone strikes across Sudan
Unknown

Beyza Binnur Donmez
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday "strongly" condemned the escalation of drone attacks across Sudan, which have killed at least 306 people and injured hundreds more in the first three weeks of October.
"The increasing use of drones, already accounting for the majority of conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan this year, is deeply disturbing and is exacting a horrifying toll," Turk said.
“Scores of civilians have been killed and vital infrastructure and services on which they depend eviscerated, driving further displacement and deepening the already severe humanitarian crisis,” he said, reiterating his call on the parties to the conflict to respect their obligations under international law.
Turk said his office had documented strikes attributed to both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), affecting residential buildings, marketplaces, medical facilities, shelters for displaced people and essential infrastructure.
The office cited recent attacks, including alleged SAF drone strikes on displacement shelters in West Kordofan between Oct. 6 and 10 that killed at least 25 civilians, an alleged RSF strike near a displacement site in Blue Nile on Oct. 9 that killed at least 31 people, and a repeated strike on a transport truck in West Kordofan on Oct. 18 that left at least 139 dead.
Turk urged both parties to comply with international humanitarian law, protect civilians and agree to a ceasefire.
He also called for an end to arms transfers contributing to violations, and stressed that a negotiated settlement centered on human rights and accountability was essential for sustainable peace. The civil war in Sudan has continued since 2023 and has led to one of the world's worst humanitarian disasters.

Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture designs "fluid" skyscraper Lilli for Miami waterfront
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture designs “fluid” skyscraper Lilli for Miami waterfront
US studio Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture has unveiled its latest skyscraper for Miami, designed to display “quiet refinement” on a slender site on the city’s waterfront.
Called Lilli, the residential skyscraper development is the latest in Miami from Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture (AS+GG). The studio is known for designing some of the world’s tallest buildings, including the world’s upcoming tallest skyscraper, the Jeddah Tower.
At 636 feet tall (193 metres), Lilli is planned for a narrow site in Miami’s Edgewater neighbourhood.
The luxury skyscraper will feature rounded edges and will have terraces on the water-facing side, with larger patios running up the opposite face.
Its design is characterised by rounded edges and large spans of glass interrupted by metallic floor plates.
“Our vision is for Lilli’s interior design to feel inseparable from its architecture,” said AS+GG design partner Juan Betancur.
“The fluidity of the building carries through the interior spaces, while a restrained palette of natural materials allows light, landscape, and views of Biscayne Bay to become part of the experience.”
“The result is a sense of quiet refinement that feels distinctly connected to its waterfront setting.”
The skyscraper will house 117 residences of varying sizes, spread across its 53 storeys, as well as amenities including lounges, pools and spas.
The ground floor will have a lobby for residents with large metallic columns and minimalist detailing.
At the top of the skyscraper, a pool will sit on the edge of a terrace underneath a bulkhead with the same reflective metal treatment seen elsewhere in the exterior.
Lilli is the latest in a series of residential skyscrapers being designed by the studio, which recently completed a “yacht-inspired” building in the city.
Residential skyscraper development has proceeded at a steady pace in Miami, with Bugatti recently unveiling its first branded skyscraper in the city.
The images are by Darcstudio.

Addressing the opening of the 9th Istanbul Mediation Conference in Istanbul, Fidan said occupation in Gaza and the West Bank continues and is met with impunity.

Speaking on the recently signed Mecca defense agreement, a pact between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, Fidan said: “The Mecca alliance aims to secure the region's peace, prosperity and future.”
“Its foundation in regional ownership gives these efforts a stronger chance of success,” he noted.
“Also rooted in regional ownership, the Balkans Peace Platform can turn sincere dialogue among Balkan nations into practical results,” according to the top diplomat.
Fidan stressed that Türkiye has consistently worked to elevate mediation from a diplomatic instrument into a strategic discipline, and built the institutional architecture to match that ambition.
“We do not seek to impose outcomes, but to create the conditions in which parties can reach their own,” he said. “Because mediation is not about deciding who wins, who loses, or who makes concessions. It is about finding common ground and working towards a win-win solution for all parties.”
Türkiye's experience based on sincere dialogue, sustained engagement, and regional ownership demonstrated how this approach can contribute to regional and global security, Fidan added.
