Kenyan world marathon champion Jepchirchir provisionally suspended over doping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:27:59 UTC
23:27:59 KST

Andrew Wasike 
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Kenya's reigning world marathon champion and former Olympic gold medalist Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for a banned performance-enhancing substance, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) announced on Friday.
"The AIU has provisionally suspended reigning World and former Olympic champion, Peres Jepchirchir, after an out-of-competition sample, collected in Kenya prior to her recent Sydney Marathon victory, returned an adverse analytical finding for EPO," the organization said in a statement.
Erythropoietin (EPO) is a prohibited substance that stimulates the production of red blood cells, increasing the body's capacity to transport oxygen and potentially improving endurance performance.
The AIU said the sample was collected in Kenya before Jepchirchir's victory at the Sydney Marathon in Australia earlier this year.
The provisional suspension prevents the athlete from competing while the case proceeds through the anti-doping disciplinary process. It does not constitute a final ruling on whether she committed an anti-doping rule violation.
Jepchirchir, 33, won the women's marathon title at the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, adding to the Olympic gold medal she secured at the Tokyo Games in 2021.
The Kenyan athlete is also a former world record holder in the half-marathon and has won four major international marathons.
According to the AIU, her victories include the New York Marathon in 2021, Boston Marathon in 2022, London Marathon in 2024 and Sydney Marathon in 2026.

====================================================================================================

Kyiv needs EUR 1.5 bln for winter - energy expert
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:27:49 EEST
23:27:49 KST

Kyiv has spent more than UAH 16 billion on strengthening its energy security since the start of 2026, compared with UAH 2 billion last year, and plans to spend another UAH 4.5-5 billion by year-end, Managing Director of the Energy Industry Research Center Oleksandr Kharchenko has said.
However, the city needs a further EUR 1.5 billion to complete the necessary work, Kharchenko said at a discussion hosted by Interfax-Ukraine on Friday.
"This is effectively a tenfold increase in investment, specifically in security measures. This includes protecting high-voltage substations and providing backup power for core sewage and heating systems," he said.
The preparations have been funded mainly from the city budget, with the central government accounting for only about 10%, Kharchenko said.
"The national budget is not in very good shape, and payments through Treasury accounts were blocked for more than a month. This hit all local authorities hard, including their preparations for winter," he said.
As a result, some equipment that cities had planned to install by November or December will be commissioned later because of the four-week pause.
Kharchenko said Kyiv's entire internal generating capacity was physically destroyed in January 2026. Before that, the city had about 1.3 gigawatts of generating capacity, while electricity demand reaches about 2 GW at temperatures of minus 10 degrees Celsius and is around 1.2 GW in milder weather.
Without in-city generation, the metro and water utility pumping stations switch to backup power, limiting their ability to provide full services, he said.
Kharchenko said the city had protected key systems against major technological failures. However, maintaining water circulation and filling reservoirs does not necessarily ensure adequate pressure in elevated districts such as Pechersk. That requires the main power supply lines serving water utility facilities to remain operational, he said.
"Some inconvenience this winter is almost inevitable," Kharchenko said.
Most cities cannot complete energy security projects in a single seven- to eight-month season because of engineering and regulatory requirements. Such projects take two to three years, he said.
Ukraine as a whole may need UAH 250-300 billion annually for at least another two years to strengthen its energy security, Kharchenko said.

Petro Poroshenko, a member of the Ukrainian Parliament and leader of the European Solidarity party, handed over five Ai-Petri data transmission and electronic warfare systems to strengthen Kyiv's defense against air attacks by Russian occupiers.
"Today we are handing over five systems, manufactured with funds from a grant from the city of Kyiv, to the leadership of the Ground Forces and other units. I thank Kyiv community and Kyiv City Council for this cooperation. All of them will help defend the capital's airspace," Poroshenko said on Facebook on Friday.
According to him, since late September and early October, the enemy has been employing new tactics for which Ukraine was not entirely prepared: it is making massive use of Shahed drones and new Kometa multi-channel antennas, which significantly complicate the operation of Ukrainian electronic warfare and air defense systems.
"This requires a concentrated effort, constant modernization, and technological improvements; it forces us to switch to three-shift operations and relocate production, particularly to underground workshops. We are modernizing not only our countermeasures against technical reconnaissance but also our electronic intelligence capabilities: direction-finding equipment, new high-frequency amplifiers, and transmitters. When used correctly, they disrupt network communications and blind attack systems," Poroshenko said.

Each system includes the counter-surveillance device itself, a pickup truck, a charging station, a generator, and the necessary electronics. In March 2025, Poroshenko announced a contract with the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, and on June 29 of that year, he announced the start of cooperation with the command of the Ukrainian Ground Forces regarding the supply of these systems to the military. On September 9, 2026, the Ai-Petri counter-surveillance system was unveiled for the first time at the MSPO 2026 security and defense technology exhibition, held in Kielce, Poland.
As reported, following a massive Russian strike on Kyiv on the night of Thursday, October 22, damage was recorded in six of the capital's ten administrative districts. One fatality and 24 injuries were reported, 16 of whom were hospitalized.
According to the Air Force, Russian occupiers launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine overnight, using Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 attack UAVs and decoy drones. Kyiv was the main target of the attack. As of 09:00, air defenses had shot down and neutralized 181 enemy UAVs (including 87 jet-powered ones), but strikes were recorded at 32 locations, and debris was found at eight locations. Serhiy "Flash" Beskrestnov, an advisor to the President of Ukraine on defense technologies, said the occupiers used an Iskander ballistic missile with a cluster warhead to strike the center of Kyiv.
On Thursday night, air defense forces shot down and neutralized via electronic warfare 140 out of 176 drones of various types that Russian troops had used to attack Ukraine.

Israeli elections: Arab voters weigh participation against abstention in bid to oust Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:21:49 UTC
23:21:49 KST

Amid fears over hardline Israeli policies, Palestinian citizens of Israel see the upcoming Israeli elections as a chance for change, with calls for higher Arab turnout to prevent incumbent Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from forming another government, Anadolu reports.
In a series of field interviews conducted by Anadolu on the streets of various Arab cities and towns in Israel, citizens emphasized that participating in this election is particularly crucial, given the “worsening racism and marginalization” against them.
While some plan to vote for the first time in hopes of bringing about political change, others continue to abstain, questioning whether elections can alter their circumstances and arguing that successive governments have failed to address their demands.
Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
Many say they have faced discrimination for years, but view the current government as a more dangerous phase, strengthening their desire to replace it through the ballot box.
Polls suggest Arab parties could win around 15 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while Arab politicians hope higher turnout will weaken the chances of small right-wing parties seeking to support Netanyahu.
Calls for participation, change
Palestinian Imad Bashnaq said the upcoming election was “decisive and extremely important,” particularly for Arab society.
He argued that the rise in racism and fascism since Oct. 7, 2023, had made conditions intolerable.
“I have always maintained that we — as Arabic speakers — are the only ones capable of bringing about change in the Middle East, not just here within this country,” Bashnaq said, arguing that “a few madmen” have taken control of the government and now seek to dictate the course of an entire region.
“We are the original rightful owners, and there is no dispute about that.
“But we are a minority in a state, and this state is a reality we have to deal with,” he added.
OPINION: Israel’s election: The Arab vote and Netanyahu’s politics of exclusion
‘Every vote makes difference’
Areen Ghanayem said she would vote for the second time, maintaining that “every vote makes a difference.”
She said Arab society needed broad participation given the problems it faces and what she described as the government’s failure to pay sufficient attention to its concerns.
“We need to have a voice and someone who speaks on our behalf and demands the rights that should be ours,” she said.
Ghanayem expressed concern that the current government could return to power, saying it marginalized Arab society.
Citizens, she added, did not want to feel excluded from political life but sought to assert their presence and ability to influence decisions.
Occupier attacks
Mohammed Ahmad Abboud said he would take part in the upcoming election, as he had in the past, with the aim of “removing the racist government.”
He said the current election differed from previous ones because of what he described as “escalating violations,” pointing to Israeli occupiers’ attacks in the occupied West Bank.
Abboud also voiced concern over statements by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich regarding the “Judaization” of the Negev and the Galilee — regions located in the south and north of Israel, respectively.
Occupier attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have escalated since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
The attacks have included the killing of Palestinians, the burning of homes, vehicles, and mosques, the destruction of agricultural land, preventing farmers from reaching their land, and the forced displacement of Palestinian communities.
These attacks have coincided with Israeli military operations involving arrests, the demolition of Palestinian homes and structures, and the expansion of illegal settlements.
Between hope and despair
In the northern city of Acre, a resident known as “Jojo” urged Arab citizens to participate in the election, arguing that voting was necessary to bring about change.
“We must vote to bring about change — real change,” he said, expressing optimism that the upcoming election could produce better results.
READ: Racism controversy erupts in Israeli election campaign after broadcaster calls Eisenkot a ‘monkey’
Separately, Saeed Abu Sultan, also from Acre, said that many years of participating in elections have not brought about any change in the reality faced by citizens.
“Some people might be able to make a difference, but as for us, we’ve grown accustomed to things as they are. We haven’t felt any change for 30 years,” Abu Sultan added.
Arab voter turnout expected to rise
Experts expect Palestinian citizens’ participation in the upcoming election to increase compared with the 2022 vote.
Experts and politicians estimate turnout among Palestinian citizens could reach 60% to 61%, up from 53% in 2022, while Arab parties hope participation will rise even further.
Arab politicians say higher turnout could alter the balance of power and reduce the chances of small Israeli right-wing parties crossing the electoral threshold and entering parliament, potentially weakening Netanyahu’s ability to form a government.
The Joint List, comprising the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality, the Arab Movement for Change, and the Balad party, is contesting the election under the leadership of Yousef Jabareen. Polls project it could win nine seats.
The United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, is also running, with projections suggesting it could win between five and six seats.
The election is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 27, to choose the 120 members of the Knesset, with Netanyahu’s bloc competing primarily against the Jewish opposition parties led by Gadi Eisenkot.
The election comes as Netanyahu’s bloc has been losing ground in opinion polls.
Forming a government in Israel requires the support of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 members.
Cooperation between the Jewish opposition and Arab parties could prevent Netanyahu from forming a government.
However, most opposition leaders reject such cooperation, while Netanyahu and Eisenkot have so far also ruled out alliances with Arab parties.
Arab lawmakers have outlined conditions for supporting any government, including ending wars, advancing a political process with the Palestinians, and ending discrimination against Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Ukrainian Troops Battle Russians Inside Gas Pipeline for Months Near Kupiansk in “Operation Impossible”
Ukrainian troops from the 425th Separate Assault Regiment “Skelya” spent several months fighting inside an underground gas pipeline near the eastern Ukrainian city of Kupiansk in Kharkiv region, the regiment reported on October 22.
Skelya detailed the operation, which its troops called “Operation Impossible,” in footage published on its YouTube channel. The regiment stated that its troops cleared Russian forces from several kilometers of the pipeline and blocked further infiltration toward the city.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“During the months-long operation, our soldiers conducted assault operations underground, living and fighting in darkness, cold, and dirt,” the regiment stated. “At the same time, assault groups held positions in Radkivka to prevent the enemy from using the entrance to the pipeline near the settlement.”
Skelya troops eventually cleared the section of pipeline of Russian forces and prevented them from continuing to use it as an underground route toward Kupiansk.
The conditions inside the pipeline forced soldiers to remain in extremely confined spaces for days at a time. “For several days, we were constantly in a horizontal position, so the first thing we wanted to do after getting out was simply stand up,” one of the operation’s participants described.
The operation was aimed at denying Russian troops an underground approach to Kupiansk while Ukrainian assault groups simultaneously held the surrounding ground positions needed to secure access points to the pipeline, according to Skelya.
The fighting inside the pipeline came as Ukrainian forces increasingly turned underground infrastructure into an active part of operations around Kupiansk. On October 22, the 2nd Khartiia Corps reported that troops had traveled more than 15 kilometers underground during the separate Operation VELES before emerging behind Russian positions, while Ukrainian units attacked simultaneously on the surface.

Finland Prepares 36th Military Aid Package for Ukraine, Decision Expected by Year-End
Unknown

- Category
- World
Finland Prepares 36th Military Aid Package for Ukraine, Decision Expected by Year-End
Finland is preparing its 36th military aid package for Ukraine, with a decision on its approval expected before the end of 2026, Militarnyi reported on October 23.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo announced the plans during a joint press conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on October 22.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"We are currently preparing the 36th package in close cooperation with the Ukrainian military. We plan to make a decision by the end of this year," Orpo stated.
The Finnish government is coordinating the contents of the upcoming package directly with Ukraine's military to address its operational requirements. Details of the equipment and weapons under consideration have not yet been disclosed.
Orpo noted that Finland had already provided Ukraine with five military aid packages in 2026. He confirmed that Helsinki would continue supplying military equipment and supporting the training of Ukrainian personnel.
The planned delivery is part of Finland's continued military assistance to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Previous shipments have included artillery ammunition, armored vehicles, and other military equipment.
Among the Finnish weapons already deployed by Ukrainian forces are 120 KRH 85 92 mortars and Crotale air defense systems, designated ItO 90M in Finnish service. The Crotale systems are designed to intercept low-altitude aerial targets, including aircraft, helicopters, and drones.
Finland approved its 35th military assistance package on October 9 in response to an urgent Ukrainian request. That shipment contained a single type of defense equipment from Finnish military stocks, while preparations for a larger follow-up package were already underway.
The upcoming package builds on a sharp increase in the scale of Finnish assistance earlier this autumn.
On September 15, Finland allocated its 34th package, worth approximately $335 million, its second-largest defense allocation to Kyiv since the full-scale invasion began. Part of the equipment was purchased directly from the Finnish defense industry, while the contents and delivery schedule remained confidential for operational security.
That decision raised the total value of Finnish defense aid to roughly $4.15 billion, up from about $3.68 billion after President Alexander Stubb approved the $138.5 million 33rd package on May 29.

Russia Has Lost 241 More Square Kilometers Than It Captured Since September, ISW Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:13:30 UTC
23:13:30 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Has Lost 241 More Square Kilometers Than It Captured Since September, ISW Says
Russia’s offensive in Ukraine has effectively gone into reverse in recent weeks, with Moscow losing more territory than it has captured since the beginning of September while its personnel losses continue to climb, according to an October 22 assessment by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
ISW estimates that since September 1, Russian forces have lost a net 241 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory—meaning Ukrainian gains have exceeded Russian advances by that amount.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The pace of Russia’s territorial progress has also slowed sharply compared with 2025. During 2026, Russian forces have advanced at an average rate of only about 0.25 square kilometers per day.
At the same time, Ukrainian forces have increasingly regained the initiative on several sections of the front.
One of the most significant recent examples was Operation Vivaldi on the Lyman axis. Ukrainian forces recaptured more than 270 square kilometers of territory during the operation and disrupted Russian plans to threaten Ukraine’s so-called Fortress Belt in the Donetsk region.
Russia’s manpower situation is also deteriorating. ISW noted that monthly personnel losses are rising while recruitment is struggling to keep pace.
Since the beginning of October 2026, Russia has already lost nearly 37,000 troops, according to Ukrainian estimates cited in the assessment. For comparison, Russia’s personnel losses during the entire month of October 2025 totaled 31,270.
ISW assessed that the Kremlin could face increasing pressure in the coming months if Ukraine continues to seize the initiative and disrupt Russian offensive plans.
If current trends persist, Russian commanders may push more aggressively for some form of additional mobilization as battlefield losses increasingly outpace Moscow’s ability to replace personnel.
The broader picture, according to ISW, is that Russia is continuing to expend large numbers of troops without producing corresponding territorial gains—a trend that could become increasingly difficult for Moscow to sustain if Ukraine maintains its recent momentum.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces traveled more than 15 kilometers through underground infrastructure before emerging behind Russian positions during Operation VELES, a counteroffensive operation on the Kupiansk axis coordinated by the 2nd Khartiia Corps of Ukraine’s National Guard.

Saudi Arabia postpones UN data, Saudi statistics forums until 2027 amid Houthi attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:13:22 UTC
23:13:22 KST

Emre Demiral and Rania Abushamala
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Saudi Arabia announced Friday that the UN World Data Forum and the Saudi Statistics Forum, scheduled for November in Riyadh, have been postponed until 2027.
The Saudi General Authority for Statistics said in a statement on the US social media company X that the decision was made “in coordination with the United Nations Statistics Division.”
Both forums were due to take place from Nov. 9 to 12. New dates will be announced later through official channels, it added.
The authority said the postponement reflects its commitment to delivering an experience that meets the expectations of the data and statistics community and enables broad international participation by speakers, experts and partners.
This would strengthen the intended impact of the UN World Data Forum, it said.
The authority confirmed that the Road to Riyadh activities leading up to the UN forum will continue.
The postponement came amid an ongoing escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi group since July, alongside renewed fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s government against the Houthis since March 2015.
The group has controlled the capital, Sanaa, and other parts of Yemen since September 2014.

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping sent a message to the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) on Friday.
The world is undergoing accelerated transformation unseen in a century, and the deficits in peace, development, security and governance are growing rather than diminishing, Xi said.
"I have put forward the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) to promote the building of a more just and equitable global governance system and a better world," he said.

People visit the China Great Wall Museum in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 23, 2026.
The renovated China Great Wall Museum held its opening ceremony on Friday at the foot of the Badaling section of the Great Wall in Beijing.
With a construction area of about 16,000 square meters, the museum displays exhibits on the Great Wall's history, culture and spirit. Its permanent exhibition features more than 700 artifacts and sets of artifacts from 24 museums across China, highlighting the Great Wall's role as a symbol of Chinese civilization and national unity.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:10:00 UTC
23:10:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Temporary restrictions on aircraft arrivals and departures were imposed at Moscow’s Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Sheremetyevo airports, Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) reported.
At present, Vnukovo and Domodedovo airports are accepting and dispatching flights in coordination with the relevant authorities. Restrictions at Zhukovsky and Sheremetyevo airports have been lifted.
Passengers were evacuated from the Sheremetyevo International Airport following an air raid alert issued due to the threat of a drone attack, the press service reported.
TASS has compiled the key information on the situation at the airports.
Restrictions imposed
- Temporary restrictions on aircraft arrivals and departures were imposed at Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Sheremetyevo airports, the Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) said.
- According to its statement, the restrictions were necessary to ensure flight safety.
- Moscow’s Sheremetyevo Airport warned passengers about possible changes to flight schedules and longer wait times due to the restrictions, the press service noted.
- As of now, Vnukovo and Domodedovo airports are accepting and dispatching flights in coordination with the relevant authorities, Rosaviatsiya said in a statement on its Max channel.
- Zhukovsky and Sheremetyevo airports have also resumed accepting and dispatching aircraft.
Evacuation at Sheremetyevo
- An air raid alert was declared at the Sheremetyevo Airport, the press service reported.
- Passengers were evacuated, and access to the secure areas of all terminals was restricted.
- Sheremetyevo Airport staff assisted passengers in moving to safe areas and provided updates on the current situation, the press service noted.
- Airport officials clarified that instructions for staff and passengers were displayed on screens throughout the terminals.
- The air raid alert has now been lifted.
Situation at airports
- The situation in the terminals is calm.
- Passengers have access to drinking fountains, water purifiers, water coolers, and free mother-and-child rooms in the terminals of Moscow’s airports.
- Airport information desks and call centers are operating.
- More than 20 flights bound for Moscow airports were diverted to other cities due to current restrictions, Moscow airports told TASS.
Airline actions
- Airlines are adjusting their schedules due to restrictions at airports in the Moscow Region, Rosaviatsiya noted.
- Aeroflot and Rossiya airlines confirmed that they are adjusting their schedules due to airport restrictions.
- Rossiya noted that the schedule changes are related to restrictions at Moscow and other Russian airports.
- According to Aeroflot, some flights have been diverted to alternate airports and will resume once the restrictions are lifted.
- Pobeda is adjusting its schedule due to ongoing restrictions in Russian regions and at Moscow hub airports, the carrier’s press office said.
- It operates at full capacity, providing information and assistance to customers in accordance with all regulations and standards.
- Passengers are asked to check their flight status before heading to the airport via the chatbot, on the departure airport’s website, and via the email address provided at the time of booking.
- The forced change and refund service allows passengers to change or refund their tickets on their own with just two clicks, even for non-refundable fares, the airline noted.
Monitoring
- Civil aviation operations in the Moscow region are under special monitoring by the Transport Ministry and Rosaviatsiya.
- The Transport Prosecutor’s Office is monitoring compliance with passenger rights in connection with restrictions at Moscow’s airports, the press service told TASS.
Handling of flights bound for Moscow
- Nizhny Novgorod’s Chkalov Airport, which serves as the main alternate airport for Moscow’s air hub, handled 13 flights bound for the capital, the press service said.
- St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport served as an alternate airport for 25 flights bound for Moscow, the company that operates the airport pointed out.

France to field twelve SAMP/T NG air defence units
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:00:55 BST
23:00:55 KST

France has ordered four additional SAMP/T NG firing units, taking its total order for the ground-based air and missile defence system to twelve, according to eurosam.
The Organisation for Joint Armament Cooperation, known as OCCAR, placed the contract on behalf of France with eurosam, the Franco-Italian grouping formed by MBDA France, MBDA Italy and Thales. The units will be delivered to the French Air and Space Force in a multi-layer configuration combining Aster and MICA VL missiles.
The company said: “This order is an additional step towards the renewal of the European Long-Range Air and Missile Defence ground capabilities, following the SAMP/T NG development launched in 2021.”
It added: “OCCAR-EA, eurosam and its members, MBDA and Thales will continue to lead the way in state of the art and sovereign air and Missile defence systems for the benefit of European defence. These advanced air defence systems are crucial in the current global context to respond to increasingly challenging threats.”
A SAMP/T NG firing unit holds up to forty-eight Aster missiles ready to fire, carried across up to six launcher modules of eight rounds each, alongside a multi-function radar and identification module able to detect and identify targets beyond 350km, and an engagement module. The whole system is mobile and eurosam says it can be operational in under thirty minutes, offering 360-degree coverage and engaging targets beyond 150km.
The system is designed around the Aster 30 B1 and the newer Aster B1NT. The B1NT uses a Ka-band seeker and new interception algorithms to give what the company describes as a hit-to-kill capability against short and medium range ballistic missiles, low manoeuvring targets and hypersonic missiles.
Britain has a stake in the wider programme, since the United Kingdom is a participant in the FSAF-PAAMS arrangement that OCCAR manages, and the fourteenth amendment to that contract, signed in Paris in January 2024, covered supplementary procurement of equipment allowing Britain to carry out mid-life upgrades to its own Aster missiles. Aster is the weapon carried by the Royal Navy’s Type 45 destroyers as part of the Sea Viper system, which HMS Diamond used against Houthi missiles and drones in the Red Sea.
France and Italy have supplied SAMP/T systems to Ukraine, where the type has engaged Russian ballistic missiles.
The order lands while Britain has no ground-based long-range air defence system assigned to the defence of the United Kingdom. Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, confirmed this week that a further £790 million will be invested in homeland integrated air and missile defence, covering enhanced command and control, improved sensing and radar systems, counter-drone capabilities and more effective layered defences.
The Defence Committee reported yesterday that anti-strike capabilities for shooting down ballistic, hypersonic and cruise missiles and drones are among the capabilities European NATO members lack in sufficient numbers, and that replacing American military capabilities with European weapons has been costed by the Kiel Institute at an extra €50 billion each year over the next decade.
Sky Sabre gives the British Army a medium range ground-based system, currently deployed in Poland and the Falkland Islands. This publication has reported on continuing work on the potential of British destroyers in the ballistic missile defence role and on when those destroyers will receive their missile upgrades.

====================================================================================================

Testosterone may help new brain cells survive, and timing could matter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:00:33 UTC
23:00:33 KST

New research in male rats suggests that the timing and duration of testosterone exposure may influence whether newly born brain cells survive to maturity. The study, published in Neuroscience, indicates that testosterone may be most effective at boosting the survival of young neurons during the later stages of their development, particularly within a part of the hippocampus involved in spatial learning and memory. These findings offer new insight into how male sex hormones support brain plasticity in adulthood.
Adult neurogenesis is the biological process by which the mature brain generates new functional nerve cells, or neurons, from dividing stem cells. This process takes place largely inside the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure located deep within the brain’s temporal lobe that is essential for learning, memory formation, and stress regulation. Specifically, new cells are born along a thin band of tissue called the subgranular zone, located within a subregion of the hippocampus known as the dentate gyrus.
Once these precursor cells divide, they migrate into the neighboring granule cell layer and begin extending communication fibers to other parts of the hippocampus. Over several weeks, the surviving cells mature into functional neurons that are highly excitable and adaptable, helping the brain form new circuits and store new memories. However, roughly half of all newly generated cells in the hippocampus naturally die off within the first month before they can fully integrate into the brain’s network.
Hormones are among the major internal factors that regulate how many of these young cells survive. Testosterone, the primary male sex hormone, naturally declines as men age, and low circulating levels of the hormone are associated with an elevated risk of age-related memory decline and dementia, although results from clinical trials testing testosterone treatment for memory in older men have been mixed. In the body and brain, testosterone can act directly on androgen receptors or be converted by enzymes into other active hormones, such as estradiol, a form of estrogen, or dihydrotestosterone, a potent androgen.
“Growing clinical evidence has shown that testosterone can improve or sustain memory in aging men, potentially reducing the risk and severity of age-related memory loss, including Alzheimer’s disease,” senior study author Mark D. Spritzer, a professor of biology at Middlebury College, told PsyPost. “One mechanism by which testosterone may be having these effects is by acting as a neuroprotectant in the brain. The hippocampus is a region of the brain that is essential for learning and memory, and it is an area that degrades with age.”
Previous experiments in male rats have shown that removing the testes, and with them the main source of testosterone, does not change the rate at which new hippocampal cells are born, but it substantially reduces how many of those new cells survive. Restoring testosterone through daily injections for 30 consecutive days reliably rescues these young neurons. In contrast, several studies using shorter treatment windows of 15 to 21 days found no benefit for cell survival, while a recent experiment by the same research group showed that a brief five-day burst of testosterone given between days 11 and 15 after cell birth did improve survival.
This pattern raised questions about whether testosterone needs to build up over a full month to protect new neurons, or if young cells are simply more sensitive to the hormone during specific developmental stages. Between 11 and 30 days after birth, maturing neurons go through a sensitive window where they begin forming active connections, or synapses, with other brain regions. During this same timeframe, chemical signals from a neurotransmitter called GABA shift from exciting the young cells to inhibiting them, a transition that promotes proper maturation.
“We had previously shown that testosterone injections can improve levels of adult neurogenesis (proliferation and maturation of new neurons) within the hippocampus,” Spritzer explained. “However, we did not know whether or not specific periods of neuron development were more strongly influenced by testosterone. Therefore, the current experiment involved giving rats testosterone during different stages of neural development to assess the effects on adult neurogenesis. The ultimate goal is to better understand how testosterone influences the brain and cognition.”
To resolve the contradictions in earlier work, Spritzer, lead author Tatum W. Hamilton, and their colleagues at Middlebury College designed an experiment to test how different windows of testosterone exposure affect neuron survival at 30 days of age. They directly compared a full 30-day treatment against two 15-day treatments covering either the first half or the second half of the cells’ 30-day maturation period.
The researchers worked with 43 adult male Sprague-Dawley rats that were approximately 60 days old at the start of the study. All rats were housed individually to control for social variables, as prior work showed that testosterone’s effects on the brain are easier to detect in individually housed animals. One week after arriving at the laboratory, all of the rats underwent surgical castration to remove their natural source of testosterone, allowing the scientists to precisely control hormone levels through injections.
Eleven days after surgery, every rat received a single abdominal injection of bromodeoxyuridine, a synthetic compound commonly known as BrdU. When cells divide, they incorporate BrdU into their newly synthesized DNA, which permanently tags the exact batch of cells born during the brief window after the injection. By waiting 30 days and then counting how many BrdU-tagged cells remain in the brain, scientists can measure the survival rate of that specific generation of cells.
Starting the day after the BrdU injection, the rats were divided into six groups of six to eight animals each. Half of the groups received daily injections of testosterone propionate at a high physiological dose of 0.500 milligrams per rat; earlier work by the same group found that a lower dose of 0.125 milligrams had no effect on new neuron survival. The other half received inert sesame oil injections as a comparison control. These injections were administered during one of three time windows following the BrdU tag: an early period (days 1 to 15), a late period (days 16 to 30), or the full period (days 1 to 30).
On day 31, the researchers collected blood samples to verify hormone levels and extracted the rats’ brains for microscopic analysis. They sliced the entire hippocampus into thin sections and used chemical staining techniques to make the BrdU-tagged cells visible under a light microscope. A researcher who was blinded to which treatment each rat received counted the labeled cells across the granule cell layer and subgranular zone, as well as in an adjacent area called the hilus to check whether any changes were specific to the neurogenic zone.
The team also divided their cell counts between the dorsal (top/front) and ventral (bottom/back) portions of the dentate gyrus, because these two zones serve different functions. The dorsal hippocampus is primarily involved in spatial navigation and memory, whereas the ventral hippocampus mainly regulates stress and anxiety. Finally, using a laser-scanning confocal microscope and fluorescent markers, the researchers examined 50 randomly selected BrdU-tagged cells per rat to see how many also contained NeuN, a nuclear protein found in mature neurons.
Blood tests confirmed that rats receiving testosterone during the late period and the full 30-day period had elevated serum testosterone concentrations at the end of the experiment, averaging about 5.7 nanograms per milliliter, compared to less than 0.3 nanograms per milliliter in the oil-treated groups and the early-period testosterone group, which had stopped receiving hormone injections 16 days earlier.
Across the entire dentate gyrus, rats treated with testosterone had higher numbers of surviving BrdU-labeled cells in the neurogenic zone than rats given oil. Planned statistical comparisons between the hormone and oil groups within each time window showed that only the full 30-day testosterone treatment produced a statistically significant increase across the whole structure. Rats given testosterone during the late window (days 16 to 30) showed a trend toward higher cell survival across the whole dentate gyrus that fell just short of statistical significance, while early treatment (days 1 to 15) had no effect.
“The results suggest that testosterone may have an additive effect, which is a novel finding,” Spritzer noted. “Namely, longer exposure to testosterone increased neurogenesis to a greater degree.”
When the researchers examined the dorsal and ventral regions separately, a more specific pattern emerged. In the dorsal dentate gyrus, testosterone increased cell survival in both the full 30-day group and the late 16-to-30-day group, while the early 1-to-15-day group showed no benefit over oil injections. In the ventral dentate gyrus, testosterone had no effect on cell survival during any of the three treatment windows, although rats injected during the early period unexpectedly had fewer surviving cells in this region than rats injected during the late or full periods regardless of whether they received hormone or oil.
Fluorescent microscopy confirmed that roughly 79 to 87 percent of the surviving BrdU-tagged cells had matured into NeuN-positive neurons across all groups, regardless of whether the rats received testosterone or oil. Because the hormone did not alter the proportion of new cells that became neurons, the higher BrdU counts can be read as a greater number of surviving new neurons. No treatment differences were found in the overall tissue volume of the dentate gyrus or in cell counts within the neighboring hilus region.
Together, these results suggest that maturing neurons in the dorsal hippocampus are especially responsive to testosterone when they are between two and four weeks old. Because the dorsal hippocampus governs spatial learning, the authors note that this regional sensitivity aligns with past behavioral experiments showing that testosterone improves spatial working memory in male rats. The hormone may help preserve new cells during this late window by blocking programmed cell death, boosting supportive growth proteins like brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or aiding the transition of GABA signals as young neurons wire into existing brain circuits.
“We demonstrated that testosterone enhances adult neurogenesis, with the effects being strongest during the later stages of neuronal development,” Spritzer said. “These results suggest that testosterone may be a useful therapeutic target for helping to sustain neuroplasticity, among men in particular.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. First, the experiment was conducted in surgically castrated young adult rats housed in social isolation, which does not mirror the gradual, partial hormone decline experienced by aging men in daily life. Second, the blood and brain tissue were collected 24 hours after the final testosterone injection for the full and late groups, but 16 days after the final injection for the early group. The authors raise the possibility that this gap helps explain why early treatment showed no benefit, but note that this explanation would require new cells to die off at a steady rate throughout development, which earlier research does not support.
“This was preclinical research conducted with rats, so it cannot be extrapolated directly to humans,” Spritzer cautioned. “However, it is suggestive that testosterone may have therapeutic value. Of importance was that we used a high physiological dose of testosterone, and the effects of dose levels have not been considered carefully in past human clinical studies involving testosterone.”
Spritzer also pointed out that boosting cell survival without limit is not necessarily the goal. “One challenge with neurogenesis research is the assumption that more is always better,” he added. “There is likely an optimal level of adult neurogenesis for best brain functioning.”
In addition, the overall statistical analysis did not show that testosterone’s effect differed across the three time windows, so the conclusions about timing rest on separate comparisons within each window, each involving only six to eight rats per group. The study also did not directly measure the molecular pathways inside the cells, so it remains uncertain whether testosterone acted through androgen receptors, estrogen receptors, or downstream growth factors during that 16-to-30-day window. Nor did it test whether the extra neurons translated into better learning or memory. Future research will need to test these specific molecular mechanisms and examine whether similar timing effects apply to older animals or females.
“Now that we know more about the stages of neural development that are influenced by testosterone, assessing the molecular mechanism will be important,” Spritzer said. “Testosterone is metabolized in the brain and likely has many effects on neuronal development, which should be explored.”
The study, “Effects of testosterone upon the survival of new neurons in the dentate gyrus of adult male rats,” was authored by Tatum W. Hamilton, Ezra J. LeMole, Grace K. Nadecki, Jordan M. Gardner, Quinn P. Kennedy, Kathryn A. Blek, and Mark D. Spritzer.

UK households are being urged to stock up on bottled water, canned food, and other essential supplies to prepare for emergencies amid growing concerns over severe weather, cyberattacks, and potential disruptions to food supplies.
Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Friday that people should take sensible measures to ensure they have enough supplies at home to cope with difficult situations as storms batter parts of the country.
He said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common," adding, "it's not about panic buying... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."
The government's recommendations advise households to keep enough essential supplies to last three days, including nine liters of water per person and non-perishable food such as canned meat, vegetables, and dried fruit.
The guidance also recommends keeping a battery-powered or wind-up FM radio, a torch, blankets, a first aid kit, hand sanitizer, wet wipes, toiletries, and a charged power bank.
Households are also advised to keep cash on hand in case electronic payment systems fail, alongside copies of important documents, and essential supplies for babies and pets.
The advice comes after the National Audit Office warned that Britain's food supply chain faces growing risks from cyberattacks and the climate crisis, saying the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs had not done enough in recent years to strengthen resilience.
Burnham, however, rejected the claims that the government had failed to prepare adequately.
He pointed to the need for greater public preparedness amid increasingly frequent unexpected events, including severe weather and power outages.
Burnham said he kept beans and soup in his cupboard and also recommended Twiglets as part of his personal emergency supplies.

The localized ceasefire will begin Thursday, Oct. 29.
Russia and Ukraine have not commented on the first lady's announcement. But Ukrainian officials indicated that there has been a tentative agreement in the Russian-occupied territory in southern Ukraine.
The first lady's office says she worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire."
"The situation in Oleshky is dire," the first lady said in a statement. "Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."
The first lady's office said she "initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement's objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary."

Türkiye eyes COP31 to attract green investment, advance industrial transformation

Mucahithan Avcioglu
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Türkiye sees COP31 as an opportunity to attract international green investment and accelerate industrial transformation, officials said on Friday, highlighting opportunities in renewable energy manufacturing, electric mobility and recycling.
Speaking at the Investment Summit Towards COP31 in Istanbul, Ahmet Burak Daglioglu, president of Türkiye’s Investment and Finance Office, said the conference would help present the country’s investment potential to global businesses and financing providers.
“We have a very strong story,” he said, adding that Türkiye needs to communicate its green transition policies more effectively to international partners.
Climate-friendly investment gains momentum
Climate-friendly investments are a priority under Türkiye’s international direct investment strategy through 2028, with 94 projects attracted under that heading so far, Daglioglu said.
The office also assesses and scores projects in its portfolio against sustainability principles, he added.
Türkiye’s ambitions extend beyond generating renewable energy to manufacturing equipment needed for the transition.
The country has Europe’s largest solar panel production capacity and an extensive wind energy equipment manufacturing ecosystem serving domestic and international markets, Daglioglu said.
Battery production capacity is expected to expand, while automotive policies support existing manufacturers’ transformation and new players such as electric vehicle producer Togg, he added.
Daglioglu highlighted recycling and upcycling opportunities arising from Türkiye’s industrial base and integration into global supply chains.
Under the Zero Waste initiative launched in 2017, 90 million tons of waste has been recycled, while the recovery rate has reached about 37%, he said. Türkiye aims to raise that rate to 60% by 2035.
Green development can support growth
Mehmet Emin Birpinar, Türkiye’s special representative for COP31 at the Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, said climate action presents an economic opportunity.
“Climate change is not an obstacle to our development,” he said, pointing to the direction of global financing flows.
Birpinar compared green development with earlier waves of industrialization and information technology that helped countries build wealth, warning that missing the transition could leave Türkiye further behind.
He stressed the need to reduce emissions while adapting infrastructure and economic activity to changing climate conditions.
Rising cooling demand illustrates how climate impacts can increase energy consumption and potentially emissions when electricity comes from fossil fuels, he added.

OPEC Fund approves record $250M loan for Istanbul North Rail Crossing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:51:23 UTC
22:51:23 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
The OPEC Fund for International Development has approved a $250 million loan for the Istanbul North Rail Crossing project, marking the largest single financing commitment in the institution’s history.
According to a fund statement, the loan is part of a broader approved package of up to $500 million to build a new railway bypassing the Istanbul metropolitan area.
The 127-kilometer (79-mile) double-track, electrified line will run between Cayirova on the Asian side and Catalca on the European side, crossing the Bosphorus via the Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge.
Carrying both passengers and cargo, the link addresses a critical bottleneck in Asia-Europe rail traffic. Currently, freight trains only use the Marmaray tunnel during limited nighttime hours, restricting annual capacity to 3 million tons.
The new line will expand this to 50 million tons, cutting freight journey times between Cayirova and Catalca from 13 hours to 3.6 hours.
It will also link Istanbul Airport and Sabiha Gokcen Airport to the national rail network, reducing inter-airport transit time from two hours to 65 minutes.
Strengthening global trade corridors
The railway provides an integral missing link for three international rail-served trade corridors crossing Istanbul: the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor linking China and Central Asia with Europe; the Iraq Development Road connecting Asia and the EU via the Middle East and Türkiye; and the Türkiye-EU corridor, which accounts for a third of Türkiye’s international trade.
Shifting freight from road to lower-carbon electrified rail will ease congestion and strengthen Türkiye’s position as a logistics hub linking Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.
The $8.3 billion project is backed by the Turkish government and a World Bank-led consortium including the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), Islamic Development Bank (IsDB), European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), and European Investment Bank (EIB).
"Türkiye has been an important partner of the OPEC Fund for nearly five decades," said OPEC Fund President Abdulhamid Alkhalifa, noting the record financing supports infrastructure that boosts connectivity and sustainable growth.
Since 1979, the OPEC Fund has approved nearly $850 million for Turkish projects across transport, agriculture, health, and energy.

Iran slams IAEA for silence towards attacks on its sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:50:39 UTC
22:50:39 KST

The statement criticized the IAEA for applying double standards and discriminatory approaches, emphasizing that the Statute is a binding legal document and must not be used as a political instrument to serve the interests of certain powerful states.
Iran also condemned the unacceptable silence of the Agency’s governing bodies regarding the military attacks by the US and the Zionist regime on its peaceful nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026. Furthermore, it highlighted the IAEA's failure to address the lack of comprehensive safeguards on the Zionist regime’s nuclear activities.
The Islamic Republic also called for the full, balanced, and non-discriminatory implementation of the IAEA Statute for all member states, particularly regarding technical cooperation and access to peaceful nuclear energy.
The full text of statement by the Iranian permanent mission in Vienna is as follows:
Permanent Mission of the Islamic Republic of Iran  
  
to the United Nations and other International Organizations in Vienna 
 
PRESS RELEASE  
   
On the Anniversary of the Approval of the IAEA Statute   
   
23 October 2026  
   
Seventy years after the adoption of the Statute of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) 
 
on 23 October 1956, a fundamental assessment is required as to the level and extent of the 
 
adherence to the principles and objectives of the Agency’s founding document. 
This anniversary must therefore be more than an occasion for commemoration; it must serve as 
 
a moment of critical reflection, institutional accountability and a renewed commitment to the full, 
 
impartial and non-discriminatory implementation of the Statute. 
The Statute: A Binding Mandate, Not a Political Instrument
The continued relevance of the IAEA Statute lies in the objective it establishes and the principles 
 
it enshrines. It implementation over the past seven decades has produced achievements in 
 
important areas. However, the failure to implement it fully, consistently, effectively and without 
 
discrimination, under all circumstances and with respect to all Member States, has caused the 
 
Agency to drift away from its core objective and priorities, undermine the principles governing its 
 
conduct, compromise its professionalism, and tarnish its authority and credibility. 
The undeniable fact is that the Statute is the Agency’s constitution, not a document to be invoked 
 
selectively or interpreted according to the interests of powerful States or a group of States. 
Beyond Safeguards: Upholding the IAEA’s Full Statutory Mandate
Article II establishes the Agency’s fundamental objective: to accelerate and enlarge the 
 
contribution of atomic energy to peace, health and prosperity throughout the world. Article III.A.1 
 
requires the Agency to encourage and assist research, development and the practical application 
 
of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. Article III.B.3 further requires the Agency to allocate its 
 
resources efficiently to achieve the greatest possible general benefit, with due regard to the special 
 
needs of developing countries. 
While safeguards are part of the IAEA’s mandate, the Agency is not merely a “watchdog” 
 
organization, as some Member States, in contravention of the Statute, seek to portray it. Such a 
 
narrow and politically motivated characterization distorts the Agency’s mandate and shifts its 
 
priorities away from its broader statutory objective that is the promotion of peaceful nuclear 
 
applications and international scientific and technical cooperation. Verification must not eclipse 
 
peaceful nuclear cooperation, development and the legitimate rights of Member States. An Agency 
 
that concentrates on scrutiny while failing to advance its key statutory responsibilities cannot claim to be fulfilling its mandate in a balanced manner.
Sovereign Equality Cannot Coexist with Double Standards
Article IV.C expressly establishes that the Agency is based on the sovereign equality of all its 
 
members and requires them to fulfil their statutory obligations in good faith. Article III.C prohibits 
 
the Agency from making assistance subject to any political, economic, military or other conditions 
 
incompatible with the Statute. Article III.B.1 requires the Agency to conduct its activities in 
 
accordance with the purposes and principles of the United Nations, while Article III.D requires 
 
due observance of the sovereign rights of States. 
These provisions are neither optional nor subordinate to geopolitical calculations. Sovereign 
 
equality requires that every State be treated fairly and without discrimination under the legal 
 
instruments applicable to it, free from double standards, selective interpretation and politically 
 
motivated action. 
A clear example is the continuing disparity between the scrutiny applied to Iran and the absence 
 
of comprehensive safeguards covering all nuclear activities of the Israeli regime, which remains 
 
outside the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. This disparity raises 
 
fundamental questions about the credibility and consistency of the international nuclear non-
 
proliferation norms. A credible, comprehensive and non-discriminatory approach to nuclear 
 
verification throughout the Middle East is a legitimate demand and a longstanding objective of 
 
regional countries that are parties to the NPT. Regional security cannot be built on selective 
 
scrutiny and unequal expectations. 
Peaceful Nuclear Cooperation: A Right, Not a Political Privilege
Peaceful nuclear cooperation must not be subject to political pressure. Article III.C of the Statute 
 
is clear: assistance must not be subjected to conditions incompatible with the Agency’s legal 
 
mandate. Political pressure and geopolitical rivalries must not obstruct legitimate scientific 
 
cooperation or turn access to peaceful nuclear technology into a privilege reserved for selected 
 
countries. The Agency is expected to defend the integrity of its technical cooperation mandate 
 
and ensure that its programs serve the development needs of all Member States fairly and without 
 
discrimination. 
Attacks on Nuclear Facilities and Unacceptable Institutional Silence
Attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities demand strong and unequivocal condemnation. The 
 
military attacks by the U.S. and the Israeli regime against Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026 constituted serious and material breaches of peremptory norm of international law on the 
 
prohibition of aggression.  They presented a grave challenge to nuclear safety, nuclear security, 
 
peaceful uses of nuclear energy, the credibility of the IAEA and its safeguards system.  
The Agency’s General Conference and Board of governors has repeatedly adopted resolutions 
 
expressly stating that armed attacks on, or threats against, nuclear facilities devoted to peaceful 
 
purposes violate the principles of the UN Charter, international law and the Agency’s Statute. 
 
Nevertheless, the Agency’s governing bodies and Secretariat failed to issue even a simple statement to condemn clear acts of aggression against Iran’s nuclear facilities – unprecedented in the Agency’s history. This failure represents a serious institutional shortcoming and raises troubling questions about the consistent application of the principles the Agency is mandated to uphold. 
The Agency cannot credibly defend the integrity of safeguards while treating attacks against 
 
facilities subject to those safeguards as a secondary concern. The Agency must therefore 
 
unequivocally reaffirm that attacks against peaceful nuclear installations are unlawful and 
 
unacceptable and must not be tolerated under any pretext.
Safeguarding the IAEA’s Independence, Integrity and Confidentiality Principle
Independence, confidentiality and professional integrity must be protected. Article VII.F of the 
 
Statute prohibits the Director General and Agency staff from seeking or receiving instructions 
 
from external sources. It also requires the protection of confidential information acquired in the 
 
course of their official duties and obliges Member States to respect the international character of 
 
their responsibilities and refrain from seeking to influence them improperly. 
These are concrete institutional safeguards, not ceremonial principles. Reports, assessments and 
 
decisions must be based on verifiable evidence, sound technical analysis and applicable legal 
 
obligations—not political demands, unsupported allegations or selective approaches. Any breach 
 
of confidentiality or attempt to instrumentalise safeguards information undermines cooperation, 
 
erodes trust and may compromise the safety and security of nuclear activities. The Agency must 
 
address credible concerns, protect sensitive information and ensure accountability. 
Restoring the IAEA’s Credibility: From Selective Implementation to Full Compliance
Cooperation must be matched by institutional responsibility. Iran recognises the importance of 
 
credible safeguards and professional verification and remains committed to engagement within 
 
the framework of its applicable legal obligations and its inherent and sovereign rights and interests. 
However, cooperation requires good faith, mutual respect, professional integrity and the 
 
consistent implementation of agreed legal commitments.  
On this anniversary, Iran calls upon Agency, particularly the Board of Governors and the Director 
 
General to end double standards, resist politicisation, protect confidential information, condemn 
 
attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities, and restore the full and balanced implementation of the 
 
Agency’s statutory mandate. Iran also calls for an effective and non-discriminatory technical 
 
cooperation policy that enables all Member States, particularly developing countries, to benefit 
 
from nuclear science and technology. 
The Agency’s credibility cannot rest solely on its authority to inspect. It depends equally on its 
 
adherence to the law, its impartiality, its independence and its willingness to uphold the legitimate 
 
rights of all its members. 
The Statute must be implemented as a whole, equally and in good faith—not selectively, not 
 
conditionally and not according to political convenience. The Agency owes this obligation to every 
 
Member State. On the seventieth anniversary of the Statute’s adoption, the Agency is expected to 
 
honour letter, spirit, object and purpose of the Statute through concrete action, not merely words, 
 
and to uphold its principles without political selectivity, discrimination or exception. 
MNA
Seventy years after the adoption of its Statute, the IAEA’s credibility rests on upholding its Statute 
 
in full, serving all Member States equally, and demonstrating that international law and statutory 
 
principles cannot be sacrificed to political convenience.

Finland nearing opening of world’s first permanent nuclear waste repository
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:50:26 UTC
22:50:26 KST

Finland nearing opening of world’s first permanent nuclear waste repository
Facilities are being built in many countries, but Finland is the first to licence its underground storage facility.
Finland has granted an operating licence for the world’s first permanent underground repository for spent nuclear fuel.
The government handed Onkalo, in western Finland, the licence on Thursday, waste management company Posiva said.
Although the move does not allow the opening of the facility, it is expected to start operations soon, the firm said. However, 22 years after construction began, no exact date has been decided yet.
“This is a great and historic day for both Posiva and Finland,” the company’s Chief Executive Officer Ilkka Poikolainen said in a statement.
“Before final disposal begins, Posiva will finalise the commissioning stage, carrying out the necessary tests and inspections which STUK [the Finnish Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority] also needs to verify and approve.”
With space for 6,500 tonnes of uranium, Onkalo, which means “cave” in Finnish, will provide permanent storage for spent fuel from Finland’s five nuclear reactors.
The fuel will be enclosed in copper canisters that are highly resistant to corrosion inside the geological repository. The canisters will then be lowered into holes drilled into the bedrock, which will be filled with bentonite clay and finally sealed with a steel-reinforced concrete plug.
The waste will remain highly radioactive for tens of thousands of years. After about 100,000 years, the levels will be about the same as the uranium ore of which the fuel is made, according to Posiva.
Countries have been wrestling with what to do with dangerous nuclear by-products since the first plants were built in the 1950s. Currently, most of it is in temporary storage.
Final repositories are being built in other countries, including neighbouring Sweden and France, but Finland is expected to be the first to open its underground storage facility.
The cost of the Onkalo site has been estimated at $1.16bn.

City of Kyiv launches 85 MW of power generation for winter readiness – expert
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:50:00 EEST
22:50:00 KST

Kyiv has already commissioned approximately 85 MW of generating capacity, which will help the city get through the fall-winter period of 2026/2027, while preparations for winter under the concept provisionally dubbed "dark but warm" are approximately 80% complete, Managing Director of the Energy Industry Research Center Oleksandr Kharchenko said.
"During the off-season, Kyiv has essentially already commissioned approximately 85 MW of capacity, which is a fairly good pace. Kyiv has also managed to arrange backup power supplies for all critical infrastructure to ensure its basic operation," Kharchenko said during an online discussion on the special topic "Survival Mode: What Will Help Kyiv and the Region Get Through This Winter?" hosted by the Centre for Economic Strategy on Thursday.
According to him, this means that some residential buildings in certain parts of Kyiv may have no water, but water will continue circulating through the system; there simply will not be enough pressure to pump it up into the buildings.
Kharchenko said reserves had also been created to ensure that sewage systems and heating continued to operate.
He said that Kyiv's winter preparation concept was provisionally dubbed "dark but warm" and was approximately 80% complete.
At the same time, the Energy Industry Research Center director added that approximately 5,000 buildings equipped with backup heating supplies would be able to maintain indoor temperatures of plus 10–14 degrees Celsius when outdoor temperatures fall to minus 5–10 degrees Celsius. This, he said, is much better than having no heating at all. Kharchenko previously said that 3,000 buildings in the capital have no backup heating supplies and are at risk.
"I try to be as objective as possible, and I believe that Kyiv is now one of the best-prepared cities for winter in the face of attacks. If we had made investments and worked at the same pace over the past four years, we would now be able to watch Russian ballistic missiles fly overhead without worrying about our critical infrastructure. I am genuinely angry because this was not done a couple of years ago," the expert said.
At the same time, he expressed the view that western Ukraine had prepared significantly less effectively for the season because of an "underlying feeling that things were calm here."
"These drones pose a significant threat to many relatively small cities where, unfortunately, the level of preparedness is lower than, say, in central or eastern Ukraine. Mykolaiv, which has prepared and has significantly better-protected critical infrastructure than many cities in western Ukraine, could unexpectedly find itself in a better situation than, for example, Ternopil or Khmelnytsky," the Energy Industry Research Center director said.
He added that these areas would still face fewer shelling attacks, but "in terms of water supply and heating, Kyiv may sometimes be more comfortable."
As reported earlier, Kharchenko said that by the New Year, Kyiv would have approximately 200 MW of gas-fired cogeneration capacity, "which will ensure the operation of the water utility and heating systems."

Rabeh said that the gunman targeted passersby at three separate locations, including a playground. Forensic investigators were also seen examining evidence at a gas station.
The alleged shooter was arrested in the nearby town of Coignieres. Nuñez said the attack lasted just under 15 minutes and was stopped by five officers from the anti-crime brigade.
Officials initially said four people had been wounded, but Rabeh told reporters there were five, including three who were very seriously injured, with their lives in danger.
A 12-year-old girl was seriously wounded after being shot eight times, but is in stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told the Agence France-Presse news agency.
Rabeh said that the person killed was "of African origin" and one of the wounded, "in critical condition, is of North African origin."
Nuñez said the gunman "clearly" committed "a terrorist crime" that may have been racially motivated. Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims.
They said they have opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise."
Bursts of gunfire and "loud bangs"
A police source told AFP that the gunman had fired in bursts from his vehicle around 10:30 a.m. local time.
Samy, a resident of Trappes, about 13 miles west of Paris, told AFP he saw a body on the ground from his window.
His mother, he said, saw a gray Renault Clio car speeding by and heard "loud bangs."
Writing on X, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the case was "very serious" and that "all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised."
President Emmanuel Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."
Trappes previously experienced tensions after a teacher there reported receiving threats after writing that the state did not do enough to protect another teacher, Samuel Paty. Paty was beheaded by a radical Islamist in 2020 in another Paris suburb after he showed his class caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad.
France on edge after street violence and protests
The shooting came with France on edge following riots that erupted amid mass protests over the cost of living, which saw some of the worst street violence in recent years. Demonstrators, including students, labor union members and activists from France's "Yellow Vest" movement, are expected to take to the streets again Saturday.
French police have promised a larger presence to maintain order after a week of overnight curfews across the country. Nuñez said authorities would deploy some 70,000 law enforcement officers and gendarmes. Elite police units will help secure public buildings, he said. Other resources, including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons, will also be deployed.
Nuñez said at a news conference that officials will be "absolutely uncompromising" with those involved in violence, looting or vandalism. Police will have a "very firm approach to making arrests, and there will be legal consequences," he said.
Major Paris museums, including the Louvre, will be closed. Art Basel Paris has canceled its weekend program due to safety concerns, the AP reported.
