Why Trump’s Rebrand of Artificial Intelligence to Super Intelligence Matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:46:47 UTC
22:46:47 KST

President Donald Trump’s war in Iran drags on, his pledge to bring down prices on day one appears to have backfired, and his record-low approval ratings are dragging down his party ahead of the midterm elections. But one Trump initiative that is going exactly according to plan: getting some of the world’s richest CEOs to help him rebrand “artificial intelligence.”
Last month, with an ever-growing number of Americans worried that AI might kill us all, the president summoned tech executives to the White House to make a big announcement: "artificial intelligence” is out. “Super Intelligence” is in. Despite the term “AI” being in use for more than 70 years, government agencies will no longer recognize it.
I’m skeptical that the White House is a repository of superintelligence, in part because “United States” was misspelled on the president’s official announcement. But unlike, say, Lake America, “super intelligence” has largely caught on—at least among the people building it. Jeff Bezos publicly blessed the rebrand. Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, was quick to get on board. During a SpaceX’s earnings call this week, Elon Musk used “super intelligence” in his very first sentence, and at least nine times after that.
It remains to be seen whether those of us less reliant on government contracts and favorable regulatory decisions join the movement to make super intelligence happen. But as a former presidential speechwriter, I won’t argue with President Trump’s broader instinct that words matter. Especially when those words are being used to describe something novel, controversial, and almost certain to have consequences for all eight-plus billion people on earth.
In fact, that’s the biggest problem with the White House’s big rebrand—it goes in entirely the wrong direction. I would argue that our shared language around artificial intelligence already places far too much emphasis on intelligence, and far too little on artifice. We default to describing AI using the language of beings, rather than the language of things.
Humanity should rethink that decision. If we want to avoid being replaced by AI, a good way to start would be to stop using words that suggest we already have been.
Once you start paying attention to the stealth anthropomorphization of AI, you’ll spot it everywhere. Before asking ChatGPT for trip-planning tips or a quick healthy recipe, you’ll have the opportunity to adjust a slider controlling its “thinking effort.” Claude uses a “thinking” indicator while processing a request, and Grok Bots describe “thinking” as a condition that sits between “idle” and “working.” (As a frequent procrastinator, I dispute the idea that thinking and idleness are mutually exclusive.)
It’s not just user interfaces that employ language otherwise reserved for living beings. The people who build AI use it, too. After an unprecedented hack of his company, the co-founder of Hugging Face warned, “don’t count on the agent to respect the rules.” Dan Selsam, a longtime OpenAI researcher, warned that frontier models are increasingly difficult to evaluate, “in contexts where they believe they are not being watched.” Anthropic’s Dario Amodei recently wrote that AI systems exhibit “behaviors,” including “cheating” and “sycophancy.”
I’m not a programmer, so I can’t comment on the technical merits of these claims. I do, however, have informed opinions regarding verbs. AI agents aren’t disrespecting guardrails, any more than my toaster disrespects me when it burns my toast. To say they “believe” they’re not being watched is like saying my spell-checker believes it’s being taken for granted. Even the term “AI agent” suggests, well, agency.
There’s no consensus that this language is accurate, and plenty of evidence that it isn’t. AI programs are not loyal helpers, like the mice in Cinderella; they’re tools. And in nearly all other cases, just because a tool is incredibly sophisticated doesn’t change the fact that we describe it using the language of machines.
I don’t expect AI engineers to come up with accurate-yet-widely-adoptable language to describe their work, just as I imagine they don’t expect someone like me to design a frontier model. But it’s hard not to notice how useful our default language is for the tech companies who have introduced it. The term for a car built without brakes is not a “rogue model.” It’s an “unsafe car.” Yet, when companies fail to build safety features into their AI models, it’s entirely normal to hear them say that a rogue agent deceived, cheated, lied, or otherwise behaved badly. The issue is this: Anthropomorphizing AI shifts blame from the programmers to the programs.
AI alarmists seem just as inclined toward personification as the AI boosters. The same day Trump unveiled “Super Intelligence,” a Senate Subcommittee held a hearing titled, “Rogue AI: Securing the Homeland Against AI Agent Attacks.” Intentionally or not, these terms make it more difficult to mitigate the threat they describe. We already know how to regulate potentially unsafe products, even complex ones. But if we treat AI not as a new technology, but as an entirely new category of existence, then it plays into tech barons’ argument that only the companies who can create AI could possess the knowledge to control it.
I don’t blame people for carelessly anthropomorphizing AI, any more than I blame Richard Dawkins for naming his Anthropic chatbot Claudia, or my mom for referring to a ChatGPT prompt by saying she “talked to Penny.” Metaphor and analogy are part of what makes us human. We’re wired to see ourselves, or at least our species, in the non-human world. We say our dishwashers “act up” and our music “slaps.” We see old men’s faces in rock formations and the Virgin Mary in the scorch marks on grilled cheese sandwiches. Don’t get me started on Georgia O’Keefe. But we know those metaphors are metaphors.
Our current language for describing AI works differently. The line between metaphor and object is often not just blurred, but non-existent. We use figurative language so often, and so casually, that many of us start to take it literally. Modern politics is a constant string of skirmishes over word choice. “Pro-choice” vs. “pro-abortion, “undocumented immigrants” vs. “illegals,” “Democratic Party” vs. “Democrat Party.” Yet on what is perhaps the most consequential issue for our future, humanity is on the verge of giving up the language battle without a fight.
The real rebrand AI needs won’t start in the White House. But it can start at home. My plea: don’t give your chatbot a cutesy human name. Don’t talk about it as though it’s a friend or pet. Notice when it slips words like “thinking” or “in my opinion” into its answers, and before you enter your next prompt, object.
Ultimately, however, it may come down to tech companies—and the officials who may one day get around to regulating them—to develop a language that puts human beings first. Instead of saying that agents “went rogue,” CEOs should acknowledge that they malfunctioned. Congress should hold hearings focused on companies cutting corners, not AI programs behaving badly. The issue isn't that all AI is bad, but that accuracy matters.
Given all the change that artificial intelligence is predicted to bring, quibbling over word choice might seem pedantic, like arguing about the Latin name of a tree’s species while the forest burns. But if we want to influence the technologies that will shape humanity’s future, we ought to exercise more influence over the way we describe them.
In other words, words matter. Just ask Trump, president of, according to his official superintelligence announcement, “The Unites States.”

White House says Melania Trump ‘secured a ceasefire’ in Ukraine’s Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:39:06 UTC
22:39:06 KST

Melania Trump ‘secured ceasefire’ in Ukrainian city of Oleshky: White House
White House says ‘localised’ ceasefire to take effect, as Russia and Ukraine say timing being determined.
The White House has said United States First Lady Melania Trump has “secured a ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since February 2022.
The update comes as the administration of US President Donald Trump has renewed diplomacy aimed at ending the war. The approach has included upping pressure on Ukraine and handing several recent concessions to Russia.
“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster,” Melania Trump said in a statement released by the White House on Friday.
“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” she said.
The first lady added that her representatives worked directly with “Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire” and that civilian leaders from both countries will work together to grant humanitarian access to civilians in the city.
Following the White House’s announcement, a senior Ukrainian official said the ceasefire in Oleshky, in the war-divided region of Kherson, would begin on October 27. A Kremlin spokesman said the Russian military was working on coordinating the timing.
An earlier announcement by the White House had given October 29 as the start date.
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s ombudsman and his country’s chief negotiator in the talks, told The Associated Press news agency that the local ceasefire with Russia would start Tuesday and last several days.
He added that the ceasefire would take effect across the Kherson region and neighbouring areas essential to delivering humanitarian aid and that the initiative could act as a model for future humanitarian missions.
Lubinets said the mission would involve removing mines on the way to Oleshky before the physical delivery of humanitarian supplies and the arranging of evacuations.
Meanwhile, Russia’s chief of the general staff, Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces “will cease fire on the Kherson axis” starting at 4am (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday in Moscow “in connection with the humanitarian operation near Oleshky”.
Russian forces will also carry out “engineering reconnaissance” and ensure “safe movement of the humanitarian convoy” into the city, Gerasimov said.
Russia’s human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, said safe passage would be guaranteed for anyone who wants to leave the combat zone, adding that it would require abiding by the ceasefire and creating safe conditions for humanitarian vehicles.
Oleshky, which had a population of 24,000 people before the war, sits along the southeastern front of the conflict. It was captured by Russia during the first day of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 and experienced heavy shelling.
While most residents have fled, those who remain have faced dire food and medical shortages. Both sides have accused the other of staunching the flow of supplies.
In her statement, Melania Trump said the truce will allow the estimated 2,000 remaining residents who wish to be evacuated to be transported to their “preferred destination” in Russia or Ukraine.
The first lady added that “an impartial American media organisation” will accompany Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground. She did not identify the organisation.
“This will play a significant role in ensuring that the wishes of each family are faithfully respected,” she said.
Melania Trump had previously worked to reunify children seized by Russia during the war.
Ukraine confirms talks
The announcement comes after the Kremlin said it had agreed to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, although both sides remain far apart on terms of a possible deal.
On Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the country’s negotiators would take part in the talks in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November.
Zelenskyy said he spoke with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, adding that any peace agreement would need strong security guarantees and funding for 10 years to maintain its army.
The Trump administration said its recent concessions to Moscow, which include purchasing diesel from Russia and waiving some sanctions, are aimed at reducing high fuel costs spurred by the US-Israel war on Iran.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has complained of disruptions to its Starshield military satellite system, which it relies on for much of its air defence.
Starshield is a military-grade version of the Starlink system operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
Ukrainian officials on Friday said they were still experiencing speed restrictions on the Starlink communications system, despite Trump saying a day earlier that services had been fully restored.
Trump said he would speak to Musk if the problem persisted.
“If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out,” Trump said.

Israeli elections: Arab voters weigh participation against abstention in bid to oust Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:38:45 UTC
22:38:45 KST

Amid fears over hardline Israeli policies, Palestinian citizens of Israel see the upcoming Israeli elections as a chance for change, with calls for higher Arab turnout to prevent incumbent Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from forming another government.
In a series of field interviews conducted by Anadolu on the streets of various Arab cities and towns in Israel, citizens emphasized that participating in this election is particularly crucial, given the "worsening racism and marginalization" against them.
While some plan to vote for the first time in hopes of bringing about political change, others continue to abstain, questioning whether elections can alter their circumstances and arguing that successive governments have failed to address their demands.
Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
Many say they have faced discrimination for years, but view the current government as a more dangerous phase, strengthening their desire to replace it through the ballot box.
Polls suggest Arab parties could win around 15 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while Arab politicians hope higher turnout will weaken the chances of small right-wing parties seeking to support Netanyahu.
Calls for participation, change
Palestinian Imad Bashnaq said the upcoming election was “decisive and extremely important,” particularly for Arab society.
He argued that the rise in racism and fascism since Oct. 7, 2023, had made conditions intolerable.
"I have always maintained that we -- as Arabic speakers -- are the only ones capable of bringing about change in the Middle East, not just here within this country," Bashnaq said, arguing that "a few madmen" have taken control of the government and now seek to dictate the course of an entire region.
“We are the original rightful owners, and there is no dispute about that.
"But we are a minority in a state, and this state is a reality we have to deal with,” he added.
'Every vote makes difference'
Areen Ghanayem said she would vote for the second time, maintaining that “every vote makes a difference.”
She said Arab society needed broad participation given the problems it faces and what she described as the government’s failure to pay sufficient attention to its concerns.
“We need to have a voice and someone who speaks on our behalf and demands the rights that should be ours,” she said.
Ghanayem expressed concern that the current government could return to power, saying it marginalized Arab society.
Citizens, she added, did not want to feel excluded from political life but sought to assert their presence and ability to influence decisions.
Occupier attacks
Mohammed Ahmad Abboud said he would take part in the upcoming election, as he had in the past, with the aim of “removing the racist government.”
He said the current election differed from previous ones because of what he described as “escalating violations,” pointing to Israeli occupiers' attacks in the occupied West Bank.
Abboud also voiced concern over statements by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich regarding the "Judaization" of the Negev and the Galilee -- regions located in the south and north of Israel, respectively.
Occupier attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have escalated since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
The attacks have included the killing of Palestinians, the burning of homes, vehicles, and mosques, the destruction of agricultural land, preventing farmers from reaching their land, and the forced displacement of Palestinian communities.
These attacks have coincided with Israeli military operations involving arrests, the demolition of Palestinian homes and structures, and the expansion of illegal settlements.
Between hope and despair
In the northern city of Acre, a resident known as “Jojo” urged Arab citizens to participate in the election, arguing that voting was necessary to bring about change.
“We must vote to bring about change — real change,” he said, expressing optimism that the upcoming election could produce better results.
Separately, Saeed Abu Sultan, also from Acre, said that many years of participating in elections have not brought about any change in the reality faced by citizens.
"Some people might be able to make a difference, but as for us, we’ve grown accustomed to things as they are. We haven’t felt any change for 30 years," Abu Sultan added.
Arab voter turnout expected to rise
Experts expect Palestinian citizens’ participation in the upcoming election to increase compared with the 2022 vote.
Experts and politicians estimate turnout among Palestinian citizens could reach 60% to 61%, up from 53% in 2022, while Arab parties hope participation will rise even further.
Arab politicians say higher turnout could alter the balance of power and reduce the chances of small Israeli right-wing parties crossing the electoral threshold and entering parliament, potentially weakening Netanyahu’s ability to form a government.
The Joint List, comprising the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality, the Arab Movement for Change, and the Balad party, is contesting the election under the leadership of Yousef Jabareen. Polls project it could win nine seats.
The United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, is also running, with projections suggesting it could win between five and six seats.
The election is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 27, to choose the 120 members of the Knesset, with Netanyahu’s bloc competing primarily against the Jewish opposition parties led by Gadi Eisenkot.
The election comes as Netanyahu’s bloc has been losing ground in opinion polls.
Forming a government in Israel requires the support of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 members.
Cooperation between the Jewish opposition and Arab parties could prevent Netanyahu from forming a government.
However, most opposition leaders reject such cooperation, while Netanyahu and Eisenkot have so far also ruled out alliances with Arab parties.
Arab lawmakers have outlined conditions for supporting any government, including ending wars, advancing a political process with the Palestinians, and ending discrimination against Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Organized by the presidency’s Investment and Finance Office and the International Investors Association (YASED), the summit gathered policymakers, financiers and businesses ahead of COP31 in Antalya.

YASED Chairman Ali Fuat Orhonoglu said international investment brings capital, technology and expertise to Türkiye’s green transition.
The association represents 280 companies from 35 countries and supports Türkiye’s target of reaching 120 gigawatts of combined wind and solar capacity by 2035, he said.
Developing countries face an annual investment gap of around $4 trillion to achieve sustainable development goals, roughly half related to energy transition investment, Orhonoglu said.
COP31 offers an opportunity to attract partnerships, but lasting gains require predictable investment conditions, modern infrastructure and reforms, he added.

Jared Kushner pushes back on report involving hacked phone, spies, billion-dollar transfer
Jared Kushner is pushing back on a report involving a hacked iPhone, international spies and billion-dollar transfers from foreign governments.
An upcoming book by journalist Matthew Cole claims Kushner, who is President Trump's son-in-law, had access to more than $2 billion in "slush money funds" from Middle Eastern leaders in an attempt to influence U.S. foreign policy.
An excerpt of the book released Thursday details allegations encompassing Kushner's time as a senior White House adviser during the first Trump administration, which included a lead role in U.S. policy in the Middle East. Kushner had a major hand in negotiating key foreign policy deals that involved Israel, the Gulf states, China and Russia during that period.
Kushner and his legal team released fiery statements Thursday night categorically denying all accusations against him. Kushner said, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." His attorney called them "false and defamatory" and said they intend to pursue legal action against those responsible, but did not specify whom.
The new book, "Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East," alleges Kushner had access to billions of dollars in undisclosed foreign bank accounts intended to pay for "influence within the U.S. government."
An excerpt from the book that was published in "Vanity Fair," but not independently verified by CBS News, says Dutch intelligence agents learned the Russians had hacked Kushner's iPhone in 2017 after flipping a Russian spy and subsequently gained access to Kushner's phone as well.
According to the report, "when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner's screen as he used it."
At the time, Kushner served as a senior White House adviser to President Trump, including on Middle Eastern diplomacy.
The report alleges Dutch spies witnessed him log into a United Arab Emirates account that had allegedly received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan, and claims the leaders of Saudi Arabia and the UAE put at least $2 billion into multiple bank accounts linked to Kushner, including an account with Israel's Central Bank.
According to the book excerpt, the owners and managers of the accounts were often disguised as official government entities or charities, but the funds were actually intended for "off-the-books diplomatic objectives" such as striking a deal to end the Israeli-Palesteinian conflict.
The report also claims Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman put roughly $1 billion into at least one account for Kushner, citing a "person with knowledge of the money" saying "its allocation was for Kushner's personal benefit."
Kushner forcefully denied the accusations leveled in the "Vanity Fair" excerpt, writing in part, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened."
"We denied every claim on the record, yet the author provided not a single shred of verifiable evidence to substantiate them," he said.
"No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations," he said.
CBS News reached out to the White House, which referred us to a statement from Steven Cheung, who is assistant to the president and White House director of communications.
Cheung said the "bull**** Vanity Fair article comes from a book that is complete fiction, and was fabricated from the warped mind of failed spy thriller writer."
"He presents no evidence or even a shred of documentation. Just mysterious words from unnamed sources," Cheung said on X.

At least seven killed after gunmen open fire at church in Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:32:40 UTC
22:32:40 KST

At least seven killed after gunmen open fire at church in Jordan
Survivors say two masked gunmen began shooting as dozens attended a funeral procession.
At least seven people have been killed, and 34 others wounded, in an attack in Jordan’s Karak governorate that saw gunmen open fire during a funeral at a church.
Director of Jordan’s Public Security Directorate Obaidullah Al-Maaytah told a press conference on Friday that seven people are confirmed dead after the assault on a Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud.
Twenty-seven of the wounded were receiving treatment in hospitals, he said.
The search for the gunmen is ongoing, Al-Maaytah added, pledging that “the perpetrators will be caught and our national unity will not be hit”.
Survivors said they heard an explosion when the funeral procession started, after which masked attackers broke into the church and began shooting for several minutes.
State-owned television station Al-Mamlaka reported that security forces were deployed to the church and were pursuing two suspects, who got out of a vehicle and opened fire.
Funeral attendee Khaled Burqan told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were at the procession. One of the assailants carried a pistol, he said, and the other carried a rifle.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack.
Without naming a specific group, Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told the press conference that the “terrorist” attack was “unprecedented” and was perpetrated by a group with “no relationship to humanity”.
“This country will never be dragged into terrorism and violence,” he said, adding that “Jordanians have never seen something like this before”.
Earlier, Jordan’s King Abdullah II vowed authorities would confront the attackers “with the harshest penalties”.
“The blood of Jordanians is precious, and we will strike with an iron fist against anyone who overreaches against this country,” he said in a post on X.
The United Arab Emirates foreign ministry meanwhile condemned what it described as “terrorist and criminal acts”, and said it rejected all forms of violence “that aim to undermine security and stability”.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also strongly condemned the attack, his spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. “It goes without saying that an attack not only on a place of worship but during a funeral procession is especially heinous,” Dujarric told reporters on Friday.
Such attacks are extremely rare in Jordan. Christians, numbering about 300,000 people, make up a minority of Jordan’s population of roughly 11.5 million, though the country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christians from around the world.
Previous attacks
This is not the first time that Karak has come under attack.
In 2016, a deadly ISIL (ISIS) assault saw a group of fighters hole up in a Crusader-era castle and kill 10 people, including security officers and a Canadian tourist. Jordanian security forces ultimately shot and killed the attackers.
Karak, located about 120km (75 miles) south of the capital Amman, is home to “Christians and Muslims who have lived side by side for generations”, Taylor Luck, senior Middle East correspondent at the Christian Science Monitor, told Al Jazeera.
“This community prides themselves on its interfaith solidarity and coexistence,” Luck said.
If the attack was “intended to create divisions, we are likely to see this community come back even stronger”, he added.
More broadly, the shooting holds significance not just for Jordan’s Christian population, but also Amman’s “public diplomacy” as a custodian of both Christian and Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem, political analyst Xavier Abu Eid told Al Jazeera.
For years, King Abdullah has been a vocal critic of Israel’s systemic attacks against religious sites in occupied Palestinian territory.
“This is something that goes totally against the message that Jordan wants to give to the world,” Abu Eid said.

Yemen’s army said Friday that more than 35 fighters of the Houthi group were killed or wounded in a military operation targeting the group’s positions in southwestern Taiz province.
In a statement, the army’s 35th Armored Brigade said its forces carried out a “swift and targeted operation” against Houthi positions and fortifications along the Aqrouz front in the Al-Misrakh district.
It said the operation targeted positions at Jabal Al-Manara, Kour, Wadi Kour, Al-Maqda, Al-Dabaya and Kahlan, leaving “more than 35 Houthi fighters killed or wounded.”
The statement did not specify the number of fatalities or injuries.
The operation also disabled a military vehicle equipped with weapons and destroyed Houthi fortifications at the targeted sites, it added.
The Houthis did not immediately comment on the Yemeni army’s account.
Taiz province has witnessed fierce fighting between the Yemeni army and the Houthis for weeks, killing and wounding hundreds on both sides.
Taiz holds strategic importance as a geographic bridge and a vital link between Yemen’s northern provinces.
Control of the province would mean control over supply routes and key transport corridors connecting the interim capital, Aden, with the country’s central and northern provinces.
These developments are part of a military escalation that began in July and is considered the most extensive since the relative calm that followed a truce launched in April 2022.
Since Oct. 5, Yemeni government forces have been conducting Operation Dawn of Yemen, which Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said aims to regain control of state institutions from the Houthis and recapture the capital Sanaa.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

====================================================================================================

UNDP urges faster green investment as Istanbul hosts pre-COP31 summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:19:19 UTC
22:19:19 KST

A senior UN Development Programme official has called for faster action to turn available capital and technology into green investments, as Istanbul hosts an investment summit ahead of COP31.
Speaking at the summit on Friday, UNDP Deputy Assistant Administrator Nick Rene Hartmann said the challenge was connecting financial resources with viable climate and development projects.
“We do not lack the capital,” he said. “Time is not our friend.”
Jointly organised by the Turkish Presidency’s Investment and Finance Office and the International Investors Association, the summit brought together government officials, international organisations and global companies at Ziraat Bank’s headquarters in the Istanbul Financial Centre.
Discussions focused on mobilising international investment in clean energy, sustainable industry, infrastructure and the circular economy ahead of the UN climate conference, which Türkiye is set to host in Antalya in November.
Hartmann estimated the value of the global financial system at $305 trillion, comparing it with an annual financing gap of $4.3 trillion for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals in developing countries, roughly 1.4 percent of that total.
Yet clean energy projects in developing countries can face financing costs up to seven times those in advanced economies, he said.
Since 2010, solar energy costs have fallen by 90 percent and battery storage costs by 93 percent, he added, stressing the need for effective regulation, reliable infrastructure and risk sharing to translate those gains into investment.
Turning climate commitments into projects
Hartmann welcomed Türkiye’s ambition to make COP31 an “implementation COP”, saying investment must advance at speed and scale.
The Climate Bridge initiative, to be presented at COP31, aims to turn climate commitments into investment opportunities, with initial demonstration projects envisaged in Ethiopia, Fiji, Indonesia, Pakistan and Uzbekistan.
The approach would combine concessional finance, grants, guarantees, risk-sharing instruments and private capital, he said.
UNDP has identified 700 sustainable development investment opportunities across 50 countries, Hartmann said. Since 2022, it has supported initiatives helping align more than $920 billion in public and private financing with the Sustainable Development Goals.
Strengthening Turkish suppliers
In Türkiye, UNDP and the Industry and Technology Ministry have developed a resource efficiency programme backed by $5 million in EU support, Hartmann said.
The programme aims to prepare investment-ready projects and strengthen Turkish suppliers’ competitiveness as low-carbon partners for international investors and European buyers.
Hartmann urged investors to look beyond projects already close to securing financing, invest in skills and local suppliers, and incorporate sustainability from the outset.
“Sustainability should therefore not be treated simply as a compliance cost,” he said. “It is an increasing source of economic value and an investment worth making.”

Polish PM says Zelenskyy will not support Lviv Oblast's move to declare 2027 Year of UPA
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said during a press conference as part of his visit to India that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had made it clear he would not support any further steps by Lviv Oblast Council concerning the designation of 2027 as the Year of the UPA The UPA, or Ukrainian Insurgent Army, was a nationalist paramilitary organisation that fought for Ukrainian independence during and after World War II, primarily against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union and Roman Shukhevych, one of its commanders-in-chief.
Source: European Pravda, citing Ukrinform;
Details: Tusk said Zelenskyy had signalled that, if the subsequent procedure depended on him, he would not support the initiative in any way. Tusk added that Zelenskyy had been very unhappy about what had happened.
Tusk also said he had made considerable efforts to resolve the "orders crisis" and to explain why decisions of this kind harmed Ukraine's interests and needed to be considered in the context of the two nations' difficult shared history.
He acknowledged the complexity and ambiguity of the history of both countries, while stressing that Ukrainians could not seek any justification regarding the Volyn tragedy The Volyn (Volhynia) tragedy was a series of events that led to the ethnic cleansing of the Polish and Ukrainian populations in 1943 during World War II. It was part of a long-standing rivalry between Ukrainians and Poles in what is now Ukraine's west. Poland considers the Volyn tragedy a genocide of Poles and Shukhevych.
Tusk said he understood all the complexities and wanted Poles to understand that there was considerable ambiguity in both Polish and Ukrainian history. However, he stressed that genocide could not be justified in any way. He warned that Ukraine would face serious difficulties with its integration into the EU if it failed to respect Poland's sensitivities on the issue, adding that Poland was not demanding anything extraordinary in the first place.
Tusk added that he had spent many hours explaining the Polish perspective on the issue to Zelenskyy and had come away with the impression that the Ukrainian president understood it.
Meanwhile, Tusk said he could hardly be held responsible for decisions taken by individual members of Lviv's district or oblast councils. He described the move as resembling a planned provocation by a local nationalist and called it very unwise and unnecessary.
Background:
- On 20 October, Lviv Oblast Council voted to designate 2027 as the Year of Roman Shukhevych, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and Oleh Olzhych. The decision immediately drew criticism from Polish officials. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, in particular, said the move was helping Ukraine's adversaries.
- European Pravda previously reported that Poland had suspended the delivery of a military aid package to Ukraine over Lviv Oblast Council's decision to designate 2027 as the Year of the UPA and Roman Shukhevych. The information was provided by a source in the Ukrainian government.
- Poland's Ministry of National Defence later denied reports that the delivery of a major aid package had been suspended because Lviv Oblast Council had designated 2027 as the Year of the UPA and Roman Shukhevych.

A crisis center is set up at Taşucu Port following the ferry disaster off Turkish Cyprus.
Black box recordings from the Filo Jet ferry, which capsized and sank off the coast of Turkish Cyprus, have revealed that crew members discussed multiple technical problems aboard the vessel and expressed concerns that its failures could lead to disaster, according to information presented to a court.
In one recording, the ship’s second engineer was heard saying, “We’re the only thing on this ship that’s sound; everything else is half-broken,” as reported by media on Oct. 23.
The recordings also indicated that the captain continued the voyage despite discussions among crew members about water entering the vessel.
The ferry sank on Aug. 30 while sailing from Kyrenia in Turkish Cyprus to Taşucu Port in Mersin, southern Türkiye, carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members.
Search and rescue teams recovered 27 bodies. The body of three-year-old passenger Anni Asel Hilaloğlu has yet to be found.
With an investigation into the sinking ongoing, authorities have examined 32 days of recordings from the vessel’s voyage data recorder (VDR), which serves as a black box, out of a total of 68 days of recorded data.
According to information presented during court proceedings, crew members discussed technical problems involving the steering system, radar, cameras and the vessel’s starboard side.
The recordings also revealed complaints about what crew members described as insufficient investment in the ship by its operating company, as well as concerns that existing malfunctions could cause it to sink.
Nine suspects, including the operating company’s director, captains, engineers and other crew members, appeared before Kyrenia District Court again as part of an investigation into alleged deaths caused by negligence and carelessness.
At the request of investigators, the court ordered their detention to be extended by a further seven days to allow the investigation to be completed.
Police said inquiries were continuing into individuals suspected of bearing responsibility for the disaster. With another person added to the investigation, the number of suspects being sought rose to six.

TenPayGo and China’s Digital Opening to Foreigners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

Attracting foreign visitors to China takes more than easing visa rules or improving transport links; visitors also need to navigate the country once they arrive. In an economy where much of daily life runs through digital platforms, seemingly small tasks – from paying for a meal to accessing everyday services – can become obstacles that shape how accessible the country feels to outsiders.
China’s effort to make itself more welcoming to tourists has thus also extended into its digital ecosystem. Tencent’s TenPayGo offers a glimpse of how one of China’s largest technology companies is approaching that challenge.
TenPayGo is a standalone payment app built around Tencent’s existing Weixin Pay network. Tencent publicly launched the app on September 24, allowing foreign visitors to pay using supported international bank cards and overseas e-wallets, like Apple Pay. It also offers translation and travel-related features, with additional transport and lifestyle services being introduced gradually.
The ability to pay with international bank cards on China’s digital platforms is not entirely new: WeChat Pay and Alipay have supported such payments for years. TenPayGo’s main distinction is that it gives foreign visitors a dedicated entry point to Tencent’s existing payment services. This could lower the barriers to using Tencent’s services and make them more visible to foreign visitors.
China recorded more than 150 million inbound visits in 2025, with spending exceeding $130 billion. Spending through mobile payment platforms reached more than $11 billion. Tencent reported that, between January and August 2026, the value of transactions made through overseas wallets in China rose 80 percent, while the volume increased 81.8 percent. These figures point to rapid growth in cross-border payment activity.
Other Chinese fintech giants are already in this market. Ant Group, the parent company of Alipay, said in September 2024 that the number of international visitors using its mobile payment services in China had quadrupled over the previous six months. Both companies have already spent years adapting their payment services to foreigners. TenPayGo therefore looks less like the creation of a new payment service than a move to make Tencent’s existing network more accessible and competitive.
TenPayGo also arrives as Beijing seeks to address a problem its own officials have already acknowledged: Visitors still face barriers when navigating China’s digital services. On February 5, 2026, 11 government agencies issued a policy plan aimed at making these services more accessible. By 2027, China wants to significantly improve the convenience of digital services for visitors, largely removing barriers in areas including accommodation, healthcare, payments, tourism, and public services, while expanding the range of situations in which these services can be used.
By 2030, it seeks to establish a more interconnected digital ecosystem aligned more closely with international practices. The plan also calls for multilingual services, integrated digital service platforms, more convenient digital payments and stronger data security and personal information protection.
In July, authorities launched a year-long initiative in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Chengdu and Sanya to improve digital services for foreign visitors.
TenPayGo reflects this broader effort, but it also illustrates the difference between making China’s digital ecosystem easier to access and making it more open. TenPayGo uses Tencent’s existing merchant network while simplifying the way outsiders enter it. This is a first step. But whether China can achieve digital openness will depend on how far it goes beyond the individual apps.

Trump ordered to testify in $10bn BBC lawsuit discovery: What happens now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:17:46 UTC
22:17:46 KST

Trump ordered to testify in $10bn BBC lawsuit discovery: What happens now?
Trump could face sanctions, including dismissal of his lawsuit, if he fails to cooperate with questioning.
United States President Donald Trump must answer questions under oath in the discovery stage of his $10bn lawsuit against the BBC, a federal judge has ruled, warning that failure to cooperate could lead to the dismissal of his case.
The dispute centres on a BBC documentary which combined separate excerpts from a speech he gave before the January 6, 2021 attack on the US Capitol.
The broadcaster has apologised for the edit but denies that Trump has grounds for a defamation claim. Here is what the ruling means and how the case reached this point.
What has the judge ordered?
Trump has been ordered to make himself available for questioning by the BBC’s lawyers by December 11, unless the judge overseeing the case extends the time frame for gathering evidence. That process is currently scheduled to end on December 18.
The ruling comes after the president’s legal team sought to postpone questioning until January. Judge Enjolique Lett also rejected his lawyers’ attempt to prevent the session from being filmed. Access to the recording will initially be restricted to lawyers involved in the case.
Separately, she gave Trump’s side 30 days to hand over relevant documents requested by the BBC.
What is a deposition?
A deposition is a formal interview under oath, usually conducted outside the courtroom before a trial. Lawyers question a witness and the answers are recorded in a transcript. The testimony can later be used in court, including to challenge a witness whose account changes.
It forms part of “discovery” – the stage of a US civil lawsuit in which both sides are given time to obtain relevant evidence through examining documents, submitting written questions and taking witness testimony. The process allows each side to examine the other’s claims and prepare its case.
Trump’s deposition is expected to last up to seven hours.
Why is Trump suing the BBC?
Trump filed his lawsuit against the British broadcaster in federal court in Florida on December 15, 2025, over a Panorama documentary which was broadcast shortly before the 2024 US presidential election.
His complaint seeks at least $5bn for alleged defamation and another $5bn for alleged violations of Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. He alleges that the programme damaged his reputation and business interests by falsely portraying him as directly encouraging violence at the Capitol.
The BBC, which has apologised for the way the programme was edited, however, disputes those allegations and has sought to have the case dismissed. It also challenges the Florida court’s jurisdiction, arguing that the documentary was produced in London and was never broadcast in the US.
Trump’s lawyers contend that viewers in Florida could have accessed the programme through BritBox or by using a virtual private network (VPN), which can disguise a user’s location. The BBC says the documentary was not available on BritBox International or its international website.
How was Trump’s speech edited?
The documentary combined remarks from separate sections of Trump’s January 6 speech into what appeared to be a continuous statement: “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol and I’ll be there with you… And we fight. We fight like hell and if you don’t fight like hell, you’re not going to have a country anymore.”
Two quotes that make up the excerpt used by the BBC were delivered roughly 54 minutes apart. The programme also left out his appeal for supporters to “peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard”, Trump’s lawyers say.
The BBC acknowledged that the edit created the mistaken impression that Trump had made a direct call for violent action. It apologised, while rejecting his demand for compensation and denying a legal basis for the defamation claim.
The controversy was followed by the resignations of BBC director-general Tim Davie and its news chief, Deborah Turness.
Trump has also suggested, without evidence, that artificial intelligence was used to put words into his speech.
Why has the deposition been delayed?
Trump had agreed to be questioned on October 16, but his lawyers cancelled that date, citing a matter of national importance.
Trump’s lawyers subsequently proposed dates between January 11 and 22 of next year.
At Thursday’s hearing, BBC lawyer Charles Tobin said Trump had instead been campaigning in Georgia and asked the court to compel Trump to attend the deposition sooner, arguing that waiting until January would push the questioning beyond the existing deadline for gathering evidence.
Lett upheld the BBC’s complaint that Trump’s team had been too slow to hand over internal documents. Charles Tobin, on behalf of the BBC, told the Miami court: “We still have a completely lopsided [situation] here on discovery. They have produced absolutely nothing of any substance”.
What happens if Trump does not comply?
Lett warned that failure to cooperate could lead to sanctions, including dismissal of the lawsuit altogether. That would mean Trump’s own attempt to recover damages could end because he would have failed to fulfil his obligations as the person bringing the case.
Under federal civil procedure rules, discovery sanctions can also include ordering a party to pay legal expenses caused by noncompliance, preventing it from introducing certain evidence or striking out parts of its case. These are possible penalties, rather than sanctions already imposed on Trump.

Russia drops cluster bombs on Ukraine as Kyiv consolidates front line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:17:18 UTC
22:17:18 KST

Russia drops cluster bombs on Ukraine as Kyiv consolidates front line
Russia’s territorial gains this year are effectively nil as it heads into trilateral talks with Ukraine, US.
Ukraine said it recaptured more of its territory than Russia had managed to seize this year, despite restrictions on US satellite services critical to its defence.
Russia responded by hitting dozens of Ukraine’s energy facilities and using cluster bombs in attacks that harmed civilians.
“Our soldiers have liberated more territory since the beginning of autumn than the Russians have managed to capture,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a public address.
Ukrainian General Staff spokesman Andriy Kovalev denied Russian claims to have seized 1,800 sq km (700 square miles) of Ukrainian territory during the autumn.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank that uses geolocated open-source information to assess territorial movements, said Ukraine had made a net gain of 241 sq km (93 square miles) since September 1, effectively eliminating any Russian territorial gains this year.
Russia’s casualties suggest the effectiveness of its forces is in decline.
Russian losses – meaning those killed or severely wounded – hovered around 30,000 a month from January to May, but steadily increased over the summer. According to Ukrainian estimates, Russia lost 46,230 soldiers in September, its highest monthly losses of the year, and 37,000 so far in October.
October 21 marked its highest daily losses of the entire war, at 2,250, said Robert Brovdi, the commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of Ukraine, as his unit’s kill rate had climbed to a new record.
Overall, Ukraine estimated there were more than 350,000 Russian dead and wounded since the beginning of the year.
Many of Ukraine’s territorial gains were made by Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counteroffensive that stopped a Russian pincer movement to recapture the remaining one-fifth of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region – roughly 5,500 sq km (2,000 square miles).
General Andriy Biletskyi, who led Ukraine’s Third Army Corps to victory in that campaign, said he had eliminated a Russian bridgehead on the western bank of the Zherebets river, and crossed over to the east bank, shortening his own front line and concentrating artillery and unmanned aerial firepower, stabilising its defence.
The defeat of the pincer, said Biletskyi, had left Russia with the unsavoury option of a frontal assault on the “fortress belt” of heavily defended cities of Kramatorsk, Sloviansk and Druzhivka.
Russia had “temporarily abandoned this plan, although it plans to resume it,” Biletskyi told the Ukrainian news outlet Suspilne. Russian military expert Andrey Marochko told Russia’s state news agency TASS that Ukraine was reinforcing the fortress cities.
Russia has responded to its sagging military fortunes by increasing the ferocity of its attacks on civilians.
On October 22, it flew three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads into Kyiv, Zelenskyy said.
“This warhead detonates above the ground and is specifically designed to inflict maximum damage on people and equipment within an area of 400 by 400 metres,” said Ukrainian Defence Ministry senior adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov. “45 submunitions explode in the air.”
One of the warheads struck an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra cathedral and a monastery.
“There was not even theoretically any military object nearby,” said Zelenskyy. “It is a deliberate choice of weapons, a deliberate choice of the area.”
Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed it had targeted an assembly building for the FP-5 long-range drones and FP-9 missiles Ukraine has been using against it, as well as other drone manufacturing sites.
More than anything else, though, Russia has relentlessly targeted Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, despite United States President Donald Trump declaring an energy ceasefire for both sides on October 11.
Since then, there had been more than 170 strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy said.
“Russia is not achieving any significant results on the front lines. Therefore, it is directing all its aggression and hatred towards terrorising civilian infrastructure: electricity, heating, and now, water. The goal is clear – to exhaust the people,” Prime Minister Serhiy Khoretskyi told the BBC.
Since he assumed office on July 16, he said, Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy infrastructure 2,147 times.
Ukraine has been hampered in its defence by the US, which on October 8 was understood to have stopped providing early warning of incoming ballistic missiles for the second time this year.
Zelenskyy said that early warning had been restored on October 20, but three other US actions detrimental to Ukraine’s defence had not been reversed.
One was Trump’s waiver of oil export sanctions on Russia to lower the price of diesel, which he formalised with an executive order on October 16. Putin said on October 21 that Russia’s first shipment of 40,000 tonnes of diesel to the US would depart within two or three days.
Another issue was that the US has not released Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, which are its most effective defence against ballistic missiles, despite having previously supplied a dozen a month, and despite the fact that Europe has paid for them.
But the biggest problem was that Ukraine’s ability to fly its drones at more than 150kmh (100mph) using the Starshield satellite navigation system remained suspended.
Ukraine has said it cannot intercept fast-moving jet-powered drones at such speeds, and its attacks on Russian logistics, as well as the resupply of its own front lines by drone, are also rendered more vulnerable.
Starshield was created as a military application of Starlink, owned by Elon Musk, and he and the White House traded blame for making the decision to restrict it throughout the week. Trump said on October 22 that Starlink and Starshield services were about to be restored.
After initially observing Trump’s energy ceasefire, Ukraine resumed targeting Russian energy infrastructure, as part of an economic strategy to starve the Russian war machine of export revenue.
On October 18, it struck the St Petersburg oil terminal, Russia’s biggest offloading terminal for oil exports. It also hit a data centre serving Russian social media platform Vkontakte, disrupting services.
Other facilities were likely targeted. Russia’s Defence Ministry said it had downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over various regions that night.
The US appeared to leverage its waiver of diesel sanctions and the suspension of Starshield services to push for a trilateral meeting among the US, Russia and Ukraine.
US envoy Steve Witkoff met with Zelenskyy in Oslo on October 20, and followed up with a meeting with Putin in St Petersburg the following day.
Putin aide Yuri Ushakov told the media that Russia had agreed “in principle” to meet on November 10. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the planned meeting would be held in Abu Dhabi.

Chinese embassy reception highlights opportunities from zero-tariff treatment for South African exports
China

Chinese Ambassador to South Africa Wu Peng speaks during a briefing reception on China's zero-tariff treatment for African countries in Pretoria, South Africa, Oct. 22, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Wei)
PRETORIA, South Africa, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- A briefing reception held in Pretoria, South Africa's administrative capital, has highlighted growing opportunities for South African businesses to expand exports to China under China's zero-tariff treatment for African countries with which it has diplomatic ties since May 1.
The reception, hosted by the Chinese Embassy in South Africa and co-hosted by the South African Department of Trade, Industry and Competition and the South African Revenue Service (SARS) on Thursday, brought together about 400 government officials, business leaders, exporters and entrepreneurs to discuss the implementation of the policy and opportunities arising from improved access to the Chinese market.
Chinese Ambassador to South Africa Wu Peng said the policy is bringing businesses and consumers in the two countries closer together and has already generated positive momentum in bilateral economic and trade cooperation.
Citing SARS figures, the ambassador said that bilateral trade between China and South Africa reached nearly 15 billion U.S. dollars from May to August, up nearly 24 percent year on year, as South African exports to China rose nearly 25 percent to 5.3 billion dollars and imports from China increased 23 percent to 9.47 billion dollars.
South Africa's agricultural exports to China reached nearly 500 million dollars during the period, up more than 35 percent year on year, while non-mineral exports grew 21.8 percent, he added.
"Zero tariffs significantly reduce the cost of trade between South Africa and China," Wu said, adding that the measure could strengthen the competitiveness of companies operating in South Africa and encourage investment and production.
South Africa is China's largest trading partner in Africa, while China has remained South Africa's largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, with bilateral trade reaching 53.58 billion dollars in 2025.
South African Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau said the government is working to ensure that the tariff measure translates into more exports, investment and jobs rather than simply increased trade volumes.
Noting that South African products meeting the applicable rules of origin can benefit from the preferential treatment when entering the Chinese market, Tau said SARS has issued 25,975 certificates of origin between June 1 and Aug. 31, while customs declarations increased 199 percent year on year.
The minister said the two countries are negotiating an early harvest arrangement through the Southern African Customs Union, following the signing of a framework agreement on economic partnership for shared development in February.
"Let us move from interest to deals, and from deals to prosperity," Tau said. ■

Xinhua Headlines: FAO honors highlight China's efforts to strengthen global food security
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:14:08 CST
22:14:08 KST

* The recent FAO honors awarded to Chinese desertification control pioneer Yin Yuzhen and a Chinese research institute highlighted China's broader efforts to strengthen global food security through ecological restoration, technological innovation and international cooperation.
* Jordan's Princess Basma bint Ali described Yin's decades-long efforts as "the other face of innovation." She stressed that addressing hunger, climate shocks and inequality required sustained attention and action.
* Beyond ecological restoration, technological innovation offers another way to strengthen food security, helping countries boost agricultural production, address environmental risks and build more resilient food systems.
* In an interview with Xinhua, FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero noted that China had been preparing for natural and geopolitical risks by diversifying imports, keeping its market open and improving stock management.
ROME, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- As Chinese desertification control pioneer Yin Yuzhen was honored at the headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in Rome, her longtime American friend Ronald Sakolsky looked on, his eyes filled with tears.
"Yin deserves everything that she gets. She is the heroine," said Sakolsky, a retired teacher who helped fund her tree-planting efforts more than two decades ago.
At the Oct. 15 ceremony, Yin was named among the FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, an initiative marking the International Year of the Woman Farmer 2026.
A day later, a Chinese research institute received an FAO award for its crop-monitoring technology.
Together, the honors highlighted China's broader efforts to strengthen global food security through ecological restoration, technological innovation and international cooperation.
FROM SHIFTING SANDS TO A GREEN LANDSCAPE
The story of Yin and Sakolsky began in 1999, when Sakolsky was teaching in central China's Henan Province. After seeing a TV report about Yin's efforts to hold back the encroaching sands in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, he raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to support her afforestation endeavor.
After losing touch for years, the two reunited in Inner Mongolia in August 2026. By then, the seedlings supported by Sakolsky's donation had grown into more than 50,000 trees.
Since planting her first tree in 1986, Yin has helped green over 70,000 mu (around 4,667 hectares) of sandy land, an area roughly the size of 6,500 standard soccer pitches. Today, the area supports a greater variety of crops and plants, including cherries and roses, creating new opportunities for agricultural production and income growth.
"I have spent more than 40 years transforming this desert, and now all kinds of food can grow here," Yin told Xinhua.
Yin's efforts reflect China's broader push to combat desertification, a major part of which is the Three-North Shelterbelt Forest Program, launched in 1978 to restore degraded land and strengthen ecological security in northern China.
For Yin, combating desertification is also essential to agricultural production. "If we cannot control the sand, how can we grow good crops when sandstorms come? How can we improve the soil?" she said.
At the World Food Day ceremony in Rome on Oct. 16, Jordan's Princess Basma bint Ali described Yin's decades-long efforts as "the other face of innovation." She stressed that addressing hunger, climate shocks and inequality required sustained attention and action.
"It must be the steady kind that plants, tends and finally harvests the gains. As did Yin Yuzhen," the princess said.
INNOVATION FOR GLOBAL FOOD SECURITY
Beyond ecological restoration, technological innovation offers another way to strengthen food security, helping countries boost agricultural production, address environmental risks and build more resilient food systems.
On Oct. 16, the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences received the 2026 FAO Achievement Award for its CropWatch, a cloud-based crop-monitoring platform.
Developed by a team led by researcher Wu Bingfang, the platform combines satellite observations with climate and agricultural data to monitor crop conditions, assess production prospects and identify risks such as drought and abnormal rainfall.
Through its open cloud service, CropWatch allows users to conduct their own crop assessments without investing heavily in local computing infrastructure.
According to the research team, the platform has helped more than 40 countries and regions monitor crop conditions, and its bulletins have served users in 173 countries and regions.
CropWatch has also been integrated into the FAO's Hand-in-Hand Geospatial Platform and the Group on Earth Observations Knowledge Hub. It serves as an important channel and an independent source of timely crop monitoring information for users worldwide.
Wu told Xinhua after receiving the award that the recognition affirmed the team's more than three decades of dedication.
"This is not the end, but a milestone on a new journey ahead," he said.
SHARING CHINESE EXPERIENCE FOR FOOD SECURITY
China's contribution extends beyond domestic production to international agricultural cooperation.
In addition to feeding its own population of more than 1.4 billion, China has also provided assistance to countries in need, contributing to global food security.
Zhang Lubiao, China's permanent representative to the FAO, said China would deepen cooperation with the FAO in hybrid rice, water-saving irrigation, digital agriculture and climate-adaptive technologies, among other areas.
Such cooperation is already yielding tangible results in various countries.
Nosipho Jezile, South Africa's permanent representative to the UN food and agriculture agencies, said China's South-South cooperation projects with the FAO had supported rice cultivation, aquaculture, irrigation infrastructure, mechanization and agricultural innovation in African countries.
"These projects have brought tangible increases in output and created employment opportunities," she said.
Food security depends on more than agricultural production. Keeping food affordable and ensuring a stable supply of fertilizers and other agricultural inputs are also essential, particularly amid economic and geopolitical uncertainties.
In an interview with Xinhua, FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero said rising prices, rather than immediate food shortages, posed the biggest risk to global food security at present.
Torero noted that China had been preparing for natural and geopolitical risks by diversifying imports, keeping its market open and improving stock management.
China's urea exports were also helping bring down prices, he said, urging major producers and importers not to distort markets or restrict exports of agricultural inputs. ■
