My Word: When Europe fiddles and burns - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:33:33 UTC
21:33:33 KST

It was a searing image. The sight of the historic city hall in Limoges, France, going up in flames, and the spire collapsing into the blazing building was haunting.
Two different news clips captured two sides of the story: In one, the crowd of onlookers could be heard cheering as the tower fell; in the other, someone called out in a shocked voice: “It’s fallen!” I wondered whether he was referring just to the spire or to French civilization in general.
According to Smithsonian Magazine, the city hall first opened its doors on Bastille Day in 1883, and “has been celebrated as an architectural wonder. Well-known for its tall spire and ornate metal belfry, the 143-year-old building gained historic monument status in 1975 as a prime example of late 19th-century French architecture and civic pride.”
There’s something sadly symbolic in the beautiful building that opened on the French National Day all those years ago being burned down in the 2026 French riots. Beautiful architecture and civic pride are being willfully destroyed.
For the masked assailants, arsonists, and looters rampaging throughout France – and elsewhere in Europe – this is a modern version of Bastille Day. The mobs are ruling through fear and violence.
Whatever initially triggered the riots – ostensibly highschoolers complaining about their conditions – the flames are being fanned from other directions. This is not about the cost of living, the price of fuel, or crowded classrooms.
News footage showed shocked storekeepers along the iconic Champs-Élysées helplessly looking on as their stores were looted and trashed. Not only were their livelihoods being stolen, but their very way of life.
It’s not by chance that symbols of the government, and of France itself, were attacked. The Statue of the Republic was defaced in Paris; the marble bust of Marianne was damaged in an attack in the historic Marseilles City Hall building; and the tourist office in Lyon, housed in a 19th-century architectural gem, was also destroyed – not that the city can expect an influx of tourists any time soon.
France has seen demonstrations before, even violent ones, but “vive la difference” – these were not French students holding philosophical discussions as they marched in May 1968; nor were they “the Yellow Vests,” protesting fuel prices in the mass rallies that petered out with COVID 19 restrictions; and today’s rioters are not the workers who took to the streets three years ago to protest the planned rise of the retirement age.
The Yellow Vests have made a comeback, but these riots are not quintessentially French. Thanks to immigrants and illegal migrants, and their children and grandchildren, foreign flags of former colonies like Morocco and Algeria rival the French tricolor, and Palestinian flags and keffiyehs are prevalent.
I couldn’t help but note the guest appearance last week by keffiyeh-clad, omni-activist Greta Thunberg. She is now absorbed by the global political climate rather than the world’s weather.
More than ever, when protesters chant, “From the river to the sea,” the question is which river and sea they are referring to. Anarchists and jihadists are agents of chaos and destruction – they create a lethal combination.
In some French cities, the lingua franca of the rioters was Arabic. There’s a word for it: “Intifada.” The Intifada has been globalized, and the results can be seen on the streets of France, where hundreds of protesters and police officers have been injured, and damage could reach a billion euros.
The current conflagration in France is not (yet) specifically an attack on Jews, but the writing was spray-painted on the wall years ago, along with the slogan “Free Palestine.”
When French President Emmanuel Macron last year declared his unconditional recognition of a State of Palestine, he did not strengthen France and French values; he rewarded terrorism and violence. No wonder there are jokes and memes about first implementing a “Two-state solution” in France.
Newsweek and other media noted the appearance of protest videos featuring the song “MRH” by rapper BORO700, which refers to jihadist Mohamed Merah, who murdered 30-year-old teacher Rabbi Jonathan Sandler and his two young sons along with eight-year-old Myriam Monsonego at a Jewish school in Toulouse in 2012, as well as killing French soldiers in other attacks.
The lyrics also praise a perpetrator of the November 2015 jihadist assault in Paris, in which 130 people were murdered, including those at a concert at the Bataclan hall, at a football stadium, and at cafés and bars. The victims were not chosen specifically, but the targets were carefully selected to include all that the young, carefree, French way of life represents.
What's causing the French riots?
As Abe Greenwald put it in Commentary, trying to explain “the real cause” of the riots in France is “kind of like trying to determine the official cause of death in someone who suffered from multiple fatal conditions at the end of his life. That someone is Europe, and the conditions are progressive, in more than one sense of the word.
“There are the real crises: welfare-state failure, education collapse, the disappearance of community, an unsustainable old-age dependency ratio, and unassimilated immigration. Then there are the isms, the activist theologies ensuring that solutions remain out of reach: socialism, anarchism, Islamism, Palestinianism, and antisemitism…
“This indecipherable convergence of radical pursuits is now everywhere in the West, and it’s been with us for a while…
“In the years since 2011, the storm has been fueled by Black Lives Matter, Antifa, gender radicalism, anti-Israel mania, and jihad fandom… The riots in France will add something new, too.”
Macron had his “let them eat cake” moment last week, attending a Celine Dion concert with his wife Brigitte as the riots worsened. Perhaps it was more like Nero fiddling as Rome burned. The French president is quacking like the lame duck he is ahead of the scheduled April 2027 elections.
Both far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon and far-Right front-runner Marine Le Pen are hoping to gain from the current protests. Neither bodes well for the Jewish community.
Marseilles-born rector of Bar-Ilan University Prof. Cyrille Cohen, speaking on Reshet Bet’s “International Hour” radio show, pointed out that polarization is not a byproduct of the riots but an aim.
Whether the Right or the Left wins, there is likely to be a wave of aliyah. Bar-Ilan, like other Israeli universities, is already absorbing more French-speaking students, he noted. Cohen quipped about a French cartoon ahead of the presidential elections showing Jews “undecided how to vote: whether to choose Jerusalem or Netanya.”
Those Israelis threatening to leave the country if next week’s general election doesn’t bring about their desired results, should keep in mind that there is no guarantee of a safe haven and a warm welcome for Jews anywhere in the global village, no matter which camp they belong to.
Israelis also need to be aware that outside forces – including Iran, Russia, Turkey, and Qatar – are happy to foster Israeli divisions and foment unrest as a way of weakening the Jewish state.
The attacks on Israel have long morphed into an assault on Judeo-Christian values. Ahead of November 11, the British Commonwealth’s Remembrance Day for its war dead, it is customary to wear poppy pins. Indeed, November 11 is also known as Poppy Day.
This year, the Palestinians and their supporters have hijacked that too, selling a poppy badge in Palestinian colors while claiming the poppy-anemone is the Palestinian national flower. It’s not; it’s Israel’s national flower, and the red anemones that carpet the Negev in the spring have come in particular to symbolize the 1,200 slaughtered in the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led invasion and mega-atrocity.
Europe is discovering that the nightmare wasn’t a bad dream but reality of its own making. It needs to wake up and smell the burning buildings. Violent riots are not demonstrations of free speech and democracy. This is war. But the world has yet to internationalize the message of the French maxim, “En la guerre comme en la guerre.”

IDF, Defense Ministry drafting resolution to protect reservists and families' benefits through 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:33:10 UTC
21:33:10 KST

The IDF and Defense Ministry are drafting a government resolution to protect the benefits and entitlements of reservists and their families whose service spans 2026 and 2027, following a Walla investigation that exposed gaps in eligibility, Walla learned on Thursday.
Alongside the government resolution, the IDF and Defense Ministry are advancing legislation in the Knesset, which they hope to expedite after the elections, during the Knesset's first session.
The move follows Walla's revelation that reservists could lose benefits and entitlements despite serving for extended periods. Because their reserve duty is divided between two calendar years, some soldiers fail to meet the minimum number of service days required to qualify for grants and benefits in either year.
As a result, a reservist serving nearly 100 consecutive days could fail to meet the eligibility requirements, despite having completed a substantial period of service.
The IDF and Defense Ministry are pursuing two parallel approaches: drafting a government resolution to regulate the calculation of reserve duty days and eligibility for benefits, while also advancing legislation in the Knesset.
While the legislative process is expected to take longer, the government resolution is intended to allow eligibility issues to be resolved sooner, subject to government approval.
Despite these efforts, the wives of reservists have criticized the proposed timetable. They argue that there is no justification for forcing families to wait until the legislative process is completed while soldiers continue accumulating reserve duty days and their families contend with the financial and personal consequences of prolonged service.
They are demanding that the IDF and Defense Ministry bridge the eligibility gaps during the interim period, providing assistance similar to that available to families of reservists who accumulate a large number of service days within a single calendar year.
Tank battalion reservists face loss of benefits
At the center of the controversy are soldiers from Battalion 363 of an armored brigade, some of whom have been called up for their fifth or sixth round of reserve duty since the start of the war.
As Walla previously reported, the soldiers received orders for 99 days of reserve duty beginning November 22, 2026, with 40 days falling in 2026 and another 59 days in 2027.
The division between the two years could affect their eligibility for various benefits, including reimbursements for mental health treatment, grants related to extending maternity leave, student grants, and vacation vouchers.
Some benefits require 45 to 50 days of reserve duty per year, while others require 60 days or more.
In response, the soldiers' wives sent a letter to IDF Personnel Directorate head Maj.-Gen. Dado Bar Kalifa and Chief Reserve Officer Brig.-Gen. Benny Ben Ari, demanding a solution to prevent their families from losing their entitlements.
"It is unacceptable that families who continue to shoulder the burden time and again should be harmed because of bureaucracy and dates over which they have no control," the women wrote.
They also emphasized that the benefits were not luxuries but assistance intended to help families cope with the price they pay for prolonged reserve duty.
IDF promises eligibility will not be affected
In response to an inquiry from Walla, the IDF Spokesperson's Unit said the issue was known and being addressed, and that reservists' eligibility for benefits would not be harmed because their service was divided between calendar years.
The IDF said the military and Defense Ministry were finalizing a draft government resolution concerning benefits for reservists.
Once the process is completed, the resolution will be submitted for government approval, after which the IDF will work to implement the entitlements in accordance with the approved framework.
Regarding battalions whose reserve duty spans two calendar years, particularly Battalion 363, the IDF clarified that service days completed in 2026 and those scheduled for 2027 would be taken into account under the framework to be established.
For a battalion that accumulated 40 days of reserve duty in 2026 and continues serving in 2027, service days will be calculated across both years, allowing eligibility for benefits in 2027 to be assessed based on the total number of service days and the provisions ultimately approved.
The IDF also clarified that reservists who have already exercised their eligibility for benefits based on service in 2026 and perform additional reserve duty in 2027 will remain eligible for benefits under the conditions to be established.
The proposed framework also addresses eligibility for emotional support and treatment when reserve duty is calculated across calendar years.
The IDF is preparing to advance the government resolution to allow reservists to receive their benefits as soon as possible.
At the same time, a dedicated briefing will be held for commanders and relevant personnel. The briefing will outline the assistance currently available, clarify the eligibility mechanism, and provide answers to reservists' questions.
Despite the IDF's commitment that reservists' rights will not be affected, the government resolution has yet to be approved, and the legislative process remains ahead.
Reservists' wives are demanding an interim solution to ensure that their families are not left without the benefits and assistance to which they are entitled.
Wives say no solution has been provided for 2026
The wives of reservists serving in Battalion 363 responded to the IDF Spokesperson's Unit's statement, arguing that despite the impression that a solution had been found, they had yet to receive an answer concerning their entitlements for 2026.
According to the women, the battalion is preparing for its sixth round of reserve duty after hundreds of days of service, during which their husbands are expected to be away from home for 99 consecutive days.
The women described the difficulties of raising children, working, and managing their households alone.
"We are not looking for special treatment, but are asking to receive support and assistance from the IDF and the state in dealing with our situation," they said.
According to the women, they even requested that the call-up be brought forward by five days to preserve their entitlements.
They are demanding a clear commitment that no benefits or rights belonging to reservists and their families will be affected in either 2026 or 2027.

France in flames: As Paris lectures Israel, riots leave its Jews fearing for their safety - opinion

France likes to speak in the name of the human conscience. It lectures other countries, hands out moral grades, and proudly invokes its national promise of liberty, equality, and fraternity.
But when its streets are burning, stores are being looted, and Jews fear for their safety, the disgraceful gap between France’s international posture and its domestic reality is exposed. A world power that seeks to teach others how to manage conflicts is struggling to protect its citizens’ storefronts.
This is more than a governance crisis. It is an indictment of French President Emmanuel Macron and a leadership that has replaced responsibility with empty rhetoric.
The student protests and anger over the cost of living may have originated in genuine hardship. Precisely for that reason, allowing them to become a pathway to arson and looting is a betrayal of the public that came to protest.
No shortage of classrooms justifies burning businesses, and no electricity bill justifies attacking police officers. Anyone who wraps criminality in the flag of social justice is not a revolutionary. He is granting legitimacy to lawlessness.
A government that cannot protect both the right to protest and the victims of violence has failed in its most basic duty.
Amid the chaos, the question arises once again: Why are Jews expected to pay the price?
Rioters vandalized a synagogue in Paris’ 19th arrondissement. The Torah ark was forced open, and religious items were thrown to the floor. There is no moral path leading from student hardship to attacks on Jews. When such a path emerges, protest has become a refuge for hatred and antisemitism.
There is no reason to condemn all the protesters. But the Palestinian flags and chants of “Free Palestine” provide ample evidence of what parts of the demonstration became. Once again, French Jews are expected to answer for the actions of the IDF and the Israeli government.
The citizenship of French Jews has been subjected to racist tests before, during the infamous Vichy regime. Nor should anyone forget the Dreyfus affair.
The figures on antisemitism demolish the excuses offered by the French leadership. France recorded 1,320 antisemitic acts in 2025. The synagogue in La Grande Motte was attacked, and a police officer was injured in an explosion.
These are not isolated incidents. They constitute a reality demanding national introspection. When the state must place security around Jewish institutions, it should begin examining its own failures. Jews do not need another emotional speech after the next attack.
Evasion is not tolerance when confronting Islamism. According to a survey conducted in 2025, 44% of Muslim respondents said they placed the rules of their religion above French law, while some expressed a preference for Sharia law.
A country cannot accept a situation in which its laws become recommendations and a minority seeks to dictate the legal rules. There must be no street where the law retreats in the face of threats or where police officers fear to enter certain areas. A Paris whose streets are in flames is the victim of state failure.
In France, as in Britain, politicians fear losing the Muslim electorate. When politicians exchange principles for electoral calculations, and when a leader softens his opposition to extremism for fear of losing support, he also abandons moderate Muslims.
A leadership that purchases temporary calm through moral ambiguity is selling its country’s future.
Macron’s presidency will be remembered with disgrace. The riots, the burning of stores, and the resurgence of antisemitism are the consequences of his failed leadership and that of the government he heads.
The importance of the presidency
Macron has forgotten that the presidency is more than a title, a palace and a flag. The images coming from France are a political humiliation for the president and the French leadership.
Anyone seeking to embody European leadership must explain why citizens in his own country are forced to pray that the next protest will pass over their businesses.
Israel remembers French moralizing all too well. On the eve of the Six Day War, France imposed an arms embargo and withheld Mirage aircraft ordered by Israel. Fifty Mirage 5 jets ordered in 1966 were never delivered under the agreement and instead entered French service.
From an Israeli perspective, this was a betrayal of trust by a major supplier at a moment of danger. Behind the lofty language of balance and responsibility stood a decision demonstrating how friendship can become conditional on diplomatic convenience.
France does not enter this debate with clean hands.
In Algeria, France operated a system that enabled torture and disappearances, as Macron himself acknowledged in the case of Maurice Audin. In Paris in October 1961, police killed dozens of Algerian demonstrators, including victims who were thrown into the Seine and drowned.
The colonial stain and hypocrisy did not end in Algeria. In Madagascar, France brutally suppressed the 1947 uprising, killing thousands. President Francois Hollande later acknowledged the brutal repression and its victims.
Behind the slogan of a civilizing mission stood a reality in which demands for independence were answered with military force. The liberty France presented as a universal value ended when people under French rule sought to exercise it themselves.
It is difficult to imagine a sharper contradiction between declaration and action: liberty for the ruling nation and subjugation for the people it ruled.
The depth of that betrayal was also exposed in Senegal. In December 1944, French forces opened fire on African soldiers at the Thiaroye military camp after those men had served France and demanded the pay owed to them.
Men who had risked their lives for France discovered that their service did not guarantee equal treatment. Macron recognized the incident as a massacre in 2024, 80 years after it occurred.
That recognition was important, but the delay remains painful. It took decades to call the killing by its proper name. This was not only colonial brutality. It was also state-sanctioned ingratitude.
The philosopher and author Maarten Boudry published a powerful monologue on X/Twitter about the riots in Europe:
“Before long, we will all know what it feels like to be Jewish. In France, they already know. This will be the punishment we deserve for abandoning the Jews, ignoring their warnings, turning against them, and even marching alongside their oppressors.
“For three years, you useful idiots marched with Palestinian flags, wore keffiyehs, screamed ‘From the river to the sea,’ and recognized a fictitious Palestinian state as a reward for the Hamas massacre of Oct. 7. You boycotted the world’s only Jewish state, defamed the Jewish people’s right to self-determination, and spread the blood libel of ‘genocide in Gaza.’
“Did you think that if you fed the crocodile enough Jewish flesh, it would eventually be satisfied? All you did was strengthen the monster and further stimulate its appetite.
“The Palestinian flag has become a flag of victory, proudly raised among the ruins of historic buildings that were looted and vandalized. It is a symbol of hatred toward our culture and everything it represents. It never ends with the Jews.”
France is paying, and will continue to pay, the price of its arrogance. Human rights were presented as a noble promise but were repeatedly subordinated to the interests of those in power.
There is now a simple demand of France’s leaders. Before presenting yourselves as judges of the world, acknowledge your own responsibility. Open the archives and give the victims a place more dignified than a footnote in a ceremonial speech.
Even if France eventually withdraws its support for the forces of evil represented by Palestinian terrorists who murdered, raped, mutilated, and abducted approximately 1,500 innocent Israeli and foreign civilians, history will not forget.

Japanese writer Ryu Murakami dies at 74
Japanese writer Ryu Murakami died on October 17, 2026, at the age of 74, according to a notice released by GENTOSHA publishing house on October 23, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Murakami made his literary debut in 1976 with Almost Transparent Blue, which won the Gunzo Prize for New Writers and the prestigious Akutagawa Prize. The novel became a bestseller, selling approximately 3.5 million copies.
His other notable works include Coin Locker Babies, In the Miso Soup and Kyoko. His writing explored social issues and the darker aspects of contemporary society, earning recognition in Japan and internationally.

China earmarks 80 mln yuan for Xizang quake relief, recovery efforts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:28:43 CST
21:28:43 KST

A villager receives a folding bed at a temporary resettlement site of an earthquake-hit village in Maru Township of Baqen County, Nagqu City, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Oct. 23, 2026. China has allocated 50 million yuan (about 7.5 million U.S. dollars) in emergency disaster relief funds and earmarked another 30 million yuan for recovery efforts following a 7.0-magnitude earthquake in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. The earthquake struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, leaving 16 people dead and 54 injured. (Xinhua/Tenzin Nyida)
BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China has allocated 50 million yuan (about 7.5 million U.S. dollars) in emergency disaster relief funds and earmarked another 30 million yuan for recovery efforts following a 7.0-magnitude earthquake in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region.
The earthquake struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, leaving 16 people dead and 54 injured.
The Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Emergency Management jointly allocated 50 million yuan to support rescue operations and assistance to affected residents, while the National Development and Reform Commission earmarked the additional 30 million yuan from the central budget to help restore damaged infrastructure and public service facilities.
The country has upgraded its national earthquake emergency response from Level IV to Level III.
On Friday afternoon, the emergency management ministry, in a separate statement, also announced an upgrade of the national natural disaster relief response to Level III, saying that additional joint working groups were dispatched to disaster areas to guide relief efforts.
It said that on top of the 5,000 relief items previously allocated by the central government, an additional 5,000 central relief items, including tents, coats and folding beds were allocated.
By coordinating efforts with other relief agencies and companies, the ministry said it has also promptly allocated 43,000 other relief items, including mobile toilets, heating stoves, food and fuel, to ensure that affected people are properly resettled.
China's national comprehensive fire and rescue force has dispatched a total of 350 rescuers and 83 vehicles for rescue operations. The emergency management ministry has guided Xizang's emergency management department in arranging for Wing Loong drone deployment to the quake-hit area for disaster reconnaissance.
As of 6:30 a.m. on Friday, 120 rescuers and 27 vehicles had arrived in the quake-hit area, while the remaining 230 rescuers and 56 vehicles from the Xizang fire and rescue corps were en route as reinforcements, having all entered Nagqu's administrative area.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said it has worked swiftly to organize local telecom operators to carry out emergency repair and restoration work on affected communications facilities.
As of 10:30 a.m. Friday, all of the 628 base stations that went out of service due to the quake in the city of Nagqu have been restored, it said. "At present, emergency command communications at all levels of government are unimpeded, and public communications services are functioning normally."
Earlier, as of 4:30 a.m. on Friday, authorities had mobilized relief supplies at the central, regional, municipal and county levels, and delivered them in batches to the affected area.
These supplies included 1,000 prefabricated housing units, 3,239 tents, 2,821 folding beds and 4,280 quilts, among other essentials. ■

ALMATY, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Monetary Policy Committee of the National Bank of Kazakhstan on Friday lowered the base rate to 15.75 percent per annum, the central bank said in a press release.
Annual inflation in Kazakhstan has declined for 12 consecutive months, reaching 9.3 percent in September. Monthly inflation stood at 0.6 percent, unchanged from August, while seasonally adjusted monthly inflation eased to 0.7 percent from 0.9 percent in the previous month, according to the national bank.
The bank aims to bring inflation back to its 5 percent target in 2028, the statement said.
Kazakhstan's gross domestic product grew by 4.2 percent year on year in January-September 2026, driven by non-resource sectors, primarily construction, manufacturing and transport. Fixed capital investment rose by 7 percent, while investment in the non-resource sector, excluding budget funds, increased by 25 percent, it said. ■

Greek parliament approves social media ban for under-15s from January
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:28:36 CST
21:28:36 KST

ATHENS, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Greek parliament has approved legislation banning children under 15 from accessing social media from Jan. 1, 2027, Greek media reported Friday.
The legislation requires social media platforms to implement age-verification measures to ensure compliance. Companies that fail to meet the requirements could face fines of up to 6 percent of their global annual turnover.
Addressing parliament ahead of the vote on Thursday evening, Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence Minister Dimitris Papastergiou described the measure as a necessary step that is compatible with the European Union's (EU) existing regulatory framework.
"It would have been very easy to do absolutely nothing today and wait for the perfect European law. But the challenge is here. Children are sinking into the internet every day, and I believe a responsible government must do what it is obliged to do," he said.
Minister of State Akis Skertsos said technology should be regulated in ways that give children greater freedom to grow up safely.
Meanwhile, Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis described digital addiction as a public health challenge. Excessive use of social media can negatively affect children's sleep, concentration, social relationships and psychological development, he said.
The legislation forms part of broader government efforts to protect children from harmful online content, cyberbullying and platform features that encourage excessive use.
Greece aims to become the first EU member state to introduce such a ban, the government has said.
The French parliament passed legislation on July 21 aimed at protecting minors from the risks associated with social media use. However, the French Constitutional Council ruled on Aug. 14 that the key provision banning under-15s from accessing social media was unconstitutional. ■

IDF names two soldiers killed in deadly shooting attack near Hebron
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:28:36 UTC
21:28:36 KST

The IDF cleared for publication the names of two soldiers killed in the shooting attack near Hebron: Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman, 23, from Ashkelon, a squad commander in the Ari Battalion (775) of the Search and Rescue Brigade, and Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem, 20, from Hod Hasharon, a combat soldier in the same battalion. Both were killed in the attack at Yehuda Junction.
The IDF said three other people wounded in the attack were also soldiers and that their injuries were classified as minor. The families of the casualties have been notified.
David Roytman, Ron's brother, said: "He was a star. Everyone loved him wherever he went. People always say things like that about someone who has fallen, but he was always number one. He fought to become a combat soldier. He wasn't even supposed to enlist in a combat role. He spent a year volunteering with at-risk youth and was injured while playing soccer. They told him there was no way he could become a combat soldier. He said, 'That's not going to happen.'"
His brother added: "He went through everyone, from junior officers all the way to the chief medical officer, and he managed to become a combat soldier. He was a commander of recruits and went with them to the battalion. He was always dreaming and striving for more. He took every opportunity to serve in the most dangerous areas of Judea and Samaria. That's what he pushed for."
David himself served as a combat soldier in the Combat Engineering Corps, while their older sister served in the Caracal Battalion, a mixed-gender combat unit.
"We're all a family of fighters," David said.
Ron attended the Kadoorie Youth Village boarding school in northern Israel.
"He was someone with a zest for life, someone who loved living. He was my best friend," his brother said.
Staff Sgt. Roytman, 23, will be laid to rest Sunday at 11 a.m. at the military cemetery in Ashkelon.
Hod Hasharon Mayor Amir Kochavi paid tribute to Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem.
"With profound sorrow and heavy hearts, we received the devastating news that Hod Hasharon resident Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem had fallen in battle with terrorists at Yehuda Junction," Kochavi wrote.
"Yuval was the son of Sivan and Amnon, a loving brother to Shira and Itamar, a devoted grandson, cousin and beloved friend. He was born and raised in Hod Hasharon.
"The Hod Hasharon municipality and community bow their heads in grief and share in the profound sorrow of our colleagues Amnon and Sivan, their children Shira and Itamar and the entire family."
Two Palestinian terrorists arrived at the scene, got out of a vehicle and opened fire. The gunbattle lasted more than 20 minutes, during which additional forces arrived, including the deputy commander of the Ari Battalion and a company commander from the battalion. The soldiers worked together to flank the terrorists and killed them.
A search of the terrorists' vehicle uncovered a large quantity of ammunition. Authorities believe the attackers had planned a major attack against civilians and intended to reach the main roads before proceeding into Israel's interior.
However, investigators are still examining whether the attackers were part of a cell directed by an outside organization or acted on their own initiative. Because both terrorists were killed, the investigation is continuing in an effort to determine their intended destination.
Magen David Adom paramedics and emergency medical technicians, working alongside an IDF medical team, treated the wounded at the scene before evacuating them to Shaare Zedek and Hadassah Ein Kerem hospitals in Jerusalem.
Ofer Ohana, a medic who arrived Friday morning at the scene of the attack at Yehuda Junction on Route 35, managed to film the exchange of fire while under live fire himself.
"The terrorist keeps shooting. The exchange of fire between the terrorist and our forces is continuing. We can't get the wounded out. There has been active gunfire for more than 20 minutes," he can be heard shouting in the footage.
Meanwhile, a photographer for the French news agency AFP captured footage of the two terrorists reloading their weapons during the exchange of fire and later filmed their bodies lying on the ground after they were killed.
The IDF will examine the AFP photographer's account to determine whether he happened upon the scene by chance or had received advance information about the attack.
AFP categorically denies that the photographer who captured images of the terrorists in the West Bank had any prior knowledge of the attack, insisting that he has not even been questioned by security forces.
Moshe Butavia, Kiryat Arba's security chief, took part in the gunbattle with the terrorists.
"We received a report of a shooting attack targeting a military force on Route 35, with casualties. Security forces from the area rushed to the scene, including me," Butavia told ynet. "The terrorists arrived in a vehicle, stopped at a spot where they couldn't be seen, quickly got out and opened fire."
He added: "In the morning, residents are traveling along the road, including buses taking students to schools in Kiryat Arba. I arrived at the scene about 15 minutes after the incident began. When I got there, I joined the fighting. Two terrorists were firing from an elevated position, and we engaged them for about 20 minutes until a force commanded by the sector's deputy battalion commander killed them."
Describing the scene, Butavia said: "The terrorists arrived in a decommissioned vehicle with yellow Israeli license plates. The soldiers at the scene prevented the attack from spreading to the main road and endangering passing motorists. That prevented a much greater disaster."
Butavia praised the security forces, saying: "The army works hard every night, carrying out numerous operations to maintain residents' security and protect the roads and communities. We must remain vigilant."
IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir praised the soldiers of the Home Front Command's Ari Battalion who killed the two Palestinian terrorists in the shooting attack near Hebron.
"The soldiers' swift actions prevented an even more serious attack and additional casualties among civilians and security forces," Zamir said during a situational assessment at the IDF's Judea Brigade headquarters.
Following the attack, Israeli forces imposed a closure on Hebron and Halhul, prohibiting entry to and exit from both cities.
At the same time, the military implemented a procedure known as "Gray Bolt" throughout Central Command, under which Palestinian vehicles entering main roads are subjected to security checks. The measures also apply to the Jenin, Nablus and Jericho areas as part of efforts to prevent further attacks.
Security forces began extensive searches, engineering operations and mapping the homes of the attackers, Hamouda al-Jaaba, 27, and Firas al-Jaaba, 27, both from Hebron. The two belonged to the same extended family and lived near each other.
As part of the investigation, authorities are expected to make arrests among people connected to the attackers while examining possible links to other individuals or organizations.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who visited the scene with Defense Minister Israel Katz, said: "We warned several weeks ago about attempts by our enemies to harm us, our civilians and our soldiers ahead of the elections. That is what they tried to do here. IDF soldiers stopped them with their own bodies and were also hit. The soldiers not only stopped the terrorists but also charged at them heroically and killed them."
Netanyahu added: "First, we will act to demolish this place and completely transform it. But we will also do something that has not been done until now. We are going to implement the successful, aggressive model we used in the refugee camps, which are effectively terrorist strongholds.
"That is exactly what we will do here, in a neighborhood of Hebron from which the terrorists came. We will evacuate the residents, go house to house, remove the weapons and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure."
The Home Front Command's Ari Battalion was established over the past year in response to the need to increase the number of combat troops deployed across various operational sectors, while also providing additional forces for missions on the home front. It is the fifth battalion in the IDF's Search and Rescue Brigade.
Shortly after the battalion's first company completed its operational training, the unit was placed on rescue alert as part of Operation Roaring Lion to provide support in northern Israel.
Once its formation was complete, the battalion joined the brigade's other battalions conducting routine operations in the IDF's Judea and Samaria Division.
Over the past week, the battalion's soldiers began their first operational deployment after completing several months of initial training, including specialized instruction for the unit's combat soldiers.
The battalion commander, Lt. Col. L., said Friday morning: "The battalion's soldiers acted professionally and were deployed effectively throughout the area as part of the effort to protect the residents of the State of Israel."
He added: "Already during their first operational deployment, the battalion's soldiers demonstrated the importance of their mission and their operational readiness. The soldiers maintained a high level of alertness and operational readiness, engaged the enemy and acted swiftly and decisively to neutralize the threat. They prevented harm to civilians, protected the population and successfully completed their mission.
"We will continue to operate responsibly and remain vigilant as part of our mission to defend Israel's residents."

CANBERRA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Australia's health care and social assistance sector has become the country's largest industry in current-price terms, generating 265.2 billion Australian dollars (about 172 billion U.S. dollars) in gross value added in 2025-26, new data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed on Friday.
The sector accounted for 9.6 percent of Australia's total economic activity and was also the country's largest employer, with 2.58 million jobs, or 15.8 percent of total employment.
The ABS said the latest estimates incorporated more detailed industry surveys and administrative data, allowing it to better measure market-based services such as private health care, aged care and disability services.
The revised methodology lifted the sector's estimated economic value by 13.9 billion Australian dollars for 2023-24 compared with previous estimates.
In real terms, the sector has more than tripled in size over the past three decades. ■

China strengthens protection for growing snow leopard population
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:27:46 CST
21:27:46 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's snow leopard population has doubled to about 5,000 from around 2,500 in 2013, reflecting progress in protecting the species and its habitat.
The latest figures were released by the National Forestry and Grassland Administration on Friday on the occasion of the International Day of the Snow Leopard which falls on Oct. 23.
Snow leopards typically inhabit rugged terrain at elevations of 3,000 to 5,000 meters and serve as an important indicator of the health of high-altitude mountain ecosystems. The species is classified as "vulnerable" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List of Threatened Species and receives the highest level of wildlife protection in China.
China has the world's largest snow leopard population and protects more than 60 percent of the species' global habitat, according to the administration. Its habitat covers about 2.08 million square kilometers across eight provincial-level regions.
China has taken a systematic approach to snow leopard conservation since 2013. Its protection network includes two national parks and 78 other important protected areas in key snow leopard habitats. More than 800,000 square kilometers of habitat are under strict protection, while nearly 40 percent of the species' potential habitat is under standardized management.
The country is also using technologies such as infrared cameras and DNA analysis of fecal samples to monitor snow leopard populations, track their movements and study their breeding activity.
Sustained conservation efforts have improved snow leopard habitat quality and ecosystem integrity, alongside growth in the population and its reproductive vitality, the administration said.
In April, infrared cameras in the Helan Mountains in northwest China captured a reintroduced female snow leopard with her cub, marking the first time a snow leopard reintroduction project worldwide has resulted in cubs being born and successfully raised in the wild.
Native to the Helan Mountains, snow leopards disappeared from the area in the 1950s due to habitat destruction and human disturbance. To restore the population, eight snow leopards have been introduced to the mountains so far. Several snow leopards, including those arriving naturally, have since established territories and hunt independently.
Signs of the species' presence are also emerging elsewhere. In Muli County of Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Sichuan Province, footage recorded this year confirmed the first sighting of a snow leopard in the prefecture, extending the known southeastern edge of the species' range, the administration said.
Looking ahead, China will focus on improving connectivity between habitats, protecting genetic diversity and refining measures to prevent and address human-wildlife conflict to sustain snow leopard population recovery, the administration said. ■

Kindergarten shelters reserved exclusively for education participants – Cabinet
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:25:49 EEST
21:25:49 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers has regulated the use of civil protection shelters at kindergartens and general secondary education institutions by people other than participants in the educational process.
Under Resolution No. 1288 of October 15, the government amended the procedure for establishing and maintaining the civil protection shelter fund.
In particular, in accordance with the law on preschool education, shelters at preschool institutions are to be used exclusively to protect participants in the educational process.
School shelters are also available exclusively to participants in the educational process while in-person classes are being held, the resolution says.
At the same time, school shelters may be used to accommodate both participants in the educational process and other members of the public only by decision of local executive authorities or local self-government bodies, and in accordance with procedures established by the institution's owner or operator.
If a decision is made to use a school shelter for both students and other members of the public, the operator must ensure that teachers, a psychologist if available, and police or security personnel if available remain with the children throughout the shelter period. It must also separate the areas occupied by students and other people where possible, minimize or eliminate overlapping routes to and from the shelter, provide separate functioning toilets, and make available a separate room or designated area for children with special educational needs to help regulate their emotional state and provide psychological support, as well as psychological, pedagogical and developmental services. The operator must also ensure the safety of all participants in the educational process.

Divers exploring oldest warship off Sweden find "new clues"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:23:32 UTC
21:23:32 KST

Divers exploring oldest warship found off Sweden find "new clues"
Bubbles rise through the murky green water as divers tenderly explore a rare 15th-century shipwreck off Stockholm's coast, believed to be the oldest warship found off Sweden.
"It's a very big ship, it was around 40-45 meters when it sailed probably," project leader and marine archaeologist Hakan Altrock from Sweden's Museum of Wrecks said, overseeing the dives down to the skeletal remains of what is known as Vrak 5, or Shipwreck 5, on a cool October day.
Located off Haringe Castle south of Stockholm, the vessel is thought to be the oldest warship found off Sweden or Denmark, which were joined in a union with Norway in the 15th century.
First discovered in the late 1800s, the shipwreck is one of five lying on the seabed in the Landfjarden sound, most of which have been dated to the 1600s and 1700s.
But in February 2025, researchers were able to date Vrak 5 to the 1480s, or possibly even the 1460s.
"It's not possible to say if it is Swedish, it could also be Danish," Altrock said, noting that the timber used to build it comes from the area that is now southeastern Sweden.
"This is the first example of a ship in the Baltic that has been built with the carvel technique... in Scandinavia that we know of," he said.
He was referring to a boat-building technique where hull planks are laid edge-to-edge rather than overlapping, which made it possible to build bigger and sturdier vessels — necessary with the advent of heavy cannons on ships.
Researchers have produced a 3D scan of the wreck, which can be seen here.
"This is the most historically interesting wreck in the area," Altrock said. "Every time we can examine part of it, we have the opportunity to find new clues."
Sunk in battle?
Marine archaeologists excavated the wreck this week in order to better document it, find out more about how it was built, and as part of a special project about food on board.
Archaeologists aim to "search for the ship's kitchen and gain new clues about how the ship was built and sank," the museum said in a statement.
Among other things, they used special pumps to vacuum up sediment and expose parts of the construction.
Divers found bricks that suggested they had found the galley, in addition to parts of the ship's rigging.
Matilda Jarl, a PhD student in marine archaeology also at the site, said the crew would have eaten fish, meat and porridge on board.
"A lot of the food would be boiled. So there would be a lot of pottage, which is basically anything that is cooked in a pot," she said.
"With the food they would also drink beer. The people with a higher status on board would be drinking wine also, but the general crew would be drinking beer instead of water as it kept better," she added.
It is not yet known why the ship sank where it did.
Altrock said rumors from when the wreck was found in the 19th century referred to a fire on board.
"Perhaps it was sunk when they (the Danes) attacked the Haringe Castle behind us in 1501," he said. "That's one theory."
"Maybe we'll find traces of where it burned. We'll see."
Other shipwrecks found in region
Several other wrecks and relics have been found in the region recently.
In April, officials announced that a 16th century shipwreck providing "unique historical and archaeological information" had been discovered off Sweden's southeastern coast. The ship is believed to have been built in the late 1500s, which would make it older than Sweden's iconic 17th century warship "Vasa" on display in Stockholm after being salvaged in the 1960s. The navy vessel HMS Belos found the wreck during a military exercise.
In February, a Swedish Navy shipwreck buried underwater in central Stockholm for 400 years became visible due to unusually low Baltic Sea levels.
In July 2024, a team of divers discovered a massive haul of champagne and wine on a shipwreck on the floor of the Baltic Sea off Sweden. The precious cargo was later declared off limits by the government.
That same year, researchers exploring an ancient shipwreck off the coast of Sweden discovered centuries-old artifacts, including a weapons chest and pieces of armor.

Denmark to buy cheap U.S. cruise missile built in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:22:11 UTC
21:22:11 KST

- Denmark will buy Covenant’s ground-launched Anthem cruise missiles, to be built in Leipzig, Germany, alongside Kongsberg Joint Strike Missiles for its F-35s.
- Germany’s defense ministry is also in talks with Covenant as the Bundeswehr evaluates low-cost cruise missiles for its own long-range strike needs.
Denmark will buy Anthem ground-launched cruise missiles from U.S. defense company Covenant Industries, giving the Danish military its first land-based option for striking targets deep inside enemy territory, the Danish Ministry of Defense announced on Oct. 22, 2026.
The ministry said the purchase is meant to strengthen Denmark’s national and collective deterrence, describing the new missiles as long-range precision weapons that NATO has asked allies to provide. They use advanced navigation to hit targets accurately over long distances and can both deter an attack and strike back deep inside an enemy’s territory if necessary, and the acquisitions follow a recommendation from Denmark’s chief of defense.
“The acquisitions are a significant step in making Denmark better able to defend itself and carry our share of the burden in NATO, and at the same time we are sending a strong signal that we have the ability to strike back,” said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus, in remarks translated from Danish.
Officials told reporters at the announcement that the contracts have already been signed, but withheld quantities, prices and delivery dates for security reasons. They said one reason for choosing the weapon was that it can be delivered relatively quickly and at a competitive price, and the Anthem missiles for Denmark will be built in Leipzig, Germany, where Covenant is setting up its European production line.
Anthem is a jet-powered cruise missile designed from the start for low cost and mass production. Covenant says it can carry a 200 kg (440-pound) warhead for precision strikes deep in enemy territory, and the missile reportedly has a range of more than 1,000 km (620 miles), with some media reports putting it as high as 1,500 km (930 miles). The company plans to sell it for a six-figure sum, under $1 million per missile, compared with the several million dollars typically charged for comparable cruise missiles.
Anthem first flew in August 2025, and Covenant says it has since been used in more than 200 tests, including several flight tests with U.S. forces in the United States and abroad, although the missile has not yet been used in combat. Choosing it marks a departure for Denmark, which has traditionally bought proven, production-ready systems for its armed forces.
Covenant opened a 10,000-square-meter (108,000-square-foot) plant in Leipzig earlier this month to build missiles for European NATO allies. Production is set to begin in 2027, with the company planning 1,000 missiles in the first year and 5,000 in 2028, and Covenant aims to source more than 95% of the components for its European version from inside Europe, with the Leipzig facility handling assembly and warheads integrated later at customer locations.
Germany is also studying the missile, and the German defense ministry has said it is in talks with Covenant about closing its own long-range strike gap, although no German order has been publicly confirmed. Lt. Gen. Christian Freuding, the head of the German Army, has confirmed that the Bundeswehr wants to buy new low-cost cruise missiles for mass use and is evaluating two systems already on the market, though he did not name them. Anthem has been reported as one of the candidates, alongside the Flamingo cruise missile from Ukrainian company Fire Point, and Covenant has brought in Andreas Marlow, a retired lieutenant general and former deputy commander of the German Army, as an adviser.
Denmark is pairing Anthem with a second, air-launched weapon, the Joint Strike Missile, built by Norway’s Kongsberg with Raytheon. The stealthy JSM fits inside the internal weapons bays of Denmark’s F-35 fighters, weighs 416 kg (917 pounds) with a 120 kg (265-pound) warhead and has a range of more than 350 km (217 miles). It is derived from Kongsberg’s Naval Strike Missile, which Denmark already operates on its frigates and for coastal defense.
Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin responded quickly to the announcement, saying Danish policy is built on confrontation and preparation for a possible conflict with Russia, and calling it a dangerous illusion to think precision strike weapons could pose a military threat to a nuclear power.
Denmark’s military planning has traditionally focused on defending its own territory, and the new missiles give it a way to strike targets in an adversary’s rear areas for the first time. With Covenant’s Leipzig line due to start production in 2027, the first Anthem missiles for Denmark are expected to come from that plant.

Macron, who on Oct. 22 announced that only union demonstrations would be authorised this weekend, was to hold a meeting of his defence council of top ministers and officials and also meet security forces.
He was also set to host for the first time representatives of high school pupils, whose protests over conditions at their schools sparked a movement that has broadened nationwide into a show of anger against the government at the rising cost of living.
The protests have come at a critical moment for France six months ahead of elections to replace Macron, with a new poll underlining far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner and showing her position has been strengthened by the latest events.
Adding to tensions, Le Pen is at the weekend due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orleans, with thousands of supporters expected but local authorities fearing clashes as opponents head to the city.

Demonstrations in Marseille in the south and Lyon in the southeast have been banned at the weekend, while in Paris protesters will only be allowed to march a limited route between Bastille and Nation squares.
Marseille authorities however reversed a decision to halt all public transport in the city on Oct. 24. But in the capital, leading museums including the Louvre will be closed on Oct. 24 while the Art Basel art fair is being cut short.
"In a country governed by the rule of law, the police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder," said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressing alarm over reports of children being severely injured by crowd-control weapons.
The violence has tarnished the image of France ahead of elections that could be a turning point in its modern history, with the government's debt pile also troubling investors.
A new poll by Harris Interactive for M6/RTL made after the violence showed Le Pen soaring ahead on 33-35 percent in the first round of voting for the presidential elections.
It predicted that hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon was on course to face her in the run-off where Le Pen would emerge as an easy winner on some 70 percent of the vote.

Are parents in France and Italy liable for damage caused by student protesters?
Parents in Italy could face financial penalties if their children participate in vandalism or looting during protests.
As high school student protests began in France last month, footage soon spread on social media of angry parents dragging their children away from demonstrations.

Here’s what we know.
What are the protests in France and Italy about?
In late September, high school students in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis began protesting about the state of their school buildings and teacher shortages. They were particularly angry about the proposed government budget which includes millions of euros in cuts to public spending.
Students in Paris, and later in other French cities, erected barricades around their schools and caused hundreds of closures during the first week of October.
Later, the protests spread nationwide as public sector workers joined demonstrations to oppose planned pay freezes. Now the protests have widened again, with those angry about the rising cost of living, petrol shortages and fuel prices joining demonstrations which have frequently descended into rioting, looting and arson.
French President Emmanuel Macron said last week that “nothing justifies” violence and that local officials could ban certain street gatherings if deemed necessary. French authorities also announced curfews.
But last Saturday, hundreds of thousands of protesters in France, Italy, Spain, Belgium and Portugal took part in largely uncoordinated demonstrations against rising living costs.
Initially peaceful weekend protests in Milan descended into riots, with groups of mainly young people looting shops, smashing windows and clashing with police. Masked protesters threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Riots were also reported in the Italian cities of Bologna and Turin.
Official figures on the expected costs of the damage in both France and Italy have yet to be established.
What has Italy announced?
On Tuesday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government approved a series of measures in response to the unrest, including sending 500 soldiers to Milan until the end of the year and increasing financial liability on parents whose children were involved in vandalism and looting.
Under new rules, anyone taking part in a group of at least five people and endangering public safety during protests faces up to five years in prison and a maximum fine of 20,000 euros ($22,460).
Protesters aged 14 to 18 can now be subject to administrative detention, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence that they pose a danger, extending powers that previously applied only to adults.
In part of the decree, which includes the phrase “You break it, you buy it”, Italy also strengthened the law holding parents responsible for criminal damage by their children.
Article 2048 of the civil code already states that parents and guardians are liable for damages caused by the “unlawful act of unemancipated minor children or persons subject to guardianship who live with them. The same provision applies to the foster parent”.
In Italy, authorities may enforce these laws through asset and wage attachments.
The new measure permits the state to directly fine parents or claim damages for any resulting loss against parents’ property or by deducting public subsidies the family receives.
What is the situation in France?
Under article 1242 of the French Civil Code, parents who live with their children and exercise parental authority also have a civil liability for damage that their children cause.
“Parents, in their capacity as holders of parental authority, are by right jointly and severally liable for damage caused by their minor children, except when the latter have been entrusted to a third party by an administrative or judicial decision,” the law states.
Last year, a new law amended article 1242 to strengthen parents’ role during youth justice proceedings. It removed the cohabitation requirement for parents for civil liability to apply.
In France, compensation from parents for damage caused by children can be enforced through civil proceedings, and can include the seizure of assets if not covered by civil liability insurance, which is often tied to housing insurance, subject to the terms of the policy agreement.
On Friday, French radio station RFI reported that a new bill known as “rioters pay” is now also being proposed by the government in response to the violent protests.
The government is scheduled to debate the draft bill on October 27.
If the law is passed, those found responsible for vandalism could be required to pay up to 10,000 euros ($11,200) in compensation. In the case of criminal damage by minors, parents could be held responsible.
A provision to the bill could also introduce collective civil liability, potentially requiring someone in a group responsible for damage to pay, even if they did not cause it themselves, on the same financial terms as those who caused the damage, RFI reported.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu described the legislation as “absolutely essential” to ensure taxpayers do not pay for damage caused by protests.
Where else does this happen?
Several other countries also hold parents financially liable for damages their children cause.
For example, in Sweden, parents or legal guardians may be held financially liable, subject to statutory conditions and limits, for certain injuries or property damage caused by a child who commits a crime.
In the United States, subject to state-specific conditions and limits, laws addressing parental responsibility specify that if a minor intentionally destroys public property, businesses, or vehicles, victims or local government can sue the parents in civil court.

Ukraine to team up with Finnish firms as Starshield problems, started amid Trump-Zelenskyy jibes, continue.
Ukraine has announced it plans to build an independent satellite communications system, as it reported that issues affecting the United States-operated Starshield system continue.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Friday that his country has agreed to partner with Finnish firms to develop the system. The same day, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence complained of lingering issues with Starshield military services.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that tech mogul Elon Musk had restored access to the satellite internet service, which plays a key role in Kyiv’s war effort and air defences.
Ukraine has been exploring its military defence options as Russian attacks have intensified in recent months, and questions over the Trump administration’s support have risen.
Zelenskyy reported on Friday that he had agreed with Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo that “[Ukraine] will use more of Finland’s satellite capabilities. This is important for our defence, for Ukraine’s resilience.
“We agreed on this with Nokia and ICEYE. Thank you for the willingness to support our logistics and energy sector – these are key targets for Russia right now,” Zelenskyy added.
The Finnish companies signed a letter of intent with the Ukrainian Defence Ministry during Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s visit to Kyiv on Thursday, the DPA news agency reported.
ICEYE Chief Executive Officer Rafal Modrzewski said in a statement that Ukraine needed a secure satellite communications system that it controls. The company said its satellites provide reconnaissance data regardless of weather or time of day.
On October 13, Ukrainian officials announced that sudden restrictions on Starlink services had left the country’s military scrambling. Although the system came back online, connectivity has reportedly remained spotty.
Questions have persisted about where the decision to restrict access came from, with Musk and Trump administration officials trading blame. The restrictions came amid a deepening feud between Trump and Zelenskyy, with Trump instead exploring talks with Putin.
A source in the Ukrainian Defence Ministry told reporters on Friday that “instances of signal loss are still being observed” regarding Starshield, the military arm of Musk’s Starlink system.
The role of the system has become increasingly central to Ukraine’s defence against the Russian invasion.
The four-and-a-half-year war has become dominated by drone warfare. Ukraine recently launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of Kyiv’s largest aerial attacks in the war, while Starshield is also key to defences as Russia rains bombs on Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine daily.

Felix Savon: From Olympic boxing legend to convicted sex offender facing poverty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:04:44 UTC
21:04:44 KST

Felix Savon, a heavyweight boxer who won three Olympic gold medals and six consecutive world amateur championships, is one of the greatest amateur boxers in history. He brought tremendous honor to his native Cuba, a country whose leaders have always been eager to use sports to showcase the strength of the regime and the nation.
Savon was a loyal citizen, fiercely devoted to his homeland and communist ideology. He received dozens of offers to defect, turn professional and face opponents such as Mike Tyson and Evander Holyfield. He turned them all down. No one could buy him, not even for tens of millions of dollars. According to several reports, legendary boxing promoter Don King offered Savon an eight-figure sum to turn professional, but Savon remained loyal to Fidel Castro.
But in recent months, reports have mounted about Savon's deteriorating health and personal hygiene. He has appeared abandoned, dirty and unkempt. Last week, a 17-second video surfaced online showing a man said to be Savon rummaging through garbage bins. The man filming recognized him and asked what he was doing. Savon replied that he was looking for food. It should be noted, however, that despite the video's millions of views, the man's identity has not been conclusively verified, nor is there clear documentation of when the footage was recorded.
The images of Savon apparently searching for food in garbage bins sparked outrage among Cubans. Some collected food, clothing and Bibles to provide immediate assistance. Others expressed anger that the Cuban authorities were no longer looking after an athlete who had brought so much honor to the country and resisted the temptation to leave.
Before shedding any tears, however, it is worth remembering who Savon is. In 2018, he was sentenced to 11 years in prison for sexual assaults involving at least one child under the age of 12. He was released on parole in 2024.
When the spotlight fades
Savon, nicknamed "Ninote" ("the big kid") by his fans, celebrated his 59th birthday last month. He is one of only three boxers in history to win three Olympic gold medals, claiming his titles in 1992, 1996 and 2000. The other two are Hungary's Laszlo Papp and fellow Cuban Teofilo Stevenson, whom Savon idolized.
Savon was also a clear contender for gold at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, but Cuba decided to boycott those Games. He finished his career with a record of 362 wins and 21 losses, having managed to avenge his defeats against all but two of the boxers who beat him.
In 2001, the Manic Street Preachers became the first Western rock band to perform in Cuba. With Fidel Castro in the audience, the band dedicated its song "You Love Us" to Savon, who had recently retired from boxing.
Savon is not the only famous Cuban athlete facing severe poverty and hunger. As long as he and other athletes were useful to the government, they received generous stipends and housing. But once they were no longer of use, their financial support dwindled to a pittance — around $25 a month, an amount insufficient to cover even two weeks of living expenses, particularly given U.S. sanctions and the rising cost of living.
Savon holds a university degree awarded to him by the regime, but he cannot even write his own name. The only work he is qualified to do to earn a living is coaching children, an option that is clearly no longer available to him in light of the crimes for which he was convicted. From there, the descent into hunger and destitution is a short one.
It is hardly unusual to find athletes who earned hundreds of millions of dollars only to lose their entire fortunes after retirement. The reasons vary. Athletes financially support their entourages and families, fall prey to bad business deals and fail to hire professionals to guide their financial decisions. They also continue living the same lifestyles they enjoyed at the height of their careers.
That means extravagant spending on homes, cars, restaurants, entertainment and vacations, both for themselves and their entourages. The difference is that millions of dollars are no longer flowing into their bank accounts every month.
Usually, however, the outcome is bankruptcy, financial hardship, the need to find new employment and a major adjustment in lifestyle. The case of a legendary boxer searching for food in the trash is an extreme one.
It is true that Savon never earned millions, but the government took care of him — and also ensured he received a remarkably short period of imprisonment for the crimes he committed. Nevertheless, the video was shocking. And even in this respect, he is not alone.
The video that sparked an outcry:
Unlike athletes such as Michael Oher, Dennis Rodman, Jimmy Butler and even Kurt Warner, who experienced homelessness at one point or another before overcoming the odds to become professional athletes and earn millions, there are plenty of athletes whose lives have followed the opposite trajectory.
Former NBA player Delonte West earned more than $16 million during his career in the league. He was diagnosed with bipolar disorder while still playing professionally and has also said he suffers from clinical depression. He attributed some of his struggles to the pressures of competing in a demanding professional sports league.
After his career ended, West, who had been involved in drug and weapons offenses since his teenage years, was seen on several occasions wandering the streets, dressed like a homeless man. Those painful images of West were also among the reasons the NBA decided to introduce programs and seminars designed to help players dealing with psychological distress.
Boxers Mike Tyson and Iran Barkley also lost their fortunes, were evicted from their homes and were forced to sleep in homeless shelters or even subway stations.
Former football player Kevin Johnson lost the millions he had earned during his career and spent an extended period homeless. He was eventually murdered at a homeless encampment earlier this year, at just 55 years old.
Savon, as noted, is a different case. His loyalty to his country "cost" him tens of millions of dollars. After all, this was a boxer who once claimed that Mike Tyson would not have stood a chance against him.
He did not lose a fortune he had accumulated. Rather, the country to which he had been so fiercely loyal simply failed to show him the same loyalty in return.

Through it, we are demonstrating to the bank’s clients—our international partners—that Ukrainian cultural heritage (such as the unfinished Karpenko-Kary University building, you have all seen this large structure on Lvivska Square) represents a national cultural heritage asset that is ripe for investment and can be transformed into a culturally attractive destination," Berezhna stated at the 10th Ukrainian Women’s Congress.
In this same context, she also mentioned the Hetman’s Inn near Pidhirtsi Castle in Lviv region.
"Could it not become a hotel that attracts a great number of tourists and visitors? Certainly, it could. That is what we are discussing with the EBRD," the Deputy Prime Minister added.

The SNP is not serious about independence or defence and is taking its supporters for fools, Labour MP Graeme Downie has said, responding to an interview in which the party’s Westminster leader confirmed he has written and costed a plan for an independent Scottish army, navy and air force but is holding it back until the next independence referendum debate, in a statement to the UK Defence Journal.
Downie, who has represented Dunfermline and Dollar since 2024 and whose constituency contains the Rosyth yard where the Type 31 frigates are being built, said: “This interview just sums up that the SNP aren’t serious about independence or defence and are taking their supporters for fools.
“They claim to have yet another secret plan for something they have no clue about. For years the SNP have failed to support UK defence, instead choosing to focus on petty ideology.
“They say they want to be in NATO and enjoy protection from a nuclear umbrella but not have it based in Scotland. They say they want to support defence jobs but have taken no action to build the skills the defence industry needs. They say they support our armed forces but stop Cadet units from building valuable community links by banning activity inside state schools.
“This is the same story from the SNP. Secrecy, fantasy and no serious plan for Scotland’s security.”
Dave Doogan, the SNP’s Westminster leader and the member for Angus and Perthshire Glens, told this publication that he drafted and costed the plan about two and a half years ago, that it now needs a refresh, and that he would publish it once enough people were asking the question. “Why not release the defence plan now? Well, a good reason is that it needs a refresh, but it’s designed to answer a question when enough people are asking that question, and that will come when we’re having the next independence referendum debate,” he said.
The plan assumes a budget of around five and a half billion pounds a year, drawn from Scotland’s existing share of British defence spending, and a conventional three service structure generated over time. Doogan also said an independent Scotland would not press a claim on British military equipment if doing so damaged what remained of the United Kingdom, telling this publication that “if we were to claim our share of eight per cent or whatever of UK assets, and that caused major difficulties for the UK, well, we just wouldn’t do it because it’s not intelligent.”
On skills, the Scottish Government confirmed this month that it will match fund two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges, one on each coast, after Luke Pollard offered the money in March as part of a £50 million Scotland Defence Growth Deal. The Scottish Affairs Committee reported in September that progress on the colleges had fallen behind equivalent work in England and urged both governments to act with greater urgency, and this publication has reported that Scotland risks missing out on the defence spending boost without a bigger skills base.
Downie has been among the more active Scottish Labour members on defence since the election, pressing on submarine dismantling at Rosyth and on the industrial base. Wes Streeting told the Commons yesterday that he wants the Defence Technical Excellence Colleges backed with £50 million in England to expand to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and offered to work with the Scottish Government on the defence of the United Kingdom regardless of constitutional differences.
