Moshe Botavia, the security chief of Kiryat Arba, took part in the gunbattle during Friday morning's shooting attack at the Yehuda Junction near Hebron, in which five people were wounded, two of them critically.
"We received a report of a shooting attack targeting a military force on Route 35, with casualties. Security forces from the area rushed to the scene, including me," he told ynet. "The terrorists arrived in a vehicle, stopped at a point where they could not be seen, quickly got out and opened fire."
Watch footage from his helmet camera:
"In the morning, residents are traveling along the road, including buses taking students to schools in Kiryat Arba. I arrived at the scene about 15 minutes after the incident began. When I got there, I joined the fighting. Two terrorists were firing from higher ground, and we exchanged fire for about 20 minutes until a force commanded by the deputy battalion commander responsible for the area killed the terrorists.
Describing the scene, Botavia said, "The terrorists arrived in a 'mashtuba' (an illegally operated, deregistered) vehicle with a yellow Israeli license plate. The soldiers at the scene prevented the attack from spreading to the main road and endangering passersby. That prevented a much greater disaster."
He praised the security forces, saying, "The army works hard every night, carrying out numerous operations to maintain residents' security and protect roads and communities. We must remain vigilant."
Since Friday morning, troops from the IDF's Duvdevan undercover unit, Paratroopers Brigade and Search and Rescue Brigade, along with Border Police forces in the West Bank, have been conducting offensive counterterrorism operations in Hebron and surrounding villages. The forces are also preparing to expand their operations.
So far, a full lockdown has been imposed on the cities of Hebron and Halhul, dozens of roadblocks have been set up across the area and the IDF's elite Maglan unit has been deployed to the Judea Regional Brigade to reinforce counterterrorism and defensive operations. In addition, work has begun to clear and demolish all illegal infrastructure at the site of the attack.
Police said a situation assessment had been completed under the leadership of Judea and Samaria District Commander Maj. Gen. Moshe Pinchi. Pinchi assigned the investigation to the district's Central Investigations Unit minority affairs division, which will also assist the Shin Bet security agency in investigating the attack.
He also ordered investigators to focus on the use of a "mashtuba" vehicle, an Arabic term referring to a vehicle that has been taken off the road, for example because it was stolen or had become too old for legal use, but continues to be driven illegally.
The attackers used such a vehicle, which had been taken off the road but bore an Israeli license plate.
"This is a phenomenon that must be eradicated," Pinchi said.
District police forces will step up enforcement on roads, including inspections of vehicles and suspects and the seizure of "mashtuba" vehicles.

French associations challenge Macron's call to ban non-union protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:28:18 UTC
20:28:18 KST

French associations have filed an urgent legal appeal against President Emmanuel Macron’s call to ban demonstrations not organised by trade unions ahead of nationwide protests planned for Saturday, October 24.
The Association for the Defence of Constitutional Freedoms (Adelico) and the Magistrates’ Union filed an application with the Council of State, France’s highest administrative court, broadcaster Franceinfo reported on Thursday.
The associations asked the court to suspend Macron’s decision and any instructions issued to enforce it. They argued that the president had no legal authority to establish a policy of banning demonstrations.
Jean-Baptiste Soufron, a lawyer representing Adelico, described the announcement as an “abuse of power”, according to the appeal.
The associations also challenged what they said was a distinction between trade unions and other citizens, arguing that unions do not have a monopoly on organising demonstrations and that the right to protest belongs to everyone.
The Council of State has 48 hours to rule on the appeal.
Security tightened ahead of protests
Macron announced on Thursday that demonstrations not organised by trade unions would be banned in the coming days, particularly on Saturday, “wherever possible”.
Prefects were instructed to examine union requests and propose alternative routes to protect city centres.
Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon said restrictions on non-union demonstrations would be decided on a case-by-case basis.
Several local authorities have already imposed restrictions. According to Franceinfo, authorities in Paris approved only one of two routes requested for Saturday, while all gatherings were banned in Lyon and parts of Nice city centre.
The prefecture of Bouches-du-Rhone also banned demonstrations across the department, including in Marseille, on Saturday, even those concerning issues other than purchasing power.
In Lille, authorities announced a ban on all demonstrations and gatherings in the city centre.
Around 70,000 security personnel expected
Meanwhile, BFMTV reporte on Friday that police academy trainees nearing the end of their training will be deployed as reinforcements during Saturday’s demonstrations.
The trainees will guard buildings and perform administrative duties at police stations, allowing experienced officers to focus on more sensitive operations.
They will not be deployed for crowd control or public order duties, which are prohibited under a 2022 law. Several dozen trainees have volunteered, according to the broadcaster.
The government plans to deploy around 70,000 security personnel mobilised during protests on October 17, which resulted in damage to businesses and public buildings.
Jean-Didier Berger, minister delegate to the Interior Ministry, said security deployments on Saturday would be 20 percent higher than on October 17. Sentinelle military personnel, specialist units GIGN and RAID, and riot police are also expected to be deployed.
Authorities have introduced additional restrictions across the Paris metropolitan area, including bans on transporting fuel and flammable gases, carrying protective equipment within 100 metres of a school, and possessing fireworks mortars.
Paris police have also imposed a curfew for adults and minors around Place de la Republique and Les Halles, from 11 pm to 6 am, running from Thursday evening until Sunday.

Red Cat adds attack drone boat to U.S.-built USV lineup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:27:55 UTC
20:27:55 KST

- Red Cat’s Blue Ops opened orders for its 18-foot B-18 attack and reconnaissance USV and its 39-foot B-39 vessel, already in low-rate production.
- The flagship B-26, formerly Variant 7, remains in full-rate production at Blue Ops’ plant in Valdosta, Georgia.
Red Cat Holdings’ maritime division, Blue Ops, has opened orders for two new uncrewed surface vessels, an 18-foot boat built for reconnaissance and one-way attack missions and a 39-foot vessel already in low-rate production, as part of a new B-Series lineup named after each boat’s length.
The company announced the family on Oct. 22, 2026. The B-18 has completed sea trials and is available for orders ahead of its original schedule, the B-39 is in low-rate production and also available for orders, and the flagship B-26, previously called Variant 7, is already in full-rate production. Blue Ops said the designations follow the traditional American approach of naming vessels by length in feet, which puts the three boats at roughly 5.5 meters, 7.9 meters and 11.9 meters.
The B-18 is the smallest and most aggressive of the three. Blue Ops said it is built around the internationally recognized form factor for one-way attack vessels, the explosive-laden drone boats designed to ram their targets, and that it was developed with U.S. Navy requirements in mind, including deployment from Littoral Combat Ships. Its listed missions are tactical reconnaissance, shipboard launch and recovery, and one-way attack, using a Modular Open Systems Approach architecture that lets operators swap in different payloads and equipment.
The company pitched the B-18 at a U.S. Navy that, in Blue Ops’ words, is reassessing its autonomous surface vessel requirements and looking at more capable, cost-effective options.
The B-39 is aimed at longer missions. It is built on an established commercial vessel platform with an existing manufacturing base, and Blue Ops said it offers more range, endurance and payload capacity than its smaller boats for persistent maritime surveillance, integrated defense systems and logistics, with room to add sensors, mission payloads and command-and-control systems.
“The Navy doesn’t need examples of what autonomous vessels might deliver years from now. It needs affordable, reliable systems that perform in real-world conditions and are available today,” said Barry Hinckley, president of Blue Ops. “That’s exactly what we’re building at Blue Ops. From one-way attack and tactical reconnaissance to maritime defense and logistics, our B-Series vessels are designed to meet immediate operational needs. Combined with Red Cat’s aerial assets, we’re delivering a complete family of systems that gives U.S. and allied forces the capabilities and flexibility to operate across air and sea.”
The B-26 is the most established boat in the family. As the Variant 7, it was described by Hinckley earlier this year as a 7.8-meter vessel with a stated range of 800 nautical miles (1,480 km) at 40 knots and a payload capacity of 1,800 pounds (816 kg), and Red Cat CEO Jeff Thompson said a base configuration costs about $700,000 before weapons or counter-drone payloads are added. The boat moved into full-rate production in May 2026, and Blue Ops has since added Kymeta multi-orbit satellite communications and a Volvo Penta diesel propulsion option.
Red Cat launched Blue Ops in August 2025, building its first prototypes with Hodgdon Shipbuilding in Maine before moving production to a 155,000-square-foot plant in Valdosta, Georgia, which marked its first year of operation in September. Red Cat told investors in March that it aims to build more than 100 USVs in 2026 at the Georgia site.
Blue Ops is now taking orders for both the B-18 and B-39, with the B-26 continuing in full-rate production in Valdosta.

European, regional powers to discuss maritime security at Istanbul meeting: German FM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:26:43 UTC
20:26:43 KST

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Friday that a first-of-its-kind meeting bringing together four European countries and four regional powers in Istanbul aims to explore ways to resolve stalled regional conflicts.
Speaking before his meetings in Istanbul, Wadephul stressed that the gathering would focus on safeguarding freedom of navigation in international waters, developments in the Black Sea, and other conflicts.
“At our first meeting in this format we Europeans and the four regional powers want to jointly explore how we can bring movement into the conflicts in the Strait of Hormuz, at Bab al Mandab and in the Black Sea,” he said.
The meeting is being held on the initiative of Germany and Türkiye, Wadephul noted, bringing together the foreign ministers of the E4 states — Germany, France, the UK and Italy — and the R4 partners Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye.
“The eight of us are taking a stand together: We will not accept Iran and the Houthi militias holding global trade to ransom and maintaining their stranglehold on the world’s supply of energy and fertilisers,” the minister underlined.
“These indiscriminate attacks on free navigation and neighbouring countries must come to an end,” he insisted. “For the people in the region, those suffering from hunger or fearing that they are no longer safe even within their own homes, this persistent insecurity is unacceptable.”
Attacks on shipping routes are also felt in Europe, from prices at gas stations to supermarket shelves, he noted. Delays in fertiliser deliveries risk increasing the danger of famine in some regions, Wadephul warned.
Black Sea grain shipments under pressure
Wadephul also accused Russia of targeting free navigation in the Black Sea and of threatening global food security through attacks on grain shipments.
”By attacking grain shipments, Russia is knowingly risking food shortages in the Global South,” he said. “This hits the world’s poorest, whose survival depends heavily on wheat, as well as our partners, such as Türkiye, which is the largest processor of wheat for the global market.”
Attacks on civilian ships and port infrastructure since July 2026 have nearly halted Ukrainian grain exports via the Black Sea, which previously accounted for about 30 percent of global wheat trade, according to official figures.
Alternative routes can only partly make up the shortfall. Houthi attacks have intensified since July 2026. Bab al Mandab handles about 12 percent of world seaborne trade, while the Strait of Hormuz carries roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption.

Japanese authorities deny entry to Palestinian American comedian over visa issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:25:15 UTC
20:25:15 KST

Palestinian American comedian Sammy Obeid said on Friday that Japanese authorities denied him entry and detained him for nearly 24 hours over a visa issue linked to planned stand-up performances in Tokyo.
“The Japanese government denied me entry and held me in solitary confinement for 24 hours over a standup comedy show with 40 attendees,” Obeid wrote in a five-part thread on X.
Obeid said he arrived in Tokyo two days before the shows with two other comedians, who were allowed to enter. Immigration officials questioned him through an interpreter about his work, travel plans and activities in Japan.
He said authorities demanded an hour-by-hour itinerary and later told him he lacked the visa required to work as an entertainer.
Japanese authorities had not publicly commented on his account as of Friday, and his description of the detention conditions could not be independently verified.
He acknowledged responsibility
Obeid acknowledged some responsibility for the visa issue, saying he had been unable to secure the sponsorship required for the relevant visa because the venues were small.
He said nobody in Japan was paying him directly and tickets were sold through a US-based platform, leading him to believe he would be allowed entry based on advice and previous travel experience.
“And yeah, it’s on me for not seeing this coming,” he wrote.
Japanese immigration rules classify entertainment performances under the “Entertainer” residence status. Short-term visits for tourism or business cannot include paid activities, while the entertainer visa process generally requires a Certificate of Eligibility.
Obeid said officials offered him the option to appeal the refusal, but told him the process could take 72 hours, during which he would remain confined. He chose to leave instead.
He claimed he was kept alone for about 22 hours without food, a shower, his phone, laptop or reading and writing materials. Officials also searched his luggage for weapons and drugs, he said.
Obeid said authorities required him to return to the US on the airline he had arrived with, rejecting his request to continue his tour in Hong Kong or Taiwan.
Although he accepted that authorities had identified a visa violation, he questioned whether he had been singled out and cancelled his weekend shows, offering ticket holders refunds, admission to another performance or access to a future virtual show.
Obeid, who describes himself as Lebanese-Palestinian-Syrian-Italian-American, has appeared on Conan, America’s Got Talent and Netflix’s 100 Humans. His comedy also addresses Palestine and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

One of Earth’s most powerful supervolcanoes is refilling with fresh magma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:23:19 UTC
20:23:19 KST

One of Earth’s most powerful supervolcanoes is refilling with fresh magma
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Kobe University
- Summary:
- Deep beneath Japan’s Kikai caldera, a massive magma reservoir is refilling 7,300 years after one of the most powerful volcanic eruptions in Earth's recent geological history. Scientists used underwater seismic surveys to reveal a vast store of magma that appears to have accumulated since the ancient catastrophe. The discovery could help explain how supervolcanoes like Yellowstone and Toba rebuild their magma supplies.
- Share:
One of Earth's most powerful supervolcanoes is slowly refilling its enormous underground magma reservoir, thousands of years after producing one of the largest volcanic eruptions in recent geological history. Scientists at Kobe University have discovered evidence that fresh magma is accumulating beneath Japan's Kikai caldera, which unleashed a catastrophic eruption about 7,300 years ago.
The discovery offers a rare look at how giant volcanic systems rebuild their magma supplies after massive eruptions. It could also provide important clues about the behavior of other supervolcanoes, including Yellowstone in the United States and Toba in Indonesia, potentially helping scientists improve their ability to recognize warning signs of future eruptions.
How Supervolcanoes Store Enormous Amounts of Magma
Some volcanic eruptions are so immense that they dramatically reshape the landscape. The amount of magma released can be staggering, enough to bury all of New York City's Central Park beneath a layer roughly 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) thick.
When such enormous volumes of magma escape from underground, the rock above the emptied reservoir can collapse, leaving behind a broad, relatively shallow depression known as a caldera. These features are associated with some of the most powerful eruptions in Earth's history.
Famous examples include Yellowstone, Toba, and Japan's Kikai caldera, most of which lies beneath the ocean. Kikai last experienced a giant eruption approximately 7,300 years ago, producing the largest known volcanic eruption of the Holocene, the geological epoch that began roughly 11,700 years ago and continues today.
Although scientists know that giant caldera volcanoes can erupt more than once, they still have an incomplete understanding of how the enormous quantities of magma required for these events accumulate underground. This makes it extremely difficult to anticipate when another major eruption might occur.
"We must understand how such large quantities of magma can accumulate to understand how giant caldera eruptions occur," says Kobe University geophysicist Nobukazu Seama.
Scientists Discover a Massive Magma Reservoir Beneath Japan
Kikai's underwater location might seem like an obstacle to studying the volcano, but it actually gives researchers an important advantage. The surrounding seafloor allows scientists to carry out extensive geological surveys across the volcanic structure.
"The underwater location allows us to implement systematic, large-scale surveys," Seama explains.
To investigate what lies beneath Kikai, researchers from Kobe University collaborated with the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC). They used powerful airgun arrays to generate seismic pulses that traveled through the crust beneath the ocean floor.
Instruments called ocean bottom seismometers recorded how these waves moved through the underground rock. Because seismic waves travel differently through solid rock and regions containing molten material, scientists can analyze their behavior to investigate structures that cannot be observed directly.
The findings, published in Communications Earth & Environment, revealed a substantial region containing a high proportion of magma directly beneath the site of Kikai's massive eruption 7,300 years ago.
By examining the seismic measurements, the team was able to determine the approximate size and shape of the underground reservoir. Its position and extent suggest that it occupies the same magma storage system involved in the ancient eruption.
"Due to its extent and location it is clear that this is in fact the same magma reservoir as in the previous eruption," Seama says.
Fresh Magma Is Recharging the Ancient Supervolcano
Perhaps the most intriguing finding is that the magma currently beneath Kikai does not appear to be simply leftover material from its catastrophic eruption thousands of years ago.
Previous investigations revealed that a new lava dome has been developing near the center of the caldera over approximately the past 3,900 years. A lava dome forms when relatively thick, viscous lava accumulates around a volcanic vent rather than flowing freely across the surrounding landscape.
Chemical analyses also showed that volcanic material from this dome and other more recent activity differs in composition from the material released during Kikai's giant eruption.
That difference provides an important clue. It suggests that the magma now stored beneath the volcano was supplied by new injections of molten rock from deeper within Earth's crust or mantle, rather than remaining unchanged since the previous eruption.
"This means that the magma that is now present in the magma reservoir under the lava dome is likely newly injected magma," summarizes Seama.
Together, the seismic observations and chemical evidence help researchers develop a clearer picture of how a giant volcanic system can gradually rebuild its underground magma supply following a massive eruption.
This replenishment process does not mean that another catastrophic eruption is imminent. Instead, it reveals how a magma reservoir can be recharged over thousands of years, an important process that scientists need to understand before they can reliably assess the long-term behavior of supervolcanoes.
What the Discovery Could Reveal About Yellowstone
The findings could have implications far beyond Japan.
Researchers believe the process identified beneath Kikai may help explain why other enormous caldera systems, including Yellowstone and Toba, also contain large magma reservoirs relatively close to Earth's surface.
"This magma re-injection model is consistent with the existence of large shallow magma reservoirs beneath other giant calderas like Yellowstone and Toba," says Seama.
The proposed model suggests that, following a giant eruption, new magma can gradually enter and replenish an existing underground reservoir. Understanding how this happens could reveal important patterns in the long-term cycles of magma accumulation, volcanic activity, and major eruptions.
Researchers now hope to improve the seismic techniques used at Kikai so they can investigate the movement and storage of magma in greater detail.
"We want to refine the methods that have proved to be so useful in this study to more deeply understand the re-injection processes. Our ultimate goal is to become better able to monitor the crucial indicators of future giant eruptions."
By revealing how fresh magma accumulates beneath a volcano responsible for one of Earth's most extraordinary eruptions, the research brings scientists closer to understanding the processes that eventually make such colossal events possible.
This research was funded by the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) (The Third Earthquake and Volcano Hazards Observation and Research Program (Earthquake and Volcano Hazard Reduction Research)) and the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (grant 20H00199). It was conducted in collaboration with researchers from the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC).
Story Source:
Materials provided by Kobe University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Akihiro Nagaya, Nobukazu Seama, Gou Fujie, Satoru Tanaka, Hiroko Sugioka, Shuichi Kodaira. Melt re-injection into large magma reservoir after giant caldera eruption at Kikai Caldera Volcano. Communications Earth, 2026; 7 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s43247-026-03347-9

Without IDF soldiers stopping two Hamas terrorists on Friday morning, a major attack would likely have been made targeting civilians, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said.

After the attack, Netanyahu had announced that Likud events which had been scheduled for Friday morning would be canceled. He also ordered the IDF and security forces to establish a cordon around the city of Hebron and to block off all travel through the West Bank.

Parashat Lech Lecha: There is no wisdom like that gained through experience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:22:58 UTC
20:22:58 KST

Parashat Lech Lecha opens with the first test through which God puts Abraham, the father of the Jewish nation. He is commanded to leave his home, his surroundings, and his homeland, and to journey to an unknown land, as the verse states (Genesis 12:1): “To the land that I will show you.” The Mishnah in Pirkei Avot (5:3) states accordingly: “Abraham our forefather, may he rest in peace, was tested with 10 trials.”
These trials are among the defining foundations of the Jewish nation. They are not merely historical events in the life of the nation’s founding father, but chapters in the shaping of the believing individual, whose influence remains evident to this day. Each trial presented Abraham with a new challenge, requiring him to discover additional inner strength, deepen his faith, and elevate his life to a higher level.
His struggles belong not only to the past; they also laid the foundations for the ability of future generations to face their own challenges.
What is a 'test'?
To understand the deeper meaning of these trials, we must examine the very concept of a “test.” Our sages, in the Midrash, explore the connection between a test and elevation, between facing a challenge and the ability to grow through it.
The Midrash states: “It is written: ‘You have given those who fear You a banner to raise, because of the truth, forever’ (Psalms 60:6). One trial after another, and one stage of growth after another, in order to test them in the world and to elevate them in the world, like the mast of a ship” (Bereishit Rabbah, Vayera 55:1).
According to this understanding, a trial is not merely an examination intended to test a person, but also a means of helping that person grow and rise to a higher level. Just as a ship’s mast rises high and can be seen from afar, so too can a person rise through the trials he experiences and discover strengths within himself that he never knew he possessed.
Precisely when he feels confronted by a difficulty that exceeds his abilities, an opportunity may be presented to him, so that he can reach a level he could never have attained by any other means.
To understand why Abraham was given these trials and what their purpose was, it is worth examining Nachmanides’s commentary on the verse describing the trial of the Binding of Isaac (Genesis 22:1): “And God tested Abraham.”
According to the Ramban, God does not need a test to know what lies in a person’s heart; the test is intended for the person himself. There is a difference between a capacity that exists within someone as a potential that has not yet been realized, and a capacity that has already been revealed through an actual deed.
A person may believe himself to be courageous, loyal, or deeply faithful, but only when called upon to act with courage do these qualities become a tangible part of his character.
Trials are not just for personal growth, there's more at play
THIS IDEA takes on an even broader significance in the words of Rabbi Yaakov, author of the Ba’al Haturim, who draws a connection between Abraham’s 10 trials and the 10 utterances through which the world was created. The trials are not merely a personal journey of spiritual growth, but part of a broader process of repairing the world and bringing it toward its ultimate purpose.
According to this interpretation, the first trial, “Lech Lecha” (“Go forth”), corresponds to the first divine utterance in Creation: “Let there be light.” This parallel offers an important key to understanding how a person should face life’s challenges.
When a person encounters a trial, he may feel as though darkness has enveloped him and the light has disappeared from his world. The familiar path is no longer clear. The answers he once had no longer suffice, and he struggles to see how he can move forward.
It is precisely in these moments that he must remember that just as Creation began with light, so too a trial may mark the beginning of a new revelation. This does not mean that every difficulty quickly disappears, or that we can always understand why events unfolded as they did.
However, we can believe that even amid uncertainty, a path exists, and that facing a challenge may open up possibilities within a person and his world that would otherwise never have emerged.
Abraham, our forefather, is commanded to journey to an unknown land, and God tells him, “that I will show you.” God’s light will illuminate the way for him, provided he believes that God watches over and guides everything, for He is the master of the universe.
A person is not always given a complete map of the future. To move forward, he must take one step at a time, seeking clarity along the way, and trusting that what he does not yet understand may become clear later.
Sometimes, life’s trials are the light that a person must follow, for hidden within them is a great light that he is called upon to discover. ■
The writer is the rabbi of the Western Wall and holy sites.

Parashat Lech Lecha: Having the courage to stand alone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:22:52 UTC
20:22:52 KST

It takes courage to stand alone against the beliefs of an entire society. Few experienced this loneliness as deeply as Abraham. In a world steeped in idolatry, he introduced humanity to belief in one God. Abraham was the first lonely man of faith.
The other side
His radical ideas enraged those around him, who tried to burn him alive. Miraculously, he survived. He later left his homeland and journeyed toward the land of God, crossing treacherous terrain and the great rivers of the Tigris and Euphrates.
He became known as Avraham Ha’Ivri, a name that reflected three aspects of his identity. By ancestry, he descended from Eber, a descendant of Noah. The word Ivri also means someone from the other side, “ever.”
Geographically, Abraham had traveled from beyond the great rivers, leaving his homeland to settle in a new land. Ideologically, he stood on one side of a great divide, bravely opposing an entire civilization that could not imagine a single God. Abraham came from the other side of the river and had the courage to stand on the other side of the world.
Soon after arriving in the Land of Israel, Abraham found himself caught up in a regional war. The conflict became personal when his nephew Lot was taken captive. Abraham joined the battle and defeated four powerful warlords who had conquered and enslaved five neighboring populations. With his small force, he confronted armies far more powerful than his own.
The name Avraham Ha’Ivri now took on another meaning. Beyond his ancestry and journey across rivers, he stood on one side against powerful enemies on the other. Significantly, the only time the Torah explicitly calls him Avraham Ha’Ivri is during this war.
A nation apart
Abraham’s willingness to stand alone would become a defining feature of our nation. As his descendants, we would desperately need that same strength. We were meant to be a different people, committed to the values God taught us even when others challenge them.
We were chosen for responsibility rather than privilege, expected to live by higher standards and reflect the dignity of a life lived in God’s presence. Throughout history, we would face a choice between Abraham’s courage to remain different despite our loneliness and the temptation to surrender that difference for acceptance.
Exile intensified this loneliness. Scattered in small communities, we lived as guests in other people’s homelands, often regarded as outsiders. Empires rose and great religions spread while we remained small and vulnerable. Yet we preserved our identity and faith, following Abraham’s example. Wherever we lived, we held firmly to our faith and traditions, even when doing so set us apart from the surrounding society. The price of remaining different was often high.
With the birth of Israel, that loneliness began to ease in two ways. We could finally live together in our homeland, speaking a common language and sharing a national identity. We could preserve our distinctiveness while enjoying the dignity of sovereignty. We no longer had to explain why our lives were different.
At the same time, Israel gradually gained acceptance abroad. Over 75 years, our military strength, economy, and technological achievements earned international respect. Diplomatic relationships expanded. Countries sought our expertise, welcomed our innovations, and increasingly treated Israel as a valuable partner even when old prejudices lingered. We felt less alone both because we had one another and because the wider world seemed increasingly willing to accept us.
Alone again
Oct. 7 shattered much of that confidence in our “acceptance.” The massacre in the South had barely ended, yet by October 8, protesters were already condemning Israel and portraying us as the aggressors. As we fought a just war against those who attacked us, we faced fierce condemnation and spurious accusations of terrible crimes. Israel has been sidelined, marginalized, and boycotted. Even our right to exist has been questioned, a challenge rarely directed at other nations.
After decades in which we believed that our legitimacy had become an accepted fact, we discovered how quickly old arguments could reappear. Once again, we find ourselves in the footsteps of Avraham Ha’Ivri, standing on the other side of a world that struggles to accept us.
This renewed Ivri status extends far beyond Israel. Across the Western world, opposition to Israel has frequently spilled over into antisemitism. Jewish students face intimidation on campuses, Jewish institutions require heightened security, and many Jews feel increasing pressure to conceal their identity. Generations of hard-won acceptance suddenly feel fragile. Jews who once felt completely at home in their countries are discovering how quickly they can be made to feel like an outsider.
Whether in Israel or abroad, we are once again being called upon to follow in the footsteps of our common ancestor Abraham and summon the courage to be Ivrim, even when that means standing alone.
The courage to be different
Most Jews are answering the Ivri call. Since Oct. 7, hostility toward Jews has only strengthened the Jewish identity of many who had previously felt disconnected from our people. Many Jews who had placed great faith in liberal democracies and their promises of equality have begun to reconsider that confidence.
We cannot always rely on others to defend our rights nor can we assume that social justice movements will also stand up for Jews. Sadly, many who champion the rights of other minorities show little concern for Jewish vulnerability. This painful awakening has drawn many Jews closer to their people.
While many Jews have embraced the courage of Avraham Ha’Ivri, standing firm in the face of a hostile world, others remain uncomfortable with the prospect of standing apart. Eager for acceptance, some have distanced themselves from Israel, even turning against its very legitimacy. There is a painful irony in disavowing a state that has become a vital anchor of Jewish identity and security. In their desire to be accepted by others, they are distancing themselves from their own people.
The price of acceptance
This sad pattern has tragic precedents. Throughout history, many Jews seeking acceptance in the wider world have been willing to sacrifice their faith and surrender core elements of their Jewish identity. In their desire to belong, they sometimes abandoned the core traditions and beliefs that had sustained our people for generations.
In the Hellenistic era, some Jews concealed their circumcision to fit into Greek society. During the Christian Middle Ages, some Jews converted to Christianity, viewing baptism as a ticket of entry into a Christian-dominated world.
In the 19th century, as Jews were invited to participate more fully in European society, many surrendered aspects of their Jewish culture and identity to feel more comfortable in the emerging culture of modern Europe. Later, in Eastern Europe, some Jews enthusiastically joined the Communist revolution, exchanging their Jewish identity for a place in a movement they believed would usher in a new era of equality and progress.
Today, we are witnessing another version of this familiar pattern. In some social and cultural circles, public opposition to Israel has become a badge of acceptance. Some Jews feel that gaining approval in these environments, particularly on social media, requires them to distance themselves from Israel or even openly condemn it. The barter has changed, but the tragedy remains: Jewish identity is once again being traded for public acceptance.
Abraham taught us that standing alone requires courage. After Oct. 7, we are once again discovering that our identity and our future cannot depend upon the approval of others. To be an Ivri is to remain faithful to our convictions even when the world stands against us.■
The writer is a rabbi and educator at Yeshivat Har Etzion (Gush). Find his latest book, Echoes of Rashi: Bereishit, at mtaraginbooks.com

Dental implants can hijack your immune system, scientists discover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:12:28 UTC
20:12:28 KST

Dental implants can hijack your immune system, scientists discover
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Rutgers University
- Summary:
- Researchers have uncovered a surprising reason dental implant infections often resist antibiotics: the implants themselves can contribute to the problem. Bacteria corrode titanium implants, releasing microscopic particles that hijack immune cells, trigger destructive inflammation, and accelerate jawbone loss.
- Share:
For tens of millions of people, dental implants have provided a way to replace missing teeth with a full set of fixed, functional teeth rather than removable dentures. However, an estimated 10% to 20% of implant patients eventually develop peri-implantitis, a serious infection that damages the surrounding jawbone.
Antibiotics frequently fail to control this condition, and scientists have struggled to understand why. Now, researchers believe they have uncovered the mechanism responsible.
A new study published in PNAS Nexus by scientists at the Rutgers School of Dental Medicine reveals that bacteria can gradually corrode dental implants, releasing microscopic titanium particles into nearby tissues. These particles interfere with the immune cells responsible for fighting infection, trapping them in a state of excessive inflammation that progressively destroys jawbone.
The researchers examined human tissue samples, studied human immune cells in the laboratory, and conducted experiments using genetically engineered mice. Their investigation identified a calcium channel in macrophages, the immune cells that engulf bacteria, that becomes activated by titanium particles. When this channel was disabled in mice, the disease was prevented.
This discovery provides the first credible drug target for a condition that affects as many as one in five dental implant recipients and costs healthcare systems worldwide more than $1 billion annually.
"For the first time, we show why all the antibiotic treatments that work around teeth do not work around implants," said Georgios Kotsakis, senior author of the study and assistant dean for clinical research at Rutgers School of Dental Medicine. "Now that we know the cause, we can start developing therapeutics."
Why Dental Implant Infections Resist Antibiotics
One of the biggest mysteries surrounding peri-implantitis has been its similarity to periodontitis, the gum disease that develops around natural teeth. Both conditions begin with the same types of bacteria found in the mouth, yet they respond very differently to treatment.
For natural teeth, antibiotics combined with routine professional cleaning can resolve the infection. Around dental implants, however, the same medications are successful in fewer than half of cases. Even when treatment is attempted, the underlying jawbone may continue to deteriorate.
For the past two decades, scientists have largely concentrated on the bacteria responsible for these infections. Researchers in Kotsakis' laboratory decided to investigate another possible contributor: the implant material itself.
Their work showed that bacteria accumulating on implant surfaces create acidic biofilms that slowly damage the titanium. Over time, this corrosion can release billions of microscopic metal particles, each smaller than a red blood cell.
Titanium particles can also be dislodged during routine dental cleaning. This is particularly concerning when instruments designed for natural teeth are used on implants, because they can scrape and damage the metal surface.
How Titanium Particles Hijack the Immune System
Once released into the gums, the tiny titanium fragments attract a bacterial toxin known as lipopolysaccharide, which coats their surfaces. This combination creates a deceptive target for the immune system, making the particles resemble unusually large bacteria that cannot be broken down.
Macrophages, the white blood cells responsible for engulfing and destroying harmful microorganisms, attempt to consume these particles. But because the cells cannot digest titanium, they become stuck in a prolonged state of excessive inflammation.
As a result, the macrophages produce large quantities of inflammatory signaling molecules, including interleukin-1 beta. This protein is also associated with inflammatory processes involved in rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's disease.
The resulting immune response gradually breaks down the bone supporting the dental implant. At the same time, the macrophages become less effective at fighting the bacteria that triggered the infection in the first place.
Laboratory experiments revealed just how severely their defenses were disrupted. Macrophages exposed to titanium particles engulfed fewer than half as many bacteria as immune cells that had not encountered the particles.
"These particles are little magnets that attract the bacterial toxin, and they hijack the immune system, preventing it from clearing bacteria," said Kotsakis. "You have a perfect storm that defies antibiotics."
Scientists Identify a Potential New Treatment Target
After uncovering how titanium particles disrupt immune defenses, the researchers investigated the molecular pathway responsible for the damaging reaction.
They traced the process to TRPC1, a calcium channel (a specialized, pore-forming protein structure within cell membranes) found in macrophages. This channel plays a central role in the inflammatory response triggered by titanium particles and bacterial toxins.
To test its importance, the team used genetically engineered mice that lacked TRPC1. When these animals were exposed to the same combination of titanium particles and bacteria, their immune systems responded much more effectively.
The mice developed dramatically smaller abscesses, produced fewer inflammatory signaling molecules, and regained the ability to clear bacteria. Disabling the channel prevented the destructive disease process observed when TRPC1 was present.
The results point toward a potentially new approach to treating peri-implantitis by targeting the immune system response rather than relying exclusively on antibiotics.
With funding from the National Institutes of Health, Kotsakis and his colleagues are now evaluating potential drugs that act on the same molecular pathway in human cells.
Why Proper Dental Implant Cleaning Matters
Although the research opens the door to future therapies, it also reinforces an important preventive measure for people who already have dental implants.
Regular professional cleaning remains the strongest known protection against peri-implantitis. However, the instruments and techniques used during those appointments can make a significant difference.
Until approximately a decade ago, many dentists routinely cleaned implants with the same metal scalers used to remove deposits from natural teeth. Research by the Rutgers team and other scientists has since demonstrated that these tools can damage and corrode titanium surfaces, potentially releasing additional particles and accelerating the disease.
Today, nonabrasive cleaning methods have become standard practice, helping protect implant surfaces while reducing the risk of complications.
By revealing how corroded titanium can interfere with immune defenses, the findings offer a new explanation for why some dental implant infections are so difficult to treat and identify a promising direction for developing more effective therapies.

Deaths of 2 CIA agents in Mexico lead to treason charges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:07:39 UTC
20:07:39 KST

Deaths of 2 CIA agents in Mexico lead to treason charges against former state attorney general
A former Mexican state attorney general could face trial for treason over accusations that he illegally launched a joint operation with the CIA without telling the federal government.
The operation to dismantle a drug lab in the state of Chihuahua in northern Mexico in April drew attention after two CIA agents and two state officials died in a car accident on their way back.
That raised questions about the Trump administration's actions on Mexican soil, and outraged President Claudia Sheinbaum, who has made a strong defense of national sovereignty a centerpiece of her administration. The state district attorney, César Jáuregui, resigned, saying he wanted to clear the way for an inquiry into the operation.
He was arrested Oct. 17 on state charges of illegal exercise of public office, which a judge ruled Thursday can go to trial. Federal officials later added the treason charge, and a federal judge will decide Saturday whether to allow the indictment.
Earlier this year, a statement from Mexico's Ministry of Security said one U.S. agent entered Mexico as a visitor while the other entered with a diplomatic passport.
"None had formal accreditation to participate in operational activities in national territory," the security ministry said.
 Mexico has long worked with the U.S. in its fight against organized crime, but that's caused fears at times that American agencies do not respect the country's sovereignty. Sheinbaum and her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador have made legal changes that aimed to stop foreign agencies from operating in Mexico without the federal government's consent.
Jáuregui held at a maximum-security prison
Héctor Villasana, one of Jáuregui's defense attorneys, said federal prosecutors told the court in a closed hearing this week that they were seeking an exemplary punishment to prevent a situation like the United States' removal of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
The U.S. State Department told The Associated Press that it is aware and watching Jáuregui's case but didn't make a link between the case and the CIA deaths.
Here's how a traffic accident in the mountains of Chihuahua led to a charge of treason - a crime Mexico has not successfully brought to trial in decades despite one recent attempt.
An accident in the Chihuahua mountains
On April 19, the Chihuahua Attorney General's Office reported the dismantling of a drug lab in the municipality of Morelos, in the mountains of that state. On the way back, a vehicle in the convoy veered off the road and fell into a ravine. Two state agents and two Americans were killed.
In a news release, the state attorney general's office identified the two Mexican casualties as first commander of the state investigation agency Pedro Román Oseguera Cervantes and officer Manuel Genaro Méndez Montes. The U.S. agents killed were "instructor officers" who "were carrying out training tasks" as part of binational anti-drug cooperation, Jáuregui told reporters at the time. Jáuregui called the targeted labs "one of the largest sites found in the country where chemical drugs were produced."
The Federal Security Cabinet reported the dismantling of laboratories there during a joint operation by the state prosecutor's office and the army but did not provide details.
The operation ended without arrests because the criminals fled.
Treason is a hard-to-prove crime
According to the federal prosecutor's office, Jáuregui endangered national security by authorizing the participation of U.S. agents in the field operation, a decision that only the federal government can make. Experts say it is a political decision ahead of the 2027 Mexican midterm elections.
The charge carries from 5 to 40 years in prison, but it is very difficult to prove.
Samuel González, a former chief prosecutor for organized crime and an analyst, said that Jáuregui may have failed to fulfill his obligations by not informing the federal government or by allowing the foreign agents to carry weapons in violation of the law. But "even if that were the case, it would not constitute treason," a wartime crime.
Luis Villegas, the former prosecutor's defense coordinator, said it was unacceptable for the federal prosecution to compare the presence of the agents to a foreign "invasion."
Carlos Pérez Ricart, a professor at the Mexican university CIDE and author of the book "A Hundred Years of Spies and Drugs," said that even if the case is ultimately dismissed, its public impact will be huge.
Mr. Trump has repeatedly said Mexico isn't doing enough against the cartels. Sheinbaum's opponents, including Chihuahua's governing National Action Party, have claimed that she's running a "narco-government."
Pérez Ricart said the case could set back the country's fight against drugs and organized crime because it "sends a very bad signal to Washington," while the discussion should center on "more or better" collaboration with the U.S.
Official contradictions about the agents' role
Villegas said that the two Americans who died were officials providing training related to intelligence and drones. U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson just stated that they were "embassy personnel." Multiple people familiar with the matter later confirmed to CBS News they were CIA agents. The CIA declined to comment.
According to Jáuregui's defense team, the federal prosecutor's office said the agents were close to the person who led the operation, the Chihuahua investigations chief, who was one of two deceased Mexicans.
The day of the operation there were two other U.S. agents in the convoy traveling in another vehicle, who were later expelled from the country. The president said none of them had permission to operate in Mexico and that the military was unaware of the foreigners' presence.
The next day, Sheinbaum said she was unaware of the operation. Jáuregui clarified that the Americans had joined the group after it.
Presence of U.S. agencies in Mexico
The presence of U.S. agencies in Mexico has been a constant for decades, although former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador (2018–2024) limited their activities, and Sheinbaum amended the Constitution to prohibit field operations without the express authorization and cooperation of the Mexican government. The law does not allow members of U.S. agencies to be armed.
Ricart, the professor, said that, beyond official relations, there have always been anti-drug agents involved in operations of this kind, "often without the federal government's knowledge."
"These actions happen, have happened, and will continue to happen" because they are based on U.S. trust with state or local officials and facilitate ongoing collaboration," he said.
"However, since there are no clear rules, they can lead to abuses."
Mexico has announced the dismantling of numerous drug labs in recent months after Mr. Trump threatened possible military action to curb drug trafficking.
In February, Mexican naval personnel discovered a hidden drug laboratory in the country's Durango region and "neutralized" over 5,000 pounds of methamphetamine. In January, authorities announced more than 1,500 pounds of meth were seized from clandestine laboratories in the states of Durango, Sinaloa and Michoacán.

France to deploy 70,000 police as country braces for weekend protests
Interior minister pledges crackdowns on violence as cities issue curfews, crowd restrictions.
French authorities are preparing for a massive police deployment and warning of crackdowns on violence as the country prepares for nationwide demonstrations on Saturday.
President Emmanuel Macron was due to hold a meeting on Friday with his defence council – made up of top ministers and officials – and was planning to meet with security forces, as cities across the country issued restrictions on gatherings and public transport. Macron, who has blamed “seditious” ultra-left groups for the unrest, was due to announce “additional decisions” following the defence council meeting, his office said.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said about 70,000 police would be deployed nationwide on Saturday, roughly 10,000 more than last weekend, with elite units, mounted police, helicopters, drones, armoured vehicles and water cannon.
“We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all those who commit acts of violence,” he told reporters, adding that “ultra-left” groups were urging activists online to target public buildings.
“We are not talking about a nice, friendly demonstration,” he said. “We will be extremely vigilant, extremely firm, and we will let absolutely nothing pass.” Curfews imposed in some sensitive areas this past week will remain in force.
Macron’s announcement on Thursday that only union demonstrations would be authorised at the weekend has prompted harsh criticism from student groups whose demonstrations in recent weeks against conditions in schools were joined by groups denouncing high living costs and other grievances.
More than 500,000 people gathered across France last Saturday for demonstrations that were marred by violence and looting.
Paris has extended a nighttime curfew until Monday, while France’s third-largest city, Lyon, has banned gatherings in central areas and introduced curfews and public transport restrictions for Saturday. In the coastal city of Marseille, which had also banned protests, authorities said on Friday they would allow one union-organised march on an “exceptional basis”.
In advance of the planned protests, Macron met with high school students for the first time on Friday.
Nathanael Combary, president of the campaign group High School Renewal, said Macron had been “attentive”, but that students were awaiting proposals in talks with the prime minister on Monday.
“We are not satisfied,” he said, urging pupils to “continue to mobilise”.
‘Trampling on freedoms’
Despite the restrictions, France’s national student union, UNEF, has called for rallies on Saturday. The Yellow Vest movement, an anti-establishment force that first emerged in 2018, was planning a march through central Paris.
Police have authorised only one union demonstration along a limited route in Paris and rejected requests for rallies organised by UNEF and the Yellow Vest movement, the Reuters agency reported. UNEF said its rallies would go ahead.
In the city of Orleans south of the capital, 20,000 to 30,000 people are expected to protest against Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally as it holds its party congress there, but the prefecture said the gathering would be barred from the city centre.
Amnesty International called the restrictions “a slide toward authoritarian practice” that jeopardise the right to demonstrate peacefully, and Human Rights Watch expressed alarm over reports of children severely injured by crowd-control weapons. Marylise Leon, general secretary of the French Democratic Confederation of Labour union, said the bans were “counterproductive” given the level of anger.
“Macron is trampling upon the freedom to protest in our country, and is spitting on the values of the republic he claims to defend,” UNEF said.
Shops and businesses in major cities have been urged to close. The Louvre and the Louis Vuitton Foundation will be closed on Saturday, while the Paris edition of the Art Basel fair will end on Friday, two days ahead of schedule.
Since last Saturday’s violence, 2,700 people have been arrested, according to the Ministry of Justice.

Israel’s election is being cast as a historic showdown - but four trends tell a different story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:04:33 UTC
20:04:33 KST

Night after night, or at least on the nights he anchors Channel 12’s nightly news, Danny Kushmaro introduces the election segment by calling them the most fateful elections in Israel’s history.
And he is not alone. “Israel’s most important elections” or “Israel’s most fateful elections” has become a refrain of this campaign.
It brings to mind a verse from Ecclesiastes (7:10): “Don’t say, ‘How was it that the former days were better than these?’ You would be asking an unwise question.”
Kohelet cautions against romanticizing the good old days. Here’s a related lesson for Tuesday’s election: don’t assume that the current one is more fateful or important than all those that came before. That would be an unwise assumption.
Besides, we seem to say that about almost every election.
What about the December 1973 election, two months after the Yom Kippur War? That wasn’t critical? The 1977 election, which forever changed this country’s political landscape and brought Menachem Begin to power, wasn’t fateful? How about the 1996 election, just months after Yitzhak Rabin’s assassination? Or Ariel Sharon’s defeat of Ehud Barak in 2001, as the peace process with the Palestinians unraveled and the Second Intifada gathered force?
Every election feels like the most fateful and important one. Ever.
But perspective is needed.
How 'fateful' elections turns political battles into existential wars
And why does that matter? Because calling this the most important and fateful election ever turns the political competition, the battle between the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs, into nothing less than an existential matter. Defeat becomes harder to regard as a setback that can be corrected next time. Instead, it begins to sound like something the country cannot survive.
And that can make accepting the outcome harder.
Therein lies the problem.
Since Naftali Bennett formed his government in 2021, Israel has struggled with more than the question of who should govern. It has struggled with whether the losing side will give the other side a chance to do so.
Before Bennett’s government was even sworn in, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu branded its formation “the greatest election fraud.” He meant broken campaign promises, not stolen ballots. But the message cast a government formed legitimately through the parliamentary process as fraudulent and, therefore, illegitimate.
From the minute Bennett’s government took office, the opposition worked tirelessly to bring it down. The main arena was the Knesset, where the coalition’s slim majority made every vote consequential.
As a result, the opposition sometimes voted against legislation it supported, believing it would weaken the government. In recordings published in May 2022, Likud MK Miri Regev defended voting against measures benefiting soldiers and vulnerable groups because the overriding objective was to topple the coalition.
The government spent much of its short life fighting for survival.
Then Netanyahu won the 2022 election and formed his hard-right government. Suddenly, the shoe was on the other foot.
Yair Lapid conceded the election and arranged an orderly handover. But as opposition to the judicial overhaul brought masses into the streets, the language of illegitimacy crept in again.
For instance, at a massive demonstration in Tel Aviv in April 2023, former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) director Yuval Diskin said that while the government had been elected legally, it was morally illegitimate because of its “appalling composition and reprehensible actions.”
By August, the Kaplan protest leadership was also calling the government illegitimate, amid questions about whether Netanyahu would obey the High Court. Once again, the distinction between fighting a government’s policies and denying its legitimacy was becoming blurred.
Will Israel's next government have room to govern?
That leaves a question hanging over Tuesday’s vote: will whichever government emerges be given room to govern, both in the Knesset and in the streets?
Calling this election “the most fateful ever” hardly prepares the ground for that.
If voters are told that the future of the country, and indeed the Jewish people, hangs in the balance, accepting defeat becomes that much harder.
Are these elections consequential? Of course. So were many of those that came before. But at this critical juncture, the country also needs to accept and live with the results. Israel desperately needs a government given the space to govern.
Accepting the outcome does not mean supporting the next government, abandoning opposition, or refraining from protest. Nor does winning an election give a government a blank check.
But opposing a government’s policies is different from treating its very existence as illegitimate. There is a difference between working to replace a government and, from the outset, seeking to make governing impossible.
That distinction must hold for whichever side wins.
Magnifying the stakes may bring voters to the polls. But it may also do something this country can ill afford: make it harder afterward for the losing side to accept the results and let the winners govern.
That is one takeaway from this campaign. Here are three more.
Election's fiercest battles taking place within blocs
Despite the characterization of these elections as the most fateful ever, the campaign has been relatively subdued: no televised debates between the leading candidates, no massive outdoor rallies. Much of the action has consisted of social media clips, interviews, and leaks to the press.
And some of the fiercest fighting has taken place inside the blocs: Netanyahu vs Ofer Winter, Gadi Eisenkot vs Avigdor Liberman.
In the anti-Netanyahu bloc, three candidates who regard themselves as worthy of the premiership have periodically sniped at one another: Eisenkot, Bennett, and Liberman. They share an interest in replacing Netanyahu, but each wants to be the one to do it.
The sharper fighting, however, has been on the Right, where Netanyahu and Religious Zionist Party head Bezalel Smotrich have spent considerable energy trying to persuade Winter and his People of Israel party to withdraw.
The stated concern is the electoral threshold. If Winter fails to cross the 3.25% bar, votes coming predominantly from the Right will not translate into seats.
The cautionary tale is April 2019, when Bennett and Ayelet Shaked’s New Right narrowly missed the threshold. Had it crossed, Netanyahu could have formed a coalition, and the country would have been spared the dizzying spiral of repeat elections.
But Winter also presents Netanyahu with an uncomfortable challenge from within his own political camp.
The anti-Netanyahu parties say this government failed: failed to prevent October 7 and failed to achieve its declared objectives afterward, with Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Iranian regime still standing. Netanyahu can dismiss those charges as the familiar carping of his opponents.
That is harder when Winter delivers a similar message from the Right.
Winter’s emphasis on new faces – his list includes no one who has previously served in the Knesset – reflects his contention that the political leadership associated with October 7 needs to be replaced. His indictment extends across the Knesset, but it also challenges Netanyahu’s claim to be the leader best equipped to keep the country safe.
The competition is therefore about more than whether Winter will waste right-wing votes. It is also about whether he will persuade right-wing voters that their own leadership has failed.
The rival across the political divide challenges your policies. The rival on your own side challenges your claim to speak for your own camp.
Polls are shaping Israel’s election, not just measuring it
Polls are supposed to measure public opinion. Good polls reflect what the public thinks.
In this campaign, however, polls don’t merely reflect opinion. They help shape it. And Israel’s electoral threshold gives them particular power to do so.
Israelis famously don’t want to be freiers – suckers. They don’t want to vote for a party that falls below the 3.25% threshold and wins no representation, because they will feel, and are repeatedly told, that they wasted their vote.
So voters wait to see whether polls show Winter’s party, or Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha’s party, crossing the threshold before deciding whether to support them. If the party looks likely to pass, they may vote for it. If not, they look elsewhere.
The result is a circular process: voters consult the polls to decide whether a party is viable, while its viability depends on whether they will vote for it.
A poll showing a small party below the threshold can frighten away the very voters who might otherwise put it over. One showing it above the threshold can give hesitant supporters the confidence to vote for it.
At that point, the polls are doing more than reflecting opinion. They are shaping it.
Their influence also extends to the choices available on the ballot. Benny Gantz’s withdrawal this week followed polls consistently showing his party below the threshold. The fledgling party led by Gilad Erdan and Yuli Edelstein withdrew before the lists were finalized, against a similar polling backdrop.
Polls are critical in elections. They become a problem when they start to decide those elections.
The airwaves and newspapers have been filled with candidate interviews. Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Lapid, Winter – everybody is getting airtime.
And everybody is being asked a version of the same question: whom will you refuse to sit with in a coalition?
It is a natural and legitimate question. Voters are entitled to know which government their vote might help bring into being.
But insisting on unequivocal answers encourages candidates to make commitments before they know the parliamentary arithmetic they will have to work with.
If candidate X promises never to sit with party Y or candidate Z, and then does precisely that, the recording of his promise will be played on an endless loop. The candidate will be branded a liar.
Bennett’s signed pledge before the 2021 election not to allow Lapid to become prime minister, even through a rotation, and not to form a government dependent on Mansour Abbas is the obvious example. He subsequently formed precisely such a government.
Did he break a campaign pledge? Obviously. But his defense was that the election results left a choice between breaking that promise and sending the country into yet another election. So here’s a formula for understanding politics: politicians don’t break promises; they encounter changed circumstances.
That line might invite a knowing smirk, but it makes a serious point: coalition government requires compromise, and the election results determine which compromises will be necessary.
If everyone adheres to every coalition veto issued during this campaign, the country may end up with plenty of promises intact and no government for a very long time. Politicians should leave room for compromise before the election, rather than making absolute promises they may have to abandon afterward for the good of the country.
Changing course does not necessarily mean a lack of backbone. Sometimes it is what separates a functioning government from yet another round of inconclusive elections.

Netanyahu bloc falls to 48 seats as opposition reaches 54, days before election - poll

The gap between Israel's coalition and opposition blocs has widened to six seats ahead of Tuesday's Knesset election, despite the two largest parties being separated by just two seats, according to a Maariv poll by Lazar Research published Friday.
The coalition bloc receives just 48 seats this week, following the failure of Ofer Winter's People of Israel party to cross the electoral threshold. The party receives 3% of the vote, below the required 3.25%. Meanwhile, the opposition's change bloc has strengthened to 54 seats. Recent polling averages have shown the two political blocs nearly tied, highlighting the fluctuations in the election race.
The poll also shows that United Torah Judaism and Otzma Yehudit each lost one seat, polling 7 mandates, while Likud (19), Shas (8), and the Religious Zionist Party (7) each gained one. Overall, the coalition bloc has weakened by three seats compared with the previous week's poll.
Within the opposition bloc, the most significant change is the two-seat jump by Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad party, which rises to 15 seats. The Democrats also gained one seat this week, reaching 10. In contrast, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party (21) and Yisrael Beytenu (8) remain unchanged. Other election surveys published on Wednesday also placed Eisenkot's party ahead of Likud.
The poll also shows that the Reservists or the New Economic Party narrowly crosses the electoral threshold, winning four seats.
This distribution of seats between the blocs depends on the Reservists-Economic Party crossing the electoral threshold. Given its narrow margin above the threshold in the current poll, if the party fails to qualify, the distribution is expected to shift to 50 seats for the coalition, 56 for the Zionist opposition, and another 14 for the Arab parties.
In addition to People of Israel (3%), the Haredi Public party (0.9%), Noam LeYisrael (0.5%), and Tzomet Beit Yisrael (0.5%) also fail to cross the electoral threshold.
Voter turnout intentions continue to rise
The Maariv poll also found that the proportion of Israelis who are certain they will vote in Tuesday's Knesset election continues to rise, reaching 81%. The figure suggests a potential increase in voter turnout compared with the 2022 election, when turnout stood at 71%.
As in the October 8 poll, the percentage of respondents certain they will vote is higher among opposition party supporters (87%) than among those intending to vote for coalition parties (83%).
Of particular note is the significant increase in the proportion of Arab party supporters who say they are certain to vote, rising from 74% on October 8 to 81% in the current poll, matching the national average.
These figures could result in the Arab party bloc winning significantly more seats in the upcoming election than it holds in the current Knesset. Arab voter turnout has emerged as a significant issue in the election campaign, amid concerns over crime and political distrust in Arab communities.
Eisenkot maintains lead over Netanyahu
The Maariv poll also found that Gadi Eisenkot continues to lead Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a head-to-head matchup for prime minister, with 49% support compared with Netanyahu's 41%.
Naftali Bennett, who was tied with Netanyahu at 43% in the previous poll, now leads him by 45% to 43%.
Against Avigdor Liberman, Netanyahu continues to lead, although the gap has narrowed slightly, with Netanyahu receiving 44% compared with Liberman's 39%.
Majority of Israelis prefer unity government over new election
As in the previous poll, most Israelis (60%) would prefer a unity government to be formed if the Knesset election produces no clear result.
Of those surveyed, 33% want such a government to be headed by a leader from the change bloc, while 19% want Netanyahu to lead a unity government. Another 8% have no preference regarding who leads it, provided that a unity government is established.
Only 23% would prefer another election in the event of a deadlock, down from 27% in the previous poll. Another 17% said they did not know. A previous Maariv poll published on October 16 also found majority support for a unity government, with 27% preferring another election.
A breakdown of the findings by political bloc shows a decline in the proportion of coalition voters who would prefer another election, from 32% to 25%.
Opposition voters, meanwhile, remain consistent in their preferences, with a majority (55%) favoring a unity government headed by a leader from their own bloc.
The poll was conducted between October 19 and 22 among a representative sample of Israel's population aged 18 and older, including Jewish and Arab respondents. The initial sample consisted of 1,000 participants, while the final sample included 1,048. Data were collected from the general population using Panel4All's online respondent panel. A total of 580 people were contacted, 188 responded (30%), and 78 completed the survey (41%). The researchers also conducted supplementary telephone polling among the Arab population. A total of 687 telephone calls were made, 308 people responded (45%), and 100 completed the survey (32%). The poll's maximum margin of sampling error was 3%.

The upcoming winter of 2026-2027 in terms of energy supply will be difficult, but not catastrophic and no more difficult than the last one, and it will be successfully navigated, believes Oleksandr Kharchenko, Director of the Center for Energy Research (CER).
"I am absolutely certain that we will get through the season. Despite all the challenges, there is an understanding of how to proceed. And I do not think that the winter will be more difficult than the last one. Rather the opposite," he said during a discussion on "Ukraine on the Threshold of Winter: Energy, Defense, and the New Diplomatic Reality" at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Friday.
According to the expert, the main factor of uncertainty for the energy sector right now is the weather. At temperatures of minus 10 degrees Celsius, scheduled power outages can reach 10-12 hours. In energy-deficient regions such as Kyiv, Odesa, and parts of Sumy and Chernihiv regions, scheduled outages may be quite long. At the same time, with milder weather, the restrictions will correspondingly be softer.
"Another truly risky component is heating. There are high risks that there will be attacks on large thermal facilities in Kyiv; they will undoubtedly happen, they happen constantly," Kharchenko emphasized.
However, according to him, a significant part of the capital's heat infrastructure is protected, and power engineers understand how to act after facilities are damaged.
"Whatever we could protect, we protected; whatever we couldn't – well, let's say, we know how to maneuver with that," he added.
At the same time, in those cities where there are actually only two or three boiler houses, if they are destroyed, a significant threat to heat supply will arise, and much in critical conditions will depend on how these cities prepared for winter.
In turn, as Kharchenko explained, energy engineers have more or less come to terms with the factor of Russian missile and drone attacks and understand that the intensity of these attacks will neither increase nor decrease cardinally.
"That is, they are not capable of inflicting more massive strikes than they are currently inflicting," he believes.
The expert added that these strikes have their own periodicity and a certain rhythm, and energy engineers understand how to respond to them, how to restore power supply to consumers as quickly as possible, and how to return core municipal infrastructure systems to operation as soon as possible.
