Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:10:11 UTC
19:10:11 KST

Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- American Academy of Neurology
- Summary:
- A seven-year study found that people with Parkinson’s disease who were more physically active experienced slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Those exercising more than eight hours per week showed almost no average cognitive decline, suggesting that staying active may offer important benefits as the disease progresses.
- Share:
People with Parkinson's disease who are more physically active may experience slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement, according to a new study published October 7, 2026, in Neurology, the official medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology.
The findings suggest that staying active could offer two important advantages for people living with Parkinson's. However, researchers emphasize that the study identified a connection between physical activity and slower symptom progression. It does not establish that exercise directly causes the disease to progress more slowly.
"Parkinson's disease is a brain disorder that causes movement and cognitive problems that gradually worsen leading to disability and a loss of independence," said study author Dong-Woo Ryu, MD, PhD, of the University of Cincinnati in Ohio. "Previous research has shown associations between physical activity and movement symptoms. Our study found physical activity may have dual benefits, with associations with slower declines in movement and cognition."
Tracking Exercise and Parkinson's Symptoms Over Seven Years
The research involved 294 adults with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease. Participants were 66 years old on average, and researchers monitored their health for up to seven years.
To understand their activity habits, participants completed questionnaires estimating how many hours each week they spent being physically active. The questions covered activities performed at work, around the home, and during hobbies or recreation.
Researchers classified activities by their intensity. Moderate activities included brisk walking, doubles tennis, leisurely swimming, and household tasks such as cleaning windows, vacuuming, or mowing the lawn. More demanding activities included running, cycling at higher speeds, participating in team sports, playing singles tennis, shoveling, and carrying heavy objects.
The team examined physical activity in three ways. First, they calculated the total time participants spent doing moderate or vigorous activities. Second, they estimated overall activity volume by combining duration with intensity, giving greater weight to strenuous exercise. Third, they separately measured the amount of time spent doing vigorous activities.
Based on total weekly activity time, participants were placed into three categories. Those in the least active group reported up to four hours per week, the moderately active group reported four to eight hours, and the most active group reported more than eight hours.
Each year, participants also completed assessments designed to track changes in thinking and memory, along with tests evaluating the severity of their Parkinson's symptoms.
More Activity Linked to Slower Memory Decline
One of the most striking differences emerged in cognitive performance. Researchers used a 30-point test of thinking and memory, with lower scores reflecting poorer cognitive function.
Among participants in the least active group, scores fell by an estimated average of 0.478 points each year. The moderately active group experienced a much smaller annual decline of 0.090 points.
For the most active participants, the estimated average yearly decrease was only 0.007 points, indicating that their cognitive scores remained nearly unchanged over time.
The researchers also examined changes in Parkinson's movement symptoms using an assessment scored from zero to 132. Higher numbers represented more severe symptoms, and participants began the study with an average score of 23.
In the least active group, symptom scores increased by an estimated 0.143 points annually, indicating a slight worsening. By contrast, scores decreased by 0.225 points per year in the moderately active group and by 0.783 points in the most active group.
Even after accounting for participants' age, sex, and how long they had been living with Parkinson's, the researchers found that the most active group experienced slower cognitive decline and less worsening of movement symptoms than the least active group.
The connection was not limited to one measure of exercise. Higher total activity time, greater overall activity volume, and more time spent exercising vigorously were each associated with slower deterioration in both thinking abilities and movement symptoms.
Why Consistent Physical Activity May Matter
The results suggest that remaining physically active over time could be especially important for people with Parkinson's disease. Researchers noted that even relatively small differences in the rate of decline might become more significant when they accumulate over several years.
"The possible benefits of physical activity for people with Parkinson's disease may depend on how long they stay active and whether they continue exercising over time," said Ryu. "While our study found small differences between activity levels, these differences may become more meaningful over time. Since participants generally had good thinking and memory skills at the start of the study, our results should be interpreted with caution and further studies are needed."
The researchers also identified an important limitation. Physical activity levels were based on participants' own reports rather than direct measurements, meaning some estimates may have been inaccurate.
Although the findings strengthen the evidence connecting physical activity with better long-term outcomes in Parkinson's disease, additional research will be needed to determine whether exercise itself can slow the progression of symptoms.
Funding for the study came from a grant provided by the Gardner Family Foundation and the Precision Medicine in Neurodegenerative Diseases Fund.
Story Source:
Materials provided by American Academy of Neurology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Dong-Woo Ryu, Kevin R. Duque, Luca Marsili, Jesus Abanto, Nathaly Chinchihualpa Paredes, Heba A. Deraz, Andrea Herrera Gorriti, Emily J. Hill, Abhimanyu Mahajan, Andrew Duker, Alberto J. Espay. Physical Activity and Motor and Cognitive Progression in Parkinson Disease. Neurology, 2026; 107 (9) DOI: 10.1212/WNL.0000000000218682

Russia develops advanced Titan robotic demining system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:09:44 UTC
19:09:44 KST

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russian specialists have created the Titan advanced robotic demining system, the system’s developer told TASS.
"To address the challenge of clearing mine and explosive obstacles using robotic systems amid the enemy’s widespread use of anti-personnel mines and improvised explosive devices in the special military operation zone, the latest robotic demining system, Titan, has been developed. The use of electric motors, a low-profile design, and all-round fragmentation protection against all known performed fragments of anti-personnel engineering munitions ensure stealth during missions and the necessary survivability. The system has increased blast resistance. According to our information, there are no counterparts with comparable quality of equipment and protection being used on either side of the line of contact," a company representative stated.
The system is designed to clear a continuous route through anti-personnel minefields by sweeping away the main types of anti-personnel mines. "The Titan enables the sweeping of mines equipped with pressure-action, pull-action, and break-wire target-sensors," he noted.
He specified that the system has successfully completed testing and is expected to be deployed in the special military operation zone. "Work is currently underway to improve the level of protection, add new controls, and refine the design of the sweeping equipment," he added.
The system’s total weight is 2.3 metric tons, and its payload capacity is one ton. "The Titan’s maximum speed with the sweeping equipment is seven km/h, and without it - 14 km/h. The system is capable of operating autonomously for at least 3.5 hours. The sweep width is two meters. If necessary, the Titan can be equipped with electronic warfare capabilities. The system’s control range depends on the type of communication used but is at least 500 meters," the developer added.

Pope Leo XIV will skip an interfaith peace gathering in the Italian town of Assisi next week as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery, with doctors advising him against the helicopter journey from the Vatican.
The 71-year-old pope had been scheduled to attend Tuesday's event, titled “Disarmed and Disarming Peace,” which marks the 40th anniversary of a landmark interfaith prayer meeting convened by St. John Paul II in 1986.
The Vatican said Friday that a follow-up chest X-ray showed Leo was recovering well, but his medical team recommended avoiding the trip as a precaution because of the short time since his operation.
Instead, Leo will send a message to organizers, religious leaders and other participants, expressing his support for the gathering and reaffirming the importance of dialogue and peaceful coexistence amid ongoing conflicts.
The meeting brings together representatives of different faiths to pray for peace and renew the spirit of the 1986 gathering. Assisi, the birthplace of St. Francis of Assisi, has long served as a symbol of interfaith dialogue.
The cancellation is the latest adjustment to Leo's schedule following surgery last week to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, where doctors had found a malignant nodule. Tests confirmed adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
The Vatican said subsequent examinations found that the cancer was localized and that Leo would not need further treatment. His activities, however, will continue to be guided by medical advice as he recovers.
Leo returned to the Vatican on Saturday after the operation. Although he has appeared in good health during public appearances since his return, speaking clearly and with a strong voice, doctors are taking precautions while his lungs heal.
The decision to avoid the Assisi trip also comes as the pope prepares for a planned visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov. 6 to 17. The trip is expected to involve about a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high-altitude destinations.
His surgeon previously said there were no clinical reasons to rule out the Latin American journey. Thoracic surgeons often advise patients to avoid flying for about three weeks after lung surgery, a recovery period that would leave Leo little margin before his scheduled departure.
The Vatican said the pope remains close to those attending the Assisi gathering and believes its message is particularly relevant at a time of international conflict.

China Great Wall Museum in Beijing reopens after renovation, upgrade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:03:14 CST
19:03:14 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- The China Great Wall Museum at the foot of the renowned Badaling Great Wall in Beijing reopened to the public on Saturday after an extensive renovation and upgrade.
Located in Yanqing District on the outskirts of the Chinese capital, the museum first opened in 1994 and closed in April 2022 for redevelopment.
Construction began in December 2023, with a building built to better blend the museum into the surrounding mountains and vegetation.
The museum, with a floor area of 16,000 square meters, features exhibition areas, educational and public service areas, collection storage areas and research spaces.
Its permanent exhibition and special thematic displays explore the Great Wall's history and culture. The permanent exhibition features more than 700 cultural relics, including many on loan from museums across China.
The displays trace over 2,000 years of the Great Wall's construction efforts and showcase how its preservation methods have advanced, from emergency protection to systematic conservation.
Visitors can also better understand the Great Wall's historical roles. Beyond its function as a military defense structure, it also gradually became a site of exchanges and integration among China's ethnic groups.
On the museum's second floor, visitors can enjoy expansive views of the imposing Badaling section outside the venue through glass curtain walls.
The Great Wall, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, stretches more than 20,000 kilometers across 15 provinces, municipalities and autonomous regions. Beijing has about 520 kilometers of Great Wall sections in total, and the Badaling section is the most visited. ■

Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on military technology, said last week that SpaceX had introduced a speed limit overnight without warning.
"Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation and this led to the disruption of several missions," Beskrestnov wrote in a post on Telegram.
Trump told reporters this week that he would speak to Musk if access to Starlink had not been restored.
On Tuesday, Zelenskyy also addressed reported restrictions on US intelligence sharing during a press conference with Nordic leaders, saying he was "thankful" that "intelligence works now."
"I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," he said.
Russian strikes kill two
It comes as Ukrainian authorities announced that two people had been killed and 18 were injured in Russian strikes on the Donetsk region.
"On 23 October, the Russians killed two residents of Donetsk Oblast: in Sloviansk and Kramatorsk," regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on Saturday morning. "A further 18 people in the region were injured over the past 24 hours."
Ukraine hits back
Ukrainian forces hit back on Friday and overnight with strikes on the Tolyattikauchuk chemical plant, a Proton-Electrotex building in Oryol, and an aircraft at the Yeysk air base in Krasnodar Krai, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
The General staff said the strikes on the chemical plant and Proton-Electrotex building would disrupt supply chains and production processes for Russian missiles.

Cloud House by Peter Morris brings "fairytale flamboyance" to London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Cloud House by Peter Morris brings “fairytale flamboyance” to London
Marshmallow-pink walls, sweeping arches and turquoise detailing influenced by a trip to Miami animate architect Peter Morris‘s self-designed home in Gospel Oak, London.
Named Cloud House, the eccentric project combines two offset residences, one for Morris and his partner, producer Emily Kennedy, and a second for a neighbour who shares their love of colour.
According to the architect, the goal of the project was to bring joy to passersby, while giving his “love of postmodernism a chance to reveal itself fully”.
“The key goal was to make a beautiful building which I hoped might create a little moment of joy for anyone walking past it on the street,” Morris told Dezeen.
“It’s easy to dismiss colour and pattern in architecture as frivolous, but there’s something about this visual language that triggers an emotional response that’s different from what you’ll get with elegant modernism,” continued Morris.
“For me, that alone tells us we should push for more variety in the built environment and be open – as Camden Council have been with this project – to the idea of more fairytale flamboyance on our streets,” he continued.
Cloud House occupies the site of a now-demolished Victorian home, adjacent to a distinctive church and school, where the couple have lived since 2016.
Its bold colour palette and cloud-like forms were inspired by the couple’s honeymoon in Miami and the city’s vast collection of art deco architecture.
“Emily and I honeymooned in Miami, where we loved the art deco curves of the buildings, and the pink and turquoise colours everywhere,” Morris explained. “In a way this building is an architectural love letter to my wife, so it felt appropriate to have some of that honeymoon spirit in the mix.”
According to Morris, the project also draws on the curved forms of the neighbouring Grade II-listed school and Grade I-listed St Martin’s Church, which Morris said are “fabulously eccentric buildings”.
“The school, which sits in St Martin’s Hall, has a frontage that looks like a Medieval castle,” he said.
“And the church – described by the historian Nikolaus Pevsner as ‘the craziest of London’s Victorian churches’ – has a knock-out interior, with a brightly coloured chancel ceiling and a nave with dramatic wooden arches.”
Cloud House’s main structure is composed of structural steel and blockwork.
This is clad in decorative arches made of polystyrene, sprayed with a waterproof layer and a textured top coat to match the bright pink render on the elevations, and positioned in place by the architect himself.
Morris’s home is the smaller of the pair, located on the right side of the plot. It measures 133 square metres.
The home is accessed from an entrance on its front elevation. It has a large, open-plan ground floor, comprising a lounge, kitchen and the architect’s studio.
Its two upper floors are each fitted with a bedroom and bathroom, while a roof terrace crowns the home, complete with an outdoor bathtub.
Next door, the adjoining 165-square-metre home is accessed by a side entrance and has an upside-down arrangement.
Its ground floor contains a home office with a kitchenette, and a guest ensuite bedroom at the rear. Above is the main bedroom.
The main bedroom has a dressing room and ensuite, and sits alongside another smaller ensuite bedroom.
Meanwhile, the social space with seating, dining and cooking spaces is on the top floor, with an adjoining terrace. A second larger terrace tops the home.
While the interiors of Morris’s house boldly match its vibrant exterior, the interiors for the neighbour’s home were left blank and ready for them to customise.
Interior highlights of the architect’s home include turquoise epoxy floors, colour-drenched bathrooms and an emerald-green striped kitchen.
Cloud House was featured on the TV show Grand Designs in September and has been shared widely on social media. Morris said the response to the project is sharply divided.
“I know that not everyone will love the Cloud House as much as we do – the reactions to it on social media have been either overwhelmingly positive or overwhelmingly negative, with nothing in between,” he reflected.
“My final goal, and hope, is that some of the people that do love it might one day be keen to commission me to create something colourful and joyful for them too.”
Other pink dwellings featured on Dezeen include a concrete “fun house” on the English coast by RX Architects and a guesthouse in the Azores contained within a converted stable.

Our Brains Weren’t Built for This Much Comparison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

More than 20? Or less than 75? As I scan my feedback on a recent social media post, my brain just can’t seem to help registering the number of “likes.” I’m not alone.
Under a recent settlement that Meta recently reached with states, Facebook and Instagram are about to look different for minors Among the new protections, one seemingly modest change caught my eye. By default, users under 18 will no longer be able to see likes and other reactions in response to their posts or those of others. The reforms are designed for children and teenagers, but touch on a psychological phenomenon just as relevant to adults. As a psychiatrist, I found myself wondering: Why does that little number beneath your post matter so much?
The answer has less to do with social media and more to do with an ancient human tendency: social comparison. Social comparison is the psychological process by which people assess themselves, including their own abilities, opinions, and achievements, in relation to those of others. Likes can both reward us and rank us. They show us that people are validating our posts and also quantify that validation.
We know how much approval we receive relative to what we might have expected, what we got the last time we posted, and what others receive. Feedback is scored. Likes are just one example. Follower counts, views, and shares are other metrics that make social information measurable. When social approval is numerically valued, comparison becomes harder to avoid.
From an evolutionary perspective, social comparison may have served an adaptive purpose. Humans evolved in social groups. Knowing where you stood relative to others might have helped you identify what behaviors were approved, whether you belonged, and how to navigate hierarchy. But moving beyond prehistoric time to the last century, comparison still had constraints. Your 25-year high school reunion? It happened once in your lifetime, maybe in a city far away from you, with only your fellow classmates in attendance. Now, the high school reunion lives in the device in our hands, capable of giving anyone quantitative signals from a vast reference group at any moment on our personalized scoreboards of social approval. If the subjective question is whether we belong, what can feel like an objective answer is the 100 likes our post gets from 2,500 followers. The scale, frequency, quantification, and accessibility of social comparison have all changed.
Our brains weren’t built for this much comparison. Neuroimaging studies show that our brains allocate value to how we believe we stack up next to others. Downward social comparison, in which we learn someone performs worse than us, can engage neural circuits associated with reward and valuation. Upward comparison, in which we learn someone performs better than us, can engage neural circuits associated with processing unpleasant emotions. These are ways in which our brains process social outcomes much like other kinds of gains or losses.
But our brains don’t just register numbers; we also tend to evaluate their meaning. In one study, likes functioned as a type of currency that adult users compared themselves on, shaping how they felt in that moment. In another set of studies, adults who made more frequent and extreme upward comparisons reported an immediate decline in self-evaluation and cumulative declines in self-esteem and life satisfaction over a browsing session. Research has also found that across generational groups, greater user tendency to engage in social comparison, together with greater maladaptive ways of coping with emotions, is associated with more symptoms of anger, anxiety, and depression.
Social comparison isn’t inherently harmful. But as repeated opportunities to compare mount, the mental health effects can add up.
While hiding likes may not eliminate social comparison, it does remove a metric from the scoreboard. The instinct to compare or desire to belong won’t just vanish. But even if we might wonder where we stand next to who’s performing better, there’s a difference between wondering and a number answering that question for us.
Social media didn’t invent our instinct to compare ourselves to others. We’ve had that for millennia. What it did was shift the environment surrounding our instincts, encoding one form of social feedback into numbers we can monitor.
That's why changing our relationship with social comparison will mean more than adapting digital platforms. What do we value? What gives us purpose? What makes our lives matter?
The cultural shift that lies ahead is to ask the questions about our social worth that don’t need a scoreboard to answer.

Breadcrumb
El-Fasher becomes ‘ghost town’ as RSF crimes continue on anniversary of takeover
One year on from the Rapid Support Forces' (RSF) takeover of North Darfur's capital, El Fasher, Amnesty International is warning that the situation remains dire, with unlawful killings, arbitrary detentions, and torture rife, while the population has dropped significantly.
In a report released on Friday, Amnesty said fewer than 70,000 people remain in the city that once had 1 million inhabitants, with humanitarian access remaining limited, and the risk of arrest for returnees high, despite claims by the paramilitary group that people are free to return.
"What we found is that El Fasher is still very much a ghost town," Laura Mills, the author of the report, told The New Arab.
Amnesty's report is based on the testimonies of 25 civilians, including six humanitarian workers, with 15 having fled the city between July and August 2026, and one who remained in the city.
Mills said part of the reason for the desertion of the city was the high risks of being there, which many of the testimonies confirmed.
"We found that many people were detained, including those who tried to return to the city. Often, men were held in prisons and detention centres where they faced torture and truly horrific conditions.
"Women and children were typically held in schools that had been converted into de facto detention centres," she said, with the report noting high levels of malnutrition in said centres.
"Moving around the city, people didn't feel safe; they felt surveilled," Mills added.
Seventeen of the 19 residents Amnesty spoke to had been arbitrarily detained, with the ethnic minority Zaghawa and Masalit people more likely to be detained. Both groups have been targeted by the RSF since the beginning of the war.
RSF killings during the fall of the city have been described as a massacre, with the UN saying that there were "hallmarks of genocide".
Mills said that ethnic minorities are automatically suspected by the RSF of being close to the country's military, which the group is fighting against in the civil war.
Amnesty spoke to those who were detained and put in prison, with many of them stating that RSF soldiers tortured and committed unlawful killings. Mamoun, a 33-year-old Zaghawa man held in Shala prison, said that the group arbitrarily shot prisoners.
Those detained are often released because families pay ransoms to the RSF, which Mills said reach up to $10,000.
She noted that these abuses by the paramilitary group are widespread across RSF-controlled Darfur, though El Fasher's years-long siege fending off the RSF has contributed to widespread suspicion of the city's residents by the group.
Humanitarian workers still operate in the city, though closely monitored by the group, which restricts their movements and prevents aid workers from speaking with residents.
Despite this, humanitarian assessments place the city, alongside much of North Darfur province, in danger of reaching IPC Level 5 famine, the highest threshold possible, in the coming months.
Mills told The New Arab that the international community had all the tools it needed to safeguard El-Fasher's residents and alleviate suffering in the country, but that it was unwilling to use them.
This includes pushing for a ceasefire and talks between the RSF and the military, which was rejected earlier in October by military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, as well as an arms embargo on the country.
"It just really feels like we have all the tools at our disposal, but the world is just sort of looking on as this horrific disaster continues to unfold, and what happened in El Fasher can easily happen somewhere else," Mills said.

Forget the Live Aid image, Africa is only a broken continent in the minds of the west | Moky Makura
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:31 UTC
19:00:31 KST

Thirty years ago, shortly after South Africa emerged from apartheid, I left London for Johannesburg in search of a better life. Not long afterwards, a friend who was preparing to visit from the UK called with an intriguing question: do they have ATMs in South Africa?
After I picked myself off the floor, I explained that not only did South Africa have ATMs, but in many respects its banking system was far more advanced than the one I had left behind in Britain. She was surprised and – dare I say – delighted that she wouldn’t have to lug a wad of cash around South Africa after all.
That moment has stayed with me far longer than it should, because I’ve witnessed too many moments where the continent has persistently surprised and delighted the uninitiated. That’s because, for much of the world, the image of Africa still owes more to Live Aid’s legacy than to the reality.
A study we commissioned by social psychologist Dr Adam Hahn at the University of Bath helps explain why. When people in Britain and the US think about Africa, they disproportionately associate it with economic and political dysfunction, harsh environments and a lack of modernity and culture. Those associations affect whether they want to visit the continent, buy its products or engage with its culture. In their minds, Africa remains a place that is broken, dependent, lacking in agency and apparently in ATMs, too.
Britain may have more ATM’s and higher conventional bank-account ownership, but it was Africa that pioneered one of the biggest innovations in modern finance: mobile money. Kenya showed that millions of people could, in effect leapfrog traditional banking altogether, using their phones to store, send and receive money. Today, sub-Saharan Africa remains the centre of the global mobile-money revolution. And when it comes to new money, Nigeria now ranks third in the world for cryptocurrency adoption, while Britain ranks 17th.
Global investors have noticed the continent’s leadership when it comes to finance and are moving in. We have produced a surprisingly high number of fintech “unicorns” – privately owned startups valued at more than $1bn (£760). Nigeria alone has Flutterwave, OPay, Moniepoint and Interswitch. Investors are not putting billions into African financial technology out of charity; they are backing the entrepreneurs who are not waiting for help to create viable, profitable solutions.
One of those is Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, who has been all over the global media for the world-class refinery he built in Nigeria. The $20bn Dangote refinery is the largest single-train refinery in the world, built in a country that, despite being Africa’s biggest oil producer, spent decades exporting crude oil only to import much of its refined fuel.
Dangote is exceptional in his wealth, the scale of his ambition and visibility he has garnered. But he is not exceptional in spirit. There are thousands of smaller “Dangotes” on the continent: entrepreneurs who see a gap, build something to fill it and, in doing so, move their country forward.
Take Siny Samba, a Senegalese entrepreneur who launched an infant food brand after wondering why virtually all the baby food in her country was imported. She started in her kitchen with banana and millet and in 2018 launched Le Lionceau, creating new markets for local farmers and women’s cooperatives.
In Tanzania, Diana Orembe looked at fruit and vegetables being thrown away and saw fish food. Her company, NovFeed, turns that waste into affordable feed in the agriculture sector and has worked with at least 200 farmers.
In Maiduguri, northern Nigeria, Mustapha Abubakar Gajibo started by converting petrol-powered tricycles to electric. Today his company, African Motor Works, designs and builds electric vehicles, producing about 200 units a month.
Samba, Orembe, Gajibo and thousands like them who are contributing to their countries’ growth, will probably never make international headlines. And that may be one of Africa’s most overlooked challenges: not the absence of progress, but the lack of visibility.
Development experts talk endlessly about Africa’s many gaps – the infrastructure gap, financing gap, skills gap – but perhaps the most consequential gap is the visibility gap: the distance between the Africa today (the one that surprises and delights) and the Africa the world imagines.
Addressing the visibility gap is why the Opportunity Africa initiative was started earlier this year. Its mandate; to make the continent’s progress impossible to overlook by spotlighting the many people – such as Samba, Orembe and Gajibo – the places, the policies and the initiatives moving Africa forward.
Places such as Rwanda, which has rebuilt its reputation around innovation, tourism and digital government. Ethiopia has transformed its agricultural sector and sharply reduced its dependence on imported wheat. Kenya now generates up to 91% of its electricity from renewable sources.
Then there are the policies, the unglamorous government decisions that rarely make headlines: Benin keeping more of its cashews for local processing; Namibia requiring more of its lithium to be processed at home; and Zambia removing fees from state education.
And progress is happening continent-wide through ambitious initiatives. Fifty countries have ratified the African Continental Free Trade Area, making it easier for African businesses to trade with each other. A pan-African payments system now lets them settle transactions in local currencies. And 38 countries have joined the single African air transport market, helping create 108 new intra-African routes since 2022.
And this is just the tip of the iceberg. If my friend was surprised by South Africa 30 years ago, imagine what else has changed and progressed. Through the recent Correct the Map campaign led by Togo, we challenged the world to see Africa differently – quite literally. Now we are asking the world to see us as we truly are.
The #NotWaiting campaign is where you will find the proof point: stories of a continent already building, solving, producing and moving forward.

Since his return, Kean has been accused of avoiding the media spotlight. His campaign denied a New York Times reporter entry to an event attended by other media outlets in August; he refused to take questions from reporters after participating in a livestreamed debate against Bennett, his Democratic opponent.
The Guardian sent two emails to Kean’s campaign requesting an interview, or the opportunity to attend a campaign event. They went unanswered.
Harrison Neely, Kean’s campaign manager, did not respond to an initial text message containing the same requests earlier this week. He did, however, respond to a second message asking for a brief interview on Thursday.
“I think the narrative that congressman Kean doesn’t engage with the press is simply false,” said Neely, adding that the campaign prefers to communicate with voters directly. (On Thursday, New York Magazine published an article saying its multiple requests for an interview went ignored.)
Kean does give interviews, mostly to local reporters, and the campaign has invited local outlets to cover events. Neely said the campaign most recently challenged Bennett to a debate on WRNJ, a local radio station. However, the Bennett campaign declined to participate.
“So you know, I think it’s basically fair to say that congressman Kean does more local press engagements than any sitting member of the New Jersey delegation,” Neely said.
Bennett, a political newcomer, is cautiously optimistic that she can flip a battleground district in New Jersey for the Democrats in next month’s midterm.
“We’re going to do everything we can for the next 16 days to flip the seat, but we are feeling good about where we are,” Bennett told reporters after a meet-and-greet with voters in Basking Ridge last Sunday. “We’re seeing a ton of momentum and enthusiasm on the ground.”
Bennett, 39, is a former Navy helicopter pilot and aircraft commander. She’s also a former executive at an online healthcare company.
Democrats in the state are hopeful her moderate stance can appeal to the district’s voters, especially because many 2024 Trump voters have expressed discontent with the economy.
Bennett said she often hears “deeply frustrated” voters bring up Kean’s willingness to let Trump unleash his agenda, such as voting for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, continuing the war with Iran or not doing enough to stop Trump from halting funding for the Gateway Hudson Tunnel Project between New Jersey and New York.
Mostly, she focuses her messaging on promoting affordability.
“I understand the challenges that we’re facing because my family is dealing with them too,” said Bennett. “My oldest kid’s in public school. My youngest is in daycare. And so when we talk about the cost-of-living crisis we’re dealing with, this is not abstract talking points on a page – this is my life.”
But nothing is certain in New Jersey’s seventh congressional district, which has seesawed between Republican and Democratic representatives since 2018. The district voted for Trump by a slim majority in 2024, and also elected Mikie Sherrill – its Democratic governor – in 2025.
The Congressional Leadership Fund – the Super Pac dedicated to helping House Republicans – and the Safety and Affordability Pac, affiliated with Trump, have reportedly canceled remaining funding for Kean’s district.
When asked about the pulled funding by the New Jersey Globe, Kean dismissed concerns, pointing to $6.2m in funding from the National Republican Congressional Committee.
Neely also expressed confidence. “If you take a step back and look at the facts, Republicans have outspent Democrats in this district to this point,” he said. “Our campaign is fully funded down the home stretch, and will be matching the Bennett campaign dollar for dollar on the airwaves.”
As Kean’s campaign pushed back against the claim he doesn’t engage with the media, before reaching Neely by phone this week, the Guardian spent time driving around the district one weekend earlier this month.
There appeared to be something in the air: a lack of Tom Kean Jr lawn signs in the Trump-friendly Bedminster area, and an autumnal breeze that appeared more present than his campaign.

Fine ‘headphone dodgers’ if you will, but to really tackle antisocial behaviour, Britain should look to Japan | Emily Bratt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:30 UTC
19:00:30 KST

There are two types of people who listen to music in public: those who wear headphones and those who … are a word I probably can’t use here. “Loudcasting” – playing audio, watching videos or talking on speakerphone in public spaces – is a form of antisocial behaviour that drives eight in 10 of people in the UK crazy, and I’m glad Andy Burnham is one of those eight. But while I welcome his policy to fine “headphone dodgers”, I’m not convinced it will solve the problem.
This behaviour isn’t only a nuisance, but a grave indicator of a deeper societal issue: the erosion of empathy. You can’t legislate civic pride into an individualistic culture where feelings of social disconnection are widespread.
From 2019 to 2021 I lived in Japan, where keeping the peace is paramount and you can be reprimanded just for talking on the bus. When I returned to England, I felt shock and shame at how we treat one another and our public spaces. I still do. We watch our dogs defecate in the street and walk away. We use public bathrooms as if we’re feral two-year-olds. We inflict the soundtrack of our mindless social-media scrolling on an entire train carriage.
Japanese society is not without its flaws; I often chafed at the level of deference I witnessed. But living there also highlighted to me just how selfish we can be in Britain. Last week, I saw someone had smeared dog poo into the communal carpeted entrance of their own block of flats. Some on the far right love to cast other cultures as primitive, but I think we need to look at ourselves.
We could learn from Japan. As a broadly collectivist society, it favours social harmony and group responsibility. One guiding principle is meiwaku wo kakenai: the idea that you should avoid inconveniencing others.
I worked in Japanese state schools and was astonished when students as young as five diligently began stacking chairs and clearing apparatus as sports day wrapped up. Nobody told them to. Additionally, Japanese schools don’t completely rely on cleaners: the students sweep the halls, wipe down desks, empty bins and even disinfect and scrub the bathrooms. This cleaning practice, a component of tokkatsu (special activities), forms part of a wider approach to holistic education and teaches children personal responsibility for, and pride in, their environment.
It’s important to add that a teenager is still a teenager, no matter the country. It’s a myth that all Japanese children are innately disciplined perfect little angels. But the wider impact of these social ethics is obvious. Crime rates in Japan are (comparatively) low, public spaces are meticulously maintained and litter is a rarity. It’s not a myth that Japanese streets are so clean you could lick them. Lick an English street and, bam! Dysentery.
The UK government’s crackdown on content-blaring can only work in conjunction with a wider effort. First, fines have to actually be imposed by those in authority – and they need to feel safe and incentivised to do so. Train managers have been hot on calling out fare dodgers for years (one made me cry when I was 19 for not having my student railcard, such was his wrath). Now they need to bring the same resolve to headphone dodgers. Burnham’s policy states that drivers would not be expected to enforce such rules – it’s a job for safety officers or the police. But unless someone is there to enforce the rules in the moment, the policy becomes little more than an empty threat.
Second, we need to rebuild social norms so that consideration for others is instinctive. The word etiquette seems antiquated, but given that almost half of us in the UK play content from our phones without headphones – and that this behaviour bothers most of us – etiquette education is still necessary. Maybe, so we don’t feel we’re in a Jane Austen novel, we call it something else. Perhaps in schools, it’s civic responsibility class, or lessons in caring about others, or simply learning how to not be a twat. It doesn’t require major educational reform. Copying Japan’s approach to school-cleaning, for example, could be a good (and easy) place to start.
The onus, of course, isn’t only on schools – parents have to lead by example. But imagine the ripple effect if British schoolchildren were given the responsibility of caring for their classrooms and corridors.
Unfortunately, there’s also a deeper issue. Some loudcasters are simply oblivious, but others are deliberately rage-baiting. The latter is a product of a disaffected society, which Burnham’s fines by themselves could exacerbate. Nobody likes being told off, but especially not angry people.
We don’t need to become Japan. But in an increasingly divided world, consideration for others and respect for our surroundings are what can still hold us together.
- Emily Bratt is a freelance journalist

Young country diary: A red squirrel examines a nut, right in front of me | Tom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:30 UTC
19:00:30 KST

Every October my family have an annual trip to Brownsea Island. We go in autumn because this is a good time to see the red squirrels. In the other seasons, they are high up, hidden in the trees. We catch the ferry from Poole Harbour, and we know we are close when we can see the castle come into view. When we arrive we’re greeted by nosy chickens and attention-seeking peacocks on the lawns.
We go behind the little church into the woods. It is a different world there. There is a mix of crunchy and soggy brown leaves on the ground and little mushrooms popping up from the earth. Some mushrooms are sprouting from rotting logs.
The red squirrels scurry at high speed. If we are at a distance or very quiet then we get good views of them. We were lucky that they stopped right in front of us on a dead log to examine a nut. A beam of sunlight hit a squirrel giving its body a golden outline. They stay still when they spot us, waiting to see if we are friend or foe. Then they continue their busy work when they realise we are just watching.
Red squirrels enjoy eating seeds from pine cones, nuts, bugs and berries. Although they don’t hibernate, they do slow down in winter and stay in their dreys (homes) to avoid the bad weather and eat all food they stockpiled. I think red squirrels are smart and resilient creatures. I love watching them get their winter food while keeping watch for any predators nearby. This shows how clever they are.
 
Tom, 10
